Scientific Learning.q: Describe the steps of the scientific method using the example of a plant that wilts.
Scientific Learning.r: (i) Observation: a plant in the corner wilts. (ii) Problem: why does it wilt? (iii) Hypothesis: it is not getting enough water. (iv) Experiment: water one pot and leave an identical pot unwatered. (v) Analysis and conclusion: if the watered plant recovers and the other wilts, the hypothesis is supported. Any four steps in order, with the example, earn full marks.

Scientific Learning.q: Which one is the correct order of the first three steps of the scientific method?
Scientific Learning.w: we first state the problem, then observe, then form a hypothesis.

Scientific Learning.q: The SI unit of temperature is
Scientific Learning.w: the kelvin is the SI unit of temperature.

Scientific Learning.q: The least count of a screw gauge with pitch 0.5 mm and 50 circular divisions is
The variable that a scientist keeps the same in a fair test is called the
Scientific Learning.w: controlled variables are kept constant so that the test is fair.

Scientific Learning.q: Technology is best described as
Scientific Learning.w: technology uses knowledge to make useful things.

Scientific Learning.q: Differentiate between accuracy and precision.
Scientific Learning.r: Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value. Precision is how close repeated measurements are to one another. A measurement can be precise but not accurate if there is a systematic error.

Scientific Learning.q: What is the least count of an instrument? Write the least count of a metre rule marked in millimetres.
Scientific Learning.r: The least count is the smallest value that an instrument can measure correctly. For a metre rule marked in mm it is 1 mm (0.1 cm).

Scientific Learning.q: What is a control group? Why is it used?
Scientific Learning.r: A control group is the set of subjects kept under normal conditions without the change being tested. It is used for comparison, so we can tell whether the change really caused the result.

Scientific Learning.q: Describe the steps of the scientific method with a suitable example.
Scientific Learning.r: Steps: identify the problem, observe and collect information, form a hypothesis, experiment, record and analyse data, draw a conclusion, report. Example: if seeds are kept with and without water, the problem is "do seeds need water to germinate?", the hypothesis is "seeds need water", two sets are kept with the same conditions except water, germination is counted, and the conclusion is that seeds without water do not germinate.

Scientific Learning.q: A vernier calliper has 10 vernier divisions equal to 9 main-scale divisions, each main division being 1 mm. The main-scale reading is 2.5 cm and the 7th vernier line coincides. Find the least count and the reading. If the instrument has a zero error of +0.02 cm, find the corrected reading.
Scientific Learning.r: Least count = 1 mm - 0.9 mm = 0.1 mm = 0.01 cm. Reading = 2.5 + 7 × 0.01 = 2.57 cm. Corrected reading = 2.57 - 0.02 = 2.55 cm.

Scientific Learning.q: A stone of mass 150 g is lowered into a measuring cylinder. The water level rises from 40 mL to 100 mL. Find the volume and the density of the stone in g cm⁻³ and in kg m⁻³.
Scientific Learning.r: Volume = 100 - 40 = 60 mL = 60 cm³. Density = 150 / 60 = 2.5 g cm⁻³ = 2500 kg m⁻³.

Scientific Learning.q: Describe the steps of the scientific method with a suitable example. Why are a control and a fair test important?
What is a vernier calliper? Explain its parts, least count and the method of taking a reading, with a worked example.

Classification of Living Beings.q: The five-kingdom classification was proposed by
Which kingdom contains organisms without a true nucleus?
Classification of Living Beings.w: Monera are prokaryotes: no nuclear membrane.

Classification of Living Beings.q: The cell wall of fungi is made of
Classification of Living Beings.w: chitin is the fungal wall material; cellulose belongs to plants.

Classification of Living Beings.q: In the name Homo sapiens, sapiens is the
Classification of Living Beings.w: the first word is the genus (Homo), the second the species.

Classification of Living Beings.q: Amoeba belongs to the kingdom
Classification of Living Beings.w: Amoeba is a single-celled eukaryote, so it is a protist.

Classification of Living Beings.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
Classification of Living Beings.w: yeast is a unicellular fungus; a mushroom is a fungus, bacteria are Monera and ferns are plants.

Classification of Living Beings.q: An organism that makes its own food and has a cell wall of cellulose is placed in
Classification of Living Beings.w: plants are autotrophs with cellulose cell walls.

Classification of Living Beings.q: Write two differences between Monera and Protista.
Classification of Living Beings.r: Monera are prokaryotes with no nuclear membrane (bacteria); Protista are unicellular eukaryotes with a true nucleus (Amoeba). Monera lack membrane-bound organelles; Protista have them.

Classification of Living Beings.q: Why is the kingdom Fungi separate from Plantae? Give two reasons.
Classification of Living Beings.r: Fungi cannot make their own food (heterotrophic, saprophytic) whereas plants are autotrophs. The fungal cell wall is made of chitin whereas the plant cell wall is cellulose.

Classification of Living Beings.q: Describe the five-kingdom system of classification with one example for each kingdom.
Classification of Living Beings.r: Whittaker (1969) divided life into five kingdoms. Monera: prokaryotic, unicellular (bacteria). Protista: unicellular eukaryotes (Amoeba). Fungi: heterotrophic, chitin wall (mushroom). Plantae: multicellular autotrophs (mango). Animalia: multicellular heterotrophs without cell wall (cow). Four creditable points: kingdoms with their basis and an example each.

Classification of Living Beings.q: Who is called the father of taxonomy?
Classification of Living Beings.w: Linnaeus introduced binomial nomenclature and the ranks.

Classification of Living Beings.q: The cell wall of fungi is made of
Which kingdom includes Paramecium?
Classification of Living Beings.w: Paramecium is a ciliated unicellular eukaryote.

Classification of Living Beings.q: Which group of plants bears naked seeds?
Define taxonomy and binomial nomenclature.
Classification of Living Beings.r: Taxonomy is the branch of biology that identifies, names and classifies organisms. Binomial nomenclature is the system of naming an organism with two words, the genus and the species.

Classification of Living Beings.q: Write any two differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
Classification of Living Beings.r: Prokaryotic cells have no true nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells have a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.

Classification of Living Beings.q: Why is Whittaker's five-kingdom system better than the older two-kingdom system?
Classification of Living Beings.r: It uses cell type, number of cells, mode of nutrition and body organisation; so bacteria, fungi and unicellular organisms like Euglena get proper places which they did not have in the plant-animal system.

Classification of Living Beings.q: Name the four shapes of bacteria with one example each.
List any two characteristics of fungi.
Classification of Living Beings.r: They have a chitin cell wall and no chlorophyll; they feed by absorption; they reproduce by spores.

Classification of Living Beings.q: Describe the characteristics of the kingdom Monera and Protista.
Classification of Living Beings.r: Monera: prokaryotic and unicellular; cell wall present; no mitochondria or chloroplast; nutrition autotrophic or heterotrophic; binary fission; examples bacteria and cyanobacteria. Protista: unicellular eukaryotes with a true nucleus; live in water or moist places; locomotion by pseudopodia, cilia or flagella; nutrition autotrophic or heterotrophic; binary fission; examples Amoeba, Paramecium, Euglena.

Classification of Living Beings.q: Differentiate between plants and animals on the basis of four points.
Classification of Living Beings.r: Plants have a cell wall, animals do not; plants are autotrophic, animals heterotrophic; plants have chlorophyll, animals do not; plants do not move from place to place, most animals do; plants store starch, animals glycogen.

Classification of Living Beings.q: Write the taxonomic hierarchy with a suitable example and state the rules for writing scientific names.
Classification of Living Beings.r: Kingdom Animalia → Phylum Chordata → Class Mammalia → Order Primates → Family Hominidae → Genus Homo → Species Homo sapiens. Rules: Latin; italics (or underlined); genus name begins with a capital letter and species with a small letter; genus first, then species.

Classification of Living Beings.q: Classify the vertebrates into classes with two characteristics and an example of each.
Classification of Living Beings.r: Pisces: scales and gills, rohu. Amphibia: moist skin, lungs and skin in adult, frog. Reptilia: dry scaly skin, lungs, lizard. Aves: feathers, warm-blooded, pigeon. Mammalia: hair, mammary glands, warm-blooded, human.

Classification of Living Beings.q: Describe the five-kingdom system of classification with the main characteristics and examples of each kingdom.
Classify the plant kingdom into its main divisions and differentiate between monocot and dicot plants.

Honey Bee.q: The only egg-laying female of a bee colony is the
Honey Bee.w: workers are sterile females; the queen lays all eggs.

Honey Bee.q: A drone develops from egg to adult in
Which species is domesticated and native to Nepal?
Honey Bee.w: Apis cerana is native and kept in hives; A. dorsata and A. florea are wild.

Honey Bee.q: The main duty of the drone is to
Honey Bee.w: a drone mates with a virgin queen and dies afterwards.

Honey Bee.q: The sac in which the queen stores sperm is the
Honey Bee.w: the spermatheca keeps sperm alive for her whole life.

Honey Bee.q: Honey bees belong to the order
Honey Bee.w: bees, wasps and ants are Hymenoptera.

Honey Bee.q: The correct order of the bee life cycle is
Honey Bee.w: complete metamorphosis: egg, larva, pupa, adult.

Honey Bee.q: Name the three castes of a honey bee colony and state one duty of each.
Honey Bee.r: Queen: lays eggs. Worker: collects nectar and pollen, builds comb, feeds larvae. Drone: mates with the queen.

Honey Bee.q: Write any two uses of honey bees to humans.
Honey Bee.r: Honey bees give honey, wax and royal jelly. They also pollinate crops, which raises fruit and seed yield.

Honey Bee.q: Describe the life cycle of a honey bee, with the days each worker stage takes.
Honey Bee.r: A honey bee passes through four stages (complete metamorphosis): egg, larva, pupa, adult. For the worker: egg 3 days, larva about 6 days, pupa about 12 days, so adult emerges after 21 days (queen 16, drone 24). The egg is laid in a cell; the larva is fed by nurse workers; the pupa is sealed in the cell with a wax cap; the adult chews its way out. A labelled four-stage diagram earns a mark.

Honey Bee.q: Which honey bee species is domesticated in Nepal?
Honey Bee.w: Apis cerana (and A. mellifera, introduced) are kept in hives.

Honey Bee.q: A worker bee develops from egg to adult in
Drones develop from
Honey Bee.w: drones are haploid, from unfertilised eggs.

Honey Bee.q: The device that stops the queen entering the honey chamber is the
Honey Bee.w: the queen is too large to pass the excluder.

Honey Bee.q: The shape of the cells in a honey comb is
Honey Bee.w: hexagons need the least wax and leave no gaps.

Honey Bee.q: Name the three castes of honey bees.
What is the function of the queen in the colony?
Honey Bee.r: The queen lays eggs (1,000–2,000 per day) to keep up the population; she also releases pheromone that holds the colony together.

Honey Bee.q: What is the difference between swarming and absconding?
Honey Bee.r: In swarming, the old queen and part of the workers leave to form a new colony because the hive is crowded. In absconding, the whole colony leaves the hive because of shortage of food, pests or disturbance.

Honey Bee.q: Give any four uses of honey bee products.
Honey Bee.r: Honey as food and medicine; beeswax for candles and cosmetics; royal jelly as a tonic; propolis as an antiseptic; pollination of crops.

Honey Bee.q: Why are the cells of the comb hexagonal?
Honey Bee.r: A hexagon fits with others without a gap and gives the largest storage space for the least wax.

Honey Bee.q: Explain the division of labour among the members of a bee colony.
Honey Bee.r: The queen lays eggs; drones mate with the queen; workers do all the other work, by age: cleaning, nursing, comb building and honey storing, guarding the entrance, and foraging for nectar, pollen and water. Division of labour gives an efficient colony.

Honey Bee.q: A queen lays 1,500 eggs a day for 20 days; 4% of the eggs fail to hatch. How many larvae hatch? On what date would a worker emerge from an egg laid on 10 May?
Honey Bee.r: Eggs = 1,500 × 20 = 30,000. Failed = 4% × 30,000 = 1,200. Hatched = 28,800. Worker emerges 21 days after 10 May = 31 May.

Honey Bee.q: Write the equipment required for modern bee keeping and mention how bee keeping benefits farmers.
Honey Bee.r: Movable-frame hive with frames and foundation, queen excluder, smoker, veil and gloves, hive tool, bee brush, uncapping knife and honey extractor. Benefits: income from honey, wax and other products; higher crop yield from pollination; low cost, small space; suitable for women and landless people.

Honey Bee.q: Describe the social organisation of a honey bee colony and the life cycle of a honey bee.
Explain the importance of honey bees and beekeeping to a farmer in Nepal. Write eight points.
Which part of the honeybee body is used to make wax for constructing honeycombs?
Honey Bee.w: Special glands in the abdomen of worker bees produce wax for constructing honeycombs.

Honey Bee.q: Honeybees communicate the location of food sources through a dance. What is this dance called?
Honey Bee.w: The waggle dance is used by honeybees to communicate the direction and distance of food sources.

Honey Bee.q: Which type of bee in the hive has a barbed stinger that tears away when used?
Honey Bee.w: Worker bees have a barbed stinger that typically tears away from their body after stinging, leading to their death.

Heredity.q: The father of genetics is
Heredity.w: Gregor Mendel, from his pea experiments.

Heredity.q: The sex chromosomes of a human female are
The sex of a child is decided by the chromosome contributed by the
Heredity.w: the mother gives only X; the father gives X or Y.

Heredity.q: Down syndrome results from
Colour blindness is more common in males because the gene is
o: recessive and on the X chromosome
Heredity.w: a male has one X, so a single recessive gene shows; a female needs two.

Heredity.q: State Mendel's law of segregation.
Heredity.r: The two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation, so each gamete carries only one allele of each gene.

Heredity.q: A man with normal vision marries a woman who is a carrier of colour blindness. Give the possible genotypes of their sons.
Heredity.r: Father $X^{N}Y$; mother $X^{N}X^{c}$. Sons get the father's Y and one of the mother's X: $X^{N}Y$ (normal) or $X^{c}Y$ (colour-blind), each with probability 1/2.

Heredity.q: Show with a Punnett square the cross between two heterozygous tall pea plants (Tt × Tt). State the genotypic and phenotypic ratios.
Heredity.r: Gametes: T, t from each parent.

Heredity.q: Explain how the sex of a baby is determined.
Heredity.r: Human cells have 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes: XX in females, XY in males. Every egg carries X. Half the sperms carry X and half carry Y. If an X sperm fertilises the egg the baby is XX (girl); if a Y sperm does, the baby is XY (boy). So the father's sperm decides the sex, with equal chance of each.

Heredity.q: Who is called the father of genetics?
The sex of a human baby is decided by
Heredity.w: the sperm carries X or Y.

Heredity.q: Down's syndrome is caused by
o: a gene on the X chromosome

Heredity.q: A plant with the genotype Tt is called
Differentiate between genotype and phenotype.
Heredity.r: Genotype is the genetic make-up (e.g. Tt); phenotype is the visible character (e.g. tall).

Heredity.q: Why is colour blindness more common in males than in females?
Heredity.r: The gene is recessive and on the X chromosome. A male has one X, so one copy of the allele shows; a female needs two copies.

Heredity.q: Explain Mendel's monohybrid cross between pure tall and pure dwarf pea plants up to the F₂ generation with a Punnett square.
Heredity.r: P: TT × tt. Gametes T and t. F₁: all Tt (tall). F₁ self: gametes T, t from each parent; Punnett square gives TT, Tt, Tt, tt. F₂: 3 tall: 1 dwarf, genotypic ratio 1: 2: 1.

Heredity.q: In a dihybrid cross of RrYy × RrYy, find the phenotypic ratio. If there are 800 offspring, how many are wrinkled green?
Heredity.r: 9 round yellow: 3 round green: 3 wrinkled yellow: 1 wrinkled green. Wrinkled green = 1/16 × 800 = 50.

Heredity.q: A colour-blind man marries a normal woman who is not a carrier. Find the genotypes and phenotypes of their children.
State and explain Mendel's law of segregation using a monohybrid cross of tall and dwarf pea plants up to the F2 generation.
Explain how the sex of a child is determined in human beings. Describe Down syndrome, Turner syndrome and Klinefelter syndrome.
Which law states that during the formation of gametes, pairs of hereditary factors separate so that offspring inherit one factor from each parent?
Heredity.w: The Law of Segregation, proposed by Mendel, describes how alleles of a gene segregate randomly into reproductive cells.

Heredity.q: What is the name given to an organism that possesses two different alleles of a gene, one dominant and one recessive?
Heredity.w: Heterozygous organisms have two different alleles for a particular gene.

Physiological Structure and Life Process.q: The functional unit of the nervous system is the
Physiological Structure and Life Process.w: a neuron carries nerve impulses; the nephron belongs to the kidney.

Physiological Structure and Life Process.q: The hormone that lowers the blood sugar level is
Physiological Structure and Life Process.w: insulin from the pancreas; glucagon raises sugar.

Physiological Structure and Life Process.q: The chamber of the heart that pumps oxygenated blood to the body is the
Physiological Structure and Life Process.w: the left ventricle drives blood through the aorta to the body.

Physiological Structure and Life Process.q: A reflex action is controlled by the
Physiological Structure and Life Process.w: the reflex arc passes through the spinal cord, bypassing thinking.

Physiological Structure and Life Process.q: The functional unit of the kidney is the
Physiological Structure and Life Process.w: each kidney has about a million nephrons.

Physiological Structure and Life Process.q: The universal blood donor group is
Physiological Structure and Life Process.w: group O red cells carry no A or B antigens.

Physiological Structure and Life Process.q: Fertilisation in humans normally takes place in the
Physiological Structure and Life Process.w: the ovum meets the sperm in the fallopian tube, then travels to the uterus.

Physiological Structure and Life Process.q: Differentiate between voluntary and reflex actions.
Physiological Structure and Life Process.r: A voluntary action is controlled by the cerebrum and is done by will (writing). A reflex action is rapid, involuntary and controlled by the spinal cord (withdrawing a hand from a hot pan).

Physiological Structure and Life Process.q: Name two hormones and the glands that secrete them.
Physiological Structure and Life Process.r: Insulin from the pancreas; thyroxine from the thyroid gland (also adrenaline from the adrenal gland).

Physiological Structure and Life Process.q: Describe the path of blood through the human heart, naming the four chambers and the main vessels.
Physiological Structure and Life Process.r: Deoxygenated blood enters the right atrium from the vena cava, passes to the right ventricle, then through the pulmonary artery to the lungs. Oxygenated blood returns by the pulmonary vein to the left atrium, goes to the left ventricle and is pumped to the body through the aorta. Valves keep the flow in one direction. A labelled sketch of the four chambers earns the diagram mark.

Physiological Structure and Life Process.q: Explain how the kidney removes waste from the blood.
Physiological Structure and Life Process.r: Blood enters each kidney by the renal artery. In each nephron, the glomerulus filters water, glucose, salts and urea into the Bowman's capsule. As the filtrate passes along the tubule, useful substances (all glucose, most water and salts) are reabsorbed into the blood. The remaining water, urea and excess salts form urine, which goes through the ureter to the bladder and leaves by the urethra.

Physiological Structure and Life Process.q: The part of the brain that controls balance of the body is the
Physiological Structure and Life Process.w: the cerebellum controls balance and posture.

Physiological Structure and Life Process.q: The hormone that lowers blood sugar is
Physiological Structure and Life Process.w: insulin lowers blood glucose; glucagon raises it.

Physiological Structure and Life Process.q: Fertilisation in human beings takes place in the
Physiological Structure and Life Process.w: the egg is fertilised in the fallopian tube.

Physiological Structure and Life Process.q: The blood vessel that carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart is the
Physiological Structure and Life Process.w: the pulmonary vein is the one vein with oxygenated blood.

Physiological Structure and Life Process.q: The functional unit of the kidney is the
Physiological Structure and Life Process.w: each kidney has about a million nephrons.

Physiological Structure and Life Process.q: The blood group known as the universal donor is
Physiological Structure and Life Process.w: group O has no A or B antigens.

Physiological Structure and Life Process.q: What is a reflex action? Give two examples.
Physiological Structure and Life Process.r: A reflex action is a quick, automatic response to a stimulus controlled by the spinal cord without thinking. Examples: pulling the hand from a hot object; blinking.

Physiological Structure and Life Process.q: Why is the pituitary called the master gland?
Physiological Structure and Life Process.r: It controls the work of many other endocrine glands (thyroid, adrenal, gonads) through its hormones.

Physiological Structure and Life Process.q: Differentiate between an artery and a vein (two points).
Physiological Structure and Life Process.r: An artery carries blood away from the heart; its wall is thick and it has no valves. A vein carries blood to the heart; its wall is thin and it has valves.

Physiological Structure and Life Process.q: Define homeostasis. How does sweating help in homeostasis?
Physiological Structure and Life Process.r: Homeostasis is the keeping of a constant internal environment. Sweat evaporates from the skin and takes heat from the body, so the temperature stays near 37 °C.

Physiological Structure and Life Process.q: Draw and label a neuron. Describe the path of a reflex arc.
Physiological Structure and Life Process.r: Neuron: dendrites, cell body with nucleus, axon with myelin sheath, axon terminals. Reflex arc: stimulus → receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord (relay neuron) → motor neuron → effector (muscle) → response.

Physiological Structure and Life Process.q: Describe the 28-day menstrual cycle.
Physiological Structure and Life Process.r: Days 1–5: menstruation. Days 6–13: the uterus lining rebuilds and an egg ripens under FSH and oestrogen. Day 14: ovulation. Days 15–28: the lining thickens under progesterone; if there is no fertilisation, hormone levels fall and menstruation begins again.

Physiological Structure and Life Process.q: A person's heart beats 75 times per minute and pumps 68 mL per beat. Calculate the cardiac output in litres per minute and the blood pumped in one hour.
Physiological Structure and Life Process.r: Cardiac output = 75 × 68 = 5,100 mL = 5.1 L per minute. In one hour: 5.1 × 60 = 306 litres.

Physiological Structure and Life Process.q: Explain how urine is formed in the nephron.
Physiological Structure and Life Process.r: Ultrafiltration of blood in the glomerulus to Bowman's capsule (about 180 L/day); selective reabsorption of glucose, water, amino acids and salts in the tubule; tubular secretion of extra wastes. The remaining fluid is urine (about 1.5 L/day), sent to the bladder via the ureter.

Physiological Structure and Life Process.q: Describe how blood sugar is kept constant in the body.
Physiological Structure and Life Process.r: When blood sugar rises after a meal, the pancreas releases insulin and the liver stores glucose as glycogen. When blood sugar falls, the pancreas releases glucagon and the liver turns glycogen into glucose. This is negative feedback; lack of insulin causes diabetes.

Physiological Structure and Life Process.q: Describe the human nervous system. Explain a reflex action and the path of a reflex arc.
Describe the structure of the human heart and explain double circulation. Calculate the cardiac output of a person.
Describe the structure of a nephron and explain the formation of urine. What is dialysis and when is it needed?

Nature and Environment.q: The gas mainly responsible for global warming is
Nature and Environment.w: CO₂ is the most abundant added greenhouse gas.

Nature and Environment.q: The ozone layer is mainly damaged by
Nature and Environment.w: chlorine released from CFCs breaks down ozone.

Nature and Environment.q: Which is a biodegradable waste?
Nature and Environment.w: vegetable waste decays by microbes; the others do not.

Nature and Environment.q: In a food chain, the producer is
Write two measures to reduce solid waste at home.
Nature and Environment.r: Follow the 3R principle: reduce use of single-use plastics, reuse containers and bags, and compost kitchen waste.

Nature and Environment.q: What is acid rain? Write its causes, two harmful effects and two preventive measures.
Nature and Environment.r: Acid rain is rain with a pH below 5.6. Cause: sulphur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen from factories, vehicles and burning coal dissolve in rain to form sulphuric and nitric acids. Effects: it damages buildings and statues, harms crops and forests, and acidifies lakes so fish die. Prevention: use low-sulphur fuel, install scrubbers in chimneys, and reduce vehicle emissions.

Nature and Environment.q: Describe the causes and effects of ozone layer depletion.
Nature and Environment.r: Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs harmful ultraviolet rays. CFCs from old refrigerators, air-conditioners and aerosol sprays rise to the stratosphere; ultraviolet light breaks them to release chlorine, which destroys ozone. Effects: more UV reaches Earth, causing skin cancer and eye cataracts, reducing crop yield and harming plankton. Remedy: phase out CFCs (the Montreal Protocol).

Nature and Environment.q: The gas mainly responsible for the greenhouse effect is
Nature and Environment.w: CO₂ is the main greenhouse gas from human activity.

Nature and Environment.q: The ozone layer is depleted mainly by
According to the 10% law, if the producers store 5,000 kJ, the energy at the secondary consumer level is
The first national park of Nepal is
Which one is a biodegradable waste?
Nature and Environment.w: vegetable peel is decayed by bacteria.

Nature and Environment.q: Define ecosystem and food chain.
Nature and Environment.r: An ecosystem is a community of living things interacting with each other and with the non-living environment. A food chain is the sequence of organisms in which each is eaten by the next, so that energy passes along.

Nature and Environment.q: What is the greenhouse effect? Name two greenhouse gases.
Nature and Environment.r: The trapping of the Earth's heat by gases in the atmosphere, which keeps the Earth warm. Two gases: carbon dioxide and methane.

Nature and Environment.q: What is acid rain? State one harm it causes.
What are the 3 Rs of waste management?
Differentiate between in-situ and ex-situ conservation with one example each.
Nature and Environment.r: In-situ: protecting the species in its natural home, e.g. Chitwan National Park. Ex-situ: protecting outside its home, e.g. the Central Zoo.

Nature and Environment.q: Explain the causes, effects and control of air pollution.
Nature and Environment.r: Causes: vehicle smoke, brick kilns, factories, burning of waste, dust, firewood smoke. Effects: asthma, lung disease, eye irritation, acid rain, smog, global warming, damage to crops and buildings. Control: public and electric vehicles, vehicle testing, clean stoves and biogas, filters on chimneys, tree planting, ban on burning waste.

Nature and Environment.q: What is global warming? Describe its causes and four effects.
Nature and Environment.r: Global warming is the rise of the average temperature of the Earth due to the increase of greenhouse gases. Causes: burning fossil fuels, deforestation, agriculture (methane, nitrous oxide), CFCs. Effects: glaciers melt; sea level rises; floods and droughts; harm to crops and biodiversity; spread of diseases.

Nature and Environment.q: In the food chain grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle, 50,000 kJ of energy is stored in the grass. Find the energy received by the snake and by the eagle. Draw an energy pyramid.
Nature and Environment.r: Grasshopper = 10% of 50,000 = 5,000 kJ; frog = 500 kJ; snake = 50 kJ; eagle = 5 kJ. Pyramid: widest base grass (50,000), then grasshopper (5,000), frog (500), snake (50), top eagle (5).

Nature and Environment.q: Describe the methods of waste management that can be used at home and in the community.
Nature and Environment.r: Reduce, reuse and recycle; segregate waste at source into biodegradable, recyclable and hazardous; compost kitchen waste or use vermicompost; make biogas from dung and kitchen waste; sanitary landfill for the remaining waste; avoid open burning; treat sewage; e-waste to authorised recyclers.

Nature and Environment.q: What is environmental pollution? Describe the causes, effects and control of air, water and soil pollution with examples from Nepal.
Explain the conservation of biodiversity in Nepal. Write eight points and mention the in-situ and ex-situ methods.

Motion and Force.q: A force of 20 N acts on a 5 kg body. Its acceleration is
The momentum of a 3 kg body moving at 4 m s⁻¹ is
Which law explains why a passenger jerks forward when a bus stops suddenly?
Motion and Force.w: inertia: the body tends to keep moving.

Motion and Force.q: With $g=10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, the weight of a 6 kg object is
A stone is dropped from rest. With $g=10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, its speed after 3 s is
State Newton's third law of motion with an example.
Motion and Force.r: To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction, and they act on different bodies. Example: a rocket pushes gases down and the gases push the rocket up.

Motion and Force.q: Find the weight of a 50 kg body on Earth ($g=10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$) and on the Moon ($g=1.67\ \text{m s}^{-2}$).
Motion and Force.r: Earth: $W=mg=50\times10=500$ N. Moon: $W=50\times1.67=83.5$ N. (Mass stays 50 kg.)

Motion and Force.q: A car of mass 1500 kg accelerates uniformly from rest to $20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in 10 s. Find the acceleration and the force acting on it.
A bullet of mass 20 g is fired from a gun of mass 4 kg with a velocity of $300\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Calculate the recoil velocity of the gun and state the principle used.
Motion and Force.r: Principle: conservation of linear momentum. Total momentum before firing is zero, so $m_1v_1+m_2v_2=0$.

Motion and Force.q: Which of these has the greatest inertia?
Motion and Force.w: a loaded truck has the greatest mass.

Motion and Force.q: The value of $g$ at the centre of the Earth is
Motion and Force.w: attractions from all sides cancel at the centre.

Motion and Force.q: If the distance between two masses is doubled, the gravitational force becomes
Why do passengers fall forward when a moving bus stops suddenly?
Motion and Force.r: The passengers' bodies are moving with the bus. When the bus stops, the feet stop with the floor, but the upper body keeps moving forward because of inertia of motion.

Motion and Force.q: State Newton's third law and give one example.
Motion and Force.r: To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Example: when a gun fires a bullet forward, the bullet pushes the gun backward (recoil).

Motion and Force.q: Define momentum. What is its SI unit?
Motion and Force.r: Momentum is the product of mass and velocity, $p = mv$. Unit: kg m s⁻¹.

Motion and Force.q: Differentiate between mass and weight (any two points).
Motion and Force.r: Mass is the quantity of matter and is measured in kg; weight is the force of gravity on the body and is measured in N. Mass is constant everywhere; weight changes with $g$.

Motion and Force.q: Why does a cricketer pull his hands back while catching a fast ball?
Motion and Force.r: Pulling back the hands increases the time of stopping the ball. Since $F = \Delta p / t$, a longer time means a smaller force on the hands, so they do not get hurt.

Motion and Force.q: A force of 30 N acts on a body of mass 6 kg for 4 s. Starting from rest, find
Motion and Force.r: (a) $a = F/m = 30/6 = 5$ m s⁻². (b) $v = u + at = 0 + 5 \times 4 = 20$ m s⁻¹. (c) $p = mv = 6 \times 20 = 120$ kg m s⁻¹ (also $Ft = 30 \times 4 = 120$ N s).

Motion and Force.q: A bullet of mass 25 g leaves a rifle of mass 5 kg at 400 m s⁻¹. Calculate the recoil velocity of the rifle.
Motion and Force.r: $m_b = 0.025$ kg. Momentum is conserved: $0 = 0.025 \times 400 + 5 v$, so $v = -10/5 = -2$ m s⁻¹. The rifle recoils at 2 m s⁻¹.

Motion and Force.q: State Newton's law of gravitation and derive an expression for the acceleration due to gravity on the Earth's surface.
Motion and Force.r: Law: $F = Gm_1m_2/d^2$ (state in words). Derivation: pull of the Earth on mass $m$ is $GMm/R^2$; this equals $mg$; cancelling $m$ gives $g = GM/R^2$.

Motion and Force.q: A ball is thrown upward with a velocity of 30 m s⁻¹ ($g = 10$ m s⁻²). Find the maximum height it reaches and the time taken to return to the thrower.
Motion and Force.r: $H = u^2/2g = 900/20 = 45$ m. Time up $= u/g = 3$ s; total time $= 6$ s.

Motion and Force.q: State Newton's three laws of motion. Explain each with an example and solve a numerical problem on the second law.
What is gravitation? Differentiate between mass and weight. Explain free fall with the help of the equations of motion and a numerical.
What is the term used to describe the rate of change of velocity with respect to time?
Motion and Force.w: Acceleration is defined as the rate of change of velocity over time.

Motion and Force.q: According to Newton's second law of motion, what is the relationship between force, mass, and acceleration expressed by the formula $F = ma$?
o: Force is inversely proportional to mass and directly proportional to acceleration.
Force is directly proportional to both mass and acceleration.
Force is directly proportional to mass and inversely proportional to acceleration.
Force is inversely proportional to both mass and acceleration.
Motion and Force.w: Newton's second law states that force equals mass times acceleration, indicating direct proportionality to both mass and acceleration.

Motion and Force.q: Which statement correctly defines inertia?
o: The ability of an object to resist changes to its state of motion.
The rate at which an object's speed changes.
The force required to maintain an object's speed.
The distance an object travels in a given time.
Motion and Force.w: Inertia is the property of matter that resists any change in its motion.

Motion and Force.q: If two objects collide and there are no external forces acting on them, which law does this scenario best illustrate?
Motion and Force.w: In the absence of external forces, the total momentum before and after collision remains constant, illustrating the conservation of momentum.

Pressure.q: A force of 500 N acts on an area of 0.25 m². The pressure is
The hydraulic press works on the principle of
Pressure.w: Pascal's law transmits pressure through the confined oil.

Pressure.q: A barometer is used to measure
An iron nail sinks but a huge iron ship floats because the ship
o: displaces water weighing as much as the ship
Pressure.w: the floating ship's weight equals the weight of water it displaces.

Pressure.q: A sharp knife cuts better than a blunt one because the sharp edge has
Pressure.w: for the same force, smaller area gives larger pressure.

Pressure.q: Why does a nail with a sharp point go into wood more easily than a blunt one?
Pressure.r: The pointed tip has a very small area, so for the same force the pressure ($P=F/A$) is much greater and the nail penetrates.

Pressure.q: In a hydraulic press, the small piston has an area of 5 cm² and the large piston 500 cm². A force of 100 N is applied to the small piston. Find the force on the large piston.
A block of volume $0.002\ \text{m}^3$ is completely immersed in water ($\rho=1000\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$). Find the upthrust. If the block weighs 30 N in air, what is its apparent weight in water?
Pressure.r: Upthrust $=V\rho g=0.002\times1000\times10=20$ N. Apparent weight $=30-20=10$ N.

Pressure.q: The SI unit of pressure is
The pressure in a liquid at a given depth depends on
Pressure.w: $P = h\rho g$; shape and area do not matter.

Pressure.q: Hydraulic brakes work on
Pressure.w: pressure on the brake fluid is transmitted equally to all wheels.

Pressure.q: A body floats in a liquid when
o: its density is more than the liquid
its density is less than the liquid
Pressure.w: a body with lower density than the liquid floats.

Pressure.q: State Pascal's law. Write one application.
Pressure.r: Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally and undiminished in all directions. Application: the hydraulic jack (or hydraulic brake).

Pressure.q: Why does a nail have a pointed tip and a broad head?
Pressure.r: The pointed tip has a very small area, so a small force gives a large pressure that helps it enter the wood. The broad head has a large area, so the pressure on the hand is small and does not hurt.

Pressure.q: Why does the pressure of the atmosphere decrease with height?
Pressure.r: The column of air above becomes shorter and the air becomes thinner, so there is less weight of air above.

Pressure.q: A box weighing 400 N rests on a floor with a contact area of 0.5 m². Calculate the pressure it exerts. If it is turned to rest on a face of area 0.2 m², what is the new pressure?
Pressure.r: $P_1 = 400/0.5 = 800$ Pa. $P_2 = 400/0.2 = 2000$ Pa. The pressure is larger on the smaller area.

Pressure.q: Derive the expression $P = h\rho g$ for the pressure at a depth in a liquid.
Pressure.r: See the derivation box: volume $Ah$, mass $\rho Ah$, weight $\rho Ahg$, divide by $A$ to get $P = h\rho g$.

Pressure.q: The areas of the small and large pistons of a hydraulic press are 10 cm² and 1000 cm². A force of 50 N is applied to the small piston. Find
p: the force on the large piston and

Pressure.q: A solid cube of side 10 cm and mass 0.5 kg is placed in water. Will it float or sink? Find the upthrust when it floats. ($\rho_w = 1000$ kg m⁻³, $g = 10$ m s⁻².)
Pressure.r: Volume $= (0.1)^3 = 0.001$ m³. Density $= 0.5/0.001 = 500$ kg m⁻³, which is less than 1000, so it floats. Upthrust = weight $= 0.5 \times 10 = 5$ N. Half the cube is under water.

Pressure.q: State Pascal's law. Explain the working of a hydraulic jack and solve a numerical problem on it.
State Archimedes' principle and explain the floating and sinking of bodies. Describe how a mercury barometer measures atmospheric pressure.

Heat.q: Heat reaches us from the Sun mainly by
Heat.w: radiation travels through the vacuum of space.

Heat.q: Water has its maximum density at
Heat.w: anomalous expansion: water is densest at 4 °C.

Heat.q: Sea breeze blows from the sea to land during the day because
o: land heats up faster than water
water heats up faster than land
Heat.w: warm air rises over land and cooler sea air flows in; land has a lower specific heat.

Heat.q: Which material is the best conductor of heat?
Heat.w: copper is a metal with free electrons.

Heat.q: Define specific heat capacity and write its SI unit.
Heat.r: Specific heat capacity is the heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C (or 1 K). Unit: J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

Heat.q: Why does water in a pond freeze from the top while the bottom stays at about 4 °C?
Heat.r: Water is densest at 4 °C. On cooling, water above 4 °C sinks until the whole pond reaches 4 °C; below 4 °C the cooler water becomes lighter and stays on top, so ice forms at the surface while the bottom stays near 4 °C.

Heat.q: At which temperature does water have the maximum density?
Heat from the Sun reaches the Earth by
Heat.w: only radiation can cross empty space.

Heat.q: During melting of ice at 0 °C, the temperature of the ice-water mixture
Heat.w: heat goes into latent heat, not into raising temperature.

Heat.q: Convection takes place in
Heat.w: fluids can flow and carry heat.

Heat.q: Define specific heat capacity and state its SI unit.
Heat.r: It is the heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C (or 1 K). Unit: J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

Heat.q: Why are gaps left between railway rails?
Heat.r: Rails expand in hot weather. Gaps give room to expand freely; otherwise they would bend and damage the track.

Heat.q: Why does the sea breeze blow during the day?
Heat.r: Land has a lower specific heat capacity, so it gets hot faster than the sea. Air over the land rises and cool air from the sea moves in to take its place.

Heat.q: Why do we wear white clothes in summer?
Heat.r: White surfaces reflect most of the heat and absorb little, so we stay cooler.

Heat.q: Why does a steam burn hurt more than a burn from boiling water at the same temperature?
Heat.r: Steam at 100 °C gives out its latent heat of vaporisation (2.26×10⁶ J kg⁻¹) when it condenses on the skin, in addition to the heat from cooling, so it supplies much more heat.

Heat.q: Explain the anomalous expansion of water and state its importance for aquatic life.
Heat.r: On heating from 0 °C to 4 °C water contracts; above 4 °C it expands. So its density is maximum at 4 °C. In a cold lake, 4 °C water sinks to the bottom and colder water stays on top and freezes. The ice layer insulates the water below, which stays at about 4 °C, so fish survive.

Heat.q: Compare conduction, convection and radiation with an example of each.
Heat.r: Use the comparison table: conduction in solids (iron rod), convection in fluids (sea breeze, boiling water), radiation without a medium (sunlight).

Heat.q: Define specific heat capacity and latent heat. Derive the heat equations and solve numerical problems on each.
Describe conduction, convection and radiation with examples. Explain how a vacuum flask keeps liquids hot or cold.
What is thermal expansion? Explain eight effects and applications of expansion of solids.
Which of the following materials would have the highest thermal conductivity?
Heat.w: Metals like copper are generally excellent conductors of heat compared to non-metals and insulators.

Heat.q: If the heat transfer coefficient (h) increases, what happens to the rate of heat transfer through convection?
Heat.w: The rate of heat transfer through convection is directly proportional to the heat transfer coefficient.

Wave.q: A wave of frequency 50 Hz has wavelength 6.8 m. Its speed is
Sound cannot travel through
Wave.w: sound is a mechanical wave and needs a medium.

Wave.q: An echo is heard 3 s after a shout. If the speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹, the reflecting wall is at
The power of a convex lens of focal length 0.5 m is
Short-sightedness (myopia) is corrected by a
Wave.w: a concave lens diverges rays so the image falls on the retina.

Wave.q: The bending of light as it passes from air to glass is called
Wave.w: refraction is bending due to a change of speed.

Wave.q: White light splits into seven colours in a prism because
o: every colour has a different speed in glass
Wave.w: dispersion: each colour has a different refractive index in glass.

Wave.q: Differentiate between transverse and longitudinal waves.
Wave.r: In a transverse wave the particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of the wave (light, waves on a string). In a longitudinal wave they vibrate parallel to it (sound).

Wave.q: State the laws of reflection of light.
Wave.r: (i) The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. (ii) The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence lie in the same plane.

Wave.q: A ship sends an ultrasonic pulse towards the sea bed and receives the echo after 0.8 s. If the speed of sound in sea water is $1500\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, find the depth of the sea.
Wave.r: The pulse travels down and back, so the distance is $2d=vt$:

Wave.q: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. Find the image distance and the magnification.
Wave.r: Using $\dfrac{1}{f}=\dfrac{1}{u}+\dfrac{1}{v}$ with real distances positive: $\dfrac{1}{v}=\dfrac{1}{10}-\dfrac{1}{30}=\dfrac{3-1}{30}=\dfrac{1}{15}$, so $v=15$ cm (a real image beyond the lens). Magnification $m=\dfrac{v}{u}=\dfrac{15}{30}=0.5$, so the image is real, inverted and half the size.

Wave.q: Sound waves in air are
Wave.w: air particles vibrate along the direction of the wave.

Wave.q: The speed of light in a medium of refractive index 2 is
The image formed by a convex mirror is always
The unit of power of a lens is
A short-sighted person should use
Wave.w: a concave lens moves the image back onto the retina.

Wave.q: Why can sound not travel in a vacuum?
Wave.r: Sound is a mechanical wave and needs particles to pass the vibration on. A vacuum has no particles.

Wave.q: What is total internal reflection? Write its two conditions.
Wave.r: Complete reflection of light back into a denser medium at its boundary with a rarer one. Conditions: light goes from denser to rarer medium, and the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle.

Wave.q: Why does a diamond sparkle?
Wave.r: Diamond's refractive index (2.42) is very high, so its critical angle (24.4°) is very small. Light entering it is totally internally reflected many times inside before coming out, making it sparkle.

Wave.q: A wave has a frequency of 256 Hz and wavelength of 1.33 m. Find the speed of the wave.
A man fires a gun and hears the echo from a hill after 3 s. If the speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹, find the distance of the hill.
Wave.r: Distance travelled $= 340 \times 3 = 1020$ m; hill distance $= 1020/2 = 510$ m.

Wave.q: What is a wave? Differentiate between transverse and longitudinal waves. Explain the characteristics of sound and solve numericals on the wave equation and echo.
State the laws of refraction. Explain image formation by a convex lens, the lens formula, and the defects of the human eye.

Electricity and Magnetism.q: A 12 V battery drives a current through a 4 Ω resistor. The current is
A 2 kW heater runs for 3 hours. The energy used is
A step-up transformer has
Electricity and Magnetism.w: more secondary turns raise the voltage.

Electricity and Magnetism.q: A generator works on the principle of
Electricity and Magnetism.w: a coil turning in a magnetic field has an induced emf.

Electricity and Magnetism.q: The direction of force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field is found by
Electricity and Magnetism.w: Fleming's left-hand rule gives the direction of the force.

Electricity and Magnetism.q: Write two differences between a motor and a generator.
Electricity and Magnetism.r: A motor converts electrical energy to mechanical energy (works on Fleming's left-hand rule); a generator converts mechanical energy to electrical energy (works on electromagnetic induction).

Electricity and Magnetism.q: Explain the working of a step-down transformer. A transformer has 1000 primary turns on a 220 V mains. How many secondary turns are needed for 11 V?
Electricity and Magnetism.r: A step-down transformer has fewer turns on the secondary than on the primary. An alternating current in the primary produces a changing magnetic flux in the iron core, which induces a smaller alternating emf in the secondary (electromagnetic induction). $\dfrac{V_p}{V_s}=\dfrac{N_p}{N_s}\Rightarrow\dfrac{220}{11}=\dfrac{1000}{N_s}\Rightarrow N_s=\dfrac{1000\times11}{220}=50$ turns.

Electricity and Magnetism.q: The SI unit of resistance is
Which rule gives the direction of force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field?
Electricity and Magnetism.w: thumb force, forefinger field, middle finger current.

Electricity and Magnetism.q: A transformer works on
Electricity and Magnetism.w: only a changing current gives a changing flux.

Electricity and Magnetism.q: In an AC generator, the output current reverses direction because of
Electricity and Magnetism.w: as the coil rotates, each side alternately moves up and down through the field, reversing the induced current every half turn.

Electricity and Magnetism.q: Why are household appliances connected in parallel?
Electricity and Magnetism.r: Each appliance receives the full supply voltage (220 V) and can be switched on or off independently of the others.

Electricity and Magnetism.q: What is a fuse? Where is it connected in a circuit?
Electricity and Magnetism.r: A fuse is a wire of low melting point that melts and breaks the circuit when the current is too large. It is connected in series with the live wire.

Electricity and Magnetism.q: State Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction.
Electricity and Magnetism.r: The emf induced in a circuit is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linked with it.

Electricity and Magnetism.q: Why is electricity transmitted at high voltage?
Electricity and Magnetism.r: At high voltage the current is small for the same power, so the heat loss $I^2R$ in the wires is much smaller.

Electricity and Magnetism.q: An electric iron of 1000 W, 220 V is used for 3 hours a day. Find the energy used in 30 days and the cost at Rs 12 per unit.
Electricity and Magnetism.r: Energy per day $= 1 \text{ kW} \times 3 \text{ h} = 3$ kWh. In 30 days: 90 kWh. Cost $= 90 \times 12 =$ Rs 1080.

Electricity and Magnetism.q: A step-down transformer has 1000 turns in the primary and 50 turns in the secondary. If the input voltage is 220 V, find the output voltage. If the output current is 4 A, find the input current.
Electricity and Magnetism.r: $V_s = 220 \times \dfrac{50}{1000} = 11$ V. $I_p = \dfrac{V_sI_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{11 \times 4}{220} = 0.2$ A.

Electricity and Magnetism.q: Explain the working of a DC motor with the help of Fleming's left-hand rule.
Electricity and Magnetism.r: Describe the coil in the magnetic field, split-ring commutator, brushes. Forces on the two sides are opposite by the left-hand rule, which turn the coil; the commutator reverses the current each half turn, so the rotation continues in one direction.

Electricity and Magnetism.q: State Ohm's law. Derive the formulae for resistors in series and in parallel and solve a numerical problem. Calculate the cost of electrical energy.
Explain electromagnetic induction. Describe the working of an AC generator and a transformer, and the use of transformers in Nepal's power supply.
If the current flowing through a conductor is doubled, what happens to the magnetic field produced by the conductor?
Electricity and Magnetism.w: The strength of the magnetic field is directly proportional to the current.

Electricity and Magnetism.q: Which of the following materials is NOT a good conductor of electricity?
Electricity and Magnetism.w: Rubber is an insulator, not a conductor.

Electricity and Magnetism.q: What is the SI unit of electric charge?
Electricity and Magnetism.w: Electric charge is measured in Coulombs.

Electricity and Magnetism.q: According to Ohm's law, if the resistance in a circuit is halved while the voltage remains constant, the current will:
Electricity and Magnetism.w: Current is inversely proportional to resistance when voltage is constant.

Universe.q: A light year is a unit of
Universe.w: a light year is the distance light travels in a year.

Universe.q: Our galaxy is called the
Universe.w: the Milky Way contains our Sun.

Universe.q: The planet nearest to the Sun is
Universe.w: Mercury orbits closest to the Sun.

Universe.q: The theory that explains the origin of the universe from a hot, dense state is the
Energy in the core of the Sun is released by
Universe.w: hydrogen nuclei fuse to helium in the core.

Universe.q: A man-made body orbiting the Earth is called
Universe.w: satellites are artificial; the Moon is natural.

Universe.q: Write any two uses of artificial satellites.
Universe.r: Telecommunication (TV, phone and internet signals) and weather forecasting; also GPS navigation and remote sensing.

Universe.q: A star is 4 light years away. Express the distance in kilometres. (1 ly $=9.46\times10^{12}$ km)
Describe the Big Bang theory and give two pieces of evidence for it.
Universe.r: The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot, dense point that expanded rapidly; as it expanded it cooled, and matter formed atoms, stars and galaxies. Evidence: (i) galaxies are moving apart, so the universe is expanding (red shift of light from distant galaxies); (ii) cosmic microwave background radiation fills space, the cooled remnant of the early universe.

Universe.q: A light year is a unit of
Universe.w: it is the distance light travels in a year.

Universe.q: The planet nearest to the Sun is
Universe.w: Mercury is 0.39 AU from the Sun.

Universe.q: The most accepted theory of the origin of the universe is the
Universe.w: supported by red shift and the microwave background.

Universe.q: The star at the end of a Sun-like star's life is a
Universe.w: a Sun-like star sheds its outer layers and leaves a white dwarf.

Universe.q: A geostationary satellite has a period of
Universe.w: it matches the Earth's rotation, so it stays above one spot.

Universe.q: Define a light year. How long does light from the Sun take to reach the Earth?
Universe.r: A light year is the distance travelled by light in one year in vacuum ($9.46\times10^{12}$ km). Sunlight takes about 8 min 20 s (500 s).

Universe.q: Why do stars twinkle but planets do not?
Universe.r: The light of stars is refracted by the moving layers of the atmosphere, so its apparent position and brightness keep changing. Planets are nearer and look like small discs; the changes from different points average out.

Universe.q: Name the types of galaxy. To which type does the Milky Way belong?
Universe.r: Spiral, elliptical and irregular. The Milky Way is a spiral galaxy.

Universe.q: Why is Pluto not called a planet?
Universe.r: Pluto has not cleared its orbit of other bodies, so in 2006 it was classified as a dwarf planet.

Universe.q: Give any two uses of artificial satellites.
Universe.r: Any two: communication, weather forecasting, navigation (GPS), remote sensing, TV broadcast.

Universe.q: Describe the life cycle of a star like the Sun and of a massive star.
Universe.r: Sun-like: nebula → protostar → main sequence → red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf. Massive: nebula → protostar → main sequence → red supergiant → supernova → neutron star or black hole.

Universe.q: State the Big Bang theory and give two pieces of evidence for it.
Universe.r: Statement: the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago from a hot, dense state and has been expanding. Evidence: red shift of distant galaxies (they recede, faster if farther); cosmic microwave background of 2.7 K; abundance of hydrogen and helium.

Universe.q: A star is 8.6 light years away. Find its distance in kilometres and the time light from it takes to reach us.
A planet is 9 AU from the Sun. Find the time it takes to go once round the Sun.
What is a geostationary satellite? Write the conditions it must satisfy and two uses.
Universe.r: A satellite that appears fixed above one point of the Earth. Conditions: orbit above the equator at about 36,000 km, revolves west to east, period 24 h. Uses: TV and communication, weather watching.

Universe.q: Describe the Big Bang theory and the evidence supporting it.
Describe the solar system, with a table of its planets. Explain the life cycle of a star and the future of the Sun.

Information and Communication Technology.q: The brain of the computer is the
Information and Communication Technology.w: the CPU processes instructions.

Information and Communication Technology.q: Which memory loses its data when power is switched off?
Information and Communication Technology.w: RAM is volatile.

Information and Communication Technology.q: The full form of URL is
Information and Communication Technology.w: Uniform Resource Locator, the address of a web page.

Information and Communication Technology.q: Buying goods through a website is called
Information and Communication Technology.w: e-commerce is trade over the internet.

Information and Communication Technology.q: Sending false messages to steal a person's bank details is
Information and Communication Technology.w: phishing tricks users into giving private information.

Information and Communication Technology.q: Which is an output device?
Information and Communication Technology.w: a printer outputs information; the others are input devices.

Information and Communication Technology.q: The worldwide network of connected computers is the
Information and Communication Technology.w: the internet connects networks worldwide; a LAN is local.

Information and Communication Technology.q: Differentiate between RAM and ROM.
Information and Communication Technology.r: RAM is temporary (volatile) memory used while a program runs and is lost when power goes off. ROM is permanent (non-volatile) memory holding start-up instructions.

Information and Communication Technology.q: What is cyber crime? Mention three safe-use rules for the internet.
Information and Communication Technology.r: Cyber crime is a crime committed using computers or the internet, such as hacking, phishing or spreading viruses. Rules: use strong, private passwords; do not share personal details or open links from unknown senders; keep anti-virus software updated; log out of public computers.

Information and Communication Technology.q: Which of the following is an output device?
Information and Communication Technology.w: a monitor displays results; the others are input devices.

Information and Communication Technology.q: The memory that loses its contents when the power is switched off is
Information and Communication Technology.w: RAM is volatile.

Information and Communication Technology.q: A network that covers a school building is a
Information and Communication Technology.w: a local area network covers a small area such as a building.

Information and Communication Technology.q: 1 byte is equal to
Information and Communication Technology.w: 1 byte = 8 bits.

Information and Communication Technology.q: A fake e-mail used to steal bank details is called
Information and Communication Technology.w: phishing tricks users into giving private information.

Information and Communication Technology.q: Differentiate between hardware and software.
Information and Communication Technology.r: Hardware is the physical, touchable parts of a computer (monitor, keyboard); software is the set of programs that instruct the hardware (Windows, MS Word).

Information and Communication Technology.q: What is the difference between the internet and the WWW?
Information and Communication Technology.r: The internet is the worldwide network of connected computers; the WWW is the collection of linked web pages that we view through a browser, one of the services on the internet.

Information and Communication Technology.q: Define e-commerce. Give two examples of e-commerce websites in Nepal.
Information and Communication Technology.r: E-commerce is buying and selling of goods and services over the internet. Examples: Daraz, Sastodeal (also Hamrobazar).

Information and Communication Technology.q: What is cyber crime? Give two examples.
Information and Communication Technology.r: A crime done using a computer or the internet. Examples: hacking, phishing, online fraud.

Information and Communication Technology.q: Write two uses of ICT in the field of health.
Information and Communication Technology.r: Telemedicine (consulting doctors by video) and digital medical imaging or electronic patient records.

Information and Communication Technology.q: A video file of 600 MB is downloaded at 16 Mbps. How long does it take?
Information and Communication Technology.r: $600\ \text{MB} = 600 \times 8 = 4800$ megabits. Time $= 4800/16 = 300$ s $= 5$ minutes.

Information and Communication Technology.q: Convert $10110_2$ into decimal and $19_{10}$ into binary.
List four advantages and two disadvantages of e-commerce.
Information and Communication Technology.r: Advantages: 24-hour service, saves time and travel, wide choice, home delivery. Disadvantages: risk of fraud, cannot touch the goods before buying, depends on the internet.

Information and Communication Technology.q: Why is cyber ethics necessary? Explain any four rules of good conduct on the internet.
Information and Communication Technology.r: Cyber ethics protects users and keeps the internet safe and respectful. Rules: be polite; do not spread false news; respect copyright and do not plagiarise; do not enter other people's accounts; protect privacy.

Information and Communication Technology.q: Describe the main parts of a computer system. Differentiate between primary and secondary memory.
What is ICT? Explain eight uses of ICT in Nepal, with a note on its disadvantages and on cyber safety.
Which law states that the number of transistors on a microchip doubles about every two years, though the cost of computers is halved?
Information and Communication Technology.w: Moore's Law predicts the trend in the number of transistors on integrated circuits.

Classification of Elements.q: The modern periodic law states that properties of elements are a periodic function of their
Classification of Elements.w: Moseley's work led to atomic number as the basis.

Classification of Elements.q: An element with electronic configuration 2, 8, 7 is in
Classification of Elements.w: three shells give period 3; seven valence electrons give group 17.

Classification of Elements.q: Which group contains the noble gases?
Classification of Elements.w: helium, neon, argon and the rest are in group 18.

Classification of Elements.q: Down a group the atomic size
Classification of Elements.w: each period down adds a shell.

Classification of Elements.q: Which element is an alkali metal?
Classification of Elements.w: sodium is in group 1; calcium is group 2.

Classification of Elements.q: Atoms of elements in the same group have the same
Classification of Elements.w: the same valence electrons give similar properties.

Classification of Elements.q: The number of periods in the modern periodic table is
State the modern periodic law.
Classification of Elements.r: The physical and chemical properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers.

Classification of Elements.q: Why are noble gases chemically inert?
Classification of Elements.r: Their outermost shells are complete (2 electrons in helium, 8 in the rest), so they neither gain, lose nor share electrons.

Classification of Elements.q: The atomic numbers of X and Y are 11 and 17. Write their electronic configurations, groups and periods, and the formula and type of bond in the compound they form.
Classification of Elements.r: X (11): 2, 8, 1 — group 1, period 3 (sodium). Y (17): 2, 8, 7 — group 17, period 3 (chlorine). X loses one electron to become X⁺ and Y gains it to become Y⁻, giving XY (NaCl) with an ionic bond.

Classification of Elements.q: Describe how atomic size and metallic character change across a period and down a group.
Classification of Elements.r: Across a period (left to right): nuclear charge increases while the shell number is the same, so atomic size decreases and metallic character decreases. Down a group: extra shells are added, so atomic size increases and metallic character increases.

Classification of Elements.q: Who proposed the law of triads?
The modern periodic law is based on
Classification of Elements.w: Moseley showed atomic number is the basis.

Classification of Elements.q: The number of elements in the third period is

Elements of group 17 are called
Write any two limitations of Newlands' law of octaves.
Classification of Elements.r: (i) It worked only up to calcium. (ii) It did not leave places for new elements such as the noble gases; unlike elements were placed together.

Classification of Elements.q: Why does atomic size decrease from left to right in a period?
Classification of Elements.r: The number of shells remains the same, but the nuclear charge increases by one at every step. The stronger pull draws the electrons nearer to the nucleus.

Classification of Elements.q: Define ionisation energy. How does it change down a group?
Classification of Elements.r: It is the minimum energy needed to remove the outermost electron from an isolated gaseous atom. It decreases down a group because the outer electron is farther away and shielded by more inner shells.

Classification of Elements.q: Write the electronic configuration of Mg (Z = 12) and Cl (Z = 17). State the period, group and valency of each, and write the formula of the compound they form.
Classification of Elements.r: Mg: 2, 8, 2; period 3, group 2, valency 2. Cl: 2, 8, 7; period 3, group 17, valency 1. Mg loses two electrons, Cl gains one each, so two Cl atoms combine with one Mg: MgCl₂.

Classification of Elements.q: Describe the merits and demerits of Mendeleev's periodic table.
Classification of Elements.r: Merits: similar elements in one group; gaps left and properties of Ga, Sc, Ge predicted correctly. Demerits: position of hydrogen uncertain; no place for isotopes; some higher-mass elements placed before lower-mass ones (Co before Ni); unlike elements in one group.

Classification of Elements.q: Compare the elements Na, Mg, Al in terms of atomic size, ionisation energy and metallic character. Give reasons.
Classification of Elements.r: All are in period 3, so the number of shells is constant while the nuclear charge increases from Na (+11) to Al (+13). Atomic size decreases (Na > Mg > Al); ionisation energy increases (Na < Mg < Al, roughly); metallic character decreases (Na > Mg > Al).

Classification of Elements.q: The atomic masses of Li and K are 7 and 39. Using Dobereiner's law, find the atomic mass of Na and state whether it fits.
Classification of Elements.r: Mass of Na = (7 + 39) / 2 = 46 / 2 = 23. The actual atomic mass of sodium is 23, so it fits the law exactly.

Classification of Elements.q: Compare Mendeleev's periodic table with the modern periodic table. State the modern periodic law and the merits and demerits of Mendeleev's table.
Explain the variation of atomic size, ionisation energy and metallic character across a period and down a group, with examples from the first 20 elements.

Chemical Reaction.w: acid and base give salt and water.

Chemical Reaction.w: citric acid changes blue litmus to red.

Chemical Reaction.q: Write four factors that affect the rate of a chemical reaction, with one example each.
Chemical Reaction.r: (i) Temperature: milk sours faster in a warm room. (ii) Concentration: concentrated acid reacts faster with marble than dilute acid. (iii) Surface area: powdered marble reacts faster than a lump. (iv) Catalyst: MnO₂ speeds the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide.

Chemical Reaction.q: The reaction CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ is a
Chemical Reaction.w: two substances join to form one.

Which is the balanced equation?
Chemical Reaction.w: 4 H and 2 O on each side.

Chemical Reaction.q: Why does powdered zinc react faster with acid than a lump of zinc?
Chemical Reaction.r: Powder has a larger surface area, so more particles are exposed to the acid and more collisions occur per second.

Chemical Reaction.q: A student burns 12 g of carbon and obtains 44 g of CO₂. How much oxygen reacted? State the law used.
Chemical Reaction.r: Oxygen = 44 - 12 = 32 g. Law of conservation of mass.

Chemical Reaction.q: Distinguish between exothermic and endothermic reactions with one example each.
Chemical Reaction.r: Exothermic: releases heat (burning of coal). Endothermic: absorbs heat (decomposition of CaCO₃).

Chemical Reaction.q: Explain with examples four factors that affect the rate of a chemical reaction.
Chemical Reaction.r: Concentration (more concentrated acid reacts faster with marble); surface area (powdered chalk faster than a lump); temperature (food cooks faster at higher temperature); catalyst (MnO₂ speeds up decomposition of H₂O₂). Each is explained by more or harder collisions.

Chemical Reaction.q: Describe the properties of acids with the help of equations.
Chemical Reaction.r: Sour taste; blue litmus turns red; reaction with metals gives hydrogen (Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂); with carbonates gives CO₂ (CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂); with bases gives salt and water (HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O).

Chemical Reaction.q: Write the steps to balance Fe + O₂ → Fe₂O₃ and give the balanced equation.
Chemical Reaction.r: Fe₂O₃ has 2 Fe and 3 O. Put 2 before Fe: 2Fe. Oxygen is 3 on the right and 2 on the left; take the lowest common multiple 6: 3O₂ on the left and 2Fe₂O₃ on the right; then Fe is 4, so 4Fe. 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃.

Chemical Reaction.q: Explain the pH scale and state how you would find whether a liquid is acidic, basic or neutral using litmus paper.
Chemical Reaction.r: pH is a scale from 0 to 14 that shows acidity or basicity: below 7 acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 basic. With litmus: if blue litmus turns red, the liquid is acidic; if red litmus turns blue, it is basic; if neither changes, it is neutral.

Chemical Reaction.q: Describe the main types of chemical reaction with a balanced equation and an example of each.
What are acids, bases and salts? Explain indicators, the pH scale and neutralisation, with the uses of neutralisation in daily life.
Which law states that at constant temperature, the volume of a given mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure?
Chemical Reaction.w: Boyle's Law describes the inverse relationship between pressure and volume of a gas at constant temperature.

Chemical Reaction.q: What is the term used to describe a reaction where two or more substances combine to form a single new substance?
Chemical Reaction.w: A synthesis reaction involves the combination of two or more substances to form a new compound.

Chemical Reaction.q: According to the law of conservation of mass, what happens during a chemical reaction?
Chemical Reaction.w: The law of conservation of mass states that mass cannot be created or destroyed in a chemical reaction.

Chemical Reaction.q: What type of reaction occurs when a substance reacts with oxygen to release heat energy?
Chemical Reaction.w: A combustion reaction involves the reaction of a substance with oxygen, often releasing heat and light.

Gases.q: Write the chemical test for carbon dioxide.
Gases.r: Pass the gas through lime water: it turns milky because insoluble calcium carbonate forms. Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ ↓ + H₂O.

State Boyle's law and write its mathematical form.
Gases.r: At constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure; $P_1V_1 = P_2V_2$.

Gases.q: Why is the Kelvin scale used in Charles' law?
Gases.r: The volume of a gas is proportional to the absolute temperature; the Kelvin scale starts from absolute zero, so that V/T is a constant.

Gases.q: How is lime water used to test CO₂? Write the equation.
Gases.r: Passing CO₂ through lime water makes it milky: Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ ↓ + H₂O.

Gases.q: Why is dilute sulphuric acid not used to prepare CO₂ from marble?
Gases.r: Calcium sulphate is slightly soluble and forms a coat on the marble that stops the acid reaching it.

Gases.q: A gas of volume 300 cm³ at 1 atm is compressed to 2 atm at constant temperature. Find the new volume.
Describe the laboratory preparation of oxygen. Give the equation, one test and two uses.
Gases.r: Heat KClO₃ with MnO₂ in a hard glass tube; collect over water. 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂ ↑. A glowing splinter relights. Uses: respiration support, welding.

Gases.q: A gas occupies 250 cm³ at 17 °C. At what temperature will it occupy 300 cm³ at constant pressure?
State Boyle's law and Charles' law. Explain them with experiments or examples and solve a numerical problem on each.
Describe the laboratory preparation, properties, tests and uses of hydrogen, oxygen and carbon dioxide.

Metal and Non-metals.w: both are needed; iron(III) oxide forms.

Metal and Non-metals.q: Brass is an alloy of
Metal and Non-metals.w: brass is copper and zinc; bronze is copper and tin.

Which metal does NOT displace hydrogen from dilute acids?

Which non-metal is a good conductor of electricity?
Metal and Non-metals.w: graphite has free electrons between its layers.

Metal and Non-metals.q: Why is sodium stored under kerosene?
Metal and Non-metals.r: Sodium is very reactive and reacts vigorously with oxygen and moisture of air, so it is kept under kerosene to keep air and water away.

Metal and Non-metals.q: Why do aluminium utensils not corrode easily?
Metal and Non-metals.r: Aluminium forms a thin, tough layer of aluminium oxide on its surface, which protects the metal below from further attack.

Metal and Non-metals.q: What is rusting? State the conditions needed and two methods to prevent it.
Metal and Non-metals.r: Rusting is the slow corrosion of iron in damp air to form reddish-brown hydrated iron(III) oxide. It needs both oxygen and water. Prevention: painting or oiling; galvanising (zinc coating); making alloys like stainless steel.

Metal and Non-metals.q: Describe the extraction of aluminium from its ore by electrolysis.
Metal and Non-metals.r: The ore is bauxite (Al₂O₃·2H₂O), purified to alumina (Al₂O₃). Alumina is dissolved in molten cryolite (which lowers the melting point) and electrolysed in a steel tank lined with carbon (cathode) using carbon anodes. At the cathode, Al³⁺ gains electrons to give molten aluminium that collects at the bottom; at the anode, oxygen is released and burns the carbon anodes to CO₂.

Differentiate between a mineral and an ore.
Metal and Non-metals.r: A mineral is any natural substance that contains a metal compound; an ore is a mineral from which the metal can be extracted profitably.

Metal and Non-metals.q: Why are sodium and potassium kept under kerosene?
Metal and Non-metals.r: They react violently with oxygen and moisture of the air; kerosene keeps them away from both.

Metal and Non-metals.q: Write the balanced equation for the reaction of zinc with dilute sulphuric acid and name the gas formed.
Why does aluminium not corrode easily even though it is reactive?
Metal and Non-metals.r: Aluminium forms a thin, strong layer of Al₂O₃ on its surface that protects the metal beneath.

Metal and Non-metals.q: Write two differences between metals and non-metals.
Metal and Non-metals.r: Metals are good conductors, malleable and ductile; non-metals are poor conductors and brittle.

Metal and Non-metals.q: Describe the extraction of iron from haematite in a blast furnace. Give the reactions.
Metal and Non-metals.r: Charge: haematite, coke, limestone from the top; hot air from bottom. C + O₂ → CO₂; CO₂ + C → 2CO; Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂; CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂; CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃ (slag). Molten iron and slag are tapped from the bottom.

Metal and Non-metals.q: What is corrosion? Explain the conditions for rusting of iron and four methods of prevention.
Metal and Non-metals.r: Corrosion: slow destruction of a metal by air, moisture or chemicals. Rusting needs oxygen and water together (nail experiment). Prevention: painting or oiling, galvanising with zinc, electroplating, alloying (stainless steel), sacrificial protection.

Metal and Non-metals.q: What is the reactivity series? Explain two of its uses with an example for each.
Metal and Non-metals.r: The reactivity series ranks metals by decreasing reactivity. (i) Displacement: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu. (ii) Reaction with acid: Mg and Zn give H₂ with dilute acids but Cu does not. (iii) It chooses the extraction method.

Metal and Non-metals.q: Find the mass of aluminium obtainable from 204 kg of alumina (Al = 27, O = 16).
Metal and Non-metals.r: Molar mass of Al₂O₃ = 102; it contains 54 of aluminium. Mass of Al = (54 / 102) × 204 = 54 × 2 = 108 kg.

Metal and Non-metals.q: Differentiate between metals and non-metals. Explain the reactivity series and its uses.
Describe the extraction of iron in a blast furnace. Explain corrosion of iron and the methods of preventing it.

Hydrocarbon and its Compounds.q: What is a homologous series? Give one example.
Hydrocarbon and its Compounds.r: A homologous series is a family of organic compounds with the same functional group and similar properties, in which successive members differ by CH₂. Example: alkanes (CH₄, C₂H₆, C₃H₈).

Hydrocarbon and its Compounds.q: Write the molecular formulae of the first four alkanes.
Hydrocarbon and its Compounds.r: Methane CH₄, ethane C₂H₆, propane C₃H₈, butane C₄H₁₀ (general formula $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}$).

Hydrocarbon and its Compounds.q: Write four differences between alkanes and alkenes.
How is ethanol converted to ethanoic acid? Name the acid's functional group, and state how it reacts with ethanol.
Hydrocarbon and its Compounds.r: Ethanol (C₂H₅OH) is oxidised by an oxidising agent such as acidified potassium dichromate to ethanoic (acetic) acid, CH₃COOH. The functional group is carboxyl, –COOH. With ethanol, in the presence of concentrated H₂SO₄, it forms an ester and water: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH → CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O.

Hydrocarbon and its Compounds.q: Which gas is produced when calcium carbide reacts with water?
Vinegar contains
Which compound will decolourise bromine water?

What is a homologous series? Give two characteristics.
Hydrocarbon and its Compounds.r: A family of organic compounds with the same functional group and general formula, in which successive members differ by CH₂. Characteristics: gradual change in physical properties; similar chemical properties.

Hydrocarbon and its Compounds.q: Write the molecular formula and structural formula of ethyne.
How would you distinguish ethane from ethene in the laboratory?
Hydrocarbon and its Compounds.r: Shake each with bromine water: ethene decolourises it; ethane does not.

Write the preparation, two properties and two uses of ethanol.
