Hydrocarbon and its Compounds.q: Compare alkanes, alkenes and alkynes in terms of general formula, bond type, example and type of reaction.
Describe the laboratory preparation of ethyne and write two of its reactions.
Hydrocarbon and its Compounds.r: CaC₂ + 2H₂O → C₂H₂ + Ca(OH)₂, gas collected over water. Reactions: 2C₂H₂ + 5O₂ → 4CO₂ + 2H₂O; C₂H₂ + 2H₂ → C₂H₆ (Ni).

Hydrocarbon and its Compounds.q: Write the formulae of the alkane, alkene and alkyne with 6 carbon atoms and calculate the molecular mass of the alkane (C = 12, H = 1).
Hydrocarbon and its Compounds.r: Alkane C₆H₁₄, alkene C₆H₁₂, alkyne C₆H₁₀. Mass of C₆H₁₄ = 72 + 14 = 86.

Hydrocarbon and its Compounds.q: What is a hydrocarbon? Describe alkanes, alkenes and alkynes with their general formulae, examples, properties and uses.
Describe ethanol: its preparation by fermentation, properties and uses. Write short notes on biogas as a hydrocarbon fuel.

Chemicals used in Daily Life.q: Why is gypsum added to cement?
Chemicals used in Daily Life.r: Gypsum slows down the setting of cement so that the mortar can be worked before it hardens.

Chemicals used in Daily Life.q: Write any two differences between soap and detergent.
Chemicals used in Daily Life.r: Soap is the sodium salt of a fatty acid; detergent is a synthetic salt of sulphonic acid. Soap forms scum in hard water; detergent does not, and works in hard and soft water.

Chemicals used in Daily Life.q: Describe the manufacture of soap (saponification).
Chemicals used in Daily Life.r: Oil or fat is heated with sodium hydroxide solution. The ester bonds break (saponification) to give glycerol and sodium salts of fatty acids (soap): fat + 3NaOH → glycerol + 3 soap. Common salt is added to make the soap separate as a layer (salting out); it is then moulded, perfumed and dried.

Chemicals used in Daily Life.q: Name the three main nutrients in NPK fertilisers and state one function of each. Mention two harmful effects of overuse.
Chemicals used in Daily Life.r: Nitrogen (N) promotes leaf and stem growth; phosphorus (P) helps roots and flowering; potassium (K) improves disease resistance and fruit quality. Overuse pollutes water (eutrophication), harms soil organisms and can burn crops.

Chemicals used in Daily Life.q: The process of making soap from fat and alkali is called
Gypsum is added to cement to
Which of the following is a thermosetting plastic?
The raw material for glass is
Detergents are better than soap in
Chemicals used in Daily Life.w: detergents do not form scum with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺.

Chemicals used in Daily Life.q: What is a fertiliser? Name the three primary nutrients.
Chemicals used in Daily Life.r: A substance added to soil to supply nutrients to plants. Nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium.

Chemicals used in Daily Life.q: Why is annealing done in glass making?
Chemicals used in Daily Life.r: The glass is cooled slowly to remove internal stress, so that it does not break easily.

Chemicals used in Daily Life.q: Differentiate between thermoplastic and thermosetting plastic.
Chemicals used in Daily Life.r: A thermoplastic softens on heating and can be re-moulded (polythene); a thermosetting plastic sets permanently after heating once (Bakelite).

Chemicals used in Daily Life.q: Why does soap not lather well in hard water?
Chemicals used in Daily Life.r: Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions react with soap to form insoluble scum, so soap is wasted before it can lather.

Chemicals used in Daily Life.q: Write two problems caused by the excess use of plastics.
Chemicals used in Daily Life.r: Plastics are non-biodegradable and pollute soil; they block drains and harm animals; burning releases toxic gases.

Chemicals used in Daily Life.q: Describe the manufacture of soap. Explain the cleaning action of soap.
Chemicals used in Daily Life.r: Saponification: boil oil or fat with NaOH; add salt to separate soap (salting out); wash, add perfume and mould. Cleaning: tails dissolve in grease, heads stay in water, grease is broken into micelles and rinsed away.

Chemicals used in Daily Life.q: Describe how Portland cement is made, stating the raw materials and the role of gypsum.
Chemicals used in Daily Life.r: Limestone and clay are ground, mixed and heated at 1400 to 1500 °C in a rotary kiln to form clinker; clinker is ground with 2 to 3 % gypsum. Gypsum slows the setting.

Chemicals used in Daily Life.q: A farmer needs 92 kg of nitrogen. How much
p: ammonium nitrate (35 % N) would be needed?
Chemicals used in Daily Life.r: (a) Urea = 92 / 0.46 = 200 kg. (b) Ammonium nitrate = 92 / 0.35 = 262.9 kg (about 263 kg).

Chemicals used in Daily Life.q: What is a polymer? Explain the types of plastics with two examples each and suggest four ways to manage plastic waste.
Chemicals used in Daily Life.r: A polymer is a large molecule formed from many monomers. Thermoplastics (polythene, PVC) soften on heating; thermosetting plastics (Bakelite, melamine) do not. Management: reduce, reuse, recycle, refuse; ban thin bags; use jute or paper bags.

Unit 2: Development and the Foundations.w: The percentage increase in output is $\frac{18-15}{15} \times 100 = 20\%$.

Mother Teresa served the poor, the sick and the dying in Kolkata and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979. Martin Luther King Jr. led the civil rights movement for equality of black Americans through peaceful protest. Lesson. All four show that equality, peace and service are stronger than hatred. Unit 5: Civic Consciousness.r: Composition. The Federal Parliament is the President together with two houses. The House of Representatives has 275 members: 165 elected by first-past-the-post and 110 by proportional representation, for five years. The National Assembly has 59 members for six years, and one-third retire every two years. How a bill becomes law. (i) A bill is introduced in one house. (ii) It is discussed in the house and in a committee. (iii) It is passed by a majority. (iv) The other house considers and passes it. (v) It goes to the President for assent. (vi) After assent it becomes an Act. Conclusion. Both houses and the President take part, so no law is made hastily.

Unit 7: Our Past.r: Introduction. The revolution of 2007 BS ended 104 years of Rana rule. Causes. (i) The Ranas ruled by family and kept people poor and uneducated. (ii) Political parties such as the Nepali Congress worked for democracy. (iii) King Tribhuvan supported the movement and left for India. (iv) Indian independence in 1947 encouraged change. Results. (i) Rana rule ended. (ii) The Delhi Agreement (Falgun 2007) set up a Rana–Congress interim cabinet and promised a Constituent Assembly. (iii) Democracy came to Nepal, remembered on Democracy Day (7 Falgun). Conclusion. The revolution opened the way to citizens' rights, although political instability followed in the first decade.

Unit 9: Our International Relations and.r: Introduction. The UN was founded on 24 October 1945, has 193 members and its headquarters in New York. Nepal joined in 1955. Role. (i) The Security Council acts for peace and security; its five permanent members hold the veto. (ii) UN peacekeeping missions keep ceasefires, and Nepal contributes troops. Unit 10: Population and Its Management.r: Introduction. Population and environment affect each other. Effects of population on environment. (i) More people need more land and firewood, causing deforestation. (ii) Urban growth causes air, water and noise pollution and waste. (iii) Greater use of fossil fuel adds to climate change. Family planning, community forestry, the 3Rs (reduce, reuse, recycle) and clean energy. Conclusion. Managing population size and protecting nature must go together.

A double-stranded DNA molecule contains 1200 base pairs, of which 30 % of the bases are guanine. Calculate the number of adenine, thymine, guanine and cytosine bases in it, and the length of the molecule in nanometres.
Biomolecules and Cell Biology.r: Total bases $= 2 \times 1200 = 2400$. Guanine is 30 % of all bases, so $G = 0.30 \times 2400 = 720$, and by Chargaff $C = 720$. The remaining bases are $2400 - 1440 = 960$, shared equally, so $A = T = 480$. Length $=$ number of base pairs $\times\ 0.34\ \text{nm} = 1200 \times 0.34 = 408\ \text{nm}$.

Biomolecules and Cell Biology.q: What is an enzyme? Describe the effect of temperature and of pH on enzyme activity.
Biomolecules and Cell Biology.r: Definition: a protein catalyst that lowers activation energy and is unchanged at the end. Temperature: activity roughly doubles for each 10 °C rise up to the optimum (about 37 °C in mammals) as molecular collisions increase; above it the tertiary structure denatures and activity falls steeply and irreversibly. pH: each enzyme has a narrow optimum (pepsin 2, salivary amylase 6.8, trypsin 8) because extreme pH alters the charges that hold the active site in shape.

Floral Diversity.w: glycogen, exactly as in animals; answering "starch" here is the standard slip.

Floral Diversity.q: The cell wall of a typical fungus is made of
Floral Diversity.w: chitin, a nitrogen-containing polysaccharide, again shared with animals (insect cuticle).

Floral Diversity.q: A fungal mycelium in which the hyphae have no cross walls is described as
Floral Diversity.w: coenocytic (aseptate), as in Mucor and Rhizopus; a multinucleate tube with no cross walls.

Floral Diversity.q: The asexual spores produced inside a sporangium of Mucor are
Floral Diversity.w: sporangiospores are formed inside a sac; conidia are formed externally in chains (Penicillium).

Floral Diversity.q: Penicillin, the first antibiotic, was obtained from
Yeast (Saccharomyces) reproduces asexually mainly by
Floral Diversity.w: budding; a small outgrowth pinches off with a nucleus.

Floral Diversity.q: A lichen is a symbiotic association between
o: a fungus and an alga or cyanobacterium
Floral Diversity.w: mycobiont plus phycobiont, an obligate mutualism.

Floral Diversity.q: In a lichen the fungal partner is called the
Floral Diversity.w: mycobiont; the alga is the phycobiont and makes the food.

Floral Diversity.q: What is binomial nomenclature? Write any four rules of it.
Write any four economic importances of fungi.
What is a lichen? Describe the nature of the association between its partners.
Why are bryophytes called the amphibians of the plant kingdom?
Differentiate between gymnosperms and angiosperms under any four heads.
Write the floral characters and any two economic importances of the family Brassicaceae.
Write the floral formula of Fabaceae and explain, whorl by whorl, how you would recognise a member of the family in the field.
Give an account of the taxonomic hierarchy with a suitable example.
Distinguish between artificial, natural and phylogenetic systems of classification.
Write any four differences between monocotyledonous and dicotyledonous plants.
Describe the family Solanaceae under the heads of habit, vegetative characters, floral characters and economic importance. Give its floral formula.
What is alternation of generations? Describe the life cycle of a moss (Funaria) to illustrate it.
Describe the general characters of algae and give an account of their economic importance.
Describe the general characters of pteridophytes and explain why they are considered the first true vascular land plants.
Give any four general characters of Bryophyta and explain why bryophytes are called the amphibians of the plant kingdom.
Floral Diversity.r: Any four of: the plant body is a haploid gametophyte, thalloid or leafy, with no true roots (only rhizoids) and no vascular tissue; sex organs are multicellular and jacketed (antheridium and archegonium); fertilisation needs external water; the zygote forms an embryo and then a sporophyte of foot, seta and capsule which stays attached to and dependent on the gametophyte; spores formed by meiosis germinate into a protonema. They are called amphibians because, like frogs, they live on land but must return to water to reproduce — the biflagellate antherozoids can only reach the egg by swimming through a film of water, so bryophytes are confined to moist, shaded habitats.

Floral Diversity.q: What is a lichen? Name its two components, state the contribution of each, and give two uses of lichens.
Floral Diversity.r: A lichen is a stable symbiotic association of a fungus and a photosynthetic partner forming a thallus unlike either alone. The mycobiont (usually an Ascomycete, 90–95 % of the thallus) forms the body, absorbs and retains water and minerals, and protects the alga from desiccation and intense light; the phycobiont (a green alga such as Trebouxia, or a cyanobacterium such as Nostoc) photosynthesises and, if a cyanobacterium, also fixes nitrogen. Uses (any two): source of litmus from Roccella tinctoria; bio-indicators of SO₂ air pollution; food and fodder (Cetraria, Cladonia rangiferina); perfumery (Evernia); the antibiotic usnic acid; pioneers of xerophytic succession on bare rock.

Floral Diversity.q: Describe the family Solanaceae under the headings habit, leaf, inflorescence, flower (calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium), fruit and floral formula, and give four points of economic importance with named examples.
Floral Diversity.r: Habit: mostly annual or perennial herbs and shrubs, rarely small trees, with a tap root; potato has an underground stem tuber and Solanum xanthocarpum is prickly. Leaf: alternate, simple, exstipulate, entire or lobed, with bicollateral vascular bundles. Inflorescence: usually a cymose inflorescence (helicoid or scorpioid cyme), solitary and axillary in Datura. Flower: ebracteate, pedicellate, complete, bisexual, actinomorphic, hypogynous, pentamerous. Calyx: 5 sepals, gamosepalous, valvate, persistent and enlarging in fruit. Corolla: 5 petals, gamopetalous, rotate or infundibuliform, valvate or twisted.

Floral Diversity.q: Explain the three domains of life, binomial nomenclature and Whittaker's five-kingdom classification, with the taxonomic hierarchy.
Describe the general characters, classification and economic importance of fungi, and explain lichens.
Compare algae, bryophytes, pteridophytes and gymnosperms, and explain alternation of generations.
Distinguish monocots from dicots, and describe the characters of the families Brassicaceae, Fabaceae, Solanaceae and Liliaceae.

Introductory Microbiology.q: Bacteria were first observed and described by
Introductory Microbiology.w: Leeuwenhoek, 1676, with his own single-lens microscope; Pasteur and Koch came two centuries later.

Introductory Microbiology.q: A spherical bacterium is called a
Eight cocci arranged in a cube of two layers form a
Introductory Microbiology.w: sarcina is the 8-celled cube; a tetrad is a flat group of four.

Introductory Microbiology.q: A comma-shaped bacterium such as Vibrio cholerae belongs to the morphological type
Introductory Microbiology.w: vibrio, a curved comma; a spirochaete is a long flexible spiral.

Introductory Microbiology.q: A small extra-chromosomal circular DNA of a bacterium is a
Introductory Microbiology.w: plasmids carry genes for antibiotic resistance and are the vectors of genetic engineering.

Introductory Microbiology.q: Transfer of DNA from one bacterium to another through a bacteriophage is
Introductory Microbiology.w: transduction is phage-mediated; transformation is uptake of naked DNA, conjugation is transfer through a pilus.

Introductory Microbiology.q: The commonest mode of asexual reproduction in bacteria is
Introductory Microbiology.w: binary fission, which under ideal conditions can occur every twenty minutes.

Introductory Microbiology.q: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in the root nodules of legumes belong to the genus
Introductory Microbiology.w: Rhizobium; Nitrosomonas is a free-living nitrifier and belongs to a different step of the cycle.

Introductory Microbiology.q: The term virus, meaning poison, and the discovery of the tobacco mosaic agent are credited to
Introductory Microbiology.w: Ivanowsky (1892) showed the agent passed a bacterial filter, Beijerinck (1898) named it contagium vivum fluidum.

Introductory Microbiology.q: The protein coat of a virus is called the
Introductory Microbiology.w: the capsid is built of repeating protein subunits called capsomeres.

Introductory Microbiology.q: Viruses are regarded as being on the borderline of living and non-living because they
o: can be crystallised yet multiply inside a host cell
Introductory Microbiology.w: outside a host a virus is an inert chemical that can be crystallised; inside one it replicates and mutates.

Introductory Microbiology.q: A virus that infects a bacterium is a
Introductory Microbiology.w: bacteriophage, literally "bacteria eater"; T₄ phage of E. coli is the standard example.

Introductory Microbiology.q: The genetic material of the tobacco mosaic virus is
Introductory Microbiology.w: TMV was the first virus discovered and contains single-stranded RNA.

Introductory Microbiology.q: Which of the following diseases is not caused by a virus?
Introductory Microbiology.w: tuberculosis is bacterial (Mycobacterium tuberculosis); the other three are viral.

Introductory Microbiology.q: Differentiate between Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria (any four points, with one example of each).

A culture of Escherichia coli containing $2 \times 10^{4}$ cells is grown for 2 hours at 37 °C, where its generation time is 20 minutes. Calculate the final number of cells, and state how many generations occurred.
Why is a virus said to lie on the borderline between living and non-living? Give two characters of each kind.
Introductory Microbiology.r: Living: they possess nucleic acid and so show heredity and mutation, and they multiply to give thousands of progeny inside a host. Non-living: they can be crystallised and stored like a chemical, and they have no cytoplasm, no respiration and no enzyme system of their own, so they cannot grow on a nutrient medium.

p: Draw a well-labelled diagram of the T4 bacteriophage.
Describe the lytic cycle of a bacteriophage, and explain how it differs from the lysogenic cycle.

Introductory Microbiology.q: Describe the economic importance of bacteria under the headings agriculture, industry, medicine and disease, giving the scientific name of the organism in each case.
Describe the structure, nutrition and reproduction of bacteria, and give eight points of their economic importance.
Describe the structure of a virus and the lytic and lysogenic cycles of a bacteriophage, and compare viruses with living and non-living things.
Describe the impacts of biotechnology in microbiology, giving eight applications.

Ecology.q: The term ecosystem was coined in 1935 by
Ecology.w: Tansley, 1935; Lindeman later quantified the energy flow.

Ecology.q: The study of a single species in relation to its environment is
Ecology.w: autecology is one species, synecology a whole community.

Ecology.q: Which of the following is an edaphic factor?
Ecology.w: edaphic means soil-related; the other three are climatic.

Ecology.q: Green plants of an ecosystem are called
Ecology.w: producers, also called transducers of solar energy, but the standard CDC term is producers.

Ecology.q: Decomposers are also known as
Ecology.w: saprotrophs feed on dead organic matter by external digestion.

Ecology.q: A food chain that begins with dead organic matter is a
Ecology.w: the detritus food chain; in a forest it actually carries more energy than the grazing chain.

Ecology.q: In the chain grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle, the frog occupies the trophic level
Ecology.w: grass 1st, grasshopper 2nd, frog 3rd. Counting the producer as zero is the usual error.

Ecology.q: Food chains rarely exceed four or five links because
o: so much energy is lost as heat at every transfer
Ecology.w: only about a tenth passes on, so the fifth level has too little energy to support a viable population.

Ecology.q: The ten per cent law of energy transfer was given by
If the producers of an ecosystem store 20,000 kJ, the energy available to the tertiary consumers under the ten per cent law is
Ecology.w: 20,000 → 2,000 (herbivore) → 200 (secondary) → 20 kJ (tertiary). Stopping one step early gives (b), the commonest wrong answer.

Ecology.q: Gross primary productivity minus respiration of the producers equals
Ecology.w: NPP = GPP - R; only NPP is available to the next level.

Ecology.q: The pyramid of biomass in a pond ecosystem is inverted because
o: the phytoplankton have a small standing crop but a very high turnover rate
Ecology.w: the tiny algae are eaten as fast as they grow, so at any instant their standing biomass is less than that of the fish they support.

Ecology.q: Energy flow in an ecosystem is
Ecology.w: unidirectional, by the second law of thermodynamics; only nutrients are cycled.

Ecology.q: Conversion of atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia is
Ecology.w: nitrogen fixation, biological (Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Anabaena) or physical (lightning).

Ecology.q: Define an ecosystem and describe its biotic components with one example of each.
Ecology.r: Definition as in the text. Producers — autotrophs that fix solar energy, e.g. grass, Hydrilla. Consumers — heterotrophs: primary (herbivore, e.g. chital deer), secondary (primary carnivore, e.g. frog), tertiary (top carnivore, e.g. Royal Bengal tiger). Decomposers — saprotrophic bacteria and fungi that mineralise dead matter and return nutrients to the soil.

Ecology.q: What is an ecological pyramid? Explain, with a reason, why the pyramid of biomass in a pond ecosystem is inverted.

The producers of a pond fix $8000\ \text{kJ m}^{-2}\ \text{yr}^{-1}$, of which they respire $5600\ \text{kJ m}^{-2}\ \text{yr}^{-1}$. Calculate the net primary productivity, and the energy that would reach a fish at the third trophic level under the ten per cent law.
Ecology.r: $\text{NPP} = \text{GPP} - R = 8000 - 5600 = 2400\ \text{kJ m}^{-2}\ \text{yr}^{-1}$. The energy passed on is taken from the NPP, so the second trophic level receives $0.10 \times 2400 = 240\ \text{kJ m}^{-2}\ \text{yr}^{-1}$ and the third trophic level receives $0.10 \times 240 = 24\ \text{kJ m}^{-2}\ \text{yr}^{-1}$.

Ecology.q: List any four morphological and anatomical adaptations of xerophytes, naming a plant that shows each.
Ecology.r: (i) Long, deeply penetrating branched roots — Acacia catechu. (ii) Leaves reduced to spines with a photosynthetic phylloclade — Opuntia. (iii) Very thick cuticle and multilayered epidermis with sclerenchymatous hypodermis — Nerium oleander. (iv) Stomata few and sunken in hairy pits — Nerium, Casuarina. A fifth, physiological, point: CAM photosynthesis with stomata open only at night — Aloe vera.

p: Draw a labelled diagram of the nitrogen cycle.
Explain nitrogen fixation, nitrification and denitrification, naming the bacteria responsible for each, and state what happens to soil fertility if denitrifying bacteria become very active.

Ecology.q: Describe the components of an ecosystem, the flow of energy through it, and ecological pyramids.
Describe the nitrogen cycle and the carbon cycle with diagrams in words, and give the human effects on them.
What is global warming? Describe the causes, effects and control measures, with eight points on the effects, and its impact on Nepal.

Vegetation.q: The vegetation of Nepal is chiefly determined by
o: altitude and the rainfall that goes with it
Vegetation.w: Nepal rises from about 60 m to 8848 m in under 200 km, so altitude compresses all the vegetation belts of Asia into one country.

Vegetation.q: Sal (Shorea robusta) forest is the characteristic vegetation of
o: the Terai and Bhabar up to about 1000 m
Vegetation.w: sal is the dominant hardwood of the Terai, Bhabar and lower Siwalik.

Vegetation.q: The tropical vegetation zone of Nepal extends up to an altitude of about
Vegetation.w: tropical up to about 1000 m, sub-tropical 1000–2000 m, temperate 2000–3000 m, sub-alpine 3000–4100 m, alpine above that.

Vegetation.q: Rhododendron arboreum, the national flower of Nepal, is typical of the
Vegetation.w: Laligurans forms whole forests between about 2000 and 3500 m.

Vegetation.q: The zone above the tree line, dominated by low shrubs, herbs and cushion plants, is the
Vegetation.w: the alpine zone lies above the tree line, roughly above 4100 m.

Vegetation.q: Abies, Betula and Juniperus are characteristic genera of the
Vegetation.w: fir, birch and juniper are the sub-alpine indicators.

Vegetation.q: Conservation of a species inside its own natural habitat is called
Vegetation.w: in-situ: national parks, wildlife reserves, conservation areas, biosphere reserves.

Vegetation.q: Which of the following is an example of ex-situ conservation?
Vegetation.w: a zoo keeps animals outside their habitat; the other three are protected areas, so in-situ.

Vegetation.q: A seed bank or gene bank is a method of
Vegetation.w: the material is stored away from the habitat, which is the definition of ex-situ.

Vegetation.q: The largest national park of Nepal by area is
Vegetation.w: Shey Phoksundo, 3555 km², in Dolpa and Mugu; Chitwan is the oldest (1973) but smaller.

Vegetation.q: Shifting cultivation, known in Nepal as khoriya, damages vegetation mainly by
o: repeated burning and clearing that prevents forest regeneration
Vegetation.w: the fallow period is now too short for the soil and the forest to recover.

Vegetation.q: The most important direct cause of deforestation in the hills of Nepal is
o: clearing for agriculture, fuelwood and fodder
Vegetation.w: a rural household needs land, firewood and fodder, and takes all three from the forest.

Vegetation.q: Community forestry in Nepal is significant because it
o: hands over management of a patch of national forest to a local user group
bans all use of forest products
replaces forests with plantations of a single exotic species
Vegetation.w: a Community Forest User Group manages and harvests the forest and keeps the income; Nepal's programme is studied worldwide.

Vegetation.q: Shorea robusta is the dominant tree of the
Vegetation.w: Sal is the dominant tree of the Terai, Bhabar and Dun valleys, below 1000 m.

Vegetation.q: Name the six altitudinal vegetation zones of Nepal with their altitude ranges, and give one indicator species of each.
Vegetation.r: Tropical, below 1000 m — Shorea robusta. Subtropical, 1000–2000 m — Schima wallichii or Pinus roxburghii. Temperate, 2000–3000 m — Quercus semecarpifolia or Rhododendron arboreum. Subalpine, 3000–4000 m — Abies spectabilis or Betula utilis. Alpine, 4000–5000 m — Rhododendron anthopogon with Kobresia meadow. Nival, above 5000 m — mosses and lichens only.

Vegetation.q: Differentiate between in-situ and ex-situ conservation, giving two named Nepali examples of each.
Vegetation.r: In-situ = conserved inside the natural habitat, so the whole ecosystem is saved and the species keeps evolving; cheap per species but needs large areas. Examples: Chitwan National Park, Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve. Ex-situ = conserved outside the natural habitat, under human care; useful for species too rare to survive in the wild, but expensive and only a few individuals can be held. Examples: National Botanical Garden, Godawari; National Gene Bank, Khumaltar (or the Central Zoo, Jawalakhel).

Vegetation.q: The mean annual temperature at Pokhara (altitude 820 m) is 20 °C. Using a lapse rate of 6 °C per 1000 m, estimate the temperature at Ghorepani (2,870 m), and name the vegetation zone and the indicator tree species you would expect to find there.
Vegetation.r: Height gained $= 2870 - 820 = 2050\ \text{m}$. Temperature fall $= 6 \times 2050/1000 = 12.3\ ^\circ\text{C}$, so $T = 20 - 12.3 = 7.7\ ^\circ\text{C}$. At 2,870 m Ghorepani lies in the temperate zone, where the expected species are Quercus semecarpifolia (khasru), Rhododendron arboreum (lali gurans) and Pinus wallichiana (gobre salla).

Vegetation.q: List any four human activities that degrade the vegetation of Nepal, and state one control measure for each.
Vegetation.r: (i) Deforestation and encroachment — hand the forest to community forest user groups and register boundaries. (ii) Overgrazing — fix a stocking limit and rotate the kharka, and promote stall feeding on fodder trees. (iii) Forest fire — build fire lines, train community fire-fighting groups and ban pre-monsoon burning. (iv) Over-collection of NTFPs such as yarsagumba — issue harvesting permits with a closed season, and cultivate the species instead of digging it from the wild. (A fifth: invasive species such as Mikania micrantha — manual uprooting before flowering and replanting with native species.)

p: Describe the protected area system of Nepal, naming the categories, their numbers and one example of each.
Describe any two ex-situ conservation facilities of Nepal, stating where each is and what it conserves.

Vegetation.q: Describe the factors that decide vegetation and explain the vegetation zones of Nepal with their altitude and typical plants.
Explain the damage done to vegetation by human activities, and the methods of in-situ and ex-situ conservation.

Introduction to Biology.q: The term biology was introduced independently in 1802 by
Introduction to Biology.w: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck and Gottfried Treviranus, both in 1802, from Greek bios (life) and logos (study).

Introduction to Biology.q: Aristotle is called the
Introduction to Biology.w: Aristotle is the father of zoology and of biology as a whole; his pupil Theophrastus is the father of botany.

Introduction to Biology.q: The branch of biology that deals with the functions of the parts of an organism is
Introduction to Biology.w: physiology is function; anatomy is internal structure revealed by dissection.

Introduction to Biology.q: The study of the form and external structure of organisms is
Introduction to Biology.w: morphology; if you cut it open to see inside, it becomes anatomy.

Introduction to Biology.q: The study of fossils is
Introduction to Biology.w: palaeontology supplies the direct evidence of evolution.

Introduction to Biology.q: The study of birds is
Introduction to Biology.w: ornithology; ichthyology is fish, herpetology reptiles and amphibians.

Introduction to Biology.q: The study of insects is
Introduction to Biology.w: entomology. Note etymology, option (b), is the study of the origin of words — a deliberate trap.

Introduction to Biology.q: The study of animal behaviour is
Introduction to Biology.w: ethology; ethnology, option (c), is the study of human races and cultures.

Introduction to Biology.q: The application of statistics to biological data is
Which of the following is not a characteristic of all living things?
Introduction to Biology.w: plants are living but do not move from place to place; all living things show the other three.

Introduction to Biology.q: Biology is related to chemistry most directly through the branch
Introduction to Biology.w: biochemistry studies the molecules and reactions of life.

Introduction to Biology.q: Sensitivity, or irritability, is best defined as
o: the ability to detect and respond to a change in the surroundings
Introduction to Biology.w: detecting a stimulus and responding to it; a plant bending towards light counts.

Introduction to Biology.q: The term "biology" is derived from the Greek words
Introduction to Biology.w: bios = life, logos = study or discourse.

Introduction to Biology.q: Aristotle is regarded as the
Introduction to Biology.w: Aristotle is the Father of Zoology (and of Biology as a whole); Theophrastus is the Father of Botany.

Introduction to Biology.q: Define biology, and name any four branches of biology based on the aspect of life studied, with one line on each.
Introduction to Biology.r: Biology is the science that deals with living organisms — their structure, function, origin, growth, reproduction, classification, behaviour, evolution and relation with the environment. Four aspect-based branches: morphology, the external form and structure of organisms; physiology, the functions and processes of the living body; genetics, heredity and variation; ecology, the relation between organisms and their environment. (Anatomy, cytology, embryology, taxonomy or biochemistry are equally acceptable.)

Introduction to Biology.q: Explain the relation of biology with physics and chemistry, with two examples of each.
Introduction to Biology.r: Physics supplies the instruments — the compound and electron microscopes, the centrifuge, the X-ray crystallography that revealed the structure of DNA — and explains the electrical nerve impulse, the fluid dynamics of blood flow and the optics of the eye; medical imaging is applied physics. The overlap is biophysics. Chemistry: living matter is carbohydrate, lipid, protein and nucleic acid; respiration is a series of oxidation–reduction reactions, enzymes are catalysts, and blood pH is held by buffers. The overlap is biochemistry.

Introduction to Biology.q: A compound microscope has a 15× eyepiece and a 40× objective.
p: A structure appears 24 mm long in the field of view at this magnification; find its real length in micrometres.
State one reason why this microscope cannot show a virus.
Introduction to Biology.r: (a) $M = 15 \times 40 = 600\times$. (b) Real length $= 24\ \text{mm} / 600 = 0.04\ \text{mm} = 40\ \mu\text{m}$. (c) A light microscope cannot resolve detail finer than about 0.2 μm because of the wavelength of light, and a virus is only about 0.1 μm across — so it lies below the resolution limit, no matter how much the image is magnified.

Introduction to Biology.q: State any four applied fields of biology and name, for each, one course or institution in Nepal where it is studied.
Introduction to Biology.r: Any four: medicine — MBBS or B.Sc. Nursing, entered through the MECEE-BL examination; agriculture — B.Sc. Ag at Agriculture and Forestry University, Rampur; forestry — B.Sc. Forestry at the Institute of Forestry, Pokhara; veterinary science — B.V.Sc. & A.H. at AFU, Rampur; biotechnology / microbiology — B.Sc. Microbiology at TU or B.Tech. Biotechnology at Kathmandu University; fisheries — B.Sc. Aquaculture, AFU; conservation — Environmental Science, with employers such as DNPWC, NTNC and WWF Nepal.

Introduction to Biology.q: Define biology and classify its branches, with a table showing at least six branches based on the group of organisms studied and six based on the aspect of life studied, giving one line of definition for each.

p: Describe the relation of biology with physics, chemistry, mathematics and geology, naming the interdisciplinary field created by each overlap.
Explain the scope and importance of biology in the context of Nepal.

Introduction to Biology.q: What is life? Explain the characteristics of living organisms and distinguish between living and non-living things.
Define biology. Describe its main branches, its relation to other sciences, and the role of the microscope, with a numerical.

Evolutionary Biology.q: The theory that life originated from non-living matter under the conditions of the early Earth is
Evolutionary Biology.w: chemical or abiogenic evolution, the modern scientific account.

Evolutionary Biology.q: The theory of chemical origin of life was proposed by
Evolutionary Biology.w: A. I. Oparin (1924) and J. B. S. Haldane (1929), independently; the "hot dilute soup".

Evolutionary Biology.q: The primitive atmosphere of the Earth is believed to have been
Evolutionary Biology.w: reducing; free oxygen would have oxidised the organic molecules as fast as they formed.

Evolutionary Biology.q: The theory that life came to Earth as spores from outer space is
Evolutionary Biology.w: the cosmozoic or panspermia theory of Richter and Arrhenius. It only moves the problem elsewhere.

Evolutionary Biology.q: Spontaneous generation was finally disproved by the swan-necked flask experiment of
Evolutionary Biology.w: Pasteur, 1864; the broth stayed sterile because dust could not climb the bend.

Evolutionary Biology.q: Organs of different animals that have the same basic structure and origin but different functions are
Evolutionary Biology.w: homologous: same origin, different function, showing divergent evolution from a common ancestor.

Evolutionary Biology.q: The wing of a bird and the wing of an insect are
Evolutionary Biology.w: analogous: same function (flight), completely different structure and origin.

Evolutionary Biology.q: Homologous organs are evidence of
Evolutionary Biology.w: divergent evolution, or adaptive radiation; analogous organs show convergent evolution. Swapping these two is the standard mistake.

Evolutionary Biology.q: The forelimbs of a whale, a bat, a horse and a human are a classic example of
Evolutionary Biology.w: the same bones — humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, phalanges — put to swimming, flying, running and grasping.

Evolutionary Biology.q: The vermiform appendix in humans is an example of
Evolutionary Biology.w: vestigial: reduced and functionless in humans, but a working cellulose-digesting caecum in a rabbit.

Evolutionary Biology.q: Archaeopteryx is important because it is a connecting link between
Evolutionary Biology.w: it had feathers and a wishbone like a bird, and teeth, a long bony tail and clawed fingers like a reptile.

Evolutionary Biology.q: Peripatus is regarded as a connecting link between
Evolutionary Biology.w: it has the segmented body and nephridia of an annelid with the tracheae and claws of an arthropod.

Evolutionary Biology.q: A living fossil among the following is
Evolutionary Biology.w: Latimeria, the coelacanth, caught alive in 1938; the others are extinct fossils.

Evolutionary Biology.q: "Ontogeny repeats phylogeny" — the biogenetic law — was stated by
Evolutionary Biology.w: Haeckel's recapitulation theory: the embryo passes through the ancestral stages.

Evolutionary Biology.q: Differentiate between homologous and analogous organs, giving one animal and one plant example of each.
Evolutionary Biology.r: Homologous — same basic structure and embryonic origin, different function, by divergent evolution from a common ancestor: forelimbs of man, whale, bat and horse; thorn of Bougainvillea and tendril of Cucurbita. Analogous — different structure and origin, same function, by convergent evolution: wing of a bird and of an insect; sweet potato (root tuber) and potato (stem tuber). Homology proves relationship, analogy only adaptation.

Evolutionary Biology.q: Describe the Miller–Urey experiment and state precisely what it proved.
Evolutionary Biology.r: Sealed glass system: boiling water feeds vapour into a chamber charged with CH₄, NH₃ and H₂, tungsten electrodes spark for a week at about 800 °C, a condenser returns the products to a U-trap. Result: amino acids (glycine, alanine, aspartic acid) with urea, sugars and fatty acids. It proved that the monomers of life form spontaneously from inorganic gases — it did not produce a cell, a protein or a nucleic acid.

Evolutionary Biology.q: In a population of 2000 people, 320 cannot roll the tongue, a recessive character. Assuming Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, calculate both allele frequencies and the expected number of heterozygotes.
What is industrial melanism, and how does it demonstrate natural selection?
Evolutionary Biology.r: Industrial melanism is the rise in frequency of a dark form in a polluted area. In Biston betularia the melanic carbonaria was almost unknown before 1848; soot killed the lichens and by 1895 about 98 % of Manchester moths were black. Kettlewell's 1955 mark–recapture recovered 27.5 % of carbonaria against 13.0 % of typica in sooty Birmingham and the reverse in unpolluted Dorset: birds ate whichever form was conspicuous. After the Clean Air Act of 1956 the melanic form fell back. It is directional natural selection, because a pre-existing heritable variation changed in frequency through differential survival in a direction set by the environment.

Evolutionary Biology.q: State the Hardy–Weinberg principle and the conditions under which a population stays in genetic equilibrium.
Evolutionary Biology.r: In a large, randomly mating population the allele and genotype frequencies at a locus stay constant across generations, with $p + q = 1$ and $p^{2} + 2pq + q^{2} = 1$. Conditions: very large population, random mating, no mutation, no migration, no natural selection. Breaking any one makes the population evolve.

p: State the postulates of Darwin's theory of natural selection.
Explain the long neck of the giraffe first on Lamarck's theory and then on Darwin's, and say why only one explanation is accepted.
Evolutionary Biology.r: (a) Prodigality of reproduction; struggle for existence (intraspecific, interspecific, environmental); variation; natural selection, or survival of the fittest; inheritance of the useful variations; origin of new species by their accumulation. (b) Lamarck: the short-necked ancestor stretched its neck for high foliage, the stretch was acquired and passed on, and the offspring stretched further — the environment created the long neck. Darwin: the population already varied in neck length; when low foliage grew scarce the longer-necked individuals fed better and left more offspring, so mean neck length rose each generation — the environment only selected among existing variations.

Evolutionary Biology.q: Give an account of human evolution from Dryopithecus to Homo sapiens sapiens with the approximate age and cranial capacity of each stage, and list four trends shown by the series.
Evolutionary Biology.r: Stages, ages and cranial capacities as in the table of section 7.4, in that order, with the branching of the figure. Trends: erect posture and complete bipedalism, which came before the large brain; progressive increase in cranial capacity; shortening of the jaws and face with reduced canines, loss of the brow ridges and appearance of a chin; forward shift of the foramen magnum with an S-shaped spine, broad pelvis and arched foot; and tool making, fire and speech, so that cultural evolution replaces biological.

Evolutionary Biology.q: Describe the origin of life according to the chemical evolution theory, with the Miller-Urey experiment.
Compare Lamarckism and Darwinism, and explain Darwin's theory of natural selection with an example.
Describe the evidences of organic evolution from comparative anatomy, embryology, palaeontology and biogeography.
Describe the stages of human evolution with the characters of each.

Faunal Diversity.q: Paramecium moves by means of
Faunal Diversity.w: some 10,000–14,000 cilia over the whole pellicle, beating in metachronal waves.

Faunal Diversity.q: The locomotory organelle of Amoeba is the
Faunal Diversity.w: temporary pseudopodia formed by sol–gel changes of the cytoplasm.

Faunal Diversity.q: The osmoregulatory organelle of a freshwater protozoan is the
Faunal Diversity.w: the contractile vacuole pumps out the water that constantly enters by osmosis.

Faunal Diversity.q: Paramecium is unusual among protozoans in having
o: two kinds of nuclei, a macronucleus and a micronucleus
Faunal Diversity.w: nuclear dimorphism: a large kidney-shaped macronucleus and one or more micronuclei.

Faunal Diversity.q: Asexual reproduction in Paramecium is by
Faunal Diversity.w: transverse binary fission in Paramecium; Euglena divides longitudinally. Examiners set this pair together deliberately.

Faunal Diversity.q: Conjugation in Paramecium is significant because it
o: brings about nuclear reorganisation and genetic recombination
Faunal Diversity.w: no increase in number takes place; conjugation only reshuffles genes and rejuvenates the animal, which is why Paramecium is said never to grow old.

Faunal Diversity.q: The infective stage of Plasmodium injected into a human by the mosquito is the
Faunal Diversity.w: sporozoites from the mosquito's salivary gland; merozoites are produced later inside the human.

Faunal Diversity.q: Malaria is transmitted by the bite of
Faunal Diversity.w: only the female takes a blood meal, which she needs for her eggs.

Faunal Diversity.q: In the life cycle of Plasmodium, the human being is the
Faunal Diversity.w: the mosquito is the primary host because the sexual cycle takes place in it; the human is secondary. This is inverted by most students.

Faunal Diversity.q: The most dangerous species of malarial parasite, causing malignant tertian malaria, is
Faunal Diversity.w: P. falciparum causes cerebral malaria and most malarial deaths.

Faunal Diversity.q: The bursting of red blood cells that releases merozoites and toxins causes
o: the periodic chill and fever of malaria
Faunal Diversity.w: the synchronous rupture of the infected erythrocytes releases haemozoin, which triggers the chill-and-fever paroxysm.

Faunal Diversity.q: Animals in which the cells are not organised into tissues show the
Faunal Diversity.w: the cellular level, as in Porifera, where the cells are loosely aggregated.

Faunal Diversity.q: Radial symmetry is characteristic of
Faunal Diversity.w: Cnidaria; Porifera are mostly asymmetrical, Annelida and Arthropoda bilateral.

Faunal Diversity.q: The body cavity lined on all sides by mesoderm is a
Faunal Diversity.w: a true coelom or eucoelom, lined entirely by mesodermal peritoneum.

Faunal Diversity.q: Distinguish between acoelomate, pseudocoelomate and coelomate animals, giving one example of each.
Faunal Diversity.r: Acoelomate — no body cavity, the space packed with mesodermal parenchyma (Planaria). Pseudocoelomate — a cavity present but a persistent blastocoel, lined by mesoderm on the body-wall side only (Ascaris). Coelomate — a true coelom within the mesoderm, lined by peritoneum on both body wall and gut (Pheretima).

Faunal Diversity.q: How does Paramecium keep its water content constant in pond water?
Faunal Diversity.r: Pond water is hypotonic, so water enters by osmosis. Two contractile vacuoles, each fed by radiating canals, collect it and discharge through a temporary pore, contracting alternately every 10–20 s. Their role is osmoregulation, not excretion: ammonia leaves by diffusion.

Faunal Diversity.q: State four diagnostic characters of phylum Arthropoda and name two examples.
Faunal Diversity.r: (i) Jointed appendages. (ii) A chitinous exoskeleton that is moulted (ecdysis). (iii) A haemocoel with an open circulation. (iv) Segmented body, typically head, thorax and abdomen, with compound eyes. Examples: Periplaneta americana, Palaemon.

Faunal Diversity.q: List the external apertures of Pheretima posthuma with their positions.
Faunal Diversity.r: Mouth on the peristomium (segment 1); anus on the last segment; female genital pore mid-ventral on segment 14; one pair of male genital pores on segment 18; four pairs of spermathecal pores in grooves 5/6, 6/7, 7/8 and 8/9; many nephridiopores; mid-dorsal pores from groove 12/13 backwards.

Faunal Diversity.q: Describe the three types of nephridia found in the earthworm.
Faunal Diversity.r: Septal nephridia, on both faces of the septa from segment 15 backwards, open into the intestine (enteronephric). Integumentary nephridia, on the inner body wall from segment 3 back and most numerous in the clitellum, open on the skin (exonephric). Pharyngeal nephridia form three paired tufts in segments 4–6, lack nephrostomes and open into the buccal cavity and pharynx.

Faunal Diversity.q: The earthworm is hermaphrodite, yet it cannot fertilise itself, and its fertilisation is external. Explain.
Faunal Diversity.r: Both sets of gonads occur in one worm, but it is protandrous — sperm mature before the ova of the same animal — so cross-fertilisation is obligatory. During copulation each worm charges the other's spermathecae. Later the clitellum secretes a cocoon; as the worm backs out, the cocoon collects ova at segment 14 and stored sperm at segments 6–9, so the gametes meet inside the cocoon, outside both parents.

Faunal Diversity.q: Explain the three modes of respiration in the frog and state when each is used.
Faunal Diversity.r: Cutaneous respiration through the moist vascular skin works in water and air, is the only method during hibernation and aestivation, and accounts for most of the year's gas exchange. Buccopharyngeal respiration across the buccal lining is used at rest on land. Pulmonary respiration serves the active animal, air being driven in by a buccal force pump.

Faunal Diversity.q: Describe the structure, locomotion, nutrition, osmoregulation and reproduction of Paramecium caudatum.
Explain the basis of animal classification and describe the nine major phyla with examples.
Describe the external features and the digestive, circulatory, excretory and reproductive systems of the earthworm Pheretima posthuma.
Describe the external features, digestive, respiratory, circulatory and reproductive systems of the frog Rana tigrina, and its economic importance.

Biota and Environment.q: The change in an organism that fits it better to its surroundings is
Biota and Environment.w: adaptation is heritable and evolutionary; acclimatisation is a reversible adjustment within one lifetime.

Biota and Environment.q: Streamlined body, fins and a swim bladder in a fish are adaptations for
Biota and Environment.w: the streamlined shape cuts drag, the fins steer and the swim bladder holds the fish at any depth without effort.

Biota and Environment.q: Pneumatic (hollow) bones and air sacs are flight adaptations of
Biota and Environment.w: birds; pneumatic bones cut weight and the air sacs give a one-way flow of air through the lungs.

Biota and Environment.q: The blubber of a whale or a seal is an adaptation for
Biota and Environment.w: a thick subcutaneous fat layer that insulates in cold water and makes the animal buoyant.

Biota and Environment.q: Cryptic colouration, in which an animal matches its background, is an example of
Biota and Environment.w: camouflage; mimicry is resembling another organism, not the background.

Biota and Environment.q: An innate, unlearned, stereotyped response of the whole animal to a stimulus is
Biota and Environment.w: instinct is inborn and needs no practice, unlike all forms of learning.

Biota and Environment.q: The waggle dance by which a honeybee tells the hive the direction and distance of food was decoded by
Biota and Environment.w: von Frisch, who shared the 1973 Nobel Prize with Lorenz and Tinbergen.

Biota and Environment.q: A duckling following the first moving object it sees after hatching shows
Biota and Environment.w: imprinting, described by Konrad Lorenz; it happens only in a short critical period and cannot be reversed.

Biota and Environment.q: Pavlov's dog salivating at the sound of a bell is an example of
Biota and Environment.w: classical conditioning: a neutral stimulus is paired with a natural one until it alone produces the response.

Biota and Environment.q: The seasonal, two-way movement of animals along a regular route is
Biota and Environment.w: migration is periodic and two-way; emigration is one-way and permanent.

Biota and Environment.q: A fish that lives in the sea and migrates into rivers to breed, such as the salmon, is called
Biota and Environment.w: anadromous, "running up" the river to breed.

Biota and Environment.q: The eel Anguilla, which lives in fresh water and breeds in the sea, is
Biota and Environment.w: catadromous, "running down" to the sea; the European eel breeds in the Sargasso Sea.

Biota and Environment.q: Air pollution caused by sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides leads chiefly to
The Bhopal gas tragedy of 1984 was caused by the leak of
Biota and Environment.w: methyl isocyanate from the Union Carbide plant, the worst industrial accident on record.

Biota and Environment.q: Describe any four adaptations of a bird for aerial life, stating the function of each.
Biota and Environment.r: Any four, each with its function: pneumatic bones — hollow and air-filled, reducing weight without losing strength; feathers — light, form the aerofoil and insulate; keeled sternum — gives a large surface for the origin of flight muscles; pectoralis major and minor — depress and raise the wing; nine air sacs — one-way airflow so oxygen is extracted during both inhalation and exhalation, and the body is cooled; no urinary bladder and uric acid excretion — saves weight.

Biota and Environment.q: Differentiate between innate and learned behaviour, with two examples of each.
Biota and Environment.r: Innate: inherited, present at birth, identical in all members, rigid, needs no practice (a spider spinning its first web; a herring gull chick pecking the red spot). Learned: acquired by experience, differs between individuals, flexible, can be forgotten (Pavlov's dog salivating at a bell; a monkey opening a latch by trial and error). Award one mark per contrasted pair and one for examples.

Biota and Environment.q: A herd of 500 blue sheep grows exponentially with an intrinsic rate of natural increase $r = 0.08\ \text{yr}^{-1}$. Calculate
p: the doubling time of the herd.

Biota and Environment.q: What is eutrophication? Explain, step by step, how it kills the fish of a lake.
Biota and Environment.r: Eutrophication is the over-enrichment of a water body with nutrients, chiefly nitrate and phosphate. Sequence: fertiliser, detergent and sewage run in → algae and water hyacinth bloom → the surface mat blocks light so submerged plants die → aerobic bacteria decompose the huge dead mass → BOD rises sharply and dissolved oxygen falls below about 4 mg L⁻¹ → fish and other aerobic animals suffocate and die.

Biota and Environment.q: Distinguish between bioaccumulation and biomagnification, and give one example of a pollutant that shows both.
Biota and Environment.r: Bioaccumulation is the gradual build-up of a persistent pollutant within a single organism, because intake exceeds excretion. Biomagnification is the stepwise rise in its concentration from one trophic level to the next along a food chain, because each consumer eats many individuals of the level below and retains almost all of the poison. DDT (also methyl mercury, PCBs) shows both: about 0.000003 ppm in water but 25 ppm in a fish-eating bird.

p: Define adaptation and distinguish it from acclimatisation.
With the help of a labelled diagram, describe the adaptations of a bony fish for aquatic life.
State Bergmann's rule and Allen's rule, giving one Himalayan example of each.
Biota and Environment.r: (a) Adaptation is an inherited, population-level feature produced by natural selection over generations; acclimatisation is a reversible physiological adjustment made by one individual within its own lifetime (extra red cells at high altitude). (b) Expect the labelled fish diagram plus streamlining and mucus, fins for propulsion and balance, counter-current gills, air bladder, and the opposite osmoregulatory strategies in fresh and sea water. (c) Bergmann — in colder regions bodies are larger, so the surface-to-volume ratio and heat loss are lower (the yak compared with lowland cattle).

p: Explain the logistic model of population growth and sketch the curve, marking the carrying capacity.

A fish population in Phewa Tal has a carrying capacity $K = 8000$ and an intrinsic rate of increase $r = 0.30\ \text{yr}^{-1}$. Find $dN/dt$ when $N = 2000$ and when $N = 4000$, and state the population size at which the growth rate is greatest.
Biota and Environment.r: (a) The logistic model adds the braking factor $(K-N)/K$ to exponential growth: $dN/dt = rN(K-N)/K$. When $N$ is small the factor is nearly 1 and growth is almost exponential; as $N \to K$ the factor $\to 0$ and growth stops. The curve is sigmoid with lag, log, deceleration and stationary phases, levelling off at $N=K$.

Biota and Environment.q: Describe air pollution under the headings: major pollutants and their sources; three global effects; the particular situation of the Kathmandu Valley; and control measures.
Describe the adaptations of animals to aquatic, desert and cold (high-altitude) environments with examples from Nepal.
What is animal behaviour? Describe innate and learned behaviour with examples, including Pavlov's experiment.
What is environmental pollution? Describe the causes, effects and control of air and water pollution, and give eight points on the effects.

Conservation Biology.q: Conservation biology is best defined as the scientific study of
o: the protection, restoration and sustainable management of biodiversity
Conservation Biology.w: it is an applied, goal-driven science: describe biodiversity, find why it is being lost, and act.

Conservation Biology.q: Biodiversity has three levels, namely
Conservation Biology.w: genetic (within a species), species (number and abundance), ecosystem (variety of habitats).

Conservation Biology.q: The greatest single cause of the loss of biodiversity today is
Conservation Biology.w: habitat loss, then invasive species, pollution, over-exploitation and climate change. Remember them as HIPPO.

Conservation Biology.q: IUCN stands for the
o: International Union for Conservation of Nature
Indian Union for Control of Nature
Institute for the United Conservation of Nature

Conservation Biology.q: The IUCN publication that lists the conservation status of species is the
Conservation Biology.w: the Red Data Book, now the online Red List.

Conservation Biology.q: The IUCN category for a species facing an extremely high risk of extinction in the wild is
Conservation Biology.w: critically endangered (CR) is the highest risk short of extinction.

Conservation Biology.q: A species that no longer occurs in the wild but survives only in cultivation or captivity is
The correct order of increasing risk among IUCN threatened categories is
Conservation Biology.w: VU → EN → CR in order of increasing risk; the full ladder is LC, NT, VU, EN, CR, EW, EX.

Conservation Biology.q: A species found naturally in one geographical area and nowhere else is
Conservation Biology.w: endemic; an exotic species is one introduced from elsewhere, which is the usual confusion.

Conservation Biology.q: Spiny babbler (Turdoides nipalensis), the only bird endemic to Nepal, is important because it
o: is found in no other country
Conservation Biology.w: it is Nepal's only endemic bird, rediscovered by Dillon Ripley in 1948 after being thought lost.

Conservation Biology.q: The national bird of Nepal is
Conservation Biology.w: the Himalayan monal or danphe, Lophophorus impejanus.

Conservation Biology.q: The one-horned rhinoceros of Nepal has the scientific name
Conservation Biology.w: Rhinoceros unicornis, the greater one-horned rhinoceros of Chitwan and Bardiya.

Conservation Biology.q: Which of the following is the first national park of Nepal?
Conservation Biology.w: Chitwan, gazetted in 1973, also Nepal's first World Heritage natural site.

Conservation Biology.q: Koshi Tappu Wildlife Reserve was established mainly to protect the
Conservation Biology.w: the last population of wild water buffalo (Bubalus arnee) in Nepal.

Conservation Biology.q: Define conservation biology and state its three levels of biodiversity with one Nepali example of each.
Conservation Biology.r: Conservation biology is the applied science that studies the loss of biological diversity and develops methods to protect, restore and sustainably manage species, habitats and ecosystems. Levels: genetic — the many rice landraces of Jumla and the Terai; species — the 208 mammals and 867 birds recorded in Nepal; ecosystem — the 118 ecosystems from Terai sal forest to trans-Himalayan steppe.

Conservation Biology.q: Differentiate between in-situ and ex-situ conservation on any four bases, giving one Nepali example of each.
Conservation Biology.r: Any four of: meaning (in habitat / outside habitat); unit protected (whole ecosystem / individuals, seeds, gametes); evolution (natural selection continues / relaxed, behaviour may be lost); cost (low per species / very high); numbers supported (large / small). Examples: Chitwan National Park (in-situ); Central Zoo Jawalakhel or the Kasara gharial breeding centre (ex-situ).

Conservation Biology.q: A sample of 100 birds from Koshi Tappu contains 50 of species A, 25 of species B, 15 of species C and 10 of species D. Calculate the Shannon–Wiener index and the evenness.
List the IUCN Red List categories in order and explain the difference between Extinct in the Wild and Critically Endangered.
Conservation Biology.r: EX, EW, CR, EN, VU, NT, LC (plus DD and NE, which are not risk ratings). Extinct in the Wild means no individual survives in the natural habitat and the species persists only in cultivation, captivity or a naturalised population outside its past range. Critically Endangered means wild individuals still exist but the species faces an extremely high risk of extinction in the immediate future, for example a population reduction of 80 % or more over three generations.

Conservation Biology.q: Why is a small population at risk even after the original threat has been removed? Explain any four reasons.
Conservation Biology.r: Any four: inbreeding depression — mating between close relatives exposes harmful recessive alleles and lowers fertility and survival; genetic drift / bottleneck effect — random loss of alleles leaves the population unable to adapt; demographic stochasticity — chance runs of one sex or of deaths matter enormously when numbers are small; Allee effect — below a threshold density individuals fail to find mates, so per-capita growth becomes negative; environmental stochasticity and catastrophes — one flood, fire or epidemic can remove the whole population.

p: Describe the protected-area system of Nepal, naming the categories, the number in each and one example of each.
Explain how the buffer-zone programme makes local people partners in conservation.
Conservation Biology.r: (a) Nepal's protected areas are managed under the National Parks and Wildlife Conservation Act, 2029 (1973) and cover 23.39 % of the country. National parks (13) give the strictest protection of a whole ecosystem, with hunting, grazing and resource removal prohibited — example, Chitwan (1973), a World Heritage Site. Wildlife reserve (1) protects particular species and their habitat — Koshi Tappu, home of the wild water buffalo. Hunting reserve (1) permits licensed, quota-controlled hunting — Dhorpatan, for blue sheep and Himalayan tahr.

Conservation Biology.q: Describe the major threats to the wildlife of Nepal and the conservation measures taken against each. Support your answer with the example of either the tiger or the vulture.
Conservation Biology.r: Expected content — six threats with matched measures. Poaching and illegal trade in rhino horn, tiger bone, musk pods and pangolin scales: army posts inside parks, community-based anti-poaching units, informant networks, the CITES Act 2073 and CITES Appendix I listing. Habitat loss and fragmentation: the Terai Arc Landscape links Nepali and Indian parks through biological corridors, and new highways carry wildlife underpasses. Human– wildlife conflict: relief and compensation payments, predator-proof corrals, biofences and electric fences. Invasive species: manual clearing of Mikania micrantha and grassland management in Chitwan.

What is meant by atomic mass unit? Calculate the mass in grams of one molecule of carbon dioxide.
Foundation and Fundamentals.r: 1 u = 1/12 of the mass of a ¹²C atom = 1.66054 × 10⁻²⁴ g. For CO₂, M = 12 + 32 = 44, so one molecule has mass 44 × 1.66054 × 10⁻²⁴ g = 7.31 × 10⁻²³ g.

Foundation and Fundamentals.q: Distinguish between empirical formula and molecular formula with two examples each. A compound has the empirical formula CH₂ and molecular mass 56; find its molecular formula.
Foundation and Fundamentals.r: Empirical formula mass of CH₂ = 12 + 2 = 14, so n = 56/14 = 4 and the molecular formula is C₄H₈.

Foundation and Fundamentals.q: Calculate the percentage composition of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃, and hence the mass of calcium oxide obtainable from 1 tonne of pure limestone. (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
Foundation and Fundamentals.r: M(CaCO₃) = 40 + 12 + 48 = 100. %Ca = 40 %, %C = 12 %, %O = 48 %. On heating, CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Every 100 g of CaCO₃ gives 56 g of CaO, so 1 tonne (1000 kg) gives 560 kg of CaO.

p: Explain why chemistry is called the central science, listing four fields in which it is applied with one concrete example from Nepal in each.
State the relation between empirical formula, molecular formula and molecular mass, and use it to show that acetic acid and glucose share an empirical formula.

Foundation and Fundamentals.q: A farmer can buy either urea, CO(NH₂)₂, at Rs 1,000 per 50 kg bag or ammonium sulphate, (NH₄)₂SO₄, at Rs 600 per 50 kg bag. aCalculate the percentage of nitrogen in each.bCalculate the mass of nitrogen in one bag of each.cFind the cost per kilogram of nitrogen for each and say which is cheaper.
Explain the mole concept and Avogadro's number, and show how molar mass, molar volume and the number of particles are related, with numericals.
How are the percentage composition, the empirical formula and the molecular formula of a compound determined? Explain limiting reagent and percentage yield with numericals.
Which of the following statements best describes Avogadro's Law?
o: At constant temperature and pressure, the volume of a gas is directly proportional to the number of moles of gas.
The pressure of a gas is inversely proportional to its volume when temperature is kept constant.
The ratio of the volumes of gases reacting together, at the same temperature and pressure, is always simple and small whole numbers.
The pressure of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to its absolute temperature if the volume is constant.
Foundation and Fundamentals.w: Avogadro's Law specifically relates volume to the amount of gas at constant temperature and pressure.

Foundation and Fundamentals.q: What is the SI unit for the amount of substance?
Foundation and Fundamentals.w: The mole ($\text{mol}$) is the SI unit for the amount of substance.

Foundation and Fundamentals.q: Which law states that the pressure exerted by a gas is inversely proportional to its volume at constant temperature?
Foundation and Fundamentals.w: Boyle's Law relates the pressure and volume of a gas at constant temperature.

Foundation and Fundamentals.q: Which of the following defines the molar mass of a substance?
o: The mass of one atom of the substance
The mass of one molecule of the substance
The mass of one mole of the substance
The mass of one ion of the substance
Foundation and Fundamentals.w: Molar mass is defined as the mass of one mole of a substance.

Stoichiometry.q: The volume at STP of $8\ \text{g}$ of oxygen ($\text{O}_2$) is
The vapour density of a gas of molar mass $44\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$ is
$\text{H}_2 + \text{Cl}_2 \to 2\text{HCl}$. The mass of HCl formed from $2\ \text{g}$ of hydrogen with excess chlorine is
Stoichiometry.w: $2\ \text{g}$ is 1 mol of $\text{H}_2$, giving 2 mol HCl $= 73\ \text{g}$; (a) forgets the factor of two.

Stoichiometry.q: In CO and $\text{CO}_2$, $12\ \text{g}$ of carbon combines with $16\ \text{g}$ and $32\ \text{g}$ of oxygen. This illustrates the law of
Stoichiometry.w: the oxygen masses $16: 32 = 1: 2$ for a fixed mass of carbon.

Stoichiometry.q: If the theoretical yield is $20\ \text{g}$ and $15\ \text{g}$ is obtained, the percentage yield is
Which postulate of Dalton's atomic theory is no longer accepted?
o: atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios
atoms of different elements differ in mass
compounds form by combination of atoms
Stoichiometry.w: atoms are divisible into electrons, protons and neutrons.

Stoichiometry.q: The number of molecules in 11.2 L of any gas at STP is
Stoichiometry.w: 11.2 L is half a mole, so 0.5 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 3.011 × 10²³.

Stoichiometry.q: The vapour density of a gas is 32. Its molecular mass is
In the reaction 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, 4 g of H₂ is mixed with 16 g of O₂. The limiting reactant is
Stoichiometry.w: n(H₂) = 2, n(O₂) = 0.5; dividing by coefficients gives 1.0 and 0.5, so oxygen runs out first.

Stoichiometry.q: Which law is explained by the existence of CO and CO₂?
Stoichiometry.w: for a fixed 12 g of carbon, the oxygen masses are 16 g and 32 g, a ratio of 1: 2.

Stoichiometry.q: The empirical formula of a compound is CH₂O and its molecular mass is 60. Its molecular formula is
State the postulates of Dalton's atomic theory and mention two of its limitations.
State Avogadro's law and derive the relation: molecular mass = 2 × vapour density.
Calculate the number of moles, molecules and atoms present in 3.4 g of ammonia gas, and the volume it occupies at STP. (N = 14, H = 1)
Stoichiometry.r: M(NH₃) = 17 g mol⁻¹, so n = 3.4/17 = 0.20 mol. Molecules = 0.20 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 1.204 × 10²³. Each NH₃ has 4 atoms, so atoms = 4 × 1.204 × 10²³ = 4.82 × 10²³. Volume at STP = 0.20 × 22.4 = 4.48 L.

Stoichiometry.q: Define limiting reactant. 50 g of CaCO₃ is treated with 35 g of HCl. Which is the limiting reactant, and what mass of CO₂ is produced? (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16, H = 1, Cl = 35.5)
Stoichiometry.r: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂↑. n(CaCO₃) = 50/100 = 0.50 mol; n(HCl) = 35/36.5 = 0.959 mol. Dividing by coefficients: 0.50/1 = 0.50 and 0.959/2 = 0.479, so HCl is limiting. n(CO₂) = 0.959/2 = 0.479 mol, giving 0.479 × 44 = 21.1 g of CO₂ (equivalently 10.7 L at STP).

p: State the law of multiple proportions. Two oxides of nitrogen contain 63.6 % and 46.7 % nitrogen by mass. Show that the data illustrate the law and identify the oxides. (N = 14, O = 16)
Define theoretical yield and percentage yield, and explain two reasons why the actual yield of an industrial reaction is always less than the theoretical yield.

Stoichiometry.q: A hydrocarbon contains 85.7 % carbon and 14.3 % hydrogen by mass. Its vapour density is 21.
p: Determine its molecular mass and molecular formula.
Calculate the volume of oxygen at STP required for the complete combustion of 4.2 g of this hydrocarbon.
Stoichiometry.r: (a) C: 85.7/12 = 7.14; H: 14.3/1 = 14.3. Dividing by 7.14 gives 1: 2, so the empirical formula is CH₂ (EF mass 14).

Stoichiometry.q: State and explain the laws of chemical combination with examples and give the modern explanation by Dalton's atomic theory.
Define limiting reactant and percentage yield. Solve a full problem on the formation of ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen.
How are the empirical and molecular formulae of a compound found from its percentage composition? Work out an example.
What is the molar volume of an ideal gas at Standard Temperature and Pressure (STP)?
Stoichiometry.w: The molar volume of an ideal gas at STP is defined as $22.4 \text{ L/mol}$.

Stoichiometry.q: Which term describes the quantitative relationship between reactants and products in a chemical reaction?
Stoichiometry.w: Stoichiometry refers to the study of quantitative relationships in chemical reactions involving reactants and products.

Stoichiometry.q: If the mass of one mole of carbon atoms is $12 \text{ g}$, what would be the mass of one mole of carbon dioxide ($CO_2$) molecules?
Stoichiometry.w: The molecular weight of $CO_2$ is calculated by summing the atomic weights of $C$ and $O$, which gives $12 + (2 \times 16) = 44 \text{ g/mol}$.

Atomic Structure.q: The number of orbitals in a $d$ subshell is
Atomic Structure.w: $l = 2$ gives $2l + 1 = 5$ orbitals.

Atomic Structure.q: The maximum number of electrons in the shell with $n = 3$ is
The electronic configuration of chromium ($Z = 24$) is
Atomic Structure.w: a half-filled $d$ subshell is more stable; (a) is the unadjusted Aufbau answer.

Atomic Structure.q: The quantum number that determines the shape of an orbital is
Atomic Structure.w: $l$ gives $s$ (spherical), $p$ (dumb-bell).

Atomic Structure.q: Electrons occupy degenerate orbitals singly before pairing, according to
Atomic Structure.w: Hund's rule of maximum multiplicity.

Atomic Structure.q: The number of unpaired electrons in $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ ($Z = 26$) is
Atomic Structure.w: $\text{Fe}\ 3d^{6}4s^{2}$ loses the $4s$ pair and one $3d$ electron, leaving $3d^{5}$: five unpaired.

Atomic Structure.q: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle states that
o: position and momentum cannot both be known exactly
no two electrons have the same four quantum numbers
Atomic Structure.w: (a) is Bohr's model and (c) is Pauli's principle.

Atomic Structure.q: The electronic configuration of Cr ($Z = 24$) is
Atomic Structure.w: a half-filled 3d⁵ with 4s¹ is more stable than 3d⁴4s².

Atomic Structure.q: The number of unpaired electrons in Fe³⁺ is
Atomic Structure.w: Fe³⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵, and by Hund's rule all five are unpaired.

Atomic Structure.q: Which pair of quantum numbers is not allowed?
Atomic Structure.w: $l$ can only run from 0 to $n-1$, so $l = 2$ is impossible for $n = 2$.

Atomic Structure.q: Describe Rutherford's α-scattering experiment and state the conclusions drawn from it. Give two limitations of his model.
State the postulates of Bohr's atomic theory and mention any three defects of the theory.
Calculate the radius and energy of the second Bohr orbit of the hydrogen atom, and the wavelength of the first line of the Lyman series. ($R_H = 1.097\times10^{7}\ \text{m}^{-1}$)
Atomic Structure.r: $r_2 = 0.529\times2^{2} = 2.116\ \text{Å} = 2.116\times10^{-10}$ m and $E_2 = -13.6/4 = -3.40$ eV. First Lyman line is $n = 2 \rightarrow n = 1$: $1/\lambda = 1.097\times10^{7}(1 - 1/4) = 8.23\times10^{6}\ \text{m}^{-1}$, so $\lambda = 1.215\times10^{-7}\ \text{m} = 121.5$ nm (ultraviolet).

Atomic Structure.q: State Heisenberg's uncertainty principle. Calculate the uncertainty in the position of an electron whose velocity is known to within $1.0\times10^{5}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.
Atomic Structure.r: $\Delta x = h/(4\pi m \Delta v) = 6.626\times10^{-34}/(4\times3.1416\times9.11\times10^{-31}\times1.0\times10^{5}) = 6.626\times10^{-34}/(1.145\times10^{-24}) = 5.79\times10^{-10}$ m, i.e. about 5.8 Å — several atomic diameters.

Atomic Structure.q: Define the four quantum numbers and write the electronic configurations of Sc ($Z = 21$), Cu ($Z = 29$) and Zn²⁺.
Atomic Structure.r: Sc: [Ar]3d¹4s². Cu: [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹ (filled 3d is extra stable). Zn²⁺: Zn is [Ar]3d¹⁰4s², so removing the two 4s electrons gives [Ar]3d¹⁰.

p: State Bohr's postulates and derive expressions for the radius and the energy of the $n^{\text{th}}$ orbit of a hydrogen-like atom.
Using these, show how the Rydberg equation for the hydrogen spectrum follows, and name the series obtained for $n_1 = 1, 2$ and $3$.
