Hydrocarbons.w: 2CH₃COO⁻ → 2CH₃· + 2CO₂ + 2e⁻, and the methyl radicals couple.

Hydrocarbons.q: The C—C bond length is shortest in
Hydrocarbons.w: 120 pm, against 134 pm for C=C and 154 pm for C—C.

Hydrocarbons.q: How is ethane prepared from (i) bromoethane by the Wurtz reaction, (ii) sodium propanoate, (iii) ethene and (iv) ethyne? Give equations with conditions.
Hydrocarbons.r: (i) 2CH₃Br + 2Na --dry ether--> C₂H₆ + 2NaBr (note bromomethane, not bromoethane, is needed for ethane). (ii) CH₃CH₂COONa + NaOH --CaO, Δ--> C₂H₆ + Na₂CO₃. (iii) C₂H₄ + H₂ --Ni, 523–573 K--> C₂H₆. (iv) C₂H₂ + 2H₂ --Ni--> C₂H₆.

Hydrocarbons.q: Describe the free-radical mechanism of the chlorination of methane, naming the three stages. Why is a trace of ethane always found in the product?
State Markovnikov's rule and explain it on the basis of carbocation stability, using the addition of HBr to propene.
What is the peroxide effect? Why is it shown by HBr but not by HCl or HI?
What is ozonolysis? An alkene C₄H₈ gives only ethanal on ozonolysis. Identify it and write the equations.
Hydrocarbons.r: Ozonolysis is the addition of ozone across a C=C to give an ozonide, followed by cleavage with Zn/H₂O to give carbonyl compounds. If the only product is ethanal, both halves of the molecule must be CH₃CH=, so the alkene is but-2-ene: CH₃CH=CHCH₃ + O₃ → ozonide, then ozonide + H₂O --Zn--> 2CH₃CHO. (The isomer but-1-ene would give HCHO + CH₃CH₂CHO, and 2-methylpropene would give HCHO + propanone.)

Hydrocarbons.q: How would you distinguish between ethane, ethene and ethyne in the laboratory? Give the reagent, the observation and one equation in each case.
Hydrocarbons.r: Bromine water: no change with ethane, decolourised by ethene and ethyne. Ammoniacal AgNO₃: white precipitate with ethyne only, C₂H₂ + 2[Ag(NH₃)₂]OH → Ag₂C₂↓ + 4NH₃ + 2H₂O. So no change to bromine water = ethane; decolourises bromine water but gives no precipitate = ethene; decolourises bromine water and gives a white precipitate = ethyne.

Hydrocarbons.q: Explain the acidic character of ethyne. Write the reactions with sodium, ammoniacal silver nitrate and ammoniacal cuprous chloride, giving the colour of each precipitate.
What is Kolbe's electrolytic method? Write the anode and cathode reactions for a concentrated solution of sodium ethanoate, and state two limitations of the method.
Hydrocarbons.r: Definition as in Section 14.9. Anode: 2CH₃COO⁻ → 2CH₃COO· + 2e⁻; 2CH₃COO· → 2CH₃· + 2CO₂; 2CH₃· → C₂H₆. Cathode: 2Na⁺ + 2e⁻ → 2Na; 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. Limitations: (i) only alkanes with an even number of carbons can be made, so methane and propane are impossible; (ii) a mixture of two salts gives a mixture of three alkanes; (iii) the solution must be concentrated, or oxygen is discharged at the anode instead.

p: Describe, with equations and conditions, four laboratory methods of preparing an alkane.
What happens when ethane is (i) chlorinated in sunlight, (ii) heated with nitric acid vapour at 673 K, (iii) oxidised with O₂ over a Cu tube at 473 K and 100 atm, (iv) burnt in excess oxygen?
State Markovnikov's rule and the peroxide effect, and explain both in terms of the stability of the intermediate formed.
Complete: (i) CH₃CH=CH₂ + H₂O/H⁺ → (ii) CH₂=CH₂ + conc. H₂SO₄ →, then + H₂O, Δ → (iii) 2-methylbut-2-ene + O₃, then Zn/H₂O → (iv) CH₃CH₂CHBrCH₃ + alc. KOH →
Hydrocarbons.r: (b) (i) propan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ — Markovnikov. (ii) CH₂=CH₂ + H₂SO₄ → CH₃CH₂OSO₃H, and CH₃CH₂OSO₃H + H₂O --Δ--> C₂H₅OH + H₂SO₄. (iii) (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃ gives propanone (CH₃)₂CO and ethanal CH₃CHO. (iv) but-2-ene CH₃CH=CHCH₃ as the major product (Saytzeff) with but-1-ene as the minor product.

p: How is ethyne prepared from calcium carbide and from 1,2-dibromoethane? Give equations.
Explain, with equations, the acidic nature of ethyne and the two precipitation tests based on it.
5.6 dm³ of ethyne at STP is burnt completely. Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide formed.
Hydrocarbons.r: (c) The balanced equation is 2C₂H₂ + 5O₂ → 4CO₂ + 2H₂O. Moles of ethyne = 5.6 / 22.4 = 0.25 mol. From the equation, 2 mol of C₂H₂ gives 4 mol of CO₂, i.e. 1 mol gives 2 mol, so moles of CO₂ = 2 × 0.25 = 0.50 mol. Mass of CO₂ = 0.50 × 44 = 22 g.

Hydrocarbons.q: Describe the preparation and chemical properties of ethene, including Markovnikov's rule, the Baeyer test and ozonolysis.
Describe the preparation and properties of ethyne and compare alkanes, alkenes and alkynes in a table of eight points.
Explain the free-radical mechanism of the chlorination of methane, and describe the conformations of ethane.

Aromatic Hydrocarbons.q: The number of $\pi$ electrons in benzene is
Aromatic Hydrocarbons.w: one $\pi$ electron from each of the six carbons.

Aromatic Hydrocarbons.q: In nitrobenzene the $-\text{NO}_2$ group directs an incoming electrophile to the
Aromatic Hydrocarbons.w: $-\text{NO}_2$ deactivates the ring and directs meta.

Aromatic Hydrocarbons.q: Benzene does not decolourise bromine water because
o: its π electrons are delocalised and the ring is stabilised
Aromatic Hydrocarbons.w: addition would destroy the aromatic sextet, and the resonance energy makes that unfavourable.

Aromatic Hydrocarbons.q: All six carbon–carbon bond lengths in benzene are
Aromatic Hydrocarbons.w: intermediate between a single and a double bond, as delocalisation requires.

Aromatic Hydrocarbons.q: Benzene is obtained when ethyne is passed through
o: a red-hot iron tube at 873 K

Aromatic Hydrocarbons.w: the carbon of —COOH is doubly bonded to oxygen, so the group is -R and deactivating.

Aromatic Hydrocarbons.q: The number of isomers of dichlorobenzene, C₆H₄Cl₂, is
State Hückel's rule and its conditions. Apply it to cyclobutadiene, benzene, the cyclopentadienyl anion and cyclooctatetraene.
Aromatic Hydrocarbons.r: A cyclic, planar, fully conjugated ring with (4n + 2) delocalised π electrons is aromatic. Cyclobutadiene 4 π = 4n, antiaromatic; benzene 6 π, aromatic (n = 1); cyclopentadienyl anion 4 π from two C=C plus the lone pair = 6 π, aromatic; cyclooctatetraene 8 π = 4n and tub-shaped, therefore non-aromatic.

Aromatic Hydrocarbons.q: Give three pieces of evidence that support the Kekulé structure of benzene and three that contradict it.
Aromatic Hydrocarbons.r: For: it accounts for C₆H₆; benzene adds exactly 3H₂ to give cyclohexane; ozonolysis gives three molecules of glyoxal; only one monosubstituted product C₆H₅X exists. Against: benzene does not decolourise bromine water or Baeyer's reagent; its heat of hydrogenation is 152 kJ mol⁻¹ too small; all six C—C bonds are 139 pm, not alternating; the structure predicts two different ortho isomers but only one is found.

Aromatic Hydrocarbons.q: What is resonance energy? How is the resonance energy of benzene obtained from heats of hydrogenation, and what does it explain about benzene's chemistry?
Aromatic Hydrocarbons.r: Resonance energy is the extra stability of the delocalised hybrid over the most stable single contributing structure. ΔH for three isolated double bonds = 3 × (-120) = -360 kJ mol⁻¹, while benzene measures -208 kJ mol⁻¹; the difference, 152 kJ mol⁻¹, is the resonance energy. It explains why benzene resists addition and prefers substitution, which restores the delocalised system.

Aromatic Hydrocarbons.q: How is benzene prepared from (i) sodium benzoate, (ii) phenol and (iii) ethyne? Give equations with conditions.
Describe the mechanism of the nitration of benzene, naming the electrophile, the intermediate and the rate-determining step.
Aromatic Hydrocarbons.r: Step 1: HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ ⇌ NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻. Step 2 (slow, rate determining): the π cloud attacks NO₂⁺ to give the arenium ion (σ-complex), a non-aromatic carbocation whose positive charge is delocalised over three carbons. Step 3 (fast): HSO₄⁻ removes H⁺ from the sp³ carbon and aromaticity is restored, giving C₆H₅NO₂.

Aromatic Hydrocarbons.q: What are Friedel–Crafts reactions? Write the alkylation and acylation of benzene with equations, and give two limitations of alkylation.
Why is —NO₂ meta-directing while —OH is ortho–para directing? Explain in terms of the resonance effect.
Aromatic Hydrocarbons.r: In phenol the oxygen lone pair is delocalised into the ring (+R), and the resonance structures put the negative charge specifically on the ortho and para carbons, so the electrophile attacks there. In nitrobenzene the -NO₂ group withdraws density (-R), and the resonance structures put the positive charge on the ortho and para carbons; the meta positions are least depleted, so attack occurs there.

p: State Hückel's rule and explain, with reasons, why cyclobutadiene is antiaromatic, benzene is aromatic and cyclooctatetraene is non-aromatic.
Discuss the Kekulé structure of benzene: what it explains, what it fails to explain, and how resonance resolves the difficulty.
Aromatic Hydrocarbons.r: (a) Cyclobutadiene is planar, cyclic and conjugated but holds 4 π electrons (4n), so it is destabilised relative to the open chain — antiaromatic. Benzene holds 6 π (4n + 2 with n = 1) in a regular planar hexagon — aromatic. Cyclooctatetraene has 8 π (4n) and escapes antiaromaticity by folding into a tub shape; since it is no longer planar, its p orbitals cannot overlap all round the ring and it behaves as an ordinary polyene — non-aromatic.

p: Describe the general mechanism of electrophilic aromatic substitution, using nitration as the example.
Write equations with reagents and conditions for the sulphonation, bromination, alkylation and acylation of benzene, naming the electrophile in each case.
Aromatic Hydrocarbons.r: (b) Sulphonation: C₆H₆ + H₂SO₄ (fuming) --Δ--> C₆H₅SO₃H + H₂O, electrophile SO₃. Bromination: C₆H₆ + Br₂ --anhyd. FeBr₃, dark--> C₆H₅Br + HBr, electrophile Br⁺. Alkylation: C₆H₆ + CH₃Cl --anhyd. AlCl₃--> C₆H₅CH₃ + HCl, electrophile CH₃⁺. Acylation: C₆H₆ + CH₃COCl --anhyd. AlCl₃--> C₆H₅COCH₃ + HCl, electrophile CH₃CO⁺.

p: Explain the terms activating, deactivating, o,p-directing and m-directing, giving two examples of each class.
Predict the major product of (i) nitration of toluene, (ii) nitration of nitrobenzene, (iii) bromination of phenol.
7.8 g of benzene is completely burnt in oxygen. Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide produced at STP.
Aromatic Hydrocarbons.r: (c) The balanced equation is 2C₆H₆ + 15O₂ → 12CO₂ + 6H₂O. Molar mass of benzene = 78 g mol⁻¹, so moles of benzene = 7.8 / 78 = 0.10 mol. From the equation 2 mol of benzene gives 12 mol of CO₂, i.e. 1 mol gives 6 mol, so moles of CO₂ = 6 × 0.10 = 0.60 mol. Volume at STP = 0.60 × 22.4 = 13.44 dm³.

Aromatic Hydrocarbons.q: Describe the structure of benzene. Explain the Kekule structure, its limitations, the resonance and the molecular orbital picture, and give the evidence for it.
Describe the electrophilic substitution reactions of benzene (nitration, halogenation, sulphonation, Friedel-Crafts) with the mechanism of nitration, and explain the directive effect of substituents.

Fundamentals of Applied Chemistry.q: A batch process is one in which
o: feed enters and product leaves continuously
the reactor is charged, the reaction is completed, and the product is removed
a small-scale plant used to test a process before scale-up
Fundamentals of Applied Chemistry.w: it tests a process on a small scale first.

Fundamentals of Applied Chemistry.q: Large-volume products such as ammonia are usually made by
Acid rain is mainly caused by
Fundamentals of Applied Chemistry.w: $\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{NO}_x$ form sulphuric and nitric acids in the air.

Fundamentals of Applied Chemistry.q: Which of the following is a fixed cost of a chemical plant?
Fundamentals of Applied Chemistry.w: depreciation is paid whether or not the plant produces anything.

Fundamentals of Applied Chemistry.q: The stage at which a reaction is first tested on the kilogram scale is the
Fundamentals of Applied Chemistry.w: the pilot plant is the kg-scale trial between bench and full plant.

Fundamentals of Applied Chemistry.q: Which process would normally be operated batchwise?
Fundamentals of Applied Chemistry.w: small tonnage, many different specifications, batch traceability needed.

Fundamentals of Applied Chemistry.q: The lowest point of the cumulative cash-flow curve of a project occurs at
o: the end of the plant's life
Fundamentals of Applied Chemistry.w: the plant is fully paid for but has not yet sold anything.

Fundamentals of Applied Chemistry.q: Define the chemical industry. Classify chemical products into four groups with one example of each.
List, in order, the stages in producing a new chemical product, and state why a pilot plant is needed even when the bench reaction works perfectly.
Fundamentals of Applied Chemistry.r: Market research → bench synthesis → pilot plant → process and plant design → construction and commissioning → full production → marketing and review. The pilot plant is needed because heat transfer, mixing, corrosion, catalyst life and solids handling do not scale with volume: the surface-to-volume ratio falls as size rises, so a reaction that is easy to cool in a flask can run away in a large reactor.

Fundamentals of Applied Chemistry.q: Distinguish between batch and continuous processing under any five headings.
A plant has fixed costs of Rs 60 million per year. The variable cost is Rs 28 per kg and the selling price is Rs 40 per kg. Find
p: the break-even output in tonnes and
the profit at an output of 8,000 tonnes per year.
Fundamentals of Applied Chemistry.r: Contribution $= 40 - 28 =$ Rs 12 per kg. (a) $n_{\text{BE}} = 60\times10^{6}/12 = 5.0\times10^{6}$ kg $= 5000$ tonnes per year. (b) $P = 8.0\times10^{6}(12) - 60\times10^{6} = 96\times10^{6} - 60\times10^{6} =$ Rs 36 million per year.

Fundamentals of Applied Chemistry.q: State four environmental impacts of the chemical industry, giving one chemical equation or species responsible for each and one method of control.
Fundamentals of Applied Chemistry.r: Any four from the impact table — e.g. acid rain (SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃; controlled by lime scrubbing), global warming (CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ in cement kilns; controlled by energy integration), water pollution (Cr⁶⁺, Pb²⁺ in effluent; controlled by precipitation and neutralisation), dust (cement dust; controlled by electrostatic precipitators).

p: Draw and explain the cash-flow diagram for the production cycle of a new chemical product, marking the research, construction, start-up, break-even and profit regions.
Explain the factors that must be considered when choosing the site and designing a new chemical plant.
Define atom economy and percentage yield and distinguish between them.

Ethanoic acid can be made by CH₃OH + CO → CH₃COOH or by CH₃CH₂OH + O₂ → CH₃COOH + H₂O. Calculate the atom economy of each route. ($M$: CH₃OH = 32, CO = 28, CH₃COOH = 60, CH₃CH₂OH = 46, O₂ = 32, H₂O = 18.)
State which route a manufacturer would prefer on environmental grounds and why.

Fundamentals of Applied Chemistry.q: Describe the stages in producing a new chemical product, from the laboratory idea to the plant, and explain the economics and cash flow of production.
Compare continuous and batch processes, explain the factors in designing a chemical plant, and discuss the environmental impact of the chemical industry.
A sample of an ideal gas occupies a volume of 22.4 L at STP. What is the number of moles of the gas?
Fundamentals of Applied Chemistry.w: At STP, 1 mole of any ideal gas occupies 22.4 L.

Modern Chemical Manufactures.q: In the diaphragm cell, chlorine is liberated at the
The usual temperature of the Haber process is about
Modern Chemical Manufactures.w: a compromise between rate and yield for an exothermic reaction.

Modern Chemical Manufactures.q: The temperature of the catalytic oxidation of $\text{NH}_3$ in Ostwald's process is about
Modern Chemical Manufactures.w: the gauze glows red-hot, so the reaction is self-sustaining.

Modern Chemical Manufactures.q: The catalyst used in the contact process is
Modern Chemical Manufactures.w: V₂O₅ is cheap and, unlike platinum, is not poisoned by traces of arsenic.

Modern Chemical Manufactures.q: In the Haber process, increasing the pressure increases the yield of ammonia because
o: the number of gas molecules decreases
Modern Chemical Manufactures.w: 4 mol of gas become 2, so by Le Chatelier's principle higher pressure shifts the equilibrium right.

Modern Chemical Manufactures.q: Sulphur trioxide is absorbed in concentrated sulphuric acid rather than water because
o: water does not react with SO₃
the reaction with water is endothermic
a persistent acid mist is formed with water
Modern Chemical Manufactures.w: direct absorption in water gives a fine mist of H₂SO₄ that will not condense and escapes up the stack.

Modern Chemical Manufactures.q: In the diaphragm cell the product formed at the cathode is
Modern Chemical Manufactures.w: water is reduced in preference to Na⁺, so hydrogen is evolved; sodium metal needs molten NaCl.

Modern Chemical Manufactures.q: The least soluble substance formed in the carbonating tower of the Solvay process is
Modern Chemical Manufactures.w: sodium hydrogencarbonate crystallises out, which is what drives the whole process.

Modern Chemical Manufactures.q: The percentage of nitrogen in urea is closest to
State Le Chatelier's principle and use it to explain the choice of temperature and pressure in the Haber process. Why is a catalyst used even though it cannot change the yield?
Modern Chemical Manufactures.r: Le Chatelier: if a system at equilibrium is disturbed, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that opposes the disturbance. The forward reaction N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ is exothermic, so a low temperature would give the highest equilibrium yield; but at low temperature the rate is uneconomically slow, so 450–500 °C is chosen as a compromise. Four moles of gas become two, so a high pressure shifts the equilibrium right and speeds the reaction — 200 atm is used, limited only by the cost and safety of the vessels. The iron catalyst lowers the activation energy of forward and reverse reactions equally, so $K_p$ is unchanged;

Modern Chemical Manufactures.q: Describe, with equations, the purification of the gas in the contact process, and state why each impurity must be removed.
Modern Chemical Manufactures.r: Burner gas is passed through: a dust chamber (steam and electrostatic precipitation) to settle dust, which would coat and deactivate the catalyst; cooling pipes, to drop the temperature to about 100 °C and recover heat; a washing tower (water spray) to dissolve out soluble impurities; an arsenic purifier where Fe(OH)₃ adsorbs As₂O₃, because arsenic is a permanent catalyst poison; a testing box to confirm purity; and a drying tower where concentrated H₂SO₄ removes water vapour, which would otherwise form acid mist and dilute the product. The reaction to be protected is 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ over V₂O₅.

Modern Chemical Manufactures.q: Explain the function of the diaphragm and of the difference in brine level in a diaphragm cell. Write the electrode reactions and name the by-products.
Modern Chemical Manufactures.r: The diaphragm is a porous asbestos layer on the perforated steel cathode. It lets ions and liquid through but prevents bulk mixing of the anolyte and catholyte, which is essential because Cl₂ + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaOCl + H₂O would destroy both products. The anode compartment is kept at a higher liquid level, so brine percolates continuously from anode side to cathode side; this bulk flow opposes the electrical migration of OH⁻ towards the anode and sweeps hydroxide away from the chlorine. Electrode reactions: anode 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻; cathode 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻. By-products: chlorine and hydrogen.

Modern Chemical Manufactures.q: Why is ammonia not consumed in the Solvay process? Write the equations for the two steps in which it is used and recovered, and name the only large waste product.
Modern Chemical Manufactures.r: Ammonia is used in the ammoniation/carbonation step, NaCl + NH₃ + CO₂ + H₂O → NaHCO₃↓ + NH₄Cl, and is recovered from the filtrate by warming with milk of lime, 2NH₄Cl + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCl₂ + 2NH₃↑ + 2H₂O. The recovered ammonia is returned to the ammoniation tower, so only make-up ammonia for mechanical losses is bought. The only large waste is calcium chloride solution.

Modern Chemical Manufactures.q: Describe the manufacture of sulphuric acid by the contact process. Include a labelled flow sheet, all balanced equations, the conditions with reasons, and explain why a much lower pressure is used than in the Haber process.
Modern Chemical Manufactures.r: Outline. Stage 1: S + O₂ → SO₂ (or 4FeS₂ + 11O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃ + 8SO₂) in the burner. Stage 2 — purification: dust chamber → cooling pipes → washing tower → arsenic purifier (Fe(OH)₃ removes As₂O₃, a catalyst poison) → testing box → drying tower (conc. H₂SO₄). Stage 3: 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃, ΔH = -196 kJ mol⁻¹, over V₂O₅ at 450 °C and 2 atm. Temperature is a compromise: the reaction is exothermic so a low temperature favours SO₃, but below ~400 °C the catalyst is too slow. Stage 4: SO₃ + H₂SO₄ → H₂S₂O₇ (oleum), then H₂S₂O₇ + H₂O → 2H₂SO₄; direct absorption in water is avoided because it forms an uncondensable acid mist.

p: With a labelled diagram, describe the manufacture of sodium hydroxide by the diaphragm cell, giving the electrode reactions and the composition of the cell liquor.
A cell carries 50 kA for 10 hours at 95% current efficiency. Calculate the mass of NaOH produced and the volume of chlorine at STP.
Modern Chemical Manufactures.r: (a) Steel tank; titanium (RuO₂-coated) anode; perforated steel cathode carrying an asbestos diaphragm; saturated 25% brine fed to the anode compartment and held at a higher level. Anode: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻. Cathode: 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻. Overall: 2NaCl + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂ + Cl₂. The diaphragm and the level difference keep OH⁻ away from Cl₂. Cell liquor drawn off contains about 11% NaOH and 16% NaCl; it is evaporated, the less soluble NaCl crystallises and is recycled, and 50% caustic liquor is obtained. (b) Q = 50 000 A × 36 000 s = 1.8 × 10⁹ C. n(e⁻) = 1.8 × 10⁹ ÷ 96 500 = 1.865 × 10⁴ mol; useful = 0.95 × 1.865 × 10⁴ = 1.772 × 10⁴ mol.

p: What is a chemical fertilizer? Classify chemical fertilizers with one example and the N–P₂O₅–K₂O grade of each class.
Describe the manufacture of urea from ammonia and carbon dioxide with a flow-sheet diagram and balanced equations.
Calculate the mass of urea that can be made from 340 kg of ammonia if the conversion is 75%.
Modern Chemical Manufactures.r: (a) A fertilizer is a substance added to soil to supply one or more elements needed for plant growth in an absorbable form. Classes: nitrogenous — urea, 46–0–0; phosphatic — triple superphosphate, 0–46–0; potassic — muriate of potash (KCl), 0–0–60; mixed/complex — DAP, 18–46–0. (Straight versus complex, and quick- versus slow-acting, are acceptable alternative classifications.) (b) NH₃ and CO₂ from the adjacent ammonia plant are compressed to 150–200 atm and fed to an autoclave at 180–190 °C: 2NH₃ + CO₂ → NH₂COONH₄ (fast, exothermic), then NH₂COONH₄ ⇌ NH₂CONH₂ + H₂O (slow, endothermic).

Modern Chemical Manufactures.q: Describe the manufacture of ammonia by Haber's process, explaining the conditions in terms of Le Chatelier's principle, and the production of urea.
Describe the manufacture of nitric acid by Ostwald's process and sulphuric acid by the contact process.
Describe the manufacture of sodium carbonate by the Solvay process and sodium hydroxide by the diaphragm cell.
Which law is used to describe the equilibrium constant expression for a chemical reaction involving gases?
Modern Chemical Manufactures.w: The Law of Mass Action relates the concentrations of reactants and products at equilibrium.

Modern Chemical Manufactures.q: What is the primary purpose of using fractional distillation in the petrochemical industry?
o: To increase the viscosity of crude oil
To separate components based on their boiling points
To enhance the octane rating of gasoline
Modern Chemical Manufactures.w: Fractional distillation separates components in crude oil based on differences in their boiling points.

Modern Chemical Manufactures.q: In the Haber process, which catalyst is commonly used to increase the yield of ammonia?
Modern Chemical Manufactures.w: Iron, often promoted with potassium oxide, is used as a catalyst in the Haber process for ammonia synthesis.

Modern Chemical Manufactures.q: Which of the following is a correct definition of a polymer?
o: A molecule consisting of repeated structural units connected by covalent chemical bonds
A compound made up of ions held together by ionic bonds
A substance that conducts electricity when dissolved in water
A pure form of carbon with high electrical conductivity
Modern Chemical Manufactures.w: Polymers are large molecules composed of many repeating subunits bonded covalently.

Chemistry: Unit-wise Objective Question.q: The number of moles in $11\ \text{g}$ of $\text{CO}_2$ is
The shape of the methane molecule is
The gas liberated at the cathode during electrolysis of brine in a diaphragm cell is
The hybridization of carbon in ethyne is
Chemistry: Unit-wise Objective Question.w: each carbon forms one $\sigma$ bond to H and one to C, with two $\pi$ bonds.

Chemistry: Unit-wise Objective Question.q: Calculate the mass of $\text{CaO}$ obtained by heating $50\ \text{g}$ of $\text{CaCO}_3$.
Chemistry: Unit-wise Objective Question.r: $\text{CaCO}_3 \to \text{CaO} + \text{CO}_2$; $50\ \text{g} = 0.5$ mol; one mole of CaCO₃ gives one mole of CaO; mass of CaO $= 0.5\times56 = 28\ \text{g}$.

Chemistry: Unit-wise Objective Question.q: State Le Chatelier's principle and apply it to the Haber process for pressure and temperature.
Chemistry: Unit-wise Objective Question.r: If a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts to oppose the disturbance. $\text{N}_2 + 3\text{H}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3$ ($\Delta H < 0$, fewer moles on the right): high pressure favours ammonia; low temperature favours ammonia but slows the rate, so about $450^{\circ}\text{C}$ with an Fe catalyst is the compromise.

Chemistry: Unit-wise Objective Question.q: Write the Lewis structure idea and shape of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and explain why its bond angle is below $109.5^{\circ}$.
Chemistry: Unit-wise Objective Question.r: Oxygen has six valence electrons, two used in bonds, so there are two bond pairs and two lone pairs ($sp^{3}$). Lone pair–lone pair and lone pair–bond pair repulsion exceeds bond pair–bond pair repulsion, squeezing the angle to $104.5^{\circ}$; the shape is bent.

Chemistry: Unit-wise Objective Question.q: Distinguish between ethane, ethene and ethyne by two chemical tests.
Chemistry: Unit-wise Objective Question.r: Bromine water: ethene and ethyne decolourise it, ethane does not. Ammoniacal $\text{AgNO}_3$: only ethyne gives a white precipitate. Baeyer's reagent is decolourised by ethene and ethyne but not ethane.

Chemistry: Unit-wise Objective Question.q: Describe the manufacture of sulphuric acid by the contact process with the reactions, conditions and a flow sheet.
Chemistry: Unit-wise Objective Question.r: Steps: (i) Sulphur dioxide: $\text{S} + \text{O}_2 \to \text{SO}_2$ (or roasting pyrites, $4\text{FeS}_2 + 11\text{O}_2 \to 2\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 + 8\text{SO}_2$); the gas is purified and dried. (ii) Oxidation: $2\text{SO}_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{SO}_3$, $\Delta H = -197\ \text{kJ}$, over $\text{V}_2\text{O}_5$ at $400$–$450^{\circ}\text{C}$ and 1–2 atm; excess oxygen and removal of heat favour the yield. (iii) Absorption: $\text{SO}_3$ is dissolved in conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ to give oleum: $\text{SO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \to \text{H}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_7$. (iv) Dilution: $\text{H}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_7 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \to 2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$.

Chemistry: Unit-wise Objective Question.q: Describe the Solvay process for sodium carbonate, giving the reactions and the role of ammonia recovery.
Chemistry: Unit-wise Objective Question.r: Brine is saturated with $\text{NH}_3$ in an ammonia tower. In the carbonating (Solvay) tower $\text{CO}_2$ is passed in: $\text{NaCl} + \text{NH}_3 + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \to \text{NaHCO}_3 + \text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$; sparingly soluble $\text{NaHCO}_3$ separates and is filtered. Heating gives soda ash: $2\text{NaHCO}_3 \to \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$ (the $\text{CO}_2$ is recycled). $\text{CO}_2$ comes from heating limestone, $\text{CaCO}_3 \to \text{CaO} + \text{CO}_2$, and the lime slakes to $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$. Ammonia is recovered: $2\text{NH}_4\text{Cl} + \text{Ca(OH)}_2 \to 2\text{NH}_3 + \text{CaCl}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Chemistry: Unit-wise Objective Question.q: What is the pH of a 0.01 M solution of HCl?
Chemistry: Unit-wise Objective Question.w: The pH is calculated as -log[H+], and since HCl is a strong acid, [H+] = 0.01 M.

General and Physical Chemistry.q: A compound contains $40.0\ \%$ carbon, $6.7\ \%$ hydrogen and $53.3\ \%$ oxygen, and its molar mass is $180\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$. Find its empirical and molecular formulae.
General and Physical Chemistry.r: Moles in $100\ \text{g}$: C $= 40/12 = 3.33$; H $= 6.7/1 = 6.7$; O $= 53.3/16 = 3.33$. Divide by $3.33$: $1: 2: 1$. Empirical formula $\text{CH}_2\text{O}$ (mass $30$). $n = 180/30 = 6$. Molecular formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$.

General and Physical Chemistry.q: State Bohr's postulates. Calculate the wavelength of the photon emitted when the electron of a hydrogen atom falls from $n = 3$ to $n = 2$ ($E_n = -13.6/n^{2}\ \text{eV}$; $hc = 1240\ \text{eV nm}$).
General and Physical Chemistry.r: Postulates: (i) electrons revolve in fixed circular orbits of definite energy without radiating; (ii) the angular momentum is quantized, $mvr = \dfrac{nh}{2\pi}$; (iii) energy is absorbed or emitted only when an electron jumps between orbits, $\Delta E = h\nu$. $\Delta E = 13.6\left(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{9}\right) = 13.6\times\dfrac{5}{36} = 1.89\ \text{eV}$. $\lambda = \dfrac{1240}{1.89} = 656\ \text{nm}$ (the red $\text{H}_\alpha$ line of the Balmer series).

General and Physical Chemistry.q: Write the four quantum numbers of the last electron of chlorine ($Z = 17$) and state why $n = 2$, $l = 2$ is not allowed.
General and Physical Chemistry.r: Cl: $1s^{2}2s^{2}2p^{6}3s^{2}3p^{5}$; the last electron is in $3p$: $n = 3$, $l = 1$. Filling the three $p$ orbitals ($m_l = -1, 0, +1$) with $\uparrow$ first and then pairing, the fifth electron has $m_l = 0$ and $m_s = -\tfrac{1}{2}$. For $n = 2$, $l$ may be only $0$ or $1$ ($l = 0$ to $n - 1$), so $l = 2$ is not allowed.

General and Physical Chemistry.q: Explain why the first ionization energy of nitrogen is higher than that of oxygen, and why that of magnesium is higher than that of aluminium.
General and Physical Chemistry.r: N: $2p^{3}$ is half-filled and extra stable; O: $2p^{4}$ has a paired electron, and pair repulsion makes it easier to remove, so $\text{IE}_{N} > \text{IE}_{O}$. Mg: $3s^{2}$ is a full subshell; Al: the outer electron is in the higher-energy, better shielded $3p$, so $\text{IE}_{Mg} > \text{IE}_{Al}$.

General and Physical Chemistry.q: Using VSEPR theory, predict and explain the shapes of $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, and account for their bond angles.
General and Physical Chemistry.r: Electron pairs around the central atom repel and arrange as far apart as possible. $\text{NH}_3$: four pairs (three bond, one lone), tetrahedral arrangement, trigonal pyramidal shape, angle $107^{\circ}$. $\text{H}_2\text{O}$: four pairs (two bond, two lone), tetrahedral arrangement, bent shape, angle $104.5^{\circ}$. Repulsion order: lone–lone $>$ lone–bond $>$ bond–bond, so lone pairs squeeze the angle below $109.5^{\circ}$ (more lone pairs, smaller angle).

General and Physical Chemistry.q: State Faraday's laws of electrolysis. Find the mass of copper deposited by a current of $2\ \text{A}$ in $30$ minutes from $\text{CuSO}_4$ solution ($1\ \text{F} = 96\,500\ \text{C}$).
General and Physical Chemistry.r: First law: the mass deposited is proportional to the charge passed, $m = ZIt$. Second law: for the same charge, masses deposited are proportional to equivalent masses. $Q = It = 2\times1800 = 3600\ \text{C}$. $\text{Cu}^{2+} + 2e^{-} \to \text{Cu}$: $63.5\ \text{g}$ needs $193\,000\ \text{C}$. $m = \dfrac{63.5\times3600}{193\,000} = 1.18\ \text{g}$.

General and Physical Chemistry.q: A gas occupies $500\ \text{cm}^{3}$ at $27^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $1\ \text{atm}$. Find its volume at STP, and state the law used.
General and Physical Chemistry.r: Charles' law with Boyle's law (combined gas law): $\dfrac{P_1V_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{P_2V_2}{T_2}$. $V_2 = \dfrac{500\times1\times273}{300\times1} = 455\ \text{cm}^{3}$.

General and Physical Chemistry.q: In the reaction $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}_2$ at equilibrium, $[\text{N}_2\text{O}_4] = 0.04\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ and $[\text{NO}_2] = 0.12\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$. Find $K_c$ and $K_p$ at $300\ \text{K}$ ($R = 0.0821\ \text{L atm mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$).

p: State Avogadro's law and deduce the relation between molecular mass and vapour density.

Propane burns as $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8 + 5\text{O}_2 \to 3\text{CO}_2 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$. For $11.2\ \text{L}$ of propane at STP, find the volume of oxygen needed, the volume of $\text{CO}_2$ formed, and the mass of water formed.
General and Physical Chemistry.r: (a) Equal volumes of all gases under the same conditions of temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules. Vapour density is the ratio of the mass of a volume of gas to the mass of the same volume of hydrogen, so $\text{V.D.} = \dfrac{M_{gas}}{M_{\text{H}_2}}$ (equal volumes contain equal molecules). The hydrogen molecule has mass $2$ (two atoms), so $\text{V.D.} = \dfrac{M}{2}$ and $M = 2\times\text{V.D.}$ (b) $11.2\ \text{L} = 0.5$ mol propane. Moles of $\text{O}_2 = 5\times0.5 = 2.5$ mol, volume $= 2.5\times22.4 = 56\ \text{L}$. Moles of $\text{CO}_2 = 3\times0.5 = 1.5$ mol, volume $= 33.6\ \text{L}$.

General and Physical Chemistry.q: Describe the shapes of $\text{BeF}_2$, $\text{BF}_3$, $\text{CH}_4$, $\text{PCl}_5$ and $\text{SF}_6$ using VSEPR theory and the hybridization of the central atom.
General and Physical Chemistry.r: The central atom's electron pairs spread out as far as possible; hybridization is the mixing of orbitals to describe the geometry.

p: Derive the ideal gas equation from Boyle's, Charles' and Avogadro's laws.
Find the pressure exerted by $4.4\ \text{g}$ of $\text{CO}_2$ in a $10\ \text{L}$ vessel at $27^{\circ}\text{C}$.
Why do real gases deviate from ideal behaviour?
State the law of mass action.
State the effect of pressure, temperature and a catalyst on $\text{N}_2 + 3\text{H}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3$ ($\Delta H < 0$).

General and Physical Chemistry.q: Which law states that the pressure of a gas is inversely proportional to its volume at constant temperature?
General and Physical Chemistry.w: Boyle's Law specifically describes the inverse relationship between pressure and volume at a constant temperature.

General and Physical Chemistry.q: What is the term used to describe the energy required to break the intermolecular forces and convert one mole of a solid into a liquid?
General and Physical Chemistry.w: Enthalpy of fusion is defined as the energy required to convert a solid into a liquid at its melting point.

General and Physical Chemistry.q: According to Raoult's Law, what happens to the vapor pressure of a solvent when a non-volatile solute is added?
General and Physical Chemistry.w: Raoult's Law states that the vapor pressure of a solvent in a solution is decreased by the presence of non-volatile solutes.

General and Physical Chemistry.q: Which statement best describes the third law of thermodynamics?
o: The entropy of a perfect crystal at absolute zero is exactly equal to zero.
Energy cannot be created nor destroyed.
The total entropy of an isolated system always increases over time.
Heat naturally flows from hot to cold bodies.
General and Physical Chemistry.w: The third law of thermodynamics asserts that the entropy of a perfect crystal at absolute zero is exactly equal to zero.

Inorganic Chemistry.q: Describe the preparation of ozone from oxygen, its structure, and the part played by chlorofluorocarbons in ozone layer depletion.
Inorganic Chemistry.r: Preparation: dry oxygen is passed through a silent electric discharge in an ozonizer: $3\text{O}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{O}_3$, $\Delta H = +285\ \text{kJ}$ (about $10$ % conversion). Structure: a bent resonance hybrid, $\text{O}-\text{O}$ bond length $128\ \text{pm}$, angle $117^{\circ}$. Depletion: UV breaks a CFC ($\text{CF}_2\text{Cl}_2 \to \text{CF}_2\text{Cl}\cdot + \text{Cl}\cdot$); then $\text{Cl}\cdot + \text{O}_3 \to \text{ClO}\cdot + \text{O}_2$ and $\text{ClO}\cdot + \text{O} \to \text{Cl}\cdot + \text{O}_2$. Chlorine is regenerated, so one atom destroys thousands of ozone molecules.

Inorganic Chemistry.q: Describe the laboratory preparation of ammonia, with the equation, the drying agent and the test for the gas.
Inorganic Chemistry.r: Heat a mixture of ammonium chloride and slaked lime: $2\text{NH}_4\text{Cl} + \text{Ca(OH)}_2 \to \text{CaCl}_2 + 2\text{NH}_3\uparrow + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. The gas is dried with quicklime (CaO) — not conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ or $\text{CaCl}_2$, which react with it. It is collected by downward displacement of air (lighter than air). Tests: it turns moist red litmus blue; a glass rod dipped in conc. HCl gives dense white fumes of $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$.

Inorganic Chemistry.q: Write the equations for the reaction of copper with
p: concentrated nitric acid, and state the role of the acid.
Inorganic Chemistry.r: (a) Dilute: $3\text{Cu} + 8\text{HNO}_3 \to 3\text{Cu(NO}_3)_2 + 2\text{NO}\uparrow + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$. (b) Concentrated: $\text{Cu} + 4\text{HNO}_3 \to \text{Cu(NO}_3)_2 + 2\text{NO}_2\uparrow + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (brown fumes). Nitric acid acts as an oxidizing agent: the nitrogen is reduced from $+5$ to $+2$ (dilute) or $+4$ (concentrated), while copper is oxidized from $0$ to $+2$.

Inorganic Chemistry.q: Describe the brown ring test for a nitrate, with equations.
Inorganic Chemistry.r: Add freshly prepared $\text{FeSO}_4$ solution to the nitrate solution, then pour conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ slowly down the side of the tube. Nitrate is reduced: $\text{NO}_3^{-} + 3\text{Fe}^{2+} + 4\text{H}^{+} \to \text{NO} + 3\text{Fe}^{3+} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. The NO combines with excess $\text{Fe}^{2+}$: $[\text{Fe(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+} + \text{NO} \to [\text{Fe(H}_2\text{O)}_5\text{NO}]^{2+} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. A brown ring appears at the junction of the two liquids.

Inorganic Chemistry.q: Describe the laboratory preparation of chlorine and show with equations that it is a stronger oxidizing agent than bromine and iodine.
Inorganic Chemistry.r: $\text{MnO}_2 + 4\text{HCl} \to \text{MnCl}_2 + \text{Cl}_2\uparrow + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (warm; the gas is washed with water and dried with conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, collected by upward displacement). Displacement: $\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{KBr} \to 2\text{KCl} + \text{Br}_2$ (orange); $\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{KI} \to 2\text{KCl} + \text{I}_2$ (violet in $\text{CCl}_4$). Chlorine displaces both, and $\text{Br}_2$ displaces $\text{I}_2$ but not $\text{Cl}^{-}$, so the order of oxidizing power is $\text{Cl}_2 > \text{Br}_2 > \text{I}_2$.

Inorganic Chemistry.q: Describe the preparation of hydrogen sulphide in Kipp's apparatus and give three of its reactions.
Inorganic Chemistry.r: In Kipp's apparatus iron(II) sulphide reacts with dilute acid: $\text{FeS} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \to \text{FeSO}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{S}\uparrow$. The gas has a rotten-egg smell. Reactions: (a) with copper sulphate: $\text{CuSO}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{S} \to \text{CuS}\downarrow + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ (black); (b) reducing action: $\text{H}_2\text{S} + \text{Cl}_2 \to 2\text{HCl} + \text{S}$; (c) burning: $2\text{H}_2\text{S} + 3\text{O}_2 \to 2\text{SO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Inorganic Chemistry.q: Distinguish between calcination and roasting with an example and equation of each, and state what slag is.
Inorganic Chemistry.r: Calcination: heating the ore in limited or no air to remove moisture and volatile matter, e.g. $\text{ZnCO}_3 \to \text{ZnO} + \text{CO}_2$. Roasting: heating the ore in excess air, e.g. $2\text{ZnS} + 3\text{O}_2 \to 2\text{ZnO} + 2\text{SO}_2$. Slag: the fusible product of the flux and gangue, e.g. $\text{CaO} + \text{SiO}_2 \to \text{CaSiO}_3$, which floats on the molten metal and is removed.

Inorganic Chemistry.q: Explain the trend in the thermal stability of the carbonates of Group 2 elements and the solubility of their sulphates.
Inorganic Chemistry.r: Carbonates decompose on heating, $\text{MCO}_3 \to \text{MO} + \text{CO}_2$, and the stability increases down the group ($\text{BeCO}_3 < \text{MgCO}_3 < \text{CaCO}_3 < \text{SrCO}_3 < \text{BaCO}_3$) because the larger cation polarizes the carbonate ion less. Sulphate solubility decreases down the group: $\text{BeSO}_4$ and $\text{MgSO}_4$ dissolve freely, $\text{CaSO}_4$ is sparingly soluble, and $\text{BaSO}_4$ is insoluble, because the lattice energy falls less quickly than the hydration energy.

Inorganic Chemistry.q: Describe the preparation and setting of plaster of Paris and give two uses.
Inorganic Chemistry.r: Gypsum is heated to about $120^{\circ}\text{C}$: $\text{CaSO}_4\cdot2\text{H}_2\text{O} \to \text{CaSO}_4\cdot\tfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_2\text{O} + 1\tfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_2\text{O}$. On mixing with water it sets to a hard mass as it re-forms gypsum: $\text{CaSO}_4\cdot\tfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_2\text{O} + 1\tfrac{1}{2}\text{H}_2\text{O} \to \text{CaSO}_4\cdot2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ with slight expansion. Uses: plaster for fractures, moulds and casts, wall plaster.

Inorganic Chemistry.q: Name the metal ions concerned in nerve impulses, in chlorophyll and in haemoglobin, and name two toxic metals with one effect each.
Inorganic Chemistry.r: Nerve impulses: $\text{Na}^{+}$ and $\text{K}^{+}$ (sodium–potassium pump). Chlorophyll: $\text{Mg}^{2+}$. Haemoglobin: $\text{Fe}^{2+}$. Toxic metals: mercury (Minamata disease, nerve damage); lead (damage to the brain and kidney, anaemia); arsenic (skin lesions and cancer); cadmium (Itai-itai disease, kidney damage).

Inorganic Chemistry.q: Describe the extraction of sodium by Down's process, with the reactions at each electrode.
Inorganic Chemistry.r: Raw material: fused sodium chloride (m.p. $801^{\circ}\text{C}$) mixed with calcium chloride, which lowers the melting point to about $600^{\circ}\text{C}$. Cell: a steel container lined with firebrick; a graphite anode at the centre; a circular iron cathode; a nickel gauze diaphragm between them to keep sodium and chlorine apart; an inverted trough above the cathode to collect sodium; a dome over the anode to collect chlorine. Reactions: anode: $2\text{Cl}^{-} \to \text{Cl}_2 + 2e^{-}$; cathode: $\text{Na}^{+} + e^{-} \to \text{Na}$. Overall: $2\text{NaCl} \to 2\text{Na} + \text{Cl}_2$. Molten sodium floats on the electrolyte and rises into the collector. By-product: chlorine.

Inorganic Chemistry.q: Describe the chemical properties of concentrated sulphuric acid as a dehydrating agent and an oxidizing agent, with equations.
Inorganic Chemistry.r: Dehydrating agent: it removes the elements of water. Sugar: $\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11} \rightarrow\ [\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4] 12\text{C} + 11\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (black carbon). Blue vitriol turns white: $\text{CuSO}_4\cdot5\text{H}_2\text{O} \to \text{CuSO}_4 + 5\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Ethanol gives ethene at $170^{\circ}\text{C}$. Oxidizing agent (hot, concentrated): $\text{Cu} + 2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \to \text{CuSO}_4 + \text{SO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$; $\text{C} + 2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \to \text{CO}_2 + 2\text{SO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$; $\text{S} + 2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \to 3\text{SO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Sulphur is reduced from $+6$ to $+4$.

Inorganic Chemistry.q: Compare the halogens chlorine, bromine and iodine in physical state, preparation from their salts, and displacement reactions, and describe the tests for chloride, bromide and iodide ions.
Inorganic Chemistry.r: State: $\text{Cl}_2$ greenish-yellow gas; $\text{Br}_2$ red-brown liquid; $\text{I}_2$ violet-black solid (sublimes). Preparation: $\text{MnO}_2 + 4\text{HCl} \to \text{MnCl}_2 + \text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$; $2\text{NaBr} + 3\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 + \text{MnO}_2 \to 2\text{NaHSO}_4 + \text{MnSO}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{Br}_2$; similarly iodide with $\text{MnO}_2$ and conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ gives $\text{I}_2$. Displacement: $\text{Cl}_2$ displaces $\text{Br}^{-}$ and $\text{I}^{-}$; $\text{Br}_2$ displaces $\text{I}^{-}$ only. Tests (with $\text{AgNO}_3$ then ammonia): $\text{Cl}^{-}$ white $\text{AgCl}$, soluble in dilute $\text{NH}_3$;

Organic Chemistry.q: Give the IUPAC names of $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}{=}\text{CHCH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{C}{\equiv}\text{CCH}_3$.
Describe the Lassaigne test for nitrogen, sulphur and chlorine in an organic compound.
Organic Chemistry.r: The organic compound is fused with a piece of sodium, the hot tube is plunged into distilled water, boiled and filtered; this is the sodium extract, containing $\text{NaCN}$, $\text{Na}_2\text{S}$ and $\text{NaCl}$. Nitrogen: boil with $\text{FeSO}_4$, acidify with dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$; a Prussian blue colour or precipitate shows N. Sulphur: add lead acetate solution; a black precipitate of PbS shows S. Chlorine: acidify with dilute $\text{HNO}_3$, add $\text{AgNO}_3$; a curdy white precipitate of AgCl, soluble in $\text{NH}_3$, shows Cl.

Organic Chemistry.q: Write all the structural isomers of $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ and name the type of isomerism between the alcohols and the ethers.
Organic Chemistry.r: Alcohols: butan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$; butan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$; 2-methylpropan-1-ol, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{OH}$; 2-methylpropan-2-ol, $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{COH}$. Ethers: ethoxyethane, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OC}_2\text{H}_5$; 1-methoxypropane, $\text{CH}_3\text{OCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$; 2-methoxypropane, $\text{CH}_3\text{OCH(CH}_3)_2$. That is seven isomers. Alcohols and ethers are functional isomers; butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol are position isomers; butan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-1-ol are chain isomers.

Organic Chemistry.q: Explain the inductive effect with examples of $+I$ and $-I$ groups, and use it to compare the acid strengths of acetic acid and chloroacetic acid.
Organic Chemistry.r: The inductive effect is the permanent displacement of the $\sigma$ electrons along a chain due to the electronegativity difference between atoms. Alkyl groups ($-\text{CH}_3$, $-\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$) push electrons ($+I$); $-\text{Cl}$, $-\text{NO}_2$ and $-\text{COOH}$ pull electrons ($-I$). In $\text{ClCH}_2\text{COOH}$ the chlorine withdraws electrons and stabilizes the carboxylate ion, so the acid ionizes more easily; in $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ the methyl group pushes electrons and destabilizes the anion. Hence chloroacetic acid is the stronger acid.

Organic Chemistry.q: Write the equations for four methods of preparing an alkane (ethane or methane).
Organic Chemistry.r: (i) Reduction of a haloalkane: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + 2[\text{H}] \rightarrow\ [\text{Zn/HCl}] \text{C}_2\text{H}_6 + \text{HBr}$. (ii) Wurtz reaction: $2\text{CH}_3\text{Br} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow\ [\text{dry ether}] \text{C}_2\text{H}_6 + 2\text{NaBr}$. (iii) Decarboxylation: $\text{CH}_3\text{COONa} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow\ [\text{CaO},\ \Delta] \text{CH}_4 + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$. (iv) Hydrogenation: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 + \text{H}_2 \rightarrow\ [\text{Ni},\ 573\ \text{K}] \text{C}_2\text{H}_6$. (v) Kolbe: $2\text{CH}_3\text{COONa} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow\ [\text{electrolysis}] \text{C}_2\text{H}_6 + 2\text{CO}_2 + 2\text{NaOH} + \text{H}_2$.

Organic Chemistry.q: State Markovnikov's rule and the peroxide effect, and give the products of the addition of HBr to propene in each case.
Organic Chemistry.r: Markovnikov: when an unsymmetrical reagent HX adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the hydrogen attaches to the carbon with more hydrogens already. $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}{=}\text{CH}_2 + \text{HBr} \to \text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_3$ (2-bromopropane, via the more stable secondary carbocation). Peroxide effect: in the presence of peroxide only HBr adds the opposite way (free-radical mechanism): $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}{=}\text{CH}_2 + \text{HBr} \rightarrow\ [\text{peroxide}] \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ (1-bromopropane).

Organic Chemistry.q: Explain the acidic nature of ethyne, with two reactions, and give a test to distinguish ethyne from ethene.
Organic Chemistry.r: The $sp$ carbon is more electronegative than $sp^{2}$ or $sp^{3}$ carbon ($50$ % $s$ character), so the terminal $\text{C}-\text{H}$ bond is polarized and its hydrogen is weakly acidic. (a) $2\text{HC}{\equiv}\text{CH} + 2\text{Na} \to 2\text{HC}{\equiv}\text{CNa} + \text{H}_2$. (b) $\text{HC}{\equiv}\text{CH} + 2[\text{Ag(NH}_3)_2]^{+}\text{OH}^{-} \to \text{AgC}{\equiv}\text{CAg}\downarrow + 4\text{NH}_3 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (white precipitate). Ethene gives no precipitate with ammoniacal $\text{AgNO}_3$, so this distinguishes ethyne from ethene.

Organic Chemistry.q: Describe Kekulé's structure of benzene and give the evidence for the resonance hybrid.
Organic Chemistry.r: Kekulé proposed a planar hexagon of six carbon atoms, each bonded to one hydrogen, with alternating single and double bonds, and a rapid shift between two forms. Limitations of the single structure: it predicts two different 1,2-disubstituted isomers (one across a single bond, one across a double bond), but only one is known; and it predicts addition reactions of the double bonds, but benzene undergoes substitution. Evidence for resonance: all six $\text{C}-\text{C}$ bonds are equal ($139\ \text{pm}$, between single $154$ and double $134$);

Organic Chemistry.q: Explain the mechanism of the nitration of benzene.
Organic Chemistry.r: Step 1: generation of the electrophile: $\text{HNO}_3 + 2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightleftharpoons \text{NO}_2^{+} + \text{H}_3\text{O}^{+} + 2\text{HSO}_4^{-}$. Step 2: attack of the $\pi$ electrons on $\text{NO}_2^{+}$ to form a resonance-stabilized carbocation (arenium ion). Step 3: loss of $\text{H}^{+}$ from the arenium ion restores the aromatic ring: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 + \text{HNO}_3 \rightarrow\ [\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4,\ 323\ \text{K}] \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Organic Chemistry.q: Write the equations for the Friedel–Crafts alkylation and acylation of benzene.
Organic Chemistry.r: Alkylation: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 + \text{CH}_3\text{Cl} \rightarrow\ [\text{anhyd. AlCl}_3] \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3 + \text{HCl}$ (toluene). Acylation: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 + \text{CH}_3\text{COCl} \rightarrow\ [\text{anhyd. AlCl}_3] \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3 + \text{HCl}$ (acetophenone). The $\text{AlCl}_3$ generates the electrophile $\text{R}^{+}$ or $\text{RCO}^{+}$.

Organic Chemistry.q: Describe three methods for the preparation of ethene and the reactions of ethene with $\text{HBr}$, water (acid-catalysed), ozone and cold alkaline $\text{KMnO}_4$.
Organic Chemistry.r: Preparation: (i) dehydration of ethanol: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} \rightarrow\ [\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4,\ 443\ \text{K}] \text{C}_2\text{H}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$; (ii) dehydrohalogenation: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br} + \text{KOH(alc.)} \to \text{C}_2\text{H}_4 + \text{KBr} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$; (iii) partial hydrogenation of ethyne: $\text{HC}{\equiv}\text{CH} + \text{H}_2 \rightarrow\ [\text{Pd/BaSO}_4\text{ (Lindlar)}] \text{C}_2\text{H}_4$. Reactions: with HBr: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 + \text{HBr} \to \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br}$; with water: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow\ [\text{H}^{+}] \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$;

Organic Chemistry.q: Describe the preparation of benzene (two methods) and its reactions: nitration, sulphonation, halogenation, hydrogenation and combustion.
Organic Chemistry.r: Preparation: (i) sodium benzoate heated with soda lime: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COONa} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow\ [\text{CaO},\ \Delta] \text{C}_6\text{H}_6 + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$; (ii) ethyne passed through a red-hot iron tube at $873\ \text{K}$: $3\text{C}_2\text{H}_2 \to \text{C}_6\text{H}_6$; (iii) phenol distilled with zinc dust: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{Zn} \to \text{C}_6\text{H}_6 + \text{ZnO}$. Reactions: nitration — conc. $\text{HNO}_3$ + conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, $323\ \text{K}$, nitrobenzene; sulphonation — fuming $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ gives benzenesulphonic acid, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{SO}_3\text{H}$;

Organic Chemistry.q: How will you convert
p: benzene to toluene? Give equations with conditions.
Organic Chemistry.r: (a) $\text{C}_2\text{H}_6 + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow\ [\text{UV}] \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl} + \text{HCl}$; then $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl} + \text{KOH(alc.)} \rightarrow\ [\Delta] \text{C}_2\text{H}_4 + \text{KCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. (b) $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 + \text{Br}_2 \to \text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$; then $\text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + 2\text{KOH(alc.)} \rightarrow\ [\Delta] \text{HC}{\equiv}\text{CH} + 2\text{KBr} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. (c) $\text{HC}{\equiv}\text{CH} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow\ [\text{HgSO}_4,\ \text{dil. H}_2\text{SO}_4,\ 333\ \text{K}] [\text{CH}_2{=}\text{CHOH}] \to \text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$ (the unstable enol rearranges).

Organic Chemistry.q: Which of the following statements best defines the term 'isomerism'?
o: A phenomenon where compounds have the same molecular formula but different structural arrangements.
A process where compounds undergo change in their state due to temperature variations.
A reaction where two molecules combine to form a single molecule.
A method of identifying elements based on their atomic number.
Organic Chemistry.w: Isomerism refers to compounds having the same molecular formula but different structures, not changes due to temperature or combination reactions.

Organic Chemistry.q: Which of the following represents the correct definition of 'functional group' in organic chemistry?
o: A specific group of atoms within a molecule that is responsible for the characteristic chemical reactions of that molecule.
A type of bond that connects different types of atoms within a molecule.
The arrangement of electrons around the nucleus of an atom within a molecule.
A process by which molecules change their structure under high pressure conditions.
Organic Chemistry.w: Functional groups determine the chemical properties of organic compounds due to their reactivity patterns.

Organic Chemistry.q: According to Zaitsev's rule, when an alkene is formed from an alcohol via dehydration, the product will be:
o: The alkene with the most substituted double bond.
The alkene with the least substituted double bond.
The alkene with the highest boiling point.
The alkene with the lowest boiling point.
Organic Chemistry.w: Zaitsev's rule predicts the formation of the most substituted alkene during elimination reactions, leading to greater stability.

Applied Chemistry.q: Describe the stages in producing a new chemical product, from the laboratory to the full-scale plant.
Applied Chemistry.r: (i) Research and development: the reaction is tested in the laboratory (yield, catalyst, conditions). (ii) Process design and economic evaluation: flow sheet, raw material and energy balance, cost estimate. (iii) Pilot plant: a small-scale unit tests the process, corrosion and safety. (iv) Full-scale plant: design, construction, commissioning and operation. (v) Marketing and monitoring of product quality and environmental impact.

Applied Chemistry.q: Distinguish between batch and continuous processes, with one example of each.
Applied Chemistry.r: Batch: the reactor is charged with a fixed amount of reactants, the reaction is completed, and the product is withdrawn before the next charge; suited to small-volume or varied products (dyes, drugs, soap). Continuous: feed enters and product leaves without interruption, in steady state; suited to large-volume products (ammonia, sulphuric acid). Continuous plants have lower labour cost per tonne and steadier quality; batch plants are more flexible.

Applied Chemistry.q: Distinguish between fixed capital and working capital in a chemical plant.
Applied Chemistry.r: Fixed capital: the money invested in land, buildings, machinery and installation; it is not consumed in production. Working capital: the money needed to run the plant from day to day — raw materials, wages, fuel, stocks and credit; it is recovered through sales. Total investment $=$ fixed capital $+$ working capital.

Applied Chemistry.q: List five environmental effects of the chemical industry and one control measure for each.
Applied Chemistry.r: Air: $\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{NO}_x$ cause acid rain (use scrubbers, desulphurization). Water: untreated effluent poisons rivers (effluent treatment plant). Soil: solid waste and heavy metals (secure landfill, recycling). Climate: $\text{CO}_2$ emission (energy efficiency, capture). Ozone: CFCs (replace with safer coolants). Also: eutrophication from fertilizer run-off (controlled use).

Applied Chemistry.q: Write the chemistry of Ostwald's process for nitric acid.
Applied Chemistry.r: (i) $4\text{NH}_3 + 5\text{O}_2 \rightarrow\ [\text{Pt–Rh gauze},\ 800^{\circ}\text{C}] 4\text{NO} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$, $\Delta H = -905\ \text{kJ}$. (ii) NO is cooled and oxidized: $2\text{NO} + \text{O}_2 \to 2\text{NO}_2$. (iii) $\text{NO}_2$ is absorbed in water in the presence of excess air: $4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \to 4\text{HNO}_3$ ($50$–$60\ \%$ acid, which can be concentrated by distillation with conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$).

Applied Chemistry.q: Write the reactions at each electrode in the diaphragm cell for sodium hydroxide, and name the function of the diaphragm.
Applied Chemistry.r: Brine is fed into the anode compartment. Anode (titanium or graphite): $2\text{Cl}^{-} \to \text{Cl}_2 + 2e^{-}$. Cathode (steel): $2\text{H}_2\text{O} + 2e^{-} \to \text{H}_2 + 2\text{OH}^{-}$. $\text{Na}^{+}$ passes through the diaphragm to give NaOH solution at the cathode. The porous asbestos diaphragm separates the two compartments and prevents $\text{Cl}_2$ from reacting with NaOH (which would give hypochlorite and chlorate) and prevents $\text{H}_2$ and $\text{Cl}_2$ from mixing explosively.

Applied Chemistry.q: Describe the manufacture of ammonia by Haber's process, giving the principle, the conditions with reasons, and a labelled flow sheet.
Applied Chemistry.r: Principle: $\text{N}_2 + 3\text{H}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3$, $\Delta H = -92\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. Raw materials: nitrogen from liquefied air; hydrogen from steam reforming of natural gas ($\text{CH}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \to \text{CO} + 3\text{H}_2$) or electrolysis of water. Conditions: $200$ atm (high pressure favours the side with fewer moles); $450$–$500^{\circ}\text{C}$ (a compromise between yield and rate); finely divided iron catalyst with Mo or $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ promoter; the poisons (e.g. sulphur compounds, CO) are removed from the gases first.

Chemistry: Unit-wise Subjective Question.q: The product of Wurtz reaction of $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ with sodium is
How many moles and how many molecules are in $5.6\ \text{L}$ of $\text{CO}_2$ at STP?
Write the electronic configuration of $\text{Cu}$ ($Z = 29$) and of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$, and state the number of unpaired electrons in each.
Chemistry: Unit-wise Subjective Question.r: Cu: $[\text{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^{1}$, one unpaired electron (the $4s$). $\text{Cu}^{2+}$: $[\text{Ar}]3d^{9}$, one unpaired electron.

Chemistry: Unit-wise Subjective Question.q: Write the structure and IUPAC name of the product when propene reacts with HBr in the presence of peroxide.
Describe the preparation and chemical properties of ammonia.
Chemistry: Unit-wise Subjective Question.r: Preparation: laboratory — $2\text{NH}_4\text{Cl} + \text{Ca(OH)}_2 \to \text{CaCl}_2 + 2\text{NH}_3 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$, dried with CaO; industrial — Haber process. Properties: colourless gas with a pungent smell, very soluble in water (fountain experiment), lighter than air; basic: $\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_4^{+} + \text{OH}^{-}$; $\text{NH}_3 + \text{HCl} \to \text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$; reducing: $2\text{NH}_3 + 3\text{CuO} \to 3\text{Cu} + \text{N}_2 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$; burns in oxygen with a yellowish flame, $4\text{NH}_3 + 3\text{O}_2 \to 2\text{N}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (with Pt catalyst, NO is formed);

Chemistry: Unit-wise Subjective Question.q: Explain Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations, and show how Bohr's model removed them.
Chemistry: Unit-wise Subjective Question.r: Rutherford: from $\alpha$-particle scattering by gold foil — most pass straight through, a few deflect, very few bounce back — he proposed a small, dense, positive nucleus with electrons revolving around it. Limitations: (i) a revolving electron should radiate energy continuously and spiral into the nucleus, making the atom unstable; (ii) it should give a continuous spectrum, but atoms give line spectra. Bohr's remedy: electrons move only in certain stationary orbits of fixed energy without radiating; angular momentum $mvr = nh/2\pi$; radiation is emitted or absorbed only when an electron jumps between orbits, $\Delta E = h\nu$, which explains the line spectrum of hydrogen.

Chemistry: Model Question Sets and Predi.q: Describe the manufacture of sulphuric acid by the contact process.
Chemistry: Model Question Sets and Predi.r: Stages: (i) burn sulphur or roast pyrites to get $\text{SO}_2$: $\text{S} + \text{O}_2 \to \text{SO}_2$; purify and dry the gas (impurities poison the catalyst). (ii) Pass $\text{SO}_2$ with excess air over $\text{V}_2\text{O}_5$ at $450^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $1$–$2$ atm: $2\text{SO}_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{SO}_3$, $\Delta H = -197\ \text{kJ}$; heat is removed with exchangers to favour the product. (iii) Absorb $\text{SO}_3$ in conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ ($98$ %) to give oleum, $\text{H}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_7$. (iv) Dilute the oleum with water to the required strength. Water is not used for direct absorption because it forms a mist of acid.

Chemistry: Model Question Sets and Predi.q: Describe benzene's structure and the evidence for resonance.
Chemistry: Model Question Sets and Predi.r: Benzene, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_6$, is a planar hexagon of six $sp^{2}$ carbons, each bonded to one hydrogen; the six unhybridized $p$ orbitals overlap sideways to give a delocalized $\pi$ cloud of six electrons above and below the ring. Kekulé's two forms (alternating double bonds) are resonance structures; the real molecule is a hybrid. Evidence: all C–C bonds are equal ($139\ \text{pm}$); only one 1,2-disubstituted product exists; the heat of hydrogenation ($-208\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) is about $150\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ less than three times that of cyclohexene ($-360$); benzene undergoes substitution, not addition, and does not decolourize bromine water or Baeyer's reagent.

State the modern periodic law. Explain, in terms of orbital filling, why the second period contains 8 elements while the fourth contains 18.
Classification of elements and Periodic.r: Properties are periodic functions of atomic number. Period 2 fills 2s and 2p only: 1 + 3 = 4 orbitals × 2 electrons = 8 elements. Period 4 fills 4s, then 3d, then 4p: 1 + 5 + 3 = 9 orbitals × 2 = 18 elements.

Classification of elements and Periodic.q: Define ionization energy. Why is the second ionization energy of sodium (4562 kJ mol⁻¹) nearly nine times the first (496 kJ mol⁻¹)?
Classification of elements and Periodic.r: IE₁ removes the 3s¹ electron from a neutral atom. IE₂ must break into the filled 2s²2p⁶ neon core of Na⁺, where the electron is in a lower shell, feels a much larger $Z_{\text{eff}}$ and must be pulled away from a positive ion. Hence the huge jump, and hence sodium's valency of 1.

Classification of elements and Periodic.q: Why is the electron affinity of fluorine smaller than that of chlorine even though fluorine is the more electronegative element? Distinguish clearly between electron affinity and electronegativity.
Classification of elements and Periodic.r: Adding an electron to the very small fluorine atom forces it into a compact 2p subshell where inter-electronic repulsion is severe; chlorine's 3p subshell is larger, so more energy is released (F 328, Cl 349 kJ mol⁻¹). Electron affinity is an energy (kJ mol⁻¹) belonging to an isolated gaseous atom; electronegativity is a dimensionless relative number describing a bonded atom's pull on a shared pair.

p: Classify the elements into s-, p-, d- and f-blocks, giving the general outer electronic configuration and one example of each.

Classification of elements and Periodic.r: (b) Radius falls steadily 186 → 99 pm because $Z_{\text{eff}}$ climbs from 2.20 to 6.10 while $n = 3$ throughout. IE₁ rises overall 496 → 1251 kJ mol⁻¹ but dips twice. Al (578) < Mg (738): aluminium's electron comes from 3p, which is higher in energy and shielded by the filled 3s². S (1000) < P (1012): phosphorus is 3p³, half-filled and stable, whereas sulphur is 3p⁴ with one repelling pair.

p: Define ionization energy, electron affinity and electronegativity, and state how each varies across a period and down a group, with the reason.

The last electron enters 3d, so it is a d-block element, and for groups 3–10 the group number = (number of d electrons) + (number of s electrons) = 6 + 2 = group 8. Common oxidation states +2 and +3.

Chemical equilibrium.q: Give any five characteristics of dynamic chemical equilibrium.

Chemical equilibrium.r: As derived in §8.5, using $p_i = [i]RT$. $K_p = K_c$ when $\Delta n = 0$.

Chemical equilibrium.q: For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), $K_c = 4.0\ \text{mol}^{-1}\text{L}$ at 1000 K. Calculate $K_p$ at the same temperature.

p: What is meant by dynamic chemical equilibrium? Distinguish it from physical equilibrium with one example of each.
State Le Chatelier's principle and apply it to the manufacture of ammonia by the Haber process, justifying the pressure, the temperature and the use of a catalyst.
Chemical equilibrium.r: (a) See §8.1 and §8.2 — physical equilibrium involves only a change of state (ice ⇌ water), chemical equilibrium forms new substances (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃). (b) Statement of the principle, then: $\Delta n = -2$ so high pressure (200 atm) increases the yield; the forward reaction is exothermic (ΔH = -92.4 kJ mol⁻¹) so a low temperature increases the yield but lowers the rate, hence the compromise at 450–500 °C; the iron catalyst does not change the yield, only the time taken to reach it.

Chemical equilibrium.w: The equilibrium constant is independent of the concentrations of reactants and products, it depends only on temperature.

Chemical equilibrium.w: A catalyst affects the rate of reaction but does not alter the equilibrium position.

Computer Science: Unit-wise Objective Qu.q: Write the difference between RAM and ROM. Give any three points.
Computer Science: Unit-wise Objective Qu.r: RAM is read-write and volatile (it loses data at power off), holds programs and data in use, and is made of SRAM and DRAM. ROM is read-only in normal use, non-volatile, and stores start-up instructions such as the BIOS; its types are PROM, EPROM and EEPROM. RAM is also usually larger and faster to write than ROM.

Computer Science: Unit-wise Objective Qu.q: Differentiate between a compiler and an interpreter.
Computer Science: Unit-wise Objective Qu.r: A compiler translates the whole program into object code before it runs, reports all errors together, and the code then runs fast without the compiler (C is compiled). An interpreter translates and runs one statement at a time, stops at the first error, and needs the interpreter present each time (BASIC and Python are commonly interpreted).

Computer Science: Unit-wise Objective Qu.q: What is a Trojan horse? State how it differs from a worm.
Computer Science: Unit-wise Objective Qu.r: A Trojan horse is a program that looks useful or harmless but secretly performs harmful acts, such as stealing passwords or opening a back door. It does not copy itself. A worm copies itself automatically across a network without a host program and without user action, and consumes bandwidth.

o: exclusive right to make a new invention

Computer Science: Unit-wise Subjective Q.r: The 1's complement inverts every bit; the 2's complement is the 1's complement plus 1. The 1's complement has two zeros (+0 and -0) while the 2's complement has one. In subtraction the 1's complement needs an end-around carry; the 2's complement just discards the carry. The 2's complement is therefore the one used inside modern computers.

Explain why NAND is called a universal gate.
Computer Science: Model Question Sets an.r: A gate is universal if every other gate can be made from it alone. With NAND: NOT is a NAND with both inputs joined ($A \cdot A$ complemented gives $A'$); AND is a NAND followed by a NOT; OR is a NAND of the two inverted inputs, since $(A' B')' = A + B$ by De Morgan. Because NOT, AND and OR can form any logic function, NAND alone is enough. NOR is universal in the same way.

Computer Science: Model Question Sets an.q: Write any five differences between a virus and a worm.
Computer Science: Model Question Sets an.r: A virus needs a host file; a worm is stand-alone. A virus spreads when a user runs or shares the infected file; a worm spreads by itself through network weaknesses. A virus mainly corrupts or deletes files; a worm mainly consumes bandwidth and memory. A virus is activated by human action; a worm needs none. Removing a virus means cleaning the host file; removing a worm means closing the hole it used and deleting the copies.

What is a bus? Describe the three types of bus in a computer system, stating the direction of each.
Computer System.r: A bus is a set of parallel wires carrying bits between the units of a computer. The address bus is unidirectional (CPU → memory/I/O) and carries the address of the location being accessed; $n$ lines give $2^{n}$ locations. The data bus is bidirectional and carries the actual data or instruction; its width normally equals the word length. The control bus carries individual timing and command signals (READ, WRITE, CLOCK, RESET, INTERRUPT) in both directions.

Computer System.q: Differentiate between RAM and ROM. Name and describe any three types of ROM.
A computer has a 32-bit address bus and a 64-bit data bus. Its clock runs at 4 GHz and one memory transfer takes 5 clock cycles. Find
p: the maximum addressable memory in GB if each location holds one byte,
the peak transfer rate in GB s⁻¹.
Computer System.r: (a) Locations $= 2^{32} = 4{,}294{,}967{,}296$; at one byte each that is $2^{32}/2^{30} = 4\ \text{GB}$. (b) $T = 1/(4\times10^{9}) = 0.25\ \text{ns}$. (c) One transfer takes $5 \times 0.25 = 1.25\ \text{ns}$ and moves 64 bits = 8 bytes, so the rate is $8/(1.25\times10^{-9}) = 6.4\times10^{9}\ \text{B s}^{-1} = 6.4\ \text{GB s}^{-1}$.

Computer System.q: Distinguish between OMR, OCR and MICR, giving one application of each.
Computer System.r: OMR senses whether a mark has been made in a fixed position by measuring reflected light — used for MCQ answer sheets. OCR recognises the shape of printed or handwritten characters and converts them to editable text — used to digitise books and forms. MICR reads characters printed in magnetic ink in the E-13B font — used for clearing bank cheques.

p: What is a microprocessor? Explain clock speed and word length, and state how each affects performance.

A processor has a clock speed of 3.2 GHz, a 16-bit data bus and a 28-bit address bus. Calculate the clock period, the memory it can address in MB, and the number of instructions executed per second if each instruction takes 8 clock cycles.
Computer System.r: (b) $T = 1/(3.2\times10^{9}) = 0.3125\ \text{ns}$. Addressable locations $= 2^{28} = 268{,}435{,}456$; at 16 bits = 2 bytes each, total $= 2^{28}\times 2 = 2^{29}\ \text{B} = 512\ \text{MB}$. One instruction takes $8 \times 0.3125 = 2.5\ \text{ns}$, so the rate is $1/(2.5\times10^{-9}) = 4\times10^{8}$ instructions per second = 400 MIPS.

Computer System.q: Explain the memory hierarchy of a computer. Compare cache, primary memory and secondary memory on speed, cost, capacity and volatility, and explain with an example why cache memory improves performance.
Computer System.r: Sketch the pyramid: registers, L1/L2/L3 cache, RAM, SSD, HDD, tape/cloud. Going down, capacity and cost per byte improve but access time worsens by roughly a factor of ten per level. Cache is small, fast, volatile SRAM; primary memory is larger, slower, volatile DRAM; secondary memory is largest, slowest and non-volatile. Cache works because of locality of reference — a loop executed a million times is fetched into cache once and then read at cache speed, so a 90 % hit rate can cut the average access time of a 1 ns cache and a 60 ns RAM to about $0.9(1) + 0.1(60) = 6.9\ \text{ns}$.

Computer Software and Operating System.r: Software is a set of programs, procedures and documentation that tells hardware what to do. System: Windows 11, device drivers. Utility: antivirus, WinRAR. Application: MS Word, Photoshop. Web-based: Gmail, Google Docs. Mobile apps: eSewa, Khalti.

Computer Software and Operating System.q: What is an operating system? Explain any five functions of an operating system.
Computer Software and Operating System.r: An OS is system software that acts as an interface between the user and the hardware and manages all resources. Five functions: process management, memory management, file management, device (I/O) management, and security and protection. (User-interface provision and error detection also earn the mark.)

Computer Software and Operating System.q: Differentiate between multiprogramming and multitasking, and between multiprocessing and distributed processing.
Computer Software and Operating System.r: Multiprogramming vs multitasking — both keep several programs in memory on one CPU, but multiprogramming switches only when the running program waits for I/O and aims at CPU utilisation, whereas multitasking switches after a fixed time slice and aims at response time. Multiprocessing vs distributed — multiprocessing uses two or more CPUs inside one computer sharing one memory; distributed processing uses many independent computers with their own memory linked by a network.

Computer Software and Operating System.q: What is a GUI? List any six features of the Windows operating system and compare a GUI with a CLI.

What is open source software? Write any four advantages of it and name four Linux distributions.
Computer Software and Operating System.r: Open source software publishes its source code under a licence allowing anyone to run, study, modify and redistribute it. Advantages: no licence cost; security flaws are found and fixed quickly because the code is public; it can be customised (for example for Nepali); no vendor lock-in. Distributions: Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, Linux Mint (also openSUSE, Arch, Kali).

p: Define an operating system and explain its role as a resource manager and as an extended machine.

Computer Software and Operating System.r: (b) Process management — scheduling the CPU among processes (Task Manager). Memory management — allocating RAM and virtual memory (Task Manager → Performance). File management — creating, organising and protecting files (File Explorer). Device management — drivers, buffering and spooling (Device Manager). Security — accounts, passwords, firewall, antivirus (Windows Security). Computer Software and Operating System.r: (b) Installing a printer: connect the printer by USB or to the Wi-Fi network and switch it on → Settings → Bluetooth & devices → Printers & scanners → Add device → Windows searches and installs the driver → if it is not found, click Add manually and supply the driver from the manufacturer's disc or website → print a test page. Android (Google, Linux kernel, open source, apps from Google Play); iOS (Apple, Darwin kernel, closed, runs only on Apple hardware); HarmonyOS (Huawei) or KaiOS (for feature phones). Differences from a desktop OS: touch-first interface, strict power management, sandboxed apps with permissions, app-store-only installation, and hardware that cannot be upgraded by the user.

Application Package.q: Differentiate between a relative, an absolute and a mixed cell reference with one example of each, and explain why absolute references are needed.
Application Package.r: Relative (B2) changes when the formula is copied — copying =B2*2 from C2 to C3 gives =B3*2. Absolute ($B$2) never changes, because the dollar signs lock both the column and the row. Mixed (B$2 or $B2) locks only one of the two. Absolute references are needed when a formula must always refer to one fixed cell, such as a rate of tax or a full-marks value, while being copied down a column.

Application Package.q: Define database, DBMS, field, record and primary key. Name two DBMS packages.
Application Package.r: A database is an organised collection of related data; a DBMS is the software that creates and manages it; a field is one column or attribute; a record is one complete row about one entity; a primary key is a field whose value is unique and never empty, so it identifies a record. Multimedia.w: tweening, short for in-betweening.

Multimedia.w: the eye holds an image for about 1/16 of a second.
