Multimedia.w: 2²⁴ ≈ 16.7 million.

Multimedia.q: Differentiate between linear and non-linear multimedia with two examples of each.
Multimedia.r: Linear multimedia plays from beginning to end in a fixed order with no user control — examples: a cinema film, an automatically playing slideshow. Non-linear multimedia lets the user choose what to see next through menus, buttons and links — examples: a website, a computer game. Linear content is easier and cheaper to produce; non-linear content holds attention longer and suits self-paced learning.

Multimedia.q: Differentiate between raster and vector graphics with any five points.
Multimedia.r: See the comparison table in §7.2: made of pixels against mathematical shapes; blurs when enlarged against stays sharp; large file size against small; suits photographs against suits logos and maps; JPEG/PNG/GIF/BMP against SVG/AI/EPS/CDR; Photoshop or GIMP against Illustrator or Inkscape.

Multimedia.q: What is animation? Explain any four types of animation.
Multimedia.r: Animation is the illusion of movement created by displaying a rapid sequence of still images that differ slightly, the images being drawn or computed rather than captured. Types: frame-by-frame (cel), where every frame is drawn separately; tweening, where only the key frames are drawn and the software fills in the rest; path animation, where an object follows a drawn path; and morphing, where one image is gradually transformed into another.

Multimedia.q: Explain the audio and video components of multimedia, naming three file formats and one piece of software for each.
Multimedia.r: Audio is digitised sound — narration, music and effects — produced by sampling an analogue wave, typically at 44,100 Hz and 16 bits. Formats: MP3 (lossy, small), WAV (uncompressed), MIDI (instructions, not a recording). Software: Audacity. Video is a sequence of frames captured from the real world with synchronised sound, measured in frames per second and always compressed by a codec. Formats: MP4, AVI, MKV. Software: Adobe Premiere Pro (or Kdenlive).

Multimedia.q: Calculate the uncompressed size, in megabytes, of a 1600 × 1200 image stored in 24-bit colour. Explain why compression is necessary.
Multimedia.r: 1600 × 1200 = 1,920,000 pixels. At 24 bits = 3 bytes per pixel, that is 5,760,000 bytes, and 5,760,000 ÷ (1024 × 1024) = 5.49 MB. Compression is necessary because uncompressed images and especially video are far too large to store in quantity or send over a network — one second of uncompressed 1080p video at 30 fps is about 178 MB, which no ordinary internet connection could stream.

p: Define multimedia and explain the five components with one example of each.
Explain any three hardware requirements and any three software requirements of a multimedia computer.
Multimedia.r: (b) Hardware: a fast processor to decode compressed video in real time; a graphics card (GPU) to render images and 3D scenes; a sound card with speakers, and large secondary storage because media files are huge; capture devices such as a microphone, scanner, webcam or digital camera. Software: an image editor such as GIMP; a sound editor such as Audacity; a video editor such as Kdenlive; media players and an authoring tool to combine everything.

p: Explain any six applications of multimedia, with one sentence on how multimedia helps in each.
State any two advantages and any two disadvantages of multimedia.
Multimedia.r: (b) Advantages: it uses sight and sound together, so people understand and remember more; the user controls the pace, which suits self-directed learning. Disadvantages: it needs expensive hardware, software and skill to produce; the files are very large, so sharing them needs fast internet and plenty of storage.

Multimedia.q: Define multimedia. Explain its five components with examples.
Explain the applications of multimedia and state its advantages and disadvantages.
What is animation? Explain its types and the principle behind it.

Information Security and Cyber Law.q: Which is not part of the CIA triad?
Malware that replicates itself across a network without needing a host file is a:
A fingerprint scanner authenticates using something you:
A digital signature is created by encrypting the message digest with the:
Software that is free to use but whose source code is not published is:
Under the Electronic Transactions Act 2063, unauthorised access to computer materials is an offence under section:
The maximum imprisonment for publishing illegal material in electronic form under the Act is:
Stealing a very small amount from a very large number of accounts is called a:
A first information report under the Electronic Transactions Act must be filed within:
Define information security and explain the CIA triad with one example of an attack on each corner.
Information Security and Cyber Law.r: Definition as in §8.2. Confidentiality — only authorised people may read the information; attacked by a keylogger capturing a password. Integrity — the information is not altered without permission; attacked by a student changing marks in a result database. Availability — the system is usable whenever a genuine user needs it; attacked by a DDoS flood that keeps real customers off a bank's website.

Information Security and Cyber Law.q: Differentiate between a virus, a worm and a Trojan horse. State any two symptoms of a malware infection.
Information Security and Cyber Law.r: A virus attaches itself to a host file or program and spreads only when that file is copied or executed. A worm is a standalone program that copies itself across a network by itself, needing neither a host nor any user action. A Trojan horse pretends to be a useful program so the user installs it willingly; it does not replicate but opens a back door. Symptoms: sudden slowdown; files disappearing or refusing to open; unexpected pop-ups; the antivirus being disabled; programs starting on their own.

Information Security and Cyber Law.q: What is a digital signature? Explain how it is created and how it is verified.
Information Security and Cyber Law.r: Definition as in §8.7. Creation: the sender passes the message through a hash function to get a short message digest, then encrypts that digest with their own private key; the result is the digital signature, which is sent along with the message. Verification: the receiver decrypts the signature with the sender's public key to recover digest A, independently hashes the received message to get digest B, and compares. If A equals B the message is genuine and unaltered; if not, either the message was changed or the signature is forged. This gives authentication, integrity and non-repudiation.

Information Security and Cyber Law.q: Define intellectual property right and explain its four types with one example of each.
Information Security and Cyber Law.r: Definition as in §8.6. Copyright — the expression of an idea, e.g. source code, a novel or a song; automatic on creation. Patent — a new and non-obvious invention or process, e.g. a new battery chemistry; must be granted. Trademark — a name, logo or slogan identifying a source, e.g. the Nepal Telecom logo. Trade secret — confidential commercial information, e.g. a search engine's ranking algorithm; protected only while kept secret.

Information Security and Cyber Law.q: List any five offences defined by the Electronic Transactions Act 2063, giving the section number and the maximum punishment for each.

p: Define cybercrime and explain any six types of cybercrime with one sentence each.
State any four measures an ordinary user can take to protect themselves from cybercrime.
Information Security and Cyber Law.r: (b) Any four of: use long, unique passwords and enable two-factor authentication; keep the operating system, browser and antivirus updated; never open attachments or click links in unexpected messages, and never share an OTP; check for https and read the domain name before entering anything private; keep regular off-site backups; use a firewall and log out of shared computers.

Information Security and Cyber Law.q: Define cybercrime. Explain its types and the measures to protect against it.
What is information security? Explain the CIA triad, the types of malware and the methods of protection.
Explain the Electronic Transactions Act 2063 and the ICT policy of Nepal. Critically examine them.
Which of the following is NOT a type of encryption algorithm used in information security?
Information Security and Cyber Law.w: SHA-256 is a hashing algorithm, not an encryption algorithm.

Information Security and Cyber Law.q: What does the principle of 'least privilege' in information security imply?
o: Users should have access to all resources needed for their tasks
Users should have minimum necessary permissions to perform their job functions
Administrators should always monitor user activities
Data should be encrypted with the strongest possible algorithms
Information Security and Cyber Law.w: The least privilege principle means that users should have only the permissions necessary for their job functions, minimizing potential damage from accidental or intentional misuse.

Information Security and Cyber Law.q: Which protocol is primarily responsible for secure web transactions by encrypting data between the browser and the server?
Information Security and Cyber Law.w: SSL/TLS protocols are designed to secure web transactions by encrypting data exchanged between a browser and a server.

What does the idiom spill the beans mean?

Compulsory English: Unit-wise Subjective.q: Why does Aksionov refuse to name Makar Semyonitch to the governor?
Compulsory English: Unit-wise Subjective.r: He does not want to bring punishment on another man, and after twenty-six years he has accepted his fate; the refusal shows his calm, humble and forgiving character.

Compulsory English: Unit-wise Subjective.q: What is the central idea of "Corona Says"?
Compulsory English: Unit-wise Subjective.r: The central idea is that humans, not the virus, are the greater destroyers of the earth, and that the pandemic has shown human equality and the earth's power to recover.

Compulsory English: Unit-wise Subjective.q: Why do the women in Trifles hide the dead canary?
Compulsory English: Unit-wise Subjective.r: They understand that the dead bird proves Mrs Wright's motive, and they sympathise with her loneliness, so they hide it to protect her from the men.

Compulsory English: Model Question Sets.q: What does the title "Trifles" mean in the play?
Compulsory English: Model Question Sets.r: "Trifles" means small, unimportant things. The men dismiss the women's interest in kitchen details as trifles, but those details solve the crime.

Compulsory English: Model Question Sets.q: Why is Jean unhappy in "Two Little Soldiers"?
Compulsory English: Model Question Sets.r: Jean is jealous and lonely because his friend Luc has started to meet a dairymaid, and he feels left out of the friendship.

Compulsory English: Model Question Sets.q: How does the poet describe the soldier's returned "gifts" in "The Gift in Wartime"?
Compulsory English: Model Question Sets.r: The "gifts" are the smell of blood, the soldier's body, medals and loneliness. Calling them gifts is ironic, because each one is a loss.

Compulsory English: Model Question Sets.q: Write a notice of about 50 words for the school notice board announcing an inter-house quiz competition.

The Selfish Giant.q: Why did the Giant build a wall around his garden?
The Selfish Giant.r: The Giant came home after seven years and found the village children playing in his garden. He believed that "my own garden is my own garden" and would allow nobody but himself to enjoy it, so he built a high wall and put up a notice-board warning that trespassers would be prosecuted.

The Selfish Giant.q: Who lived in the garden all the year round after the wall was built, and why were they pleased?
The Selfish Giant.r: The Snow and the Frost stayed all year, and they invited the North Wind and then the Hail. They were pleased because Spring had forgotten the garden, which left them free to live there permanently and spoil it — the Snow covering the grass, the Frost silvering the trees, the Hail breaking the roof slates.

The Selfish Giant.q: What made the Giant realise how selfish he had been?
The Selfish Giant.r: One morning he heard a linnet singing and looked out to see the children sitting in the blossoming trees, having crept in through a hole in the wall. In one corner a tiny boy was crying because he could not reach the branches. That sight made the Giant's heart melt and he said, "How selfish I have been!"

The Selfish Giant.q: Why did the little boy not run away when the Giant came into the garden?
The Selfish Giant.r: He did not run because his eyes were so full of tears that he simply did not see the Giant coming. On the symbolic level, his staying suggests that innocent love does not fear, and it is this one child who remains who becomes the means of the Giant's change and salvation.

The Selfish Giant.q: What did the Giant mean when he said that winter was "merely the Spring asleep"?
The Selfish Giant.r: He meant that winter is not death but a pause: the flowers are only resting under the ground and will come back. It shows how much he has changed — the man who once complained that Spring was late can now wait patiently, because he has learned that love, like spring, returns.

The Selfish Giant.q: What were the wounds on the little boy's hands and feet, and how did he explain them?
The Selfish Giant.r: There were the prints of two nails on his palms and two on his little feet — the marks of the Crucifixion. When the Giant angrily demanded who had dared to wound him, the child answered, "Nay! but these are the wounds of Love," identifying himself as Christ, who was wounded out of love for humankind.

The Selfish Giant.q: How does Wilde use the garden and the seasons to show the inner condition of the Giant?
The Selfish Giant.r: Wilde makes the garden a picture of the Giant's inner life, so that the reader can see his moral state. While the children are welcome, all four seasons work: blossom in spring, fruit in autumn, birds in the trees. The moment he builds the wall, the garden is cut off from the ordinary year and locked into a single season. Nature is personified to make the judgement clear — the birds "did not care to sing" where there were no children, the trees "forgot to blossom", and Autumn refuses fruit with the words, "He is too selfish." Snow, Frost, the North Wind and the Hail move in as guests, so that the Giant's chosen isolation is staffed by cold, noise and damage.

The Oval Portrait.q: How did the narrator come to notice the oval portrait?
The Oval Portrait.r: At midnight the narrator was displeased with the position of the tall candelabrum and reached out to move it so that its light fell better on his book. The candles then lit a niche that had been hidden in shadow by a bed-post, and the portrait appeared in vivid light.

The Oval Portrait.q: What exactly was it about the portrait that terrified the narrator?
The Oval Portrait.r: It was not the skill of the painting nor the beauty of the face, and he did not mistake it for a living woman. What appalled him was its "absolute life-likeliness of expression" — the picture seemed to be alive, and that impression first startled, then confused and finally overcame him.

The Oval Portrait.q: Why did the painter's wife hate Art?
The Oval Portrait.r: She hated Art because it was her rival. The painter already had a bride in his Art, and the palette and brushes took him away from her, so that she was deprived of her husband's company and even of his face. When he wished to paint her, she therefore heard it as terrible news.

The Oval Portrait.q: What does the narrator mean by his "incipient delirium", and why does Poe mention it?
The Oval Portrait.r: "Incipient delirium" means a fever-madness that is just beginning. Poe mentions it so that the reader cannot be certain whether the portrait is truly uncanny or whether the narrator's sick imagination is at work. This uncertainty deepens the fear and makes the narrator unreliable.

The Oval Portrait.q: Explain the irony in the painter's words, "This is indeed Life itself!"
The Oval Portrait.r: The painter believes he has captured life on canvas, and in that instant he has — but the life came out of his wife. He shouts his triumph over a woman who has just died, and the picture is "Life itself" only because she is no longer alive. Success and disaster arrive in the same moment.

The Oval Portrait.q: Discuss "The Oval Portrait" as a story about the conflict between art and life.
The Oval Portrait.r: Poe builds the story on a single idea: that a work of art may be paid for with a human life, and he presents it literally rather than as a figure of speech. The painter already has "a bride in his Art" before he marries; the living wife is therefore a second wife from the beginning, and she knows it, for she hates only the Art which is her rival and dreads the palette and brushes that steal her husband from her. When she begins to sit in the dark turret, the exchange starts. The narrator of the book tells us that the painter "would not see" that the light withered her, and would not see that the tints he spread on the canvas were "drawn from the cheeks of her who sate beside him".

The Oval Portrait.q: Explain how Poe uses the frame narrative and the Gothic setting to produce his single effect of dread.

God Sees the Truth but Waits.q: What dream did Aksionov's wife have, and how did he react to it?
God Sees the Truth but Waits.r: She dreamt that he returned from the town and that when he took off his cap his hair had turned completely grey, and she begged him not to start that day. Aksionov laughed at her fear, joked that she was afraid he would go on a spree at the fair, called the dream a lucky sign and drove away.

God Sees the Truth but Waits.q: What evidence convinced the police-officer that Aksionov was the murderer?
God Sees the Truth but Waits.r: The police-officer found a blood-stained knife in Aksionov's bag. Added to this were the facts that Aksionov had slept in the room next to the murdered merchant, that the house was locked from inside, and that he had left the inn before dawn. His pale face and broken voice were taken as further proof.

God Sees the Truth but Waits.q: Why did Aksionov stop sending petitions to the Czar?
God Sees the Truth but Waits.r: Because his own wife asked him whether he had really committed the murder. Once the person closest to him doubted him, he decided that only God could know the truth and that it was to God alone he should appeal. He gave up all hope of help from men and simply prayed.

God Sees the Truth but Waits.q: How did Makar Semyonich betray, without meaning to, that he knew about the murder?
God Sees the Truth but Waits.r: He laughed at the idea that anyone could have hidden a knife in the bag under a sleeping man's head without waking him — a detail only the murderer could know. He also exclaimed how wonderful it was that they should meet, and asked how Aksionov had grown so old, but refused to explain his surprise.

God Sees the Truth but Waits.q: Why did Aksionov refuse to tell the Governor who had dug the tunnel?
God Sees the Truth but Waits.r: Telling the truth would have had Makar flogged almost to death, and Aksionov would not take that revenge. He replied that it was not God's will that he should tell, and that the Governor could do as he liked with him. He had also decided, after Makar's threat, to leave the matter "as God shall direct".

God Sees the Truth but Waits.q: What happened to Aksionov after Makar confessed to the authorities?
God Sees the Truth but Waits.r: Nothing that could help him. Makar confessed his guilt in spite of Aksionov's words, but by the time the official order for Aksionov's release arrived, Aksionov was already dead. His innocence was proved only after his death.

God Sees the Truth but Waits.q: Discuss the theme of forgiveness in "God Sees the Truth, but Waits".
God Sees the Truth but Waits.r: Forgiveness in this story is not a polite word but a costly act, and Tolstoy builds the whole plot so that we can measure its cost. Aksionov has lost twenty-six years, his business, his wife and his children to a crime he did not commit, and he knows exactly who is responsible. When the escape tunnel is discovered, he is given a perfect revenge: a lawful authority asks him a direct question, and one honest sentence would have had Makar flogged nearly to death, with nobody able to blame the informer. He refuses, saying only, "It is not God's will that I should tell." The second and greater act comes that night.

God Sees the Truth but Waits.q: Justify the title of the story with reference to its events.
God Sees the Truth but Waits.r: The title is a Russian proverb, and the story is arranged to prove both halves of it. "God sees the truth": from the first night, the truth about the murder exists and is known — by Makar Semyonich, and, in the story's religious sense, by God. No human being sees it. The police-officer is honest and completely wrong; the court convicts on a knife and a frightened face; even Aksionov's wife suspects him. The second half of the proverb is the harder one: "but waits". The truth is not spoken for twenty-six years. During that time an innocent man is flogged, sent to the mines, loses his wife and is forgotten by his children. Tolstoy refuses to soften this.

The Wish.q: What is the boy doing at the beginning of the story, and what does it show about him?
The Wish.r: He is sitting alone at the foot of the stairs, carefully picking the scab off his knee and examining the clean pink skin underneath. It shows that he is solitary, patient and closely interested in small, slightly unpleasant things — exactly the kind of attention he will soon turn on the carpet.

The Wish.q: What rules does the boy make for his game on the carpet?
The Wish.r: The black parts of the carpet are poisonous snakes, the red parts are red-hot lumps of coal, and only the yellow parts are safe. If he touches black he will be bitten and die; if he touches red he will be burnt. He must cross the whole carpet stepping on yellow alone.

The Wish.q: What prize has the boy promised himself for crossing the carpet successfully?
The Wish.r: He has decided that if he crosses the carpet without a single mistake, he will be given a puppy for his birthday, which falls the very next day. The smallness of this reward, set against the death he has imagined for himself, is one of the story's quiet ironies.

The Wish.q: How does Dahl show that the game has stopped being a game for the boy?
The Wish.r: Dahl stops describing what the boy pretends and starts describing what he sees: the snakes appear to stir, raise their heads and watch him, and the red looks genuinely hot. At the same time the boy's body reacts — his breathing quickens and he feels dizzy and frightened — which shows that he now believes in the danger.

The Wish.q: Why is the last stretch across the black band impossible for him?
The Wish.r: A wide band of black lies across his route, and the nearest yellow patch on the far side is further away than a normal step. He can only reach it by an enormous stretch, with one foot behind and his weight hanging over the black, which leaves him no way to recover if he wobbles.

The Wish.q: Why does Dahl end the story with the mother outside in the sunshine?
The Wish.r: Because the sudden distance is more frightening than any description of what happened. After a whole story spent inside the boy's mind, the reader is pushed outside into warm daylight, where an ordinary mother is looking for a child she cannot find. Dahl explains nothing, and the silence does the work.

The Wish.q: How does Roald Dahl build tension in "The Wish"? Discuss the techniques he uses.
The Wish.r: Dahl builds tension out of materials that are completely harmless, which is why the effect is so striking. First he establishes the rules, and makes them absolute: black means snakes and death before teatime, red means burning, yellow alone is safe. Because the reader accepts the rules, every later step can be measured against them. Second, he arranges the physical difficulty in a rising order. The early steps are simple; then the yellow patches narrow, so the boy must balance on tiptoe and on one foot; and finally a wide band of black demands a stretch no child of his size can make.

Civil Peace.q: What are Jonathan Iwegbu's five "inestimable blessings"?
Civil Peace.r: They are five heads that survived the war: his own, his wife Maria's, and those of three of his four children. The fourth child died. He counts survival itself as wealth, which shows both his gratitude and how much the war destroyed.

Civil Peace.q: Why does Jonathan treat his bicycle as a blessing, and how did he save it?
Civil Peace.r: The bicycle is the machine that restarts his life: used as a taxi between the camps and the military cemetery, it earns him a hundred and fifteen pounds in two weeks. He saved it during the war by paying two pounds to an officer who wanted to commandeer it, and then burying it in the ground until the fighting was over.

Civil Peace.q: How does the Iwegbu family earn a living after they return to Enugu?
Civil Peace.r: Everyone works. Jonathan rides his bicycle as a taxi and later opens a bar selling palm-wine in his house; Maria makes and sells akara balls; and the children pick mangoes and sell them to soldiers' wives. His old job at the coal mine no longer exists.

Civil Peace.q: What is the "egg-rasher", and how much is it?
Civil Peace.r: It is the crowd's pronunciation of "ex-gratia award", a payment of twenty pounds made by the treasury to anyone who handed in the now worthless Biafran currency. Jonathan queues for his and receives it, and it is exactly this money the thieves demand that night.

Civil Peace.q: What happens when Jonathan's family shouts for help during the robbery?
Civil Peace.r: Nothing happens. They call for neighbours, police and soldiers, and no one answers. The leader of the thieves then shouts for the police himself, in mockery, to prove to Jonathan that there is no help anywhere in the neighbourhood.

Civil Peace.q: How does Jonathan react to the loss of his money the next morning?
Civil Peace.r: He refuses to be upset. He tells the sympathising neighbours not to trouble themselves, saying that the money came to him from nowhere only a few days before, so that losing it means nothing to him; and he repeats "Nothing puzzles God." He and his family are already back at work.

Civil Peace.q: Why is the story called "Civil Peace"? Discuss the irony of the title.
Civil Peace.r: The title is ironic from beginning to end. It comes from the thief himself, who tells Jonathan through the locked door that the civil war is finished and that this time it is "Civil Peace" — meaning that nobody need be killed provided the money is handed out. Achebe's point is that for ordinary Nigerians the end of the fighting brought a change of name rather than a change of condition. In the official version, peace has returned: the treasury is paying awards, offices are open, the government has won.

Civil Peace.q: Discuss "Civil Peace" as a picture of a society just after a war.
Civil Peace.r: Achebe's post-war Nigeria is drawn in a handful of exact details, and every one of them tells us something. Physically, the country is broken: houses lie in rubble, and Jonathan's flimsy zinc house survives when stronger ones did not, so that survival looks arbitrary rather than deserved. Economically, it is in collapse: the coal mine cannot say when it will reopen, the Biafran currency is waste paper, and the government's answer is a flat twenty-pound award for everyone. Whole families therefore live on tiny trades — mangoes, fried akara, palm-wine, a bicycle taxi that earns its money carrying people to and from a military cemetery. Socially, the most disturbing fact is the silence.

Two Little Soldiers.q: Why do the two soldiers go to the same place every Sunday?
Two Little Soldiers.r: Because the place at the edge of the wood of Champioux reminds them of Brittany. The trees recall the forest of Kermarivan, a large stone recalls the dolmen of Locneuven, and the fields look like Plounivon. Being homesick conscripts, they feel happy nowhere else.

Two Little Soldiers.q: Describe the two soldiers' Sunday meal.
Two Little Soldiers.r: They buy a piece of sausage, a few cents' worth of bread and a quart of wine in Bezons and carry it wrapped in their handkerchiefs. At their usual corner they take two bricks out of a hedge, light a fire of dry branches and roast the sausage on the points of their knives, then lie on the grass side by side.

Two Little Soldiers.q: How does the dairymaid first show kindness to the soldiers?
Two Little Soldiers.r: Seeing that they always sit in the same spot, she speaks to them and teases them gently; then, returning with her pail full, she offers them milk, saying it will remind them of home. She has guessed exactly what they are missing, and both soldiers are moved.

Two Little Soldiers.q: What does Luc do during the week that puzzles Jean?
Two Little Soldiers.r: He obtains leave on a Tuesday and does not come back until ten at night, and then borrows ten sous from a comrade and takes leave again on the Friday. On Sunday he seems strange and disturbed. Jean notices all this, suspects something, but cannot guess that Luc has been meeting the dairymaid.

Two Little Soldiers.q: Why is the sentence "She did not offer him any milk that day" important?
Two Little Soldiers.r: Because it is the moment Jean's exclusion becomes complete. The milk had been the sign that the girl treated the two friends alike and understood their homesickness; withholding it, with only a careless nod, tells him wordlessly that he is now outside. Maupassant replaces any description of Jean's despair with this one small omission.

Two Little Soldiers.q: How does the story end, and what is the last line?
Two Little Soldiers.r: On the walk home they stop on the bridge at Bezons as they always do. Jean leans further and further over the railing, as if hypnotised by the water, and falls into the Seine; boatmen recover his body the same day. Luc, weeping, reports it at the barracks as an accident, and the story ends with the line "If he had only known."

Two Little Soldiers.q: Discuss "Two Little Soldiers" as a study of homesickness and friendship.
Two Little Soldiers.r: Everything the two soldiers value in the story is a substitute for Brittany. They are conscripts from a fishing and farming country, shut up in a barracks at Courbevoie, and their one pleasure is a walk to a wood that resembles the forest of Kermarivan. On the way they stop on the bridge to watch white sails that recall their fishing boats; they halt at a stone because it is like the dolmen of Locneuven; Jean says every week that the fields are just like Plounivon; and the dairymaid's milk is welcome mainly because, as she says, it will remind them of home. Maupassant sums up their condition in a single simile — the slow sorrow of a captive animal that remembers its freedom.

Two Little Soldiers.q: How does Maupassant prepare the reader for the ending of the story?
Two Little Soldiers.r: The ending is shocking but not sudden, because almost every element of it has already been planted. The bridge at Bezons is introduced in the third paragraph, and we are told that the soldiers always stop there for several minutes, bending over the railing to watch the Seine. The reader therefore accepts the final pause on the bridge as ordinary, which is precisely why it is dangerous. Maupassant also establishes the men's total silence: they walk for long stretches without a word, and their faces never betray anything, so that when Jean is destroyed we are warned that nothing will be said about it.

An Astrologer's Day.q: What does the astrologer's "professional equipment" consist of, and why does he need it?
An Astrologer's Day.r: It consists of a dozen cowrie shells, a square piece of cloth covered with mystic charts, a notebook and palmyra writing, together with the sacred ash and vermilion on his forehead and a saffron turban. None of it has any use except display: it makes him look like a holy man with occult knowledge, and so it draws customers to his mat.

An Astrologer's Day.q: How does the astrologer manage to satisfy his customers without knowing astrology?
An Astrologer's Day.r: He relies on shrewd guesswork rather than the stars. He lets the customer talk for about ten minutes first, watches him closely, and then gives advice based on what Narayan calls a working analysis of mankind's troubles — marriage, money and the tangles of human ties. Since his answers are flattering and sensible, the customers go away satisfied.

An Astrologer's Day.q: What is the wager between the astrologer and Guru Nayak?
An Astrologer's Day.r: Guru Nayak challenges him to say something worth hearing. They agree that if the astrologer answers his questions correctly he will be paid a rupee, and that if he is proved wrong he must pay back double. Guru Nayak grips his wrist to hold him to the terms.

An Astrologer's Day.q: Why does the astrologer try to back out of the bargain after the match is struck?
An Astrologer's Day.r: Because the flame of the match lights the stranger's face, and the astrologer recognises the man he stabbed and threw into a well years before in his own village. He realises he is sitting in front of someone who has come to kill him, and he wants to get away before he is recognised in turn.

An Astrologer's Day.q: What advice does the astrologer give Guru Nayak at the end of the reading, and why?
An Astrologer's Day.r: He tells him that the man he has been hunting was crushed under a lorry four months ago in a far-off town, and warns him to go home at once and never travel southward again, promising that he will then live to be a hundred. The advice is a lie, and its purpose is to keep Guru Nayak permanently away from the town where his attacker actually lives.

An Astrologer's Day.q: Why does the astrologer say that a great load has gone off him?
An Astrologer's Day.r: Because he has discovered that Guru Nayak is alive. For years he had believed he had killed a man in his village and had been living with the fear and guilt of it — indeed it was why he ran away, changed his life and became an astrologer. Meeting his victim alive removes that burden at a stroke, and he goes to bed calm enough to yawn.

An Astrologer's Day.q: Discuss the irony in "An Astrologer's Day".
An Astrologer's Day.r: Irony is not one feature of this story; it is the whole design. The largest example is situational. The astrologer is an admitted fraud who, as Narayan tells us on the first page, knows nothing whatever about the stars — and yet the reading he gives Guru Nayak is entirely accurate, down to the knife, the well and the man's own name. He can be accurate for one reason only: he is the criminal. A second irony follows immediately. Guru Nayak has spent years searching for the man who tried to kill him, and he pays that very man twelve and a half annas to be told that his enemy is dead; the victim finances his own deception, and goes away pleased.

An Astrologer's Day.q: How does Narayan prepare the reader for the twist at the end of the story?
An Astrologer's Day.r: Narayan plays fair with the reader. Every fact needed for the ending is supplied early, but none of it is emphasised. In the opening pages we are told plainly that the astrologer has no knowledge of the stars, which is what makes the later accuracy of his reading significant rather than magical. We are also told, almost in passing, that he had never intended to take up this work, that he would otherwise have lived and died a farmer, and that he left his village abruptly without telling anybody — three sentences that mean nothing on a first reading and everything on a second.

Corona Says.q: Who is the speaker in "Corona Says", and who is being addressed?
Corona Says.r: The speaker is the coronavirus itself, given a human voice by the poet. It addresses the whole human race — the repeated "you" of the poem. The poet himself never speaks directly; his opinion reaches us only through what the virus says.

Corona Says.q: What charges does the virus bring against human beings?
Corona Says.r: The virus accuses human beings of cutting down forests, poisoning rivers and the air, hunting, caging and killing other creatures, and destroying millions of their own kind in wars. Its point is that all this damage was deliberate, long-lasting and far greater than the harm a virus can do.

Corona Says.q: What changes in nature does the speaker point to as evidence for its argument?
Corona Says.r: During the lockdown the air became clear, the rivers ran cleaner, and birds and wild animals reappeared in places from which people had driven them. The earth recovered as soon as human activity stopped, which supports the virus's claim that human beings, not viruses, are the planet's real problem.

Corona Says.q: Why has the poet chosen free verse instead of a regular metre?
Corona Says.r: Free verse has no fixed metre or rhyme, so the poem sounds like ordinary speech rather than a song. That plain, calm, conversational voice makes the virus's accusation sound reasonable, and keeps the reader's attention on the terrible content instead of on pretty sound patterns.

Corona Says.q: What is a dramatic monologue? Show how "Corona Says" fits the definition.
Corona Says.r: A dramatic monologue is a poem in which an invented speaker, who is not the poet, talks at length to a silent listener whose presence we infer from the speech. In "Corona Says" the invented speaker is the virus, the silent listener is humankind, and we learn what humankind feels ("you hate me") only from the virus's words.

Corona Says.q: Discuss "Corona Says" as a satire on modern human civilisation.
Corona Says.r: Satire attacks human folly and wrongdoing by holding it up to ridicule, and that is precisely what this poem does. Its satirical method is to give the speech to the coronavirus, so that human behaviour is described from outside by somebody with no reason to flatter us. The targets are exact. First, our hypocrisy: we call the virus a murderer while conducting wars and slaughtering other species. Second, our arrogance: we believed money, technology, armies and borders had made us masters of the earth, and an organism too small to see undid that belief in weeks.

Corona Says.q: The speaker tells human beings that it does not ask whether a body belongs to a rich person or a poor one, to one religion or another, before it enters.
p: What quality of the speaker is being described here?
What comment on human society does this make?
Corona Says.r: (a) The speaker is the coronavirus, which the poet has personified and allowed to address humankind throughout the poem. (b) It describes the virus's complete indifference to human distinctions. It infects anyone, and wealth, power, caste, colour, nationality and religion give no protection. This is why the poem presents it as the one true equaliser. (c) The comment is a bitter one about human hypocrisy. Human society claims that all people are equal, yet it is organised by exactly the differences the virus ignores. It has taken a disease to give human beings the equality their own declarations promise but their behaviour denies.

A Red, Red Rose.q: What impossible conditions does the speaker use to describe how long he will love?
A Red, Red Rose.r: He says he will love her till all the seas run dry, till the rocks melt in the sun, and for as long as the sands of his own life keep running. Since none of the first two can happen, the vow means "for ever", measured against the age of the earth and then against his own lifetime.

A Red, Red Rose.q: Why does Burns write in the Scots dialect?
A Red, Red Rose.r: Scots was the everyday speech of the Ayrshire country people Burns lived and worked among. Using it keeps the poem close to real speech and to oral folk song, gives it a distinct music ("gang", "bonnie", "a'"), and asserts the dignity of ordinary Scottish life at a time when poets were expected to write polished English.

All the World's a Stage.q: Who speaks these lines, and in which play and scene do they occur?
All the World's a Stage.r: The lines are spoken by Jaques, the melancholy lord, in Shakespeare's comedy As You Like It, Act II, Scene vii. He speaks them in the Forest of Arden, to the banished Duke Senior and his followers, taking up an image the Duke has just used.

All the World's a Stage.q: List the seven ages of man in the correct order.
All the World's a Stage.r: Infant, schoolboy, lover, soldier, justice (judge), pantaloon (the lean slippered old man), and second childishness or oblivion.

All the World's a Stage.q: What does Shakespeare mean by "the bubble reputation"?
All the World's a Stage.r: It is a metaphor for fame won in battle. A bubble is bright and round and attractive, but weightless and certain to burst in a moment. The soldier will face the mouth of a cannon for something that empty, which is Shakespeare's comment on military glory.

All the World's a Stage.q: How is the schoolboy described, and what does the description suggest?
All the World's a Stage.r: He is described with his satchel and "shining morning face", "creeping like snail / Unwillingly to school". The washed, bright face shows he has been carefully prepared by others, while the snail simile shows that he has no wish to go. The gap between the two is the comedy of the second age.

All the World's a Stage.q: Why is the last age called "second childishness"?
All the World's a Stage.r: Because the very old man returns to the condition of the infant he once was. He cannot feed or look after himself, his voice has climbed back to a child's high treble, and finally memory and the senses go. Life is therefore shown as a circle rather than a straight line.

All the World's a Stage.q: Explain the effect of the repeated word "sans" in the final line.
All the World's a Stage.r: "Sans" means "without", and it is repeated four times in one short line. Each repetition removes something more — teeth, eyes, taste, and then "everything". The rhythm of the line therefore imitates the process it describes: loss after loss, until nothing at all is left.

All the World's a Stage.q: Describe the seven ages of man as Shakespeare presents them, and show how the pictures are chosen to build a single argument.
All the World's a Stage.r: Jaques presents seven pictures in time order. The infant is helpless, "Mewling and puking in the nurse's arms". The schoolboy, with satchel and shining morning face, creeps "like snail / Unwillingly to school". The lover sighs "like furnace" and writes a sad ballad to his mistress's eyebrow. The soldier, bearded like the leopard and quick to quarrel, chases "the bubble reputation" even at the cannon's mouth. The justice, with a fair round belly lined with capon and a formally cut beard, hands out borrowed wisdom in the form of "wise saws and modern instances".

All the World's a Stage.q: Discuss "All the World's a Stage" as an extended metaphor. How far do you agree that life is a performance?
All the World's a Stage.r: The speech is built on a single comparison carried through to the end, which is what an extended metaphor means. The world becomes a stage, men and women become "merely players", birth and death become "entrances" and "exits", and a lifetime becomes a play in seven acts. Once the metaphor is set, every detail follows from it: each age arrives with a costume (satchel, beard, spectacles, slippers), a voice (mewling, sighing, swearing, piping) and a set of lines (the ballad, the oaths, the proverbs).

Who are you, little i?.q: What is the child doing, and where?
Who are you, little i?.r: He is "peering" — looking hard and with concentration — out of a high window, watching the gold of a November sunset. He is alone, still, and completely absorbed in what he sees.

Who are you, little i?.q: Why does the poet choose a November sunset rather than a summer one?
Who are you, little i?.r: November is late autumn in the northern hemisphere, the last month before winter, so the year itself is ending. Putting the day's ending inside the year's ending doubles the idea of things drawing to a close, and prepares us for the poem's real subject, the end of a life.

Who are you, little i?.q: Why is the pronoun "i" written in lower case?
Who are you, little i?.r: To make the self small and humble. A capital "I" would put the speaker at the centre of the poem; the lower-case "i" matches the size of a five-year-old child at a high window and keeps him in proportion to the enormous sunset he is watching. It is one of Cummings's trademark devices, not an error.

Who are you, little i?.q: What is the effect of putting the last three lines inside brackets?
Who are you, little i?.r: The brackets turn the last three lines into a private, inner voice — the child's own feeling, thought rather than spoken. We seem to overhear it instead of being told it, which makes the poem's large statement about death sound gentle and unforced.

Who are you, little i?.q: Discuss the significance of the sunset in "who are you,little i".
Who are you, little i?.r: The sunset is the centre of the poem and its main symbol. On the surface it is simply what the child can see: the gold of the sky at the end of a November afternoon, watched from an upstairs window. But every detail is chosen to make it mean more. It is a sunset, the oldest image in poetry for the close of a life. It is in November, so the year is in its own late afternoon, with winter next. The only colour named is gold, which turns the fading light into something precious rather than something lost. And it is watched through a window, which frames it like a picture and keeps the small watcher separate from the vast sky.

Who are you, little i?.q: The child, watching the last gold light of a November evening, feels that if the day has to turn into night, this is a beautiful way for it to happen.
p: What is the child looking at?
What larger meaning does this carry?
Why are these lines placed inside brackets?
Who are you, little i?.r: (a) He is looking through a high window at the gold of a November sunset — the last light of a late-autumn day. (b) The sunset is a symbol for the end of a life, and November, the last month before winter, doubles the idea of things closing. The child's feeling — that if the ending must come, it may come beautifully — is therefore a quiet acceptance of death, arrived at innocently by someone far too young to know what he has said. Because the poet asking the question is himself an old man, that childhood acceptance becomes the answer he is looking for. (c) The brackets make the words an inner voice rather than a statement.

The Gift in Wartime.q: Who is the speaker of "The Gift in Wartime" and whom does she address?
The Gift in Wartime.r: The speaker is a young Vietnamese widow standing at the grave of the soldier she loved. She addresses him directly as "you", although he is dead and cannot answer. The poem is therefore a one-sided conversation, which is part of its sadness.

The Gift in Wartime.q: What gifts does the speaker offer?
The Gift in Wartime.r: She offers roses, which she lays on his newly dug grave, and her wedding ring. Beyond these objects she offers herself — her youth, her beauty, her love, and all the years of the life she must now live without him.

The Gift in Wartime.q: What does she receive in return?
The Gift in Wartime.r: She receives the things war hands out: the smell of blood from his uniform, his dead body returned from the field, the medals and official honours given to the families of the dead, and a lifetime of loneliness and mourning.

Because a "gift" is something freely given that the receiver wants, and nothing in the second list is wanted by anybody. Calling blood, a corpse and a medal "gifts" uses the language of love and celebration for the products of killing, and the mismatch is the poem's protest against war.

The Gift in Wartime.q: What do the roses and the wedding ring symbolise?
The Gift in Wartime.r: The roses stand for love, beauty and mourning, and — because cut flowers die quickly — for how briefly the couple's happiness lasted. The wedding ring is a circle, a symbol of a bond meant to have no end, and it is now being handed over to a grave.

The Gift in Wartime.q: Discuss the use of irony in "The Gift in Wartime".
The Gift in Wartime.r: Irony means a gap between what is said and what is actually the case, and this poem is built on one enormous example of it. The word "gift" belongs to weddings, birthdays and festivals; it implies choice, affection and pleasure. Tran Mong Tu takes that word and makes it carry the entire traffic of a war. On one side of the exchange it behaves normally: roses for a grave, a wedding ring, a young woman's love. On the other side the same word is attached to the smell of blood on a uniform, a body brought home from the field, and a medal handed to a widow in place of her husband.

The Gift in Wartime.q: The speaker brings roses to lay on a newly dug grave and offers the wedding ring she has worn through her marriage.
p: Who is the speaker and where is she?
What do these two objects symbolise?
Why does she give presents to someone who cannot receive them?
The Gift in Wartime.r: (a) The speaker is a young Vietnamese widow, and she is standing at the freshly made grave of the soldier she loved, during the Vietnam War. (b) The roses stand for love, beauty and mourning; because cut flowers wither within days, they also stand for how short her happiness was. The wedding ring is a circle with no beginning and no end, the symbol of a bond that was supposed to last a lifetime — and she is now returning it to the earth. (c) Because giving is all she has left of the marriage. Ceremony is how human beings hold on to the dead: bringing flowers, keeping anniversaries, speaking aloud at a grave.

Sharing Tradition.q: How is traditional knowledge passed from one generation to the next?
Sharing Tradition.r: It is passed on by the elders, orally and by example — through songs, names, prayers, stories and, above all, through taking part in ceremonies and dances. The learner is present, watches, is given small tasks, and slowly grows into the knowledge instead of being taught it in lessons.

Sharing Tradition.q: Why does LaPena say that knowledge must be earned?
Sharing Tradition.r: Because some knowledge is sacred and powerful, and careless handling can damage both the knowledge and the person. A learner has to show patience, respect and steadiness before more is given; certain songs, names and roles belong to particular families and are not given out generally. Earning it is part of learning to treat it properly.

Sharing Tradition.q: How does the traditional artist differ from the artist who works for a gallery?
Sharing Tradition.r: The traditional artist makes things for use — regalia, baskets, songs, paint for a ceremony — under obligations about how they are made and what may be done with them. A gallery artist makes objects to be looked at, judged and sold. The first kind of art has a job to do in the life of a community; the second is complete when it is admired.

Sharing Tradition.q: Why is a ceremonial object in a museum not the same object?
Sharing Tradition.r: Because its meaning lay in its use. Once it is taken out of the ceremony, put behind glass and labelled, it is cut off from the people, the purpose and the relationships that made it what it was. It looks the same, but it has become information about a tradition rather than a living part of one.

Sharing Tradition.q: Does LaPena believe a tradition must never change? Explain.
Sharing Tradition.r: No. He says that living traditions have always changed — new materials, new songs, new circumstances in every generation — and that a tradition which cannot change has already become a museum piece. What must stay constant is not the outward detail but the relationship behind it: the respect, the purpose and the connection to ancestors and land.

Sharing Tradition.q: What does the title "Sharing Tradition" mean in the essay?
Sharing Tradition.r: It means passing the tradition on: teaching the right things to the right people at the right time, so that the practice continues into the next generation. It does not mean making everything public. Because each generation holds the tradition in trust rather than owning it, sharing is a duty owed to the ancestors who gave it and to the children who have not yet received it.

Sharing Tradition.q: State LaPena's central argument in "Sharing Tradition" and show how he builds it.
Sharing Tradition.r: LaPena's thesis is that tradition is a living practice rather than a body of information or a collection of objects, that it belongs to a community rather than to an individual, and that anyone who receives it takes on the responsibility of living it properly and handing it on. He builds this in five moves. First he redefines the key term: instead of asking what tradition is, he asks who counts as a traditional person, and answers that it is the one who takes part, keeps the obligations and accepts the discipline — so tradition shifts from things known to things done.

Sharing Tradition.q: How does LaPena describe the relationship between art, ceremony and community? Why does he object to ceremonial objects being collected and displayed?
Sharing Tradition.r: In LaPena's account the three are not separable. Ceremony is the centre of community life: dances and songs are not entertainment but work that has to be done, to give thanks, to mark the seasons and the stages of a life, and to keep the relationship between the people and the natural world in good repair. Art exists to serve that work. Regalia, feathers, baskets, paint and song are made for use, and they come with obligations — who may make them, how, and what may be done with them afterwards. There is no separate category of "the artist" standing apart from the community and expressing a private vision; the maker is a member with a job.

Sharing Tradition.q: Discuss the style and technique of "Sharing Tradition". How does LaPena persuade a reader who is outside his culture?
Sharing Tradition.r: LaPena writes a reflective personal essay in the first person, and his authority is that of a participant rather than a researcher — he has danced, not merely studied. That position governs everything else. The tone is calm, patient and explanatory; he sets out to make an outsider understand rather than to accuse, and the restraint is persuasive, because a reader who would argue with a protest will often accept an explanation. His central technique is redefinition: he takes familiar words — tradition, art, authentic, sharing — and quietly replaces the reader's everyday meaning with his own, so that the argument is largely won at the level of vocabulary before any conclusion is stated.

How to Live Before You Die.q: What is the story about Steve Jobs' birth?
How to Live Before You Die.r: His biological mother was a young unmarried graduate student who decided to give him up for adoption, insisting that he be adopted by college graduates. The lawyer and his wife who were to take him changed their minds at the last moment because they wanted a girl, so a couple on the waiting list were telephoned in the middle of the night and asked whether they wanted "an unexpected baby boy." They said, "Of course." Because the adoptive mother had never finished college and the father had never finished high school, his biological mother refused to sign the papers, and relented only when they promised the boy would one day go to college.

How to Live Before You Die.q: What does he mean when he says, "you can't connect the dots looking forward; you can only connect them looking backward"?
How to Live Before You Die.r: He means that the usefulness of an experience is almost never visible at the time, and becomes clear only years afterwards when it turns out to have fed into something else. His own calligraphy class had no apparent purpose when he took it and became essential a decade later. Since you cannot know in advance which experiences will matter, you cannot plan a life logically forward; you can only follow curiosity and trust that the pieces will fit.

How to Live Before You Die.q: What happened when Steve Jobs turned 30?
How to Live Before You Die.r: He was fired from Apple, the company he had founded. Apple had grown in ten years into a two-billion-dollar company with over four thousand employees and had just released the Macintosh. The executive Jobs had recruited to run the company with him came to disagree with him about the future, they had a falling out, and the Board of Directors sided with the other man. Jobs was dismissed publicly, and found that the focus of his entire adult life had gone.

How to Live Before You Die.q: What does he mean by "don't settle"?
How to Live Before You Die.r: "Don't settle" means: do not accept second-best work, or a job you merely tolerate, simply because looking for the right one is difficult or slow. Jobs compares the search to a search for love — you will recognise the right thing when you find it — and insists that until you find it you should keep looking rather than making do. Settling, in his view, guarantees that you will never do great work, since great work only comes from loving what you do.

How to Live Before You Die.q: Explain: "You have to trust in something — your gut, destiny, life, karma, whatever."
How to Live Before You Die.r: He is admitting that his advice cannot be proved. Since you cannot see ahead, following curiosity instead of a plan requires an act of faith in something — instinct, fate, the divine order, karma. Jobs deliberately offers a list rather than a single name, so that listeners of any religion or none can accept the point. What matters to him is not which belief you hold but that you have enough confidence in your own path to act on it before its value is proved.

How to Live Before You Die.q: Explain: "Your time is limited, so don't waste it living someone else's life."
How to Live Before You Die.r: He means that the shortness of life makes borrowed living wasteful. Most people spend their days meeting other people's expectations, following inherited opinions, and fearing disapproval — but the time so spent is subtracted from the only life they will ever have. Since the span is fixed and unknown, Jobs argues, the only rational course is to follow your own heart and intuition rather than somebody else's plan for you.

How to Live Before You Die.q: What does the slogan "Stay Hungry. Stay Foolish." mean?
How to Live Before You Die.r: They were the farewell words on the back cover of the final issue of The Whole Earth Catalog, and Jobs adopts them as his own wish for the graduates. To "stay hungry" is to remain unsatisfied — to keep wanting to learn and to make, instead of resting on what you have already achieved. To "stay foolish" is to keep the courage to attempt what sensible, experienced people would dismiss, and to risk looking ridiculous. Together they describe a life of continuing curiosity and continuing nerve.

How to Live Before You Die.q: Which style of speech does Jobs use to persuade his audience, and why is his personal-narrative technique so effective?
How to Live Before You Die.r: Jobs uses the personal narrative or autobiographical style: instead of arguing a thesis, he tells three true stories from his own life and lets each one end in a rule. The speech is informal, conversational and plainly worded, is organised in a tripartite structure announced in advance, and moves steadily from private experience to direct second-person instruction.

What I Require from Life.q: How does the writer distinguish between a peaceful age and a heroic age?
What I Require from Life.r: A peaceful age is one in which ordinary safety can be assumed, so that a person may reasonably plan a quiet life; Haldane was born into such an age in 1892 and expected to live in it. A heroic age is one of wars, revolutions and upheavals, in which nothing can be assumed and everyone must improvise. Haldane says that since 1914 he has been living in a heroic age and sees no prospect of surviving into another peaceful one, so he must make the best of the time he has.

What I Require from Life.q: Why does the writer want more freedom of speech than most people?
What I Require from Life.r: Because he already has far more freedom than most people and can see exactly where it stops. He would like to say and write in public what he believes about Lord Blank's newspapers, Mr Dash's pills and Sir John Asterisk's beer — all of which, he says, are poisonous — and the law of libel prevents him. He wants freedom of speech not to indulge himself but to expose things that harm the public, and the invented names show him reporting the problem while still trapped by it.

What I Require from Life.q: What is the difference between desire and demand according to the writer?
What I Require from Life.r: A requirement or demand is something without which a human life is genuinely damaged: work, freedom, health, friendship. A desire is something that would be pleasant but whose absence can be borne. Haldane illustrates the difference from his own life — he would like a room of his own with books, a motor-car, a daily bath, a garden or a river nearby, but he has not got them, "and I bear up quite happily." The distinction matters because it stops the essay becoming a wish-list and keeps his political demands modest and defensible.

What I Require from Life.q: Why does the writer demand security rather than adventure for others?
What I Require from Life.r: Because he does not trust his own taste for adventure. He admits that peace and security are rightful aims and that his own desire for violent adventure is "probably merely an adaptation to the age in which I live" — a habit forced on him by living through wars, not a virtue. Calling himself "a child of my age, and all the worse for being one," he refuses to impose his own restlessness on everybody else, and asks for others the settled safety he has never had.

What I Require from Life.q: Why can Haldane not be friends with a person whose orders he must obey?
What I Require from Life.r: Because he defines friendship as the society of equals who can criticize one another freely. Where one person must obey another's orders without criticism before or after, criticism in both directions becomes impossible, and so does honesty; what remains is a relation of rank, not friendship. For the same reason he finds friendship with people much richer or poorer than himself very difficult. This is why his private definition of friendship leads directly to his public demand for equality.

What I Require from Life.q: Why does the essayist take his references from ancient philosophers?
What I Require from Life.r: For three reasons. First, they supply ready definitions he does not need to argue for: Aristotle gives him happiness as "unimpeded activity" and Socrates gives him a model of a good death. Second, they give the essay an authority older and wider than any political party, so that his demands look like ordinary human sense rather than communist doctrine. Third, they show that his question is not a modern or political one at all but the oldest question in philosophy — what does a human being need in order to live well?

What I Require from Life.q: Why does Haldane consider the death of Socrates enviable?
What I Require from Life.r: On three grounds. Socrates died for his convictions when he could easily have saved himself by betraying them; he died at about seventy, still in full possession of his faculties and having completed all the work he could reasonably hope to do; and he died laughing, since his last words were a joke. Haldane does not expect all three conditions, which are very rarely met together, but says that if he can achieve even two he will have done well — and that his friends may lament him provided they do not pity him.

What I Require from Life.q: Why does Haldane call himself a socialist? What does he want socialism to achieve, and how does he argue for it?
What I Require from Life.r: Haldane calls himself a socialist three separate times in the essay, and each time he gives a different reason, so that the three together amount to a complete case.

What I Require from Life.q: What is socialism? How is it different from capitalism?
What I Require from Life.r: Socialism is a political and economic system in which the means of production — land, factories, machines, mines, transport — are owned and controlled in common, either by the workers themselves or by the state on behalf of the whole community, and in which what is produced is distributed according to need or contribution rather than according to ownership. Capitalism is a system in which those same means of production are privately owned, in which goods and labour are bought and sold in a market, and in which the owner of capital keeps the profit generated by the work of employees.

What I Require from Life.q: Discuss the essay in terms of its language, purpose, subject, point of view and mode of writing.
What I Require from Life.r: Subject. The essay's subject is stated in its title: what a human being genuinely requires in order to live well. Haldane treats it in two halves — what he requires for himself, and what he requires for the society he lives in — and adds a short postscript on what he would require of his own death.

What I Require from Life.q: What do you require from your life to be happy and satisfied?
What I Require from Life.r: (A personal answer; what follows is a model.) Taking Haldane's own method, I would separate what I require from what I merely desire.

What I Require from Life.q: Write an essay about your dream house.

What is Poverty?.q: What is poverty according to Parker?
What is Poverty?.r: For Parker, poverty is not simply a shortage of money but a whole condition of life. It is a smell that never leaves the house; it is being always tired, with anaemia, worms and no money for medicine; it is dirt, because soap, hot water and fuel all cost money; it is insects, torn screens and a fire that must be watched all night; it is the shame of asking for help; and it is an acid that wears away pride and a chisel that chips away honour. Above all it is a trap from which every exit costs money she does not have.

What is Poverty?.q: How is poverty difficult for Parker's children? List some specific examples.
What is Poverty?.r: Her three children suffer in body, in schooling and in prospects. They have worms, infections and pink-eye all summer; they are not starving but they are malnourished; they sleep on the floor or in her single bed; the baby's skin came away with a dried nappy, another child played with broken glass and the eldest was left alone at the edge of a lake. At school they have no extra books, magazines, pencils, crayons or paper — and two of them, she says, will already be damaged before they ever get there. Looking ahead she expects her sons to drift into theft, alcohol or drugs, and for her daughter "at best, there is a life like mine."

What is Poverty?.q: How does Parker try to obtain help, and what problems does she encounter?
What is Poverty?.r: She goes to the welfare office. She circles the block four or five times before she can make herself go in, and goes only because she thinks of her children. Inside, everyone is busy; the person who eventually comes out is never the person she needs; and after telling her whole story — "spilling the whole shame of your poverty all over the desk" — she is told this is the wrong office and must begin the process again somewhere else, where it is no easier. Finally she is told to wait, and cannot take in the reason because of the shame and despair.

What is Poverty?.q: Why does Parker ask the reader to listen without pity?
What is Poverty?.r: Because pity is useless to her — "I cannot use your pity." Pity lets the listener feel kind while changing nothing, and it places the poor person below the listener as an object of charity rather than beside them as a person with a case. What Parker wants instead is first understanding ("Listen with understanding… put yourself in my shoes") and finally anger — anger that will make the reader act and speak on her behalf. The refusal of pity at the start and the demand for anger at the end frame the whole essay.

What is Poverty?.q: Explain: "Poverty is looking into a black future."
What is Poverty?.r: It means that Parker can see her children's future and it is as hopeless as her present. Respectable families will not let their children play with her sons, so the boys will attach themselves to boys who steal, and she can already picture them "behind the bars of their prison instead of behind the bars of my poverty"; or they will escape into alcohol or drugs and be enslaved by them. For her daughter the best she can imagine is a repetition of her own life. The sentence states the essay's bleakest theme — that poverty is inherited — and the word "black" carries no hope of dawn.

What is Poverty?.q: What does Parker mean by "The poor are always silent"?
What is Poverty?.r: She means that poor people do not complain, do not protest and are never heard. Earlier she has explained why: "the poor are always polite. The poor always listen" — they accept a doctor's advice they cannot afford without saying so, because objecting is dangerous and useless, and because shame keeps them quiet. Their silence is what allows comfortable people to believe whatever they like about them. This is why the essay exists: it is one of the silent speaking. And because the next sentence is "Can you be silent too?", the phrase also becomes a challenge — she has broken her silence, and the reader no longer has an excuse for keeping his.

What is Poverty?.q: Why did Parker give up her job?
What is Poverty?.r: Because working cost more than it earned and endangered her children. She was making twenty-two dollars a week, while a good nursery school for three children cost twenty dollars a week, so almost nothing remained. When she left the children with "Granny" instead, she came home to find the baby covered with fly specks in a nappy that had not been changed — so hardened that when it came off, bits of the baby's flesh came with it — one child playing with a sharp piece of broken glass and the eldest alone at the edge of a lake. The episode is her central proof that poverty is a trap rather than laziness.

What is Poverty?.q: Why are people's opinions and prejudices Parker's greatest obstacles?
What is Poverty?.r: Money, food and medicine are all things Parker could be given. Opinions cannot be, and it is opinions that decide whether she is given anything at all. That is why she calls them, in effect, her greatest obstacle.

What is Poverty?.q: How does Parker discount the usual solutions society offers for poverty — welfare, education and health clinics?
What is Poverty?.r: Parker deals with the three standard answers in turn, and in each case her method is the same: she agrees that the thing exists, and then shows that it cannot reach her.

What is Poverty?.q: What writing strategy does Parker use at the beginning of most of her paragraphs? How does she develop each paragraph, and how does the final paragraph use questions to involve the reader?
What is Poverty?.r: The opening strategy. Parker begins most of her paragraphs with the same two words — "Poverty is". "Poverty is being tired." "Poverty is dirt." "Poverty is asking for help." "Poverty is remembering." "Poverty is looking into a black future." "Poverty is an acid…" This is anaphora, and there is a clear recurring pattern: each paragraph is a fresh, complete definition of the same word. The effect is threefold. It imposes order on an experience that is otherwise shapeless; it keeps reminding the reader that the essay is answering the question in its title;

What is Poverty?.q: Using adjectives that highlight the futility of the situation, write a short definition essay on "Growing up in Poverty", imitating Parker's style.
What is Poverty?.r: (A model imitation. Notice the repeated opening, the second-person address, the concrete detail and the flat closing reason.)

Scientific Research is a Token of Humank.q: What does a scientist get instead of big money?
Scientific Research is a Token of Humank.r: Instead of a large income a scientist receives freedom, camaraderie and independence; honours and promotions that depend on his own ability far more than in other occupations; and, above all, "the overwhelming feeling of uncovering yet another one of nature's mysteries." As the essay puts it, science is an exciting adventure in which the major reward comes from the discovery itself — the satisfaction of the work is the payment.

Scientific Research is a Token of Humank.q: What was the problem that the nuclear powers had faced?
Scientific Research is a Token of Humank.r: The three nuclear powers — the Soviet Union, the United States and the United Kingdom — wanted to ban the testing of new nuclear weapons, but a ban is useless if it cannot be policed. Their problem was therefore one of verification: suppose the powers sign an agreement to stop testing, and suppose one of them breaks it by secretly setting off an underground nuclear explosion — how can the others detect the violation? Underground explosions shake the earth in much the same way earthquakes do, so the difficulty was telling the two apart.

Scientific Research is a Token of Humank.q: In which area did Keilis-Borok's theoretical knowledge have a direct application?
Scientific Research is a Token of Humank.r: In the survival of humankind — specifically, in the detection of secret underground nuclear tests. Keilis-Borok had been working in Moscow on the pure theory of seismic waves, with no thought of any practical use. Because an underground explosion produces tremors similar to those of an earthquake, his theory became the means of distinguishing a cheat's bomb from a natural event, and so made a verifiable test-ban treaty possible.

Scientific Research is a Token of Humank.q: What was the important decision that the politicians were able to take as a result of the Geneva talks?
Scientific Research is a Token of Humank.r: The nuclear test ban. The scientists at Geneva worked out a technical solution to the detection problem, and that solution, in the author's words, "eventually allowed politicians to reach one of the most important decisions of their times: nuclear test ban." The order of events matters: the experts met first, and the political decision followed from what they were able to show could be done.

Scientific Research is a Token of Humank.q: What are the natural and man-made disasters mentioned by the author?
Scientific Research is a Token of Humank.r: The author names both kinds together as threats to the survival of civilisation: earthquakes (natural), and, as man-made ones, the self-inflicted destruction of megacities, environmental catastrophes, and economic and social crises. He then gives examples of what a single modern disaster could be — a massive release of radioactivity from a nuclear waste disposal site, an earthquake in the middle of a megalopolis, or an outburst of mass violence — any of which could cause up to a million casualties, make a large part of the world uninhabitable, or trigger a global depression or a war.

Scientific Research is a Token of Humank.q: The professional addressed as "you" in "If you are so clever, why are you so poor?" refers to a (i) lawyer (ii) doctor (iii) scientist (iv) businessman. Justify your choice.
Scientific Research is a Token of Humank.r: The answer is (iii) scientist. The sentence is the essay's opening epigraph and is immediately explained by the question that follows it: why do some of us still decide to become scientists, "despite the fact that businessmen, lawyers, and doctors enjoy a much higher income"? Lawyers, doctors and businessmen are therefore named as the rich professions and cannot be the "you" of the taunt. The person who is clever but poor is the scientist, and the whole essay is his reply.

Scientific Research is a Token of Humank.q: The writer says, "I found myself in Geneva." What does it express?
Scientific Research is a Token of Humank.r: It expresses surprise, suddenness and a pleasing sense of being carried along by events rather than directing them. The passive construction — he does not say "I went to Geneva" but "I found myself in Geneva" — makes it sound as though he looked up one day and was simply there. It also expresses the essay's larger theme in miniature: a man absorbed in abstract mathematics, with no thought of the real world, is suddenly lifted out of his study and set down in the middle of international politics, because his work turned out to matter.

Scientific Research is a Token of Humank.q: How does the essayist justify that scientific research is the token of humankind's survival?
Scientific Research is a Token of Humank.r: The word token in the title means a sign and a guarantee — something that both shows survival is possible and helps bring it about. Keilis-Borok justifies the claim in three stages.

Scientific Research is a Token of Humank.q: Discuss and illustrate the writer's stand that scientists are the most practical people in the world.
Scientific Research is a Token of Humank.r: The writer takes up a familiar prejudice — the "common lore" that a person immersed in science has no practical sense — and turns it upside down.

Scientific Research is a Token of Humank.q: What can be the purpose of the essayist in using quotations in the essay? Discuss with reference to at least three of them.
Scientific Research is a Token of Humank.r: The essay is unusually full of other people's words. There are four that matter: the popular expression "If you are so clever, why are you so poor?"; Tolstoy on the writer who cannot live without writing; Frank Press on the good feeling of like-minded people working together; the French proverb "Nobody is satisfied with his wealth, everybody is satisfied with his wisdom"; and McGeorge Bundy's "Ours is the time of contest over issues not completely understood." They serve several purposes at once.

Scientific Research is a Token of Humank.q: Are the following statements true, and why? (i) Money is more powerful than intellectual resources. (ii) Intellectual resources help the survival of humankind. (iii) Basic research is a way of stalling disasters.
Scientific Research is a Token of Humank.r: (i) Not true, according to the essay — though the author admits money is the more popular belief. He states plainly that "the hope and the responsibility for breaking the stalemate rest not on the money but on intellectual resources." His evidence is that trillions of dollars a year are already being spent to contain modern disasters by all known techniques, and the dangers keep growing. Money can only buy more of what already exists; when what exists is not enough, only new knowledge can help.

Trifles.q: Do you believe that Mrs Wright killed her husband? Explain.
Trifles.r: Yes.
