The play never shows the killing, but the evidence the women assemble points only one way: the rope was the Wrights' own, there was "no sign at all of anyone having come from the outside", Minnie was in the bed beside him, and the wildly stitched quilt block shows her hands shaking that night. The broken cage and the strangled canary supply the motive — the husband killed the one thing she loved, and she answered with the same injury to his neck. Mrs Hale's protest that "I don't think she did it" is not really a claim about the facts; it is a refusal to let the word "murderer" stand for the whole of what happened in that house.

Trifles.q: Do you think Mr Wright's death would have been uncovered if Mr Hale hadn't stopped by the Wrights' home?
Trifles.r: Probably yes, but not so soon, and perhaps not in a way that would have convicted her. The Wrights lived in a lonesome hollow where "you don't see the road", and had refused a party telephone, so news travelled slowly; Minnie herself had notified nobody and was simply sitting in her rocker pleating her apron when Hale arrived. Sooner or later a neighbour, the Ladies' Aid or a delivery would have brought someone to the door. But the delay would have mattered: the kitchen might have been tidied, the bird disposed of, and the story rehearsed. Hale's accidental call on the morning after is what freezes the scene exactly as Minnie left it — which is why the kitchen can be read at all.

Trifles.q: Why does Mrs Hale think that Mrs Wright's worries about her preserves indicate her innocence?
Trifles.r: Because a woman who has just killed her husband and been dragged to jail would not, Mrs Hale reasons, still be anxious about a summer's work in jars — and because the same woman asked for an apron and her little shawl, the small belongings of an ordinary life. "Asking for an apron and her little shawl. Worrying about her fruit." To Mrs Hale these are the concerns of a housewife, not of a criminal. The judgement is of course sentimental rather than logical, and the play knows it: Mrs Hale will shortly find the dead canary. But the observation is still true in a deeper way. Minnie is not a hardened killer; she is an ordinary woman who broke once, and the preserves prove it.

Trifles.q: How does Mrs Peters' homesteading experience connect her to Mrs Wright?
Trifles.r: Mrs Peters tells how she and her husband homesteaded in Dakota and how her first baby died at two years old, leaving her with no other child: "I know what stillness is." That is the precise link. Minnie Wright lived for thirty years in a silent house with no children and a husband who wanted only "peace and quiet", and the canary was the one sound in it. Because Mrs Peters has herself lived through a stillness that nearly destroyed her, she can imagine what it would be "if there'd been years and years of nothing, then a bird to sing to you… still, after the bird was still." Her own past, not any argument of Mrs Hale's, is what turns the sheriff's wife into Minnie's defender.

Trifles.q: How do the women's perspectives on men differ?
Trifles.r: Mrs Hale judges men freely and is ready to say so aloud. She answers back to the County Attorney about the towels ("Men's hands aren't always as clean as they might be"), resents them "snooping around and criticizing" in another woman's kitchen, and describes John Wright to his neighbours' faces as "a hard man… Like a raw wind that gets to the bone." Mrs Peters begins by excusing the men at every turn — "Of course it's no more than their duty", "they've got awful important things on their minds", "the law is the law" — because she is married to the Sheriff and identifies with his authority. By the end the difference has almost vanished: Mrs Peters is the first to reach for the box.

Trifles.q: Why is the play called Trifles?
Trifles.r: The title comes from Hale's dismissive line, "Well, women are used to worrying over trifles," spoken when the men laugh at Mrs Wright for worrying about her frozen preserves. It is deeply ironic, because the trifles the men despise — the preserves, the bread, the quilt, the birdcage and the dead canary — are precisely the evidence that reveals the motive for the murder. The men search the bedroom and the barn and find nothing; the women stay among the trifles and find everything. The title therefore states the men's prejudice and the play's argument in a single word.

Trifles.q: What do the women do with the dead canary, and why?
Trifles.r: Mrs Peters first tries to hide the box in the bag she is carrying, but it is too big, and when she opens it she cannot bring herself to touch the bird; Mrs Hale then snatches the box and thrusts it into the pocket of her big coat, where it is when she speaks the last line of the play. They hide it because it is the one thing that would supply the motive the County Attorney says he needs — "something to show anger, or sudden feeling" — and because they have decided, without ever saying so, that a court which would hang Minnie Wright while never trying John Wright is not entitled to the evidence.

Trifles.q: What is the main theme of the play? Discuss it with reference to the text.
Trifles.r: The main theme of Trifles is the systematic undervaluing of women and of women's knowledge, and the injustice that follows from it. Every other theme in the play — isolation, marriage, law against justice, female solidarity — branches from this one.

Trifles.q: Discuss the symbolism used in the play.
Trifles.r: Glaspell's symbols are all ordinary household objects, which is itself part of the argument: in a world that notices nothing a woman touches, the meaning has to be hidden in plain sight.

Trifles.q: Discuss the setting of the play. Does it have an impact on the theme?
Trifles.r: The setting of Trifles is a single room: the kitchen of the Wrights' now abandoned farmhouse, on a bitterly cold morning in rural Iowa, the day after the murder. The play observes the classical unities almost exactly — one place, one continuous action, roughly real time — and every element of the setting is doing thematic work.

A Sunny Morning.q: What makes Dona Laura think that Don Gonzalo is an ill-natured man?
A Sunny Morning.r: His behaviour from the moment he enters. He grumbles that the people in the park are "idling their time away", demands a bench to himself, orders Juanito to "rout out" three priests who are sitting on "his" bench, and then walks straight through Dona Laura's pigeons, scattering the birds she is feeding. When she protests he answers, "What do I care about the birds?" and refuses even to speak to her because "we have not met". Her verdict is immediate: "What an ill-natured old man! Why must people get so fussy and cross when they reach a certain age?" She is also, of course, delighted when he fails to get the other bench — which shows she is quite as combative as he is.

A Sunny Morning.q: Why do neither Dona Laura nor Don Gonzalo reveal their true identities?
A Sunny Morning.r: Because each is ashamed of having grown old, and each wants to protect the other's memory of their youth. The two asides are almost identical in feeling. Gonzalo: "No, no, I will not reveal myself. I am grotesque now. Better that she recall the gallant horseman who passed daily beneath her window tossing flowers." Laura: "No, I am too sadly changed. It is better he should remember me as the black eyed girl tossing flowers as he passed among the roses in the garden." Their silence is therefore not deceit but consideration — each would rather be remembered beautifully than be recognised.

A Sunny Morning.q: When does Dona Laura realise that Don Gonzalo was her former lover?
A Sunny Morning.r: Laura is certain during the retelling of the duel, when Gonzalo describes "my cousin" hiding in his house, escaping to Seville and then Madrid, and writing letters that were never answered. Her aside "Gonzalo!" comes even earlier, at the words "the gallant lover". But the final, acknowledged realisation comes at the very end, when she turns her head and sees him stooping, "trembling and with a great effort", to pick up the violets she has dropped, and says to herself, "Yes, it is he!" The sequence matters: she knows who he is quite early, but she knows he still loves her only in the last few seconds.

A Sunny Morning.q: Why do Dona Laura and Don Gonzalo spin fictitious stories about themselves?
A Sunny Morning.r: For three reasons. First, self-defence — each has to explain why the lovers never met again, and the truth is unflattering: he ran off to Paris with a ballet dancer within three months, and she married someone else within two years. Second, romance — having decided to keep the past beautiful, each decorates it, turning a shabby ending into a glorious death in Africa and a tragic drowning at sunset. Third, competition, which is where the comedy lies: Laura's aside "You will not get ahead of me in decorating my own funeral" shows that once he has told a splendid lie she is determined to tell a better one.

A Sunny Morning.q: How do Dona Laura and Don Gonzalo feel about each other at the end of the play?
A Sunny Morning.r: With deep and undiminished affection, mixed with amusement and a little sadness. They begin as enemies and end unable to bear parting: they agree to meet again tomorrow on the same bench, he promises to bring crumbs for her birds, and he tells her the morning "has been a great honour and a great pleasure." The feeling is proved by actions rather than statements — his painful stooping for the violets, her "(Sweetly.) Are you coming again tomorrow?" — and it is sealed when they quote the Campoamor lines to each other and smile "as if she were again at the window and he below in the rose garden."

A Sunny Morning.q: What part do the snuff and the violets play in the action?
A Sunny Morning.r: Both are small objects that carry the whole movement of the play. The snuff ends the quarrel: he offers his box, she accepts, they sneeze three times each, and she says in an aside, "The snuff has made peace between us." It is the hinge of the play — without that shared courtesy the two would never have talked. The violets, brought by Petra from her guard, end the play: as Laura takes them a few fall, and Gonzalo stoops painfully to pick them up. That action reveals his feeling and brings about the final recognition. Together they show the Quinteros' method: feeling is conveyed through objects and gestures rather than declarations.

A Sunny Morning.q: What is the effect of the flashback in the play, when Dona Laura and Don Gonzalo learn that they were lovers in the past?
A Sunny Morning.r: The flashback in A Sunny Morning is unusual: nothing is staged, no scene changes, and no character steps back in time. The past is delivered entirely through dialogue, and — this is the crucial point — through a disguise. Gonzalo speaks of "my cousin" and Laura of "my best friend", so that the two lovers narrate their own history while pretending it belongs to other people. The effects are several and all of them are dramatic rather than decorative.

A Sunny Morning.q: Discuss how the play is built around humour and irony.
A Sunny Morning.r: The play is a comedy that keeps turning into a love scene, and the two effects are produced by the same means.

A Sunny Morning.q: How is the title "A Sunny Morning" justifiable? Discuss.
A Sunny Morning.r: The title is justified on at least four levels, and a good answer should climb from the literal to the symbolic.

Refund.q: Why does Wasserkopf demand a refund of his tuition fees from the school?
Refund.r: Because he believes the school took his money and gave him nothing in return. He had studied there for six years, eighteen years ago, and holds a leaving certificate saying he was educated; but he has just been dismissed from his job, he is penniless, and he cannot do anything. As he puts it, "Because I didn't get my money's worth, that's why! This certificate here says I got an education. Well, I didn't. I didn't learn anything and I want my money back." The immediate push came from his old classmate Leaderer, who was making money on foreign exchange and told him that if he did not even understand how, he should go and get his tuition fees back.

Refund.q: Why does Wasserkopf consider himself good for nothing?
Refund.r: Because his life has proved it to him. He has been "fired from my last job", he is "quite broke", and he says plainly, "If I get a job I can't keep it." His meeting with Leaderer was humiliating: a schoolfellow was growing rich by speculating on the fall of Hungarian money, and Wasserkopf could not even follow the explanation. He blames the school for it — "You took my money and you taught me nothing. Now I'm no good for anything, and I can't do the things that I should have learned in school" — and says bitterly that his education "made nothing but an incompetent ass out of me."

Refund.q: What did the teachers decide to do when Wasserkopf asked for a refund?
Refund.r: They decided to conspire to make him pass. The Mathematics Master saw the danger at once: "The object is to prevent him from failing, because if he fails he succeeds." So the staff agreed to stick together, ask easy questions, and — the key sentence — "Whatever his answers, we agree beforehand that they are correct," with the Mathematics Master as the judge of what counted as correct. His motive was not educational but institutional: if Wasserkopf got his money, "tomorrow there will be two more former pupils, and the next day a dozen", and the school would face a "pedagogical scandal".

Refund.q: Why did Wasserkopf give ridiculous answers, and why did the teachers accept these answers?
How does the Mathematics Master describe Wasserkopf's character?
Refund.r: He describes Wasserkopf, before the examination begins, as "a sly, crafty individual, who will try to get the better of us — and his money back — by hook or crook", a man who has "pursued advanced studies in the school of life" and must be checkmated. After the examination he reverses the description completely and calls him a "mathematical genius", because Wasserkopf worked out the total of six years of fees, to the last heller, entirely in his head. Both descriptions are accurate, and together they make the play's point: the man is genuinely able, and the school never noticed.

Refund.q: How did the teachers outwit Wasserkopf?
Refund.r: By using his own greed against him. The Mathematics Master first pretended to do exactly what Wasserkopf wanted — he rejected the answer of 2,629 litres because the correct figure was 2,628, and declared, "I refuse to pass the candidate. Mark him 'Failure.'" He then agreed that the refund was now Wasserkopf's right and asked, innocently, "How much do we owe you, Herr Wasserkopf?" Wasserkopf, "greedily, forgetting everything else", rattled off the entire account to the heller — 6,450 crowns 50 heller.

Refund.q: What is the final judgment on Wasserkopf's demand for a refund?
Refund.r: His demand is rejected completely. The Principal announces that "Herr Wasserkopf has passed with distinction in every subject, and has again shown that he is entitled to the certificate we awarded him on his graduation," and the staff accept "a large share" of the congratulations for having taught him so excellently. Since he has proved that his education was sound, there is no ground for a refund. The Principal then drops the courtesy entirely — "get out before I have you thrown out!" — and the Servant seizes him by the collar and the seat of his trousers and rushes him off the stage. He leaves without a single crown.

Refund.q: What is the theme of the play Refund? Discuss.
Refund.r: The theme of Refund is the failure of an education system that issues certificates instead of giving knowledge, and then defends itself rather than admit it. Several strands run out of that centre.

Refund.q: The play is a satire on the present-day education system. Do you think that our education system does not prepare students for life? Discuss.
Refund.r: Refund is set in a Hungarian school of the 1930s, but every Nepali student recognises it, which is itself an argument that the satire still bites.

Refund.q: Explain the following line from the play: "Because I didn't get my money's worth, that's why!"
Refund.r: The line is Wasserkopf's answer to the Principal's question, "Why do you want it back?", and it is the thesis of the whole play compressed into eight words.

Word Classes, Contracted Forms and Dicti.q: The police has arrested the two suspects.
Word Classes, Contracted Forms and Dicti.r: The police have arrested the two suspects. — police is a plural noun.

Word Classes, Contracted Forms and Dicti.q: The bus reached at Butwal at seven o'clock.
Word Classes, Contracted Forms and Dicti.r: The bus reached Butwal at seven o'clock. — reach takes a direct object, arrive takes at/in.

Word Classes, Contracted Forms and Dicti.q: The dog wagged it's tail when it saw the child.
Word Classes, Contracted Forms and Dicti.r: The dog wagged its tail … — possessive its has no apostrophe.

Word Classes, Contracted Forms and Dicti.q: Can you please explain me this rule once more?
Word Classes, Contracted Forms and Dicti.r: Can you please explain this rule to me once more? — explain cannot take an indirect object without to.

Word Classes, Contracted Forms and Dicti.q: The students hostel is behind the library. — Insert the apostrophe correctly.
Word Classes, Contracted Forms and Dicti.r: The students' hostel is behind the library. — plural possessive: apostrophe after the -s.

Word Classes, Contracted Forms and Dicti.q: The light in the classroom was too dim.
Word Classes, Contracted Forms and Dicti.r: Noun — it follows the determiner The and is the subject.

Word Classes, Contracted Forms and Dicti.q: The shop is between the bank and the post office.
Word Classes, Contracted Forms and Dicti.r: Preposition — it relates the noun phrase the bank and the post office to the shop.

Tenses: Present, Past and Future.q: The train already left when we arrived at the platform.
Tenses: Present, Past and Future.r: The train had already left when we arrived … — the earlier past action takes the past perfect.

Tenses: Present, Past and Future.q: The guests left. Then we cleaned the room. — Join with after, using the past perfect.
Tenses: Present, Past and Future.r: After the guests had left, we cleaned the room. — the earlier action takes had + V3.

Articles, Determiners and Quantifiers.q: How (much / many) sisters does Kamala have?
The water is essential for all living things.
Articles, Determiners and Quantifiers.r: Water is essential … — an uncountable noun used generally takes no article.

Modal Verbs and Semi-modals.q: Why don't we go to Godawari on Saturday? — Rewrite with shall.
Modal Verbs and Semi-modals.r: Shall we go to Godawari on Saturday? — shall makes a suggestion with we.

Modal Verbs and Semi-modals.q: Do you can help me with this sum?
Modal Verbs and Semi-modals.r: Can you help me …? — modals form questions without do.

Passive Voice and Causatives.q: The students of Grade 11 organised a blood donation programme.
Passive Voice and Causatives.r: A blood donation programme was organised by the students of Grade 11. — simple past → was/were + V3.

Passive Voice and Causatives.q: The government has banned single-use plastic in the valley.
Passive Voice and Causatives.r: Single-use plastic has been banned in the valley by the government. — present perfect → has been + V3.

Passive Voice and Causatives.q: The flood had damaged three suspension bridges.
Passive Voice and Causatives.r: Three suspension bridges had been damaged by the flood. — past perfect → had been + V3.
By whom was this window broken? — who becomes by whom and moves to the front.

Passive Voice and Causatives.q: The fields are ploughed by the oxen every Baisakh.
Passive Voice and Causatives.r: The oxen plough the fields every Baisakh. — is/are + V3 → simple present.

Passive Voice and Causatives.q: A new health post is being built by the ward office.
Passive Voice and Causatives.r: The ward office is building a new health post. — is being + V3 → present continuous.

Passive Voice and Causatives.q: The thief had been caught by the neighbours before the police arrived.
Passive Voice and Causatives.r: The neighbours had caught the thief before the police arrived. — had been + V3 → past perfect.

Passive Voice and Causatives.q: The report will have been submitted by the committee by Chaitra.
Passive Voice and Causatives.r: The committee will have submitted the report by Chaitra. — will have been + V3 → future perfect.

Passive Voice and Causatives.q: Let the gate be locked at nine.
Passive Voice and Causatives.r: Lock the gate at nine. — Let … be + V3 goes back to an imperative.

Passive Voice and Causatives.q: By whom was this letter posted?
Passive Voice and Causatives.r: Who posted this letter? — by whom becomes the subject who.

Passive Voice and Causatives.q: A carpenter repaired our main door last week. — Rewrite with had.
Passive Voice and Causatives.r: We had our main door repaired last week. — have + thing + V3.

Passive Voice and Causatives.q: The barber is cutting Bibek's hair at the moment. — Rewrite with is having.
Passive Voice and Causatives.r: Bibek is having his hair cut at the moment. — the causative in the present continuous.

Passive Voice and Causatives.q: The teacher made us to copy the notes again. — Correct the error.
Passive Voice and Causatives.r: The teacher made us copy the notes again. — active make takes the bare infinitive.

Passive Voice and Causatives.q: The road is repairing by the contractor these days. — Correct the error.
Passive Voice and Causatives.r: The road is being repaired by the contractor these days. — the passive needs being + V3.

Reported Speech.r: The teacher said that water boils at 100 °C. — a universal truth is not backshifted.

Reported Speech.q: The manager said to the clerk, "Bring the file at once."
Reported Speech.r: The manager ordered the clerk to bring the file at once. — command → to + V1.

Reported Speech.q: The doctor said to the patient, "Don't eat oily food."
Reported Speech.r: The doctor advised the patient not to eat oily food. — negative command → not to + V1.

Reported Speech.q: The guard ordered us not to park there.
Reported Speech.r: He said to us, "Don't park here." — not to + V1 becomes a negative imperative; there → here.

Reported Speech.q: The old man asked the boy where he lived.
Reported Speech.r: The old man said to the boy, "Where do you live?" — the wh- question regains its inversion and do.

Reported Speech.q: The teacher asked us where were we going.
Reported Speech.r: The teacher asked us where we were going. — a reported question uses statement order.

Conditional Sentences.q: If I had known your number, I would have called you. — Rewrite without if.
Conditional Sentences.r: Had I known your number, I would have called you. — type-3 inversion with had.

Conditional Sentences.q: If I were the mayor, I would widen this road. — Rewrite without if.
Conditional Sentences.r: Were I the mayor, I would widen this road. — type-2 inversion with were.

Conditional Sentences.q: If it will rain tomorrow, the match will be postponed.
Conditional Sentences.r: If it rains tomorrow … — no will in the if-clause of a type 1.

Conditional Sentences.q: If I would have money, I would buy a new bicycle.
Conditional Sentences.r: If I had money … — type 2 takes the simple past in the if-clause.

Conditional Sentences.q: If she would have called me, I would have gone with her.
Conditional Sentences.r: If she had called me … — type 3 takes had + V3, not would have.

Conditional Sentences.q: If I was you, I would not sign that paper.
Conditional Sentences.r: If I were you … — the type-2 subjunctive is were for all persons.

Conditional Sentences.q: If he had studied harder, he would pass the examination last year.
Conditional Sentences.r: … he would have passed the examination last year. — a past result needs would have + V3.

Conditional Sentences.q: If you will heat ice, it melts.
Conditional Sentences.r: If you heat ice, it melts. — a zero conditional uses the present in both clauses.

Relative Clauses and Connectives.q: The farmer is worried. His maize crop failed.
Relative Clauses and Connectives.r: The farmer whose maize crop failed is worried. — whose shows possession and sits next to farmer.

Relative Clauses and Connectives.q: The tea was too hot for me to drink. — Rewrite using so … that.
Relative Clauses and Connectives.r: The tea was so hot that I could not drink it. — too … to becomes so … that with a negative result clause.

Relative Clauses and Connectives.q: The boy is my cousin. He won the essay competition. — Join with a relative pronoun.
Relative Clauses and Connectives.r: The boy who won the essay competition is my cousin. — subject pronoun who, placed next to boy.

Relative Clauses and Connectives.q: The pen was lying on the desk which my uncle gave me.
Relative Clauses and Connectives.r: The pen which my uncle gave me was lying on the desk. — the clause must stand next to its own noun.

Question Tags, Questions and Subject-Ver.q: Where does he live? — Rewrite beginning Do you know …
Question Tags, Questions and Subject-Ver.r: Do you know where he lives? — an embedded question keeps statement order and drops does.

Prepositions, Adjectives and Adverbs.q: The bus reached at Birgunj at midnight.
Prepositions, Adjectives and Adverbs.r: The bus reached Birgunj at midnight. — reach takes no preposition.
The soup tastes delicious. — after a linking verb use an adjective.

Guided Writing: Stories from Outlines, C.q: The table below shows how 120 students of Grade 11 in one college spend an average weekday. Describe the information in about 150 words.
Guided Writing: Stories from Outlines, C.r: The table compares how the boys and the girls of Grade 11 in one college use the twenty-four hours of an ordinary weekday. Both groups spend exactly the same time on the two largest items: eight hours asleep and six hours at college, which together take up more than half the day. The differences lie in the remaining six hours. Girls study an hour longer at home than boys, three hours against two, and they do three times as much household work — three hours compared with one. Boys use the extra time for entertainment. They spend four hours on a mobile phone or in front of the television, twice the two hours the girls spend, and one hour more than the girls on games and outdoor play.

Functional Writing: Letters, Emails, App.q: Write a letter to the manager of a mobile phone company complaining that the handset you bought three weeks ago switches itself off, and asking for a replacement.
Functional Writing: Letters, Emails, App.r: Anisha Shrestha, Ward No. 6, Itahari · 12 Kartik 2082 · The Customer Service Manager, Him Mobile Pvt. Ltd., Putalisadak, Kathmandu · Subject: Faulty handset, invoice no. 4417 · Dear Sir or Madam, — Para 1: I bought a Him M20 handset from your Itahari showroom on 18 Asoj 2082; the invoice number is 4417 and the warranty runs for one year. Para 2: From the fourth day the handset has switched itself off without warning, between six and ten times a day, even when the battery is above eighty per cent. Your showroom reset the software on 2 Kartik, but the fault returned the same evening.

Functional Writing: Letters, Emails, App.q: Write an email to your class teacher asking for three days' leave to attend your sister's wedding, and saying how you will cover the lessons you miss.
Functional Writing: Letters, Emails, App.r: Subject: Request for leave, 14–16 Mangsir. — Dear Sir, I am writing to request three days' leave from 14 to 16 Mangsir 2082, as my elder sister's wedding takes place at our home in Gorkha and I am needed there. I have asked Sunita Adhikari to keep a copy of the notes for Physics and English, and I shall complete the laboratory report for Chemistry before I leave. I shall return to class on 17 Mangsir. I should be grateful if you would grant me leave for these three days. Yours faithfully, Prakash Bhandari, Grade 11 "A", Roll No. 17.

Functional Writing: Letters, Emails, App.q: Write a suitable subject line for an email applying for the post of Lab Assistant.
Functional Writing: Letters, Emails, App.r: Application for the post of Lab Assistant — specific, four to eight words, no full stop.

Functional Writing: Letters, Emails, App.q: What is wrong with this notice line: I want to inform all of you that the picnic is cancelled.
Functional Writing: Letters, Emails, App.r: A notice is impersonal: there is no I and no you. Write All students are informed that the picnic has been cancelled.

Free Writing: Essays, Memoirs and Critic.q: Write a memoir of about 250 words beginning I had never seen my father lose his temper before that afternoon.
Free Writing: Essays, Memoirs and Critic.r: Plan, then write to it. Setting and the ordinary day before the change (40 words) — the afternoon itself, told slowly, with two or three physical details you can see now: what was in his hands, what the room smelt of, what somebody said (110 words) — the moment his temper broke, in short sentences (50 words) — reflection: what you understood about him, or about adults, that you had not understood at breakfast (50 words). Keep the whole thing to one afternoon; resist explaining his life.

Free Writing: Essays, Memoirs and Critic.q: Which sentence is the topic sentence?
p: Water was rationed to two hours a day.
Last summer was the hardest our town has had.
The taps ran dry in Chaitra.
Free Writing: Essays, Memoirs and Critic.r: (b) — it is the general claim; (a) and (c) are the evidence for it.

Free Writing: Essays, Memoirs and Critic.q: Which kind of essay does Explain why so many young Nepalis go abroad to work ask for?
Free Writing: Essays, Memoirs and Critic.r: Expository — explain why asks for causes, not opinion.

Free Writing: Essays, Memoirs and Critic.q: Which kind does Describe the busiest street in your town ask for?
Free Writing: Essays, Memoirs and Critic.r: Descriptive — arranged in space order, built on sensory detail.

Free Writing: Essays, Memoirs and Critic.q: Name the one thing a conclusion must never contain.
Free Writing: Essays, Memoirs and Critic.r: A new point or new evidence. The conclusion restates and widens; it does not add.

Free Writing: Essays, Memoirs and Critic.q: What separates a memoir from a short story?
Free Writing: Essays, Memoirs and Critic.r: A memoir is true and ends with the writer's reflection on what the experience meant; a story is invented and ends with the event.

Free Writing: Essays, Memoirs and Critic.q: A critical response spends six of its twelve sentences retelling the plot. What mark is at risk, and why?
Free Writing: Essays, Memoirs and Critic.r: The content mark. Summary shows only that the text was read; the marks are for judgement supported by evidence.

Vocabulary, Sounds, Prefixes, Suffixes a.q: What does beat about the bush mean?
Vocabulary, Sounds, Prefixes, Suffixes a.r: To avoid coming to the main point; to talk round a subject.

Vocabulary, Sounds, Prefixes, Suffixes a.q: What does burn the midnight oil mean?
Vocabulary, Sounds, Prefixes, Suffixes a.r: To work or study late into the night.

Vocabulary, Sounds, Prefixes, Suffixes a.q: Where is the stress in record in Please record the lesson?
Vocabulary, Sounds, Prefixes, Suffixes a.r: On the second syllable — record — because it is a verb here.

Vocabulary, Sounds, Prefixes, Suffixes a.q: Where is the stress in photography?
Vocabulary, Sounds, Prefixes, Suffixes a.r: On the second syllable — photography — because -graphy pulls the stress onto the syllable before it.

Functions.q: If $f(x)=\frac{2x+1}{x-3}$, find $f^{-1}(x)$ and state the domain and range of $f$.
Functions.r: Let $y=\frac{2x+1}{x-3}$. Then $y(x-3)=2x+1\Rightarrow xy-3y=2x+1\Rightarrow x(y-2)=3y+1\Rightarrow x=\frac{3y+1}{y-2}$. So $f^{-1}(x)=\frac{3x+1}{x-2}$. Domain of $f$ is $\mathbb{R}-\{3\}$ (denominator zero at 3); range is $\mathbb{R}-\{2\}$ (the value that $f^{-1}$ cannot take).

Functions.q: If $f(x)=2x-1$ and $g(x)=x^2+3$, find $(f\circ g)(x)$ and $(g\circ f)(x)$. Show that $f\circ g\ne g\circ f$ by evaluating both at $x=2$.
Find the domain and range of $f(x)=\sqrt{9-x^2}$.
Functions.r: We need $9-x^2\ge 0$, so $x^2\le 9$ and $-3\le x\le 3$: domain $=[-3,3]$. Inside the root the value runs from $0$ (at $x=\pm3$) to $9$ (at $x=0$), so $f$ runs from $0$ to $3$: range $=[0,3]$.

Functions.w: the denominator vanishes at $x = \pm 2$, and both must be excluded.

Functions.q: Define domain, co-domain and range of a function. Find the domain and range of $f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x-3}$ and of $g(x) = \sqrt{16 - x^{2}}$.
Functions.r: The domain is the set of allowed inputs; the co-domain is the set the outputs are declared to lie in; the range is the set of outputs actually attained, always a subset of the co-domain.

Curve Sketching.w: The inflection point is defined as the point where the curvature changes direction.

Curve Sketching.q: Which of the following represents the second derivative of a function $f(x)$ at a point $x=a$ if it exists?
Curve Sketching.w: The second derivative indicates the rate at which the first derivative is changing, denoted by $\frac{d^2f}{dx^2}(a)$.

Curve Sketching.q: If a function $f(x)$ has a local minimum at $x = c$, then which of the following must be true regarding its first derivative $f'(c)$?
Curve Sketching.w: At a local minimum, the slope of the tangent line (first derivative) equals zero.

Sequence and Series.q: Derive the formula for the sum of the first $n$ terms of an arithmetic series, and hence find the sum of the first $30$ odd natural numbers.
Sequence and Series.r: Write $S_n = a + (a+d) + \cdots + l$ and again in reverse order; adding the two lines pairs every term to give $a+l$, and there are $n$ pairs, so $2S_n = n(a+l)$ and $S_n = \frac{n}{2}(a+l) = \frac{n}{2}[2a+(n-1)d]$.

Sequence and Series.q: The fourth term of a geometric progression is $24$ and the seventh term is $192$. Find the first term, the common ratio and the sum of the first $10$ terms.
If $a$, $b$, $c$ are in harmonic progression, show that $b = \dfrac{2ac}{a+c}$. Hence find the harmonic mean of $4$ and $12$.
Sequence and Series.r: $a, b, c$ in HP means $\frac1a, \frac1b, \frac1c$ are in AP, so $\frac{2}{b} = \frac1a + \frac1c = \frac{a+c}{ac}$. Cross-multiplying gives $b = \dfrac{2ac}{a+c}$.

Sequence and Series.q: The first term of an infinite geometric series is $3$ and its sum is $4$. Find the common ratio and the fourth term.
Sequence and Series.r: $\dfrac{3}{1-r} = 4$ gives $3 = 4 - 4r$, so $r = \dfrac14$ (and $|r| < 1$, so the sum is legitimate). Fourth term $= ar^{3} = 3\left(\tfrac14\right)^{3} = \dfrac{3}{64}$.

Sequence and Series.q: Express $0.3\overline{7} = 0.3777\ldots$ as a fraction in lowest terms.

p: Define a geometric progression and derive the formula for the sum of its first $n$ terms.
The sum of three numbers in geometric progression is $21$ and their product is $216$. Find the numbers.
Sequence and Series.r: (a) See the derivation in §5.1: multiply $S_n$ by $r$, subtract, and the middle terms cancel to leave $S_n(1-r) = a(1-r^{n})$, so $S_n = \dfrac{a(1-r^{n})}{1-r}$ for $r \ne 1$.

p: For two positive numbers, prove that $G^{2} = AH$ and that $A \ge G \ge H$.
The arithmetic mean of two numbers is $\dfrac{25}{4}$ and their harmonic mean is $4$. Find the numbers.
Sequence and Series.r: (a) $AH = \dfrac{a+b}{2}\cdot\dfrac{2ab}{a+b} = ab = G^{2}$. Next, $A - G = \dfrac{(\sqrt{a} - \sqrt{b})^{2}}{2} \ge 0$, so $A \ge G$; and $G - H = G - \dfrac{G^{2}}{A} = \dfrac{G(A-G)}{A} \ge 0$, so $G \ge H$. Equality throughout only if $a = b$.

p: State the condition under which an infinite geometric series has a sum, and derive the formula for that sum.
A ball is dropped from a height of $12\ \text{m}$ and on each bounce rises to $\dfrac{2}{3}$ of the previous height. Find the total vertical distance it travels before coming to rest.
Sequence and Series.r: (a) $S_n = \dfrac{a}{1-r} - \dfrac{ar^{n}}{1-r}$. If $|r| < 1$ then $r^{n} \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$, leaving $S_{\infty} = \dfrac{a}{1-r}$. If $|r| \ge 1$, $r^{n}$ does not tend to zero and no sum exists.

Sequence and Series.q: Derive the $n$th term and the sum of $n$ terms of an A.P. and of a G.P., define arithmetic and geometric means and solve worked problems.
Define A.M., G.M. and H.M. of two positive numbers, prove $A\ge G\ge H$ and $G^{2}=AH$, derive the sum of an infinite G.P. and apply it to recurring decimals and a bouncing ball.
If the third term of a geometric sequence is 16 and the sixth term is 128, what is the common ratio?
Sequence and Series.w: Using the formula for the nth term of a geometric sequence, $ar^2 = 16$ and $ar^5 = 128$, solving these gives the common ratio r=2.

Sequence and Series.q: Find the sum of an infinite geometric series if the first term is 8 and the common ratio is $\frac{1}{2}$.
Sequence and Series.w: For an infinite geometric series with $|r| < 1$, the sum is given by $S = \frac{a}{1-r}$. Plugging in the values yields 16.

Matrices and Determinants.q: Find the adjoint and the inverse of the matrix with rows $(2,1)$ and $(7,4)$, and verify that $AA^{-1} = I$.
Matrices and Determinants.r: $|A| = 2(4) - 1(7) = 1$. The cofactors are $C_{11} = 4$, $C_{12} = -7$, $C_{21} = -1$, $C_{22} = 2$, so the cofactor matrix has rows $(4,-7)$, $(-1,2)$ and $\mathrm{adj}\,A$ (its transpose) has rows $(4,-1)$, $(-7,2)$.

Matrices and Determinants.q: Solve by Cramer's rule: $\;2x + 3y = 13$, $\;3x - y = 3$.
Using properties of determinants, show that the determinant with rows $(1,a,a^{2})$, $(1,b,b^{2})$, $(1,c,c^{2})$ equals $(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)$.
Matrices and Determinants.r: The determinant is the transpose of the one in Worked example 6.10, and by P1 transposing does not change the value, so it is $(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)$. (Directly: $R_1 \rightarrow R_1 - R_2$ and $R_2 \rightarrow R_2 - R_3$, take out $(a-b)$ and $(b-c)$, then expand.)

Matrices and Determinants.q: Express the matrix with rows $(3,5)$ and $(1,7)$ as the sum of a symmetric and a skew-symmetric matrix.
Matrices and Determinants.r: $A^{T}$ has rows $(3,1)$, $(5,7)$. Then $\frac12(A+A^{T})$ has rows $(3,3)$ and $(3,7)$ — symmetric; and $\frac12(A-A^{T})$ has rows $(0,2)$ and $(-2,0)$ — skew-symmetric. Their sum has rows $(3,5)$, $(1,7)$, which is $A$.

Matrices and Determinants.q: If $A$ is a non-singular matrix of order $3$ with $|A| = 5$, find $|\mathrm{adj}\,A|$ and $|A^{-1}|$.
Matrices and Determinants.r: Take determinants of $A(\mathrm{adj}\,A) = |A|I$. By P8 and P4 (with $n = 3$),

p: Define the minor and the cofactor of an element of a square matrix, and state how the adjoint is built from them.
Find the inverse of the matrix $A$ with rows $(3,-3,4)$, $(2,-3,4)$, $(0,-1,1)$ by the adjoint method, and verify that $AA^{-1} = I$.
Matrices and Determinants.r: (a) The minor $M_{ij}$ is the determinant left after deleting row $i$ and column $j$; the cofactor is $C_{ij} = (-1)^{i+j}M_{ij}$; the adjoint is the transpose of the matrix of cofactors.

p: State any four properties of determinants.
Solve the system $\;x+2y+3z = 14$, $\;2x+3y+4z = 20$, $\;3x+4y+6z = 29$ by Gauss elimination.
Matrices and Determinants.r: (a) Any four of P1–P8 in the table above, for example: $|A^{T}| = |A|$; interchanging two rows changes the sign; two identical rows give zero; adding a multiple of one row to another leaves the value unchanged.

p: Show that $A(\mathrm{adj}\,A) = |A|\,I$ and deduce the formula for $A^{-1}$.
Matrices and Determinants.r: (a) The $(i,j)$ entry of $A(\mathrm{adj}\,A)$ is $\sum_k a_{ik}C_{jk}$. For $i = j$ this is the cofactor expansion of $|A|$ along row $i$; for $i \ne j$ it is the expansion of a determinant with row $j$ replaced by row $i$ — two identical rows — so it is $0$. Hence $A(\mathrm{adj}\,A) = |A|I$, and dividing by $|A| \ne 0$ gives $A^{-1} = \mathrm{adj}\,A / |A|$.

Inverse Circular Functions.q: Define the inverse sine function and state the domain and range of all six inverse circular functions.
Inverse Circular Functions.r: $\sin^{-1}x$ is the unique $y\in\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right]$ with $\sin y = x$, defined for $-1\le x\le 1$. The full table is the one in §9.1: $\sin^{-1},\csc^{-1}$ have range $\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right]$ (excluding $0$ for $\csc^{-1}$), $\tan^{-1}$ has $\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$, $\cos^{-1},\sec^{-1}$ have $[0,\pi]$ (excluding $\frac{\pi}{2}$ for $\sec^{-1}$), and $\cot^{-1}$ has $(0,\pi)$. Domains: $[-1,1]$ for $\sin^{-1},\cos^{-1}$; $|x|\ge 1$ for $\sec^{-1},\csc^{-1}$; $\mathbb{R}$ for $\tan^{-1},\cot^{-1}$.

Let $\sin^{-1}x=\theta$, so $\sin\theta=x$ and $-\frac{\pi}{2}\le\theta\le\frac{\pi}{2}$. Then $\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=\sin\theta=x$. Since $0\le\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta\le\pi$, the angle $\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta$ lies in the range of $\cos^{-1}$, so $\cos^{-1}x = \frac{\pi}{2}-\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}-\sin^{-1}x$, which rearranges to the result.

Let $A=\cos^{-1}\frac45$, so $\sin A=\frac35$, $\cos A=\frac45$. Let $B=\tan^{-1}\frac{5}{12}$, so $\sin B=\frac{5}{13}$, $\cos B=\frac{12}{13}$ (from the $5,12,13$ triangle). Then $\sin(A+B)=\sin A\cos B+\cos A\sin B = \frac35\cdot\frac{12}{13}+\frac45\cdot\frac{5}{13} = \dfrac{36+20}{65} = \dfrac{56}{65}$.

Product $(x+1)(x-1) = x^{2}-1$. Assuming $x^2-1<1$, $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{(x+1)+(x-1)}{1-(x^{2}-1)} = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{8}{31}$, so $\dfrac{2x}{2-x^{2}} = \dfrac{8}{31}$. Cross-multiplying: $62x = 16-8x^{2}$, i.e. $8x^{2}+62x-16=0$, or $4x^{2}+31x-8=0$. Factorising, $(4x-1)(x+8)=0$, so $x=\frac14$ or $x=-8$. Check: $x=\frac14$ gives $x^2-1 = -\frac{15}{16}<1$ and a small positive left-hand side — valid. $x=-8$ makes the left side negative while $\tan^{-1}\frac{8}{31}>0$ — reject. Hence $x=\dfrac14$.

Trigonometric Equations and General Valu.r: Write $\sqrt{3}\cos x+\sin x=R\cos(x-\alpha)$ with $R\cos\alpha=\sqrt{3}$, $R\sin\alpha=1$. Then $R=\sqrt{3+1}=2$ and $\tan\alpha=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$, so $\alpha=\frac{\pi}{6}$. The equation becomes $2\cos\left(x-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=\sqrt{2}$, i.e. $\cos\left(x-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}=\cos\frac{\pi}{4}$. Hence $x-\frac{\pi}{6}=2n\pi\pm\frac{\pi}{4}$, so $x=2n\pi+\frac{\pi}{6}\pm\frac{\pi}{4}$, that is $x=2n\pi+\frac{5\pi}{12}$ or $x=2n\pi-\frac{\pi}{12}$, $n\in\mathbb{Z}$.

Prove that if $\sin\theta = \sin\alpha$ then $\theta = n\pi+(-1)^{n}\alpha$, $n\in\mathbb{Z}$.
Trigonometric Equations and General Valu.r: $\sin\theta-\sin\alpha = 2\cos\frac{\theta+\alpha}{2}\sin\frac{\theta-\alpha}{2} = 0$. Either $\cos\frac{\theta+\alpha}{2}=0$, giving $\frac{\theta+\alpha}{2}=(2m+1)\frac{\pi}{2}$ and so $\theta = (2m+1)\pi-\alpha$; or $\sin\frac{\theta-\alpha}{2}=0$, giving $\frac{\theta-\alpha}{2}=m\pi$ and so $\theta = 2m\pi+\alpha$. The first family is $\theta = (\text{odd }n)\pi-\alpha$ and the second $\theta = (\text{even }n)\pi+\alpha$, both of which are $\theta = n\pi+(-1)^{n}\alpha$.

Trigonometric Equations and General Valu.q: Solve $2\cos^{2}\theta+\sin\theta-1 = 0$.
Trigonometric Equations and General Valu.r: Substitute $\cos^{2}\theta = 1-\sin^{2}\theta$: $2-2\sin^{2}\theta+\sin\theta-1=0$, i.e. $2\sin^{2}\theta-\sin\theta-1=0$. Factorising, $(2\sin\theta+1)(\sin\theta-1)=0$. If $\sin\theta = 1 = \sin\frac{\pi}{2}$ then $\theta = n\pi+(-1)^{n}\frac{\pi}{2}$. If $\sin\theta = -\frac12 = \sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)$ then $\theta = n\pi+(-1)^{n}\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = n\pi-(-1)^{n}\frac{\pi}{6}$.

Trigonometric Equations and General Valu.q: Solve $\cos\theta+\cos 3\theta = 2\cos 2\theta$.
Trigonometric Equations and General Valu.r: $\cos\theta+\cos 3\theta = 2\cos 2\theta\cos\theta$, so the equation is $2\cos 2\theta\cos\theta = 2\cos 2\theta$, i.e. $2\cos 2\theta(\cos\theta-1)=0$. Either $\cos 2\theta = 0 \Rightarrow 2\theta = (2n+1)\frac{\pi}{2} \Rightarrow \theta = (2n+1)\frac{\pi}{4}$; or $\cos\theta = 1 \Rightarrow \theta = 2n\pi$.

Squaring and adding, $a^{2}+b^{2} = r^{2}$, so $r=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$; dividing, $\tan\alpha = b/a$. Then $a\cos\theta+b\sin\theta = r(\cos\alpha\cos\theta+\sin\alpha\sin\theta) = r\cos(\theta-\alpha)$. Coordinates in Space.r: Complete the rectangular box on $AB$ as a space diagonal, with $M(x_2,y_2,z_1)$. $A$ and $M$ lie in the plane $z = z_1$, so $AM^{2} = (x_2-x_1)^{2}+(y_2-y_1)^{2}$. The edge $MB$ is parallel to the $z$-axis, so $MB = |z_2-z_1|$ and $MB \perp AM$. Pythagoras in $\triangle AMB$ gives $AB^{2} = AM^{2}+MB^{2}$, hence $AB = \sqrt{(x_2-x_1)^{2}+(y_2-y_1)^{2}+(z_2-z_1)^{2}}$.

Coordinates in Space.q: Find the ratio in which the $zx$-plane divides the join of $A(-2,4,7)$ and $B(3,-5,8)$.
Coordinates in Space.r: Let the $zx$-plane cut $AB$ in the ratio $k:1$. The dividing point is $\left(\frac{3k-2}{k+1},\ \frac{-5k+4}{k+1},\ \frac{8k+7}{k+1}\right)$. On the $zx$-plane $y = 0$, so $-5k+4 = 0$ and $k = \frac45$. The ratio is $4:5$ internally.

Coordinates in Space.q: A line makes angles $90^{\circ}$ and $135^{\circ}$ with the positive $x$- and $y$-axes. Find the angle it makes with the positive $z$-axis and write down its direction cosines.
Coordinates in Space.r: $l = \cos 90^{\circ} = 0$ and $m = \cos 135^{\circ} = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$. Then $n^{2} = 1-0-\frac12 = \frac12$, so $n = \pm\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ and $\gamma = 45^{\circ}$ or $135^{\circ}$. The direction cosines are $\left(0,\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$ or $\left(0,\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)$.

Coordinates in Space.q: Find the angle between the lines whose direction ratios are $(1,1,2)$ and $(\sqrt{3}-1,\ -\sqrt{3}-1,\ 4)$.
Coordinates in Space.r: $a_1a_2+b_1b_2+c_1c_2 = 1(\sqrt{3}-1)+1(-\sqrt{3}-1)+2(4) = -2+8 = 6$. The lengths are $\sqrt{1+1+4} = \sqrt{6}$ and $\sqrt{(\sqrt{3}-1)^{2}+(\sqrt{3}+1)^{2}+16} = \sqrt{(4-2\sqrt{3})+(4+2\sqrt{3})+16} = \sqrt{24} = 2\sqrt{6}$. So $\cos\theta = \dfrac{6}{\sqrt{6}\cdot 2\sqrt{6}} = \dfrac{6}{12} = \dfrac12$, giving $\theta = 60^{\circ}$.

Vectors.q: Define collinear vectors. Prove that the points $A(-2,3,5)$, $B(1,2,3)$ and $C(7,0,-1)$ are collinear, and find the ratio $AB:BC$.
Vectors.r: Collinear vectors lie on the same or parallel lines, so each is a scalar multiple of the other. Here $\vec{AB} = (1+2)\hat{i}+(2-3)\hat{j}+(3-5)\hat{k} = 3\hat{i}-\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ and $\vec{BC} = (7-1)\hat{i}+(0-2)\hat{j}+(-1-3)\hat{k} = 6\hat{i}-2\hat{j}-4\hat{k}$. Since $\vec{BC} = 2\,\vec{AB}$, the vectors are collinear; they share $B$, so $A$, $B$, $C$ lie on one line. Also $AB:BC = 1:2$.

Vectors.q: Find the position vector of the point $P$ which divides the join of $A(2,-1,4)$ and $B(7,4,-1)$ internally in the ratio $3:2$.
Vectors.r: With $m = 3$, $n = 2$: $\vec{r} = \dfrac{3(7\hat{i}+4\hat{j}-\hat{k}) + 2(2\hat{i}-\hat{j}+4\hat{k})}{5} = \dfrac{(21+4)\hat{i}+(12-2)\hat{j}+(-3+8)\hat{k}}{5} = \dfrac{25\hat{i}+10\hat{j}+5\hat{k}}{5} = 5\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+\hat{k}$, i.e. $P(5,2,1)$. It lies between $A$ and $B$, as required.

Vectors.q: Express $\vec{c} = 7\hat{i}+4\hat{j}$ as a linear combination of $\vec{a} = \hat{i}+2\hat{j}$ and $\vec{b} = 2\hat{i}-\hat{j}$, and explain why the answer is unique.
Show that the vectors $\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$, $-2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-4\hat{k}$ and $\hat{i}-3\hat{j}+5\hat{k}$ are coplanar.
If $\vec{a} = 2\hat{i}+\lambda\hat{j}+\hat{k}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{b} = \hat{i}-2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$, find $\lambda$. Hence find the projection of $\vec{b}$ on $\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$.
Vectors.r: Perpendicularity gives $2(1)+\lambda(-2)+1(3) = 0$, so $5 = 2\lambda$ and $\lambda = 5/2$. For the projection, $\vec{b}\cdot(\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}) = 1+4+6 = 11$ and $|\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}| = \sqrt{1+4+4} = 3$, so the projection is $11/3 = 3.67$ units.

Vectors.q: Two vectors of magnitudes $7$ and $8$ units act at a point at $60^{\circ}$ to each other. Find the magnitude of the resultant and the angle it makes with the $8$-unit vector.
Vectors.r: $R = \sqrt{8^{2}+7^{2}+2(8)(7)\cos 60^{\circ}} = \sqrt{64+49+56} = \sqrt{169} = 13$ units. Measuring $\alpha$ from the $8$-unit vector, $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{7\sin 60^{\circ}}{8+7\cos 60^{\circ}} = \dfrac{6.062}{11.5} = 0.5272$, so $\alpha = 27.80^{\circ}$.

Vectors.r: (a) See the derivation in §14.1: from $AP:PB = m:n$ we get $n\,\vec{AP} = m\,\vec{PB}$, i.e. $n(\vec{r}-\vec{a}) = m(\vec{b}-\vec{r})$, which rearranges to $\vec{r} = \dfrac{m\vec{b}+n\vec{a}}{m+n}$. Putting $m = n = 1$ gives the midpoint $\dfrac{\vec{a}+\vec{b}}{2}$.

Measures of Dispersion.r: Variance is the mean of the squared deviations from the mean; $\sigma$ is its positive square root. Here $n = 7$, $\sum x = 56$, so $\bar{x} = 8$.

Measures of Dispersion.q: The mean and standard deviation of the heights of the boys in a class are $160$ cm and $8$ cm; for the girls they are $150$ cm and $6$ cm. State with reasons which group is more variable in height.
Measures of Dispersion.r: The means differ, so compare coefficients of variation: $C.V._{\text{boys}} = \frac{8}{160}\times100 = 5\%$ and $C.V._{\text{girls}} = \frac{6}{150}\times100 = 4\%$. The boys' C.V. is larger, so the boys are more variable in height, even though a quick glance at the standard deviations only says their spread is larger in absolute centimetres.

Measures of Dispersion.q: For a distribution the mean is $40$, the median is $38$ and the standard deviation is $10$. Find the mode and Karl Pearson's coefficient of skewness by both formulae.
Measures of Dispersion.r: $M_o = 3M_d - 2\bar{x} = 3(38) - 2(40) = 114 - 80 = 34$. Then $S_k = \frac{\bar{x}-M_o}{\sigma} = \frac{40-34}{10} = 0.6$, and by the median form $S_k = \frac{3(40-38)}{10} = 0.6$ — the two agree. Positively skewed.

Measures of Dispersion.q: For a normal distribution, what proportion of the data falls within one standard deviation of the mean?
Measures of Dispersion.w: In a normal distribution, approximately $68\%$ of the data lies within one standard deviation of the mean.

A card is drawn from a well-shuffled pack of 52. Find the probability that it is (i) a king or a heart, (ii) neither a king nor a heart. (iii) Three coins are tossed; find the probability of exactly two heads.
Probability.r: (i) There are 4 kings and 13 hearts, and the king of hearts is counted in both, so $P=\frac{4}{52}+\frac{13}{52}-\frac{1}{52}=\frac{16}{52}=\frac{4}{13}$. (ii) $1-\frac{4}{13}=\frac{9}{13}$. (iii) The sample space has $2^3=8$ outcomes. Exactly two heads: HHT, HTH, THH, so $P=\frac{3}{8}$.

A card is drawn from a well-shuffled pack. The probability that it is a face card is
Define the mathematical and the empirical definitions of probability, giving one example of each, and state why the mathematical definition fails for the event "it will rain in Pokhara tomorrow".
Probability.r: Mathematical (classical): $P(A) = m/n$, the ratio of favourable to total equally likely cases — e.g. $P(\text{head}) = 1/2$ for a fair coin. Empirical: $P(A) = \lim_{n\to\infty} m/n$, the limiting relative frequency in repeated trials — e.g. if $25$ of $1000$ bulbs are defective, $P \approx 0.025$. The mathematical definition fails for rain because the two cases "rain" and "no rain" are not equally likely, so dividing by $2$ has no justification; only past records (an empirical estimate) can give a number.

A bag contains $4$ white, $5$ black and $3$ red balls. Two balls are drawn at random without replacement. Find the probability that
p: one is white and one is black,
Probability.r: Total $= 12$ balls, drawn without replacement. (a) $P(WW) = \dfrac{4}{12}\times\dfrac{3}{11} = \dfrac{12}{132} = \dfrac{1}{11}$. (b) One white one black, in either order: $2\times\dfrac{4}{12}\times\dfrac{5}{11} = \dfrac{40}{132} = \dfrac{10}{33}$. (c) Neither red means both come from the $9$ non-red balls: $\dfrac{9}{12}\times\dfrac{8}{11} = \dfrac{72}{132} = \dfrac{6}{11}$.

Probability.q: A card is drawn at random from a pack of $52$ cards. Find the probability that it is an ace or a red card. State clearly whether the two events are mutually exclusive.
Probability.r: A card can be both an ace and red (the ace of hearts, the ace of diamonds), so the events are not mutually exclusive. $P(\text{ace} \cup \text{red}) = \dfrac{4}{52} + \dfrac{26}{52} - \dfrac{2}{52} = \dfrac{28}{52} = \dfrac{7}{13}$.

Probability.q: In a class of $40$ students, $25$ like mathematics, $20$ like science and $10$ like both. Find the probability that a student chosen at random likes
Probability.r: With $M$ and $S$ the two events, $n(M) = 25$, $n(S) = 20$, $n(M\cap S) = 10$. (a) $n(M\cup S) = 25+20-10 = 35$, so $P = 35/40 = 7/8$. (b) Neither $= 1 - 7/8 = 1/8$ (i.e. $5$ students). (c) Mathematics only $= 25-10 = 15$ students, so $P = 15/40 = 3/8$.

p: State the addition law of probability for two events and illustrate it with a Venn diagram, writing down the special form for mutually exclusive events.
A box contains $6$ red and $4$ blue balls. Three balls are drawn one after another without replacement. Find the probability that (i) all three are red, (ii) at least one is blue.
Probability.r: (a) $P(A\cup B) = P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$. On a Venn diagram the two circles overlap in $A\cap B$; adding the two circles counts that overlap twice, so it is subtracted once. If the events are mutually exclusive the circles are disjoint, $P(A\cap B) = 0$, and $P(A\cup B) = P(A)+P(B)$.

p: State the multiplication law of probability, and explain the difference between independent and dependent events with one example of each.

Three students $A$, $B$, $C$ try to solve a problem independently with probabilities $\frac{1}{2}$, $\frac{1}{3}$ and $\frac{1}{4}$. Find the probability that (i) none of them solves it, (ii) the problem is solved, (iii) exactly one of them solves it.
Probability.r: (a) $P(A\cap B) = P(A)\,P(B|A)$; if the events are independent this becomes $P(A\cap B) = P(A)P(B)$. Independent: two tosses of a coin — the first result does not change the second. Dependent: two cards drawn from a pack without replacement — the first draw changes the composition of the pack, so $P(\text{second is an ace})$ depends on what the first card was.

Limits and Continuity.q: Evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to1}\frac{x^{5}-1}{x^{2}-1}$ and state clearly which standard limit you have used.
Limits and Continuity.r: Write both as standard forms about $a=1$: $\dfrac{x^{5}-1}{x^{2}-1} = \dfrac{(x^{5}-1)/(x-1)}{(x^{2}-1)/(x-1)}$. Using $\lim_{x\to a}\frac{x^{n}-a^{n}}{x-a} = na^{n-1}$ with $a=1$, the numerator tends to $5(1)^{4} = 5$ and the denominator to $2(1)^{1} = 2$. Hence the limit is $\boxed{5/2}$.

Limits and Continuity.q: Prove that $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x} = 1$ and hence evaluate $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{1-\cos x}{x^{2}}$.
Limits and Continuity.r: Proof. For $0 < x < \pi/2$, comparing the areas of triangle $OAB$, sector $OAB$ and the tangent triangle in a unit circle gives $\frac12\sin x < \frac12 x < \frac12\tan x$. Dividing by $\frac12\sin x > 0$ gives $1 < x/\sin x < 1/\cos x$, i.e. $\cos x < \frac{\sin x}{x} < 1$. As $x\to0^{+}$, $\cos x \to 1$, so by the squeeze theorem $\frac{\sin x}{x}\to1$. The function is even, so the left-hand limit is 1 too.

Limits and Continuity.q: A function is defined by $f(x) = 2x+3$ for $x \le 1$ and $f(x) = kx^{2}+1$ for $x > 1$. Find $k$ so that $f$ is continuous at $x=1$.

Limits and Continuity.r: Let $\varepsilon>0$. Then $|(3x-5)-7| = |3x-12| = 3|x-4|$, which is less than $\varepsilon$ exactly when $|x-4| < \varepsilon/3$. Choose $\delta = \varepsilon/3$; then $0<|x-4|<\delta \Rightarrow |(3x-5)-7| = 3|x-4| < 3\delta = \varepsilon$. Since $\delta$ exists for every $\varepsilon$, the limit is 7.

p: State the three conditions for a function to be continuous at $x = a$, and describe the three types of discontinuity with a sketch of each.
Limits and Continuity.r: (a) $f$ is continuous at $a$ iff (i) $f(a)$ is defined, (ii) $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)$ exists (LHL $=$ RHL), (iii) that limit equals $f(a)$. Removable: LHL $=$ RHL but $f(a)$ missing or different — a hole in the graph. Jump: LHL and RHL finite but unequal — a step. Infinite: a one-sided limit is $\pm\infty$ — a vertical asymptote. (See the three-panel figure in §17.3.)
