Electric Charges.q: State Coulomb's law, express it in vector form, define the coulomb and compare the electric and gravitational forces.
Describe the three methods of charging, explain the properties of electric charge and find the force on a charge due to several charges.

Electric field.q: The SI unit of electric field strength is
Electric field.w: $\text{N C}^{-1}$ and $\text{V m}^{-1}$ are the same combination of base units. Option (d) is the unit of potential.

Electric field.q: The electric field due to an infinitely long straight charged wire varies as
Electric field.w: a cylindrical Gaussian surface has area $\propto r$, so $E \propto 1/r$; only a point charge gives $1/r^2$.

Electric field.q: Two electric lines of force can never intersect because
o: the field would then have two directions at one point
Electric field.w: the tangent at a point gives the unique direction of $\vec E$ there.

Electric field.q: The electric field at $3\ \text{m}$ from a point charge of $1\ \mu\text{C}$ is
The SI unit of electric flux is
The SI unit of electric field intensity is
For an infinitely long charged straight wire, $E$ varies with distance $r$ as
Electric field.w: the cylindrical Gaussian surface gives $E = \lambda/2\pi\varepsilon_0 r$.

Electric field.q: Two electric field lines can never intersect because
o: the field would have two directions at one point
Electric field.w: a unique tangent means a unique field direction.

Electric field.q: Define electric field intensity and electric flux. State Gauss's law and name its SI units.
Using Gauss's law, derive an expression for the electric field due to an infinitely long straight uniformly charged wire.
Two point charges $+9\ \mu\text{C}$ and $-4\ \mu\text{C}$ are placed $1\ \text{m}$ apart in air. Locate the point where the resultant electric field is zero.
Electric field.r: The point lies beyond the $-4\ \mu\text{C}$ charge. With $d$ measured from it, $9/(1+d)^{2} = 4/d^{2}$ gives $3d = 2+2d$, so $d = 2\ \text{m}$ — that is, $3\ \text{m}$ from the $+9\ \mu\text{C}$ charge on the side away from it.

Electric field.q: A charge of $17.7\ \mu\text{C}$ is placed at the centre of a cube of side $10\ \text{cm}$. Calculate the electric flux through one face of the cube.
Electric field.r: Total flux $= q/\varepsilon_0 = 17.7\times10^{-6}/8.85\times10^{-12} = 2.0\times10^{6}\ \text{N m}^{2}\text{C}^{-1}$. One face gets one sixth: $3.33\times10^{5}\ \text{N m}^{2}\text{C}^{-1}$. The side length is irrelevant.

Electric field.q: A metal sphere of radius $5\ \text{cm}$ carries a charge of $2\ \mu\text{C}$. Find the field at $2\ \text{cm}$, at $5\ \text{cm}$ and at $10\ \text{cm}$ from its centre.
Electric field.r: At $2\ \text{cm}$ (inside): $E = 0$. At the surface: $E = 9\times10^{9}\times2\times10^{-6}/(0.05)^{2} = 7.2\times10^{6}\ \text{N C}^{-1}$. At $10\ \text{cm}$: $E = 9\times10^{9}\times2\times10^{-6}/(0.10)^{2} = 1.8\times10^{6}\ \text{N C}^{-1}$.

p: State Gauss's law and prove it for a point charge enclosed by a spherical surface.
Using it, obtain the electric field due to a uniformly charged conducting sphere at a point outside, on and inside the sphere, and sketch $E$ against $r$.
Electric field.r: (a) Put $q$ at the centre of a sphere of radius $r$. $E = kq/r^{2}$ is constant and parallel to $d\vec{A}$, so $\oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{A} = E(4\pi r^{2}) = q/\varepsilon_0$. (b) Outside, $E = kQ/r^{2}$; at the surface, $E = kQ/R^{2} = \sigma/\varepsilon_0$; inside, the enclosed charge is zero so $E = 0$. The graph is flat at zero up to $R$, jumps to $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$, then decays as $1/r^{2}$.

Electric field.q: Define electric field intensity, derive the field due to a point charge and state the properties of electric field lines.

Mechanics.q: Using dimensional analysis, derive an expression for the time period $T$ of a simple pendulum, assuming it depends on its length $l$, the mass $m$ of the bob and the acceleration due to gravity $g$. State one limitation of the method.
Mechanics.r: Let $T = k\,l^{a}m^{b}g^{c}$. Dimensions: $[T] = T$, $[l] = L$, $[m] = M$, $[g] = LT^{-2}$. So $T^{1}= L^{a}M^{b}L^{c}T^{-2c}$. Comparing: $M$: $b = 0$; $T$: $-2c = 1$ so $c = -\tfrac12$; $L$: $a + c = 0$ so $a = \tfrac12$. Hence $T = k\sqrt{l/g}$, independent of mass. Limitation: the dimensionless constant $k$ ($= 2\pi$) cannot be found by this method, and it fails if a quantity depends on a sum or a function such as $\sin\theta$.

Mechanics.q: Two forces of $10\ \text{N}$ and $6\ \text{N}$ act at a point with an angle of $60^{\circ}$ between them. Find the magnitude and direction of the resultant.
Mechanics.r: $R = \sqrt{P^{2} + Q^{2} + 2PQ\cos\theta} = \sqrt{100 + 36 + 2(10)(6)(0.5)} = \sqrt{196} = 14\ \text{N}$. Direction from the $10\ \text{N}$ force: $\tan\alpha = \dfrac{Q\sin\theta}{P + Q\cos\theta} = \dfrac{6(0.866)}{10 + 3} = 0.400$, so $\alpha \approx 21.8^{\circ}$.

Mechanics.q: A ball is projected with a speed of $20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ at $30^{\circ}$ above the horizontal ($g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$). Find the time of flight, the maximum height and the horizontal range.
A gun of mass $5\ \text{kg}$ fires a bullet of mass $20\ \text{g}$ at $400\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. State the principle you use and find the recoil velocity of the gun.
Mechanics.r: Principle: conservation of linear momentum (no external horizontal force). $0 = m_bv_b + Mv_g$, so $v_g = -\dfrac{m_bv_b}{M} = -\dfrac{0.020\times400}{5} = -1.6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$: the gun recoils at $1.6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ opposite to the bullet.

Mechanics.q: State the laws of solid friction. A $20\ \text{kg}$ block rests on a horizontal floor with $\mu = 0.3$. Find the horizontal force needed to move it at constant speed ($g = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$).
Mechanics.r: Laws: (i) friction opposes relative motion; (ii) limiting friction is independent of the area of contact; (iii) $F \propto R$, $F = \mu R$; (iv) kinetic friction is less than limiting friction and independent of speed. $R = mg = 20\times9.8 = 196\ \text{N}$; $F = \mu R = 0.3\times196 = 58.8\ \text{N}$.

Mechanics.q: A $2\ \text{kg}$ body is released from rest at a height of $20\ \text{m}$ ($g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$). Using energy, find its speed when it is $5\ \text{m}$ above the ground, and show that the total energy there equals the initial energy.
Mechanics.r: Fall of $15\ \text{m}$: $v^{2} = 2gh = 2(10)(15) = 300$, so $v = 17.3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. At $5\ \text{m}$: $K = \tfrac12(2)(300) = 300\ \text{J}$, $U = mgh = 2(10)(5) = 100\ \text{J}$, total $400\ \text{J}$. Initially $U = 2(10)(20) = 400\ \text{J}$, $K = 0$. Equal, so mechanical energy is conserved.

Mechanics.q: Derive an expression for the acceleration due to gravity at a height $h$ above the Earth's surface. Find $g$ at a height $R/2$ ($g_0 = 9.8\ \text{m s}^{-2}$).
Mechanics.r: At the surface $g_0 = GM/R^{2}$. At height $h$: $g = \dfrac{GM}{(R+h)^{2}}$, so $g = g_0\left(\dfrac{R}{R+h}\right)^{2} = g_0\left(1 + \dfrac{h}{R}\right)^{-2}$. For $h = R/2$: $g = 9.8\times\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^{2} = 9.8\times\dfrac{4}{9} = 4.36\ \text{m s}^{-2}$.

Mechanics.q: A car of mass $1000\ \text{kg}$ rounds a level curve of radius $50\ \text{m}$ at $10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Find the centripetal force, and the banking angle at which no friction is needed on this curve ($g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$).
Mechanics.r: $F = \dfrac{mv^{2}}{r} = \dfrac{1000\times100}{50} = 2000\ \text{N}$. With banking, $\tan\theta = \dfrac{v^{2}}{rg} = \dfrac{100}{50\times10} = 0.2$, so $\theta = 11.3^{\circ}$.

Mechanics.q: A steel wire $2\ \text{m}$ long with cross-section $1\ \text{mm}^{2}$ is stretched by $1\ \text{mm}$ by a force of $100\ \text{N}$. Find the Young modulus and the elastic energy stored.
Mechanics.r: $Y = \dfrac{FL}{A\,\Delta l} = \dfrac{100\times2}{(1\times10^{-6})(1\times10^{-3})} = 2\times10^{11}\ \text{N m}^{-2}$. Energy $= \tfrac12F\Delta l = \tfrac12(100)(10^{-3}) = 0.05\ \text{J}$.

p: Derive the three equations of uniformly accelerated motion using the velocity–time graph.
A car accelerates uniformly from $10\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ to $30\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in $200\ \text{m}$. Find the acceleration and the time taken.
Mechanics.r: (a) Draw a straight line AB on a $v$–$t$ graph from $v = u$ at $t = 0$ to $v = v$ at time $t$. Slope $= a$, so $a = \dfrac{v-u}{t}$, giving $v = u + at$. The displacement is the area under the line: a rectangle $ut$ plus a triangle $\tfrac12(v-u)t$, so $s = ut + \tfrac12(v-u)t = ut + \tfrac12at^{2}$, giving $s = ut + \tfrac12at^{2}$. The area is also the trapezoid $s = \tfrac12(u+v)t$; substituting $t = (v-u)/a$ gives $s = \dfrac{v^{2}-u^{2}}{2a}$, so $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2as$. (b) $a = \dfrac{v^{2}-u^{2}}{2s} = \dfrac{900 - 100}{400} = 2.0\ \text{m s}^{-2}$; $t = \dfrac{v-u}{a} = \dfrac{20}{2} = 10\ \text{s}$.

p: Derive an expression for the orbital speed and period of a satellite at height $h$ above the Earth.
What is a geostationary satellite? State its conditions.
For $R = 6400\ \text{km}$, $g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$ and $h = 3600\ \text{km}$, find the orbital speed and period.
Mechanics.r: (a) Gravity supplies the centripetal force: $\dfrac{mv^{2}}{R+h} = \dfrac{GMm}{(R+h)^{2}}$, so $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{R+h}} = R\sqrt{\dfrac{g}{R+h}}$ (using $GM = gR^{2}$). Period $T = \dfrac{2\pi(R+h)}{v} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{(R+h)^{3}}{GM}}$. Both are independent of the satellite's mass. (b) A satellite that appears fixed over one point of the Earth. Conditions: orbit in the equatorial plane; period $24\ \text{h}$; same sense as Earth's rotation (west to east); height about $36\,000\ \text{km}$. (c) $R + h = 10^{7}\ \text{m}$; $v = 6.4\times10^{6}\sqrt{\dfrac{10}{10^{7}}} = 6.4\times10^{6}\times10^{-3} = 6400\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

Mechanics.q: Which of the following defines the principle of conservation of momentum?
o: Total momentum before collision equals total energy after collision
Total momentum before collision equals total momentum after collision
Total momentum before collision is always greater than total momentum after collision
Total momentum after collision is always zero
Mechanics.w: Conservation of momentum states that the total momentum of an isolated system remains constant.

Mechanics.q: What does Hooke's Law describe?
o: The relationship between pressure and volume in gases
The relationship between the force applied to a spring and its extension
The relationship between velocity and time for a free-falling object
The relationship between the electric field and potential difference
Mechanics.w: Hooke's Law describes how the force applied to a spring is directly proportional to the extension of the spring.

Heat and Thermodynamics.q: Define linear, superficial and cubical expansivity. Show that $\gamma = 3\alpha$ for an isotropic solid.
Heat and Thermodynamics.r: $\alpha = \dfrac{\Delta l}{l\,\Delta\theta}$ (per unit length per kelvin); $\beta = \dfrac{\Delta A}{A\,\Delta\theta}$; $\gamma = \dfrac{\Delta V}{V\,\Delta\theta}$. A cube of side $l_0$: $V_0 = l_0^{3}$; at $\theta$, $l = l_0(1+\alpha\theta)$, so $V = l_0^{3}(1+\alpha\theta)^{3} \approx V_0(1 + 3\alpha\theta)$ (neglecting $\alpha^{2}$, $\alpha^{3}$). Comparing with $V = V_0(1+\gamma\theta)$: $\gamma = 3\alpha$. Similarly $\beta = 2\alpha$.

Heat and Thermodynamics.q: State Newton's law of cooling. A body cools from $80^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $60^{\circ}\text{C}$ in $10$ minutes in a room at $20^{\circ}\text{C}$. Estimate the time to cool from $60^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $40^{\circ}\text{C}$ using the average-temperature form.
Heat and Thermodynamics.r: The rate of loss of heat of a body is proportional to the excess of its temperature over the surroundings (for small differences). First interval: mean excess $= 70 - 20 = 50$; fall $= 20$ in $10$ min, so rate $= 2.0\ \text{K min}^{-1}$ at $50\ \text{K}$ excess, i.e. $0.04\ \text{min}^{-1}$ per kelvin. Second interval: mean $= 50^{\circ}\text{C}$, excess $30$; rate $= 0.04\times30 = 1.2\ \text{K min}^{-1}$; time $= 20/1.2 = 16.7$ min.

Heat and Thermodynamics.q: A $0.5\ \text{kg}$ metal block at $100^{\circ}\text{C}$ is dropped into $0.4\ \text{kg}$ of water at $20^{\circ}\text{C}$ and the mixture reaches $30^{\circ}\text{C}$. Find the specific heat capacity of the metal ($c_w = 4200\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$; neglect the container).

Find the heat required to change $10\ \text{g}$ of ice at $-10^{\circ}\text{C}$ into steam at $100^{\circ}\text{C}$. ($c_{ice} = 2100$, $c_w = 4200\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$, $L_f = 3.36\times10^{5}$, $L_v = 2.26\times10^{6}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}$)
Heat and Thermodynamics.r: Ice warms $-10 \to 0$: $0.010\times2100\times10 = 210\ \text{J}$. Melts: $0.010\times3.36\times10^{5} = 3360\ \text{J}$. Water $0 \to 100$: $0.010\times4200\times100 = 4200\ \text{J}$. Boils: $0.010\times2.26\times10^{6} = 22\,600\ \text{J}$. Total $= 30\,370\ \text{J} \approx 3.0\times10^{4}\ \text{J}$.

Heat and Thermodynamics.q: Define thermal conductivity. Find the rate of heat flow through a glass pane of area $2\ \text{m}^{2}$ and thickness $0.1\ \text{m}$... use $k = 0.8\ \text{W m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$ with faces $20\ \text{K}$ apart.
Heat and Thermodynamics.r: Thermal conductivity $k$: the heat flowing per second through unit area of a slab of unit thickness when the faces differ by $1\ \text{K}$ (steady state), unit $\text{W m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$. $H = \dfrac{kA\Delta\theta}{d} = \dfrac{0.8\times2\times20}{0.1} = 320\ \text{W}$.

Heat and Thermodynamics.q: State Stefan–Boltzmann's law. A black body of surface area $0.01\ \text{m}^{2}$ is at $727^{\circ}\text{C}$. Find the power radiated ($\sigma = 5.67\times10^{-8}\ \text{W m}^{-2}\text{K}^{-4}$).
Heat and Thermodynamics.r: The energy radiated per second by a black body is proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature and its area: $P = \sigma AT^{4}$. $T = 727 + 273 = 1000\ \text{K}$. $P = 5.67\times10^{-8}\times0.01\times10^{12} = 567\ \text{W}$.

Heat and Thermodynamics.q: State the zeroth law of thermodynamics and explain how it underlies the use of a thermometer.
Heat and Thermodynamics.r: If two bodies are each in thermal equilibrium with a third, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other. A thermometer is the third body: when it reads the same for two bodies they have the same temperature and no net heat flows between them. In a mercury thermometer, the mercury reaches equilibrium with the body and its column length marks the common temperature.

Heat and Thermodynamics.q: Calculate the volume of $2$ mol of an ideal gas at $27^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $1.013\times10^{5}\ \text{Pa}$ ($R = 8.31\ \text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$).

p: Derive the expression $P = \tfrac13\rho\overline{c^{2}}$ for the pressure of an ideal gas using the kinetic theory.
Deduce that the mean kinetic energy of a molecule is $\tfrac32kT$.
Find the r.m.s. speed of nitrogen ($M = 28\times10^{-3}\ \text{kg mol}^{-1}$) at $27^{\circ}\text{C}$.
Heat and Thermodynamics.r: (a) Take $N$ molecules, each of mass $m$, in a cubical box of side $l$. A molecule with velocity components $u_x, u_y, u_z$ strikes a wall perpendicular to $x$ and rebounds elastically; momentum change $= 2mu_x$. It returns to the same wall after time $2l/u_x$, so the rate of change of momentum (force) is $\dfrac{2mu_x}{2l/u_x} = \dfrac{mu_x^{2}}{l}$. For all molecules, $F = \dfrac{m}{l}\sum u_x^{2}$ and the pressure on the wall of area $l^{2}$ is $P = \dfrac{m}{l^{3}}\sum u_x^{2} = \dfrac{m}{V}\,N\,\overline{u_x^{2}}$. By symmetry $\overline{u_x^{2}} = \overline{u_y^{2}} = \overline{u_z^{2}} = \tfrac13\overline{c^{2}}$.

Heat and Thermodynamics.q: According to Charles's Law, what happens to the volume of a gas when its temperature is increased while keeping the pressure constant?
o: The volume decreases proportionally to the increase in temperature.
The volume increases proportionally to the increase in temperature.
The volume remains constant regardless of the change in temperature.
The volume increases exponentially with an increase in temperature.
Heat and Thermodynamics.w: Charles's Law states that the volume of a gas increases linearly with an increase in temperature at constant pressure.

Heat and Thermodynamics.q: Which statement best describes the Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics?
o: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted from one form to another.
If two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third system, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other.
The entropy of an isolated system not in equilibrium will tend to increase over time.
The total energy of an isolated system is always conserved.
Heat and Thermodynamics.w: The Zeroth Law defines thermal equilibrium and the concept of temperature.

Heat and Thermodynamics.q: What does the Second Law of Thermodynamics imply about the direction of heat transfer?
o: Heat can spontaneously flow from a colder body to a hotter body.
Heat will spontaneously flow from a hotter body to a colder body.
Heat transfer can occur without any net change in the temperature of both bodies.
Heat transfer is impossible between two bodies at the same temperature.
Heat and Thermodynamics.w: The Second Law states that heat naturally flows from hot to cold objects.

Waves and Optics.q: A coin lies at the bottom of a water tank $12\ \text{cm}$ deep. If $n_{water} = 4/3$, find the apparent depth. Explain why a pool looks shallower than it is.
Waves and Optics.r: $n = \dfrac{\text{real depth}}{\text{apparent depth}}$, so apparent depth $= \dfrac{12}{4/3} = 9\ \text{cm}$. Rays leaving the coin bend away from the normal on entering air, so to the eye they appear to come from a point nearer the surface.

Waves and Optics.q: Define the critical angle and total internal reflection. Find the critical angle for glass of refractive index $1.5$.
Waves and Optics.r: The critical angle is the angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the refracted ray grazes the interface (angle of refraction $90^{\circ}$). Total internal reflection occurs when light travelling in the denser medium meets the boundary at an angle greater than $C$. $\sin C = \dfrac{1}{n} = \dfrac{1}{1.5} = 0.667$, so $C = 41.8^{\circ}$.

Waves and Optics.q: A prism of angle $60^{\circ}$ and refractive index $\sqrt{2}$ is used. Find the angle of minimum deviation.
An object is $30\ \text{cm}$ from a convex lens of focal length $20\ \text{cm}$. Find the image distance and magnification. Also find the power of a concave lens of focal length $25\ \text{cm}$.
Define the dispersive power of a material. Find it for glass with $n_v = 1.532$, $n_r = 1.514$ and $n_y = 1.522$.
Waves and Optics.r: Dispersive power $\omega = \dfrac{n_v - n_r}{n_y - 1}$: the ratio of the angular dispersion to the mean deviation. $\omega = \dfrac{1.532 - 1.514}{1.522 - 1} = \dfrac{0.018}{0.522} = 0.0345$.

p: Draw the path of a ray through a prism and derive $n = \dfrac{\sin\frac{A+D}{2}}{\sin\frac{A}{2}}$.
A ray falls on a prism of angle $60^{\circ}$ at $50^{\circ}$ and emerges at $50^{\circ}$. Find the deviation and the refractive index.
Waves and Optics.r: (a) (Diagram: ray $PQ$ meets face $AB$ at $Q$, bends towards the normal, meets face $AC$ at $R$, emerges as $RS$ bending away; angles $i_1, r_1$ at $Q$ and $r_2, i_2$ at $R$; the deviation $D$ is between the incident ray $PQ$ extended and $RS$.) Deviation at the first face $= i_1 - r_1$; at the second $= i_2 - r_2$, so $D = (i_1 + i_2) - (r_1 + r_2)$. In the quadrilateral $AQNR$ (normals meeting at $N$), $r_1 + r_2 = A$. So $D = i_1 + i_2 - A$. At minimum deviation the ray passes symmetrically: $i_1 = i_2 = i$ and $r_1 = r_2 = r = A/2$, so $D_m = 2i - A$, or $i = \dfrac{A + D_m}{2}$. Snell's law $n = \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r}$ gives $n = \dfrac{\sin\frac{A+D_m}{2}}{\sin\frac{A}{2}}$.

Waves and Optics.q: Derive the mirror formula $\dfrac{1}{u} + \dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f}$ for a concave mirror and show that $f = R/2$. [6] Find $R$ if an object $20\ \text{cm}$ away gives a real image $60\ \text{cm}$ away.
Waves and Optics.r: (Diagram: object $AB$ beyond $C$; ray $AD$ parallel to the axis reflects through $F$; ray $AP$ strikes the pole and reflects with equal angle; image $A'B'$ between $F$ and $C$.) Use the real-is-positive convention: $PB = u$, $PB' = v$, $PF = f$. The ray $AP$ hits the pole at angle $\theta$ and reflects at the same angle, so right triangles $ABP$ and $A'B'P$ are similar: $\dfrac{AB}{A'B'} = \dfrac{u}{v}$. The ray $AD$ (with $DP = AB$) passes through $F$, so right triangles $DPF$ and $A'B'F$ are similar: $\dfrac{AB}{A'B'} = \dfrac{DP}{A'B'} = \dfrac{PF}{FB'} = \dfrac{f}{v - f}$. Equating, $\dfrac{u}{v} = \dfrac{f}{v-f}$, so $uv - uf = vf$.

Electricity and Magnetism.q: State Coulomb's law. Find the force between two $2\ \mu\text{C}$ charges placed $3\ \text{cm}$ apart in air ($k = 9\times10^{9}\ \text{N m}^{2}\text{C}^{-2}$).
Electricity and Magnetism.r: The force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them, along the line joining them: $F = k\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r^{2}}$. $F = \dfrac{9\times10^{9}\times(2\times10^{-6})^{2}}{(0.03)^{2}} = \dfrac{9\times10^{9}\times4\times10^{-12}}{9\times10^{-4}} = 40\ \text{N}$ (repulsive).

Electricity and Magnetism.q: Define electric field intensity. Find the field at $0.30\ \text{m}$ from a point charge of $5\ \text{nC}$, and the force on a $2\ \text{nC}$ charge there.
Electricity and Magnetism.r: The force per unit positive test charge at that point, $E = F/q$ (unit $\text{N C}^{-1}$). $E = \dfrac{kq}{r^{2}} = \dfrac{9\times10^{9}\times5\times10^{-9}}{0.09} = 500\ \text{N C}^{-1}$. $F = qE = 2\times10^{-9}\times500 = 1.0\times10^{-6}\ \text{N}$.

Electricity and Magnetism.q: Define electric potential and the volt. Find the work done in taking a $2\ \mu\text{C}$ charge through a potential difference of $100\ \text{V}$.
Electricity and Magnetism.r: Potential at a point is the work done per unit positive charge in bringing it from infinity to that point. One volt is one joule per coulomb. $W = qV = 2\times10^{-6}\times100 = 2\times10^{-4}\ \text{J}$.

Electricity and Magnetism.q: Derive the energy stored in a capacitor. Find it for $10\ \mu\text{F}$ charged to $100\ \text{V}$.
Electricity and Magnetism.r: Raising the charge on the plates from $q$ to $q + dq$ against the potential $V = q/C$ needs work $dW = \dfrac{q}{C}\,dq$. Total: $W = \int_0^Q\dfrac{q}{C}\,dq = \dfrac{Q^{2}}{2C} = \tfrac12CV^{2} = \tfrac12QV$. $U = \tfrac12(10\times10^{-6})(100)^{2} = 0.050\ \text{J}$.

Electricity and Magnetism.q: A cell of emf $12\ \text{V}$ and internal resistance $1\ \Omega$ is connected to a $5\ \Omega$ resistor. Find the current, the terminal potential difference and the power dissipated in the external resistor.
Electricity and Magnetism.r: $I = \dfrac{E}{R + r} = \dfrac{12}{6} = 2.0\ \text{A}$. Terminal p.d. $V = E - Ir = 12 - 2 = 10\ \text{V}$. $P = I^{2}R = 4\times5 = 20\ \text{W}$.

Electricity and Magnetism.q: State Ohm's law and explain why it fails for a filament lamp. Find the resistance of a copper wire $2\ \text{m}$ long, $0.5\ \text{mm}^{2}$ in area ($\rho = 1.7\times10^{-8}\ \Omega\,\text{m}$).
Electricity and Magnetism.r: Ohm's law: at constant temperature the current through a conductor is proportional to the potential difference across it. A filament heats up, so its resistance rises with current and the $V$–$I$ graph is not a straight line. $R = \dfrac{\rho l}{A} = \dfrac{1.7\times10^{-8}\times2}{0.5\times10^{-6}} = 0.068\ \Omega$.

p: Derive the capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor, $C = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d}$.
Show that the energy density is $\tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^{2}$.
Plates of area $0.02\ \text{m}^{2}$ are $1\ \text{mm}$ apart in air; find $C$ and the energy at $100\ \text{V}$ ($\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}\ \text{F m}^{-1}$).
Electricity and Magnetism.r: (a) For large plates the field between them (area $A$, charge $\pm Q$) is $E = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0} = \dfrac{Q}{\varepsilon_0A}$ (Gauss's law). The potential difference is $V = Ed = \dfrac{Qd}{\varepsilon_0A}$. By definition $C = \dfrac{Q}{V} = \dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d}$. (b) $U = \tfrac12CV^{2} = \tfrac12\dfrac{\varepsilon_0A}{d}(Ed)^{2} = \tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^{2}\,(Ad)$. The volume between the plates is $Ad$, so the energy per unit volume is $\tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^{2}$. (c) $C = \dfrac{8.85\times10^{-12}\times0.02}{1\times10^{-3}} = 1.77\times10^{-10}\ \text{F} = 177\ \text{pF}$. $U = \tfrac12CV^{2} = \tfrac12(1.77\times10^{-10})(10^{4}) = 8.85\times10^{-7}\ \text{J}$.

p: State Kirchhoff's current law and voltage law and name the principle each expresses.
A $12\ \text{V}$ battery (negligible internal resistance) is connected to a $4\ \Omega$ resistor in series with a parallel pair of $6\ \Omega$ and $3\ \Omega$. Find the current in each resistor.

Electricity and Magnetism.q: What is the unit of magnetic flux density?
Electricity and Magnetism.w: Tesla (T) is the SI unit of magnetic flux density.

Modern Physics.q: Define half-life and decay constant, and derive the relation between them.
Modern Physics.r: Half-life $T_{1/2}$: the time in which half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample decay. Decay constant $\lambda$: the probability of decay of a nucleus per unit time (fractional decay rate). From $N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}$, at $t = T_{1/2}$, $N = N_0/2$: $\tfrac12 = e^{-\lambda T_{1/2}}$, so $\ln2 = \lambda T_{1/2}$ and $T_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{\lambda}$.

Modern Physics.q: A radioactive sample of mass $80\ \text{g}$ has half-life $4$ days. How much remains after $12$ days?

Calculate the binding energy and the binding energy per nucleon of $^{4}_{2}\text{He}$ ($m_p = 1.007825\ \text{u}$ for hydrogen atom, $m_n = 1.008665\ \text{u}$, $m_{He} = 4.002603\ \text{u}$, $1\ \text{u} = 931.5\ \text{MeV}$).
Distinguish between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion.
Using band theory, distinguish between a conductor, a semiconductor and an insulator.
Explain what happens to the resistance of a semiconductor and a metal as temperature rises, and why.

p: State the law of radioactive decay and derive $N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}$.
Draw the decay curve and mark $T_{1/2}$.
A sample of $64\ \text{g}$ is reduced to $8\ \text{g}$ in $18$ days. Find the half-life and the decay constant.
Modern Physics.r: (a) Law: the rate of decay of a radioactive sample is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei present. $-\dfrac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N$. Separating variables, $\dfrac{dN}{N} = -\lambda\,dt$. Integrating from $N_0$ at $t = 0$ to $N$ at $t$: $\ln\dfrac{N}{N_0} = -\lambda t$, so $N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}$. (b) (Graph: an exponential curve falling from $N_0$ at $t = 0$; mark $N_0/2$ at $t = T_{1/2}$, $N_0/4$ at $2T_{1/2}$, $N_0/8$ at $3T_{1/2}$.) (c) $\dfrac{64}{8} = 8 = 2^{3}$, so $18\ \text{days} = 3T_{1/2}$ and $T_{1/2} = 6\ \text{days}$. $\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{6} = 0.1155\ \text{day}^{-1}$.

Modern Physics.q: According to Planck's quantum theory, the energy of a photon is directly proportional to its frequency. What is the proportionality constant in this relation?
Modern Physics.w: Planck's constant ($h$) is the proportionality constant in the equation $E = hf$.

Modern Physics.q: What does the de Broglie hypothesis state about particles?
o: Particles can exist in two places at once.
Particles can only absorb discrete amounts of energy.
Modern Physics.w: De Broglie hypothesized that all particles exhibit wave-like behavior.

Modern Physics.q: The uncertainty principle implies which of the following about the measurement of a particle’s properties?
o: The more accurately we know a particle's momentum, the less accurately we can know its position.
The more accurately we know a particle's position, the more accurately we can know its momentum.
We can measure both the position and momentum of a particle with absolute precision.
The uncertainty principle applies only to macroscopic objects.
Modern Physics.w: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle states there is an inherent limit to the precision with which certain pairs of physical properties can be known simultaneously.

Modern Physics.q: Which law describes the emission spectrum of hydrogen?
Modern Physics.w: Rydberg's law predicts the wavelengths of spectral lines of various chemical elements, especially hydrogen.

A body of mass $4\ \text{kg}$ moving at $6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ collides inelastically with a $2\ \text{kg}$ body at rest and they move together. Find the common velocity and the loss of kinetic energy.
Find the equivalent resistance of $4\ \Omega$ and $12\ \Omega$ in parallel, and the current from a $6\ \text{V}$ source through it.
Find the temperature rise of $0.2\ \text{kg}$ of water when it absorbs $4200\ \text{J}$ of heat ($c = 4200\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$).
State Snell's law and find the refractive index if the angle of incidence is $45^{\circ}$ and of refraction $30^{\circ}$.
Physics: Unit-wise Subjective Question B.r: The ratio $\sin i/\sin r$ is constant for a given pair of media, and the incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in one plane. $n = \dfrac{\sin45^{\circ}}{\sin30^{\circ}} = \dfrac{0.7071}{0.5} = 1.41$.

Physics: Unit-wise Subjective Question B.q: Derive the work–energy theorem for a constant force and use it to find the stopping distance of a $1000\ \text{kg}$ car moving at $20\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ when a constant braking force of $5000\ \text{N}$ is applied.
Physics: Unit-wise Subjective Question B.r: For a constant force $F$ producing acceleration $a$ over displacement $s$: $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2as$ with $a = F/m$ gives $Fs = \tfrac12mv^{2} - \tfrac12mu^{2}$: the work done by the net force equals the change in kinetic energy. Braking: $-5000\,s = 0 - \tfrac12(1000)(400) = -2.0\times10^{5}$, so $s = 40\ \text{m}$.

Physics: Unit-wise Subjective Question B.q: Define the principal focus of a convex lens, derive the thin-lens formula and find $f$ if an object at $40\ \text{cm}$ gives a real image at $24\ \text{cm}$.
Physics: Unit-wise Subjective Question B.r: The principal focus is the point on the axis at which rays parallel to the axis converge after refraction. Derivation: for an object $AB$ at $u$, ray $AO$ through the optical centre is undeviated; the ray parallel to the axis refracts through $F$. From similar triangles $ABO \sim A'B'O$: $\dfrac{h_o}{h_i} = \dfrac{u}{v}$; from $COF \sim A'B'F$: $\dfrac{h_o}{h_i} = \dfrac{f}{v - f}$. So $\dfrac{u}{v} = \dfrac{f}{v-f}$, giving $uv - uf = vf$ and $\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{u} + \dfrac{1}{v}$ (real-is-positive). Numerical: $\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{40} + \dfrac{1}{24} = \dfrac{3 + 5}{120} = \dfrac{1}{15}$, so $f = 15\ \text{cm}$.

Physics: Unit-wise Subjective Question B.q: If an object is thrown vertically upward with an initial velocity of $20\,ms^{-1}$, how high does it go before starting to fall back down?
Physics: Unit-wise Subjective Question B.w: At the highest point, final velocity is $0$. Using the equation $v^2 = u^2 - 2gh$, we substitute $v=0$, $u=20\,ms^{-1}$, and $g=9.8\,ms^{-2}$ to find $h = \frac{u^2}{2g} = 20.4\,m$.

Model Set 1.q: According to Newton's Second Law of Motion, what is the relationship between force ($F$), mass ($m$), and acceleration ($a$)?
Model Set 1.w: Newton's Second Law states that the net force acting on an object equals the product of its mass and acceleration.

Model Set 1.q: What does Hooke's Law describe?
o: The relationship between current and voltage in a conductor
The relationship between pressure and volume in gases
The relationship between stress and strain in elastic materials
The relationship between gravitational force and distance between two masses
Model Set 1.w: Hooke's Law defines the linear relationship between stress and strain within the elastic limit of a material.

Model Set 1.q: In the context of conservation of energy, which statement best describes the law?
o: Energy can be created but not destroyed
Energy can be destroyed but not created
Energy can neither be created nor destroyed
Energy can be both created and destroyed
Model Set 1.w: The law of conservation of energy asserts that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed from one form to another.

Model Set 1.q: Which equation represents Ohm's Law?
Model Set 1.w: Ohm's Law states that the current through a conductor between two points is directly proportional to the voltage across the two points.

A $60\ \text{kg}$ person stands on a lift accelerating upward at $2\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. Find the apparent weight ($g = 10$).
Physics: Model Question Sets and Predict.r: $R - mg = ma$, so $R = m(g + a) = 60\times12 = 720\ \text{N}$ (apparent weight, compared with $600\ \text{N}$ at rest).

Physics: Model Question Sets and Predict.q: Find the equivalent resistance between the ends when $2\ \Omega$ is in series with the parallel pair $3\ \Omega$ and $6\ \Omega$.
A sample has $5\ \text{g}$ left after $12$ days from $40\ \text{g}$. Find its half-life.
Derive the expression for the energy stored in a charged capacitor and find the energy released when a $20\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor charged to $50\ \text{V}$ is discharged.
Physics: Model Question Sets and Predict.r: Charging from $q$ to $q + dq$ against the p.d. $V = q/C$ needs $dW = \dfrac{q}{C}\,dq$. Total work $W = \int_0^Q\dfrac{q}{C}\,dq = \dfrac{Q^{2}}{2C} = \tfrac12CV^{2}$, stored as electric field energy. $U = \tfrac12(20\times10^{-6})(50)^{2} = 0.025\ \text{J}$, which is released as heat or light on discharge.

Physics: Model Question Sets and Predict.q: Derive the relation between the focal length and radius of curvature of a concave mirror and find the image formed by an object $30\ \text{cm}$ from a concave mirror of $f = 10\ \text{cm}$.
Physics: Model Question Sets and Predict.r: A ray parallel to the axis strikes the mirror at $D$; the radius $CD$ is the normal, so the angle of incidence and reflection are equal, $\theta$. The reflected ray cuts the axis at $F$. In $\triangle CDF$, $\angle FCD = \angle CDF = \theta$ (since $DA \parallel CP$), so $CF = FD$; for a small aperture $FD \approx FP$, hence $CP = CF + FP = 2FP$ and $f = R/2$. Numerical: $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{10} - \dfrac{1}{30} = \dfrac{2}{30}$, so $v = 15\ \text{cm}$ (real, inverted); $m = -\dfrac{15}{30} = -0.5$ (diminished).

Recent Trends in physics.q: The quark composition of a neutron is
Flat rotation curves of spiral galaxies are evidence for
Recent Trends in physics.w: the extra unseen mass keeps the outer stars moving fast.

Recent Trends in physics.q: What is an antiparticle? Describe pair production and annihilation, giving the threshold energy for electron–positron pair production.
Recent Trends in physics.r: Outline: an antiparticle has the same mass and spin as its particle but opposite charge and opposite quantum numbers (§26.1). In pair production a photon passing close to a nucleus turns into a particle–antiparticle pair; for $e^{-}e^{+}$ the photon must carry at least $2m_ec^{2} = 1.02\ \text{MeV}$, and the nearby nucleus is needed to take up recoil momentum. In annihilation an electron and a positron meet and vanish, and two photons of $0.511\ \text{MeV}$ go out in opposite directions so that momentum is conserved.

Recent Trends in physics.q: Distinguish between baryons and mesons, and show that the quark contents $uud$ and $u\bar{d}$ give the correct charges of the proton and the $\pi^{+}$.
Recent Trends in physics.r: Outline: baryons are three quarks with baryon number $+1$; mesons are a quark and an antiquark with baryon number $0$, and all mesons are unstable. Charges: $uud = \frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{3} = +1$ for the proton; $u\bar{d} = \frac{2}{3}+\frac{1}{3} = +1$ for the $\pi^{+}$.

Recent Trends in physics.q: Why was the neutrino proposed, and why is it so difficult to detect? What does neutrino oscillation tell us about its mass?
Recent Trends in physics.r: Outline: beta-decay electrons emerge with a continuous energy spectrum, so Pauli (1930) proposed an unseen neutral particle carrying off the missing energy and momentum. The neutrino is chargeless and interacts only weakly, so its chance of interacting in a detector is minute. Oscillation between flavours is possible only if at least two neutrino states have non-zero mass.

Recent Trends in physics.q: What is dark matter? Give two pieces of observational evidence for it.
Recent Trends in physics.r: Outline: dark matter is matter that has mass and therefore gravitates, but neither emits nor absorbs light, so it is seen only through its gravity (§26.2). Evidence: (i) flat galactic rotation curves — outer stars orbit far faster than the visible mass allows, requiring $M(r) \propto r$ out to large radii; (ii) gravitational lensing by clusters, which bends background light by far more than the luminous mass could; (iii) the speeds of galaxies inside clusters (Zwicky, Coma cluster), which are too high for the cluster to stay bound on visible mass alone.

Recent Trends in physics.q: Show that a star orbiting at radius $r$ inside a galaxy of enclosed mass $M(r)$ has speed $v = \sqrt{GM(r)/r}$, and explain why a flat rotation curve requires $M(r) \propto r$.
Recent Trends in physics.r: Gravity supplies the centripetal force, $GM(r)m/r^{2} = mv^{2}/r$. Cancelling $m$ and multiplying by $r$ gives $v^{2} = GM(r)/r$, so $v = \sqrt{GM(r)/r}$. If $v$ is constant then $M(r) = v^{2}r/G$, which is proportional to $r$: mass keeps accumulating outside the visible disc.

Recent Trends in physics.q: A gravitational wave of strain $1.0\times10^{-21}$ crosses a detector whose arms are $4.0\ \text{km}$ long. Calculate the change in length of one arm.
Recent Trends in physics.r: $\Delta L = hL = 1.0\times10^{-21}\times4.0\times10^{3} = 4.0\times10^{-18}\ \text{m}$, roughly one four-hundredth of a proton diameter.

Plant Anatomy.q: What basis would you apply to distinguish a meristematic tissue from a permanent tissue?
o: losing the ability of cell division
Plant Anatomy.w: meristematic cells are the ones that activate cell division; option (d) describes a permanent cell, the very opposite.

Plant Anatomy.q: Which parenchyma makes aquatic plants light and helps them to float?
Plant Anatomy.w: aerenchyma has large air spaces. Stellate parenchyma is a kind of aerenchyma with star-shaped cells (banana petiole), but the general tissue that gives buoyancy is aerenchyma. Assimilatory parenchyma (chlorenchyma) is for photosynthesis.

Plant Anatomy.q: What is the role of the endodermis in the roots of a plant?
o: to store excess water and starch
to facilitate gas exchange for respiration
to regulate the movement of water and minerals into the root
Plant Anatomy.w: endodermal cells with Casparian strips force water to pass through the living protoplast, so the endodermis controls what enters the stele. Option (a) is the starch sheath of a stem, a different endodermis.

Plant Anatomy.q: What is the name of the lateral meristem responsible for secondary growth in stems?
Plant Anatomy.w: the vascular cambium adds secondary xylem and phloem. Cork cambium is also a lateral meristem, but it makes periderm, not the vascular tissue that the word "stem growth" usually means; apical meristem gives primary growth only.

Plant Anatomy.q: A botanist observes scattered vascular bundles throughout the ground tissue of a stem. What is the most appropriate conclusion?
o: the plant has an open vascular bundle
Plant Anatomy.w: scattered bundles in undifferentiated ground tissue are the signature of a monocot stem. Option (c) is the opposite: monocot bundles are closed.

Plant Anatomy.q: Which tissue is dead at maturity and has a heavily lignified wall?
Plant Anatomy.w: sclerenchyma cells are dead and lignified. Collenchyma is living, parenchyma is living.

Plant Anatomy.q: The only living component of xylem is
Plant Anatomy.w: xylem parenchyma stores food and is alive; tracheids, vessels and fibres are dead at maturity.

Plant Anatomy.q: A sieve tube element has no nucleus. It stays alive because of the help of
Plant Anatomy.w: the companion cell, sister cell of the sieve element, supplies ATP and proteins. Bulliform and passage cells are in leaf and endodermis.

Plant Anatomy.q: Casparian strips are bands of
o: lignin on the outer wall of the epidermis
suberin on the radial and transverse walls of endodermal cells
Plant Anatomy.w: suberin on radial and transverse walls; option (a) puts it on the epidermis, which is wrong.

Plant Anatomy.q: Heartwood differs from sapwood because it
o: is dead, plugged with tyloses, tannin and resin, and gives only support
Plant Anatomy.w: heartwood is non-conducting. Option (d) describes sapwood, which is the living conducting region beneath the bark.

Plant Anatomy.q: Which leaf has mesophyll that is not differentiated into palisade and spongy tissue?
Plant Anatomy.w: isobilateral leaves of monocots have similar mesophyll on both sides. Ligustrum (privet) is a dicot with a dorsiventral leaf.

Plant Anatomy.q: Define parenchyma tissue and explain its structure and function.
Plant Anatomy.r: Definition [1]. Parenchyma is a living, simple permanent tissue made of thin-walled cells that can still divide. Structure [2]. The cells are round, oval or polygonal; the primary wall is thin cellulose; there is a large central vacuole, a peripheral nucleus and usually small intercellular spaces. Functions [1]. storage of food (cortex of potato tuber), photosynthesis (chlorenchyma in leaf), buoyancy (aerenchyma in aquatic plants), healing of wounds and regeneration, and secretion.

Plant Anatomy.q: Differentiate between simple permanent tissue and complex permanent tissue on the basis of structure, types, cell composition and functions.
Define vascular bundle. What type of vascular bundle is present in a monocot root? Mention any two functions of a vascular bundle.
Plant Anatomy.r: Definition [1]. A vascular bundle is a strand of conducting tissue made up of xylem and phloem (with or without cambium) that runs through the plant body. Type in monocot root [1]. radial, with many (polyarch, more than six) separate patches of xylem and phloem on alternate radii; the xylem is exarch. Functions [2]. (i) Xylem conducts water and minerals upward; phloem conducts prepared food to all parts. (ii) The lignified xylem gives mechanical strength; the cambium, where present, produces secondary tissue.

Plant Anatomy.q: Write four differences between a dicot stem and a monocot stem. (original)
Write four differences between a dicot root and a monocot root. (original)
Describe the secondary growth in a dicot stem with the help of labelled diagrams. (predicted: no long question on anatomy has appeared yet, which makes the unit overdue)
Xylem and phloem lying on alternate radii is characteristic of
Plant Anatomy.w: radial bundles are the defining feature of a root; stems and leaves have conjoint bundles.

Plant Anatomy.q: The Casparian strip is found in the
Plant Anatomy.w: the strip of suberin and lignin lies on the radial and tangential walls of the endodermis.

Plant Anatomy.q: Bulliform cells occur in the
o: upper epidermis of a grass leaf
lower epidermis of a dicot leaf
Plant Anatomy.w: large thin-walled motor cells in the upper epidermis of grasses; they lose turgor and roll the leaf.

Plant Anatomy.q: Distinguish between collenchyma and sclerenchyma under four headings.
Plant Anatomy.r: Table of four rows. Cell state — collenchyma living, sclerenchyma dead. Wall material — cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin (collenchyma) versus lignin (sclerenchyma). Thickening — uneven, at corners or on particular walls, versus uniform and heavy with a narrow lumen. Function and location — flexible support in a still-growing dicot organ (hypodermis, petiole) versus rigid support in a mature organ (fibres, sclereids, bundle caps).

Plant Anatomy.q: Describe the structure and function of the endodermis and pericycle of a dicot root.
What is an annual ring? Explain how spring wood and autumn wood differ, and state one limitation of using annual rings to age a tree in Nepal.
Plant Anatomy.r: Definition, then the contrast: spring wood has wide, thin-walled vessels and is light-coloured and less dense; autumn wood has narrow, thick-walled vessels and is dark and dense. One of each = one year. Limitation: in the Terai and the tropics the cambium may work almost continuously, so the rings are faint or absent, and a mid-season drought can lay down a false ring — so ring counts are reliable only where the growing season is sharply defined.

Plant Anatomy.q: Give four anatomical differences between a dorsiventral and an isobilateral leaf.
Define bark. Distinguish between periderm and bark, and explain the function of lenticels.
Name the four elements of xylem and state one function of each.
Plant Anatomy.r: Tracheids — dead, tapering, bordered pits; conduction and support, and the only conducting element in gymnosperms. Vessels — dead, wide tubes with perforated end walls; efficient conduction, characteristic of angiosperms. Xylem fibres — dead, sclerenchymatous; mechanical support. Xylem parenchyma — living; storage of starch and tannin, and radial conduction.

Lateral roots are said to be endogenous while stem branches are exogenous. Explain what this means and why it matters.

Plant Anatomy.q: Describe the secondary growth of a dicot stem. Explain the formation of the cambial ring, the activity of the cambium, annual rings and the formation of bark.
