Plant Physiology.q: Two cells P and Q lie in contact, separated by a semi-permeable membrane. The osmotic pressure of P is 15 atm and of Q is 12 atm; the turgor pressure of P is 10 atm and of Q is 6 atm. In which direction will water move?
Plant Physiology.w: DPD of P = 15 - 10 = 5 atm, of Q = 12 - 6 = 6 atm. Water moves towards the larger DPD, so P → Q. Option (c) is the trap of comparing only the osmotic pressures or only the turgor pressures: P is larger in both, which gives a false "P is stronger" instinct. It is the difference that matters.

Plant Physiology.q: Which one of the following parts is not responsible for transpiration in plants?
Plant Physiology.w: transpiration is loss from aerial parts; roots absorb water. Option (d) is true of transpiration, not its opposite.

Plant Physiology.q: A cell has an osmotic pressure of 12 atm and a turgor pressure of 8 atm. Its DPD is
Plant Physiology.w: DPD = OP - TP = 12 - 8 = 4 atm. Option (a) adds instead of subtracting.

Plant Physiology.q: The cohesion–tension theory of the ascent of sap was proposed by
Plant Physiology.w: Dixon and Joly (1894). Münch proposed the pressure-flow hypothesis for phloem; Went is auxin.

Plant Physiology.q: Loss of liquid water from leaf margins through hydathodes at night is
Plant Physiology.w: guttation is from hydathodes and needs root pressure. Bleeding is from a cut stem.

Plant Physiology.q: Stomata open in the morning because
o: K⁺ enter the guard cells, water follows and they become turgid
starch is formed in guard cells
Plant Physiology.w: in light, K⁺ and malate accumulate, the guard cells take in water and bulge, pulling the stoma open. Option (c) is the closing signal.

Plant Physiology.q: A plant cell is placed in a 10 % NaCl solution. The cell will
Plant Physiology.w: the outside solution is hypertonic, water leaves, the protoplast shrinks away from the wall: plasmolysis. Bursting (a) is what animal cells do in hypotonic water.

Plant Physiology.q: Some C4 plants show the diagnostic feature of Kranz anatomy. Which of these plants has it?
Plant Physiology.w: maize is a C4 plant with a wreath (Kranz) of bundle-sheath cells. Wheat, barley and oats are C3 grasses, a favourite distractor set.

Plant Physiology.q: The oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from
Plant Physiology.w: photolysis of water (Hill reaction; ¹⁸O in water appears in O₂). Students pick CO₂ because it is the gas that is "used".

Plant Physiology.q: The reaction-centre chlorophyll a of photosystem I is
Plant Physiology.w: P700 for PS I, P680 for PS II. P870 is bacterial.

Plant Physiology.q: Cyclic photophosphorylation produces
Plant Physiology.w: electrons return to PS I, so there is no NADPH and, with no photolysis, no O₂.

Plant Physiology.q: For the fixation of one molecule of CO₂ in the Calvin cycle the plant needs
Plant Physiology.w: 3 ATP + 2 NADPH per CO₂, so 18 ATP and 12 NADPH for one glucose.

Plant Physiology.q: In a C4 plant the enzyme that first fixes CO₂ in the mesophyll cell is
Plant Physiology.w: PEP carboxylase, which has no affinity for O₂, fixes HCO₃⁻ into oxaloacetate; RuBisCO works later, in the bundle sheath.

Plant Physiology.q: The net gain of ATP from glycolysis of one glucose molecule is
Plant Physiology.w: 4 ATP made, 2 spent: net 2. Option (b) is the gross yield.

Plant Physiology.q: Differentiate between transpiration and guttation.
How does diffusion differ from osmosis on the basis of the types of molecules involved across a cell membrane? Explain how environmental factors influence the rate of diffusion.
Plant Physiology.r: Difference [2]. Diffusion is the net movement of molecules of any substance — solid, liquid or gas, solute or solvent — from a region of higher to lower concentration. It needs no membrane. Osmosis is the movement of water (solvent) molecules only across a selectively permeable membrane from higher water potential to lower water potential. Environmental factors [2]. (i) Temperature: heat raises the kinetic energy of molecules and speeds diffusion. (ii) Concentration gradient: a steeper gradient makes it faster. (iii) Density of the medium and size of the molecule: small molecules move faster through a thinner medium (gases diffuse faster than liquids).

Plant Physiology.q: Describe any four practical importances of seed dormancy in agriculture and horticulture.
Plant Physiology.r: Seed dormancy is useful because (any four): (i) it keeps seeds from germinating in an unfavourable season (winter, drought) and saves the seedling; (ii) it allows seeds to be stored and transported to distant places; (iii) it spreads germination over time, so a single bad spell cannot kill all seedlings; (iv) it prevents sprouting on the mother plant (vivipary) during a rainy harvest; (v) in horticulture, knowing the dormancy type lets growers break it by scarification or stratification, which gives uniform germination of apple, rose and many forest seeds; (vi) it lets seed banks keep germplasm for years.

Plant Physiology.q: Which influencing factors must be provided for the normal germination of seeds? What happens when seeds are kept at low temperature?
Plant Physiology.r: Factors [3]. Water (imbibition softens the coat and activates enzymes), oxygen (for aerobic respiration that supplies energy), a suitable temperature (25–30 °C for most seeds; at best an optimum), plus a viable seed with a mature embryo and, for a few seeds (lettuce), light. Low temperature [1]. Enzymes work slowly, respiration and metabolism fall, so germination is delayed or stops and the seed stays dormant (and may be injured by freezing). Chilling for some weeks (stratification) breaks dormancy in apple and pear.

Plant Physiology.q: Differentiate between C3 and C4 plants (any four points). (original)
The source of oxygen in photosynthesis is water, not carbon dioxide. Explain with reasons. Briefly describe the Hill reaction.
Plant Physiology.r: Reasons [2]. (i) Van Niel's comparison. Purple sulphur bacteria photosynthesise with H₂S and release sulphur, not oxygen: CO₂ + 2H₂S → (CH₂O) + H₂O + 2S. So in green plants the hydrogen donor must be water, and the gas released must come from it: CO₂ + 2H₂O → (CH₂O) + H₂O + O₂. (ii) Ruben and Kamen (1941) used heavy oxygen. Chlorella given water labelled with ¹⁸O released ¹⁸O₂; when the CO₂ was labelled and the water was ordinary, the oxygen released was not labelled. So O₂ comes from H₂O. Hill reaction [6]. Robert Hill (1937) showed that isolated chloroplasts can release oxygen in the light, without any CO₂, if a suitable hydrogen acceptor is provided. Experiment.

Plant Physiology.q: The light-independent reactions of photosynthesis convert carbon dioxide into glucose. Explain the steps involved and how ATP and NADPH from the light reaction are used.
Plant Physiology.r: The light-independent (dark) reaction is the Calvin–Benson cycle, in the stroma. Steps [5]. 1. Carboxylation. CO₂ joins ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP, 5C); RuBisCO forms an unstable 6-carbon compound that splits into two molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PGA), the first stable product. 2. Reduction. ATP phosphorylates 3-PGA to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate; NADPH then reduces it to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (G3P), a triose sugar. 3. Regeneration. Of every six G3P, five are rearranged using ATP to regenerate three RuBP; one G3P leaves the cycle and becomes glucose, sucrose or starch. Three turns fix three CO₂ and yield one G3P; six turns give one glucose. Use of ATP and NADPH [3].

Plant Physiology.q: How do the different photosynthetic pigments help in capturing light energy? Explain how cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation generate ATP and NADPH, and illustrate them with suitable charts.
Plant Physiology.r: Pigments [2]. Chlorophyll a (blue-green) is the main pigment and the reaction-centre molecule (P680, P700). Chlorophyll b and the carotenoids (carotene, xanthophyll) are accessory pigments: they absorb other wavelengths (blue and green-blue) and pass the energy on to chlorophyll a, so the usable range of the spectrum widens; the carotenoids also shield chlorophyll from photo-oxidation. Non-cyclic photophosphorylation [3]. Light excites P680 of photosystem II; its electron travels through phaeophytin, plastoquinone, cytochrome b₆f and plastocyanin to photosystem I, releasing energy that pumps H⁺ into the thylakoid lumen; ATP synthase uses the gradient to make ATP (chemiosmosis).

Plant Physiology.q: Describe the link reaction and the Krebs cycle. Calculate the ATP, NADH and FADH₂ formed from one molecule of glucose in these stages. (predicted: the Krebs cycle and electron transport have not yet been the long question)
Plant Physiology.r: Link reaction [2]. In the mitochondrial matrix each pyruvate is decarboxylated and oxidised and joined to coenzyme A: pyruvate + NAD⁺ + CoA → acetyl CoA + CO₂ + NADH (pyruvate dehydrogenase). Krebs cycle [4]. Acetyl CoA (2C) + oxaloacetate (4C) → citrate (6C) → isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate (5C) (CO₂, NADH) → succinyl CoA (4C) (CO₂, NADH) → succinate (GTP, which makes ATP) → fumarate (FADH₂) → malate → oxaloacetate (NADH), ready for the next turn. Accounting [2].

Plant Physiology.q: Define water potential and name its four components, stating the sign of each. Why is the working equation for a vacuolated cell only $\Psi_w = \Psi_s + \Psi_p$?
A 0.2 M sucrose solution is prepared at 22 °C. Calculate its solute potential, and state what would happen to a plant cell of $\Psi_w = -0.9$ MPa placed in it.
Give four reasons why root pressure cannot account for the ascent of sap in a tall tree. What is its accepted function in modern plant physiology?
Describe the mechanism of stomatal opening in terms of potassium ion movement. Why is the starch–sugar interconversion theory no longer accepted?
Differentiate between guttation and dew under any four heads.
Distinguish cyclic from non-cyclic photophosphorylation under four heads, and explain why a chloroplast needs both.
Why is the modern ATP yield of aerobic respiration given as 30–32 rather than 38? Explain both the change from 38 and the reason for the range.
Explain, with the balanced equation, why the respiratory quotient of tripalmitin is about 0.7 while that of malic acid is 1.33.
Write short notes on:

The 38 assumed integer P/O ratios (3 per NADH, 2 per FADH$_2$), a pre-chemiosmotic requirement. Since about 10 H$^+$ are pumped per NADH and 4 consumed per ATP, P/O = 2.5; for FADH$_2$, 6/4 = 1.5. The range 30–32 arises from the shuttle used for cytoplasmic NADH: malate–aspartate (Complex I, 2.5 each) gives 32; glycerol-3-phosphate (ubiquinone, 1.5 each) gives 30.
Describe the light reaction of photosynthesis. Draw and explain the Z-scheme, state exactly where ATP, NADPH and oxygen are produced, and compare cyclic with non-cyclic photophosphorylation.

Describe the Calvin cycle under its three phases and derive the ATP and NADPH requirement per molecule of glucose. Then explain how C4 and CAM plants each overcome the limitation of RuBisCO, and tabulate the differences between C3, C4 and CAM plants.

Give an account of the aerobic respiration of one molecule of glucose, naming the site, the substrates and the products of each of the four stages, and calculate the total ATP yield showing why the answer is 30–32 and not 38.
Explain the ascent of sap. Evaluate the vital-force and capillarity theories, state the evidence that refutes them, and describe the cohesion–tension theory under its three pillars.
Explain the cohesion–tension theory of the ascent of sap and show why root pressure, vital-force and capillarity theories fail.
Compare C3, C4 and CAM photosynthesis in a table and explain how C4 and CAM plants overcome photorespiration.
Describe the four stages of aerobic respiration and calculate the ATP yield of one glucose molecule, explaining the figures 38 and 30–32.

Genetics.q: Two pea plants with red flowers, genotypes unknown, are crossed and give red and white flowers in the ratio 3: 1. What are the genotypes of the parents?
Genetics.w: Rr × Rr gives 3 red: 1 white. Two homozygotes (a) or one of each (b) would give no white offspring at all.

Genetics.q: Marriage of a man of normal vision with a colour-blind woman will produce
Which of the following genetic disorders is caused by a point mutation?
Genetics.w: sickle-cell anaemia is one base change (GAG → GTG), Glu → Val. Down, Turner and Klinefelter are chromosome-number changes.

Genetics.q: In the Hershey–Chase experiment the DNA of the bacteriophage was labelled with
Genetics.w: phosphorus is in DNA; sulphur is in protein, so ³⁵S labels the protein coat. Choosing ³⁵S is the classic slip.

Genetics.q: A DNA sample contains 30 % adenine. The percentage of guanine is
The number of hydrogen bonds between guanine and cytosine is
Genetics.w: G≡C has three, A=T has two.

Genetics.q: One complete turn of B-DNA is
Genetics.w: 10 bp × 0.34 nm = 3.4 nm; (d) is the diameter.

Genetics.q: E. coli grown for many generations in ¹⁵N medium is shifted to ¹⁴N medium. After two generations of division the DNA is
Genetics.w: the first generation is all hybrid (¹⁵N/¹⁴N); the second is half hybrid and half light. Semi-conservative replication never gives all-heavy after a shift.

Genetics.q: Short fragments formed on the lagging strand are joined by
Genetics.w: DNA ligase seals the nicks between Okazaki fragments. Primase makes the primers; helicase unwinds.

Genetics.q: Which of these is a stop codon?
Genetics.w: the stop codons are UAA, UAG, UGA. AUG is the start codon and also codes Met; UGG is Trp.

Genetics.q: If the codon on the mRNA is GCA, the anticodon of the tRNA is
Genetics.w: the anticodon pairs with the codon: G–C, C–G, A–U gives CGU. Option (b) contains T, which tRNA does not have.

Genetics.q: The enzyme that synthesises mRNA from a DNA template is
Genetics.w: transcription uses RNA polymerase; reverse transcriptase makes DNA from RNA.

Genetics.q: The grandson of a colour-blind man can receive the gene only through
o: his carrier mother, who got it from the colour-blind man
Genetics.w: the colour-blind man gives his X only to his daughters; she passes it to her son (criss-cross). Option (a) is wrong because a father gives his son a Y.

Genetics.q: Drosophila melanogaster was chosen for genetic studies mainly because it
o: has a short life cycle, few chromosomes and many progeny
Genetics.w: 2n = 8, a life cycle of about 10–14 days, and hundreds of offspring per mating.

Genetics.q: If you were assigned to make a Watson and Crick model of DNA, what essential components would you use to make the exact structure?
Genetics.r: Components [2]. A nucleotide = one deoxyribose sugar + one phosphate + one nitrogenous base. Four kinds of base are needed: the purines adenine (A) and guanine (G), drawn as double rings, and the pyrimidines thymine (T) and cytosine (C), as single rings. Building the model [2]. (i) Join the nucleotides by phosphodiester bonds (3′ carbon of one sugar to the 5′ phosphate of the next) into two long chains of sugar–phosphate backbone. (ii) Pair the bases across the two chains by hydrogen bonds: A with T (two bonds) and G with C (three bonds), so that a purine always faces a pyrimidine and the ladder keeps a uniform width of 2 nm.

Genetics.q: Explain the mechanism of incomplete dominance up to the F₂ generation with a suitable example. How does it differ from complete dominance?
Genetics.r: Mechanism [2]. In incomplete dominance neither allele masks the other, so the heterozygote is intermediate. In the four o'clock plant (Mirabilis jalapa), RR (red) × rr (white) gives an F₁ that is all Rr, pink. On selfing the F₁:

Genetics.q: In which process are linked genes inherited together from one generation to another with parental and non-parental combinations? Explain the process with a suitable example.
Genetics.r: The process is linkage. Definition. Genes that lie on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together; they do not assort independently. Because crossing over separates some of them, the offspring show parental combinations more often than recombinants. Example (Morgan, Drosophila). Grey body and long wings (b⁺b⁺ vg⁺vg⁺) × black body and vestigial wings (bb vgvg) gives F₁ grey long. A test cross of the F₁ female with a black-vestigial male gave 965 grey-long and 944 black-vestigial (parental, 83 %) but only 206 grey-vestigial and 185 black-long (recombinant, 17 %). If the genes had assorted independently the four classes would have been 25 % each.

Genetics.q: Explain in brief the significance of polyploidy with examples.
Genetics.r: Polyploidy is the presence of more than two complete sets of chromosomes. Significance: (i) it makes cells and organs larger — bigger fruits, flowers and seeds (gigas effect), as in polyploid tomato and sugar beet; (ii) autotriploids are sterile and so give seedless fruit: banana (3n) and watermelon; (iii) it restores the fertility of hybrids: triticale, an allopolyploid of wheat × rye, combines the yield of wheat and the hardiness of rye; (iv) it is a source of new species in nature — bread wheat is hexaploid (6n = 42) and more than a third of flowering plants are polyploid; (v) colchicine treatment lets breeders produce polyploids on purpose.

Genetics.q: Write four reasons why Drosophila melanogaster is chosen for genetic studies. (original)
Genetics.r: (i) Small and cheap to keep in bottles on banana or cornmeal medium; (ii) a short life cycle of about 10–14 days, so many generations can be followed in a few months; (iii) one mating gives hundreds of offspring, so ratios are reliable; (iv) only four pairs of chromosomes (2n = 8), and the giant salivary-gland chromosomes can be seen with banding; (v) males and females are easily told apart, and there are many visible mutant traits (white eye, vestigial wing, yellow body).

Genetics.q: Distinguish between a point mutation and a frame-shift mutation, with an example of each. (original)

Why is Drosophila melanogaster selected for genetical study? "The inheritance of a sex-linked trait follows the criss-cross pattern." Justify this statement with special reference to the eye colour of Drosophila.

Explain how colour blindness is inherited as a sex-linked trait in humans. Illustrate it by suitable genetic crosses and analyse the phenotypic outcomes. On that basis justify why the pattern is called criss-cross inheritance.
How can chromosomal mutations alter the number and structure of chromosomes? Discuss the types of chromosomal mutation and analyse their significance.
Genetics.r: Definition [1]. A chromosomal mutation is a change in the structure or number of whole chromosomes. Types [4]. Structural: deletion (loss of a piece: cri-du-chat syndrome); duplication (a piece repeated: Bar eye of Drosophila); inversion (a piece turned through 180°, paracentric or pericentric); translocation (a piece moves to a non-homologous chromosome, as in the Philadelphia chromosome). Numerical: aneuploidy — one chromosome more or less: trisomy 21 (Down's syndrome, 47), monosomy X (Turner's, 45, X), XXY (Klinefelter's, 47); euploidy/polyploidy — whole extra sets (3n, 4n), induced by colchicine; caused by non-disjunction at meiosis. Significance [3].

Genetics.q: State Mendel's law of segregation and illustrate it with a monohybrid cross in pea up to the F₂ generation, giving both ratios.
Genetics.r: Law of segregation: the two alleles of a gene, which stay together in the body cells of a heterozygote, separate from each other without being altered during gamete formation, so that each gamete receives only one of them. Cross TT (tall) × tt (dwarf) → F₁ all Tt, tall. Selfing the F₁ gives gametes T and t from each parent, so the F₂ Punnett square gives TT: Tt: Tt: tt. Phenotypic ratio 3 tall: 1 dwarf; genotypic ratio 1 TT: 2 Tt: 1 tt. The reappearance of pure dwarfs in the F₂ proves the alleles were never blended.

Genetics.q: A pure tall pea plant with round seeds (TTRR) is crossed with a dwarf plant with wrinkled seeds (ttrr). Give the F₁, the gametes of the F₁, the F₂ phenotypic ratio, and the result of test crossing the F₁.
Genetics.r: F₁ = TtRr, all tall with round seeds. The F₁ makes 2² = 4 kinds of gamete: TR, Tr, tR, tr in equal numbers. Selfing gives the F₂ ratio 9 tall round: 3 tall wrinkled: 3 dwarf round: 1 dwarf wrinkled. A test cross (TtRr × ttrr) gives 1 tall round: 1 tall wrinkled: 1 dwarf round: 1 dwarf wrinkled, i.e. 1: 1: 1: 1, which directly reveals the four gamete types of the F₁.

Genetics.q: Differentiate between DNA and RNA (any four points) and name the three types of RNA with one function each.

Define linkage and crossing over. In a test cross of a double heterozygote, 1600 offspring were obtained of which 96 were recombinants. Calculate the recombination frequency and the map distance between the two genes.
Genetics.r: Linkage is the tendency of genes on the same chromosome to be inherited together. Crossing over is the exchange of corresponding segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes at the chiasma in pachytene, producing recombinants.

Genetics.q: What is polyploidy? Differentiate between autopolyploidy and allopolyploidy with one example of each, and name the chemical used to induce polyploidy.
Genetics.r: Polyploidy is the presence of more than two complete sets of chromosomes in a cell. In autopolyploidy the extra sets come from the same species (AAAA), pairing gives multivalents and fertility is often low — e.g. tetraploid potato Solanum tuberosum (2n = 4x = 48) or triploid banana. In allopolyploidy the sets come from two different species (AABB), pairing is normal and the plant is fertile — e.g. bread wheat Triticum aestivum (2n = 6x = 42) or Raphanobrassica. Polyploidy is induced by colchicine, obtained from Colchicum autumnale, which prevents spindle formation.

Genetics.q: What is sex-linked inheritance? Explain X-linked recessive inheritance by working out a cross between a carrier woman and a normal man for colour blindness, and state the criteria by which an X-linked recessive trait is recognised in a pedigree.

In a dihybrid cross in pea, the F₂ generation of 160 plants consisted of 95 tall round, 27 tall wrinkled, 30 dwarf round and 8 dwarf wrinkled. Test whether these results agree with the expected 9: 3: 3: 1 ratio using the chi-square test, and explain what your conclusion means.
Describe semi-conservative DNA replication, naming the enzymes, and give the evidence of Meselson and Stahl.
State and explain Mendel's law of independent assortment with a dihybrid cross, and test the ratio by the chi-square method.
Explain linkage, crossing over and gene mapping, with Morgan's evidence and a worked map-distance calculation.

Embryology.q: Which of the following cells of an embryo sac degenerate after fertilisation?
o: synergids and the primary endosperm cell
antipodal cells and the primary endosperm cell
Embryology.w: synergids and antipodals have done their job and disappear; the primary endosperm cell divides to form endosperm. Option (a) is the trap: the endosperm cell is the busiest cell after fertilisation.

Embryology.q: What is the development of an embryo from an unfertilised egg called?
Embryology.w: parthenogenesis is about the egg; parthenocarpy (a) is about the fruit. The two words differ by one syllable and exam setters exploit it.

Embryology.q: In porogamy, through which structure does the pollen tube enter the ovule?
Embryology.w: micropylar entry is porogamy. In 2082 the question was reversed: "which term describes entry through the micropyle" with options mesogamy, chalazogamy, syngamy, porogamy.

Embryology.q: Which type of artificial vegetative propagation induces roots on a branch while it is still attached to the parent plant, and suits plants with soft branches lying near the soil?
Embryology.w: in simple (soil) layering the branch is bent into the soil while still attached and roots then form. Air layering works on upright branches, and grafting and cutting detach the piece at once.

Embryology.q: The number of cells and nuclei in a mature Polygonum-type embryo sac are
Embryology.w: seven cells but eight nuclei because the central cell carries two polar nuclei.

Embryology.q: Double fertilisation in angiosperms was discovered by
Embryology.w: Nawaschin (1898, Fritillaria and Lilium), confirmed by Guignard. Strasburger described the embryo sac and fertilisation, not the double event.

Embryology.q: The hard outer layer of the pollen grain, resistant to acid, alkali and heat, is made of
Embryology.w: sporopollenin, one of the most resistant organic materials. Callose is found around microspore mother cells and in pollen tubes.

Embryology.q: The nutritive layer of the anther wall that supplies food to developing pollen grains is the
Embryology.w: the tapetum; the endothecium helps dehiscence.

Embryology.q: Pollen grains from the anther of a flower reach the stigma of another flower of the same plant. This is
Embryology.w: the flowers are on the same plant, so it is geitonogamy; it is genetically autogamy but ecologically cross-pollination. Xenogamy needs two plants.

Embryology.q: Which feature is typical of a wind-pollinated flower?
o: light dry pollen and feathery stigma
Embryology.w: wind-pollinated flowers are small, dull and produce huge amounts of light dry pollen. Colour, scent and sticky pollen are insect-pollination features.

Embryology.q: The single cotyledon of a monocot embryo is called
Embryology.w: scutellum; coleoptile and coleorhiza are protective sheaths of the plumule and radicle.

Embryology.q: In the dicot embryo the portion between the plumule and the radicle is the
Embryology.w: the hypocotyl lies below the cotyledons and ends in the radicle; the epicotyl lies above them.

Embryology.q: Write the salient features of a dicot embryo in reference to its development pattern, with labelled diagrams.
Embryology.r: Development pattern [2]. The zygote divides (after a rest) to give a two-celled proembryo: the upper embryonal cell and the lower suspensor cell. The suspensor cell forms the suspensor, which pushes the embryo into the endosperm; the embryonal cell passes through the globular, heart-shaped (two cotyledons begin) and torpedo stages to the mature embryo. Features of the mature embryo [2]. It has an embryonal axis with the radicle at the lower end (covered by a root cap), the hypocotyl, the epicotyl and the plumule (shoot tip), and two cotyledons attached to the axis; the suspensor lies at the radicle end. Draw the stages figure below.

Embryology.q: What is double fertilisation? Explain it and state its significance. (original)
Embryology.r: Definition [1]. The fusion of one male gamete with the egg and the other with the two polar nuclei, both in the same embryo sac, is double fertilisation; it is found only in angiosperms. Explanation [2]. The pollen tube enters the embryo sac (usually through the micropyle, porogamy) and releases two male gametes. Syngamy: gamete 1 + egg → diploid zygote (2n) → embryo. Triple fusion: gamete 2 + two polar nuclei → triploid primary endosperm nucleus (3n) → endosperm. The synergids and antipodals then degenerate. Significance [1]. The endosperm starts to form only when fertilisation has occurred, so no food is wasted on an unfertilised ovule;

Embryology.q: Distinguish between wind pollination (anemophily) and insect pollination (entomophily). (original)
The layer of the anther wall that nourishes the developing microspores is the
Embryology.w: the tapetum supplies food and sporopollenin; the endothecium only helps in dehiscence.

Embryology.q: A typical angiosperm embryo sac is
Embryology.w: 3 antipodals + 2 synergids + 1 egg + 1 central cell with 2 nuclei = 7 cells, 8 nuclei.

Embryology.q: Describe the development of the male gametophyte from the microspore mother cell to the pollen tube.
Embryology.r: Sporogenous tissue → microspore mother cells (2n) → meiosis → tetrad of four haploid microspores (microsporogenesis). Each microspore builds a two-layered wall — sporopollenin exine with germ pores, and cellulose intine. Its nucleus then divides unequally by mitosis into a large vegetative (tube) cell and a small generative cell; the grain is usually shed at this 2-celled stage. On the stigma the grain germinates, the intine grows out through a germ pore as the pollen tube, and the generative cell divides into two male gametes, which travel down the tube behind the tube nucleus.

Embryology.q: What is double fertilization? Write the two fusions with the ploidy of each product and state its significance.
Embryology.r: Double fertilization is the occurrence of two fusions in the same embryo sac. Syngamy: one male gamete (n) + egg (n) → zygote (2n) → embryo. Triple fusion: the second male gamete (n) + two polar nuclei (n + n) → primary endosperm nucleus (3n) → endosperm. It was discovered by Nawaschin (1898). Significance: the food-storing endosperm is laid down only after the egg is fertilised, so no reserves are wasted on an ovule that will not become a seed; the triploid endosperm is also vigorous and gives the young seedling a strong start. It is found only in angiosperms.

Embryology.q: An anther contained 250 microspore mother cells. How many pollen grains, male gametes and ovules could it at most fertilise, and how many seeds could result?
Embryology.r: Each microspore mother cell gives 4 pollen grains:

Embryology.q: Differentiate between a dicot and a monocot embryo (any four points), and define coleoptile and coleorhiza.
What is pollination? Describe the different agents of cross-pollination with the flower characters and examples of each, and explain any four contrivances that plants use to ensure cross-pollination.
Embryology.r: Outline. (i) Definition — pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma; self (autogamy), geitonogamy and cross (xenogamy). (ii) Anemophily — wind: small, dull, scentless flowers, versatile anthers, enormous amounts of light dry pollen, feathery stigmas — maize, grasses. (iii) Hydrophily — water: unwettable pollen, often thread-like — Vallisneria, Hydrilla, Zostera. (iv) Entomophily — insects: large, brightly coloured, scented flowers with nectar, sticky spiny pollen and sticky stigma — Salvia, mustard, Ficus. (v) Ornithophily — birds: large red tubular flowers with copious watery nectar and no scent — Bombax ceiba, Butea monosperma.

Embryology.q: Describe the development of a dicot embryo in Capsella bursa-pastoris with labelled diagrams, and compare it with a monocot embryo. What is endosperm, and how do the three types of endosperm development differ?
Embryology.r: Outline. (i) The zygote divides transversely into a small apical cell and a large basal cell. (ii) The basal cell forms the suspensor, whose lowest cell becomes the vesicular haustorium and whose top cell, the hypophysis, gives the radicle tip. (iii) The apical cell divides by two vertical and one transverse wall into an octant; the four epibasal cells give the plumule and cotyledons, the four hypobasal cells give the hypocotyl. (iv) Periclinal divisions give dermatogen, periblem and plerome. (v) The embryo passes through globular → heart-shaped → torpedo → mature stages, ending with two cotyledons, a plumule and a radicle.

Embryology.q: Describe the development of the male gametophyte (microsporogenesis and microgametogenesis) from the structure of the anther.
Describe the development of the female gametophyte (embryo sac) in a typical angiosperm and draw a labelled mature embryo sac.
What is double fertilization? Explain the process, the formation of endosperm and embryo, and give eight points of its significance.

Biotechnology.q: In an economically important plant species embryo mortality is very high. Which method would you suggest to check the mortality?
Biotechnology.w: embryo culture rescues weak or aborting embryos by growing them on medium. Meristem culture (d) gives virus-free plants, a different aim.

Biotechnology.q: Who proposed the concept of totipotency of plant cells?
Biotechnology.w: Gottlieb Haberlandt (1902). Skoog and Miller found kinetin; Murashige and Skoog gave the medium.

Biotechnology.q: A high concentration of cytokinin relative to auxin in the medium promotes
Biotechnology.w: high cytokinin: auxin → shoots; the reverse → roots; a balance → callus. Reversing the ratio is the usual error.

Biotechnology.q: Virus-free plants are obtained by culturing
Biotechnology.w: the apical meristem is usually free of virus because it has no vascular connection.

Biotechnology.q: Haploid plants are produced in the laboratory by
Biotechnology.w: anther (or pollen) culture gives haploids, which doubling then turns into homozygous diploids.

Biotechnology.q: Somatic hybrids are produced by the fusion of
o: two gametes of the same plant
Biotechnology.w: protoplast fusion bypasses sexual barriers (pomato). Fusion of gametes is ordinary fertilisation.

Biotechnology.q: The first generation of a cross between two pure lines often grows better than both parents. This is called
Biotechnology.w: heterosis or hybrid vigour; inbreeding depression is the opposite.

Biotechnology.q: The cry gene in Bt cotton comes from
Biotechnology.w: the cry gene codes Cry protein, toxic to bollworm. Agrobacterium supplies the vector, which is why (a) tempts.

Biotechnology.q: A common vector used to introduce a foreign gene into a dicot plant is
Biotechnology.w: the Ti plasmid transfers T-DNA into dicot cells.

Biotechnology.q: The enzyme that cuts DNA at specific base sequences is
Biotechnology.w: restriction endonuclease; ligase joins, it does not cut.

Biotechnology.q: Which of the following is used as a green manure crop in Nepal?
Biotechnology.w: Sesbania (dhaincha) is ploughed in while green; wheat and maize are grain crops.

Biotechnology.q: Azolla is used as a biofertiliser because it lives with a nitrogen-fixing
Biotechnology.w: Azolla fixes nitrogen through Anabaena azollae. Rhizobium lives in legume nodules.

Biotechnology.q: Golden Rice was developed to overcome the deficiency of
Biotechnology.w: Golden Rice makes β-carotene, the precursor of vitamin A.

Biotechnology.q: Food that is free from toxins and disease-causing organisms is a matter of
Biotechnology.w: safety is about hazards; security (a) is about availability and access.

Biotechnology.q: Describe the process of micropropagation to rapidly produce a large number of identical plantlets and how it can be used in the conservation of endangered plant species.
Biotechnology.r: Process [2]. Micropropagation is the rapid clonal multiplication of a plant from a small piece (explant, e.g. shoot tip or node) in sterile conditions. Steps: (1) choose a healthy mother plant and surface-sterilise the explant; (2) place it on sterile MS medium with sugar and growth regulators for shoot multiplication (high cytokinin); (3) transfer the shoots to a rooting medium (high auxin); (4) harden the plantlets in a greenhouse and move them to soil. Thousands of genetically identical plantlets come from one explant. Conservation [2].

Biotechnology.q: How can GMOs be used to address food-security challenges, and what are the possible environmental concerns and health risks associated with them?
Biotechnology.r: Use for food security [2]. GM crops can carry genes for insect resistance (Bt cotton, Bt maize), herbicide tolerance, drought or salt tolerance and extra nutrients (Golden Rice: vitamin A), raising yield, cutting losses and improving nutrition. Concerns [2]. Environmental: gene flow to wild relatives, loss of biodiversity, evolution of resistant pests and superweeds, harm to non-target insects. Health: possible allergens, unknown long-term effects of new proteins, antibiotic-resistance marker genes. Social: patent control by seed companies and dependence of farmers.

Biotechnology.q: Distinguish between a biofertiliser and a biopesticide, giving two examples of each. (original)
What is plant tissue culture? Describe the steps of tissue culture technique and mention its applications. (predicted)
What is micropropagation? List its steps in order and give two advantages over conventional propagation.
Biotechnology.r: Micropropagation is the rapid multiplication of plants in vitro from small explants using tissue culture. Steps: (i) select and surface-sterilise the explant with 0.1 % HgCl₂ or sodium hypochlorite; (ii) inoculate on MS medium with a high cytokinin: auxin ratio to get shoots (through callus if needed); (iii) transfer the shoots to a high auxin medium for rooting; (iv) harden the plantlets in a greenhouse, then transfer to the field. Advantages: thousands of genetically identical, disease-free plants from one mother plant in a small space, all the year round; it works for species that are sterile or slow to propagate, such as banana and orchids.

Biotechnology.q: Differentiate between vertical and horizontal resistance in plants, with one example of each.
Biotechnology.r: | Vertical resistance | Horizontal resistance | |---|---| | Governed by one or a few major R genes | Governed by many minor genes (polygenic) | | Complete immunity, but only to certain races | Partial, slows the disease down | | Breaks down when a new race appears | Durable across races | | Easy to transfer by breeding | Difficult, needs many crosses | | Example: Sr stem-rust genes in wheat | Example: field resistance to late blight of potato |

Biotechnology.q: Explain how the Bt toxin kills a caterpillar but is harmless to human beings.
Biotechnology.r: Bacillus thuringiensis makes a crystalline protoxin (Cry protein) that is inactive as made. The caterpillar eats leaf tissue containing it. The insect midgut is strongly alkaline (pH about 9–10), so the crystal dissolves there and gut proteases cut it into the active toxin. The toxin binds to specific receptors on the midgut epithelium and makes pores, so the cells swell and burst; the insect stops feeding and dies. The human stomach is strongly acidic (pH 1.5–3), the crystal does not dissolve, the activating proteases are absent and human gut cells carry no receptor for it — so the protein is simply digested like any other protein.

Biotechnology.q: A PCR tube contains 8 copies of a target sequence and is run for 25 cycles at full efficiency. Calculate the number of copies formed, and state why the actual yield is lower after about 35 cycles.
Biotechnology.r: Copies $= N_0 \times 2^n = 8 \times 2^{25}$. $2^{25} = 33{,}554{,}432$, so $N = 8 \times 33{,}554{,}432 = 268{,}435{,}456 \approx 2.68 \times 10^{8}$ copies. After about 35 cycles the primers and dNTPs are used up, Taq polymerase loses activity from repeated heating, and the many product strands re-anneal to each other instead of to primers, so the reaction enters the plateau phase and the number of copies stops doubling.

Biotechnology.q: Distinguish between green manure and bio-fertilizer, giving two examples of each.
Biotechnology.r: | Green manure | Bio-fertilizer | |---|---| | A green crop grown and ploughed back into the same field | A preparation of living micro-organisms applied to seed, soil or root | | Adds organic matter, nitrogen and improves soil structure | Supplies nutrients by fixing N₂ or solubilising phosphate | | Acts after decomposition, over one season | Acts as long as the organism stays alive in the soil | | Examples: Sesbania aculeata (dhaincha), Crotalaria juncea (sunn hemp) | Examples: Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Azolla–Anabaena, mycorrhiza |

Biotechnology.q: Describe the steps of recombinant DNA technology. Mention the role of restriction endonuclease, DNA ligase and a cloning vector, and explain how recombinant cells are selected.
Biotechnology.r: Outline. (i) Isolation of DNA — lyse cells with lysozyme or cellulase, digest protein with protease and RNA with ribonuclease, precipitate DNA with chilled ethanol. (ii) Cutting — a restriction endonuclease such as EcoRI cuts both the donor DNA and the vector at the same palindromic sequence (G↓AATTC), giving complementary sticky ends. (iii) Ligation — the sticky ends base-pair and DNA ligase seals the phosphodiester bonds, producing recombinant DNA. (iv) Vector — the plasmid (pBR322) or Ti plasmid carries an ori so it replicates in the host, selectable marker genes, and unique restriction sites.

Biotechnology.q: Describe plant tissue culture under the headings: principle, medium, steps and applications.
Biotechnology.r: Principle: totipotency — every living plant cell carries the whole genome and can regenerate a complete plant under the right conditions. Medium: Murashige and Skoog (1962) medium supplying macronutrients, micronutrients, 2–3 % sucrose, vitamins, myo-inositol, agar and growth regulators; autoclaved at 121 °C and kept at pH 5.6–5.8. Steps: choose the explant (shoot tip, node, anther, embryo) → surface sterilise → inoculate aseptically → callus induction with 2,4-D → organogenesis: high cytokinin: auxin gives shoots, high auxin gives roots → subculture → hardening and transfer to soil. Types: callus, suspension, meristem, anther (haploids), embryo rescue and protoplast culture.

Biotechnology.q: Define food safety and food security. Explain the four pillars of food security and describe four ways in which biotechnology can improve food safety and food security in Nepal.
Biotechnology.r: Food safety means food that is free from biological, chemical and physical hazards and is fit to eat. Food security (FAO, 1996) exists when all people, at all times, have physical, social and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food for an active, healthy life. Four pillars: availability (enough food produced or imported); access (people can afford and reach it); utilisation (the body can use it — safe food, clean water, balanced diet); stability (the first three do not fail in drought, flood or price shock). Contribution of biotechnology in Nepal: (i) tissue culture supplies disease-free potato, banana and orchid planting material, raising yield;

Biotechnology.q: Describe the steps of plant tissue culture and give eight applications.
Describe the steps of recombinant DNA technology, naming the tools, and explain how human insulin is produced.
Explain the principle and steps of PCR and of gel electrophoresis, with their uses.

Animal Tissues.q: Which of the following tissues possesses fat globules?
Animal Tissues.w: adipose tissue stores fat globules. Areolar tissue (a) is the commoner distractor because it is also loose and sits beside fat.

Animal Tissues.q: Which of the following tissues lacks a blood supply?
Animal Tissues.w: cartilage is avascular and is fed by diffusion from the perichondrium. Bone (c) has Haversian canals full of vessels.

Animal Tissues.q: Which pair of white blood cells contains phagocytic cells?
Animal Tissues.w: neutrophils and monocytes (which become macrophages) are the professional phagocytes; eosinophils are weakly phagocytic, lymphocytes are not.

Animal Tissues.q: Which epithelium forms the inner lining of the vagina?
Animal Tissues.w: the vagina is a moist internal passage, so its stratified squamous epithelium is non-keratinised. Keratinised squamous (c) is the epidermis.

Animal Tissues.q: Which epithelium lines the air sacs (alveoli) of the lung?
Animal Tissues.w: a single flat layer keeps the diffusion distance small. Cuboidal lines kidney tubules.

Animal Tissues.q: The epithelium that can stretch when the urinary bladder is filled is
Animal Tissues.w: transitional epithelium lets the cells slide over one another.

Animal Tissues.q: Tendon and ligament are both
Animal Tissues.w: both are dense regular connective tissue rich in collagen; they differ in what they join. Fibrocartilage (d) is found in the disc.

Animal Tissues.q: A ligament connects
Animal Tissues.w: ligament is bone to bone; tendon is muscle to bone (option a).

Animal Tissues.q: The cartilage in the external ear (pinna) is
Animal Tissues.w: elastic cartilage springs back; hyaline is at the articular ends and trachea.

Animal Tissues.q: The cells of bone that lie in lacunae are
Animal Tissues.w: osteocytes sit in lacunae. Osteoblasts make matrix and become osteocytes; chondrocytes belong to cartilage.

Animal Tissues.q: Muscle fibres that are striated and branched and join end to end through intercalated discs are
Animal Tissues.w: cardiac muscle. Skeletal fibres are long, unbranched and multinucleate.

Animal Tissues.q: The fatty insulating sheath around an axon in peripheral nerves is formed by
Animal Tissues.w: Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system; oligodendrocytes do the same in the central nervous system.

Animal Tissues.q: The type of cell that makes up about 99 % of the formed elements of blood is
Animal Tissues.w: red cells outnumber white cells by about 600: 1.

Animal Tissues.q: Squamous epithelium is also called pavement epithelium because
o: its flat cells fit edge to edge like paving stones
Animal Tissues.w: flat cells, tightly joined, resemble a paved floor. The word has nothing to do with a pavement outside.

Animal Tissues.q: How would you elaborate the different types of simple epithelial tissues in animals? Support with diagrams.
Animal Tissues.r: Simple epithelium is a single layer of cells resting on a basement membrane. Types [3]: - Squamous — flat, plate-like cells with a central nucleus; lining of alveoli, blood vessels (endothelium), Bowman's capsule; diffusion and filtration. - Cuboidal — cube-shaped cells with a round central nucleus; thyroid follicles, kidney tubules (brush border in the PCT), ducts of glands; secretion and absorption. - Columnar — tall, narrow cells with a basal nucleus; stomach and intestine (goblet cells secrete mucus; microvilli absorb); secretion and absorption. A ciliated form lines the trachea and oviduct and moves mucus or eggs. - Glandular — single cells (goblet cells) or sheets that secrete.

Animal Tissues.q: Compare and contrast areolar and adipose connective tissues.
Compare and contrast voluntary and involuntary muscles.
Name the three types of cartilage and state where each is found; why does cartilage heal slowly? (original)
Animal Tissues.r: Hyaline cartilage — the commonest: ends of long bones (articular), nose, trachea, larynx, ribs; glassy matrix. Elastic cartilage — pinna of the ear, epiglottis; yellow elastic fibres. Fibrocartilage — intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis; dense collagen, strongest. Slow healing [1]. Cartilage is avascular; its cells are fed by diffusion from the perichondrium, so repair is slow.

Animal Tissues.q: Describe the three types of muscular tissue with labelled diagrams. (predicted)
Define epithelial tissue and give four general characters of it.
Distinguish between a tendon and a ligament under four heads.
Animal Tissues.r: Tendon — white collagen fibres, straight parallel bundles, inextensible, joins muscle to bone. Ligament — yellow elastic fibres, branching, elastic, joins bone to bone.

Animal Tissues.q: Draw a labelled T.S. of a Haversian system and name any four parts.
Give four differences between cardiac muscle and smooth muscle.
Animal Tissues.r: Cardiac: branched fibres, one central nucleus, intercalated discs present, found only in the heart, never fatigues. Smooth: spindle-shaped unbranched cells, one central nucleus, no discs, no striations, found in gut, uterus and blood vessels.

Animal Tissues.q: Why is cartilage slow to heal while bone heals comparatively fast?
Animal Tissues.r: Cartilage is avascular: its chondrocytes receive food and oxygen only by slow diffusion through the solid matrix from the perichondrium, and they divide slowly. Bone is richly supplied with blood through the Haversian and Volkmann's canals, and the periosteum contains osteoblasts that can lay down new matrix quickly, so a fracture unites in weeks.

p: Classify epithelial tissue with one example and one location for each type.
Draw a labelled diagram of pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium and explain why it is not a stratified epithelium.
Describe the structure of a myelinated motor neuron with a labelled diagram.
What is a synapse? Explain how an impulse crosses it and why transmission is one-way.

Animal Tissues.q: Classify epithelial tissue. Describe the types, structure, location and function of each with examples.
Describe connective tissue: its general structure, its types, and give eight points of function.
Describe the three types of muscular tissue and the sliding-filament mechanism of muscle contraction.

Developmental Biology.q: What are the sequential steps involved in gametogenesis?
Developmental Biology.w: multiplication, growth, maturation. Option (c) puts growth first; it is tempting because in ordinary life "growth" precedes "maturity".

Developmental Biology.q: In the frog, the coelom is derived from which embryonic layer?
Developmental Biology.w: the coelom is a mesodermal cavity (it forms by a split in the mesoderm). Mesogloea (d) is a jelly layer of cnidarians, not a germ layer.

Developmental Biology.q: What happens during spermiogenesis in spermatogenesis?
o: secondary spermatocytes form from primary spermatocytes
Developmental Biology.w: spermiogenesis is the conversion of a spermatid into a spermatozoon (no division). Options (a)–(c) are the division steps of the multiplication and maturation phases.

Developmental Biology.q: Which is the correct sequence of embryonic development in a frog?
Developmental Biology.w: morula → blastula → gastrula. The blastula follows the morula because the cavity forms inside the solid ball.

Developmental Biology.q: Immediately after fertilisation, a frog zygote undergoes
Developmental Biology.w: cleavage is the first series of mitoses, without growth. Gastrulation comes several stages later.

Developmental Biology.q: One primary spermatocyte gives rise to
Developmental Biology.w: meiosis I and II give four haploid spermatids, each becoming a sperm.

Developmental Biology.q: One primary oocyte finally gives rise to
o: one ovum and three polar bodies
two ova and two polar bodies
Developmental Biology.w: oogenesis is unequal: one large ovum and three small polar bodies.

Developmental Biology.q: In humans the secondary oocyte is arrested at
Developmental Biology.w: the secondary oocyte stops at metaphase II and completes meiosis only after the sperm enters.

Developmental Biology.q: The cleavage of a frog egg is holoblastic and unequal because
o: the yolk is concentrated in the vegetal half and slows division there
Developmental Biology.w: yolk slows the cleavage furrows, so vegetal cells are larger. Microlecithal (c) means little yolk.

Developmental Biology.q: The cavity of the blastula is called
Developmental Biology.w: blastocoel is the cavity of the blastula; archenteron belongs to the gastrula.

Developmental Biology.q: The cavity formed inside the embryo during gastrulation is the
Developmental Biology.w: the archenteron becomes the gut. Students confuse it with the blastocoel, which it gradually replaces.

Developmental Biology.q: The nervous system of the frog develops from
Developmental Biology.w: the neural plate, then the neural tube, arises from ectoderm; the notochord is mesodermal and induces it.

Developmental Biology.q: Metamorphosis of a frog tadpole into an adult is controlled by
Developmental Biology.w: thyroxine from the thyroid; if the gland is removed, tadpoles remain tadpoles.

Developmental Biology.q: Fertilisation in the frog is
Developmental Biology.w: the male clasps the female (amplexus) and sperm are shed over the eggs in water.

Developmental Biology.q: Define blastulation. Write the process of blastulation during the development of the frog.
Developmental Biology.r: Definition [1]. Blastulation is the stage of development in which the morula is converted into a hollow blastula with a central cavity, the blastocoel. Process [3]. After the 32–64-cell morula forms, the cells rearrange and fluid accumulates among the smaller animal-pole cells (micromeres). The fluid-filled blastocoel appears and lies towards the animal pole, pushed off-centre by the bulky yolky vegetal cells (macromeres). The wall of the blastula is formed of several layers of cells: a roof of small micromeres, a floor of large macromeres and a marginal zone between them; such a blastula is a coeloblastula. The embryo, still the size of the egg, is ready for gastrulation.

Developmental Biology.q: What is coelom? How is it formed in the development of the frog?
Developmental Biology.r: Coelom [1]. The coelom is the body cavity lying between the body wall and the gut, lined with mesoderm. Formation [3]. In the frog the coelom is schizocoelic. During gastrulation the mesoderm arises from the roof and sides of the archenteron (and from cells rolling in at the lips of the blastopore) and spreads between ectoderm and endoderm. The mesoderm splits into two layers: an outer somatic (parietal) layer against the ectoderm and an inner splanchnic (visceral) layer against the endoderm. The space between the two layers is the coelom; it later holds the heart, gut and other viscera.

Developmental Biology.q: Write about the process of neurulation in the development of the frog.
Developmental Biology.r: Neurulation is the formation of the nervous system that follows gastrulation. The notochord (mesoderm) induces the overlying ectoderm to thicken into the neural plate. The edges of the plate rise as neural folds, with the neural groove between them. The folds meet and fuse in the mid-line, turning the groove into a hollow neural tube, which sinks below the ectoderm; its front end swells into the brain, the rest becomes the spinal cord. The remaining ectoderm closes over as the epidermis.

Developmental Biology.q: Define the term in-vitro fertilisation and describe its process.
Developmental Biology.r: Definition [1]. In-vitro fertilisation (IVF) is the fertilisation of an egg by a sperm outside the body, in a laboratory dish, followed by return of the embryo to the uterus. Process [3]. (i) The woman receives hormones (FSH-like drugs) to produce many eggs; the eggs are collected from the ovary. (ii) The man gives semen, from which active sperm are selected. (iii) Eggs and sperm are mixed in a culture dish, where fertilisation takes place. (iv) The zygotes are grown for 2–5 days to form embryos at the 8-cell or blastocyst stage. (v) One or two healthy embryos are placed in the uterus (embryo transfer); the pregnancy is confirmed by test.

Developmental Biology.q: Describe gastrulation in the frog. (predicted)
Developmental Biology.r: Gastrulation converts the blastula into a gastrula with the three germ layers. It begins when a crescent-shaped groove, the dorsal lip of the blastopore, appears near the grey crescent. Cells of the animal hemisphere spread (epiboly) and roll in (invagination, involution) over the dorsal lip, forming the roof of a new cavity, the archenteron (future gut); the blastocoel is squeezed out. The lip extends round as a circle enclosing the large yolky cells as the yolk plug. By the end, ectoderm covers the outside, endoderm lines the archenteron, and mesoderm lies between them.

Developmental Biology.q: Describe the development of the frog from fertilisation to the formation of the neurula. (predicted)
Define gametogenesis. With the help of a flow chart, compare spermatogenesis and oogenesis in any four respects.
Developmental Biology.r: Gametogenesis is the formation of haploid gametes from diploid germ cells in the gonad. Flow chart: gonium ($2n$) → mitosis → primary gametocyte ($2n$) → meiosis I → secondary gametocyte(s) ($n$) → meiosis II → 4 spermatids / 1 ootid + 3 polar bodies. Four differences: site (testis / ovary); growth phase (slight / enormous with yolk); cytokinesis (equal / unequal); yield (4 sperms / 1 ovum + 3 polar bodies). A fifth mark-worthy point is the extra phase of spermiogenesis in the male.

Developmental Biology.q: A frog has $2n = 26$. Trace the chromosome number through one primary spermatocyte, one secondary spermatocyte, one spermatid and the zygote, and state how many sperms 250 primary spermatocytes will produce.
Developmental Biology.r: Primary spermatocyte $= 26$ chromosomes (52 chromatids, since DNA is replicated). Secondary spermatocyte $= 13$ chromosomes (26 chromatids). Spermatid $= 13$ chromosomes (13 chromatids). Zygote $= 13 + 13 = 26$ chromosomes. Sperms from 250 primary spermatocytes: $250 \times 4 = \mathbf{1000}$ sperms.

Developmental Biology.q: What is the grey crescent? Explain why it is important in the development of the frog.
Developmental Biology.r: The grey crescent is the crescent-shaped, lightly pigmented area that appears on the surface of the fertilised frog's egg opposite the point of sperm entry, formed when the pigmented cortex rotates about 30° towards the entry point. Importance: (i) it marks the future dorsal side; (ii) the first cleavage furrow passes through it and divides it equally, so each of the first two blastomeres can form a complete embryo; (iii) the dorsal lip of the blastopore — Spemann's organiser — develops from it, so it fixes the body axis.

Developmental Biology.q: Describe the cleavage of the frog's egg up to the 8-cell stage, mentioning the plane of each furrow. Why is it called holoblastic unequal cleavage?
Developmental Biology.r: First furrow — vertical (meridional), passing through both poles and bisecting the grey crescent → 2 equal blastomeres. Second furrow — vertical, at right angles to the first → 4 equal blastomeres. Third furrow — horizontal (latitudinal) but above the equator → 4 small micromeres at the animal pole and 4 large macromeres at the vegetal pole. It is holoblastic because the furrow cuts completely through the egg, and unequal because the yolk at the vegetal pole slows the furrow, so the resulting blastomeres are of different sizes.

Developmental Biology.q: Distinguish between epiboly and emboly. Name the three germ layers formed at the end of gastrulation and give one derivative of each.
Developmental Biology.r: Epiboly is the downward spreading of the small, rapidly dividing animal micromeres as a sheet over the vegetal cells; they become ectoderm. Emboly is the inward movement of marginal cells over the lip of the blastopore by involution and invagination; they become mesoderm and endoderm. Germ layers and one derivative each: ectoderm → brain and spinal cord (or epidermis); mesoderm → skeletal muscle (or kidney, blood); endoderm → lining of the alimentary canal (or liver, lungs).

Developmental Biology.q: Write short notes on the role of thyroxine in the metamorphosis of the frog.
Developmental Biology.r: Thyroxine (T₄, converted to the more active T₃) is secreted by the tadpole's thyroid gland under the control of TSH from the anterior pituitary, and its synthesis requires iodine absorbed from the water. It triggers the whole of metamorphosis: resorption of the tail and gills by lysosomal enzymes, growth of hind and then fore limbs, replacement of gills by lungs, shortening of the intestine as the animal changes from herbivore to carnivore, and development of eyelids. Feeding thyroxine to a young tadpole causes precocious metamorphosis into a tiny frog; removing the thyroid or withholding iodine gives a permanent giant tadpole. Prolactin acts against thyroxine and keeps the larva larval.

Developmental Biology.q: Describe the process of gametogenesis in animals. Draw a labelled flow chart of spermatogenesis and oogenesis showing the chromosome number at each stage, and tabulate any four differences between the two processes.
Developmental Biology.r: Outline. (i) Define gametogenesis; name the two types and their sites. (ii) Multiplication phase — repeated mitosis of primordial germ cells giving spermatogonia / oogonia, all $2n$. (iii) Growth phase — one gonium enlarges into a primary spermatocyte or primary oocyte, still $2n$; in the female this involves massive storage of yolk, RNA and organelles, which is why the oocyte may be a thousand times the volume of a spermatocyte. (iv) Maturation phase — meiosis I is reductional ($2n \to n$) and meiosis II is equational;

Developmental Biology.q: Describe the development of the frog from the fertilised egg up to the formation of the gastrula. Draw labelled diagrams of the blastula and the late gastrula, and state the fate of each germ layer.
Developmental Biology.r: Outline. (i) Fertilisation — external, in water, during amplexus; monospermic; cortical reaction lifts the fertilisation membrane; the pigmented cortex rotates and the grey crescent appears opposite the entry point; male and female pronuclei ($n = 13$ each) fuse to give a zygote with $2n = 26$. (ii) Cleavage — holoblastic and unequal: first and second furrows vertical and at right angles giving 4 equal blastomeres, third furrow horizontal above the equator giving 4 micromeres and 4 macromeres, then 16, 32 and a solid morula. No growth occurs, so the blastomeres get steadily smaller.

Developmental Biology.q: Describe spermatogenesis in mammals with the structure of a mature sperm.
Describe oogenesis in a human female and compare it with spermatogenesis in a table of eight points.
Describe the development of a frog from fertilisation to the formation of the three germ layers, and give the fate of each layer.

Human Biology.q: Which enzyme is needed for the digestion of milk protein in human beings?
Human Biology.w: rennin curdles casein in infants; lactase (b) digests the milk sugar, which is the trap. Pepsin also acts on protein but the classic milk-protein answer is rennin.

Human Biology.q: If the cerebellum of a person is injured, which physiological function is affected?
Human Biology.w: the cerebellum coordinates movement and balance. Respiration belongs to the medulla, memory to the cerebrum, smell to the olfactory bulb.

Human Biology.q: The vas deferens carries spermatozoa from the cauda epididymis to the ejaculatory duct. What happens if it is surgically disconnected?
Human Biology.w: sperms are still made and still stored, so the semen carries none; the fluid from the seminal vesicles and prostate still comes. Option (d) is wrong because spermatogenesis goes on in the testis.

Human Biology.q: In the middle ear of a human being there are three ear ossicles. Which set is arranged in the correct sequence?
Human Biology.w: malleus, incus, stapes from the tympanum inward. The cochlea and saccule are not ossicles.

Human Biology.q: Pancreas is a gland with exocrine and endocrine functions; its exocrine part is the pancreatic acini. What is the endocrine part?
Human Biology.w: the islets of Langerhans make insulin and glucagon. Zona glomerulosa and zona reticularis are adrenal cortex layers, adenohypophysis is the anterior pituitary.

Human Biology.q: Show the correct path of origin and conduction of the heart beat in the human heart.
o: AV node, SA node, bundle of His, Purkinje fibres
SA node, AV node, bundle of His, Purkinje fibres
SA node, AV node, Purkinje fibres, bundle of His
AV node, bundle of His, Purkinje fibres, SA node
Human Biology.w: SA node (pacemaker) → AV node → bundle of His → Purkinje fibres.

Human Biology.q: Which enzymes are likely to act in order on soyabean sprouts eaten by a man as they move down the alimentary canal?
Human Biology.w: pepsin (stomach) → trypsin (duodenum) → peptidases (intestinal brush border). Reversing the stomach and the intestine gives (b)–(d).

Human Biology.q: What would happen if the frontal lobe of the cerebrum were accidentally damaged?
Human Biology.w: the frontal lobe handles thinking, planning and memory. Option (a) is the occipital and temporal lobes; (b) the medulla; (c) the hypothalamus.

Human Biology.q: What is the primary role of a surrogate mother in the context of IVF?
o: to provide emotional support to the biological mother
to carry the pregnancy to full term
Human Biology.w: a gestational surrogate carries the embryo to term. Donating ova is the role of an egg donor, and fertilisation happens in the laboratory.

Human Biology.q: What would happen if the oxyntic cells of the gastric glands became non-functional?
o: protein digestion does not take place
the pH of the stomach falls
Human Biology.w: oxyntic (parietal) cells make the HCl; without it pepsinogen is not converted to active pepsin and the acidity needed for protein digestion in the stomach is lost. Option (d) is the nearest distractor: the chief cells still release pepsinogen, so the real failure is activation, not secretion.

Human Biology.q: Show the correct path for the flow of urine.
o: renal pelvis, ureter, urinary bladder, urethra
renal pelvis, ureter, urethra, urinary bladder
renal pelvis, urinary bladder, urethra, ureter
renal pelvis, urethra, ureter, urinary bladder
Human Biology.w: pelvis → ureter → bladder → urethra. The bladder lies between the ureter and the urethra.

Human Biology.q: A person has a puffy appearance, a moon face, low body temperature and intolerance to cold. What is he suffering from?
Human Biology.w: myxoedema is adult hypothyroidism: puffy face, cold intolerance, low metabolic rate. Graves' is hyperthyroidism. Hashimoto's is an autoimmune cause of hypothyroidism, but the puffy-face description is the textbook picture of myxoedema.

Human Biology.q: What is the substance sampled during amniocentesis?
Human Biology.w: a needle takes amniotic fluid to test for chromosome and gene disorders. Placental cells are sampled in chorionic villus sampling.

Human Biology.q: After digestion in the duodenum, the fat-rich milky fluid absorbed into the lacteals is called
Human Biology.w: chyle. Chyme is the acidic food mass leaving the stomach, bolus is the swallowed mass.

Human Biology.q: Justify the statement "the sino-auricular node is a natural pacemaker". What would you suggest if the natural pacemaker does not function normally? How do you test the blood group in human beings?
Human Biology.r: SA node [3]. The sino-atrial node is a small mass of modified cardiac muscle in the wall of the right atrium near the opening of the superior vena cava. It is myogenic: it fires on its own about 70–75 times a minute, faster than any other part, so it sets the rate of the whole heart. Each impulse spreads over the atria (atrial systole), reaches the AV node (delayed 0.1 s), and passes by the bundle of His, its branches and the Purkinje fibres to the ventricles (ventricular systole). Hence the SA node is the natural pacemaker. If it fails [2].

Human Biology.q: Distinguish between breathing and respiration. Define tidal volume and vital capacity, giving their normal values in an adult.
Human Biology.r: Breathing is the mechanical movement of air in and out of the lungs; respiration is the enzyme-controlled oxidation of food inside the cell to release ATP. Breathing is physical, involves no enzymes and happens in the lungs; respiration is chemical, needs enzymes and happens in every cell. Tidal volume = volume of air breathed in or out in one quiet breath ≈ 500 ml. Vital capacity = maximum volume that can be expelled after the deepest possible inspiration = IRV + TV + ERV ≈ 4500 ml (about 3500 ml in women).

Human Biology.q: Describe the events of one cardiac cycle and give the duration of each of its three phases.
Human Biology.r: One cycle lasts 0.8 s at 75 beats per minute. Atrial systole (0.1 s): atria contract, pushing the last 30 % of blood through the open AV valves into the ventricles. Ventricular systole (0.3 s): ventricles contract, AV valves shut (first sound, "lubb"), pressure rises isovolumetrically until the semilunar valves open and about 70 ml is ejected into the aorta and pulmonary trunk. Joint diastole (0.4 s): ventricles relax, semilunar valves shut (second sound, "dupp"), AV valves open and the chambers refill passively.

Human Biology.q: Two points on a nerve 12 cm apart are stimulated in turn; the muscle responds after 1.0 ms and 2.0 ms respectively. Calculate the conduction velocity in m s⁻¹ and state, with a reason, whether the fibre is myelinated.
Human Biology.r: The extra 12 cm of nerve added 1.0 ms to the latency, so

Human Biology.q: Name the disorders caused by the hyper- and hyposecretion of thyroxine and of growth hormone, and give one sign of each.
Human Biology.r: Thyroxine — hypersecretion: Graves' disease (exophthalmic goitre), sign = protruding eyeballs with rapid pulse and weight loss; hyposecretion: myxoedema in the adult, sign = puffy dry skin and low BMR, or cretinism in the infant, sign = stunted growth with mental retardation. Growth hormone — hypersecretion before the epiphyses close: gigantism, sign = abnormal height; after they close: acromegaly, sign = enlarged jaw, hands and feet; hyposecretion in childhood: pituitary dwarfism, sign = very short stature with normal body proportions and normal intelligence.

Human Biology.q: Describe the structure of a myelinated neuron. With the help of a graph of membrane potential against time, explain the origin and conduction of a nerve impulse, naming the value of the resting potential, the threshold and the peak.
Human Biology.r: Diagram as in Figures 12 and 13. Structure: a cyton (cell body) containing the nucleus and Nissl granules; many short branched dendrites that receive impulses; and one long axon that carries the impulse away. The axon is wrapped in a fatty myelin sheath laid down by Schwann cells, interrupted every 1–2 mm at the nodes of Ranvier; it ends in synaptic knobs holding neurotransmitter vesicles. Resting state: the Na⁺–K⁺ pump throws 3 Na⁺ out for every 2 K⁺ in, and the membrane leaks K⁺ outward, leaving the inside at -70 mV — polarised. Depolarisation: a stimulus that brings the membrane to the threshold of -55 mV opens voltage-gated Na⁺ channels;

Human Biology.q: Describe the menstrual cycle of a human female under the headings menstrual, proliferative, ovulatory and secretory phases, and explain the hormonal control of each. What happens to the corpus luteum if fertilisation occurs?
Human Biology.r: Graph as in Figure 21. The cycle averages 28 days, counted from the first day of bleeding. Menstrual phase (days 1–5). The corpus luteum of the previous cycle has degenerated, so oestrogen and progesterone fall sharply. The endometrium can no longer be maintained; it breaks down and is shed with 50–80 ml of blood. Proliferative / follicular phase (days 6–13). FSH from the anterior pituitary ripens one Graafian follicle, which secretes oestrogen. Oestrogen repairs and thickens the endometrium and restores its glands and blood vessels. Ovulatory phase (day 14). The peak of oestrogen acts by positive feedback on the pituitary to produce a sudden LH surge.

Human Biology.q: Describe the structure of the human heart and explain the cardiac cycle with its timing, heart sounds and cardiac output.
Describe the structure of a nephron and explain the formation of urine in its three steps.
Explain how a nerve impulse is generated and conducted, and how it crosses a synapse.
Describe the menstrual cycle with the hormones that control it.

Human Population and Health Disorders.q: When an organ transplantation occurs between two genetically identical individuals, what is the type of transplantation?
Human Population and Health Disorders.w: genetically identical individuals (identical twins) give an isograft. Autograft (a) is from the same individual, allograft (b) from the same species, heterograft (c) from another species.

Human Population and Health Disorders.q: Overpopulation has adverse consequences in society. Which of the following can control it?
Human Population and Health Disorders.w: family planning controls birth. Early marriage and polygamy raise births; food supply supports growth.

Human Population and Health Disorders.q: Which organ transplant has the lowest risk of rejection because the tissue lacks blood vessels?
Human Population and Health Disorders.w: the cornea has no blood vessels and sits behind the immune system's surveillance; rejection is rare.

Human Population and Health Disorders.q: The movement of individuals into a population from outside, which increases its size, is
Human Population and Health Disorders.w: immigration increases and emigration decreases the population; natality is births only.

Human Population and Health Disorders.q: A population has 1000 individuals. In a year there are 40 births, 10 deaths, 5 immigrants and 15 emigrants. The net increase is
Human Population and Health Disorders.w: births - deaths = 30; immigration - emigration = -10; net = 30 + (-10) = 20. Option (b) forgets the net migration.

Human Population and Health Disorders.q: A population pyramid with a broad base and a narrow top represents
Human Population and Health Disorders.w: a broad base means many young people: an expanding population. A narrow base would be declining.

Human Population and Health Disorders.q: The skin graft transferred from one part of the body of a burn patient to another part is an
Human Population and Health Disorders.w: same individual, so an autograft; no immune rejection.

Human Population and Health Disorders.q: HIV mainly destroys
Human Population and Health Disorders.w: HIV binds CD4 on helper T cells; as they fall, infections take over.

Human Population and Health Disorders.q: The vector of the malaria parasite is
Human Population and Health Disorders.w: the female Anopheles bites at night; the male feeds on plant juices. Aedes carries dengue.

Human Population and Health Disorders.q: The antibodies received by a baby through breast milk give
Human Population and Health Disorders.w: antibodies come ready-made from the mother (natural) and the baby made none (passive).

Human Population and Health Disorders.q: Kwashiorkor is caused by the deficiency of
Human Population and Health Disorders.w: protein deficiency with adequate energy gives oedema and a swollen belly; marasmus is protein and energy lack.

Human Population and Health Disorders.q: Which is the most common reason for adolescents to start smoking?
Human Population and Health Disorders.w: peer pressure; the question type also appears as a planning task (see the subjective chapter).

Human Population and Health Disorders.q: Define population growth. Explain the factors that influence the size of a human population. (original)
Human Population and Health Disorders.r: Definition [1]. Population growth is the change in the number of individuals in a population over a period. Factors [3]. growth = (natality - mortality) + (immigration - emigration). Natality (birth rate) rises with early marriage, desire for sons, poor use of contraception; mortality (death rate) falls with better health care, vaccination and nutrition; immigration and emigration (Nepal has large labour migration abroad). Education of girls, age at marriage, economic conditions and government policy (family planning) set these rates; the sum is shown in the demographic transition model.

Human Population and Health Disorders.q: What is AIDS? State how it is transmitted and how it can be prevented. (original)
Human Population and Health Disorders.r: AIDS [1]. Acquired Immuno-Deficiency Syndrome, caused by HIV, an RNA retrovirus that destroys CD4 helper T cells, so the body cannot fight infections. Transmission [1.5]. Unprotected sexual contact; contaminated blood or blood products; shared needles and syringes; from an infected mother to her child (pregnancy, birth, breast-feeding). It is not spread by handshake, mosquito bite or sharing food. Prevention [1.5]. Safe sex and condom use; screening of donated blood; use of a new syringe for each injection; antiretroviral drugs for pregnant women to protect the baby; AIDS education and counselling.

Human Population and Health Disorders.q: Explain malaria: the causative agent and its life cycle in man and mosquito, symptoms, and control measures. (predicted: a communicable-disease long question appears in every paper — the three seen so far covered typhoid, cholera and TB; malaria, hepatitis and AIDS are the others on the syllabus)
The definitive host of the malarial parasite is
Human Population and Health Disorders.w: fertilisation and sporogony occur in the female Anopheles.

Human Population and Health Disorders.q: AIDS is diagnosed when the CD4⁺ T-cell count falls below
Human Population and Health Disorders.w: below 200 cells mm⁻³ the patient is defined as having AIDS.

Human Population and Health Disorders.q: Define crude birth rate, crude death rate and rate of natural increase. A district of 480,000 people registered 8160 live births and 3360 deaths in one year; find all three rates.
Human Population and Health Disorders.r: Definitions as in §9.1.1. $\text{CBR} = \frac{8160}{480000}\times 1000 = 17.0$ per 1000; $\text{CDR} = \frac{3360}{480000}\times 1000 = 7.0$ per 1000; $\text{RNI} = 17.0 - 7.0 = 10.0$ per 1000, i.e. 1.0 % per year (doubling time $\approx 70$ years).

Human Population and Health Disorders.q: What is a population pyramid? Draw and label the pyramid of a rapidly growing population and state two features that identify it.
Explain the four stages of the demographic transition model and state, with a reason, which stage Nepal is in.
Human Population and Health Disorders.r: Outline: Stage 1 both rates high, growth near zero; Stage 2 death rate falls (clean water, vaccines) while birth rate stays high, growth fastest; Stage 3 birth rate falls (contraception, female education), growth slows; Stage 4 both rates low, growth near zero. Nepal is in late Stage 3 — CDR is already low (about 6 per 1000) and the birth rate has fallen to about 19 per 1000 with TFR 2.1, so natural increase is small but still positive.

Applied Biology.q: Which one of the following sets contains bacterial diseases only?
Applied Biology.w: tuberculosis, typhoid and cholera are all bacterial. Candidiasis is a fungal disease and hepatitis and influenza are viral, so every other option hides one wrong member.

Applied Biology.q: Which pair of diseases is spread through contaminated food and water?
Applied Biology.w: typhoid and cholera spread by the faeco-oral route. Tuberculosis and influenza are airborne; candidiasis is fungal.

Applied Biology.q: The indigenous honeybee of Nepal, kept in log and box hives, is
Applied Biology.w: Apis cerana is the hive bee of Nepal's hills. A. mellifera is the introduced European bee.

Applied Biology.q: In a honeybee colony, drones develop from
Applied Biology.w: drones are haploid, from unfertilised eggs (parthenogenesis); queen and workers are diploid.

Applied Biology.q: A larva becomes a queen bee because it is fed throughout on
Applied Biology.w: royal jelly for the whole larval life makes a queen; workers get it only for the first days.

Applied Biology.q: The silkworm Bombyx mori is fed on the leaves of
Applied Biology.w: mulberry (Morus). Castor feeds the eri silkworm.

Applied Biology.q: The two proteins of the raw silk thread are
Applied Biology.w: fibroin forms the thread and sericin glues it.

Applied Biology.q: In composite fish culture catla, rohu and mrigal are stocked together because they
o: feed at different depths of the pond
Applied Biology.w: catla is a surface feeder, rohu a column feeder, mrigal a bottom feeder, so they use the whole pond without competing.
