The earthworm commonly used for vermicomposting is
Applied Biology.w: Eisenia fetida (red wiggler) is an epigeic composting worm. Pheretima is a burrower.

Applied Biology.q: Lac is obtained from
Applied Biology.w: the lac insect Kerria lacca secretes lac on twigs.

Applied Biology.q: The causative organism of typhoid is
Applied Biology.w: Salmonella typhi. Vibrio cholerae causes cholera.

Applied Biology.q: The test used for the diagnosis of typhoid is
Applied Biology.w: Widal detects antibodies to S. typhi antigens; Mantoux is for TB.

Applied Biology.q: The first line of treatment of dehydration in cholera is
Applied Biology.w: ORS replaces water and salts; antibiotics are secondary.

Applied Biology.q: What are pullets? How would you express the scope of poultry farming in Nepal?
Applied Biology.r: Pullets [1]. Young female chickens (fowls) that have not yet started laying eggs, usually from about 8 weeks to the start of laying. Scope in Nepal [3]. (i) Eggs and meat are an affordable source of protein, and demand is rising with urban growth and tourism; (ii) poultry needs a small land area and capital and can be kept in backyards, so it gives self-employment, especially for women and in the hills; (iii) poultry waste is a good manure and a feed for fish; (iv) farms, hatcheries, feed mills and marketing provide jobs and reduce the import of eggs and chicken; (v) improved breeds (White Leghorn for eggs;

Applied Biology.q: Name any two indigenous fish species of Nepal. Discuss how integrated fish farming is advantageous over traditional fish farming.
Applied Biology.r: Indigenous fish [1]. Asala (snow trout, Schizothorax) and Sahar (golden mahseer, Tor putitora); also Katle. Advantages of integrated fish farming [3]. It combines fish culture with another farm enterprise, such as poultry, duck, pig or paddy and vegetables. (i) The waste of the animals falls in the pond as manure and feed, cutting the cost of fish feed and fertiliser; (ii) the nutrient-rich pond water and mud can irrigate and fertilise the crop; (iii) the same land gives more than one product and more income; (iv) it makes use of waste and saves money, which a traditional single-crop pond cannot do.

Applied Biology.q: Describe the three castes of the honeybee and their functions. (original)
Applied Biology.r: Queen — one per colony, large fertile female with long abdomen; she lays up to 1500–2000 eggs a day and produces the pheromone that holds the colony together; she eats royal jelly throughout life. Workers — sterile females (2n), the smallest and most numerous; they collect nectar and pollen, make honey and wax, build comb, feed the brood, guard and clean the hive, and ventilate it. Drones — males, haploid, hatched from unfertilised eggs, larger eyes; their only function is to mate with the queen (during the nuptial flight), and they are driven out or killed after the season.

Applied Biology.q: Describe the life cycle of the silkworm Bombyx mori and state the stage at which silk is obtained. (original)
Applied Biology.r: The silkworm shows complete metamorphosis: egg (laid by the moth, about 400–500 eggs) → larva (caterpillar) that feeds greedily on mulberry leaves and moults four times → pupa inside a cocoon spun from a single continuous thread of fibroin and sericin from its salivary glands → adult moth. Silk is obtained from the cocoon: the pupa is killed by hot air or steam before the moth emerges (otherwise it cuts the thread), and the cocoons are boiled to soften the sericin and the thread is reeled off.

Applied Biology.q: What is vermicomposting? Explain its method and advantages. (original)
Applied Biology.r: Vermicomposting [1]. Preparation of compost from organic waste using earthworms. Method [2]. A shaded pit, box or bed is filled with a bedding of partly decomposed dry leaves and cow dung; kitchen and farm waste is added in layers; about 1000 worms (Eisenia fetida) are released per square metre; the bed is kept moist (60–70 %) and covered with jute; after 45–60 days the dark, crumbly vermicast is sieved out. Advantages [1]. Cheap, rich in NPK and humus, improves soil structure, recycles waste, and gives extra income from worms.

Applied Biology.q: Why is typhoid called enteric fever? Illustrate its causative agent, mode of transmission, symptoms and preventive measures. (NEB model 2079; asked again in NEB 2081 as: name the causative agent, transmission, symptoms, prevention, and the organ affected in severe cases)
Applied Biology.r: Why enteric [1]. The disease is caused by an organism that lives in the intestine (enteron), and the fever starts when bacteria invade the intestinal wall and the blood; hence enteric fever. Causative agent [1]. Salmonella Typhi (written Salmonella typhi in older books), a motile, rod-shaped Gram-negative bacterium. Transmission [2]. The faeco-oral route: food and water contaminated with the faeces or urine of patients or carriers (Typhoid Mary was a famous carrier); flies carry bacteria to food; poor sanitation and unwashed hands; street food and untreated water. Symptoms [2].

Applied Biology.q: Explain cholera as an acute diarrhoeal disease. Discuss its causative agent, mode of transmission and symptoms. Mention its control measures.
Applied Biology.r: Cholera [1]. An acute diarrhoeal disease with sudden, profuse, watery diarrhoea that can kill through dehydration within hours. Causative agent [1]. Vibrio cholerae, a comma-shaped Gram-negative bacterium with a single polar flagellum; its enterotoxin makes the intestinal cells pump out water and salts. Transmission [2]. Faeco-oral: water contaminated with faeces (wells, rivers after floods, the monsoon), uncooked food and shellfish, flies and unwashed hands; epidemics in crowded places. Symptoms [2]. Sudden rice-water stools, vomiting, severe dehydration (sunken eyes, dry mouth, loss of skin turgor), muscle cramps, low blood pressure, rapid pulse and collapse;

Applied Biology.q: Mention the causative agent, mode of transmission and symptoms of pulmonary tuberculosis. Highlight the strategies for its prevention. Why is it called a "disease of poverty"?
Applied Biology.r: Causative agent [1]. Mycobacterium tuberculosis, a rod-shaped acid-fast bacillus. Transmission [2]. Airborne droplets when a person with active lung TB coughs, sneezes or talks; sometimes infected milk (M. bovis); the risk rises in crowded, badly ventilated rooms. Symptoms [2]. Cough for more than two weeks, sometimes with blood in the sputum, evening fever, night sweats, weight loss, loss of appetite, chest pain and fatigue. Prevention [2]. BCG vaccination at birth; finding and treating cases early with DOTS (directly observed treatment, short course: rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for two months, then rifampicin and isoniazid, six months in all) to cut the source;

Applied Biology.q: Define apiculture. Name any two species of Apis found in Nepal and state one difference between them.
Applied Biology.r: Apiculture is the rearing and management of honey bees in hives for honey, wax and pollination. Any two of Apis cerana, A. mellifera, A. dorsata, A. laboriosa, A. florea. A usable difference: A. cerana builds several combs inside a cavity and can therefore be kept in a hive, while A. dorsata builds a single open comb on a tree or cliff and cannot.

Applied Biology.q: What is bee space, and why did its discovery matter? Describe the castes of a honey bee colony.
Describe the life cycle of Bombyx mori and explain why the pupa is killed before the moth emerges.
Applied Biology.r: Egg (10–14 d) → larva, five instars and four moults, feeding only on mulberry (29–30 d) → spins a cocoon over 2–3 days and pupates inside → adult moth, which does not feed and cannot fly. The pupa is killed by stifling because an emerging moth secretes a softening fluid and bites its way out, cutting the single continuous filament into useless short lengths so the cocoon can no longer be reeled.

Applied Biology.q: What is composite fish culture? Give the six species used and the feeding zone of each.
Applied Biology.r: See the table in §10.1: silver carp — surface, phytoplankton; catla — surface and mid-water, zooplankton; rohu — column, omnivore; grass carp — margins, macrophytes; mrigal — bottom, detritus; common carp — bottom, omnivore. The point of the arrangement is that the six occupy different feeding niches, so all layers of the pond's food are harvested and no two species compete.

Applied Biology.q: Why do carps fail to breed in ponds, and how is the problem overcome?
Applied Biology.r: Carps mature in a pond but do not spawn, because still water gives none of the riverine stimuli — rising level, current, monsoon turbidity — needed for final maturation and the release of gametes. The problem is overcome by induced breeding: an injection of pituitary extract or of a synthetic GnRH analogue with domperidone (Ovaprim) into ripe brooders, which then spawn in a hapa or circular hatchery within a few hours.

Applied Biology.q: Write short notes on the three ecological groups of earthworms and state which is used in vermicomposting, with a reason.
Differentiate between a broiler and a layer. Name Nepal's three indigenous chicken breeds.
State Koch's postulates and give one limitation of them.
Why are antibiotics ineffective against viral infections? Name two antibiotics with their target site.
Applied Biology.r: Because every antibiotic target is a prokaryotic structure — peptidoglycan wall, 70S ribosome, DNA gyrase, bacterial folate synthesis — and a virus has none of them; it is acellular and replicates using the host cell's own machinery, so antivirals are required instead. Two examples: penicillin inhibits cell-wall synthesis; streptomycin binds the 30S ribosomal subunit. (Also acceptable: erythromycin — 50S; ciprofloxacin — DNA gyrase; rifampicin — RNA polymerase; sulfonamide — folate synthesis.)

Applied Biology.q: Distinguish between the primary and the secondary immune response, and explain why a booster dose is given.
Describe apiculture under the headings: bee species of Nepal, castes of a colony, the movable-frame hive, and economic importance.
Write an account of vaccines and antibiotics: what each is, how each works, the main types of each, and why an antibiotic cannot be used to treat COVID-19.
Applied Biology.r: Vaccine = preparation of a pathogen or its antigen that provokes a primary response and leaves memory cells, i.e. artificial active immunity; Jenner 1796 (cowpox), Pasteur coined the word 1881. Types with examples: live attenuated, killed, subunit/conjugate, toxoid, mRNA, viral vector. Mechanism: primary response slow and IgM; secondary fast, 100–1000× larger, IgG — hence boosters. Antibiotic = substance from one microorganism that kills or inhibits another; Fleming 1928, Florey and Chain 1940–41, Nobel 1945. Targets: cell wall, 70S ribosome (30S and 50S), DNA gyrase and RNA polymerase, folate synthesis; broad vs narrow spectrum, bactericidal vs bacteriostatic.

a: Explain in brief the significance of polyploidy with examples.
Paper 2079 General Stream.r: Differences between transpiration and guttation. | Transpiration | Guttation | |---|---| | loss of water as vapour from aerial parts | loss of water as liquid drops | | occurs mainly through stomata (also cuticle and lenticels) | occurs through hydathodes at leaf margins and tips | | takes place mostly in the daytime, in sunlight | takes place mainly at night or in the early morning, when humidity is high | | caused by the pulling force of evaporation (transpiration pull) | caused by root pressure | | the water is pure (nearly) | the water contains dissolved sugars, salts and organic matter | | a physical process controlled by guard cells | not controlled by guard cells;

p: Write the salient features of the dicot embryo in reference to its development pattern with labelled diagrams.
Paper 2079 General Stream.r: Development pattern of the dicot embryo (2 marks). The development of the embryo (embryogeny) is by repeated divisions of the zygote inside the embryo sac, in the sequence: 1. The zygote rests for a while and then divides transversely into a large basal cell (toward the micropyle) and a small terminal cell (toward the chalaza). 2. The basal cell divides transversely many times to form a row of 6 to 10 cells, the suspensor, which pushes the embryo into the nutritive endosperm. Its first cell, next to the micropyle, is swollen and anchors the embryo (haustorium), and the cell next to the embryo forms the radicle tip (hypophysis). 3.

p: The source of oxygen in photosynthesis is the water but not the carbon dioxide. Explain with reasons. Briefly describe the Hill reaction. ## Section II: Zoology ### Group 'B'
Paper 2079 General Stream.r: Source of O₂ is water, not CO₂ (2 marks). 1. Van Niel (1931): purple sulphur bacteria use H₂S instead of H₂O, giving sulphur and no oxygen: CO₂ + 2H₂S → (CH₂O) + 2S + H₂O. He generalised the reaction as CO₂ + 2H₂A → (CH₂O) + 2A + H₂O, so in green plants the "A" liberated is O₂ from H₂O (6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ + 6H₂O). 2. Ruben and Kamen (1941), isotope experiment with the alga Chlorella: when water labelled with ¹⁸O (H₂¹⁸O) and ordinary CO₂ was given, the O₂ evolved was labelled with ¹⁸O; when ordinary water and C¹⁸O₂ were given, the O₂ evolved was not labelled (the ¹⁸O was found in the carbohydrate and water). So the oxygen comes from the photolysis of water. Hill reaction (6 marks).

p: How would you elaborate the different types of simple epithelial tissues in animals? Support with diagrams.
Paper 2079 General Stream.r: Simple epithelium consists of a single layer of cells resting on a basement membrane. It lines body cavities and ducts, and is classified by the shape of its cells. | Type | Structure | Location | Function | |---|---|---|---| | Simple squamous | single layer of flat, polygonal cells with a central bulging nucleus; fits like a pavement | alveoli of lungs, lining of blood vessels (endothelium), Bowman's capsule, mesothelium | diffusion and filtration | | Simple cuboidal | cube-shaped cells with a round central nucleus;

p: Describe the process of oogenesis in animals with a diagram.
a: Define the term in-vitro fertilization. Describe its process.
Paper 2079 General Stream.r: Oogenesis is the formation of mature ova (eggs) in the ovary of the female. It has three phases. 1. Multiplication phase: in the embryonic ovary the germinal epithelium forms primordial germ cells which divide by mitosis to form millions of oogonia (2n). This phase is finished before birth; no new oogonia are formed afterwards. 2. Growth phase: each oogonium enlarges, stores yolk and becomes a primary oocyte (2n), which starts meiosis I but stops at prophase I. It is surrounded by follicle cells (a primary follicle) and remains in this state until puberty; of about 2 million at birth only 300,000 to 400,000 remain at puberty, and only about 400 are ovulated in life. 3.

p: Explain cholera as an acute diarrhoeal disease. Discuss its causative agent, mode of transmission and symptoms. Mention its control measures.
Paper 2079 General Stream.r: Cholera (1 mark). Cholera is an acute infection of the small intestine that causes sudden, profuse, watery diarrhoea ("rice-water stools") and rapid loss of water and salts, so that a patient can die of dehydration within hours if untreated. It occurs as epidemics in crowded places with poor sanitation, especially in the rainy season. Causative agent (1 mark). Vibrio cholerae, a comma-shaped, motile, Gram-negative bacterium with a single polar flagellum; the serogroups O1 (classical and El Tor biotypes) and O139 cause epidemics. In the intestine it releases the cholera toxin (choleragen), which makes the cells of the intestinal wall pump out large amounts of water and chloride.

p: What is the difference between hypertonic, hypotonic and isotonic solutions, and how do they affect the movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane?
What is incomplete dominance? Provide an example of a trait that shows incomplete dominance and explain how it is inherited.
Paper 2080 Technical 9101.r: Incomplete dominance is the phenomenon in which neither allele of a gene pair is completely dominant over the other, so the heterozygote ($F_1$) shows an intermediate (blended) phenotype between the two homozygous parents. It is also called partial dominance or blending inheritance and was reported by Correns in Mirabilis jalapa. Example: flower colour in the four o'clock plant (Mirabilis jalapa). The allele $R$ gives red pigment and $r$ (or $R^W$) gives no pigment (white), but $R$ is not completely dominant over $r$. Mode of inheritance. 1. Parents: a pure red-flowered plant ($RR$) is crossed with a pure white-flowered plant ($rr$). 2.

p: What is plasmolysis? Point out its significances.
Paper 2080 Technical 9101.r: Plasmolysis is the shrinkage of the protoplasm of a plant cell, due to the loss of water by exosmosis, when the cell is placed in a hypertonic solution; the plasma membrane and cytoplasm pull away from the cell wall (the opposite of deplasmolysis, in which a plasmolysed cell regains water in a hypotonic solution). Stages: limiting plasmolysis (the protoplast just begins to leave the corners of the wall), incipient plasmolysis (the protoplast has pulled away from the wall at several places) and evident (complete) plasmolysis (the protoplast is rounded and completely detached from the wall). Significance of plasmolysis. 1.

p: Draw a labelled diagram of T.S. of dicot stem and compare it with that of monocot stem.
What is diffusion? Compare it with osmosis.
Paper 2080 Technical 9101.r: Diffusion is the net movement of molecules or ions (of a solid, liquid or gas) from a region of their higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, down the concentration gradient, due to their random kinetic energy, until they are evenly distributed. It needs no energy and no membrane. Examples: spreading of the smell of perfume in a room, a drop of ink in water, exchange of O₂ and CO₂ in the leaf or alveolus. Comparison between diffusion and osmosis.

p: How can biotechnology be applied in medicine and agriculture? Analyse the potential benefits and drawbacks of using biotechnology in these fields.
Paper 2080 Technical 9101.r: Biotechnology is the use of living organisms or their parts (cells, enzymes, genes) to make products and processes useful to humans; modern biotechnology uses genetic engineering and tissue culture. Applications in medicine. Production of human insulin, growth hormone and interferon by recombinant bacteria; vaccines (hepatitis B subunit vaccine) and monoclonal antibodies; gene therapy (ADA deficiency), DNA fingerprinting, PCR-based diagnosis, stem cell therapy and antibiotics from microbes. Applications in agriculture.

p: What is amniocentesis? Why is it done? Explain the procedure of amniocentesis.
Paper 2080 Technical 9101.r: Definition (1). Amniocentesis is a prenatal diagnostic technique in which a small sample of the amniotic fluid, containing fetal cells shed from the skin, lungs and urinary tract of the fetus, is withdrawn from the amniotic sac of a pregnant woman with a hollow needle and examined, to detect genetic and chromosomal disorders in the fetus. Why it is done (1). To detect, before birth, chromosomal abnormalities such as Down syndrome (trisomy 21), Edward syndrome and Turner's or Klinefelter's syndrome, gene disorders such as cystic fibrosis, sickle cell anaemia, Tay–Sachs disease and haemophilia, neural-tube defects (raised α-fetoprotein), the maturity of the fetal lung, and fetal infection.

p: Define organogenesis. Write down the process of neurulation in the development of frog.
a: Define allograft. What are the methods used to prevent the rejection of an organ transplanted? Why is cornea transplantation easier?
Paper 2080 General Stream.r: Organogenesis is the process by which the three primary germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm) formed in gastrulation differentiate into the organs and organ systems of the body (e.g. nervous system from ectoderm, notochord, muscles and heart from mesoderm, gut lining from endoderm). Neurulation in the frog. It is the first organogenesis, in which the central nervous system is made from the dorsal ectoderm, and it occurs in the late gastrula/neurula stage. 1. Neural plate: induced by the underlying dorsal mesoderm (the notochord, called the primary organiser), the ectoderm on the dorsal side thickens into a flat neural plate. 2.

p: Compare and contrast myelinated and non-myelinated nerve fibres.

A population exhibits a characteristic pattern of its growth. Develop a model of the J-shaped growth curve of a species when introduced in a new habitat. Plan any two activities to control population growth. ### Group 'C'
Paper 2080 General Stream.r: J-shaped growth curve (exponential growth). When a species is introduced into a new habitat with plenty of food, space and no predators or disease, its population grows exponentially: the growth rate depends only on the number of individuals present and keeps on increasing until a resource suddenly runs out or the environment changes. The curve is shaped like the letter J. Model: the rate of change of population size N with time t is $$\frac{dN}{dt} = rN \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad N_t = N_0\, e^{rt}$$ where N₀ is the starting number, r the intrinsic rate of natural increase (birth rate - death rate) and e = 2.718. Worked example.

p: Explain the causative agents and modes of infection of Hepatitis-B and Tuberculosis. List the vaccines used for both the diseases.
Paper 2080 General Stream.r: Hepatitis-B - Causative agent (1): hepatitis-B virus (HBV), a partly double-stranded DNA virus of the family Hepadnaviridae (Dane particle, with surface antigen HBsAg). - Modes of infection (2): through body fluids: (i) blood transfusion of infected blood; (ii) sharing contaminated needles and syringes by drug users, unsterilised tattoo/ear-piercing instruments and razors; (iii) unprotected sexual contact; (iv) from an infected mother to the baby at birth (vertical transmission); (v) accidental needle-stick injuries to health workers. It does not spread by casual contact, coughing or sharing food. - Symptoms: jaundice, dark urine, fatigue, nausea and fever;

p: What is co-dominance? Explain it with an example.
Paper 2081 Technical 9101.r: Co-dominance is the phenomenon in which both alleles of a gene pair are fully expressed in the heterozygote; neither allele is dominant over the other, so the F₁ shows the phenotypes of both parents together. Example: ABO blood groups in humans. The gene $I$ has three alleles: $I^A$ (antigen A), $I^B$ (antigen B) and $i$ (no antigen). $I^A$ and $I^B$ are dominant over $i$, but they are co-dominant with each other. A person of genotype $I^AI^B$ has both antigen A and antigen B on the red blood cells, giving blood group AB; both alleles express themselves equally.

p: What is meristem? Write its characteristics and types.
Paper 2081 Technical 9101.r: Meristem is a group of young, undifferentiated living cells that retain the power of continuous cell division and give rise to new cells that later differentiate into permanent tissues. Characteristics of meristematic cells: - They are small, spherical, oval or polygonal, and are closely packed without intercellular spaces. - The cell wall is thin, elastic and made of cellulose. - The cytoplasm is dense with a large, prominent nucleus. - Vacuoles are absent or very small; no reserve food and no ergastic substances. - Plastids are in the proplastid stage, and metabolic activity is very high. Types of meristem: 1.

p: What is osmosis? Write its types and significances.
Paper 2081 Technical 9101.r: Osmosis is the movement of the solvent (water) molecules from a solution of lower solute concentration to a solution of higher solute concentration through a semipermeable membrane. Types: 1. Endosmosis: movement of water into a cell or an osmometer when it is placed in a hypotonic solution (the cell swells or becomes turgid). 2. Exosmosis: movement of water out of a cell placed in a hypertonic solution (the cell shrinks; plasmolysis in plant cells). Significance of osmosis: 1. Absorption of water from the soil by the root hairs, and its movement from cell to cell across the cortex into the xylem. 2.

p: How is it possible to create a disease resistant plant by using biotechnology? Explain with examples.
Paper 2081 Technical 9101.r: Disease resistant plants by biotechnology (genetic engineering). Plants can be made resistant to diseases caused by viruses, bacteria, fungi and insect pests by isolating a gene that gives resistance and transferring it into the plant by recombinant DNA technology. Steps: (1) the resistance gene is isolated from the source organism; (2) it is inserted into a vector, usually the Ti plasmid of Agrobacterium tumefaciens, or delivered by a gene gun; (3) the plant cells or protoplasts are transformed and grown on a tissue culture medium; (4) the transformed cells are regenerated into whole transgenic plants, which are then tested and selected. Examples: 1.

p: Define parenchyma tissue and explain its structure and function.
Paper 2081 General Stream.r: Definition. Parenchyma is a simple permanent tissue made of living, thin-walled, generally isodiametric cells that retain the power of division. It is the most abundant and the most primitive ground tissue of the plant body (cortex, pith, mesophyll, medullary rays and the packing cells of xylem and phloem). Structure. - The cells are living and have a prominent nucleus, a large central vacuole with cell sap, and a thin primary cell wall of cellulose and pectin. - The shape is round, oval, polygonal or elongated, and the cells are loosely packed with small intercellular spaces between them.

p: Explain the mechanism of incomplete dominance up to the F₂ generation with a suitable example. How does it differ from complete dominance?
a: Describe any four practical importances of seed dormancy in agriculture and horticulture.
Paper 2081 General Stream.r: Incomplete dominance is the inheritance in which neither allele is completely dominant over the other, so the heterozygote shows a phenotype intermediate between the two homozygous parents (Correns, 1900). Example: flower colour in Mirabilis jalapa (four o'clock plant) / snapdragon. - Parents (P): red-flowered plant (RR) × white-flowered plant (rr). - Gametes: all R from the red parent and all r from the white parent. - F₁: all Rr, with pink flowers (a blend, neither red nor white). - F₁ selfing (Rr × Rr): gametes R and r from each parent; Punnett square gives RR: Rr: Rr: rr.

p: Describe the process of micropropagation to rapidly produce a large number of identical plantlets, and describe how it can be used in conservation efforts for endangered plant species. ### Group 'C'
Paper 2081 General Stream.r: Micropropagation is the in vitro clonal multiplication of a plant from a very small part of it (explant: shoot tip, axillary bud, leaf piece) on a sterile, nutrient medium under controlled conditions. It rests on totipotency: every living plant cell can regenerate a whole plant. Steps: 1. Selection and sterilisation of the explant from a healthy mother plant (shoot tip or axillary bud, usually disease-free), surface-sterilised with ethanol and sodium hypochlorite. 2. Initiation/inoculation on a sterile Murashige–Skoog (MS) medium (sucrose, mineral salts, vitamins, agar) in culture tubes in a laminar-flow chamber. 3.

p: The light-independent reactions of photosynthesis involve the conversion of carbon dioxide into glucose. Explain the steps involved in this process and how the products of the light-dependent reactions (ATP and NADPH) are utilized.
Paper 2081 General Stream.r: The light-independent reactions are the Calvin cycle (C₃ cycle). They take place in the stroma of the chloroplast, use the ATP and NADPH formed in the thylakoid membranes (light-dependent reactions) and do not need light directly. The cycle has three phases. Steps of the Calvin cycle 1. Carboxylation (carbon fixation). CO₂ combines with the five-carbon acceptor ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP), catalysed by the enzyme RuBisCO, to form an unstable six-carbon intermediate that splits at once into two molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PGA), the first stable product (a three-carbon compound, hence "C₃"). 2. Reduction.

p: In what ways does DNA serve as the genetic material of living organisms? Discuss its double helical structure with a labelled diagram. Analyze the similarities and differences between DNA and RNA, and evaluate the significance of these molecules in genetic processes.
a: How can chromosomal mutations alter the number and structure of chromosomes? Provide a detailed discussion on the various types of chromosomal mutations. Analyze the significance of chromosomal mutation in an organism. ## Section II: Zoology ### Group 'B'
Paper 2081 General Stream.r: 1. DNA as the genetic material (1 mark). DNA qualifies as the genetic material because it: - stores information in the sequence of its bases (the genetic code); - replicates accurately (semi-conservative), so a complete copy is passed to every daughter cell and every offspring; - expresses its information by producing RNA and then proteins (transcription and translation), controlling the traits of the organism; - is stable chemically, but can change by mutation, which gives the variation needed for evolution.

p: Compare and contrast between voluntary and involuntary muscles.
Paper 2081 General Stream.r: | Voluntary (striated / skeletal) muscles | Involuntary (smooth / visceral) muscles | |---|---| | Controlled by the will; supplied by the somatic nervous system. | Not under the will; supplied by the autonomic nervous system. | | Attached to the bones by tendons; found in limbs, face, trunk. | Found in the walls of hollow organs: gut, blood vessels, bladder, uterus, iris. | | Cells are long, cylindrical, unbranched, multinucleate (syncytium). | Cells are spindle-shaped, tapering, uninucleate. | | Show dark and light cross-striations (sarcomeres). | Without striations (smooth). | | Quick, strong contraction; get fatigued easily. | Slow, rhythmic contraction; do not tire easily.

Paper 2081 General Stream.r: Coelom is the fluid-filled body cavity that lies between the body wall and the digestive tube, and is completely lined by a mesodermal epithelium (peritoneum). It holds and protects the visceral organs, allows them to grow and move independently of the body wall, and its fluid acts as a hydrostatic skeleton and a transport medium. Animals having it are coelomates (frog, man). Formation of coelom in the frog. 1. After cleavage and gastrulation, the embryo has three germ layers; the mesoderm is formed from the roof and sides of the archenteron (and the cells that roll in at the dorsal lip of the blastopore). 2.

p: Name the causative agent of typhoid. Explain its mode of transmission, symptoms and preventive measures. Mention the body organ that gets affected in severe cases.
Paper 2081 General Stream.r: Causative agent (1): the bacterium Salmonella typhi (Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi), a Gram-negative, rod-shaped, flagellated bacterium. Mode of transmission (2): typhoid spreads by the faeco-oral route. - By food and water contaminated with the faeces or urine of a patient or a carrier (a person who is healthy but keeps the bacteria in the gall bladder). - By houseflies that carry the bacteria from faeces to food; by uncooked vegetables washed in polluted water, street food and unclean hands of food handlers. - Poor sanitation and overcrowding help it to spread. Symptoms (2): the incubation period is 1–3 weeks.

p: Differentiate between simple permanent tissue and complex permanent tissue on the basis of structure, types, cell composition and functions.
Paper 2082 General Stream.r: | Basis | Simple permanent tissue | Complex permanent tissue | |---|---|---| | Structure | Made of one type of cells, uniform structure | Made of more than one type of cells working together as a unit | | Types | Parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma | Xylem and phloem | | Cell composition | Only one cell type, e.g. only parenchyma cells | Xylem: tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres and xylem parenchyma. Phloem: sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem fibres and phloem parenchyma | | Functions | Storage, photosynthesis, mechanical support, flexibility and strength | Conduction: xylem carries water and minerals upward, phloem carries food (sugars) in both directions |

p: In which process are the linked genes inherited together from one generation to another with parental and non-parental combinations? Explain the process with a suitable example.
a: How does diffusion differ from osmosis based on the types of molecules involved across a cell membrane? Explain how environmental factors influence the rate of diffusion.
Paper 2082 General Stream.r: Process: linkage and crossing over (recombination). Genes located on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together (linkage), giving parental combinations; crossing over between non-sister chromatids in prophase I of meiosis breaks the linkage and produces non-parental (recombinant) combinations. The closer the genes, the stronger the linkage. Example (Morgan's experiment on Drosophila): a grey-bodied, long-winged female (BBVV) was crossed with a black-bodied, vestigial-winged male (bbvv). The F₁ were all grey, long. A test cross of the F₁ female with a bbvv male gave: grey long 965, black vestigial 944 (parental, 83%) and grey vestigial 206, black long 185 (recombinant, 17%).

p: How can GMOs be used to address global food security challenges and what are the potential environmental concerns and health risks associated with their use?
Paper 2082 General Stream.r: Food security: GMOs raise yield and reduce losses: pest-resistant Bt cotton and Bt maize need less pesticide; herbicide-tolerant crops give easier weed control; drought-, salt- and flood-tolerant varieties grow on poor land; nutritionally improved crops (Golden Rice rich in β-carotene) fight deficiency; longer shelf life lowers post-harvest loss. Environmental concerns: gene flow to wild relatives, "superweeds" and resistant pests, harm to non-target organisms (e.g. pollinators), loss of biodiversity and dependence on a few varieties. Health risks: possible allergic reactions, toxicity of the new protein, transfer of antibiotic-resistance marker genes, and unknown long-term effects.

p: How do different photosynthetic pigments contribute to capturing light energy? Explain how cyclic and non-cyclic photophosphorylation generate ATP and NADPH, and illustrate these with appropriate charts.
Paper 2082 General Stream.r: Pigments: chlorophyll a (blue-green, the primary pigment in the reaction centres P680 and P700) absorbs mainly red (about 680–700 nm) and blue-violet light; chlorophyll b (yellow-green) and the carotenoids (carotene, xanthophyll) are accessory pigments that absorb other wavelengths (green-blue, 450–500 nm), pass the energy to chlorophyll a, widen the range of light used, and protect chlorophyll from photo-oxidation. Together they form light-harvesting antenna complexes that funnel energy to the reaction centre. Non-cyclic photophosphorylation (both photosystems, Z-scheme): light excites P680 of PS II;

p: Write about the neurulation process in the development of the frog.
a: Name any two indigenous fish species. Discuss how integrated fish farming is advantageous over traditional fish farming.
Paper 2082 General Stream.r: Neurulation is the formation of the neural tube (the future central nervous system) after gastrulation, in the late gastrula stage of the frog. 1. The ectoderm lying above the notochord thickens to form the neural plate. 2. The edges of the plate rise as the neural folds, with a neural groove between them. 3. The folds approach each other and fuse in the mid-dorsal line, closing the groove into a hollow neural tube with a cavity (neurocoel), which sinks below the surface ectoderm. 4. The anterior part of the tube enlarges into the brain vesicles, the rest forms the spinal cord. Cells at the crest of the folds form the neural crest, which gives sensory ganglia and other structures;

p: Mention the causative agent, mode of transmission and symptoms of pulmonary tuberculosis. Highlight various strategies for its prevention. Why is it called a "disease of poverty"?
Paper 2082 General Stream.r: Causative agent (1): the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis (tubercle bacillus). Mode of transmission (2): by droplet infection. An infected person releases droplets containing the bacilli when coughing, sneezing, talking or spitting, and others inhale them. Crowded, poorly ventilated places and contaminated sputum also spread it; the bacteria may also spread through unpasteurised milk (bovine TB). Symptoms (2): cough for more than two weeks with sputum (sometimes blood-stained), chest pain, evening fever, night sweats, loss of weight and appetite, weakness and shortness of breath. Prevention (2): BCG vaccination of newborns;

Volumetric Analysis.w: equivalents = 100 × 0.5 + 20 × 0.1 + 50 × 0.2 = 50 + 2 + 10 = 62 milli-equivalents in 170 mL, so N = 0.3647 and pH = -log 0.3647 = 0.44. Option (c) is the pH if the volumes were forgotten and the three normalities were simply averaged.

Distinguish between a primary and a secondary standard substance. Give two examples of each and state why sodium hydroxide cannot be a primary standard.
Volumetric Analysis.r: A primary standard is pure, stable, highly soluble and of high equivalent weight, so a standard solution follows from one accurate weighing (oxalic acid, K₂Cr₂O₇). A secondary standard must be titrated against a primary standard (HCl, KMnO₄). NaOH is deliquescent and absorbs CO₂ from the air to form Na₂CO₃, so the mass weighed is not pure NaOH.

Volumetric Analysis.q: Why is only dilute sulphuric acid used to acidify a potassium permanganate titration, and why must an oxalic acid titration be carried out hot?
Volumetric Analysis.r: HCl would itself be oxidised by permanganate (2MnO₄⁻ + 16H⁺ + 10Cl⁻ → 2Mn²⁺ + 5Cl₂ + 8H₂O), consuming extra KMnO₄ and giving a high result; HNO₃ is an oxidising agent and would oxidise the reductant in the flask. Only dilute H₂SO₄ merely supplies H⁺. The oxalate–permanganate reaction is very slow at room temperature (it is autocatalysed by the Mn²⁺ it produces), so the flask is warmed to 60–70 °C to get a sharp end point.

Ionic Equilibrium.r: Hydrolysis is the reaction of the ions of a salt with water to regenerate the parent acid or base. Na₂CO₃ is the salt of the weak acid H₂CO₃ and the strong base NaOH, so the anion hydrolyses: CO₃²⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻, releasing OH⁻ and making the solution alkaline. FeCl₃ is the salt of the strong acid HCl and the weak base Fe(OH)₃, so the cation hydrolyses: Fe³⁺ + 3H₂O ⇌ Fe(OH)₃ + 3H⁺, releasing H⁺ and making the solution acidic.

Chemical Kinetics.r: (a) Order is found by experiment and may be zero, fractional or whole; molecularity is a theoretical count of colliding molecules in one elementary step and is always a whole number (1, 2 or 3). Order refers to the overall reaction; molecularity refers to a single elementary step. (b) See the figure: a straight line sloping downwards from [A]₀, with slope -k. Chemical Kinetics.r: (a) The rate law is rate = k[P] (Q is zero order). From experiment I: k = 2 × 10⁻²/0.1 = 0.2 s⁻¹. Experiment II: 4 × 10⁻² = 0.2 × A, so A = 0.2 M. Experiment IV: 2 × 10⁻² = 0.2 × B, so B = 0.1 M. Experiment III: C = 0.2 × 0.4 = 8 × 10⁻² M s⁻¹. (b) k = 0.2 s⁻¹ (see (a)); the unit s⁻¹ shows overall first order. (c) The rate law expresses the rate as the product of the concentrations of the reactants raised to the powers m and n. m and n are found only by measuring the rate at different concentrations because the rate depends on the slow step of the mechanism, which cannot be seen in the balanced equation.

Thermodynamics.q: Define the standard heat of formation. Calculate the heat of formation of acetic acid from: C(s) + O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = -99 kcal mol⁻¹; H₂(g) + ½O₂ → H₂O(l), ΔH = -68 kcal mol⁻¹; CH₃COOH(l) + 2O₂ → 2CO₂ + 2H₂O(l), ΔH = -208 kcal mol⁻¹. [1+4]
Thermodynamics.r: The standard heat of formation is the enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states at 298 K and 1 atm. Formation reaction: 2C(s) + 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → CH₃COOH(l). The three given equations are used as follows: (i) 2C + 2O₂ → 2CO₂, ΔH = 2(-99) = -198; (ii) 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, ΔH = 2(-68) = -136; (iii) 2CO₂ + 2H₂O → CH₃COOH + 2O₂, ΔH = +208 (the combustion equation reversed). Adding (i), (ii) and (iii) gives 2C + 2H₂ + O₂ → CH₃COOH.

Thermodynamics.q: The Gibbs equation is ΔG = ΔH - TΔS.
p: Define the Gibbs free energy change.
Predict the spontaneity when ΔH and ΔS are both positive.
For a reaction ΔH = 50 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = 300 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Is it spontaneous at 15 °C?
Thermodynamics.r: (a) The Gibbs free energy change ΔG is the part of the enthalpy change that is available to do useful work at constant T and P: ΔG = ΔH - TΔS; a process is spontaneous when ΔG is negative. (b) ΔH positive makes ΔG more positive, and ΔS positive makes -TΔS negative. At low temperature the ΔH term dominates, so ΔG > 0 and the process is non-spontaneous; at high temperature the TΔS term dominates, so ΔG < 0 and the process becomes spontaneous. (Melting of ice and evaporation of water follow this pattern.) (c) T = 15 + 273 = 288 K and ΔS = 0.300 kJ mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

Which law of thermodynamics states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, but can only change from one form to another?
Thermodynamics.w: The First Law of Thermodynamics is the principle of conservation of energy.

Thermodynamics.q: Entropy is a measure of which of the following in a thermodynamic system?
Thermodynamics.w: Entropy quantifies the disorder or randomness in a system.

Thermodynamics.q: In the context of the Third Law of Thermodynamics, what happens to the entropy of a perfect crystal at absolute zero?
Thermodynamics.w: According to the Third Law, the entropy of a perfect crystal approaches zero as the temperature approaches absolute zero.

Electrochemistry.q: Four metals P, Q, R and S have standard electrode potentials -0.76 V, +0.34 V, -2.71 V and +0.80 V respectively. The correct order of decreasing reactivity is
Electrochemistry.w: the more negative the reduction potential, the more readily the metal is oxidised, so reactivity falls as E° rises: R (-2.71) > P (-0.76) > Q (+0.34) > S (+0.80). Option (a) is the same list read the wrong way round, which is the usual slip.

Electrochemistry.q: The standard electrode potentials of four elements are +0.34 V, -0.76 V, 0.00 V and -3.05 V. The order of decreasing reducing power is
Electrochemistry.w: reducing power increases as E° becomes more negative, so the most negative value heads the list.

Electrochemistry.q: When a lead storage battery is discharged,
o: the density of the acid rises
Electrochemistry.w: discharge is Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄ → 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O: sulphuric acid is consumed and its density falls, which is why the acid density is used to test the state of charge.

Electrochemistry.q: In a galvanic cell the anode is
o: positive and the site of reduction
negative and the site of oxidation
positive and the site of oxidation
negative and the site of reduction
Electrochemistry.w: in a galvanic cell electrons are pushed out of the anode, making it the negative terminal. In electrolysis the anode is connected to the positive terminal of the supply; oxidation still happens there, but the sign flips. This sign reversal is the single most-missed point in the unit.

Electrochemistry.q: If the concentration of Zn²⁺ in the Daniell cell is increased, the cell potential
Electrochemistry.w: from the Nernst equation E = 1.10 - (0.0591/2) log([Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]); raising the product-ion concentration lowers E.

Electrochemistry.q: The calomel electrode is used as
Electrochemistry.w: it is a calibrated, easily maintained electrode whose potential (+0.242 V saturated) is known relative to SHE, which is the primary standard.

Electrochemistry.q: The standard reduction potentials are E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = -0.76 V and E°(Mg²⁺/Mg) = -2.38 V.

Electrochemistry.r: (a) The standard electrode potential of an electrode is its potential when it is in contact with a 1 M solution of its ions at 25 °C (and 1 atm for gases), measured against the standard hydrogen electrode whose potential is taken as zero. (b) Mg has the more negative potential, so it is the stronger reducing agent: Mg is the anode (oxidation) and Zn the cathode (reduction).

Why is it called a reference electrode?

(b) Its potential is fixed at zero by convention, so every other electrode potential is measured relative to it. (c) Zn (more negative) is the anode and Pb the cathode.

Electrochemistry.q: The standard reduction potentials of three metals A, B and C are -0.76 V, +0.34 V and +0.80 V.
p: Give the order of reducing power of A, B and C.
Write the cell notation when B is connected to the standard hydrogen electrode.
Electrochemistry.r: (a) The standard reduction potential is the potential of a half-cell, when the reduction half-reaction takes place at it in contact with a 1 M solution of its ions at 25 °C, measured against the SHE. (b) The smaller (more negative) the E°, the stronger the reducing power: A > B > C (-0.76, +0.34, +0.80). (c) B (E° = +0.34 V) is higher than hydrogen (0.00 V), so B is reduced and the SHE is the anode:

p: Describe the lead storage battery: the anode, the cathode, the electrolyte and the reactions on discharge and on charging.
Describe the hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell, with the electrode reactions.
Why is the fuel cell used in spacecraft?
Electrochemistry.r: (a) Lead storage battery. Anode: spongy lead (Pb); cathode: lead dioxide (PbO₂) on a lead grid; electrolyte: about 38 % H₂SO₄. On discharge: Pb + SO₄²⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2e⁻ (anode); PbO₂ + 4H⁺ + SO₄²⁻ + 2e⁻ → PbSO₄ + 2H₂O (cathode). Overall: Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄ → 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O. Sulphuric acid is consumed, so its density falls. On charging (the current is reversed) the reactions are reversed: 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O → Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄. One cell gives about 2 V, so a 12 V battery has six cells in series. (b) H₂–O₂ fuel cell. Porous carbon electrodes carrying a Pt or Ni catalyst dip in hot KOH. H₂ is fed to the anode and O₂ to the cathode. Anode: 2H₂ + 4OH⁻ → 4H₂O + 4e⁻. Cathode: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻.

Electrochemistry.q: The standard electrode potential of the standard hydrogen electrode at 298 K is
Electrochemistry.w: it is the arbitrary zero of the whole scale.

Electrochemistry.q: In a galvanic cell the anode is
Electrochemistry.w: electrons are released there, so it is the negative terminal of a galvanic cell.

Electrochemistry.q: Which of these metals cannot liberate hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid?
Electrochemistry.w: copper lies below hydrogen in the electrochemical series.

Electrochemistry.q: The quantity of charge carried by one mole of electrons is about
Electrochemistry.w: one faraday, $F = N_Ae \approx 96500$ C mol⁻¹.

Electrochemistry.q: Explain with electrode reactions the working of the hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell, and state two advantages over a thermal power plant.
Electrochemistry.r: Anode: 2H₂ + 4OH⁻ → 4H₂O + 4e⁻. Cathode: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻. Overall 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, $E^{\circ}_{cell} = 1.23$ V. Advantages: much higher conversion efficiency (about 70 % against 40 %) because no heat engine is involved, and no polluting emissions — the product is pure water.

Distinguish between a galvanic cell and an electrolytic cell on any three grounds, and state Faraday's two laws of electrolysis.
Electrochemistry.r: (b) Galvanic: spontaneous, converts chemical to electrical energy, anode negative, two electrolytes joined by a salt bridge. Electrolytic: non-spontaneous, converts electrical to chemical energy, anode positive, one electrolyte. Faraday's first law: the mass liberated at an electrode is proportional to the quantity of electricity passed, $m = Zit$. Second law: with the same quantity of electricity, the masses liberated in different electrolytes are proportional to their equivalent weights.

Transition Metals.q: Transition metals are good catalysts mainly because they
o: show variable oxidation states and have partly filled d orbitals
Transition Metals.w: variable oxidation states let the metal form unstable intermediates, and partly filled d orbitals let reactants adsorb on the surface. Colour (d) is a consequence of the same d orbitals, not the cause of catalysis.

Transition Metals.q: Which ion imparts a green colour to its salts?
Transition Metals.w: Ni²⁺ is 3d⁸, partly filled, and absorbs in the red, appearing green. Zn²⁺, Sc³⁺ and Ag⁺ are all d¹⁰ or d⁰ and colourless.

Transition Metals.q: The maximum oxidation state exhibited in the 3d transition series is
Transition Metals.w: manganese, 3d⁵4s², can lose all seven outer electrons, as in KMnO₄ and Mn₂O₇.

Transition Metals.q: Which of the following ions is colourless in aqueous solution?
Transition Metals.w: Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰, with no vacancy for a d–d transition. "All transition-metal ions are coloured" is the misconception this question is built on.

Transition Metals.q: In an octahedral complex the d orbitals split into
Transition Metals.w: the three t₂g orbitals lie between the axes and are stabilised by 0.4Δo, while the two e(g) orbitals point at the ligands and are raised by 0.6Δo.

Transition Metals.q: The shape and hybridisation of [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ are
Transition Metals.w: CN⁻ is a strong-field ligand, so the 3d⁸ electrons pair up, freeing one 3d orbital for dsp² hybridisation; the ion is square planar and diamagnetic. With the weak-field Cl⁻ the same metal gives tetrahedral [NiCl₄]²⁻.

Transition Metals.q: What is a d–d electron transition? List the characteristics of transition metals. [1+4]
Transition Metals.r: A d–d transition is the excitation of an electron from a lower-energy d-orbital to a higher-energy d-orbital of the same metal ion (for an octahedral complex, from t₂g to e_g) when the ion absorbs a photon of visible light of energy equal to the crystal-field splitting Δo. The complementary colour is transmitted, so the compound is coloured. Characteristics of transition metals: 1. Variable oxidation states, because the (n-1)d and ns electrons have similar energy (Mn shows +2 to +7). 2. Coloured compounds, from d–d transitions in ions with a partly filled d subshell. 3. Complex formation, because the ions are small, highly charged and have vacant d-orbitals ([Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺, [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻). 4.

p: State the assumptions of crystal field theory.
Draw the diagram showing the splitting of the d-orbitals in an octahedral complex.
Transition Metals.r: (a) Assumptions of crystal field theory: 1. The ligands are treated as point negative charges (or dipoles), and the bond between metal and ligand is purely electrostatic. 2. In the free ion the five d-orbitals have the same energy; the approaching ligands repel the d electrons, and the orbitals split into sets of different energy according to their orientation relative to the ligands. 3. The difference in energy, the crystal field splitting Δ, depends on the ligand and on the geometry, and electrons fill the split orbitals according to Δ and the pairing energy.

p: Why does an octahedral complex of Cu²⁺ become distorted according to crystal field theory?
Which is more stable, Fe³⁺ or Fe²⁺, and why?
Why are transition metals good catalysts?
Transition Metals.r: (a) Cu²⁺ is d⁹: the t₂g set is full and the e_g set holds three electrons, with unequal occupancy of d_z² and d_x²-y². Unequal repulsion on the ligands along z and in the xy plane makes the complex elongate along the z-axis (Jahn–Teller distortion), which lowers the total energy. (b) In [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ the d–d transition absorbs light in the red-orange region, so the transmitted (complementary) colour is blue. (c) Fe³⁺ (d⁵) is more stable than Fe²⁺ (d⁶) because a half-filled d subshell gives extra exchange energy and symmetry. (d) They have variable oxidation states and vacant d-orbitals, so they form intermediate compounds with reactants and offer a surface for adsorption.

p: Write the electronic configurations of Cr and Cu and explain why they are exceptions.
Why is zinc not regarded as a transition element?
Why are Sc³⁺ and Zn²⁺ colourless?
How many d electrons has Cr in [Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺?
Transition Metals.r: (a) Cr: [Ar] 3d⁵4s¹ (not 3d⁴4s²) and Cu: [Ar] 3d¹⁰4s¹ (not 3d⁹4s²). A half-filled (d⁵) or fully filled (d¹⁰) subshell has extra stability from symmetry and exchange energy, so one 4s electron moves into the 3d subshell. (b) Zn is [Ar] 3d¹⁰4s² and forms only Zn²⁺ (3d¹⁰): its d subshell is full in both the atom and its common ion, so it does not meet the definition of a transition element (an ion with a partly filled d subshell). (c) Sc³⁺ is 3d⁰ and Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰, so there is no partly filled d subshell and no d–d transition is possible. (d) Cr³⁺ is [Ar] 3d³: three d electrons.

p: Define a transition element and write the general electronic configuration.
Explain the variable oxidation states of manganese with one compound for each state.
Explain why [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ is coloured while Sc³⁺ compounds are not.
Give two examples of catalysis by transition metals with the catalyst and reaction.
Transition Metals.r: (a) A transition element is one that has a partly filled d subshell in its atom or in any of its common ions. General configuration: (n-1)d¹⁻¹⁰ ns¹⁻² (in the 3d series, [Ar] 3d¹⁻¹⁰ 4s¹⁻²). (b) Manganese ([Ar] 3d⁵4s²) uses its 4s and 3d electrons and shows every state from +2 to +7: +2 in MnSO₄, +3 in Mn₂O₃, +4 in MnO₂, +6 in K₂MnO₄ and +7 in KMnO₄. The 4s and 3d energies are close, so successive electrons can be removed with small increases in ionisation energy; the highest state +7 equals the number of 3d + 4s electrons.

Transition Metals.q: Which of the following is not regarded as a typical transition element?
Transition Metals.w: zinc has a complete 3d¹⁰ subshell in both the atom and the Zn²⁺ ion.

Transition Metals.q: The highest oxidation state shown by manganese is
Transition Metals.w: all five 3d and both 4s electrons are used, as in MnO₄⁻.
Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰, so no d–d transition is possible.

Transition Metals.q: The oxidation state of iron in K₃[Fe(CN)₆] is
Define a transition element. State any five characteristic properties of transition metals and explain why they show variable oxidation states.
Why are most transition metal compounds coloured? Explain why Sc³⁺ and Zn²⁺ are colourless, and why the colour of MnO₄⁻ has a different origin.
Define ligand, coordination number and effective atomic number. Calculate the EAN of the metal in [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺ and [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻. ($Z$: Cu = 29, Fe = 26)
Transition Metals.r: A ligand is a molecule or ion with at least one lone pair that it donates to a central metal ion to form a coordinate bond. The coordination number is the number of such bonds. The EAN is $Z - (\text{oxidation state}) + 2(\text{CN})$.

Transition Metals.q: Distinguish between a double salt and a complex salt, using Mohr's salt and potassium ferrocyanide as examples.
State the postulates of crystal field theory. Draw the splitting of the d orbitals in an octahedral field and calculate the spin-only magnetic moment of [Mn(H₂O)₆]²⁺.
Transition Metals.r: Mn²⁺ is 3d⁵. Water is a weak-field ligand, so the complex is high spin, $t_{2g}^{3}e_{g}^{2}$, with $n = 5$ unpaired electrons:

Transition Metals.q: Why do transition metals and their compounds act as good catalysts? Give any four industrial catalysts with the process in which each is used.

p: Discuss the variation of oxidation states across the 3d series and explain why the +2 state becomes increasingly stable towards the right-hand end.
Give the hybridisation, shape and coordination number of [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺, [NiCl₄]²⁻, [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ and [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺.
State the postulates of crystal field theory. Explain the splitting of the d orbitals in octahedral and in tetrahedral fields, and state the relation between $\Delta_{t}$ and $\Delta_{o}$.
[Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺ has four unpaired electrons whereas [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ has none, although both contain Fe(II). Explain, and calculate the CFSE of each.
Transition Metals.r: (b) Fe²⁺ is 3d⁶ in both. H₂O is a weak-field ligand, so $\Delta_{o} < P$ and the electrons spread out over all five orbitals, $t_{2g}^{4}e_{g}^{2}$, leaving four unpaired: high spin, and $\text{CFSE} = [-0.4(4) + 0.6(2)]\Delta_{o} = -0.4\Delta_{o}$.

Transition Metals.q: Explain the characteristic properties of the transition metals, giving eight points, and account for their magnetic properties.

Studies of Heavy Metals.q: The Bessemer converter is used in the extraction of copper for
o: converting copper matte into blister copper
Studies of Heavy Metals.w: hot air blown through molten matte oxidises FeS to slag and then Cu₂S to blister copper: 2Cu₂S + 3O₂ → 2Cu₂O + 2SO₂, then 2Cu₂O + Cu₂S → 6Cu + SO₂.

Studies of Heavy Metals.q: The chief ore of copper is
Studies of Heavy Metals.w: CuFeS₂ supplies most of the world's copper; the others are minor ores.

Studies of Heavy Metals.q: Blue vitriol heated to 230 °C gives
Studies of Heavy Metals.w: all five water molecules are lost by 230 °C, leaving white anhydrous CuSO₄. Black CuO needs about 720 °C.

Studies of Heavy Metals.q: The red oxide of copper is
Studies of Heavy Metals.w: cuprous oxide is red; cupric oxide CuO is black.

Studies of Heavy Metals.q: Philosopher's wool is
Studies of Heavy Metals.w: zinc oxide, which sublimes as a woolly white mass; it is yellow while hot and white on cooling.

Studies of Heavy Metals.q: Zinc dissolves in hot concentrated NaOH giving
Studies of Heavy Metals.w: Zn + 2NaOH → Na₂ZnO₂ + H₂↑; zinc reacts with both acids and alkalis because it is amphoteric.

Studies of Heavy Metals.q: Cinnabar is the ore of
Studies of Heavy Metals.w: HgS, bright red, roasted in air to give the metal directly.

Studies of Heavy Metals.q: Which pair is correctly described?
Studies of Heavy Metals.w: calomel Hg₂Cl₂ is insoluble and harmless enough to have been used medicinally, while the soluble HgCl₂ is a violent poison. Solubility is what makes the difference.

Studies of Heavy Metals.q: Corrosive sublimate with a limited amount of SnCl₂ gives a
Studies of Heavy Metals.w: limited SnCl₂ reduces Hg(II) only as far as Hg(I), giving white Hg₂Cl₂; excess reduces it to grey metallic mercury.

Studies of Heavy Metals.q: The chief ore of iron is
Studies of Heavy Metals.w: haematite Fe₂O₃ contains about 70 % iron and is the main commercial source.

Studies of Heavy Metals.q: The slag formed in the blast furnace is
Studies of Heavy Metals.w: limestone decomposes to CaO, which takes up the silica gangue: CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃.

Studies of Heavy Metals.q: Iron becomes passive with concentrated HNO₃ because
Studies of Heavy Metals.w: the acid oxidises the surface to a thin, coherent film of Fe₃O₄ which seals the metal; this is why conc. HNO₃ can be carried in iron containers.

Studies of Heavy Metals.q: The carbon content of wrought iron is about
Studies of Heavy Metals.w: wrought iron is the purest commercial form, under 0.25 % carbon; cast iron holds about 4 %.

Studies of Heavy Metals.q: Iron is protected from rusting by coating it with zinc because zinc
o: is more electropositive and corrodes first
Studies of Heavy Metals.w: zinc has the more negative electrode potential, so it is oxidised in preference to iron; the protection continues even where the coating is scratched.

Studies of Heavy Metals.q: An ammonia solution is added to the sulphate of a coinage metal A. The blue precipitate B that forms dissolves in excess of the reagent to give a deep blue solution C.
p: Identify A, B and C with the reactions.
Write the electronic configuration of A.
Name a method for the purification of A.
Studies of Heavy Metals.r: (a) A = copper (Cu), in the sulphate CuSO₄. With a little NH₄OH a blue precipitate B = Cu(OH)₂ forms; excess ammonia dissolves it to the deep blue C = tetraamminecopper(II) sulphate, [Cu(NH₃)₄]SO₄. CuSO₄ + 2NH₄OH → Cu(OH)₂↓ + (NH₄)₂SO₄ Cu(OH)₂ + (NH₄)₂SO₄ + 2NH₄OH → [Cu(NH₃)₄]SO₄ + 4H₂O (b) Cu: [Ar] 3d¹⁰4s¹. (c) Electrolytic refining (after poling): impure copper is the anode, pure copper the cathode, and acidified CuSO₄ is the electrolyte; 99.95 % pure copper deposits.

Studies of Heavy Metals.q: A coinage metal M of group IB has the configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰4s¹.
p: Draw the blast furnace used for smelting its chief ore.
Explain the reactions that form the matte in the furnace.
Studies of Heavy Metals.r: (a) See the figure: the chief ore is copper pyrite, CuFeS₂, and the roasted ore is smelted with coke and silica in a small water-jacketed blast furnace. (b) The reactions that occur in the furnace: FeO + SiO₂ → FeSiO₃ (slag; silica is the flux that removes iron as a fusible silicate) Cu₂O + FeS → Cu₂S + FeO The FeO formed in the second reaction is slagged by silica. The molten matte (Cu₂S + FeS, about 45 % Cu) sinks below the lighter slag and is tapped off for the Bessemer converter. Matte forms because copper has a greater affinity for sulphur than iron has, so the sulphur stays with copper and the iron passes into the slag as FeSiO₃.

Studies of Heavy Metals.q: Write the preparation, properties and uses of corrosive sublimate. [1+3+1]
Studies of Heavy Metals.r: Preparation: (i) directly, by heating mercury in excess chlorine, Hg + Cl₂ → HgCl₂; (ii) industrially, by heating mercury(II) sulphate with sodium chloride and subliming the product, HgSO₄ + 2NaCl → HgCl₂↑ + Na₂SO₄ (a little MnO₂ is added to oxidise any mercurous salt). Properties: white crystalline, poisonous, sublimes on heating, sparingly soluble in water and largely un-ionised (covalent). Reactions: (i) with KI, a scarlet precipitate that dissolves in excess KI: HgCl₂ + 2KI → HgI₂↓ + 2KCl; HgI₂ + 2KI → K₂[HgI₄]; (ii) with SnCl₂, a white precipitate that turns grey: 2HgCl₂ + SnCl₂ → Hg₂Cl₂↓ + SnCl₄, then Hg₂Cl₂ + SnCl₂ → 2Hg + SnCl₄;

Studies of Heavy Metals.q: The metal M, [Ar] 3d¹⁰4s², is called "Jasta".
p: Identify M and its main ore.
Why is M not regarded as a transition element?
Draw the vertical retort and write the reduction reaction.
What happens to M when it is exposed to air for a long time?

Studies of Heavy Metals.q: What is rusting? Describe the electrochemical theory of the rusting of iron and give two methods of preventing it. [1+3+1]
Describe the extraction of copper from copper pyrite, giving the reactions of each stage: concentration, roasting, smelting, Bessemerisation and refining.
Studies of Heavy Metals.r: Ore: copper pyrite, CuFeS₂ (2–3 % Cu). 1. Concentration by froth flotation. The powdered ore is agitated with water, pine oil and sodium ethyl xanthate while air is blown through; the sulphide particles are wetted by oil and rise in the froth, the earthy gangue sinks. 2. Roasting in a reverberatory furnace in a limited supply of air at about 1070 K, which drives off moisture, As and Sb as oxides, and burns part of the sulphur: 2CuFeS₂ + O₂ → Cu₂S + 2FeS + SO₂; 2FeS + 3O₂ → 2FeO + 2SO₂; 2Cu₂S + 3O₂ → 2Cu₂O + 2SO₂. 3. Smelting of the roasted ore with coke and silica in a water-jacketed blast furnace: FeO + SiO₂ → FeSiO₃ (slag), Cu₂O + FeS → Cu₂S + FeO.

Studies of Heavy Metals.q: Describe the extraction of silver from argentite by the cyanide process. Write the reactions, explain why air is blown through the solution and how silver is refined.
Studies of Heavy Metals.r: Ore: argentite (silver glance), Ag₂S. 1. Concentration by froth flotation. 2. Leaching. The concentrate is agitated with a dilute (0.1–0.5 %) NaCN solution while air is blown through: Ag₂S + 4NaCN ⇌ 2Na[Ag(CN)₂] + Na₂S The reaction is reversible. The air oxidises the sodium sulphide as it forms, 2Na₂S + 2O₂ + H₂O → Na₂S₂O₃ + 2NaOH, which removes a product and drives the equilibrium to the right (Le Chatelier's principle). The silver dissolves as sodium dicyanoargentate(I). 3. Precipitation. Zinc dust displaces silver because zinc is more electropositive: 2Na[Ag(CN)₂] + Zn → Na₂[Zn(CN)₄] + 2Ag↓ 4.

Studies of Heavy Metals.q: Describe the extraction of copper from copper pyrite up to the stage of blister copper. Give balanced equations for roasting, smelting and bessemerisation, and state the role of silica.
How is zinc extracted from zinc blende? Why must the ore be roasted before reduction, and why is the zinc obtained as a vapour?
Studies of Heavy Metals.r: Concentration by froth flotation; roasting 2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂; reduction ZnO + C → Zn + CO at 1673 K in fireclay retorts; refining by liquation, distillation or electrolysis. Carbon has no affinity for sulphur and cannot reduce ZnS, so the sulphide must first become the oxide. Zinc boils at 907 °C, well below the 1400 °C of the retort, so it leaves as vapour and is condensed out of contact with air — otherwise it would re-oxidise to ZnO.

Studies of Heavy Metals.q: What happens when
p: copper is left in moist air containing CO₂,
copper is warmed with aqueous ammonia in the presence of air,
copper is added to iron(III) chloride solution? Give equations.

Studies of Heavy Metals.q: Explain, with equations, the action of heat on blue vitriol. Why is the formula of the pentahydrate better written [Cu(H₂O)₄]SO₄·H₂O?
Distinguish between calomel and corrosive sublimate under four headings, and give one chemical test that separates them.
Explain the electrochemical theory of rusting. Why does a scratched galvanised sheet still resist rust while a scratched tinned can does not?
Studies of Heavy Metals.r: A water film containing dissolved O₂ and CO₂ makes the iron surface a galvanic cell. Oxygen-poor areas are anodic, 2Fe → 2Fe²⁺ + 4e⁻; oxygen-rich areas are cathodic, O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O. The Fe²⁺ is oxidised further, 4Fe²⁺ + O₂ + 4H₂O → 2Fe₂O₃ + 8H⁺, and the oxide hydrates to rust Fe₂O₃·xH₂O. Zinc (E° = -0.76 V) is more electropositive than iron (-0.44 V), so at a scratch the zinc becomes the anode and corrodes instead of the iron — sacrificial protection. Tin (-0.14 V) is less electropositive than iron, so at a scratch the iron becomes the anode of a small cell and corrodes faster than it would on its own.

p: Describe the manufacture of steel by the Basic Oxygen Process, with the equations for the removal of carbon, silicon and phosphorus, and state the function of the lime.
Compare the Basic Oxygen Process with the Open Hearth Process under three headings.
Studies of Heavy Metals.r: (b) Oxidant: pure O₂ blown in, versus haematite added to the charge. Time: 20–40 minutes, versus 8–10 hours. Control: limited, versus excellent — the open hearth can be sampled and corrected, so it is preferred for alloy and tool steels.

p: Describe the extraction of silver from argentite by the cyanide process, with equations, and explain why air is blown through the leach solution.
How is silver chloride prepared? Give its action with aqueous ammonia, with sodium thiosulphate and with light.
Studies of Heavy Metals.r: (b) AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl↓ + NaNO₃, a white curdy precipitate. With ammonia it dissolves: AgCl + 2NH₃ → [Ag(NH₃)₂]Cl. With hypo it dissolves: AgCl + 2Na₂S₂O₃ → Na₃[Ag(S₂O₃)₂] + NaCl (photographic fixing). In light it darkens: 2AgCl → 2Ag + Cl₂.

Studies of Heavy Metals.q: An ore contains 25.0% copper pyrite by mass. Calculate
p: the percentage of copper in pure CuFeS₂,
the mass of copper in 2.00 tonnes of the ore, and
the mass of blister copper (98% pure) that this would give at 85% recovery. (Cu = 63.5, Fe = 56, S = 32)

Studies of Heavy Metals.q: Describe the extraction of iron from haematite in the blast furnace with the reactions in each zone, and compare the three forms of iron.

Haloalkanes.q: Trichloromethane reduced in a neutral medium gives
Haloalkanes.w: reduction removes one chlorine: CHCl₃ + 2[H] → CH₂Cl₂ + HCl. Option (d) is the oxidation product formed in air.

Haloalkanes.q: Which haloalkane undergoes an SN1 reaction most readily?
Haloalkanes.w: SN1 goes through a carbocation, and the tertiary cation is the most stable, so the rate order follows carbocation stability.

Haloalkanes.q: Which substrate reacts fastest by the SN2 mechanism?
Haloalkanes.w: SN2 needs the nucleophile to attack the back of the carbon; the less crowded that carbon is, the faster the reaction. The SN1 and SN2 orders are exact opposites, which is precisely what the examiner is testing.

Haloalkanes.q: Iodoethane warmed with alcoholic KCN gives
Haloalkanes.w: the cyanide ion of KCN, an ionic salt, attacks through carbon, giving the nitrile CH₃CH₂CN, which is propanenitrile.

Haloalkanes.q: Bromoethane heated with AgNO₂ gives mainly
Haloalkanes.w: AgNO₂ is largely covalent, so the nitrite attacks through nitrogen giving the nitroalkane; ionic KNO₂ would have given the nitrite ester.

Haloalkanes.q: The Wurtz reaction of chloroethane with sodium in dry ether gives
Haloalkanes.w: two ethyl groups join, so the product has 2 × 2 = 4 carbons.

Haloalkanes.q: Trichloromethane treated with concentrated nitric acid gives
Haloalkanes.w: CHCl₃ + HNO₃ → CCl₃NO₂ + H₂O; chloropicrin is a tear gas.

Haloalkanes.q: Trichloromethane heated with silver powder gives
Haloalkanes.w: two molecules lose six chlorines to the silver, joining as 2CHCl₃ + 6Ag → C₂H₂ + 6AgCl.

Haloalkanes.q: Trichloromethane is stored in dark bottles filled to the brim because in air and light it forms
Haloalkanes.w: slow photo-oxidation gives carbonyl chloride; the ethanol added destroys any phosgene formed and the full bottle excludes air.

Haloalkanes.q: The reagent that converts an alcohol into a haloalkane with gaseous by-products only is
Haloalkanes.w: thionyl chloride gives SO₂ and HCl, both gases, so the haloalkane is left pure; this is Darzen's process.

Haloalkanes.q: The correct order of reactivity of haloalkanes towards nucleophilic substitution is
Haloalkanes.w: the C–I bond is the weakest and breaks most easily; C–F is the strongest.

Haloalkanes.q: Hydrolysis of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane proceeds through
Haloalkanes.w: a tertiary substrate ionises to a planar carbocation which is attacked equally from both faces.

Haloalkanes.q: A chemical reaction occurs as CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + KOH(aq) → B + KBr.
p: Which substitution mechanism occurs, and why?
What is formed if alcoholic KOH is used instead of aqueous KOH?
How can nitropropane be obtained from the haloalkane?
Haloalkanes.r: (a) B = propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH. (b) SN2. 1-Bromopropane is a primary halide with little steric hindrance, and OH⁻ is a strong nucleophile, so it attacks the carbon from the back in a single step with inversion and no carbocation forms (a primary carbocation is unstable). (c) Alcoholic KOH gives elimination (dehydrohalogenation): CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + KOH(alc.) → CH₃CH=CH₂ + KBr + H₂O, that is propene. (d) By heating with silver nitrite: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + AgNO₂ → CH₃CH₂CH₂NO₂ + AgBr, giving 1-nitropropane.

p: Differentiate between SN1 and SN2 reactions.
State Saytzeff's rule with an example.

Haloalkanes.q: The vapour of an organic compound A causes loss of consciousness and forms a component of tear gas when heated with conc. HNO₃.
p: Prepare A from an isomer of C₂H₆O.
What happens when A is (i) exposed to air, (ii) heated with silver powder, (iii) condensed with acetone, (iv) heated with aniline in the presence of alcoholic KOH?
Give reasons: ether is stored in a bottle containing iron wire; ethanol, though organic, is soluble in water.
Haloalkanes.r: A is chloroform, CHCl₃ (anaesthetic vapour; conc. HNO₃ gives chloropicrin, the tear-gas component). (a) The isomer is ethanol (the other isomer, methoxymethane, cannot be used). CaOCl₂ + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + Cl₂; CH₃CH₂OH + Cl₂ → CH₃CHO + 2HCl; CH₃CHO + 3Cl₂ → CCl₃CHO + 3HCl; 2CCl₃CHO + Ca(OH)₂ → 2CHCl₃ + (HCOO)₂Ca. (b) (i) In air and light chloroform is oxidised to the poisonous phosgene: 2CHCl₃ + O₂ → 2COCl₂ + 2HCl. (ii) With silver powder it gives ethyne: 2CHCl₃ + 6Ag → HC≡CH + 6AgCl. (iii) With acetone in the presence of a base it gives chloretone, a hypnotic: (CH₃)₂CO + CHCl₃ → (CH₃)₂C(OH)CCl₃.

Haloalkanes.q: An unsaturated hydrocarbon C₃H₆ adds HBr according to Markovnikov's rule to give A. A on hydrolysis with aqueous alkali gives B. B with PBr₃ gives C. C reacts with AgCN (alcoholic) to give D, which on reduction with LiAlH₄ gives E.
p: Identify A, B, C, D and E with the reactions.
How does E react with nitrous acid?
Haloalkanes.r: (a) Markovnikov's rule: when an unsymmetrical reagent HX adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the hydrogen adds to the carbon that already carries more hydrogens and the halogen to the carbon with fewer hydrogens. (b) CH₃CH=CH₂ + HBr → A = 2-bromopropane, CH₃CHBrCH₃. A + aq. KOH → B = propan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃. B + PBr₃ → C = 2-bromopropane, CH₃CHBrCH₃ (3CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ + PBr₃ → 3CH₃CHBrCH₃ + H₃PO₃). C + AgCN(alc.) → D = isopropyl isocyanide (2-isocyanopropane), (CH₃)₂CH–NC + AgBr: silver cyanide is covalent, so the attack is through nitrogen. D + LiAlH₄ (or H₂/Ni) → E = N-methylpropan-2-amine, (CH₃)₂CH–NH–CH₃. (c) E is a secondary amine;

Haloalkanes.q: The number of structural isomers of C₄H₉Br is
Which haloalkane is most reactive towards nucleophilic substitution?
Haloalkanes.w: the C–I bond is the weakest (234 kJ mol⁻¹), so iodide is the best leaving group.

Haloalkanes.q: Define a haloalkane. Write the structures, IUPAC names and classification (1°, 2°, 3°) of all the isomers of C₄H₉Br, and state which one is optically active.
How is bromoethane prepared from
p: ethanol? Why is thionyl chloride the best reagent for making chloroethane from ethanol?
Haloalkanes.r: (a) Ethene + HBr → CH₃CH₂Br; the addition needs no peroxide because ethene is symmetrical, so Markovnikov's rule does not arise. (b) Ethanol is warmed with NaBr and conc. H₂SO₄, which generates HBr in the flask: C₂H₅OH + HBr → C₂H₅Br + H₂O. Thionyl chloride is best for the chloride because C₂H₅OH + SOCl₂ → C₂H₅Cl + SO₂↑ + HCl↑ — both by-products are gases and escape, so the haloalkane is obtained pure with no separation step.

Haloalkanes.q: State Saytzeff's rule. Predict and explain the major product when 2-bromobutane is heated with alcoholic KOH.
Haloalkanes.r: Saytzeff's rule: in a dehydrohalogenation the alkene with the greater number of alkyl groups on the doubly bonded carbons is the major product, because alkyl groups release electrons into the double bond (hyperconjugation and inductive effect) and stabilise it. 2-Bromobutane can lose a β-hydrogen from C1 or C3. Loss from C3 gives but-2-ene, CH₃CH=CHCH₃, which is disubstituted; loss from C1 gives but-1-ene, CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃, which is monosubstituted. But-2-ene is therefore the major product (about 80%).

Haloalkanes.q: How is chloroform prepared from propanone? Why is this route preferred to the one starting from ethanol?
Haloalkanes.r: Bleaching powder in water gives Ca(OH)₂ and Cl₂. Then CH₃COCH₃ + 3Cl₂ → CCl₃COCH₃ + 3HCl, and 2CCl₃COCH₃ + Ca(OH)₂ → 2CHCl₃ + (CH₃COO)₂Ca. Propanone is preferred because it already contains the carbonyl group, so the oxidation step needed with ethanol is unnecessary: two steps instead of three, and a higher yield.

p: How is trichloromethane prepared from ethanol? Give all three equations.
What happens when chloroform is treated with (i) air and sunlight, (ii) silver powder, (iii) conc. HNO₃, (iv) aqueous NaOH? Give equations.
Haloalkanes.r: (b) (i) 2CHCl₃ + O₂ → 2COCl₂ + 2HCl (phosgene). (ii) 2CHCl₃ + 6Ag → C₂H₂ + 6AgCl (ethyne). (iii) CHCl₃ + HNO₃ → CCl₃NO₂ + H₂O (chloropicrin). (iv) CHCl₃ + 4NaOH → HCOONa + 3NaCl + 2H₂O (sodium methanoate).

Haloalkanes.q: An organic compound A, C₃H₇Br, reacts with aqueous KOH to give B, and with alcoholic KOH to give C, C₃H₆. A with KCN gives D, and A with sodium in dry ether gives E, C₆H₁₄. Identify A to E, write all the equations, and state the mechanism by which A reacts with aqueous KOH if A is the 2-bromo isomer.
Haloalkanes.r: A = C₃H₇Br (1-bromopropane or 2-bromopropane). B = propan-1-ol or propan-2-ol, C₃H₇OH: C₃H₇Br + KOH(aq) → C₃H₇OH + KBr. C = propene, CH₃CH=CH₂: C₃H₇Br + KOH(alc.) → CH₃CH=CH₂ + KBr + H₂O. D = butanenitrile (or 2-methylpropanenitrile), C₃H₇CN: C₃H₇Br + KCN → C₃H₇CN + KBr. E = hexane, C₆H₁₄, by the Wurtz reaction: 2C₃H₇Br + 2Na → C₆H₁₄ + 2NaBr.

Haloarenes.q: Which compound reacts with chlorobenzene in the presence of concentrated H₂SO₄ to form DDT?
Haloarenes.w: chloral, CCl₃CHO (trichloroethanal), condenses with two molecules of chlorobenzene.

Haloarenes.q: Chlorobenzene is less reactive than chloroethane towards nucleophiles because
o: the C–Cl bond has partial double-bond character
Haloarenes.w: the lone pair on chlorine is delocalised into the ring, shortening and strengthening the C–Cl bond; the sp² carbon also holds the halogen more tightly.

Haloarenes.q: Benzenediazonium chloride warmed with CuCl and HCl gives chlorobenzene. The reaction is called
Haloarenes.w: copper(I) chloride is the Sandmeyer reagent; copper powder alone would make it the Gattermann reaction.

Haloarenes.q: Chlorobenzene heated with sodium in dry ether gives
Haloarenes.w: two rings couple in the Fittig reaction.

Haloarenes.q: Chlorobenzene is converted to phenol by NaOH at
Haloarenes.w: the Dow process needs severe conditions precisely because the C–Cl bond is so unreactive.

Haloarenes.q: An aromatic compound A contains one chlorine on the ring. A reacts with trichloroethanal in the presence of conc. H₂SO₄ to give an insecticide B, and A reacts with ethanoyl chloride in the presence of anhydrous AlCl₃ to give C.
p: Why does aqueous NaOH react less readily with A than with chloroethane?
Haloarenes.r: A is chlorobenzene, C₆H₅Cl. (a) C₆H₅N₂Cl + CuCl/HCl → C₆H₅Cl + N₂ (Sandmeyer reaction); Cu powder and HCl give the same product (Gattermann reaction). (b) B = DDT, 2C₆H₅Cl + CCl₃CHO → (conc. H₂SO₄) (ClC₆H₄)₂CH–CCl₃ + H₂O (1,1,1-trichloro-2,2-bis(4-chlorophenyl)ethane). C = 4-chloroacetophenone, ClC₆H₄COCH₃ (Friedel–Crafts acylation; the para isomer is the major product). (c) In chlorobenzene the carbon–chlorine bond is shorter and stronger than in chloroethane: the carbon is sp² hybridised, and the lone pair on chlorine is delocalised into the ring by resonance, giving the C–Cl bond partial double-bond character.

Haloarenes.q: How will you carry out the following conversions?
Haloarenes.r: (a) Phenol → benzene → chlorobenzene → DDT. C₆H₅OH + Zn → C₆H₆ + ZnO (distil with zinc dust) C₆H₆ + Cl₂ → (anhyd. FeCl₃) C₆H₅Cl + HCl 2C₆H₅Cl + CCl₃CHO → (conc. H₂SO₄) DDT + H₂O (b) Aniline → diazonium salt → chlorobenzene (Sandmeyer): C₆H₅NH₂ + NaNO₂ + 2HCl → (273–278 K) C₆H₅N₂Cl + NaCl + 2H₂O; C₆H₅N₂Cl + CuCl → C₆H₅Cl + N₂.

p: Explain why chlorobenzene is less reactive than chloroethane towards nucleophilic substitution.
How is chlorobenzene prepared from benzene and from benzenediazonium chloride?
Write the reaction by which DDT is made and give one use and one harmful effect of DDT.
Haloarenes.r: (a) The lower reactivity of chlorobenzene has three causes. (i) Resonance: the lone pair of chlorine is delocalised into the benzene ring, so the C–Cl bond has partial double-bond character and is stronger and shorter (about 169 pm against 177 pm in chloroethane). (ii) Hybridisation: the carbon bearing chlorine is sp² (more electronegative, holding the bond electrons closer) and not sp³. (iii) The electron-rich π cloud repels an incoming nucleophile, and the phenyl cation needed for SN1 is unstable, while backside attack for SN2 is blocked by the ring. (b) From benzene: C₆H₆ + Cl₂ → (anhydrous FeCl₃, dark) C₆H₅Cl + HCl.

Haloarenes.q: The C–Cl bond length is shortest in
Haloarenes.w: resonance gives the ring C–Cl bond partial double-bond character, so it is shortest (169 pm).
