Haloarenes.q: Chlorobenzene is treated with sodium metal in dry ether. The product is
Haloarenes.w: this is the Fittig reaction, 2C₆H₅Cl + 2Na → C₆H₅–C₆H₅ + 2NaCl.
the –I effect deactivates the ring, while the +R effect places electron density at the ortho and para carbons.

Haloarenes.q: DDT is prepared by treating chlorobenzene with
The dipole moment of chlorobenzene (1.69 D) is less than that of chloromethane (1.86 D) mainly because
o: the C–Cl bond is longer in chlorobenzene
the lone pair on Cl is delocalised into the ring and the carbon is sp²
Haloarenes.w: delocalisation opposes the inductive pull and the sp² carbon holds its electrons more tightly.

Haloarenes.q: Explain, with resonance structures, why chlorobenzene does not react with aqueous NaOH at room temperature while chloroethane does.
How is chlorobenzene prepared from aniline? Give all equations and conditions.
Haloarenes.r: Diazotise, then apply the Sandmeyer reaction. C₆H₅NH₂ + NaNO₂ + 2HCl --(273–278 K)--> C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + NaCl + 2H₂O C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ --(CuCl / conc. HCl, warm)--> C₆H₅Cl + N₂↑ The temperature must be held at 273–278 K (an ice–salt bath) or the diazonium salt decomposes to phenol. The Gattermann variant, using copper powder and concentrated HCl, gives the same product in slightly lower yield.

Haloarenes.q: Distinguish between the Fittig and the Wurtz–Fittig reaction with balanced equations. Why must the ether be perfectly dry?
Haloarenes.r: Fittig couples two aryl halides: 2C₆H₅Cl + 2Na --(dry ether)--> C₆H₅–C₆H₅ + 2NaCl Wurtz–Fittig couples an aryl halide with an alkyl halide: C₆H₅Cl + 2Na + CH₃Cl --(dry ether)--> C₆H₅CH₃ + 2NaCl The ether must be perfectly dry because sodium reacts violently with water, and the organosodium intermediate (C₆H₅Na) is instantly destroyed by moisture, giving benzene instead of the coupled product.

p: Give two methods of preparing chlorobenzene, with equations and conditions.
Explain fully why haloarenes are far less reactive than haloalkanes towards nucleophiles.
State the conditions under which chlorobenzene can be converted to phenol, and name the process.

Write balanced equations, with reagents and conditions, for the reaction of chlorobenzene with: sodium in dry ether; a mixture of sodium and chloromethane in dry ether; chloral in conc. H₂SO₄; nickel–aluminium alloy in NaOH.
Draw the structure of DDT and give its systematic name.
22.5 g of chlorobenzene reacts completely with excess chloral. Calculate the mass of DDT formed. (DDT = 354.5 g mol⁻¹)
Haloarenes.r: (a) 2C₆H₅Cl + 2Na --(dry ether)--> C₆H₅–C₆H₅ + 2NaCl (Fittig); C₆H₅Cl + 2Na + CH₃Cl --(dry ether)--> C₆H₅CH₃ + 2NaCl (Wurtz–Fittig); CCl₃CHO + 2C₆H₅Cl --(conc. H₂SO₄)--> (4-ClC₆H₄)₂CH–CCl₃ + H₂O; C₆H₅Cl + 2[H] --(Ni–Al/NaOH)--> C₆H₆ + HCl. (b) Two 4-chlorophenyl rings joined to one carbon that also carries a hydrogen atom and a –CCl₃ group; 1,1,1-trichloro-2,2-bis(4-chlorophenyl)ethane. (c) Moles of C₆H₅Cl = 22.5 / 112.5 = 0.200 mol; two moles of chlorobenzene give one mole of DDT, so moles of DDT = 0.100 mol and mass = 0.100 × 354.5 = 35.45 g.

Haloarenes.q: Explain why chlorobenzene is much less reactive than a haloalkane towards nucleophilic substitution, and describe its Fittig, Wurtz–Fittig and electrophilic substitution reactions.
Which of the following is the correct definition of haloarenes?
o: Compounds containing an aromatic ring bonded directly to a halogen atom.
Compounds where halogen atoms are attached to aliphatic chains.
Organic compounds that contain sulfur instead of halogens attached to an aromatic ring.
Inorganic compounds containing halogens and aromatic rings.
Haloarenes.w: Haloarenes specifically refer to compounds with halogen atoms directly bonded to an aromatic ring.

Alcohols.q: In Victor Meyer's test a tertiary alcohol gives a solution that is
Alcohols.w: the tertiary nitroalkane has no α-hydrogen, so it cannot form the nitrolic acid or pseudonitrole that give the colours.

Alcohols.q: In the Lucas test, immediate turbidity at room temperature indicates
Alcohols.w: tertiary alcohols form the most stable carbocation and react at once; primary alcohols need heating.

Alcohols.q: Absolute alcohol is obtained from rectified spirit by distilling it with
Alcohols.w: CaO takes up the last 4.4 % of water chemically, which simple distillation cannot remove because the mixture is an azeotrope.

Alcohols.q: Rectified spirit contains ethanol to the extent of
Alcohols.w: 95.6 % by mass, the constant-boiling mixture with water.

Alcohols.q: Power alcohol is
Alcohols.w: a petrol–ethanol blend used as a motor fuel.

Alcohols.q: Ethanol heated with concentrated H₂SO₄ at 413 K gives
Alcohols.w: the lower temperature favours intermolecular dehydration to the ether; 443 K gives the alkene.

Alcohols.q: Oxidation of propan-2-ol with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ gives
Alcohols.w: a secondary alcohol is oxidised to a ketone with no loss of carbon.

Alcohols.q: Ethanol passed over copper at 573 K gives
Alcohols.w: copper catalyses dehydrogenation, not dehydration; a primary alcohol loses H₂ to give the aldehyde.

Alcohols.q: Ethanol and phenol can be distinguished using
Alcohols.w: phenol gives a violet colour with neutral ferric chloride and ethanol gives none. Sodium reacts with both, so (a) cannot distinguish them.

Alcohols.q: Give an example of a primary and a secondary alcohol. How is Victor Meyer's test applied to distinguish between them? [1+4]
Alcohols.r: Primary: ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH. Secondary: propan-2-ol, (CH₃)₂CHOH. Victor Meyer's test. The alcohol is converted into its iodide, then the nitroalkane, then treated with nitrous acid and made alkaline:

Alcohols.q: A primary alcohol has a molecular mass of 46. Write the reaction of this alcohol with
p: state how it is distinguished from methanol. [1+1+2+1]
Alcohols.r: The primary alcohol of M = 46 is ethanol. (a) C₂H₅OH + 4I₂ + 6NaOH → CHI₃↓ (yellow) + HCOONa + 5NaI + 5H₂O (iodoform test). (b) CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O (conc. H₂SO₄, warm): ethyl ethanoate, a fruity-smelling ester. (c) With conc. H₂SO₄ at 443 K, dehydration gives ethene: C₂H₅OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O; at 413 K with excess alcohol, ethoxyethane: 2C₂H₅OH → C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + H₂O. (d) Ethanol gives the yellow iodoform precipitate with I₂/NaOH, methanol does not (it has no CH₃CH(OH)– group).

Alcohols.q: Write the structural formula and IUPAC name of a tertiary alcohol of formula C₄H₁₀O, and all isomeric alcohols of C₃H₈O with their IUPAC names. [1+2] How are the C₃H₈O isomers distinguished?
Alcohols.r: The tertiary alcohol of C₄H₁₀O is (CH₃)₃C–OH, 2-methylpropan-2-ol. The isomers of C₃H₈O that are alcohols are CH₃CH₂CH₂OH, propan-1-ol, and CH₃CH(OH)CH₃, propan-2-ol (the third isomer, methoxyethane, is an ether). They are distinguished by Victor Meyer's test: propan-1-ol gives a blood-red colour (nitrolic acid sodium salt) and propan-2-ol a blue colour (pseudonitrole).

p: Describe the preparation of ethanol by (i) the hydrolysis of a haloalkane, (ii) the reduction of ethanal and (iii) the fermentation of glucose.
Describe the action of ethanol with (i) sodium, (ii) PCl₅, (iii) conc. H₂SO₄ at two temperatures, (iv) acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, and (v) heated copper at 573 K.
Alcohols.r: (a) (i) C₂H₅Br + KOH(aq) → C₂H₅OH + KBr. (ii) CH₃CHO + H₂ → (Ni) C₂H₅OH, or with LiAlH₄. (iii) C₆H₁₂O₆ → (zymase, 303 K) 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. (b) (i) Sodium: 2C₂H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₂H₅ONa + H₂↑ (sodium ethoxide; shows the weak acidic nature). (ii) PCl₅: C₂H₅OH + PCl₅ → C₂H₅Cl + POCl₃ + HCl↑ (white fumes; a test for –OH). (iii) Conc. H₂SO₄: at 443 K, C₂H₅OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O; at 413 K with excess alcohol, 2C₂H₅OH → C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + H₂O. (iv) Acidified K₂Cr₂O₇: a primary alcohol is oxidised to the aldehyde and then the acid: CH₃CH₂OH → (O) CH₃CHO → (O) CH₃COOH (the orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ turns green Cr³⁺).

Alcohols.q: The alcohol that gives turbidity immediately with Lucas reagent is
Alcohols.w: 3° alcohols form the carbocation fastest, so the insoluble chloride appears at once.

Alcohols.q: The reagent used in Darzen's method for converting an alcohol into a chloroalkane is
Alcohols.w: SOCl₂; the by-products SO₂ and HCl are gases and escape, leaving a pure product.

Alcohols.q: Rectified spirit contains
Alcohols.w: it is the ethanol–water azeotrope, 95.6 % ethanol by mass.

Alcohols.q: Describe Victor Meyer's method for distinguishing primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols, giving the equations and the colour obtained in each case.
Alcohols.r: Outline: (i) R–OH + HI/red P → R–I; (ii) R–I + AgNO₂ → R–NO₂ + AgI; (iii) R–NO₂ + HNO₂, then excess NaOH. 1° (two α-H) → nitrolic acid R–C(NO₂)=N–OH → blood-red sodium salt; 2° (one α-H) → pseudonitrole R₂C(NO₂)(N=O) → blue; 3° (no α-H) → no reaction → colourless.

Alcohols.q: Explain why ethanol (b.p. 78 °C) boils about 120 °C higher than propane (b.p. -42 °C) although the two have almost the same molar mass, and why 2-methylpropan-2-ol boils lower than butan-1-ol.
Alcohols.r: Ethanol molecules are joined by intermolecular hydrogen bonds between the δ+ hydroxyl hydrogen and a lone pair on the oxygen of the next molecule (≈ 20 kJ mol⁻¹ each). Propane has only weak van der Waals forces, so much less energy is needed to separate its molecules. 2-Methylpropan-2-ol is a compact, nearly spherical molecule: the surface area of contact between molecules, and so the van der Waals attraction, is smaller than in the extended chain of butan-1-ol, and there is only one –OH in each case. Hence branching lowers the boiling point (117.7 °C → 82.4 °C).

Alcohols.q: What happens when
p: ethanol is warmed with I₂ and NaOH,
propan-2-ol vapour is passed over copper at 300 °C,
ethanol is warmed with ethanoic acid and conc. H₂SO₄? Write equations.
Alcohols.r: (a) Yellow ppt of iodoform: CH₃CH₂OH + 4I₂ + 6NaOH → CHI₃↓ + 5NaI + HCOONa + 5H₂O. (b) Dehydrogenation to a ketone: (CH₃)₂CHOH --Cu, 300 °C--> CH₃COCH₃ + H₂↑. (c) C₂H₅OH + SOCl₂ → C₂H₅Cl + SO₂↑ + HCl↑. (d) No reaction — the carbinol carbon of a 3° alcohol carries no hydrogen, so mild oxidation is impossible (the dichromate stays orange). (e) Esterification: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O, a fruity-smelling ester.

Alcohols.q: Distinguish between rectified spirit, absolute alcohol, denatured alcohol and power alcohol. How is absolute alcohol obtained from rectified spirit?
Alcohols.r: Rectified spirit = 95.6 % ethanol + 4.4 % water (the azeotrope from fractional distillation). Absolute alcohol = 100 % ethanol. Denatured alcohol = ethanol + about 5 % methanol, pyridine and CuSO₄, made unfit to drink so as to avoid excise duty. Power alcohol = petrol containing 20–25 % ethanol as a motor fuel, with benzene as co-solvent. Absolute alcohol is obtained by refluxing rectified spirit with quicklime (CaO) for 5–6 hours and then distilling; CaO removes the water as Ca(OH)₂. Distillation alone cannot work, because the 95.6 % mixture is a constant-boiling azeotrope.

p: How is ethanol manufactured by the fermentation of starch? Give the enzymes and equations for each stage, and state why fermentation alone cannot give alcohol stronger than about 14 %.
Describe the oxo process and the hydroboration–oxidation of ethene, and state one advantage of each over fermentation.
Alcohols.r: (a) Starch is boiled with water and treated with malt: 2(C₆H₁₀O₅)ₙ + nH₂O --diastase--> nC₁₂H₂₂O₁₁; then C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O --maltase--> 2C₆H₁₂O₆; then C₆H₁₂O₆ --zymase--> 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂↑ at 25–30 °C in the absence of air. Zymase is a protein and is destroyed (denatured) by ethanol above about 14 %, so the fermentation stops itself; the wash must then be fractionally distilled to 95.6 % rectified spirit. (b) Oxo process: CH₂=CH₂ + CO + H₂ --Co₂(CO)₈, 150 °C, 100 atm--> CH₃CH₂CHO, then CH₃CH₂CHO + H₂ --Ni--> CH₃CH₂CH₂OH. Advantage: continuous, uses cheap petrochemical feedstock, and lengthens the chain by one carbon.

p: Write balanced equations for the action of ethanol with PCl₅, sodium metal, conc. H₂SO₄ at 170 °C and acidified K₂Cr₂O₇.

An organic liquid X, C₃H₈O, does not give turbidity with Lucas reagent in the cold, gives a red colour in Victor Meyer's test, and on oxidation gives Y which turns blue litmus red. 6.0 g of X gives 1.12 dm³ of hydrogen at STP with excess sodium. Identify X and Y, verify the gas volume by calculation, and write all the equations.
Alcohols.r: (a) C₂H₅OH + PCl₅ → C₂H₅Cl + POCl₃ + HCl; 2C₂H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₂H₅ONa + H₂↑; C₂H₅OH --conc. H₂SO₄, 170 °C--> CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O; 3CH₃CH₂OH + K₂Cr₂O₇ + 4H₂SO₄ → 3CH₃CHO + K₂SO₄ + Cr₂(SO₄)₃ + 7H₂O.

Alcohols.q: Describe the laboratory preparation of ethanol and the reactions of alcohols; how are primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols distinguished?
What is the primary functional group present in alcohols?
Alcohols.w: The hydroxyl (-OH) group is characteristic of alcohols.

Phenols.q: Which reagent distinguishes phenol from a carboxylic acid?
Phenols.w: a carboxylic acid liberates CO₂ with sodium hydrogen carbonate; phenol, being weaker than carbonic acid, does not. Both dissolve in NaOH and both react with sodium, so (a) and (b) fail. This "acidic enough for NaOH but not for NaHCO₃" line is the whole point of the question.

Phenols.q: A compound X on boiling with water gives phenol and nitrogen gas. X is
Phenols.w: the diazonium group is displaced by water on warming, releasing nitrogen.

Phenols.q: The reagent used in the Reimer–Tiemann reaction is
Phenols.w: chloroform with alkali generates dichlorocarbene, which formylates the ring at the ortho position.

Phenols.q: Kolbe's reaction on sodium phenoxide gives
Phenols.w: carbon dioxide under pressure gives sodium salicylate, and acidification gives salicylic acid, the raw material for aspirin.

Phenols.q: Phenol gives a violet colour with
Phenols.w: the violet iron(III)–phenoxide complex; this is the standard identification test for a phenolic –OH.

Phenols.q: The correct order of acidic strength is
Phenols.w: the carboxylate ion is stabilised by two equivalent oxygens, the phenoxide by the ring only, and the alkoxide not at all.

p: Give the chemical reaction for the preparation of phenol from chlorobenzene.
Why is phenol nitrated more easily than benzene?
How is phenol converted into phenolphthalein?
Phenols.r: (a) Dow's process: C₆H₅Cl + 2NaOH → (623 K, 300 atm) C₆H₅ONa + NaCl + H₂O; C₆H₅ONa + HCl → C₆H₅OH + NaCl. (b) The –OH group is a strong activating group: its lone pair is delocalised into the ring (+M effect), raising the electron density at the ortho and para positions. The ring therefore attacks the NO₂⁺ electrophile more readily, and phenol is nitrated by dilute HNO₃ at room temperature, whereas benzene needs a conc. HNO₃–H₂SO₄ mixture. (c) Two molecules of phenol condense with phthalic anhydride in conc. H₂SO₄: 2C₆H₅OH + C₆H₄(CO)₂O → (conc. H₂SO₄) phenolphthalein + H₂O.

Phenols.q: Describe the FeCl₃ test, the bromine water test and the Liebermann test for phenol.
Phenols.r: FeCl₃ test: a few drops of neutral FeCl₃ with phenol give a violet (purple) colour because of a complex, [Fe(OC₆H₅)₆]³⁻. Bromine water test: aqueous bromine is decolourised and a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol forms at once. Liebermann test: phenol is warmed with conc. H₂SO₄ and a crystal of NaNO₂; a deep green or blue colour forms that turns red on dilution with water and green or blue again on adding alkali.

p: Describe three methods of preparing phenol (from chlorobenzene, from benzenediazonium chloride, from benzene sulphonic acid).
Explain the acidic nature of phenol by comparison with alcohol and water.
Write the nitration and bromination of phenol.
Phenols.r: (a) (i) From chlorobenzene: C₆H₅Cl + 2NaOH → (623 K, 300 atm) C₆H₅ONa + NaCl + H₂O, then HCl gives phenol. (ii) From diazonium salt: C₆H₅N₂Cl + H₂O → (warm, 283 K) C₆H₅OH + N₂ + HCl. (iii) From benzene sulphonic acid: C₆H₅SO₃H + 2NaOH → (fusion, 573 K) C₆H₅ONa + Na₂SO₃ + H₂O, then C₆H₅ONa + HCl → C₆H₅OH. (b) Phenol reacts with NaOH and with sodium: C₆H₅OH + NaOH → C₆H₅ONa + H₂O, but not with NaHCO₃. Phenol is more acidic than water and alcohol because its conjugate base, the phenoxide ion, is stabilised by resonance; in an alkoxide the negative charge on oxygen is intensified by the electron-releasing alkyl group. Water has pKa 15.7, ethanol 16, phenol about 10.

Phenols.q: Phenol dissolves in aqueous NaOH but not in aqueous NaHCO₃ because
o: it is a stronger acid than carbonic acid
it is a weaker acid than carbonic acid
it is not acidic at all
Phenols.w: with $\mathrm{p}K_a$ 10.0 against 6.35, phenol cannot displace CO₂ from a bicarbonate.

Phenols.q: Sodium phenoxide heated with CO₂ at 125 °C and 4–7 atm gives, after acidification,
Phenols.w: Kolbe–Schmitt reaction; CO₂ attacks the ortho position.

Phenols.q: Which one gives a violet colour with neutral ferric chloride?
Phenols.w: only a phenolic –OH forms the violet iron(III) complex.

Phenols.q: Phenol is more acidic than ethanol mainly because
o: the phenoxide ion is resonance stabilised
it has a higher molar mass
Phenols.w: the negative charge is delocalised over C-2, C-4 and C-6, which is impossible in an alkoxide ion.

Phenols.q: Explain, with resonance structures, why phenol is a stronger acid than ethanol but a weaker acid than acetic acid.
Phenols.r: In the phenoxide ion the negative charge is delocalised over the oxygen and the two ortho and one para carbons (four contributing structures), so the conjugate base is stabilised and the proton is lost more easily. In an ethoxide ion the charge stays on one oxygen and the +I effect of the ethyl group intensifies it, so ethanol ($\mathrm{p}K_a$ 15.9) is a much weaker acid. In the acetate ion, however, the charge is shared equally by two electronegative oxygen atoms, which is far more effective than spreading it onto carbon atoms — so acetic acid ($\mathrm{p}K_a$ 4.76) is stronger than phenol (10.0).

p: benzene sulphonic acid? Give equations and conditions.
Phenols.r: (a) C₆H₅Cl + 2NaOH --300 °C, 150 atm--> C₆H₅ONa + NaCl + H₂O, then C₆H₅ONa + HCl → C₆H₅OH + NaCl (Dow's process). (b) C₆H₅N₂Cl + H₂O --warm above 5 °C--> C₆H₅OH + N₂↑ + HCl. (c) C₆H₅SO₃Na + 2NaOH --fuse 300–350 °C--> C₆H₅ONa + Na₂SO₃ + H₂O, then acidify.

Phenols.q: What is the Reimer–Tiemann reaction? Give the mechanism outline, the equation and the product obtained when CCl₄ is used in place of CHCl₃.
Phenols.r: Phenol + CHCl₃ + aqueous NaOH at 60–70 °C, then acidification, gives salicylaldehyde. The alkali removes a proton from chloroform to give CCl₃⁻ which loses Cl⁻ to form dichlorocarbene:CCl₂, the electrophile. It attacks the ortho position of the phenoxide ion; hydrolysis of the resulting –CHCl₂ group gives –CHO. Overall: C₆H₅OH + CHCl₃ + 3NaOH → 2-(HO)C₆H₄CHO + 3NaCl + 2H₂O. With CCl₄ the product is salicylic acid: C₆H₅OH + CCl₄ + 5NaOH → 2-(HO)C₆H₄COONa + 4NaCl + 3H₂O.

Phenols.q: How would you distinguish between phenol, ethanol and benzoic acid using simple chemical tests?
Phenols.r: Add NaHCO₃ solution: only benzoic acid gives CO₂ effervescence. To the remaining two add neutral FeCl₃: phenol gives a violet colour, ethanol none. Confirm with bromine water (phenol → white precipitate) and with the iodoform test (ethanol → yellow CHI₃).

Phenols.q: Calculate the pH of a 0.001 M solution of phenol, $K_a = 1.0\times10^{-10}$, and state whether the solution would turn blue litmus red.
Phenols.r: $[\text{H}^{+}] = \sqrt{K_aC} = \sqrt{(1.0\times10^{-10})(1.0\times10^{-3})} = \sqrt{1.0\times10^{-13}} = 3.16\times10^{-7}\ \text{mol dm}^{-3}$. $\mathrm{pH} = -\log(3.16\times10^{-7}) = 6.5$. The solution is only very slightly acidic — litmus (which changes around pH 5–8) would show at most a very faint pink, so in practice phenol does not turn blue litmus properly red.

p: Why is phenol more reactive than benzene towards electrophilic substitution, and why does substitution occur at the ortho and para positions?
Write equations for the nitration, sulphonation, bromination and Friedel–Crafts alkylation of phenol, stating the conditions.
9.4 g of phenol is nitrated completely with excess conc. HNO₃/H₂SO₄. Calculate the mass of picric acid obtained if the yield is 70 %.
Phenols.r: (a) The oxygen lone pair is delocalised into the ring, so the ring carries more electron density than benzene and attracts electrophiles more strongly (–OH is strongly activating). The delocalisation places the extra negative charge specifically on C-2, C-4 and C-6, so the electrophile attacks there; the intermediate carbocation formed at those positions is also the only one that can be stabilised by a structure in which every atom has a complete octet. (b) C₆H₅OH + HNO₃(dil., 25 °C) → o- and p-O₂NC₆H₄OH + H₂O; C₆H₅OH + 3HNO₃ --conc. H₂SO₄--> C₆H₂(NO₂)₃OH + 3H₂O; C₆H₅OH + H₂SO₄ ⇌ HOC₆H₄SO₃H + H₂O (ortho at 25 °C, para at 100 °C); C₆H₅OH + 3Br₂ (water) → C₆H₂Br₃OH↓ + 3HBr;

Phenols.q: Explain the acidic nature of phenol by comparing it with ethanol and water, and describe Kolbe's reaction and the Reimer–Tiemann reaction.
Which of the following phenols is most acidic due to the presence of an electron-withdrawing group?
Phenols.w: The nitro group ($-NO_2$) is strongly electron-withdrawing by resonance, increasing the acidity.

Phenols.q: Which of the following statements is true regarding the reaction of phenols with bromine water?
o: Phenol does not react with bromine water at all.
Phenol gives a white precipitate of $\ce{2,4,6-Br3C6H2OH}$.
Phenol forms a colorless solution with bromine water.
Phenol produces a reddish-brown precipitate with bromine water.
Phenols.w: Phenol reacts with bromine water to give 2,4,6-tribromophenol, which is a white precipitate.

Ethers.q: Sodium phenoxide heated with methyl bromide gives
Ethers.w: the phenoxide oxygen attacks the methyl carbon, giving methoxybenzene (anisole); this is the aromatic Williamson synthesis.

Ethers.q: Williamson's synthesis works best when the halide used is
Ethers.w: the alkoxide is a strong base as well as a nucleophile, so with 2° and 3° halides elimination competes and finally wins.

Ethers.q: Ethoxyethane treated with a limited amount of cold HI gives
Ethers.w: the iodide attacks the smaller alkyl group and the oxygen leaves as an alcohol; with excess hot HI that alcohol is converted to a second iodoethane.
attack always occurs at the alkyl carbon, never at the sp² ring carbon, so the aryl group keeps the oxygen.

Ethers.q: Ethers must be tested before distillation because on long exposure to air they form
Ethers.w: auto-oxidation at the carbon next to oxygen gives peroxides which concentrate in the still and can detonate.

Ethers.q: Convert ethoxyethane from a haloalkane C₂H₅Br using Williamson's reaction.
p: What product is obtained when ethoxyethane is heated with excess HI?
Why are old samples of ether not distilled to dryness in air?
Ethers.r: Williamson's synthesis: C₂H₅Br + C₂H₅ONa → C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + NaBr, with sodium ethoxide from 2C₂H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₂H₅ONa + H₂. (a) Heated with excess HI, ethoxyethane gives two molecules of iodoethane: C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + 2HI → 2C₂H₅I + H₂O. (b) On exposure to air and light ether forms explosive peroxides, which have higher boiling points and concentrate in the residue; if the ether is distilled to dryness the peroxide residue may explode. (c) Phenol with NaOH gives sodium phenoxide, which with CH₃Br (Williamson) gives anisole: C₆H₅OH + NaOH → C₆H₅ONa + H₂O; C₆H₅ONa + CH₃Br → C₆H₅OCH₃ + NaBr.

p: Describe Williamson's synthesis and use it to prepare ethoxyethane and anisole.
Write the action of ethoxyethane with (i) excess hot HI, (ii) cold conc. H₂SO₄, (iii) air and (iv) chlorine.
Ethers.r: (a) Williamson's synthesis is the reaction of a sodium alkoxide (or phenoxide) with a primary alkyl halide, which gives an ether by SN2 substitution: R–ONa + R′–X → R–O–R′ + NaX. Ethoxyethane: C₂H₅ONa + C₂H₅Br → C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + NaBr. Anisole: C₆H₅ONa + CH₃Br → C₆H₅OCH₃ + NaBr (the phenoxide from phenol and NaOH). A tertiary halide cannot be used, because the strongly basic alkoxide would eliminate HX to give an alkene. (b) (i) C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + 2HI → (hot, excess) 2C₂H₅I + H₂O. (ii) Cold conc. H₂SO₄ dissolves ether as an oxonium salt, (C₂H₅)₂O + H₂SO₄ → [(C₂H₅)₂OH]⁺HSO₄⁻, which is how ether is separated from alkanes.

Ethers.q: The IUPAC name of C₂H₅OCH₃ is
Ethers.w: the smaller group (CH₃) becomes the methoxy substituent on the larger (ethane) chain.
same functional group, same formula, but the carbons are shared 1 + 3 against 2 + 2 about the oxygen.

Ethers.q: Anisole on refluxing with excess HI gives
Ethers.w: only the sp³ methyl carbon can undergo SN₂, so the aryl–O bond survives.

Ethers.q: Ethoxyethane boils at 34.6 °C while butan-1-ol boils at 117.7 °C because
o: the ether has a smaller molar mass
the ether cannot form intermolecular hydrogen bonds
Ethers.w: an ether has no O–H hydrogen to donate, so its molecules are held together only by weak dipole and van der Waals forces.

Ethers.q: The best pair of reagents for preparing 2-methoxy-2-methylpropane is
Ethers.w: the bulky group must be the alkoxide; (a) would give 2-methylpropene by elimination.

Ethers.q: Diethyl ether stored for a long time in a half-empty bottle becomes dangerous because it forms
Ethers.w: slow autoxidation gives CH₃CH(OOH)OC₂H₅, which explodes when the ether is distilled to dryness.

Ethers.q: What is Williamson's synthesis? Show how it is used to prepare ethoxyethane and anisole, and explain why CH₃ONa + C₆H₅Cl cannot be used.
Ethers.r: Williamson's synthesis is the SN₂ reaction of a sodium alkoxide or phenoxide with a methyl or primary haloalkane: C₂H₅ONa + C₂H₅I → C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + NaI, and C₆H₅ONa + CH₃I → C₆H₅OCH₃ + NaI. CH₃ONa + C₆H₅Cl fails because the C–Cl bond in a haloarene has partial double-bond character (the chlorine lone pair is delocalised into the ring), the ring carbon is sp², and the benzene ring blocks the backside approach that SN₂ requires.

Ethers.q: Explain why ethoxyethane (b.p. 34.6 °C) boils far below butan-1-ol (b.p. 117.7 °C) although both are C₄H₁₀O, yet the two are about equally soluble in water.
Ethers.r: Butan-1-ol has an O–H hydrogen, so its molecules are joined by intermolecular hydrogen bonds that must be broken before it boils; ethoxyethane has no O–H and is held only by dipole and van der Waals forces, so it boils about 83 °C lower — close to pentane (36.1 °C). Solubility is a different question: water supplies the hydrogen, and the ether oxygen accepts the hydrogen bond, so both compounds hydrogen-bond to water about equally well (6.5 g and 7.9 g per 100 cm³).

Ethers.q: What happens when ethoxyethane is treated with
p: air over a long period? Give equations.
Ethers.r: (a) C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + HI → C₂H₅OH + C₂H₅I. (b) C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + 2HI → 2C₂H₅I + H₂O. (c) It dissolves, forming the oxonium salt [(C₂H₅)₂OH]⁺HSO₄⁻ — the ether is acting as a Lewis base. (d) C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + 2Cl₂ → CH₃CHCl–O–CHClCH₃ + 2HCl (the two α-hydrogens are replaced). (e) Slow autoxidation: C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + O₂ → CH₃CH(OOH)OC₂H₅, an explosive peroxide.

Ethers.q: Write all the isomers of C₄H₁₀O with their IUPAC names, and state the type of isomerism shown by (i) ethoxyethane and butan-1-ol, (ii) ethoxyethane and 1-methoxypropane.
Ethers.r: Alcohols: butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol. Ethers: ethoxyethane, 1-methoxypropane, 2-methoxypropane — seven isomers in all. (i) Functional isomerism (alcohol against ether). (ii) Metamerism (2 + 2 against 1 + 3 carbons about the oxygen).

p: Define an ether and classify ethers with one example of each type. Explain metamerism using C₄H₁₀O.
Describe Williamson's synthesis of an aliphatic and of an aromatic ether, give the mechanism in outline, and explain why the halide must be primary.
How is ethoxyethane also obtained from ethanol? Why does this method fail for mixed ethers?
Ethers.r: (a) An ether has an oxygen atom bonded to two carbon atoms, R–O–R′. Simple (symmetrical): C₂H₅OC₂H₅. Mixed (unsymmetrical): CH₃OC₂H₅; aromatic mixed: C₆H₅OCH₃. Metamerism is isomerism arising from a different distribution of carbon atoms about the same functional group: for C₄H₁₀O, C₂H₅–O–C₂H₅ (2 + 2) and CH₃–O–C₃H₇ (1 + 3) are metamers. (b) C₂H₅ONa + C₂H₅I → C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + NaI; C₆H₅ONa + CH₃I → C₆H₅OCH₃ + NaI. Mechanism: the alkoxide oxygen, a strong nucleophile, attacks the carbon carrying the halogen from the side opposite the C–X bond; the transition state has the oxygen and the halogen partially bonded on opposite sides, and the halide leaves as the new C–O bond forms (SN₂).

p: Give equations for the action of ethoxyethane with HI, conc. HCl, conc. H₂SO₄, air and Cl₂, stating the conditions in each case.
3.7 g of ethoxyethane is treated with just 0.050 mol of cold HI. Name the organic products and calculate the mass of each.
Ethers.r: (a) C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + HI (cold) → C₂H₅OH + C₂H₅I; C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + 2HI (hot, excess) → 2C₂H₅I + H₂O; C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + HCl (cold conc.) → [(C₂H₅)₂OH]⁺Cl⁻, and on heating under pressure C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + 2HCl → 2C₂H₅Cl + H₂O; C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + H₂SO₄ (cold) → [(C₂H₅)₂OH]⁺HSO₄⁻, and on heating C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + 2H₂SO₄ → 2C₂H₅HSO₄ + H₂O; C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + O₂ (air, light, slow) → CH₃CH(OOH)OC₂H₅; C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + 2Cl₂ (dark) → CH₃CHCl–O–CHClCH₃ + 2HCl, and C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + 10Cl₂ (sunlight) → C₂Cl₅OC₂Cl₅ + 10HCl. (b) $n(\text{ether}) = 3.7/74 = 0.050\ \text{mol}$, and 0.050 mol of HI is supplied, so the mole ratio is 1: 1 and only one C–O bond is broken: C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + HI → C₂H₅OH + C₂H₅I.

Ethers.q: Describe the Williamson synthesis and the main reactions of diethyl ether, including its action with HI, and state its uses and hazards.
Which of the following ethers is classified as a cyclic ether?
o: Diethyl ether ($	ext{C}_2	ext{H}_5-O-	ext{C}_2	ext{H}_5$)
Methyl ethyl ether ($	ext{CH}_3-O-	ext{C}_2	ext{H}_5$)
Ethers.w: Tetrahydrofuran has a ring structure making it a cyclic ether.

Ethers.q: The Williamson synthesis is used to prepare ethers by reacting an alkoxide ion with what other compound?
Ethers.w: Williamson synthesis specifically involves the reaction of an alkoxide ion with a haloalkane.

Aldehydes and Ketones.q: Benzene → X → Y; Y warmed with ethanoic anhydride and sodium ethanoate gives an acid. That acid is
Aldehydes and Ketones.w: benzene is acylated or oxidised through to benzaldehyde (Y), and the Perkin condensation with ethanoic anhydride and sodium ethanoate gives 3-phenylprop-2-enoic acid, cinnamic acid.

Aldehydes and Ketones.q: Which compound gives a positive Tollens' test and a positive iodoform test?
Aldehydes and Ketones.w: ethanal is the only aldehyde carrying a CH₃CO– group, so it answers to both tests. Propanone gives iodoform but no mirror; methanal and propanal give a mirror but no iodoform.

Aldehydes and Ketones.q: A compound gives an orange-red precipitate with 2,4-DNP but no silver mirror with Tollens' reagent. It is
Aldehydes and Ketones.w: 2,4-DNP detects the carbonyl group in both aldehydes and ketones, so it cannot distinguish them; only Tollens' can.

Aldehydes and Ketones.q: Which compound does not reduce Fehling's solution?
Aldehydes and Ketones.w: aromatic aldehydes do not reduce Fehling's solution, although they do give a silver mirror with Tollens'. This exception is examined almost every year.

Aldehydes and Ketones.q: Tollens' reagent oxidises an aldehyde and deposits
Aldehydes and Ketones.w: free silver plates out on the glass as a mirror; Fehling's gives the red-brown Cu₂O instead.

Aldehydes and Ketones.q: Which compound undergoes the Cannizzaro reaction?
Aldehydes and Ketones.w: methanal has no α-hydrogen, so it cannot enolise and instead disproportionates to methanol and sodium formate.

Aldehydes and Ketones.q: Clemmensen's reduction is carried out with
Aldehydes and Ketones.w: zinc amalgam with concentrated HCl, so it is used for compounds stable to acid; Wolff–Kishner is the basic alternative.

Aldehydes and Ketones.q: The Rosenmund reduction converts an acid chloride into
Aldehydes and Ketones.w: the poisoned palladium catalyst stops the reduction at the aldehyde stage.

Aldehydes and Ketones.q: The reagent used to purify an aldehyde through a crystalline addition compound is
Aldehydes and Ketones.w: the sodium bisulphite adduct crystallises out and is decomposed later with dilute acid or alkali to return the pure carbonyl compound.

Aldehydes and Ketones.q: Ozonolysis of but-2-ene followed by reductive work-up gives
Aldehydes and Ketones.w: the double bond breaks in the middle of the chain, giving two CH₃CHO molecules.

Aldehydes and Ketones.q: Methanal reacts with ammonia to give
Aldehydes and Ketones.w: six molecules of methanal and four of ammonia give hexamethylenetetramine, used as a urinary antiseptic and in making RDX.

Aldehydes and Ketones.q: Benzaldehyde with alcoholic KCN gives
Aldehydes and Ketones.w: cyanide ion catalyses the coupling of two aromatic aldehyde molecules to give the α-hydroxy ketone benzoin.

Aldehydes and Ketones.q: Write a chemical equation for each of (i) carbonylation, (ii) Fehling's test, (iii) aldol condensation, (iv) Williamson's ether synthesis and (v) the 2,4-DNP test.
Aldehydes and Ketones.r: (i) Carbonylation: CH₃ONa + CO → (425 K, 3 atm) CH₃COONa. (ii) Fehling's test: CH₃CHO + 2Cu²⁺ + 5OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + Cu₂O↓ (red) + 3H₂O. (iii) Aldol: 2CH₃CHO → (dil. NaOH) CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CHO. (iv) Williamson: C₂H₅ONa + C₂H₅Br → C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + NaBr. (v) 2,4-DNP: CH₃CHO + H₂N–NH–C₆H₃(NO₂)₂ → CH₃CH=N–NH–C₆H₃(NO₂)₂ + H₂O (yellow-orange precipitate).

Aldehydes and Ketones.q: Give an example of each of
Aldehydes and Ketones.r: (a) Tollens': CH₃CHO + 2[Ag(NH₃)₂]OH → CH₃COONH₄ + 2Ag↓ (silver mirror) + 3NH₃ + H₂O. (b) Cannizzaro: 2HCHO + NaOH(conc.) → CH₃OH + HCOONa. (c) Decarbonylation (loss of CO): CH₃CH₂CHO → (Pd or Rh catalyst, heat) CH₃CH₃ + CO. (d) Reimer–Tiemann: C₆H₅OH + CHCl₃ + 3NaOH → o-HOC₆H₄CHO + 3NaCl + 2H₂O. (e) Oxo process: CH₂=CH₂ + CO + H₂ → (Co₂(CO)₈, 420 K, 100 atm) CH₃CH₂CHO, which is reduced to propan-1-ol.

Aldehydes and Ketones.q: An organic compound X reacts with methyl magnesium bromide followed by acid hydrolysis to give Y. Y on oxidation with acidified KMnO₄ gives Z. All three give a positive iodoform test.
p: Predict X, Y and Z with the reactions and IUPAC names.
What is obtained when Z reacts with dilute NaOH?
Aldehydes and Ketones.r: (a) X = ethanal, CH₃CHO; Y = propan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃; Z = propanone, CH₃COCH₃. CH₃CHO + CH₃MgBr → CH₃CH(OMgBr)CH₃ (dry ether); CH₃CH(OMgBr)CH₃ + H₂O → CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ + Mg(OH)Br. CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ + [O] → (acidified KMnO₄) CH₃COCH₃ + H₂O. Each compound contains CH₃CO– (ethanal, propanone) or CH₃CH(OH)– (propan-2-ol), so all give yellow iodoform. (b) Propanone with dilute NaOH undergoes aldol condensation: 2CH₃COCH₃ → (CH₃)₂C(OH)CH₂COCH₃, diacetone alcohol (4-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one).

Aldehydes and Ketones.q: Give one example, with reagents and conditions, of each of the following reactions.
p: an elimination reaction, (f) Cannizzaro's reaction, (g) Reimer–Tiemann reaction, (h) Friedel–Crafts alkylation. [8 × 1]
Aldehydes and Ketones.r: (a) Hydroboration–oxidation: 6CH₃CH=CH₂ + B₂H₆ → 2(CH₃CH₂CH₂)₃B; (CH₃CH₂CH₂)₃B + 3H₂O₂ + NaOH → 3CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + Na₃BO₃ (anti-Markovnikov hydration). (b) Decarbonylation: CH₃CH₂CHO → (Pd or Rh, heat) CH₃CH₃ + CO. (c) Sandmeyer: C₆H₅N₂Cl + CuCl/HCl → C₆H₅Cl + N₂. (d) Iodoform: CH₃COCH₃ + 3I₂ + 4NaOH → CHI₃↓ (yellow) + CH₃COONa + 3NaI + 3H₂O. (e) Elimination: CH₃CH₂Br + KOH(alc.) → CH₂=CH₂ + KBr + H₂O (dehydrohalogenation); or ethanol with conc. H₂SO₄ at 443 K. (f) Cannizzaro: 2C₆H₅CHO + NaOH(conc.) → C₆H₅CH₂OH + C₆H₅COONa. (g) Reimer–Tiemann: C₆H₅OH + CHCl₃ + NaOH → salicylaldehyde. (h) Friedel–Crafts alkylation: C₆H₆ + CH₃Cl → (anhydrous AlCl₃) C₆H₅CH₃ + HCl.

Aldehydes and Ketones.q: An organic compound X reacts with Grignard's reagent to give Y, which on oxidation gives Z. All three give a positive iodoform test.
p: Identify X, Y and Z with the reactions and conditions.
Why do these compounds give a positive iodoform test?
How would you convert Y into pseudonitrol?
Write any two methods for the preparation of Z.
Aldehydes and Ketones.r: (a) X = ethanal, Y = propan-2-ol, Z = propanone. CH₃CHO + CH₃MgBr → (dry ether) CH₃CH(OMgBr)CH₃; + H₂O/H⁺ → CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ + Mg(OH)Br. Then CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ + [O] → (acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ or KMnO₄) CH₃COCH₃ + H₂O. (b) The iodoform test is given by compounds with the CH₃CO– group, or the CH₃CH(OH)– group, which the hypoiodite (NaOH + I₂) first oxidises to CH₃CO–. The three α-hydrogens are replaced by iodine to give –COCI₃, which is cleaved by alkali into CHI₃ (yellow) and a carboxylate. Ethanal (CH₃CO–H), propan-2-ol (CH₃CH(OH)–) and propanone (CH₃CO–) all meet this requirement. (c) Propan-2-ol → 2-iodopropane → 2-nitropropane → pseudonitrole: CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ + I₂/red P → CH₃CHICH₃;

Aldehydes and Ketones.q: Which of the following gives Cannizzaro's reaction?
Aldehydes and Ketones.w: methanal has no α-hydrogen, so it disproportionates.

Aldehydes and Ketones.q: Describe the structure of the carbonyl group and explain, with the help of the polarity, why aldehydes and ketones undergo nucleophilic addition rather than electrophilic addition.
How do you distinguish between
p: ethanal and benzaldehyde? Give reagent, observation and equation in each case.
Aldehydes and Ketones.r: (a) Tollens' reagent: ethanal gives a silver mirror, propanone gives no change — CH₃CHO + 2[Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ + 3OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + 2Ag + 4NH₃ + 2H₂O. (b) Iodoform test with I₂/NaOH: propanone gives yellow CHI₃, propanal does not, because propanal has no CH₃—CO— group. (c) Fehling's solution: ethanal gives a red-brown Cu₂O precipitate, benzaldehyde gives none (both give Tollens').

Aldehydes and Ketones.q: What is aldol condensation? Write the mechanism for the aldol condensation of ethanal and state why benzaldehyde does not undergo it.
Compare Clemmensen's reduction with Wolff–Kishner reduction under four headings, and state which you would use to reduce 4-hydroxybutan-2-one to 4-hydroxybutane.
Aldehydes and Ketones.r: Headings: reagent, medium, by-product, when used (see the table in Section 13.8). The substrate contains an —OH group, which concentrated HCl would dehydrate or substitute, so use Wolff–Kishner (basic conditions).

p: Explain the structure and polar nature of the carbonyl group and give the general mechanism of nucleophilic addition.
Arrange HCHO, CH₃CHO, CH₃COCH₃ and C₆H₅CHO in order of decreasing reactivity towards nucleophilic addition and justify the order.
Aldehydes and Ketones.r: (b) HCHO > CH₃CHO > CH₃COCH₃ > C₆H₅CHO. HCHO has no electron-releasing alkyl group, so its carbonyl carbon carries the largest δ+ and is the least hindered. Each alkyl group added donates electron density (+I), lowering δ+, and adds steric bulk. In benzaldehyde the benzene ring donates electron density into the carbonyl group by resonance, which lowers δ+ further; propanone is therefore more reactive than benzaldehyde in practice. (Figure of hydration constants: K = 2.3 × 10³, 1.1 and 2 × 10⁻³ for the first three.)

p: How is benzaldehyde prepared from toluene? Give two methods with equations.
Write the reactions of benzaldehyde with (i) ethanoic anhydride and sodium ethanoate, (ii) alcoholic KCN, (iii) concentrated NaOH, naming each product.
Why does benzaldehyde undergo meta substitution on nitration?
Aldehydes and Ketones.r: (c) —CHO is a -I and -R group. It withdraws electron density from the ring, and the resonance structures put the positive charge at the ortho and para positions. The electrophile therefore attacks the least deactivated position, the meta position.

Aldehydes and Ketones.q: An organic compound X of formula C₄H₈O decolourises neither bromine water nor KMnO₄, gives an orange solid with 2,4-DNP, gives yellow crystals with I₂/NaOH, but does not reduce Tollens' reagent. On reduction with LiAlH₄ it gives Y, which on heating with concentrated H₂SO₄ gives Z, C₄H₈. Identify X, Y and Z with reasoning and write all the equations.
Aldehydes and Ketones.r: No decolourisation of Br₂ water or KMnO₄ ⇒ no C=C. 2,4-DNP positive ⇒ carbonyl group. Tollens' negative ⇒ not an aldehyde ⇒ a ketone. Iodoform positive ⇒ contains CH₃CO—. The only C₄H₈O ketone is butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃ = X.

Aldehydes and Ketones.q: Distinguish aldehydes from ketones, and explain the aldol condensation and the Cannizzaro reaction with mechanisms and examples.

Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.q: A compound C₃H₄O₄ on heating gives Y and CO₂; Y with P₂O₅ gives X. X is
Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.w: C₃H₄O₄ is propanedioic (malonic) acid; heating it loses CO₂ to give ethanoic acid (Y), and P₂O₅ dehydrates two molecules of that to ethanoic anhydride.

Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.q: The strongest acid among the following is
Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.w: three chlorines pull the most electron density away from the carboxylate, stabilising the anion best.

Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.q: Methanoic acid reduces Tollens' reagent because it contains
Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.w: HCOOH is the one acid in which the carboxyl carbon still carries a hydrogen, so it behaves partly as an aldehyde.

Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.q: The reagent that gives brisk effervescence with ethanoic acid but not with phenol is
Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.w: only an acid stronger than carbonic acid displaces CO₂ from a hydrogen carbonate; phenol is too weak.

Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.q: Claisen condensation of two molecules of ethyl ethanoate gives
Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.w: the carbanion from one ester attacks the carbonyl of the other, giving the β-keto ester ethyl 3-oxobutanoate.

Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.q: Ethanamide treated with bromine and NaOH gives
Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.w: the Hofmann bromamide degradation loses the carbonyl carbon, so a two-carbon amide gives a one-carbon amine.

Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.q: The most reactive acid derivative towards nucleophilic acyl substitution is
Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.w: chloride is the best leaving group of the four and the carbonyl carbon is the most electrophilic.

Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.q: Ethanoic acid reduced with LiAlH₄ gives
Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.w: lithium aluminium hydride is powerful enough to take the acid all the way down to the primary alcohol.

Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.q: Hydrolysis of an ester with NaOH is called
Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.w: alkaline hydrolysis gives the salt, which cannot react back with the alcohol, so the reaction goes to completion.

Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.q: An amide is described as amphoteric because it
o: reacts with both acids and bases
Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.w: the lone pair on nitrogen gives a weak base and the N–H a weak acid, so amides form salts with both strong acids and sodium.

Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.q: Ethanenitrile on complete hydrolysis gives
Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.w: the nitrile passes through the amide and then the acid, with ammonia released.

Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.q: An aliphatic compound A reacts with SOCl₂ to give B. B is heated with ammonia to give C. C is heated with Br₂/KOH to give D. D treated with NaNO₂/HCl at low temperature gives E, a primary alcohol that gives a positive iodoform test. Identify A to E with the reactions.
Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.r: Work backwards: E is a primary alcohol giving iodoform, so E = ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, which comes from ethylamine D by nitrous acid. Ethylamine comes by Hofmann bromamide degradation (one carbon lost) from propanamide C, so B = propanoyl chloride and A = propanoic acid. A: CH₃CH₂COOH + SOCl₂ → B: CH₃CH₂COCl + SO₂↑ + HCl↑ B + 2NH₃ → C: CH₃CH₂CONH₂ (propanamide) + NH₄Cl C + Br₂ + 4KOH → D: CH₃CH₂NH₂ (ethanamine) + K₂CO₃ + 2KBr + 2H₂O D + HNO₂ (NaNO₂ + HCl, 273 K) → E: CH₃CH₂OH + N₂↑ + H₂O

p: How is ethanoic acid prepared from (i) CH₃MgBr, (ii) CH₃CN and (iii) CH₃ONa?
Convert ethanoic acid into methanoic acid.
Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.r: (a) (i) CH₃MgBr + CO₂ → CH₃COOMgBr → (H₃O⁺) CH₃COOH. (ii) CH₃CN + 2H₂O → (H⁺ or OH⁻, heat) CH₃COOH + NH₃. (iii) CH₃ONa + CO → (425 K, 3 atm) CH₃COONa; CH₃COONa + HCl → CH₃COOH + NaCl. (b) CH₃COOH → (NH₃, heat) CH₃CONH₂ → (Br₂/KOH) CH₃NH₂ → (HNO₂) CH₃OH → (K₂Cr₂O₇/H⁺) HCOOH. (Each step loses or oxidises one carbon unit: Hofmann removes the carboxyl carbon, and oxidation of methanol gives methanoic acid.)

p: Write the Hofmann bromamide reaction for ethanamide.
Arrange acid chloride, anhydride, ester and amide in decreasing order of reactivity towards nucleophiles.
Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.r: (a) CH₃CONH₂ + Br₂ + 4NaOH → CH₃NH₂ + Na₂CO₃ + 2NaBr + 2H₂O (a primary amine with one carbon fewer). (b) An amide can accept a proton on its nitrogen lone pair (weakly basic) and can lose an N–H proton to a strong base such as sodium, forming a salt (weakly acidic); it is amphoteric. (c) Acid chloride > anhydride > ester > amide. (d) Claisen condensation: two molecules of an ester with α-hydrogens condense in the presence of sodium ethoxide to give a β-keto ester: 2CH₃COOC₂H₅ → (C₂H₅ONa) CH₃COCH₂COOC₂H₅ + C₂H₅OH (ethyl acetoacetate).

Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.q: The compound C₂H₄O₂ has two functional isomers A and B. A turns blue litmus red, and B has a fruity smell.
p: How is A formed using a Grignard reagent?
Give a test to distinguish A from methanoic acid.
Arrange CH₃COOH, ClCH₂COOH, FCH₂COOH and C₆H₅COOH in decreasing acidic strength.
Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.r: (e) A = ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH (acidic, turns blue litmus red) and B = methyl methanoate, HCOOCH₃ (an ester with a fruity smell). (a) CH₃MgBr + CO₂ → CH₃COOMgBr → (H₂O/H⁺) CH₃COOH + Mg(OH)Br. (b) Ethanoic acid is first converted to methanol, and methanoic acid is made from it: CH₃COOH → (NH₃, heat) CH₃CONH₂ → (Br₂/KOH) CH₃NH₂ → (HNO₂) CH₃OH. Part of the methanol is oxidised, CH₃OH → (K₂Cr₂O₇/H⁺) HCOOH, and the rest is esterified with it: HCOOH + CH₃OH ⇌ (conc. H₂SO₄) HCOOCH₃ + H₂O. (Any valid route scores.) (c) Tollens' test: methanoic acid gives a silver mirror; ethanoic acid does not.

p: How are an acid chloride, an amide, an ester and an anhydride prepared from ethanoic acid? Give the reaction of each.
Write the products of hydrolysis, ammonolysis and alcoholysis of ethanoyl chloride.
Arrange the derivatives in decreasing order of reactivity.
Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.r: (a) Acid chloride: CH₃COOH + SOCl₂ → CH₃COCl + SO₂ + HCl (or PCl₅, PCl₃). Amide: CH₃COOH + NH₃ → CH₃COONH₄ → (heat) CH₃CONH₂ + H₂O. Ester: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ (conc. H₂SO₄) CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O. Anhydride: 2CH₃COOH → (P₂O₅, heat) (CH₃CO)₂O + H₂O; or CH₃COCl + CH₃COONa → (CH₃CO)₂O + NaCl. (b) Hydrolysis: CH₃COCl + H₂O → CH₃COOH + HCl. Ammonolysis: CH₃COCl + 2NH₃ → CH₃CONH₂ + NH₄Cl. Alcoholysis: CH₃COCl + C₂H₅OH → CH₃COOC₂H₅ + HCl. (c) Acid chloride > anhydride > ester > amide — the better the leaving group (Cl⁻, RCOO⁻, RO⁻, NH₂⁻) and the less the lone pair donates into the carbonyl, the more reactive the derivative.

Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.q: Which reagent distinguishes ethanoic acid from phenol?
Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.w: only the acid is strong enough to liberate CO₂ from NaHCO₃; phenol is not.

Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.q: The strongest acid among the following is
Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.w: three chlorine atoms give the largest total -I effect, $pK_a$ 0.66.

Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.q: Which carboxylic acid gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent?
Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.w: methanoic acid contains a —CHO grouping and so acts as a reducing agent.

Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.q: Explain, with resonance structures, why a carboxylic acid is more acidic than both phenol and ethanol.
What is the Hell–Volhard–Zelinsky reaction? Write the equations for the conversion of ethanoic acid into chloroethanoic acid and then into glycine, and state why methanoic acid does not undergo it.
Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.r: CH₃COOH + Cl₂ --red P--> ClCH₂COOH + HCl; then ClCH₂COOH + 2NH₃ → H₂NCH₂COOH + NH₄Cl (glycine). Methanoic acid has no α-carbon, so there is no α-hydrogen to replace.

Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.q: Describe the abnormal behaviour of methanoic acid under four headings with equations.

p: Define a carboxylic acid and explain its acidic character using the resonance of the carboxylate ion.
Discuss the effect of electron-withdrawing and electron-releasing substituents on acid strength, using $pK_a$ data.
Why is benzoic acid a stronger acid than ethanoic acid?
Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.r: (c) The carbon of the benzene ring is sp² hybridised and therefore more electronegative than the sp³ carbon of a methyl group. It withdraws electron density from the carboxyl group (-I) instead of releasing it, so benzoate is better stabilised than ethanoate: $pK_a$ 4.20 against 4.76.

p: Name the four derivatives of ethanoic acid and give one equation for the preparation of each from ethanoic acid.
Compare their reactivity towards hydrolysis, explain the order, and write the equation for the alkaline hydrolysis of ethyl ethanoate and of ethanamide.
Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.r: (b) RCOCl > (RCO)₂O > RCOOR′ > RCONH₂, because the weaker the base L⁻ the faster it leaves, and the less the atom L donates its lone pair into the C=O. CH₃COOC₂H₅ + NaOH → CH₃COONa + C₂H₅OH (saponification); CH₃CONH₂ + NaOH → CH₃COONa + NH₃.

Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.q: An organic compound A of formula C₇H₈ is oxidised by hot alkaline KMnO₄ and then acidified to give B, C₇H₆O₂, which dissolves in NaHCO₃ with effervescence. B with SOCl₂ gives C; C with ammonia gives D, C₇H₇NO; D with Br₂ and excess NaOH gives E, C₆H₇N, which gives an orange dye when coupled after diazotisation. Identify A to E and write all the equations.
Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.r: C₇H₈ with a benzene ring and a side chain is toluene, C₆H₅CH₃ = A.

Carboxylic Acid and its Derivatives.q: Explain the acidity of carboxylic acids and the effect of substituents on it, and describe five characteristic reactions of acetic acid including the HVZ reaction.

Nitro Compounds.q: In the nitrous acid test a secondary nitroalkane gives a
Nitro Compounds.w: the pseudonitrole gives a blue colour; the primary compound gives the red nitrolic acid salt and the tertiary compound, having no α-hydrogen, gives nothing.
both are C₂H₅NO₂, but one has a C–N bond and the other a C–O–N linkage, so they belong to different functional classes.

p: Why is the nitro group meta-directing?
Write the products when nitrobenzene is treated with (i) Zn/NH₄Cl and (ii) LiAlH₄.
Nitro Compounds.r: (a) The NO₂ group withdraws electrons by both the -I and -M effects. In the resonance structures of nitrobenzene the ortho and para carbons carry a positive charge, so they are less electron-rich than the meta carbons. The electrophile therefore attacks the meta position, and the ring is deactivated towards substitution. (b) (i) Zn/NH₄Cl (neutral): C₆H₅NO₂ + 4[H] → C₆H₅NHOH + H₂O (N-phenylhydroxylamine). (ii) LiAlH₄: 2C₆H₅NO₂ + 8[H] → C₆H₅N=NC₆H₅ + 4H₂O (azobenzene). (c) C₂H₇N has two isomers: CH₃CH₂NH₂ (ethanamine, primary) and CH₃NHCH₃ (N-methylmethanamine, secondary).

Nitro Compounds.q: What happens when a haloalkane is treated with (i) silver nitrite and (ii) sodium nitrite in ethanol? Explain the difference.
Nitro Compounds.r: AgNO₂ gives mainly the nitroalkane (CH₃CH₂Br + AgNO₂ → CH₃CH₂NO₂ + AgBr), because the Ag–O bond is largely covalent and leaves the nitrogen lone pair as the better nucleophilic site. NaNO₂ is ionic, the nitrite ion attacks through oxygen, and the alkyl nitrite CH₃CH₂–O–N=O is the main product. The nitrite ion is ambident — it has two nucleophilic sites.

Nitro Compounds.q: How is nitrobenzene prepared from benzene? Give the equation, the conditions, and the role of concentrated sulphuric acid.
Nitro Compounds.r: C₆H₆ + HNO₃ --conc. H₂SO₄, 50–60 °C--> C₆H₅NO₂ + H₂O. Conditions: 1: 1 nitrating mixture, water bath at 50–60 °C, reflux. H₂SO₄ protonates nitric acid and removes water to generate the electrophile: HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻. Above 60 °C, m-dinitrobenzene is formed.

Nitro Compounds.q: Explain, with reasons, why nitrobenzene undergoes electrophilic substitution more slowly than benzene and gives the meta product.
Nitro Compounds.r: The –NO₂ group is electron-withdrawing both inductively (the N carries a positive charge) and by resonance (it delocalises ring π electrons onto its oxygens). The ring therefore has less electron density available for an electrophile, and the arenium-ion intermediate is destabilised — nitration is about 10⁷ times slower than for benzene. For ortho and para attack one canonical form of the intermediate places the positive charge on the ring carbon bearing the positive nitrogen, which is strongly destabilising; meta attack never does, so the meta isomer is formed.

p: Describe the reduction of nitrobenzene in acidic, neutral, strongly alkaline and electrolytic (conc. H₂SO₄) media, giving the product and a balanced equation in each case.
How are 1°, 2° and 3° nitroalkanes distinguished by the nitrous acid test?
Nitro Compounds.r: (a) Use the table in §15.4: acidic (Sn/HCl) → aniline, C₆H₅NO₂ + 6[H] → C₆H₅NH₂ + 2H₂O; neutral (Zn/NH₄Cl) → N-phenylhydroxylamine, C₆H₅NO₂ + 4[H] → C₆H₅NHOH + H₂O; strongly alkaline (Zn/NaOH excess) → hydrazobenzene, 2C₆H₅NO₂ + 10[H] → C₆H₅NHNHC₆H₅ + 4H₂O; electrolytic in conc. H₂SO₄ → p-aminophenol, C₆H₅NO₂ + 4[H] → p-H₂NC₆H₄OH + H₂O (the –NHOH formed first rearranges in strong acid). (b) 1° → blood-red nitrolic acid salt with NaOH; 2° → blue pseudonitrole; 3° → no reaction (no α-hydrogen). See Worked example 15.1.

Nitro Compounds.q: Describe the reduction of nitrobenzene in acidic, neutral and alkaline media and explain its electrophilic substitution reactions.

Amines.q: A compound gives a foul-smelling product with chloroform and alcoholic KOH. It is
Amines.w: the carbylamine (isocyanide) test is given only by primary amines; 2° and 3° amines give nothing.

Amines.q: Benzene → A → B → C, where B is aniline and C is benzenediazonium chloride. The step B → C is called
Amines.w: nitrous acid generated in situ at 273–278 K converts the –NH₂ group into –N₂⁺Cl⁻.

Amines.q: A mixture of 1°, 2° and 3° amines is separated by Hoffmann's method using
Amines.w: the ester reacts differently with each class: a solid oxamide from the 1° amine, a liquid oxamic ester from the 2°, and nothing from the 3°.

Amines.q: A secondary amine treated with nitrous acid gives
Amines.w: the N–H of a secondary amine is nitrosated; there is no hydrogen left for the further steps that release nitrogen.

Amines.q: Aniline is less basic than ethylamine because in aniline
o: the lone pair is delocalised into the ring
Amines.w: resonance delocalisation into the benzene ring reduces the electron density on nitrogen, so it accepts a proton much less readily.

Amines.q: Ethylamine treated with nitrous acid gives
Amines.w: the aliphatic diazonium ion is unstable even at low temperature and decomposes at once, releasing nitrogen quantitatively.

Amines.q: Aniline is acetylated before nitration in order to
o: control the reaction and obtain the p-isomer
Amines.w: acetylation reduces the activating power of the nitrogen and blocks oxidation by the nitrating mixture, so the para product can be isolated.

Amines.q: Ethanenitrile reduced with LiAlH₄ gives
Amines.w: the nitrile carbon is retained, so CH₃CN gives CH₃CH₂NH₂; the Hofmann route would have shortened the chain instead.

Amines.q: How would you apply Hoffmann's method for the separation of primary, secondary and tertiary amines from their mixture?
Amines.r: Hoffmann's method uses diethyl oxalate, (COOC₂H₅)₂, which reacts differently with the three classes. - Primary amine: (COOC₂H₅)₂ + 2RNH₂ → (CONHR)₂ + 2C₂H₅OH, a solid dialkyl oxamide. - Secondary amine: (COOC₂H₅)₂ + R₂NH → C₂H₅OOC–CO–NR₂ + C₂H₅OH, a liquid oxamic ester. - Tertiary amine: no reaction (no N–H), so it is recovered as such. Separation: the mixture is heated with diethyl oxalate and the products are distilled. The tertiary amine distils first (it is volatile). The liquid oxamic ester (b.p. higher) distils next, leaving the solid oxamide in the flask, or the solid is filtered off.

Amines.q: A mixture has A = CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂ and B = CH₃CH₂NHCH₃.
p: How would you separate them by Hoffmann's method?
Give the nitrous acid test to distinguish A from B.
Amines.r: (a) Heat the mixture with diethyl oxalate. Propylamine (A) forms the solid N,N′-dipropyloxamide, (CONHC₃H₇)₂, and N-methylethanamine (B) forms the liquid oxamic ester, C₂H₅OOC–CO–N(CH₃)C₂H₅. The liquid is distilled off (or the solid is filtered), and each is hydrolysed with KOH to regenerate the amine. (b) Nitrous acid test (NaNO₂ + HCl): A, a primary amine, gives colourless gas bubbles of N₂ and the alcohol: CH₃CH₂CH₂NH₂ + HNO₂ → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + N₂↑ + H₂O. B, a secondary amine, gives a yellow oily liquid, the N-nitrosoamine, with no gas: CH₃CH₂NHCH₃ + HNO₂ → CH₃CH₂N(NO)CH₃ + H₂O.

Amines.q: Write the reaction of a primary amine (ethylamine) with
Amines.r: (a) Carbylamine: C₂H₅NH₂ + CHCl₃ + 3KOH → C₂H₅NC (foul-smelling ethyl isocyanide) + 3KCl + 3H₂O. (b) Conc. HCl: C₂H₅NH₂ + HCl → C₂H₅NH₃⁺Cl⁻. (c) Acylation: C₂H₅NH₂ + CH₃COCl → CH₃CONHC₂H₅ + HCl. (d) Nitrous acid: C₂H₅NH₂ + HNO₂ → C₂H₅OH + N₂ + H₂O. (e) Alkylation: C₂H₅NH₂ + 3CH₃Br → C₂H₅N⁺(CH₃)₃Br⁻ + 2HBr (quaternary salt with excess halide).

p: Give a test to distinguish an alkyl from an aryl primary amine.
Separate ethylamine and dimethylamine from their mixture by Hoffmann's method.
Arrange propylamine, ethylmethylamine and trimethylamine in increasing order of basic strength.
Amines.r: (a) Azo-dye test with NaNO₂/HCl at 273 K followed by alkaline β-naphthol: an aryl amine gives an orange-red azo dye, an alkyl amine does not (the alkyl diazonium salt decomposes at once to an alcohol and N₂). (b) Ethylamine (primary) and dimethylamine (secondary) are heated with diethyl oxalate. Ethylamine gives the solid N,N′-diethyloxamide, (CONHC₂H₅)₂; dimethylamine gives the liquid ester C₂H₅OOC–CO–N(CH₃)₂. The liquid is distilled from the solid. Each is boiled with aqueous KOH to regenerate the amine: (CONHC₂H₅)₂ + 2KOH → 2C₂H₅NH₂ + (COOK)₂.

p: Describe two methods of preparing aniline.
Write the reactions of aniline with (i) acetyl chloride, (ii) bromine water, (iii) NaNO₂/HCl at 273 K, (iv) chloroform and alcoholic KOH.
What is a coupling reaction? Give an example.
Amines.r: (a) (i) Reduction of nitrobenzene: C₆H₅NO₂ + 6[H] → (Sn/HCl, then NaOH) C₆H₅NH₂ + 2H₂O. (ii) From phenol: C₆H₅OH + NH₃ → (anhydrous ZnCl₂, 573 K, pressure) C₆H₅NH₂ + H₂O. (b) (i) C₆H₅NH₂ + CH₃COCl → C₆H₅NHCOCH₃ (acetanilide) + HCl. (ii) C₆H₅NH₂ + 3Br₂ → 2,4,6-tribromoaniline (white precipitate) + 3HBr. (iii) C₆H₅NH₂ + NaNO₂ + 2HCl → C₆H₅N₂Cl + NaCl + 2H₂O. (iv) C₆H₅NH₂ + CHCl₃ + 3KOH → C₆H₅NC (phenyl isocyanide) + 3KCl + 3H₂O. (c) Coupling is the reaction of a diazonium salt with a phenol or an aromatic amine to form an azo compound, the parent of the azo dyes: C₆H₅N₂Cl + C₆H₅OH → (NaOH, 273 K) p-HOC₆H₄–N=N–C₆H₅ + HCl (p-hydroxyazobenzene, orange).

Amines.q: The number of structural isomers of C₃H₉N is
Which one gives brisk effervescence of nitrogen with nitrous acid at 5 °C?
Amines.w: only a 1° aliphatic amine gives an unstable diazonium salt that releases N₂.

Amines.q: The correct order of basic strength in aqueous solution is
Amines.w: the compromise between +I effect, cation solvation and steric hindrance.

Amines.q: Aniline is a weaker base than ammonia because
o: its lone pair is delocalised into the ring
Amines.w: delocalisation removes the lone pair from service, and the anilinium ion loses that resonance energy.

Amines.q: Benzenediazonium chloride is prepared at 0–5 °C because
o: it decomposes to phenol and N₂ above 5 °C

Amines.q: The Hinsberg product of a secondary amine is
Amines.w: C₆H₅SO₂NR₂ has no acidic N–H, so it cannot form a sodium salt.

Amines.q: Classify amines with one example each, and write the four structural isomers of C₃H₉N with their IUPAC names.
Amines.r: See §16.1: 1° R–NH₂ (CH₃NH₂), 2° R₂NH ((CH₃)₂NH), 3° R₃N ((CH₃)₃N). Isomers of C₃H₉N: propan-1-amine, propan-2-amine (both 1°), N-methylethanamine (2°), N,N-dimethylmethanamine (3°).

Amines.q: Describe Hoffmann's method for separating a mixture of 1°, 2° and 3° amines, with equations.
Amines.r: Warm the mixture with diethyl oxalate. 1° → solid oxamide, (COOC₂H₅)₂ + 2RNH₂ → (CONHR)₂ + 2C₂H₅OH; 2° → liquid oxamic ester, (COOC₂H₅)₂ + R₂NH → C₂H₅OOC·CO·NR₂ + C₂H₅OH; 3° does not react and distils over unchanged. Filter the solid from the liquid, then hydrolyse each with NaOH: (CONHR)₂ + 2NaOH → 2RNH₂ + (COONa)₂.

Amines.q: How will you distinguish between propan-1-amine, N-methylethanamine and trimethylamine? Give reagents, equations and observations.
Amines.r: Use NaNO₂ + dilute HCl at 0–5 °C. Propan-1-amine: brisk N₂, C₃H₇NH₂ + HNO₂ → C₃H₇OH + N₂↑ + H₂O. N-Methylethanamine: yellow oil, CH₃NHC₂H₅ + HNO₂ → CH₃N(NO)C₂H₅ + H₂O. Trimethylamine: clear solution of [(CH₃)₃NH]⁺NO₂⁻ only. Confirm the first with the carbylamine test, C₃H₇NH₂ + CHCl₃ + 3KOH → C₃H₇NC + 3KCl + 3H₂O.

Amines.q: Calculate the pH of a 0.050 mol dm⁻³ solution of ethylamine ($K_b = 5.0\times10^{-4}$).
What is diazotisation? Give the equation and explain the coupling reaction of benzenediazonium chloride with phenol.
Amines.r: Diazotisation is the conversion of a primary aromatic amine into a diazonium salt with nitrous acid at 0–5 °C: C₆H₅NH₂ + NaNO₂ + 2HCl → C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + NaCl + 2H₂O. The diazonium ion is a weak electrophile, so it attacks only a strongly activated ring. With phenol in weak alkali (pH 9–10, which generates the more reactive phenoxide) it substitutes at the para position: C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ + C₆H₅OH → p-HO–C₆H₄–N=N–C₆H₅ + HCl, an orange azo dye.

p: How is aniline prepared from nitrobenzene and from phenol? Give equations and conditions.
Compare the basicity of aniline with that of methylamine and ammonia, with reasons.
Why does bromine water give 2,4,6-tribromoaniline immediately, whereas p-bromoaniline needs a three-step route?
Amines.r: (a) C₆H₅NO₂ + 6[H] --Sn/conc. HCl--> C₆H₅NH₂ + 2H₂O (industrially 4C₆H₅NO₂ + 9Fe + 4H₂O → 4C₆H₅NH₂ + 3Fe₃O₄); and C₆H₅OH + NH₃ --ZnCl₂, 300 °C, pressure--> C₆H₅NH₂ + H₂O. (b) Basicity CH₃NH₂ ($pK_b$ 3.36) > NH₃ (4.75) > C₆H₅NH₂ (9.38). Methylamine is strengthened by the +I effect of CH₃; aniline is weakened because the lone pair is delocalised into the ring and because the anilinium ion loses that resonance stabilisation on protonation. (c) –NH₂ is so strongly activating that all three free ortho/para positions react at once with bromine water, giving the tribromo compound.

p: Give the reactions of a primary amine with chloroform and alcoholic KOH, with an acid chloride, with an alkyl halide and with nitrous acid.
8.85 g of ethanamide is subjected to the Hofmann bromamide reaction with a 70 % yield. Name the product and calculate its mass.
Amines.r: (a) Carbylamine: RNH₂ + CHCl₃ + 3KOH → RNC + 3KCl + 3H₂O. Acylation: CH₃NH₂ + CH₃COCl → CH₃NHCOCH₃ + HCl. Alkylation: CH₃NH₂ + CH₃I → (CH₃)₂NH·HI, continuing to (CH₃)₃N and (CH₃)₄N⁺I⁻. Nitrous acid: RNH₂ + HNO₂ → ROH + N₂↑ + H₂O. (b) Moles of CH₃CONH₂ = 8.85 / 59 = 0.150 mol. The product is methylamine, CH₃NH₂ (M = 31). Theoretical mass = 0.150 × 31 = 4.65 g; at 70 % yield, mass = 4.65 × 0.70 = 3.26 g.

Amines.q: Compare the basicity of aliphatic amines and aniline, explain the preparation of aniline and its conversion to a diazonium salt and an azo dye.

Organometallic Compounds.q: The first π-bonded organometallic compound to be synthesised, containing ethene, is
Organometallic Compounds.w: K[PtCl₃(C₂H₄)]·H₂O, prepared by Zeise in 1830; the ethene is held side-on by its π electrons.

Organometallic Compounds.q: Of CH₃MgI, Ni(CO)₄, C₂H₅Li, C₂H₅ONa and (C₄H₉)₂SnCl₂, the organometallic compounds are
Organometallic Compounds.w: sodium ethoxide has a Na–O bond, not a Na–C bond, so it is simply a salt. Every other compound listed has a direct metal–carbon bond, including the carbonyl of nickel.

Organometallic Compounds.q: To prepare a primary alcohol from a Grignard reagent, the carbonyl compound used must be
Organometallic Compounds.w: only methanal adds to give RCH₂OH; ethanal would give a secondary alcohol and propanone a tertiary one.

Organometallic Compounds.q: Ethylmagnesium bromide treated with water gives
Organometallic Compounds.w: water is an acid towards the carbanion-like carbon, which is protonated to the alkane. This is why the ether and the apparatus must be perfectly dry.

Organometallic Compounds.q: In a Grignard reagent the carbon attached to magnesium behaves as
Organometallic Compounds.w: magnesium is far more electropositive than carbon, so the carbon carries a partial negative charge and attacks electrophilic carbonyl carbons.

Organometallic Compounds.q: Which of the following are organometallic compounds: CH₃MgI, Ni(CO)₄, C₂H₅Li, C₂H₅ONa, (C₄H₉)₂SnCl₂? Define an organometallic compound and justify your answer. [1+4]
Organometallic Compounds.r: An organometallic compound contains at least one direct bond between a metal and a carbon atom. CH₃MgI (Mg–C), Ni(CO)₄ (Ni–C of the carbonyl), C₂H₅Li (Li–C) and (C₄H₉)₂SnCl₂ (Sn–C) are organometallic. C₂H₅ONa is not: sodium is bonded to oxygen (a metal alkoxide), so there is no metal–carbon bond.

p: How is a Grignard reagent prepared from a haloalkane and from a haloarene?
Why must the preparation be carried out in dry ether?
Write the reaction of CH₃MgBr with water.
What product results from CH₃MgBr and HCN?
Organometallic Compounds.r: (a) From a haloalkane: CH₃CH₂Br + Mg → (dry ether) CH₃CH₂MgBr. From a haloarene: C₆H₅Br + Mg → (dry ether, or THF) C₆H₅MgBr. (b) Grignard reagents are strongly basic and are destroyed by any water or alcohol; ether also dissolves the reagent by co-ordinating to magnesium. (c) CH₃MgBr + H₂O → CH₄ + Mg(OH)Br. (d) With HCN the Grignard reagent takes up the acidic hydrogen: CH₃MgBr + HCN → CH₄ + Mg(CN)Br (so HCN is a proton source; addition to a nitrile carbon needs RCN, not HCN).

Organometallic Compounds.q: How are a primary, a secondary and a tertiary alcohol prepared from Grignard reagents? Write one equation for each.
Organometallic Compounds.r: Grignard reagent + carbonyl compound, then hydrolysis: - Primary alcohol: with methanal, RMgX + HCHO → RCH₂OMgX → (H₂O) RCH₂OH. Example: CH₃MgBr + HCHO → CH₃CH₂OH (ethanol) after hydrolysis. - Secondary alcohol: with any other aldehyde, RMgX + R′CHO → R(R′)CHOH. Example: CH₃MgBr + CH₃CHO → CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ (propan-2-ol). - Tertiary alcohol: with a ketone, RMgX + R′COR″ → R(R′)(R″)COH. Example: CH₃MgBr + CH₃COCH₃ → (CH₃)₃COH (2-methylpropan-2-ol).

Organometallic Compounds.q: Which is not an organometallic compound?
Organometallic Compounds.w: sodium is bonded to oxygen, not to carbon.

Organometallic Compounds.q: A Grignard reagent reacts with methanal to give, after hydrolysis, a
Organometallic Compounds.w: HCHO supplies only one carbon substituent, so R–CH₂OH results.

Organometallic Compounds.q: The C–M bond is most ionic in
Organometallic Compounds.w: lithium has the lowest electronegativity, Δχ = 1.57.

Organometallic Compounds.q: Dry ether is used in preparing a Grignard reagent because
o: its oxygen lone pairs coordinate to magnesium
Organometallic Compounds.w: coordination stabilises the magnesium and keeps RMgX in solution.

Organometallic Compounds.q: Define an organometallic compound. Give the general formula and one example each of organolithium, organocopper and organocadmium compounds.
Explain the nature of the carbon–metal bond and use it to account for the reactivity order RLi > RMgX > R₂Cd.
Organometallic Compounds.r: Carbon (χ = 2.55) is more electronegative than the metals, so the bonding pair lies nearer carbon: Cδ⁻–Mδ⁺. The bigger the electronegativity difference the more ionic the bond and the freer the carbanion. Δχ is 1.57 for C–Li (≈46 % ionic), 1.24 for C–Mg (≈32 %) and 0.86 for C–Cd (≈17 %), giving RLi > RMgX > R₂Cd.

Organometallic Compounds.q: How is ethylmagnesium bromide prepared? State three precautions and explain why chlorobenzene does not form a Grignard reagent in ether.
Organometallic Compounds.r: C₂H₅Br + Mg --dry ether--> C₂H₅MgBr. Precautions: (i) all apparatus and the ether must be perfectly dry, since water destroys the reagent; (ii) clean Mg turnings and a crystal of iodine are used to start the reaction; (iii) the mixture is kept away from air and moisture and gently refluxed. Chlorobenzene fails because the C–Cl bond in a haloarene has partial double-bond character (resonance) and is too strong to be attacked by Mg in ether; THF at 66 °C is needed instead.

Organometallic Compounds.q: How would you obtain (i) propan-1-ol, (ii) propan-2-ol and (iii) 2-methylpropan-2-ol from a Grignard reagent? Give equations.
Organometallic Compounds.r: (i) C₂H₅MgBr + HCHO → C₂H₅CH₂OMgBr --H₃O⁺--> CH₃CH₂CH₂OH (1°). (ii) CH₃MgI + CH₃CHO → (CH₃)₂CHOMgI --H₃O⁺--> (CH₃)₂CHOH. (iii) CH₃MgI + CH₃COCH₃ → (CH₃)₃COMgI --H₃O⁺--> (CH₃)₃COH.

p: How is a Grignard reagent prepared from a haloalkane and from a haloarene? Give equations and conditions.
Describe its reactions with water, carbon dioxide, an ester and a nitrile, giving the product in each case.
Organometallic Compounds.r: (a) CH₃CH₂Br + Mg --dry ether--> CH₃CH₂MgBr; C₆H₅Br + Mg --dry ether--> C₆H₅MgBr. Absolutely anhydrous conditions, clean magnesium, a crystal of iodine to initiate; chlorobenzene requires THF at 66 °C. (b) Water: CH₃MgI + H₂O → CH₄↑ + Mg(OH)I (alkane). CO₂: C₂H₅MgBr + CO₂ → C₂H₅COOMgBr, then H₃O⁺ gives propanoic acid. Ester: two equivalents add, giving a tertiary alcohol with two identical groups, e.g. CH₃COOC₂H₅ + 2CH₃MgI → (CH₃)₃COH after hydrolysis. Nitrile: addition to C≡N gives a ketimine salt which hydrolyses to a ketone, CH₃MgI + CH₃CN → CH₃C(=NMgI)CH₃ --H₃O⁺--> CH₃COCH₃.

p: Show how 1°, 2° and 3° alcohols are prepared from Grignard reagents, using ethanal, methanal and propanone as the carbonyl compounds.
0.90 g of a compound of molar mass 90 g mol⁻¹ liberates 448 cm³ of methane at STP with excess CH₃MgI. How many active hydrogen atoms has it?
Organometallic Compounds.r: (a) HCHO + CH₃MgI → ethanol (1°); CH₃CHO + CH₃MgI → propan-2-ol (2°); CH₃COCH₃ + CH₃MgI → 2-methylpropan-2-ol (3°). Each requires acid hydrolysis of the alkoxide intermediate R–OMgI. (b) Moles of CH₄ = 0.448 / 22.4 = 0.0200 mol. Moles of compound = 0.90 / 90 = 0.0100 mol. Ratio 2: 1, so the molecule has 2 active hydrogen atoms — consistent with lactic acid, CH₃CH(OH)COOH (M = 90), which has one –OH and one –COOH hydrogen.

Organometallic Compounds.q: Describe the preparation of the Grignard reagent and its reactions with aldehydes, ketones, carbon dioxide and water, showing the synthesis of primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols.
Which of the following metals is commonly used to form Grignard reagents?
Organometallic Compounds.w: Magnesium forms Grignard reagents with alkyl halides.

Chemistry in the service of mankind.q: The monomer of Teflon is
Chemistry in the service of mankind.w: polytetrafluoroethene is made by the addition polymerisation of CF₂=CF₂; the C–F bonds give it its non-stick, chemically inert surface.

Chemistry in the service of mankind.q: Bakelite is obtained from methanal and
Chemistry in the service of mankind.w: phenol and methanal condense to a cross-linked, three-dimensional thermosetting network.

Chemistry in the service of mankind.q: Buna-S is an example of
Chemistry in the service of mankind.w: a butadiene–styrene copolymer with rubber-like elasticity.

Chemistry in the service of mankind.q: Indigo is applied to cloth as
Chemistry in the service of mankind.w: indigo is insoluble, so it is reduced in a vat to the soluble leuco form, taken up by the fibre, and re-oxidised in air.

p: Define condensation polymerisation and give the monomers of Bakelite.
How are addition and condensation polymers formed? Give one example of each.
Chemistry in the service of mankind.r: (a) Condensation polymerisation is the joining of many molecules of one or more monomers, each with two or more functional groups, with the loss of a small molecule such as water or HCl at every step. Bakelite is formed from phenol (C₆H₅OH) and methanal (HCHO). (b) Addition polymers are formed by the repeated addition of unsaturated monomers (alkenes) with no loss of atoms: n CH₂=CH₂ → (–CH₂–CH₂–)n, polythene. Condensation polymers are formed from bifunctional monomers with elimination of water: n H₂N(CH₂)₆NH₂ + n HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH → nylon 6,6 + 2n H₂O.

p: Differentiate between a homopolymer and a copolymer, with one example of each.
Name the monomers of polystyrene and Bakelite and write their molecular formulae.
Chemistry in the service of mankind.r: (a) A homopolymer is made of one kind of monomer: polythene from ethene, (–CH₂–CH₂–)n. A copolymer is made from two or more different monomers: Buna-S from buta-1,3-diene and styrene. (b) Polystyrene: styrene (phenylethene), C₆H₅CH=CH₂, molecular formula C₈H₈. Bakelite: phenol, C₆H₅OH (C₆H₆O), and methanal, HCHO (CH₂O). (c) Polystyrene is used for disposable cups, packaging foam and thermal insulation.

Chemistry in the service of mankind.q: Give the structural formula of the monomer(s) and one use of
Chemistry in the service of mankind.r: (a) Nylon 6,6: hexane-1,6-diamine, H₂N–(CH₂)₆–NH₂, and hexanedioic acid (adipic acid), HOOC–(CH₂)₄–COOH. Use: textile fibres, ropes, fishing nets, parachutes. (b) Polystyrene: styrene, C₆H₅–CH=CH₂. Use: packaging, toys, insulation. (c) A fibre is a polymer with strong intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonds in nylon) that can be drawn into long threads; nylon and terylene are synthetic fibres, and cotton and silk are natural.

p: Give the structural formulae of aspirin and DDT.
Differentiate between an antipyretic and an analgesic drug with one example of each.
What is a habit-forming drug? [1], model set B for (b))
Chemistry in the service of mankind.r: (a) Aspirin (2-acetoxybenzoic acid): a benzene ring with –COOH and –OCOCH₃ on adjacent carbons, C₆H₄(OCOCH₃)COOH. DDT: two p-chlorophenyl groups on one carbon that also carries a CCl₃ group, (ClC₆H₄)₂CH–CCl₃. (b) An antipyretic lowers raised body temperature (paracetamol); an analgesic relieves pain without loss of consciousness (aspirin, ibuprofen). Paracetamol acts as both. (c) A habit-forming drug causes physical or psychological dependence, so the user needs more and more of it (morphine, heroin, cocaine, alcohol, tobacco).

Chemistry in the service of mankind.q: Give the monomer(s), the type of polymerisation and one use of each of the following polymers: polythene, PVC, Teflon, polystyrene, nylon 6,6 and Bakelite. [6] State what elastomers are, with an example.

p: List the characteristics of an ideal drug.
Classify common drugs with one example each.
What are insecticides, herbicides and fungicides? Give an example of each.
Chemistry in the service of mankind.r: (a) An ideal drug (i) acts on the target site only, (ii) has few or no side effects, (iii) is effective in a small dose, and (iv) is non-addictive and stable. (b) Classification: analgesics (aspirin, paracetamol); antipyretics (paracetamol); antibiotics (penicillin); antiseptics and disinfectants (dettol, boric acid, chlorine); tranquillisers (diazepam); antacids (Mg(OH)₂, NaHCO₃); anaesthetics (chloroform, ether, N₂O). (c) Drug addiction is physical and mental dependence on a drug such that stopping it causes withdrawal symptoms. (d) Insecticides kill insects (DDT, malathion); herbicides kill weeds (2,4-D); fungicides kill fungi (Bordeaux mixture, CuSO₄ + Ca(OH)₂).

Chemistry in the service of mankind.q: The monomer of Teflon is
In Witt's theory, –N=N– is a
Chemistry in the service of mankind.w: the azo group carries the colour.

Chemistry in the service of mankind.q: Indigo is applied to cotton as a
Chemistry in the service of mankind.w: it is reduced to the soluble leuco form, absorbed, then air-oxidised inside the fibre.

Chemistry in the service of mankind.q: Distinguish between addition and condensation polymerisation, with two examples of each.
Chemistry in the service of mankind.r: See the table in §18.1. Addition: unsaturated monomer, nothing eliminated, same empirical formula (polythene, PVC). Condensation: bifunctional monomers, a small molecule such as H₂O eliminated, different empirical formula (nylon-6,6, bakelite).

Chemistry in the service of mankind.q: Give the monomer, type of polymerisation and one use of polythene, PVC, polystyrene and bakelite.
Chemistry in the service of mankind.r: Polythene — ethene, addition, carrier bags and water tanks. PVC — chloroethene, addition, pipes and raincoats. Polystyrene — styrene, addition, thermocol packing. Bakelite — phenol + methanal, condensation, electrical switches.

Chemistry in the service of mankind.q: What is a dye? Explain Witt's theory with methyl orange as the example, and classify dyes on the basis of their method of application.
Chemistry in the service of mankind.r: A dye is a coloured compound that can be fixed to a fabric and resists light and washing. Witt: a chromophore gives colour and an auxochrome deepens it and binds the dye to the fibre. In methyl orange the chromophore is –N=N– and the auxochromes are –N(CH₃)₂ and –SO₃Na. By application: acid, basic, direct, vat, mordant, disperse, reactive and ingrain dyes (one example each, as in §18.3).

Chemistry in the service of mankind.q: Define a drug. State four characteristics of a good drug and distinguish between an antiseptic and a disinfectant with examples.
Chemistry in the service of mankind.r: A drug is a low-molecular-mass chemical that acts on a biological target to diagnose, prevent or cure disease. Good drug: effective at a small dose, selectively toxic, few side effects, not habit-forming (also stable, cheap, excretable). An antiseptic (dettol, tincture of iodine) is applied to living tissue; a disinfectant (1 % phenol, bleaching powder) to floors, drains and instruments. Phenol is an antiseptic at 0.2 % and a disinfectant at 1 %.

Chemistry in the service of mankind.q: A sample of polythene has an average molar mass of 42,000 g mol⁻¹. Find its degree of polymerisation.
Chemistry in the service of mankind.r: Monomer is ethene, M = 28 g mol⁻¹. $n = 42000/28 = \mathbf{1500}$ units.

Chemistry in the service of mankind.q: What are habit-forming drugs? Name the four types with one example each and state two harmful effects of drug addiction.
Chemistry in the service of mankind.r: Habit-forming (addictive) drugs act on the central nervous system and cause tolerance and dependence. Stimulants — amphetamine; depressants — barbiturates; narcotic analgesics — morphine; hallucinogens — cannabis. Harmful effects: damage to liver, brain and kidneys; spread of HIV and hepatitis B through shared needles; loss of study, work and family life. Controlled in Nepal by the Narcotic Drugs (Control) Act, 2033.

p: Classify polymers on the basis of the mode of polymerisation, of physical properties and of origin, giving two examples of each class.
Write the equation for the formation of nylon-6,6 and calculate the mass of nylon obtained from 29.2 g of adipic acid with excess diamine.
Chemistry in the service of mankind.r: (a) By mode: addition (polythene, PVC) and condensation (nylon-6,6, bakelite). By physical property: elastomers (natural rubber, buna-S), fibres (nylon-6,6, terylene), thermoplastics (polythene, polystyrene), thermosets (bakelite, melamine). By origin: natural (starch, cellulose), semi-synthetic (rayon, cellulose acetate) and synthetic (nylon, PVC). (b) n H₂N(CH₂)₆NH₂ + n HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH → –[NH(CH₂)₆NHCO(CH₂)₄CO]ₙ– + 2n H₂O. Moles of adipic acid = 29.2 / 146 = 0.200 mol; repeat-unit mass = 146 + 116 - 36 = 226 g mol⁻¹; mass of nylon = 0.200 × 226 = 45.2 g (with 0.400 × 18 = 7.2 g of water).
