p: Classify dyes on the basis of structure, with an example of each.
What are pesticides? Distinguish between insecticides, herbicides and fungicides with two examples each, and give two harmful effects of using persistent pesticides such as DDT.
Chemistry in the service of mankind.r: (a) Azo (methyl orange), triphenylmethane (malachite green), indigoid (indigo), anthraquinone (alizarin), nitro (picric acid), phthalein (phenolphthalein). (b) A pesticide is a chemical used to kill or control pests. Insecticides kill insects (DDT, malathion); herbicides kill weeds (2,4-D, glyphosate); fungicides kill fungi (Bordeaux mixture, sulphur dust). Harmful effects of DDT-type pesticides: they persist for years and biomagnify up the food chain, poisoning fish and birds at the top; residues remain on food and cause chronic poisoning of farmers; pests also develop resistance. DDT is banned in Nepal for this reason.

Chemistry in the service of mankind.q: Define polymerisation, compare addition and condensation polymers, and describe the preparation and uses of polythene, PVC, Teflon, nylon-6,6 and Bakelite.
Classify drugs with examples, and distinguish insecticides, herbicides and fungicides.
What does the acronym 'PVC' stand for in the context of plastics used in construction and plumbing?
Chemistry in the service of mankind.w: PVC stands for Polyvinyl Chloride, which is widely used in construction and plumbing due to its durability and chemical resistance.

Chemistry in the service of mankind.q: Which enzyme is primarily used in the production of cheese to coagulate milk proteins?
Chemistry in the service of mankind.w: Chymosin is an enzyme that catalyzes the coagulation of casein, a major milk protein, which is crucial for cheese production.

Chemistry in the service of mankind.q: In water treatment processes, what is the primary purpose of adding chlorine to water?
Chemistry in the service of mankind.w: The main purpose of chlorination in water treatment is to disinfect the water by killing harmful microorganisms.

Cement.q: The effect of adding calcium sulphate to cement is to
Cement.w: gypsum reacts with tricalcium aluminate to form a coating of ettringite that delays hydration, giving workers time to place the concrete.

Cement.q: The constituent mainly responsible for the early strength of cement is
Cement.w: tricalcium silicate hydrates within about a week; C₂S continues for months and supplies the final strength.

Cement.q: The clinkering zone of the rotary kiln operates at about
Cement.w: about 1673–1773 K, hot enough to part-fuse the charge into clinker nodules.

Cement.q: Portland pozzolana cement contains pozzolanic material to the extent of
Cement.w: the pozzolana replaces part of the clinker, lowering the heat of hydration and improving resistance to sulphates.

Cement.q: The first cement factory established in Nepal was at
Cement.w: Himal Cement at Chobhar, commissioned in 1974.

p: Why is gypsum added to the clinker?
Name two instruments used for the quality control of cement.
Cement.r: (a) Portland cement is a fine grey powder made by burning a mixture of limestone (CaCO₃) and clay to clinker and grinding it with a little gypsum; it sets and hardens by hydration, even under water (a hydraulic cement). (b) The major components are calcium oxide (lime, 60–67 %), silica (17–25 %), alumina (3–8 %), iron oxide (0.5–6 %), magnesia and SO₃, present in the clinker as tricalcium silicate (C₃S), dicalcium silicate (C₂S), tricalcium aluminate (C₃A) and tetracalcium aluminoferrite (C₄AF). (c) Gypsum (2–5 %) acts as a retarder: without it, tricalcium aluminate reacts with water at once and the cement undergoes flash set;

p: Classify cement on the basis of setting and hardening.

Cement.q: Explain the quality control system in the manufacture of Portland cement.
Cement.r: Quality control is exercised at every stage. (i) Raw materials: samples of limestone and clay are analysed chemically and the lime saturation and the hydraulic and silica moduli are checked so that the raw mix has the correct composition. (ii) Kiln: temperature, flame and the amount of free lime in the clinker are monitored, since excess free lime causes unsoundness. (iii) Final grinding: the gypsum dose (2–5 %) and the fineness are controlled (Blaine apparatus, sieve test).

Cement.q: Describe the manufacture of Portland cement: the raw materials, the main steps with the flow sheet, the chemical composition of the clinker and the role of gypsum.
Cement.r: Raw materials: limestone (about 75 %, the source of CaO), clay or shale (SiO₂, Al₂O₃, Fe₂O₃), with sand, bauxite or iron ore to correct the composition, gypsum as a retarder, and coal or fuel oil as fuel. Steps (see the flow sheet in short answer 2): 1. Crushing and grinding. Limestone and clay are crushed and ground, dry or with water, to a fine mix (raw meal or slurry), blended so that the lime content is correct. 2. Strong heating in the rotary kiln (60–150 m long, inclined 1 in 30, turning 1–2 rpm): the charge is dried; at about 900 °C the limestone decomposes, CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂;

Cement.q: The approximate percentage of lime (CaO) in ordinary Portland cement is
Cement.w: lime is the largest single oxide.

Cement.q: Gypsum is added to cement clinker to
Cement.w: it stops the flash set caused by C₃A.

Cement.q: Which Bogue compound is mainly responsible for early strength?
Cement.w: C₃S hydrates in hours to days.

Cement.q: Nepal's largest cement plant is located in
Cement.w: the Hongshi–Shivam plant in Dhading, about 2.4 Mt yr⁻¹.

Cement.q: What is cement? Give the average composition of OPC and state the two moduli that control the raw mix.
Cement.r: See §19.1: a hydraulic binder of calcium silicates and aluminates made by burning limestone with clay at 1400–1500 °C and grinding the clinker with gypsum. CaO 60–67 %, SiO₂ 17–25 %, Al₂O₃ 3–8 %, Fe₂O₃ 0.5–6 %. Hydraulic modulus CaO/(SiO₂+Al₂O₃+Fe₂O₃) ≈ 2 and silica modulus SiO₂/(Al₂O₃+Fe₂O₃) = 2.5–4.

Cement.q: Name the raw materials used in cement manufacture and state the oxide each supplies.
Cement.r: Calcareous — limestone, chalk, marl (CaO); argillaceous — clay, shale (SiO₂, Al₂O₃, Fe₂O₃); correctives — sand (SiO₂), bauxite (Al₂O₃), iron ore (Fe₂O₃); gypsum (SO₃) added at the grinding stage.

Cement.q: Describe the zones of a rotary kiln with their temperatures and the chemical changes in each.
Cement.r: Drying zone up to 400 °C, water removed; calcination zone 900–1000 °C, CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂↑ and the clay breaks down; clinkering zone 1400–1500 °C, where 2CaO + SiO₂ → Ca₂SiO₄, 3CaO + SiO₂ → Ca₃SiO₅, 3CaO + Al₂O₃ → Ca₃Al₂O₆ and 4CaO + Al₂O₃ + Fe₂O₃ → Ca₄Al₂Fe₂O₁₀; then rapid cooling to about 100 °C.

Cement.q: What are Bogue compounds? Give their formulae and the property each controls. Why is gypsum added?
Cement.r: C₃S (3CaO·SiO₂) early strength; C₂S (2CaO·SiO₂) later strength; C₃A (3CaO·Al₂O₃) flash set, most heat, poor sulphate resistance; C₄AF (4CaO·Al₂O₃·Fe₂O₃) grey colour, little strength. Gypsum reacts with C₃A to form ettringite, coating the grains and giving a workable setting time.

Cement.q: Distinguish between OPC and PPC, and explain the chemistry by which a pozzolana improves durability.
Cement.r: See the table in §19.4. Pozzolana reacts with the Ca(OH)₂ set free during hydration: Ca(OH)₂ + SiO₂ + H₂O → calcium silicate hydrate gel. Removing the soluble calcium hydroxide and adding more gel makes the concrete denser, less permeable and more resistant to sulphate and chloride attack, while lowering the heat of hydration.

p: What are the setting and hardening reactions of cement? Write the equations for C₃S and C₂S.

A cement contains 45 % C₃S, 30 % C₂S, 12 % C₃A and 8 % C₄AF. Taking heats of hydration of 500, 260, 865 and 420 J g⁻¹, calculate the heat evolved per kilogram, and say whether this cement is suitable for a thick dam wall.
Cement.r: (a) Setting and hardening are hydration reactions producing tobermorite (calcium silicate hydrate) gel and calcium hydroxide: 2Ca₃SiO₅ + 6H₂O → Ca₃Si₂O₇·3H₂O + 3Ca(OH)₂ (fast, early strength) and 2Ca₂SiO₄ + 4H₂O → Ca₃Si₂O₇·3H₂O + Ca(OH)₂ (slow, later strength). The interlocking gel needles bind the aggregate, so the concrete must be kept wet while curing. (b) q = 0.45(500) + 0.30(260) + 0.12(865) + 0.08(420) = 225 + 78 + 103.8 + 33.6 = 440.4 J g⁻¹, so 440 kJ per kg. This is higher than an ordinary cement (≈435 kJ kg⁻¹) because of its large C₃A content, so it is not suitable for a thick dam wall; a low-heat PPC should be used instead.

Cement.q: Describe the manufacture of Portland cement by the dry process with the chemistry of the kiln, the composition of cement and the setting reactions, and mention the cement industry of Nepal.

Paper and Pulp.q: In the production of paper, removal of which component increases fibre-to-fibre bonding?
Paper and Pulp.w: lignin encrusts the fibres and prevents the hydrogen bonds between cellulose chains that give paper its strength. Removing cellulose would destroy the paper.

Paper and Pulp.q: The chemicals used in the Kraft (sulphate) process are
Paper and Pulp.w: caustic soda with sodium sulphide dissolves lignin and gives an unusually strong ("kraft" means strength) pulp.

Paper and Pulp.q: Mechanical pulping gives a yield of about
Paper and Pulp.w: nothing is dissolved away, so almost all the wood is recovered; the price is a weak, dark, short-lived paper.

Paper and Pulp.q: Sizing of paper is carried out with
Paper and Pulp.w: rosin precipitated by alum coats the fibres and makes the sheet resistant to the spread of aqueous ink.

Paper and Pulp.q: China clay is added to paper mainly to
Paper and Pulp.w: fillers occupy the spaces between fibres, raising opacity and smoothness, although they slightly reduce strength.

Paper and Pulp.q: The grammage of paper is expressed in
Paper and Pulp.w: grams per square metre; ordinary copier paper is about 70–80 GSM.

p: What are the raw materials for the production of paper?
Differentiate between the fibrous and non-fibrous raw materials.
Paper and Pulp.r: (a) Raw materials are (i) fibrous: wood (spruce, pine), bamboo, straw, bagasse, cotton rags and waste paper, which supply cellulose fibres; and (ii) non-fibrous additives: fillers (china clay, talc, CaCO₃, TiO₂), sizing agents (rosin with alum, starch), dyes and water. (b)

p: Write any two differences between paper and pulp.
Why must lignin be removed from the wood fibre?
Name the two common chemical pulping processes.

Paper and Pulp.q: Describe the stages of paper production with a flow sheet.
Paper and Pulp.r: Raw material (wood, bamboo) → debarking and chipping → pulping (cooking the chips with chemicals, for example white liquor in the Kraft process at about 170 °C, to dissolve the lignin) → washing → bleaching (Cl₂, ClO₂ or H₂O₂ removes the colour) → beating and refining (the fibres are fibrillated in water) → addition of filler, size and dye → sheet formation on a moving wire screen (Fourdrinier machine) → pressing → drying on heated rollers → calendering (smoothing between rollers) → reeling and cutting.

Paper and Pulp.q: Describe the manufacture of paper from wood by the Kraft process, giving the raw materials, the chemicals used, the stages and two properties that decide the quality of paper.
Paper and Pulp.r: Raw materials: wood (spruce, pine, eucalyptus) or bamboo as the fibrous material; white liquor (NaOH + Na₂S), bleach (ClO₂ or H₂O₂), filler (china clay), size (rosin + alum) and water. Stages: (1) Debarking and chipping: logs are debarked and cut into chips of 2–3 cm. (2) Pulping: chips are cooked in a digester with white liquor at about 170 °C and 7–8 atm for 2–4 hours; the alkali and HS⁻ break the lignin into soluble sodium salts and leave the cellulose fibres; the spent dark liquor (black liquor) is burnt to recover the chemicals. (3) Washing and screening remove the liquor and uncooked knots. (4) Bleaching with chlorine dioxide or hydrogen peroxide gives a white pulp.

Paper and Pulp.q: The chief chemical constituent of paper is
The white liquor used in the Kraft process contains
Lignin must be removed from pulp mainly because it
o: is brown and makes the paper yellow in light
Paper and Pulp.w: residual lignin oxidises in light and yellows the sheet.

Paper and Pulp.q: Causticisation of green liquor is represented by
Paper and Pulp.w: lime converts carbonate back to hydroxide.

Paper and Pulp.q: Rosin and alum are added to pulp for
The grammage of ordinary photocopy paper is about
Paper and Pulp.w: 70–80 g m⁻² is the usual office grade.

Paper and Pulp.q: What are pulp and paper? Name the raw materials used for papermaking in Nepal and state one advantage of non-wood fibre.
Paper and Pulp.r: Pulp is the fibrous cellulose mass got by breaking plant material down mechanically or chemically; paper is the sheet formed when dilute pulp is drained on a wire, pressed and dried. Nepali raw materials: babiyo (sabai) grass, rice and wheat straw, bagasse, bamboo, lokta bark and waste paper. Non-wood fibre contains much less lignin, so it needs a milder cook, less chemical and less energy.

Paper and Pulp.q: Compare mechanical and chemical pulping under yield, strength, colour stability and use.
Paper and Pulp.r: See the table in §20.3: mechanical 90–95 % yield, weak short fibres, yellows in light, used for newsprint; chemical 45–55 % yield, strong fibres, colour-stable, used for printing, writing and packaging paper.

Paper and Pulp.q: Describe the Kraft process, giving the composition of white liquor, the cooking conditions and the equations of chemical recovery.
Paper and Pulp.r: Chips are cooked with white liquor (NaOH + Na₂S) at about 170 °C and 7–8 atm for 2–4 hours; lignin dissolves, leaving cellulose. Recovery: Na₂SO₄ + 2C → Na₂S + 2CO₂↑ in the furnace; Na₂CO₃ + Ca(OH)₂ → 2NaOH + CaCO₃↓ in the causticiser; CaCO₃ --Δ--> CaO + CO₂↑ and CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ in the lime kiln.

Paper and Pulp.q: What is the purpose of (i) bleaching, (ii) beating, (iii) sizing and (iv) loading? Name one chemical used in each.
Paper and Pulp.r: (i) Bleaching removes residual lignin and whitens the pulp — ClO₂ or H₂O₂. (ii) Beating frays and swells the fibres so they bond — mechanical, no chemical. (iii) Sizing makes the sheet resist ink spread — rosin with alum, Al₂(SO₄)₃. (iv) Loading fills the gaps for opacity and smoothness — china clay, CaCO₃ or TiO₂.

Paper and Pulp.q: List six properties by which the quality of paper is judged and explain why acid-free paper lasts longer.
Paper and Pulp.r: Grammage, caliper, brightness, opacity, strength (tensile, burst, tear), sizing or Cobb value, ash content, pH, smoothness. Acid-free paper (pH 7–9) is not slowly hydrolysed at its glycosidic links, so the cellulose chains keep their length and the sheet does not become brown and brittle.

Paper and Pulp.q: Describe the manufacture of paper from wood by the sulphate (kraft) process, the stages of paper making and the qualities of paper, and mention hand-made paper of Nepal.

Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Ra.q: When a nucleus emits an α particle, its atomic number
Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Ra.w: the α particle carries away two protons and two neutrons, so Z falls by 2 and A by 4. Option (c) confuses the two numbers.

Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Ra.q: The control rods of a nuclear reactor are made of
Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Ra.w: cadmium and boron absorb neutrons strongly and so control the chain reaction; graphite and heavy water are moderators, which slow neutrons rather than absorb them.

Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Ra.q: Radiocarbon dating uses an isotope of half-life
Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Ra.w: carbon-14 decays with a half-life of 5730 years, which suits archaeological time scales.

p: Differentiate between nuclear reactions and chemical reactions.
What is artificial radioactivity? Give one example. [1+1]
Explain nuclear fission with an equation and the chain reaction.
Describe the use of nuclear energy in power generation and state how it differs from a nuclear weapon.
Give two medical and two industrial uses of radioactivity.
State one harmful effect of nuclear radiation.
Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Ra.r: (a) Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two lighter nuclei, with a large release of energy, when it absorbs a neutron: ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + 3¹₀n + 200 MeV. The three neutrons released each split another uranium nucleus, so a chain reaction is set up. If the chain is uncontrolled the energy is released in a flash (an atomic bomb); if the neutrons are absorbed by control rods (cadmium or boron) it is controlled, as in a reactor. (b) In a nuclear power plant a controlled fission chain heats water, the steam drives turbines and the turbines drive generators; a moderator (graphite or heavy water) slows the neutrons.

Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Ra.q: When a nucleus emits an α-particle, its atomic number
Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Ra.w: α emission removes 2 protons and 2 neutrons.

Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Ra.q: The moderator in a nuclear reactor is used to
Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Ra.w: slow (thermal) neutrons are captured by ²³⁵U far more readily.

Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Ra.q: Distinguish between natural and artificial radioactivity with one example of each.
Compare α, β and γ radiations under nature, charge, ionising power and penetrating power.
Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Ra.r: See the table in §21.1: α is ⁴₂He²⁺, charge +2, ionising power ≈ 10 000, stopped by paper; β is an electron, charge -1, ionising power ≈ 100, stopped by 3 mm of aluminium; γ is an electromagnetic wave, no charge, ionising power 1, needs thick lead.

Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Ra.q: Define becquerel, curie, gray and sievert, and state the relations between the SI and the older units.
Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Ra.r: Becquerel = one disintegration per second; curie = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq; gray = absorbed dose of 1 J kg⁻¹ (1 rad = 0.01 Gy); sievert = absorbed dose × quality factor (1 rem = 0.01 Sv). For β and γ, Q = 1; for α, Q = 20.

Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Ra.q: What is nuclear fission? Write the equation for the fission of ²³⁵U and explain the terms chain reaction and critical mass.
Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Ra.r: Fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into two lighter nuclei with the release of neutrons and energy: ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + 3¹₀n + 200 MeV. The three neutrons can cause three further fissions, so the process becomes self-sustaining — a chain reaction. The critical mass is the smallest mass of fissile material in which enough neutrons are retained (rather than escaping through the surface) for the chain to continue; for pure ²³⁵U it is about 15 kg.

Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Ra.q: Give four industrial and four medical applications of radioactivity, naming the isotope used in each.

p: What are nuclear fission and nuclear fusion? Write one equation for each and compare them under four headings.
Describe the parts of a nuclear reactor and the function of each, and explain why a reactor cannot explode like a bomb.
Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Ra.r: (a) Fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus (²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + 3¹₀n); fusion is the union of light nuclei (²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n + 17.6 MeV). Compare on the nuclei involved, the starting condition (a slow neutron versus 10⁷–10⁸ K), energy per nucleon (0.85 versus 3.5 MeV) and products (radioactive fragments versus helium) — see the table in §21.4. (b) Fuel (UO₂, 3–4 % ²³⁵U) provides the fissile nuclei; the moderator (graphite or D₂O) slows the fast neutrons; control rods of boron or cadmium absorb surplus neutrons and hold the multiplication factor at 1; the coolant carries heat to the boiler; the concrete-and-lead shield stops radiation.

p: Explain the principle of radiocarbon dating and state its limitations.
Each fission of ²³⁵U releases 200 MeV. Calculate the energy released when 0.50 g of ²³⁵U undergoes complete fission. (1 MeV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹³ J)

Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Ra.q: Distinguish nuclear fission from nuclear fusion, describe the working of a nuclear reactor, and solve numerical problems on radioactive decay and energy release.
Which of the following is the correct definition of radioactivity?
o: The process by which unstable atomic nuclei emit particles or energy to reach a more stable state.
The process by which an atom gains electrons to become negatively charged.
The process by which a nucleus splits into two approximately equal parts.
The process by which atoms combine to form molecules.
Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Ra.w: Radioactivity involves the emission of particles or energy from unstable nuclei.

Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Ra.q: Which law states that the rate of radioactive decay of a given substance is proportional to the amount of the substance present?
Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Ra.w: The Law of Radioactive Decay directly relates to the proportionality between the rate of decay and the quantity of substance.

Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Ra.q: In nuclear fission, what is typically split by a neutron to release energy?
Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Ra.w: Uranium-235 is commonly used in nuclear fission reactions due to its ability to sustain a chain reaction upon neutron absorption.

p: How would you apply Hoffmann's method for the separation of 1°, 2° and 3° amines from their mixture?
Paper 2079 General Stream.r: Hoffmann's method separates a mixture of 1°, 2° and 3° amines using diethyl oxalate, (COOC₂H₅)₂, which reacts with the N–H bonds. A primary amine has two N–H, a secondary has one, a tertiary has none. Step 1 — treat with diethyl oxalate. The mixture is warmed with diethyl oxalate: - A primary amine (e.g. ethylamine) replaces both ethoxy groups to give a solid, N,N′-diethyloxamide (dialkyl oxamide, a solid): 2C₂H₅NH₂ + (COOC₂H₅)₂ → (CONHC₂H₅)₂ + 2C₂H₅OH - A secondary amine replaces only one ethoxy group, because after that it has no N–H left to continue.

p: Describe the Open-Hearth process for the manufacture of steel.
Paper 2080 General Stream.r: Open-hearth process (Siemens–Martin process). It is used to convert pig iron into steel of good and controlled quality, using pig iron, scrap iron and iron ore as the charge. Furnace. A large shallow, saucer-shaped hearth, 10 to 15 m long, is built of refractory brick with a low roof. The lining is acidic (silica) if the pig iron is low in phosphorus and basic (dolomite or magnesite, MgO·CaO) if the iron is rich in phosphorus. A pair of regenerators (chambers of checker brickwork) stand at each end. Producer gas and air are pre-heated by passing through the hot bricks of one regenerator, burn over the charge and reach about 1700 K;

p: Give two chemical reactions for the preparation of chlorobenzene. Why does it give ortho and para products during electrophilic substitution reaction? Give its action on chloral.
Paper 2080 General Stream.r: Preparation of chlorobenzene (any two). 1. Direct chlorination of benzene in the dark with a halogen carrier: C₆H₆ + Cl₂ —(anhyd. FeCl₃ or AlCl₃)→ C₆H₅Cl + HCl 2. Sandmeyer reaction: benzenediazonium chloride is warmed with cuprous chloride in HCl: C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ —(CuCl / HCl, Δ)→ C₆H₅Cl + N₂↑ 3. Raschig process (industrial): C₆H₆ + HCl + ½O₂ —(CuCl₂ / FeCl₃, 500 K)→ C₆H₅Cl + H₂O Why ortho and para products? In chlorobenzene, Cl is more electronegative than carbon and withdraws electrons through the σ-bond (-I effect), which deactivates the ring overall.

p: Consider the reaction sequence: A —(SOCl₂)→ B —(NH₃, Δ)→ C —(Br₂ / KOH)→ D —(NaNO₂ / HCl)→ E The compound E is a primary alcohol which gives a positive iodoform test. Identify A, B, C, D and E.
Paper 2080 General Stream.r: E is a primary alcohol that gives the iodoform test, so it must be CH₃CH₂OH (ethanol). Working backwards: - E is formed from D by diazotisation, so D is a primary amine with the same carbon skeleton: CH₃CH₂NH₂, ethanamine. - D is formed from C by Hofmann bromamide degradation (Br₂/KOH), which removes one carbon, so C is propanamide, CH₃CH₂CONH₂. - C is formed by ammonolysis of the acyl chloride B: propanoyl chloride, CH₃CH₂COCl. - B is formed from A with SOCl₂, so A is propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH.

p: Define common ion effect and solubility product principle. Describe three main applications of common ion effect and solubility product principle.
Paper 2081 Technical 9111.r: Common ion effect: the suppression of the ionisation of a weak electrolyte by adding a strong electrolyte that has an ion in common with it. Example: adding NH₄Cl to NH₄OH decreases the OH⁻ concentration, since NH₄OH ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ is pushed to the left. Solubility product principle: in a saturated solution of a sparingly soluble electrolyte at a given temperature, the product of the molar concentrations of its ions, each raised to the power of its coefficient, is constant, $K_{sp}$. For $A_xB_y$: $K_{sp} = [A^{y+}]^x[B^{x-}]^y$. A precipitate forms when the ionic product exceeds $K_{sp}$, and a salt dissolves when the ionic product is less than $K_{sp}$. Applications (any three): 1.

p: What is meant by order of reaction? Derive the expression for the integrated rate equation of a first order reaction.
Paper 2081 Technical 9111.r: Order of reaction is the sum of the powers to which the concentration terms are raised in the experimentally determined rate law. For $aA + bB\to$ products, rate $= k[A]^m[B]^n$ and the order is $m + n$. It is an experimental quantity and may be zero, fractional or an integer. Integrated rate equation for a first order reaction. Take $A\to$ products with initial concentration $[A]_0 = a$. After time $t$ let $x$ mol L⁻¹ have reacted, so $[A] = a - x$. The rate is proportional to the first power of $[A]$: $$\frac{dx}{dt} = k(a - x)$$ Separating the variables, $$\frac{dx}{a - x} = k\,dt$$ Integrating, $$-\ln(a - x) = kt + I$$ At $t = 0$, $x = 0$, so $I = -\ln a$.

Paper 2082 Technical 9111.r: (a) The pH of a solution is the negative logarithm (to base 10) of the hydrogen ion concentration in mol L⁻¹: $\text{pH} = -\log_{10}[\text{H}^+]$. p: Derive and explain the integrated rate equation and the half-life for a zero order reaction.
Paper 2082 Technical 9111.r: Consider a zero order reaction $A \to \text{products}$. The rate is independent of the concentration of the reactant: $$\text{rate} = -\frac{d[A]}{dt} = k[A]^0 = k$$ Rearranging, $d[A] = -k\,dt$. Integrating from $t = 0$ (concentration $[A]_0$) to time $t$ (concentration $[A]$): $$\int_{[A]_0}^{[A]} d[A] = -k\int_0^t dt\ \Rightarrow\ [A] - [A]_0 = -kt$$ $$\boxed{k = \frac{[A]_0 - [A]}{t}\qquad\text{or}\qquad [A] = [A]_0 - kt}$$ This is the integrated rate equation. It is the equation of a straight line: a plot of $[A]$ against $t$ is a straight line of slope $-k$ and intercept $[A]_0$. The unit of $k$ is mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹.

Paper 2082 Technical 9111.r: (a) The standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) consists of a platinum foil coated with platinum black, dipped in a 1 M solution of H⁺ ions (1 M HCl) at 298 K, with pure hydrogen gas bubbled over the foil at 1 atm pressure. Its half cell reaction is $\text{H}^+ + e^- \rightleftharpoons \frac{1}{2}\text{H}_2$, and its potential is arbitrarily taken as exactly 0.00 V at all temperatures. (b) The major application is as a primary reference electrode: it is coupled with any other half cell, and the measured emf of the cell gives the standard electrode potential of that half cell (since $E^\circ_{\text{SHE}} = 0$). It can also be used to measure the pH of a solution.

a: Differentiate between solubility and solubility product. How is the solubility product principle helpful in the qualitative salt analysis?
Paper 2082 Technical 9111.r: Rate of a chemical reaction. It is the change in the concentration of a reactant or product per unit time: $$\text{rate} = -\frac{d[\text{reactant}]}{dt} = +\frac{d[\text{product}]}{dt}\quad(\text{mol L}^{-1}\,\text{s}^{-1})$$ Factors affecting the rate: 1. Concentration. The rate is proportional to the product of the concentrations of the reactants raised to the powers of their orders (law of mass action, $\text{rate} = k[A]^m[B]^n$). More concentrated reactants mean more molecules per unit volume, more collisions per second and a faster reaction. Magnesium burns faster in pure oxygen than in air. 2. Temperature.

p: Define instantaneous rate of reaction. Write down the rate expressions of the following reaction. 2N₂O₅(g) → 4NO₂(g) + O₂(g) If 2.24 litres of O₂ at NTP is produced in 30 minutes, what is the rate of disappearance of N₂O₅(g)?
Paper 2082 General Stream.r: Instantaneous rate: the rate of reaction at a given instant of time, $\displaystyle\lim_{\Delta t\to0}\frac{\Delta C}{\Delta t} = \frac{dC}{dt}$, the slope of the tangent to the concentration–time curve at that instant. Rate expression: $\text{rate} = -\tfrac12\dfrac{d[\text{N}_2\text{O}_5]}{dt} = +\tfrac14\dfrac{d[\text{NO}_2]}{dt} = +\dfrac{d[\text{O}_2]}{dt}$. O₂ produced = $\dfrac{2.24}{22.4} = 0.1$ mol in 30 min, so $\dfrac{d[\text{O}_2]}{dt} = \dfrac{0.1}{30} = 3.33\times10^{-3}$ mol min⁻¹ (taking a 1 L vessel, the paper gives no volume). Then $$-\frac{d[\text{N}_2\text{O}_5]}{dt} = 2\frac{d[\text{O}_2]}{dt} = 6.67\times10^{-3}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}\text{min}^{-1}.$$

p: What is rusting? Describe the electrochemical theory of rusting of iron. List any two methods for the prevention of rusting.
Paper 2082 General Stream.r: Rusting is the slow corrosion of iron in the presence of moist air, forming reddish-brown hydrated ferric oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O. Electrochemical theory: impure iron with moisture, dissolved CO₂/O₂ forms tiny galvanic cells. At the anode (pure iron): Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻. At the cathode (impurity or strained region): O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O (or O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻). The Fe²⁺ ions react: Fe²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Fe(OH)₂, then 4Fe(OH)₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4Fe(OH)₃, which loses water to give Fe₂O₃·xH₂O (rust). Prevention (any two): painting or oiling the surface; galvanising (zinc coating); electroplating with Cr/Ni/Sn; cathodic protection with a sacrificial metal such as Mg or Zn. ### Group C

Data Communication and Networking.r: The first octet 172 lies in 128–191, so it is class B (and a private address, since it is inside 172.16.0.0/12). With mask 255.255.0.0 the first two octets are the network, so the network address is 172.16.0.0 and the broadcast address is 172.16.255.255. There are 16 host bits, so $2^{16}-2 = 65{,}534$ usable hosts. An IP address is a 32-bit logical address assigned by software, used by routers between networks, and it changes when the host joins another network; a MAC address is a 48-bit physical address burned into the NIC, used by switches inside one LAN, and it never changes.
