Neighbours.q: Why did the newly-weds feel "like sojourners in a foreign land" when they first moved into the street?
Neighbours.r: Because the street was full of European migrants whose language, habits and noise were completely unfamiliar to them. They had grown up in the "expansive outer suburbs where good neighbours were seldom seen and never heard", so the daybreak watering, the spitting and the shouting of the Macedonian family made them feel that they, and not the migrants, were the outsiders.

Neighbours.q: What did the Polish widower do with his salvaged lumber for most of the story, and what did he finally build with it?
Neighbours.r: For most of the story he did nothing with it: he hammered nails into wood only to pull them out again, and added to the stack of salvaged timber in his yard without ever building with it. In the late spring he finally began to sink posts and pour cement, and by late summer he had almost completed a two-car garage — although he owned no car.

Neighbours.q: How did the couple's own parents react to the neighbourhood, and how did the couple feel about that reaction?
Neighbours.r: The parents visited and "cast shocked glances across the fence" at the migrant neighbours. The couple, who had themselves been wary only months before, felt "superior and proud" — which shows both how far they had moved and that their tolerance was at that stage still a way of feeling better than somebody else.

Neighbours.q: What did the Macedonian family teach the couple in the spring, and how did the couple behave during it?
Neighbours.r: They taught them to slaughter, pluck and dress the muscovy ducks the couple had kept through the winter. Everyone sat on blocks and upturned buckets, the men butchering and the women plucking, telling "barely understood stories"; the couple felt intoxicated in the haze of down and steam, and "found themselves shouting" — behaving at last exactly like the neighbours whose noise had once appalled them.

Neighbours.q: Why did the little boy next door make the young man nervous at first?
Neighbours.r: Because the boy behaved in ways the young man found crude and could not interpret — he urinated in the street and sprayed the cat from the back step — and because of the way he watched. He would stand at the fence with "only his cobalt eyes showing", so that the young man was observed by a child he could neither see properly nor speak to.

Neighbours.q: What did the young man see when he went outside for more wood on the evening the labour began?
Neighbours.r: In the last light of the day he saw faces at each fence, watching the house — he counted twelve of them. The Macedonian family waved and called out what sounded like their best wishes. It was the first sign that the whole street was keeping watch with him through the night.

Neighbours.q: Discuss the importance of the seasonal cycle in the structure and meaning of "Neighbours".
Neighbours.r: The story has scarcely any plot, and the seasons supply the shape that plot would otherwise give. The couple arrive and endure a period of unmarked, unhappy months; then autumn arrives with the digging and planting of the vegetable patch, which is the first occasion for contact. Winter, with its "vermilion sunsets" and the smell of wood smoke, is the season of exchange — cabbages for grappa and firewood — and the season in which the ducks are kept. Spring brings the killing of the ducks, the full entry of the couple into the life of the street, and the beginning of the pregnancy; the Polish widower's hoarded lumber also finally begins to be used.

A Respectable Woman.q: What picture of Gouvernail had Mrs. Baroda formed before meeting him, and how accurate was it?
A Respectable Woman.r: She had "unconsciously formed an image of him in her mind", picturing him tall, slim and cynical, wearing eyeglasses and carrying his hands in his pockets — and on that basis she decided that she did not like him. The picture was almost entirely wrong: he was slim, but not very tall and not at all cynical, and he wore no eyeglasses and did not keep his hands in his pockets.

A Respectable Woman.q: Why did Mrs. Baroda become "piqued" with her guest?
A Respectable Woman.r: Because he asked nothing of her. She could not understand him, and when she deliberately left him alone with her husband he "took no manner of exception" to it. A hostess whose importance depends on being needed found herself unnecessary, and the injury to her vanity turned her puzzlement into irritation.

A Respectable Woman.q: How did Mrs. Baroda recognise Gouvernail in the darkness of the garden?
A Respectable Woman.r: She could see nothing in the dark but "the approaching red point of a lighted cigar", and she knew from that alone that it must be Gouvernail, "for her husband did not smoke". Her own white gown then revealed her to him.

A Respectable Woman.q: What did Gouvernail say about his own life as he sat on the bench?
A Respectable Woman.r: He spoke of his college days with Gaston and of "the days of keen and blind ambitions and large intentions", and said that all that was left to him now was "a philosophic acquiescence to the existing order — only a desire to be permitted to exist, with now and then a little whiff of genuine life, such as he was breathing now."

A Respectable Woman.q: What reason does the narrator give for Mrs. Baroda's decision not to tell her husband?
A Respectable Woman.r: That she was sensible as well as respectable, and "she knew there are some battles in life which a human being must fight alone." Telling Gaston would have relieved her own feelings at the cost of his peace and his oldest friendship.

A Respectable Woman.q: What part does Gaston unknowingly play in bringing about the bench scene?
A Respectable Woman.r: It is Gaston who invites Gouvernail in the first place, and it is Gaston who sends Gouvernail out into the dark garden with his wife's white scarf. The husband thus arranges, in perfect innocence and out of simple kindness, the one encounter that threatens his marriage.

A Respectable Woman.q: Discuss "A Respectable Woman" as a study of the conflict between natural desire and social respectability.
A Respectable Woman.r: The story sets a natural impulse against an acquired identity and shows the identity winning — at a price. Chopin prepares the ground carefully. Mrs. Baroda's interest in Gouvernail is not presented as love; it grows out of vanity, because he does not court her good opinion, and then out of curiosity, as she tries "to penetrate the reserve in which he had unconsciously enveloped himself". On the bench, in darkness, with a voice speaking Whitman's lines about the night, the feeling becomes unmistakably physical: "Her physical being was for the moment predominant," and she wants to touch his face and lips and to whisper against his cheek — she "did not care what".

A Devoted Son.q: What did Rakesh do first when he saw the examination results, and why did Varma repeat it to every visitor?
A Devoted Son.r: He bowed down and touched his father's feet. Varma repeated it because it proved that his son, for all his new glory, was still respectful — the kind of "exemplary filial behaviour" that made the parents proud, and of which the neighbours said, "One does not often see such behaviour in sons any more."

A Devoted Son.q: Why did Varma teach his family to say "the USA" rather than "America"?
A Devoted Son.r: Because "the USA" sounded grander and more familiar, "with a grand familiarity", than "America", which was what the "ignorant neighbours" said. It shows Varma's pride in his son's success and his wish to rise above the neighbours; Desai smiles at his small snobbery.

A Devoted Son.q: What kind of wife did Rakesh's mother choose for him, and what did that show about Rakesh?
A Devoted Son.r: She chose a plump, uneducated girl from her own village, the daughter of a childhood friend: "so old-fashioned, so placid, so complaisant". That Rakesh accepted her "almost without argument" shows his obedience to his mother and his lack of interest in a foreign or educated wife.

A Devoted Son.q: How did Rakesh's supervision of his father's diet begin?
A Devoted Son.r: One day Varma, ill, had ordered soojie halwa and eaten it with a saucerful of cream. Rakesh walked in "with the confident and rather contemptuous stride of the famous doctor" and announced "No more halwa for you, papa." After that everything fried, then everything sweet, and finally everything the old man enjoyed was crossed off his diet.

A Devoted Son.q: What did old Bhatia say when Varma told him about the scales?
A Devoted Son.r: Bhatia was shocked. He asked in disbelief whether "even in this evil age" a son could refuse his own father food, and murmured "Never" and "Your own son?" He is the voice of common sense, and his amazement tells the reader that Rakesh's care has gone too far.

A Devoted Son.q: What did Varma do with the tonic Rakesh brought him at the end?
A Devoted Son.r: Varma refused it: "Keep your tonic — I want none." With a sudden, "grand" wave of his hand he swept the bottle out of Rakesh's grasp, so that it smashed and the brown syrup stained his son's white trousers.

A Devoted Son.q: Is Rakesh a "devoted son"? Give a balanced answer with evidence from the story.
A Devoted Son.r: The title names Rakesh a "devoted son", and Desai spends the first half of the story proving it. He touches his father's feet on the day of the results and again on his return from the USA; he comes home when he could have stayed abroad; he marries the girl his mother chose; he nurses his mother "at the last moment"; he brings his father's tea in his favourite tumbler, reads him the news, arranges his pillows and carries him out to the lawn on summer nights. Even the "most rancorous" neighbours admit his goodness.

A Devoted Son.q: Discuss the use of irony in Anita Desai's "A Devoted Son".
A Devoted Son.r: Irony — the gap between appearance and reality — is the method of the story. (a) The title means one thing in the first half and another in the second. (b) Verbal irony: "such a son as few women had borne", "that pearl amongst pearls", and the "radiant heights of fame and fortune" echo the community's exaggerated praise with a gentle smile. (c) Situational irony: the son who does everything right makes his father miserable; the medicine meant to prolong life prolongs a life the old man wants to end; and the mother's death is greeted with "a sigh that sounded positively happy".

The Treasure in the Forest.q: What did Evans and Hooker know about the treasure before they reached the island, and how did they learn it?
The Treasure in the Forest.r: They knew that a Spanish galleon from the Philippines had been wrecked and its ingots buried, and that Chang-hi had found and reburied them "very safe". They learned it by overhearing three Chinese men talk in pidgin English round a fire one moonlit night; later they took Chang-hi's map from him.

The Treasure in the Forest.q: What puzzled the two men about the marks on the map?
The Treasure in the Forest.r: The "little marks" looked like the plan of a house, and the "little dashes, pointing this way and that" in the corner could not be explained by either man. In fact the dashes showed where poisoned thorns had been set around the gold.

The Treasure in the Forest.q: Why did Evans and Hooker drink at the river before doing anything else?
The Treasure in the Forest.r: They had made a long night voyage in an unprovisioned canoe under a blazing sun and were almost mad with thirst — Evans said he would "have to drink sea water" and finally sucked up the water with his lips. Their physical need was stronger than their greed, for a moment.

The Treasure in the Forest.q: What did Hooker suppose had killed the dead man in the forest?
The Treasure in the Forest.r: He supposed "some poisonous snake" had killed him: "He stole a march on his friends. He came here alone, and some poisonous snake has killed him." The neck was "puffed and purple" and the hands and ankles swollen, which matches a snakebite, and this wrong guess kept the danger hidden.

The Treasure in the Forest.q: How did Hooker finally understand what was killing Evans?
The Treasure in the Forest.r: He felt a little prick on the ball of his thumb and found a slender thorn two inches long. Seeing Evans twitching and the blue body among the trees, he "thought of the little dashes in the corner of the plan, and in a moment he understood": the thorns were like those the Dyaks poison for their blowpipes.

The Treasure in the Forest.q: What is the significance of Chang-hi's grin?
The Treasure in the Forest.r: It shows that Chang-hi knew something the thieves did not: that his treasure was guarded by poisoned thorns, so that anyone who took the map would be killed. It is a moment of silent triumph, and when Hooker "understood that grin now" it becomes the key to the story.

The Treasure in the Forest.q: Discuss "The Treasure in the Forest" as a story of greed and its punishment.
The Treasure in the Forest.r: Every stage of the story shows greed leading to destruction. Evans and Hooker are "stranded British wastrels" who have seized a map by force from Chang-hi; they cross the sea without water; and on the island Evans's only reaction to the dead body is fury that "somebody has been here before". When the gold is found they think only of carrying it away. Even after Evans is pricked twice they keep on lifting ingots, and Evans refuses Hooker's wish to bury the corpse: "Let that mass of corruption bide." Each small act of greed takes them closer to the thorns.

The Treasure in the Forest.q: How does Wells use foreshadowing and suspense in the story?
The Treasure in the Forest.r: Foreshadowing is planted in every scene: the map's "little dashes"; Chang-hi's "great stress on the safety"; his "incomprehensible and startling grin"; Evans's dream of devils feeding him with burning coals and of a furnace in his mouth; the corpse's swollen neck, hands and ankles; Hooker's unease, "It scares me somehow"; Evans's two pricks; his sudden "unreasonable anger". Each looks like a small piece of description and later proves to be a clue.

My Old Home.q: Why has the narrator come back to his old home?
My Old Home.r: He has come "with the sole object of saying goodbye". The old house, in which his clan had lived for many years, has been sold and must be handed over before New Year's Day; he has come to take his mother and nephew to the place where he now works.

My Old Home.q: What picture flashes into the narrator's mind when his mother mentions Runtu?
My Old Home.r: He sees "a golden moon suspended in a deep blue sky", a seashore planted with jade-green watermelons, and in the middle a boy of eleven or twelve in a silver necklet thrusting a steel pitchfork at a zha, which dodges the blow and escapes between his legs. The boy is the young Runtu.

My Old Home.q: Who is Mrs Yang and why is she called "the Compass"?
My Old Home.r: Mrs Yang is a neighbour of about fifty who used to sit in the beancurd shop across the road and was then called the "Beancurd Beauty". She is called "the Compass" because she stands with her hands on her hips and her trousered legs apart, "just like the compass in a box of geometrical instruments".

My Old Home.q: How has Runtu changed when the narrator meets him again?
My Old Home.r: The round, crimson-faced boy of memory has become a sallow, deeply wrinkled man twice his former size, with swollen, red-rimmed eyes, a shabby felt cap, a single thin padded jacket and hands "like the bark of a pine tree". He is shivering, almost speechless and addresses the narrator respectfully as "Master".

My Old Home.q: What does Runtu ask to take from the house?
My Old Home.r: He takes two long tables, four chairs, an incense burner and candlesticks, and a balance, and asks for all the ashes from the stove, which are used as fertiliser for the sandy soil.

My Old Home.q: What question does Hongr ask in the boat, and why is it important?
My Old Home.r: Hongr asks, "Uncle, when shall we go back?" because Shuisheng has invited him to his home. It matters because the children, unlike the adults, show no class barrier between them; the question brings the narrator hope that the next generation will not be divided.

My Old Home.q: Discuss the theme of hope in the story, with special reference to the last paragraph.
My Old Home.r: Hope is the last theme of the story and is treated honestly. As the boat leaves, the narrator sees Hongr and Shuisheng as friends and hopes that "they will not allow a barrier to grow up between them"; he wants them to have "a new life, a life we have never experienced". But immediately he is "afraid": when Runtu asked for the incense burner and candlesticks, he had laughed up his sleeve at his idol-worship, yet now he sees that "what I now called hope was no more than an idol I had created myself", only more remote.

My Old Home.q: What does Lu Xun show about rural China through the character of Runtu?
My Old Home.r: Runtu is the story's portrait of the Chinese peasant. As a boy he is bright, brave and knowledgeable about nature; as a man he is "sallow", wrinkled, shivering in one thin jacket, with a hand "like the bark of a pine tree". His own words give the causes: many children, bad harvests, and taxes that mean that when he sells he loses money and when he does not sell his produce rots. The narrator adds "famines, taxes, soldiers, bandits, officials and landed gentry", all of which had "squeezed him as dry as a mummy".

The Half-closed Eyes of the Buddha and t.q: What does the tourist mean when he says that the West is indebted to the East?
The Half-closed Eyes of the Buddha and t.r: He means that the East has given the West religion, the Puranas, brass images, ivory ornaments, palm-leaf manuscripts, copperplate inscriptions, civilisation and wisdom, and has done so "innocent of the notion of ownership", while the West has taken. It is an admiring speech, but it treats the East as a giver and not as an equal.

The Half-closed Eyes of the Buddha and t.q: Why does the guide not take the tourist into the temple of Adinath?
The Half-closed Eyes of the Buddha and t.r: The tourist has already seen and "understood" such sights and even "preached" them; the temple, with its Shiva shrine, Buddha images and prayer wheels, is an example of tolerance he already admires. The guide wants to show him the reality that is not on the tourist's map: a poor farmer's house.

The Half-closed Eyes of the Buddha and t.q: What lie does the guide tell the child's parents, and why?
The Half-closed Eyes of the Buddha and t.r: He tells them that the tourist is a doctor, so that they welcome him with hope and a smile that the tourist had praised the day before. The guide lies in order to show the tourist what a smile based on hope alone is worth, since it will be "extinguished" when the visitor goes.

The Half-closed Eyes of the Buddha and t.q: What does the guide say the paralysed child "can neither give nor take"? Why does he say it?
The Half-closed Eyes of the Buddha and t.r: The child, says the guide, "can neither give nor take anything at all". He says it in answer to the tourist's claim that Easterners "always" give to the West: here is an Easterner who cannot give, and his "endurance" is not a virtue but the silence of a helpless body.

The guide says that the child's eyes are "eyes surrounded by mountains", eyes that "welcome you" and "build", and that "in these eyes hides the end of life". He ends: "They are just as beautiful as the setting sun's reflection in the eyes of the Buddha!" — uniting the boy's eyes with the image from the title.

The Half-closed Eyes of the Buddha and t.q: Compare and contrast the tourist's view of Nepal with the guide's.
The Half-closed Eyes of the Buddha and t.r: The tourist sees Nepal as a beautiful, peaceful, spiritual country: a green valley with earthen houses, a place of carved temples and eternal calm, inhabited by smiling, generous people who have always "given" to the West. He is happy, romantic, and a little drunk; he knows it from books; and he praises the country for qualities (innocence, endurance, harmony) that are comforting to a visitor. He wants the "eyes without equal" that will make his journey unforgettable.

A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings.q: Why did Pelayo go out into his courtyard at the beginning of the story?
A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings.r: After three days of rain the house was full of dead crabs, and the newborn child had a fever that the family blamed on the smell. Pelayo crossed the flooded courtyard to throw the crabs into the sea, and on his way back found the old man.

A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings.q: What did the neighbour woman say about the old man?
A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings.r: The neighbour woman, who "knew everything about life and death", said the old man was an angel who had probably come for the sick child but had been knocked down by the rain because he was so old. She also advised killing him.

A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings.q: How did Father Gonzaga test whether the old man was an angel?
A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings.r: He went into the chicken coop and greeted the old man in Latin. The old man did not understand, which made the priest suspect an impostor, since an angel should know "the language of God". He also noticed that the old man smelled, was full of parasites and was "much too human".

A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings.q: How did Pelayo and Elisenda make money from the angel?
A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings.r: Elisenda fenced in the courtyard and charged five cents admission to see the angel. Pilgrims and curious visitors came from far away, and in less than a week the couple had "crammed their rooms with money"; they later built a two-storey mansion.

A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings.q: Why did the crowd leave the angel for the spider woman?
A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings.r: The spider woman's show cost less, she answered questions, and her story of disobeying her parents was a clear moral lesson "full of so much human truth". The angel, by contrast, was silent and aloof, and his "miracles" (three new teeth for a blind man, sunflowers for a leper) were absurd.

A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings.q: How do the people in the story treat the old man, and what does this show about human nature?
A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings.r: The people treat the old man badly in many ways. The neighbours toss him food as if he were a circus animal; the crowd lets the hens peck his wings, pulls out his feathers, throws stones and burns him with a branding iron. Pelayo and Elisenda lock him in a chicken coop, sell tickets, neglect him and later chase him out of the bedroom with a broom, shouting that it is "hell full of angels". Father Gonzaga treats him as a theological question and leaves him in the coop while waiting for Rome. Only the child and the doctor come close to treating him as a living being.

A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings.q: Explain the symbolism of the angel and of the ending.

On Libraries.q: Why did Sacks call Willesden Public Library his "Ur-library"?
On Libraries.r: Ur- is a German prefix meaning "original". Willesden, the public library a five-minute walk from his home, was the first great library of his life and the standard for every library after it: there, he says, he "received my real education".

On Libraries.q: How did Sacks get into the library of the Science Museum?
On Libraries.r: The Walker Library at his school, St Paul's, had few science books, so a schoolmaster wrote him a special testimonial. With that recommendation he obtained a ticket to the Science Museum library and read the huge chemistry works of Mellor and Gmelin.

On Libraries.q: Why does the author appreciate the Queen's College library?
On Libraries.r: He appreciates it for its magnificent building (designed by Wren), its underground "maze of heating pipes and shelves", and above all its holdings: ancient books, Gesner's Historiae Animalium, Agassiz, Darwin's works in original editions, Browne, Swift, and the seventeenth- and eighteenth-century writers. The books were freely available on the shelves, and there he "really gained a sense of history, and of my own language".

On Libraries.q: Why do you think the modern students ignore the bookshelves?
On Libraries.r: Because by the 1990s they could find whatever they needed through computers, so the shelves seemed unnecessary. To them the printed books were no longer the first place to look, and few visited the stacks at all.

On Libraries.q: What made the essayist unhappy when he visited the library a couple of months ago?
On Libraries.r: He found the shelves, once overflowing, sparsely occupied; most of the books had been thrown out over a few years, with hardly any objection. He felt that a crime had been committed against centuries of knowledge.

On Libraries.q: How does the writer's family background inspire him to learn from the library?
On Libraries.r: His father's Hebrew scholarship, his parents' Ibsen society, his mother's books and his brothers' adventure books meant that shelves of books surrounded him from birth. He could pick up a book at any time, learned to read at three or four and made the oak-panelled library his favourite place — the beginning of a lifelong habit of learning in libraries.

On Libraries.q: What impression did the author have about the library at the Albert Einstein College of Medicine?
On Libraries.r: He found it spacious, which he had longed for after his cramped flat. It had a large table where he could read and write and shelves and stacks where he could wander and find "unexpected treasures, lucky finds". It was quiet, but whispered conversations led to friendships, and it gave him a sense of community, even intimacy.

On Libraries.q: What did the librarian assure the author?
On Libraries.r: The librarian, seeing his distress, assured him that everything "of worth" had already been digitised, so nothing valuable was lost.

On Libraries.q: Why does the digital library not interest the author?
On Libraries.r: He values what only a physical book can offer — "its look, its smell, its heft" — and the freedom of browsing among shelves. He does not use a computer himself, and he feels a digital copy cannot replace the book, the shelf and the reader's community.

On Libraries.q: Why was the author biased towards science?
On Libraries.r: As he grew older his interest turned to astronomy and chemistry. The essay says his reading became "increasingly biased towards the sciences", and his hunger for chemistry books that the school library lacked led him to the Science Museum library.

On Libraries.q: In the essay "On Libraries", Oliver Sacks talks about two kinds of library — the traditional library and the modern, digital one. Which do you find more impressive, and why?
On Libraries.r: Sacks describes the traditional library in loving detail: oak-panelled rooms, open shelves and stacks, quiet tables, whispered talk that turns to friendship, old books in original editions — and, at the end, a digital library in which books are scanned and the paper copies thrown away. I find the traditional library more impressive, and Sacks gives me the reasons. First, it gives freedom to browse: he "roamed the shelves" and found "unexpected treasures, lucky finds", such as Hook in the Bodleian and Liveing's Megrim in the stacks. A search returns only what you ask for; a shelf shows you what you did not know to ask.

On Libraries.q: What did libraries give Oliver Sacks at each stage of his life? Trace the development of his relationship with libraries.
On Libraries.r: Home library: books and reading became his first memories; he read at three or four and found fantasy in The Jungle Book. Willesden: his "real education"; freedom to choose; independence from the school that bored him. Walker Library and Science Museum library: his first serious training in chemistry, when his school could not supply the books. Oxford: the Bodleian gave him a subject in Theodore Hook and a quiet place to write; the Queen's College library gave him "a sense of history, and of my own language" through original editions of Darwin, Browne, Swift and others.

On Libraries.q: Do you agree with Sacks that the loss of physical books is a great loss? Give reasons from the essay and from your own experience.
On Libraries.r: I agree with Sacks that it is a great loss, though not one to be blamed on technology alone. His argument is that digitisation saves the text but destroys the book: its "look, its smell, its heft", its neighbours on the shelf and the names of earlier readers. It also destroys serendipity: he found Hook and Megrim only by wandering among real shelves. And a library that disposes of its old books cannot rediscover them later; once a book is thrown out and the scan is lost or unreadable, knowledge vanishes. In my own experience, a book on a school shelf beside the one I wanted has often taught me something I did not plan to learn.

Marriage as a Social Institution.q: In what way is marriage an institution? Explain.
Marriage as a Social Institution.r: Marriage is an institution because it is culturally patterned and integrated into the other basic institutions of society — education, the economy and politics. Its rules come from outside the couple and are supported by law, religion and custom, so the marriage of any one couple follows a pattern that everyone understands.

Marriage as a Social Institution.q: Is marriage different from other networks of relation? Give a reason.
Marriage as a Social Institution.r: Yes. Friendship and other personal ties have few rules, but marriage is defined by legal, moral and conventional assumptions that originate outside the couple and mark it off from all other relationships. Married people know what they owe each other, their children and their relatives, and others expect the same of them.

Marriage as a Social Institution.q: Why does marriage matter to men?
Marriage as a Social Institution.r: Following Durkheim, marriage matters to men because it gives structure to their lives and organises their ambitions. By restraining uncontrollable desires and tying a man to one partner and one set of duties, it gives him a "moral equilibrium" and a sense of purpose.

Marriage as a Social Institution.q: Do you think marriage is a social institution? Why, or why not? Explain briefly.
Marriage as a Social Institution.r: Yes, marriage is a social institution. It is culturally patterned, joined to education, the economy and politics, governed by rules that come from society rather than the couple, and backed by law, religion and custom. Unlike cohabitation, it gives the couple a template and creates binding obligations to kin and children.

Marriage as a Social Institution.q: What does Nock mean by "soft boundaries"?
Marriage as a Social Institution.r: "Soft boundaries" are the rules, originating outside a particular couple, that set the commonly understood limits of behaviour which distinguish marriage from all other relationships. They are "soft" because they are enforced by custom, opinion and law together rather than by force, and they allow variation within them.

Marriage as a Social Institution.q: Why does the lack of a word for an unmarried partner matter in Nock's argument?
Marriage as a Social Institution.r: Because it shows that such a relationship is not governed by convention. Married people can say "my wife" or "my husband" and everyone knows what is meant; there is no common word for an unmarried partner because society has not agreed on the rules. To Nock this suggests that cohabitation "is not an institution".

Marriage as a Social Institution.q: How is marriage a form of social capital?
Marriage as a Social Institution.r: Social capital is a network of people linked by trust and obligation. Through marriage, husbands and wives gain new kin and friends of kin, bound by obligations that last; in need, they can call on relatives for help. This asset exists only in relationships and is therefore "an individual asset" that is intangible but valuable.

Marriage as a Social Institution.q: Discuss the six dimensions of normative marriage in America.
Marriage as a Social Institution.r: Nock writes that marriage is defined by "soft boundaries", and in the last paragraph he restates the six dimensions that define normative marriage in America. First, marriage is voluntary: two people enter it by choice. Second, it is entered by mature adults, not by children. Third, it is heterosexual, between a man and a woman. Fourth, husbands are expected to be the principal earners. Fifth, both partners are expected to be sexually faithful. Sixth, married people are expected to become parents. Nock adds that many marriages depart from these ideals, but they remain "the core of normative marriage as it is expressed in law, religion, and custom".

Marriage as a Social Institution.q: Describe marriage as a social institution, with reference to Nock's essay. (Model)
Marriage as a Social Institution.r: Nock's first claim is that marriage is "much more than the sum of two spouses". It is a relationship defined by legal, moral and conventional assumptions, and it is an institution: culturally patterned and integrated into education, the economy and politics. Its rules originate outside any particular couple and set soft boundaries that distinguish it from all other relationships. Married couples are "heirs to a vast system of understood principles". A husband and wife pledge faithfulness, commitment to children and responsibility to relatives, and these pledges are "enforceable", supported by laws, religion and customs.

Marriage as a Social Institution.q: Compare marriage and cohabitation as Nock presents them. Which does he think gives more to its partners, and why?
Marriage as a Social Institution.r: Cohabitation offers freedom: there are no widely accepted boundaries, so each couple decides how to treat each other's parents, whether to share holidays, how to handle money. But it also offers no guidance: the partners, their parents and friends must invent the relationship, with no established expectations, no agreed word to introduce a partner, and no enforceable obligations. Marriage offers a template — "a pattern to follow" for domestic life — with pledges of faithfulness and commitment that law, religion and custom support. It also supplies kin networks and social capital.

Marriage as a Social Institution.q: Explain Durkheim's argument about marriage and men as it is used in the essay, and say whether you think it is convincing.
Marriage as a Social Institution.r: Durkheim argued, about a century before Nock, that once basic needs are met, human desires turn to comfort, luxury and prestige, and these have no natural limit; once one appetite is satisfied another appears. Modern society therefore needs institutions to set "legitimate boundaries" on desire, and marriage does so for men. By binding a man to one partner for life, marriage "assigns a strictly definite object to the need for love, and closes the horizon"; he cannot seek other satisfactions without "transgressing his duty", so he limits his wants and finds "moral equilibrium".

Knowledge and Wisdom.q: What is the difference between knowledge and wisdom, according to Russell?
Knowledge and Wisdom.r: According to the textbook's summary, knowledge is the acquisition of data and information, while wisdom is the practical application of that knowledge to create value. In Russell's own account, knowledge is what a specialist knows; wisdom is a comprehensive vision — a sense of proportion, awareness of the ends of life, freedom from prejudice and from the "tyranny of the here and now". Knowledge can be harmful without wisdom.

Knowledge and Wisdom.q: Why does the world need more wisdom than knowledge in the future?
Knowledge and Wisdom.r: Because "with every increase of knowledge and skill, wisdom becomes more necessary". More knowledge gives people greater power to achieve their purposes, and so greater power for evil if their purposes are unwise. Since knowledge will go on increasing, the world will need wisdom even more in the future than now.

Knowledge and Wisdom.q: Do you agree with the author that wisdom is more important than knowledge? Why, or why not?
Knowledge and Wisdom.r: Yes, I agree. Knowledge tells us what we can do; wisdom tells us what we should do. Without wisdom, knowledge can be harmful, as nuclear weapons and misused medicine show. A person with wisdom can continue to learn and will use what he knows for good, but a person with knowledge alone may harm others.

Knowledge and Wisdom.q: What is the central idea of the essay "Knowledge and Wisdom"? (Model)
Knowledge and Wisdom.r: The central idea is that knowledge and wisdom are different, that our age has gained enormously in knowledge without a corresponding increase in wisdom, and that knowledge may become harmful unless it is combined with wisdom, which can and should be taught.

Knowledge and Wisdom.q: How can wisdom be taught? Give examples. (Model)
Knowledge and Wisdom.r: Russell says it can be taught "in some degree", by giving moral teaching a larger intellectual element: in the course of teaching facts, teachers can point out the disastrous results of hatred and narrow-mindedness. For example, when teaching atomic physics they can show how the atom has been used for destruction; by applying the Samaritan parable to today's enemies, teachers can show that hatred harms the hater.

Knowledge and Wisdom.q: Why does Russell say that Hegel lacked wisdom?
Knowledge and Wisdom.r: Hegel's philosophy of history was comprehensive in time, but its chief lesson was that from 400 AD Germany had been the most important nation and the standard-bearer of progress. His national pride distorted the facts, so he lacked the awareness of the ends of human life and the freedom from prejudice that wisdom needs.

Knowledge and Wisdom.q: What point does Russell make through Mr A and Mr B?
Knowledge and Wisdom.r: Two men who hate each other and are ruined by their hatred each give an equally one-sided list of the other's vices, partly true and partly false. By showing each that the other says the same, a wise person can make both see that the other has "only the normal share of human wickedness" and that their enmity harms both. That is a "fragment of wisdom": seeing a quarrel from outside oneself.

Knowledge and Wisdom.q: What does Russell mean by "the tyranny of the here and now"?
Knowledge and Wisdom.r: It means the natural self-centredness of our senses and feelings, which tie us to our own bodies, needs and moment. An infant knows only its own hunger. Wisdom is freedom from this as far as possible, by understanding and caring about things remote in time and space.

Knowledge and Wisdom.q: Why does Russell refuse to say that it is right to hate those who do harm?
Knowledge and Wisdom.r: Because hatred makes the hater as harmful as the enemy and is unlikely to persuade anyone to give up evil ways. "Hatred of evil is itself a kind of bondage to evil." The way out is understanding, though he does not advocate non-resistance: resistance should use the smallest force compatible with preserving what is good.

Knowledge and Wisdom.q: Discuss Russell's view of wisdom and the factors that contribute to it. (Model)
Knowledge and Wisdom.r: Russell begins from the fact that our age far surpasses earlier ages in knowledge, without a corresponding increase in wisdom. He defines wisdom through its factors. The first is a sense of proportion, the capacity to take account of all the important factors in a problem and give each its due weight; specialists often lack this, as the medical researcher and the atomic physicist show. The second is awareness of the ends of human life: Hegel's comprehensive history failed because national pride bent it. The third is feeling as well as intellect, since people with wide knowledge but narrow feelings are not wise.

Knowledge and Wisdom.q: Can wisdom be taught? Explain Russell's views on wisdom, hatred and education. (Model)
Knowledge and Wisdom.r: Russell answers yes, "in some degree". The need is great, because people are taught on Sundays to love their neighbours and on other days to hate them; the Good Samaritan's lesson would be understood today only if we put "Communist or anti-Communist" in his place. He holds that hatred of evil is "a kind of bondage to evil": hate makes us as harmful as those we hate and rarely persuades them; the way out is understanding, combined with resistance using the smallest force necessary. Examples from history (Elizabeth I, Henry IV, Lincoln) show that such wisdom is not weakness.

Knowledge and Wisdom.q: Why, according to Russell, is wisdom more necessary today than ever before? Do you agree?
Knowledge and Wisdom.r: According to Russell, wisdom is more necessary than ever because the power of knowledge has grown enormously. "With every increase of knowledge and skill, wisdom becomes more necessary", since greater power to realise our purposes is also greater power to do evil if the purposes are unwise. Nuclear weapons, unknown to earlier ages, show what this means: for the first time humans can destroy themselves. Modern specialisation also narrows the vision of experts, who therefore cannot see the wider effects of their work. And if knowledge continues to grow, "the world will need wisdom in the future even more than it does now". I agree.

Humility.q: What are the universal human abilities according to Harari?
Humility.r: According to Harari, the universal human abilities are morality, art, spirituality and creativity. They are "embedded in our DNA", he says, and they began in Stone Age Africa, long before any present-day nation or religion.

Humility.q: How do the Hindu nativists oppose the claim of Chinese nationalists about human history and civilisation?
Humility.r: They "dismiss these Chinese boasts" by claiming something larger: that even airplanes and nuclear bombs were invented by ancient sages in the Indian subcontinent long before Confucius or Plato, not to mention Einstein and the Wright brothers — for instance, that Bhardwaj invented rockets and aeroplanes and Kanad was the father of atomic theory.

Humility.q: The essayist calls on readers around the world to "puncture the hot-air balloons inflated by their own tribes". What do you think is the reason behind this?
Humility.r: Harari means that every group inflates its own importance — "hot-air balloons" are full of air and nothing else — and that only the members of each group can best puncture their own pride. By criticising his own people first, he hopes to make readers honest about their own nation, culture or religion, so that they see how ridiculous exaggerated claims are.

Humility.q: Why is one not the centre of the world? Explain.
Humility.r: Because no nation, culture or religion was the source of human history. Modern civilisation developed from abilities that all humans share and that arose in Stone Age Africa, long before any present-day nation; every group makes the same claim of centrality, so all the claims cancel out. Thinking otherwise is "crass egotism".

Humility.q: What makes the author conclude that morality, art, spirituality and creativity are universal human abilities embedded in our DNA? Give your opinion.
Humility.r: He says these abilities existed before any of today's nations or religions, when humans colonised the world, domesticated plants and animals, built the first cities and invented writing and money, so they cannot belong to any one of them; they are common to all human groups and have their genesis in Stone Age Africa. In my opinion the conclusion is convincing: people of every culture paint, pray, tell stories and distinguish right from wrong, which suggests a common, very ancient inheritance.

Humility.q: Do you agree with the author's view that history has been a major debatable issue in the present world? Give your opinion. (Model)
Humility.r: Yes, I agree. History is debated because it gives pride, identity and power. Each group wants to be seen as the oldest or the most creative, and tells the past in ways that flatter it. Disputes about textbooks, monuments and ancient achievements show this, and since each version contradicts the next, history becomes contested.

Humility.q: What did the Aztecs believe about the sun, and what does Harari think of such beliefs?
Humility.r: The Aztecs believed that without the human sacrifices they offered every year, the sun would not rise and the whole universe would fall apart. Harari uses this as an extreme case of a people imagining that their rituals were part of the laws of nature — an example of crass egotism.

Humility.q: Why does Harari use the example of the Jews to illustrate his point?
Humility.r: Because, he says, "it is more polite to criticise one's own people than to criticise foreigners". He also knows the Jews best, and starting with them shows that he is not singling out anyone else. The yoga story and the belief that the cosmos exists for the rabbis' study show how ludicrous self-important narratives are, and he leaves readers to treat their own tribes the same way.

Humility.q: How do Hindu nationalists refute the Chinese claim that human history really began with the Yellow Emperor and the Xia and Shang dynasties?
Humility.r: In his catalogue of national claims, Harari first reports that Chinese nationalists say history began with the Yellow Emperor and the Xia and Shang dynasties and that whatever Westerners, Muslims or Indians achieved is a pale copy of Chinese breakthroughs. Then he reports the answer of Hindu nativists: they "dismiss these Chinese boasts" and argue that even airplanes and nuclear bombs were invented by ancient sages in the Indian subcontinent long before Confucius or Plato, not to mention Einstein and the Wright brothers. They give examples: Maharishi Bhardwaj is said to have invented rockets and aeroplanes; Vishwamitra invented and used missiles;

Humility.q: Why do you think history has been a major contested issue in the present world? Discuss with reference to the essay. (Model)
Humility.r: History is a contested issue first because it gives a group its identity and pride. Harari's catalogue shows that every group wants to be the origin of civilisation, because being first seems to give a right to respect and leadership. Second, history is used as a political tool: governments use the past to justify their authority, borders and policies, and to unite people against "others". Third, the memory of injury — conquest, colonialism, war — leaves different communities with different versions of the same events. Fourth, in the age of social media, flattering stories spread faster than careful research.

Humility.q: Discuss the title "Humility". Is it a suitable title for the essay?
Humility.r: The title "Humility" is well chosen. Humility means not thinking oneself more important than one is, and the whole essay is about its opposite, pride in one's group, which Harari calls "crass egotism". The catalogue shows proud claims from many nations; the verdict shows that they are false; the positive message is that the great human abilities belong to everyone, so no group has reason for superiority; and the method of criticising his own people first is itself an act of humility. The title is also ironic: the essay never mentions humility in its text, but it teaches the virtue by showing the absurdity of its absence.

Human Rights and the Age of Inequality.q: Who is Samuel Moyn, and what is he best known for?
Human Rights and the Age of Inequality.r: Samuel Moyn is an American professor of law and history at Yale University. He is known for critical studies of the history of human rights, such as The Last Utopia (2010) and Not Enough (2018).

Human Rights and the Age of Inequality.q: What is the difference between status equality and distributive equality?
Human Rights and the Age of Inequality.r: Status equality means everyone has the same standing and basic rights as a person, as in Article 1 of the UDHR. Distributive equality concerns how wealth is shared, including any limit on the gap between rich and poor. The UDHR has the first but not the second.

Human Rights and the Age of Inequality.q: What does Moyn mean by a "floor of protection" and a "ceiling on inequality"?
Human Rights and the Age of Inequality.r: A floor of protection is a minimum standard of living, such as food, health care and schooling, that everyone must be raised to. A ceiling on inequality is a limit on how far the richest can rise above the rest. Human rights offer the floor but not the ceiling.

Human Rights and the Age of Inequality.q: Why does Moyn call the UDHR's first article "a revolutionary act"?
Human Rights and the Age of Inequality.r: Because in a world "devastated by the evils of racism and genocide", proclaiming that every human being is born free and equal in dignity and rights was a bold break with the ideas that had justified those evils, even though it said nothing about how wealth should be shared.

Human Rights and the Age of Inequality.q: What was Roosevelt's "highest promise" in his 1944 speech, according to Moyn?
Human Rights and the Age of Inequality.r: It was not just a floor of protection for the masses but the end of "special privilege for the few", a ceiling on inequality, which Moyn says people overlook because they remember only "freedom from want".

Human Rights and the Age of Inequality.q: What irony does Moyn find in the 1974 Nobel Prize in economics?
Human Rights and the Age of Inequality.r: Myrdal, who hoped to spread welfare worldwide, and Hayek, the champion of free markets, shared the prize; but Moyn says "where one of them was forgotten, the other saw his fondest wishes come true": market fundamentalism won.

Human Rights and the Age of Inequality.q: What does the hammer-and-nail image tell us about the human rights movement?
Human Rights and the Age of Inequality.r: Human rights have become so successful that people use them as the tool for every problem, like a man who has only a hammer and treats everything like a nail. The image warns that rights are not suited to reduce inequality.

Human Rights and the Age of Inequality.q: Why does Moyn say a supplement, not a substitute, is needed?
Human Rights and the Age of Inequality.r: Because human rights law works well against repression and violence and Moyn does not want to throw that away; what is missing is a separate political force for redistribution that can stand beside rights. So a supplement is needed, not a replacement.

Human Rights and the Age of Inequality.q: Explain Moyn's argument that human rights are "not equipped to challenge global inequalities".
Human Rights and the Age of Inequality.r: Moyn's claim is that human rights law and movements aim at a floor, not a ceiling. The UDHR announced status equality ("born free and equal in dignity and rights"), but it does not mention distributive equality, any limit on the wealth gap between rich and poor. As Moyn puts it, one could "imagine one man owning everything" and still not break the current scheme of human rights, provided everyone's basic rights were met; so "even perfectly realized human rights are compatible with radical inequality."

Human Rights and the Age of Inequality.q: How does Moyn trace the history of human rights in relation to political economy?
Human Rights and the Age of Inequality.r: Moyn uses two stages. In the first, the heroic age of national welfare states (1940s-1970s), human rights were a modest, optional synonym for the welfare consensus reached "after depression and war". Roosevelt's 1944 call for a "second bill of rights" promised "freedom from want" and, more importantly, the end of "special privilege for the few", a ceiling. This worked only within nations, mostly in the North Atlantic. Even decolonisation left the wealth gap between rich and poor nations.

Human Rights and the Age of Inequality.q: Do you agree with Moyn that human rights need a supplement rather than a substitute? Give reasons with reference to Nepal.
Human Rights and the Age of Inequality.r: Moyn says human rights cannot close the wealth gap, so they need a supplement: a politics of redistribution with the power to frighten the privileged. I agree. Human rights are valuable: they protect people from torture, censorship and arbitrary arrest, and many Nepalis rely on the rights in the 2015 Constitution and on the National Human Rights Commission. But rights alone do not make a poor child in Karnali as likely to get a good school as a child in Kathmandu. Fair tax systems, public schools and hospitals, land reform, and strong trade unions and citizens' groups are political, not just legal, instruments.

Human Rights and the Age of Inequality.q: Write a paragraph on how the gap between rich and poor can be narrowed in your country.
Human Rights and the Age of Inequality.r: Suggest progressive taxes, well-funded public schools and health posts in remote districts, land and housing programmes, employment and skills training, transparent governance, and strong civic movements. End with Moyn's insight that change needs political pressure, not just good laws.

A Matter of Husbands.q: Why has the Earnest Young Woman come to the Famous Actress?
A Matter of Husbands.r: She believes her husband, the lawyer Alfred, has fallen in love with the actress, and she has come to beg the actress to "give me back my husband".

A Matter of Husbands.q: How does the actress first answer the wife's plea?
A Matter of Husbands.r: The actress pretends to be bewildered. She says she cannot return a husband she has not got, and that she knows Alfred only as the lawyer who drew up her last contract and whom she has seen backstage.

A Matter of Husbands.q: What evidence of the affair does the wife produce?
A Matter of Husbands.r: She says he sends flowers to the actress's dressing room twice a week (she learned it at the florist's), she reads a letter found on his desk ("My darling... Ten thousand kisses. Alfred"), and she has a lock of the actress's hair found in his drawer.

A Matter of Husbands.q: What does the actress say is "one of the oldest expedients in the world"?
A Matter of Husbands.r: Inventing a love affair with an actress to make a wife or sweetheart jealous and win back her affection. The actress says authors, composers, scene designers, lawyers, orchestra leaders and managers have all used it.

A Matter of Husbands.q: How does the actress explain the lock of hair?
A Matter of Husbands.r: She says men bribe her hairdresser to steal a lock, so Alfred's possession of it is part of his plan to make his wife jealous, not proof of a love affair.

A Matter of Husbands.q: What advice does the actress give the wife before she leaves?
A Matter of Husbands.r: She advises the wife not to be taken in a second time, no matter what letters, handkerchiefs, photographs or flowers she finds in his pockets, and promises not to tell Alfred about the visit.

A Matter of Husbands.q: What do the last words of the play reveal?
A Matter of Husbands.r: The actress calls out, "All right, Alfred. You can come in now. She has gone." They reveal that the husband has been hiding in her boudoir all the time, so the wife's suspicion was true and the actress has deceived her.

A Matter of Husbands.q: Why does the author call the characters "Famous Actress" and "Earnest Young Woman"?
A Matter of Husbands.r: They are types, not individuals: a woman of the theatre who lives by acting, and an ordinary, sincere woman. The labels highlight the contrast that drives the play: pretending versus plain dealing.

A Matter of Husbands.q: Discuss "A Matter of Husbands" as a comedy of deception.
A Matter of Husbands.r: The play is a comedy because it is built on deception that we enjoy watching. The wife comes to claim her husband and the actress denies any knowledge. Then the actress changes the ground: she turns each of the wife's proofs into a sign of something harmless. The wife leaves relieved; only in the last line, when the actress calls "Alfred" out of her boudoir, do we see that the wife's fears were true. The humour lies in the gap between what the wife believes and what the audience learns. There is little cruelty: the wife leaves the stage happy. The irony of the ending, that the wife thanks her rival, makes the comedy complete.

A Matter of Husbands.q: Describe how the Famous Actress persuades the Earnest Young Woman that her husband is innocent.
A Matter of Husbands.r: The actress works in five steps. First she denies everything calmly, so the wife's certainty weakens. Second, she asks whether the couple have been getting on badly of late, whether they were once affectionate and whether the wife has grown cold; the wife's "Yes" to each supplies the premise of the actress's theory. Third, she declares it a "typical case": it happens "endless times" to actresses, because men of the theatre invent love affairs to make wives jealous. This flatters the wife, making her less a victim than the target of a clever husband.

A Matter of Husbands.q: Discuss the use of irony and stage directions in the play.
A Matter of Husbands.r: Irony is the play's main method. Verbal irony: the actress says she is "neither better nor worse than any other girl in the theater" while deceiving a wife. Situational irony: the wife, who came to fight her rival, leaves grateful to her. Dramatic irony: the audience gradually suspects what the wife does not; and in the last line what we suspected becomes certain. The stage directions supply most of the acting. The wife "gulps emotionally", "extends her arms in a beseeching gesture", "fumbles in her bag", "weeps", and at the end kisses the actress "impetuously". The actress's directions show control: "without anger, slowly, regards her appraisingly", "with a gracious little laugh".

A Matter of Husbands.q: Write a paragraph describing your favourite actor or actress.
A Matter of Husbands.r: Give the name; say what he or she is famous for, three qualities of the acting (voice, emotion, range) and two or three works; end with why he or she inspires you. Use present tense and concrete examples.

Facing Death.q: Where and when is the play set?
Facing Death.r: The play is set in the dining-room of Durand's pension near Lake Léman in French Switzerland in the 1880s, on a morning when the house is bankrupt.

Facing Death.q: Why does Adèle complain when Pierre comes back from the baker?
Facing Death.r: Because Pierre brings no bread but three unpaid bills. The baker will send no more until he is paid and the butcher and grocer have also sent bills. She sees that the family's credit is finished.

Facing Death.q: Why does Antonio ask Durand whether he was born in Switzerland?
Facing Death.r: Antonio seems to have guessed that Durand may not be Swiss by birth. Durand answers "uncertainly" that he was, and later Thérèse and Durand himself reveal that he was born in France.

Facing Death.q: What does Durand do after seeing Antonio kiss Thérèse?
Facing Death.r: He lifts his stick against Antonio and tells him to choose his weapon; when Antonio leaves, Durand throws a gold piece after him, breaks his stick in two and says, "He who cannot kill must die."

Facing Death.q: What do the daughters take from Durand, and what does Thérèse give back at the end?
Facing Death.r: They take his glass of milk and his matches. At the end Thérèse says, "Here are your matches, papa--and there's your milk" and runs into his arms: the only things she has to give.

Facing Death.q: What is the meaning of the candle that Durand counts with Adèle?
Facing Death.r: The packet should hold six candles but has five; the sixth has been placed "very high up and very near" something that will burn, and will be burned out in "five minutes or so". It is the fuse that will start the fire.

Facing Death.q: What does Durand ask Adèle to do for her sisters?
Facing Death.r: He asks her to take motherly care of Thérèse and see her married soon, to find a place as a teacher for Annette, to manage the money carefully, to keep the family papers, never to tell her sisters what he has done and never to speak ill of their mother.

Smoke comes through the ceiling and bells ring outside. Adèle sees that Durand has taken poison. He asks whether she has the insurance papers and begins to say "Tell Thérèse--and Annette--" when his head falls on the table. The curtain falls.

Facing Death.q: Describe Monsieur Durand as a tragic hero.
Facing Death.r: A tragic hero is a central figure whom we pity because he suffers more than he deserves, and whose fall comes from character and circumstance. Durand is such a figure in a modern key. He is a good man: patient, honourable and tender. He buys candles for a dead child, says that he once got up at night to cover his daughters and gave them water in secret, and never speaks ill of his dead wife. Yet he is also flawed: for twenty years he has watched the family "go toward an abyss" without reaching "the engine valves"; even when an American guest assaulted Thérèse he did not act, "father-like". His fall comes from debt, a failing pension and a family that despises him.

Facing Death.q: How does Strindberg use symbols and foreshadowing to prepare for the ending?
Facing Death.r: The play prepares the ending through clues that seem ordinary until the last minutes. Foreshadowing: on the first page Durand tells Adèle to put out the fire in the stove and Adèle asks whether the fire insurance is paid; Durand wishes everything would "crash at once"; the wind is "going to blow soon"; a clanging is heard "down toward Cully"; Antonio jokes about a "sinking ship". Symbols: the candles are first a memorial for the dead child, then a fuse, since the sixth is placed "very high up and very near"; fire is destruction but also rescue; milk and matches stand for the small kindnesses the daughters withhold and Thérèse finally returns;

Facing Death.q: Is Durand's decision to kill himself justified? Discuss with reference to the play.
Facing Death.r: The play does not condemn or approve; it asks us to understand. In favour: Durand is bankrupt, unable to borrow "a sou", despised by his children and worn out by years of humiliation; his daughters face homelessness; death will bring them money, and he arranges their future carefully, with marriages and a teaching post. He also dies with dignity, protecting their picture of their mother. Against: he commits arson and fraud; he uses Adèle as an accomplice; he leaves his daughters a secret that may weigh on them; he gives up any chance of reconciliation, though Thérèse's last words show that love was possible; and suicide closes every other door.

Facing Death.q: Write a short essay on "The Sacrifices of Parents".
Facing Death.r: Open with the idea that parents give time, food and dreams before being asked. Give two examples from life and one from the play (Durand's candle, milk, death). Discuss how children can thank them. End with a short promise.

Facing Death.q: Do you think a family's poverty can destroy love? Discuss with examples.
Facing Death.r: Take a side. Poverty can strain love, as the Durand daughters' cruelty shows, but it can also reveal it: Thérèse's last gift of matches and milk. Mention support, communication and honesty as the things that protect a family.

The Bull.r: Bhimnidhi Tiwari (1911-1973) was a Nepali poet, story-writer and dramatist, and a social reformer who founded the Nepal Natak Sangh to promote Nepali plays.

The Bull.q: What is the name of the bull and who owns it?
The Bull.r: The bull is called Male. It belongs to King Ranabahadur Shah, who is very fond of bulls.

The Bull.q: Why are Laxminarayan, Jitman and Gore afraid of the king?
The Bull.r: Because the king's bull has died in their care, and the king is known to punish people severely. They fear being beheaded or shaved as a punishment, though the bull died of natural causes or rich food.

The Bull.q: What excuse does Laxminarayan give the king for moving the bull?
The Bull.r: He says the bull is ill, will not eat, move or speak, and needs a change of climate; he asks to take it to the hills. This is a lie to hide that the bull is already dead.

The Bull.q: What does Laxminarayan tell the cowherds to do before the king arrives?
The Bull.r: He tells them to massage the bull's back feet and fan it as if it were alive, and not to reveal that it is dead.

The Bull.q: How much money does the king give to Jitman and Gore?
The Bull.r: Jitman receives four hundred rupees and Gore five hundred.
Chakari is serving and flattering a person of higher rank to win his favour; it also means pleading before such a person by showing one's poverty or distress.

The Bull.q: Name two things that show the bull is treated better than the cowherds.
The Bull.r: The bull has a mattress, quilt and mosquito net and is fed fine rice and lentil soup, while the cowherds sleep on straw in winter and live in fear.

The Bull.q: Discuss "The Bull" as a satire on the feudal system.
The Bull.r: A satire exposes the faults of people or society through humour. "The Bull" exposes the feudal system, in which a king and lords hold all power. The first fault is the dehumanisation of ordinary people: the king's bull has a mattress, quilt and mosquito net, while the cowherds sleep on straw; the men's lives are at risk if the bull dies. The second is fear: Laxminarayan, Jitman and Gore are terrified of being beheaded or shaved, though the bull died without their fault. The third is chakari: Laxminarayan lies and praises the bull to please the king, and the cowherds howl with mock grief. The fourth is patriarchal privilege: Laxminarayan has seven wives and shouts for his hookah.

The Bull.q: How does Laxminarayan save himself and the cowherds? What does this tell us about him?
The Bull.r: Laxminarayan saves himself and the cowherds by controlling what the king knows. When Jitman and Gore bring the news, he keeps it secret and goes to the palace. There he says the bull is ill and praises its beauty and courage, and suggests a change of climate in the hills, so that any death could happen out of sight. When the king says he will visit Thulo Gauchar, Laxminarayan runs ahead, has the cowherds massage and fan the dead bull, and begins to grind medicine. So the king finds the bull dead in the middle of loving care. The cowherds weep loudly; Laxminarayan himself weeps. The plan works: the king rewards the cowherds and deals kindly with the doctor.

The Bull.q: Discuss the use of irony and humour in the play.
The Bull.r: Irony is the source of the humour. Dramatic irony: the audience knows from the start that the bull is dead and watches Laxminarayan lie to a king who does not know. Situational irony: men who did nothing wrong are terrified, and in the end they are rewarded for lying; a king who could have punished them pays them. Verbal irony: the cowherds declare that the bull was dearer to them than their parents, wives and children. Humour comes also from farce: the men massage and fan a corpse; from exaggeration: the cowherds' loud weeping and Gore's threat to hang himself; and from contrast: the bull's mattress and net against the cowherds' straw.

The Bull.q: Write a paragraph on "The Role of Satire in Society".
The Bull.r: Define satire; say it uses humour and exaggeration to expose faults; give examples (newspaper cartoons, comic plays, "The Bull"); explain how laughter can change attitudes more than lecture; end by noting that satire must be fair and aim at injustice, not individuals.

Question Tags and Questions.q: The programme starts at ten, isn't it?
Question Tags and Questions.r: The programme starts at ten, doesn't it? — the subject is a thing, so it, not isn't it.

Question Tags and Questions.q: Where he has gone since morning?
Question Tags and Questions.r: Where has he gone since morning? — a direct question inverts the operator and the subject.
Who broke this window? — who is the subject here, so no did.

Question Tags and Questions.q: Can you tell me when does the library open?
Question Tags and Questions.r: Can you tell me when the library opens? — an embedded question keeps statement order.

Question Tags and Questions.q: Does your father works in a bank?
Question Tags and Questions.r: Does your father work in a bank? — after does, the base form.

Question Tags and Questions.q: Why you did not attend the meeting?
Question Tags and Questions.r: Why didn't you attend the meeting? — the operator must come before the subject.

Question Tags and Questions.q: Where is the ticket counter? — Rewrite beginning Could you tell me …
Question Tags and Questions.r: Could you tell me where the ticket counter is? — the embedded clause returns to statement order.

Modal Verbs.q: Does he can come with us tomorrow?
Modal Verbs.r: Can he come with us tomorrow? — modals form questions without do.

Determiners and Quantifiers.q: The teacher gave us many informations about the scholarship.
Determiners and Quantifiers.r: … gave us much information about the scholarship. — information is uncountable.

Determiners and Quantifiers.q: The most of the villagers depend on farming.
Determiners and Quantifiers.r: Most of the villagers depend on farming. — no the before most of.

Subject-Verb Agreement and Miscellaneous.q: The list of selected candidates have been published.
Subject-Verb Agreement and Miscellaneous.r: The list of selected candidates has been published. — the subject is the list.

Subject-Verb Agreement and Miscellaneous.q: The committee have announced their decision unanimously.
Subject-Verb Agreement and Miscellaneous.r: The committee has announced its decision unanimously. — acting as one body, and unanimously shows it.

Subject-Verb Agreement and Miscellaneous.q: The teachers and the principal were present. — Rewrite beginning Not only the teachers but also …
Subject-Verb Agreement and Miscellaneous.r: Not only the teachers but also the principal was present. — the proximity rule makes the verb singular.

Adjectives, Adverbs and Adjective Order.q: The mangoes of Nepal are sweeter than India.
Adjectives, Adverbs and Adjective Order.r: The mangoes of Nepal are sweeter than those of India. — compare mangoes with mangoes.

Reported Speech.q: The guide said, "The Himalayas lie to the north of Nepal."
Reported Speech.r: The guide said that the Himalayas lie to the north of Nepal. — a permanent geographical fact does not shift.

Reported Speech.q: The teacher said to the boys, "Why are you making noise?"
Reported Speech.r: The teacher asked the boys why they were making noise. — wh-word kept, statement order, no question mark.

Reported Speech.q: The teacher said that the earth moved round the sun.
Reported Speech.r: The teacher said that the earth moves round the sun. — a universal truth stays in the present.

Reported Speech.q: The officer ordered the peon to bring the file at once.
Reported Speech.r: The officer said to the peon, "Bring the file at once." — the infinitive becomes an imperative.

Conditional Sentences.q: If you (heat) iron, it expands.
Conditional Sentences.r: heat — type 0; both clauses in the present simple.

Conditional Sentences.q: If it rains tomorrow, we (postpone) the picnic.
Conditional Sentences.r: will postpone — type 1; will goes in the main clause.

Conditional Sentences.q: If I (be) you, I would consult a doctor.
Conditional Sentences.r: were — type 2; were is used for all persons in the unreal past.

Conditional Sentences.q: If she had taken the medicine, she (recover) by now.
Conditional Sentences.r: would have recovered — type 3; the condition and the result are both past and unfulfilled. (would be well by now would be the mixed form.)

Conditional Sentences.q: If the bus (not come) on time, we would have missed the flight.
Conditional Sentences.r: had not come — type 3 if-clause; past perfect.

Conditional Sentences.q: If only he (listen) to his teachers when he was young!
Conditional Sentences.r: had listened — if only + past perfect for a past regret.

Conditional Sentences.q: If it will rain, the programme will be cancelled.
Conditional Sentences.r: If it rains, the programme will be cancelled. — no will in the if-clause.

Conditional Sentences.q: If I would have known, I would have told you.
Conditional Sentences.r: If I had known, I would have told you. — type 3 uses the past perfect.

Conditional Sentences.q: If I was a bird, I would fly over the Himalayas.
Conditional Sentences.r: If I were a bird, I would fly over the Himalayas. — unreal were.

Conditional Sentences.q: If had he apologised, she would have forgiven him.
Conditional Sentences.r: Had he apologised, she would have forgiven him. — with inversion, if is deleted.

Conditional Sentences.q: If you do not water the plants, they will die. — Use unless.
Conditional Sentences.r: Unless you water the plants, they will die. — the negative disappears with unless.

Conditional Sentences.q: If she had not helped me, I would have been in trouble. — Begin: But for …
Conditional Sentences.r: But for her help, I would have been in trouble. — but for is followed by a noun phrase.

Conditional Sentences.q: If I were rich, I would build a school in my village. — Begin: Were …
Conditional Sentences.r: Were I rich, I would build a school in my village. — if is deleted and were moves in front of the subject.

Passive Voice.q: The postman delivers the letters every morning.
Passive Voice.r: The letters are delivered (by the postman) every morning. — simple present: are + V3.

Passive Voice.q: The committee will announce the results tomorrow.
Passive Voice.r: The results will be announced by the committee tomorrow. — future: will be + V3.

Passive Voice.q: The teacher gave Sita a prize.
Passive Voice.r: Sita was given a prize by the teacher. (or A prize was given to Sita by the teacher.) — the person-first passive is preferred.

Passive Voice.q: The villagers are looking after the orphans.
Passive Voice.r: The orphans are being looked after by the villagers. — the preposition after stays with the verb.

Passive Voice.q: The window was broken by the boys.
Passive Voice.r: The boys broke the window. — the agent becomes the subject.

Passive Voice.q: A new hospital is going to be built here.
Passive Voice.r: They are going to build a new hospital here. — supply a general subject when no agent is given.

Passive Voice.q: Let the lights be switched off.
Passive Voice.r: Switch off the lights. — Let … be + V3 is the passive of an imperative.

Passive Voice.q: The letter has written by the secretary.
Passive Voice.r: The letter has been written by the secretary. — the passive needs been.

Passive Voice.q: The problem was discussed about for two hours.
Passive Voice.r: The problem was discussed for two hours. — discuss takes no about.

Passive Voice.q: The glass was broke by the cat.
Passive Voice.r: The glass was broken by the cat. — past participle, not past tense.

Passive Voice.q: The hall was crowded by students.
Passive Voice.r: The hall was crowded with students. — crowded takes with.

Prepositions, Tenses and Relative Clause.q: When we reached the theatre, the film already (start).
Prepositions, Tenses and Relative Clause.r: had already started — the earlier of two past events.

Prepositions, Tenses and Relative Clause.q: The teacher told us that the sun (rise) in the east.
Prepositions, Tenses and Relative Clause.r: rises — a universal truth does not shift after a past reporting verb.

Prepositions, Tenses and Relative Clause.q: By next June we (complete) our course.
Prepositions, Tenses and Relative Clause.r: will have completed — future perfect with by next June.

Prepositions, Tenses and Relative Clause.q: The pen is missing. I bought it yesterday. — Join with a defining clause.
Prepositions, Tenses and Relative Clause.r: The pen (that) I bought yesterday is missing. — the pronoun is the object, so it may be dropped.

Prepositions, Tenses and Relative Clause.q: The girl who is sitting near the window is my cousin. — Reduce the relative clause.
Prepositions, Tenses and Relative Clause.r: The girl sitting near the window is my cousin. — who is is deleted and the -ing form remains.

Permutation and Combination.r: (a) Fix one object in one seat; every circular arrangement can be rotated into exactly one position with that object there, so nothing is lost or double-counted. (iii) $r$ is the modulus of the complex number, $r=|z|=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}$, its distance from the origin on the Argand plane. (iv) $\theta$ is the argument (amplitude) of the complex number, the angle its radius vector makes with the positive real axis. (v) Finding powers and roots of complex numbers, for instance the $n$th roots of unity; also proving trigonometric identities for multiple angles.
