Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.w: unauthorised access is an offence under the Act.

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: In Nepal, cyber crimes are reported to the
Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.w: the Cyber Bureau handles cyber crime.

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: The record of everything you post, search and share online is your
What is computer ethics? Write any two of the Ten Commandments of computer ethics.
Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.r: Computer ethics is the set of moral rules for using computers and the Internet rightly. Any two commandments (Computer Ethics Institute, 1992): do not use a computer to harm other people; do not snoop around in other people's files; do not use a computer to steal; do not copy or use software you have not paid for; do not take other people's work as your own.

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: What is phishing? Write two signs of a phishing message.
Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.r: Phishing is tricking people into giving passwords, OTPs, PINs or card numbers through a fake message, e-mail or website that looks as if it came from a bank, wallet or office. Signs: it creates urgency ("your account will be blocked today"); it asks for an OTP, PIN or password; the sender address or link is slightly wrong; spelling mistakes; a prize you never entered for.

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: Differentiate between copyright and plagiarism.
Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.r: Copyright is the legal right of the creator of a work — a book, song, film, photo or program — to control its copying and use; in Nepal it lasts for the author's life plus 50 years. Plagiarism is presenting someone else's words or work as your own without giving credit, such as copying an essay from a website into your project.

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: What is cyber bullying? What should a student do if it happens to them?
Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.r: Cyber bullying is using phones, social media or games to insult, threaten, shame or harass someone again and again. The student should not reply, should save screenshots as evidence, block and report the bully on the platform, and tell a parent or teacher; serious cases can be reported to the Cyber Bureau.

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: Explain hacking, identity theft, software piracy and cyber bullying.
Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.r: Hacking: getting into someone's computer, account or network without permission (an offence under section 45 of the ETA). Identity theft: stealing someone's personal details — name, photo, citizenship number, password — to pretend to be them, open fake accounts or cheat others. Software piracy: copying, selling or using software without a licence. Cyber bullying: harassing or threatening someone repeatedly online.

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: Who is a digital citizen? Write any three rules for using social media safely.
Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.r: A digital citizen is a person who uses the Internet and digital technology responsibly, safely and with respect for others (1 mark). Any three rules: think before you post — posts stay for ever; keep your accounts private and share no personal details such as address, phone number or school timetable; use strong, different passwords and turn on multi-factor authentication; accept friend requests only from people you know; do not share fake news or others' photos without permission; report abuse (3 marks).

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: Computer ethics means
Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.w: ethics are moral rules; laws are made by the state.

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: The Ten Commandments of Computer Ethics were published by the
"Do not snoop around in other people's computer files" means you should not
o: look into others' files without permission
Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.w: commandment 3: do not look into others' files.

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: Getting into someone's computer or account without permission is
Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.w: hacking; punished under section 45 of the ETA.

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: A fake message that tricks you into giving your password or OTP is called
Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.w: phishing pretends to be a trusted company.

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: Copying and selling a paid program without its licence is
Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.w: software piracy breaks the copyright in a computer program.

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: Submitting a classmate's assignment as your own is
Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.w: plagiarism is using work without credit.

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: What is computer ethics? Write any two commandments of computer ethics.
Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.r: Computer ethics is the set of moral principles that guide how we use computers, networks and the Internet. Commandments (any two): do not use a computer to harm other people; do not snoop in other people's files; do not use a computer to steal; do not copy or use paid software you have not paid for; always use a computer with respect for others.

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: Differentiate between ethics and law with two points.
Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.r: Ethics are moral rules followed by choice, from conscience; laws are made by the state and everyone must obey them. Breaking an ethical rule brings shame or loss of trust; breaking a law brings a fine, prison or both.

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: What is hacking? Under which section of the ETA 2063 is unauthorised access punished, and what is the maximum punishment?
Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.r: Hacking is getting into a computer, network or account without the owner's permission. Unauthorised access is punished under section 45 of the ETA 2063, with a fine up to Rs 2 lakh, or prison up to 3 years, or both.

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: What is phishing? Write any two signs of a phishing message.
Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.r: Phishing is tricking people into giving their passwords, PINs, OTPs or card numbers through a fake message that seems to come from a trusted company. Signs (any two): a strange or misspelt web address; a demand for a password, MPIN or OTP; panic and a short deadline; "Dear customer" instead of your name; spelling mistakes; a prize that is too good to be true.

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: What is cyber bullying? Write two things a student should do if bullied online.
Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.r: Cyber bullying is using phones, chat or social media to repeatedly hurt, threaten or shame someone. The student should (any two): not reply; keep screenshots as evidence; block and report the bully on the app; tell a parent or teacher (and the police in serious cases).

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: Differentiate between copyright infringement and plagiarism.
Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.r: Copyright infringement is copying or using a work without the owner's permission; it is a legal offence under the Copyright Act. Plagiarism is using someone's work without giving credit; it is an ethical and academic offence. (Giving credit does not make unlicensed copying legal; permission does not make uncredited copying honest.)

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: What is software piracy? Write two harms of it.
Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.r: Software piracy is copying, selling or using software without the owner's licence. Harms (any two): the programmers lose the money they earned; pirated copies often carry viruses; they get no security updates; it is illegal under the Copyright Act.

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: Write the full name of Nepal's cyber law and the date it was authenticated. Name two things to which it gives legal recognition.
Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.r: The Electronic Transactions Act, 2063, authenticated and published on 22 Mansir 2063 BS (8 December 2006). It gives legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures.

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: What is a digital footprint? Give one example each of an active and a passive footprint.
Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.r: A digital footprint is the record of everything a person does online. Active: a post, comment or photo you share on purpose. Passive: your search history, location data or cookies recorded without your notice.

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: Write any four rules for the safe use of social media.
Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.r: Any four: use a strong, unique password and MFA; keep the profile private and accept only people you know; never share your address, phone number, location or ID card; think before posting; check facts before sharing; never share an OTP or MPIN; never meet an online friend alone; block and report bullies and fake accounts.

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: What is computer ethics? Explain any six of the Ten Commandments of computer ethics with an example of each.
Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.r: Computer ethics is the set of moral principles that guide the use of computers, networks and the Internet (1 mark). Any six, half a mark each: (1) do not use a computer to harm others — e.g. posting a photo to embarrass a classmate; (2) do not interfere with others' computer work — e.g. switching off a friend's computer while she works; (3) do not snoop in others' files — e.g. opening a classmate's folder; (4) do not use a computer to steal — e.g. moving money with a stolen PIN; (5) do not tell lies with a computer — e.g. spreading a false rumour; (6) do not use paid software you have not paid for — e.g. a cracked game; (7) do not use others' computer resources without permission — e.g.

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: What is cyber crime? Explain any three cyber crimes, with an example and one way of protection for each.
Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.r: Cyber crime is any illegal act done by means of a computer, phone, network or the Internet (1 mark). Any three (1 mark each): Hacking — entering a computer or account without permission, e.g. breaking into a result system to change marks; protect with strong passwords, MFA and updates. Phishing — fake messages that trick people into giving passwords or OTPs, e.g. "your eSewa account is blocked, verify here"; never click unknown links or share an OTP. Cyber bullying — repeatedly hurting someone online, e.g. a fake profile to mock a classmate; block, report, keep evidence and tell an adult. Identity theft — pretending to be someone using their details, e.g.

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: Describe the Electronic Transactions Act, 2063: when it was made, its aims, and any three offences with their punishments.
Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.r: The Electronic Transactions Act, 2063 is Nepal's cyber law. It was authenticated and published on 22 Mansir 2063 BS (8 December 2006) and has 12 chapters and 80 sections (1 mark). Aims (1 mark): to give legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures; to make electronic transactions secure and reliable; to set up a Controller and Certifying Authorities for digital signature certificates; to control computer crimes. Offences (2 marks, any three): s.44 pirating, destroying or altering source code — up to 3 years or Rs 2 lakh or both; s.45 unauthorised access — up to Rs 2 lakh or 3 years or both;

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: What is intellectual property? Explain copyright and plagiarism. How can a student avoid plagiarism in a project?
Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.r: Intellectual property is a creation of the mind, such as a book, song, photo, program, invention or brand name; the rights that protect it are intellectual property rights (1 mark). Copyright is the legal right of a creator to copy, publish and sell an original work and stop others; it is automatic, and in Nepal lasts for the author's life plus 50 years under the Copyright Act, 2059, which also protects computer programs. Plagiarism is presenting someone else's words, ideas or work as your own without credit, e.g. copying a website paragraph into a project (2 marks). To avoid plagiarism (1 mark): write in your own words; put exact words in quotation marks and name the source;

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: Who is a digital citizen? Explain netiquette and any four rules for the safe use of social media.
Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.r: A digital citizen is a person who uses the Internet and digital technology responsibly, safely and respectfully (1 mark). Netiquette is good manners online: be polite, do not write in capitals, do not spam, respect others' privacy, give credit, think before posting (1 mark). Safe use of social media (2 marks, any four): strong unique passwords and MFA; private profile and friends you know; keep address, phone, location and ID private; think before posting; check facts before sharing; never share an OTP or MPIN; never meet online friends alone; block and report bullies and keep evidence.

Computer Ethics and Cyber Law.q: What is computer ethics? Explain the ten commandments of computer ethics and the main cyber crimes.
Explain copyright, plagiarism, the Electronic Transactions Act 2063 and the rules of a good digital citizen.

Computer Virus.q: Malware that spreads by itself across a network without needing a host file is a
Computer Virus.w: a worm copies itself over networks by itself.

Computer Virus.q: A free "game" that secretly opens the computer to an attacker is a
Computer Virus.w: it hides inside something that looks useful.

Computer Virus.q: Malware that locks your files and demands money to unlock them is
Brain, the first virus for PCs (1986), came from
A keylogger, which records everything you type, is a kind of
Which of these is antivirus software?
Moving a suspicious file to a locked, safe area so it cannot run is called
The 3-2-1 backup rule is three copies, on two kinds of media, with
Computer Virus.w: one copy away from home (or in the cloud) survives fire or theft.

Computer Virus.q: Write any two ways a computer virus spreads.
Computer Virus.r: Any two: infected pen drives and memory cards; pirated or cracked software and games; e-mail attachments and links from unknown senders; fake websites and apps; files shared over a network.

Computer Virus.q: Write any four symptoms of a computer infected by a virus.
Computer Virus.r: Any four: the computer becomes very slow or hangs; programs crash or the computer restarts by itself; files go missing, change, or cannot be opened; folders on a pen drive turn into shortcuts; unwanted pop-up adverts appear; the antivirus is switched off without your knowing; messages are sent from your account without you.

Computer Virus.q: What is ransomware? Name one ransomware attack.
Computer Virus.r: Ransomware is malware that locks (encrypts) a user's files or computer and demands money (a ransom) to unlock them. Example: WannaCry, which on 12 May 2017 locked more than 200,000 computers in over 150 countries and demanded 300 US dollars in Bitcoin.

Computer Virus.q: What is antivirus software? Name two antivirus programs.
Computer Virus.r: Antivirus software is a utility program that detects, blocks and removes viruses and other malware. Examples: Microsoft Defender, Avast, Kaspersky, Norton, ClamAV (any two).

Computer Virus.q: Explain how antivirus software works, and differentiate between an antivirus and a firewall.
Computer Virus.r: How it works: it compares files with a database of signatures (patterns of known malware) and also watches the behaviour of programs for suspicious actions; its real-time scanner checks every file as it is opened or downloaded; a found threat is cleaned, deleted or put in quarantine; the signature list must be updated regularly (2 marks). Difference: an antivirus checks and cleans the files and programs inside the computer, while a firewall checks the network traffic coming in and going out and blocks unauthorised connections; the two work together (2 marks).

Computer Virus.q: Write any four ways to protect a computer from viruses and other malware.
Computer Virus.r: Any four: install an antivirus and keep it updated; turn on automatic updates for the operating system and apps; scan pen drives before opening them; download software only from official sites, never cracked copies; do not open attachments or links from unknown senders; keep backups by the 3-2-1 rule (three copies, two kinds of media, one kept elsewhere); use strong passwords with multi-factor authentication.

Computer Virus.q: A computer virus is a
Computer Virus.w: a virus is a program written by a person.

Computer Virus.q: The name "computer virus" was first used by
Computer Virus.w: Fred Cohen, on the suggestion of Leonard Adleman, 1983–84.

Computer Virus.q: Brain, the first virus for IBM PCs, appeared in
Computer Virus.w: 1986, by the Alvi brothers of Lahore.

Computer Virus.q: Malware that copies itself over a network without a host file is a
Computer Virus.w: a worm needs no host and spreads by itself.

Computer Virus.q: A harmful program disguised as a useful game or tool is a
Computer Virus.w: named after the wooden horse of Troy.

Computer Virus.q: Malware that locks your files and demands money is
What is a computer virus? Write any two ways by which it spreads.
Computer Virus.r: A computer virus is a harmful program that attaches itself to other files, copies itself when the infected file is run, and damages data without the user's knowledge. It spreads (any two) through infected pen drives, pirated software, e-mail attachments, fake links and downloads, and shared network folders.

Computer Virus.q: Differentiate between a virus and a worm.
Computer Virus.r: A virus needs a host file and spreads only when a person runs the infected file; a worm is a complete program that copies itself over a network by itself. A virus mainly damages files; a worm mainly uses up network speed and computer resources.

Computer Virus.q: What is a Trojan horse? Why is it given this name?
Computer Virus.r: A Trojan horse is a harmful program disguised as a useful or attractive one, such as a free game or a software crack; it does harm (steals data, opens a backdoor) once installed and does not copy itself. It is named after the Greek story of soldiers hidden in a wooden horse given to Troy as a gift.

Computer Virus.q: What is ransomware? Write one way to protect your files from it.
Computer Virus.r: Ransomware is malware that locks a computer or encrypts its files and demands money to unlock them. Protection (any one): keep a backup on a disk that is unplugged after use or in cloud storage; install security updates; do not open unknown attachments.

Computer Virus.q: Differentiate between spyware and adware.
Computer Virus.r: Spyware hides and secretly collects information such as passwords and browsing and sends it to someone; adware shows unwanted adverts and is very visible. Example: a keylogger is spyware; a toolbar that keeps opening shopping sites is adware.

Computer Virus.q: What is antivirus software? Name any two antivirus programs.
Computer Virus.r: Antivirus software is a utility program that detects, blocks and removes viruses and other malware. Examples (any two): Microsoft Defender, Avast, AVG, Avira, Kaspersky, Norton 360, McAfee, Bitdefender, ESET NOD32, Quick Heal, ClamAV.

Computer Virus.q: What is a virus signature? Why must antivirus software be updated regularly?
Computer Virus.r: A virus signature is the recognisable pattern of code that identifies a known virus; antivirus programs keep a database of them. It must be updated because new malware appears every day, and an antivirus can recognise by signature only the malware whose signature is already in its database.

Computer Virus.q: Differentiate between antivirus software and a firewall.
Computer Virus.r: Antivirus software checks files and programs for malware and removes or quarantines it; a firewall checks the data entering and leaving through the network and blocks unauthorised connections. Antivirus uses a signature database; a firewall uses rules about which programs and addresses may connect.

Computer Virus.q: What is a backup? Explain the 3-2-1 backup rule.
Computer Virus.r: A backup is an extra copy of files kept somewhere else so that they can be recovered after loss or damage. The 3-2-1 rule: keep 3 copies of important files, on 2 different kinds of storage, with 1 copy away from the computer (for example in cloud storage).

Computer Virus.q: What is malware? Explain any four types of malware with an example of each.
Computer Virus.r: Malware (malicious software) is any program made to harm a computer or its user (1 mark). Any four (3 marks): Virus — attaches itself to a file and spreads when the file is run; e.g. Brain (boot sector virus). Worm — a separate program that copies itself over networks by itself; e.g. the Morris worm. Trojan horse — disguised as a useful program, it does harm once installed; e.g. a fake game crack that steals passwords. Spyware — secretly records what the user does and sends it to someone; e.g. a keylogger. Adware — shows unwanted adverts and tracks browsing; e.g. a pop-up toolbar. Ransomware — locks the files and demands money; e.g. WannaCry (2017).

Computer Virus.q: Write a short history of computer viruses, describing any four important events.
Computer Virus.r: Any four, 1 mark each: 1971 Creeper — Bob Thomas's program moved between ARPANET computers showing "I'M THE CREEPER: CATCH ME IF YOU CAN"; Reaper was written to delete it. 1982 Elk Cloner — a 15-year-old's program spread on Apple II floppy disks and showed a poem. 1983–84 — Fred Cohen demonstrated a self-copying program and gave it the name computer virus. 1986 Brain — made by the Alvi brothers in Lahore, Pakistan; infected the boot sector of floppy disks; the first PC virus. 1988 Morris worm — spread over the Internet and slowed thousands of computers. 2000 ILOVEYOU — an e-mail worm that overwrote picture and music files.

Computer Virus.q: What is antivirus software? Explain how it detects and deals with malware.
Computer Virus.r: Antivirus software is a utility program that detects, blocks and removes malware (1 mark). How it works (3 marks): signature checking — it compares files with a database of known virus signatures, which must be updated regularly; behaviour (heuristic) checking — it watches for suspicious actions such as a program changing hundreds of files, to catch new malware; real-time protection — it checks every file as it is opened, downloaded or copied, including pen drives, and the user can run quick, full or custom scans; action — infected files are cleaned, quarantined (locked away where they cannot run) or deleted.

Computer Virus.q: Explain any four ways of protecting a computer from viruses and other malware.
Computer Virus.r: Any four, 1 mark each, with the reason: antivirus and firewall — real-time scanning removes malware and the firewall blocks unauthorised connections; updates — patches close the security holes that worms use, as WannaCry showed; safe browsing and downloading — official sites and stores only, no cracked software, no pop-ups or unknown attachments; scanning pen drives and switching off AutoPlay — stops the commonest school route; backups by the 3-2-1 rule — files can be recovered after ransomware or disk failure; strong unique passwords with MFA — a stolen password alone cannot open the account; standard user accounts — malware cannot easily install itself.

Computer Virus.q: A cyber café's computers have become slow, show adverts on every page, and the folders on customers' pen drives turn into shortcuts. Name the likely malware and write a plan to clean the computers and keep them safe.
Computer Virus.r: The slowness and adverts point to adware (and possibly spyware) on the computers, and the shortcut folders to a pen-drive virus or worm (1 mark). Plan (3 marks): disconnect each infected computer from the network; update the antivirus and run a full scan, quarantining or deleting what it finds; uninstall unknown programs and browser extensions and reset the browsers; scan customers' pen drives and show hidden files so they can recover the real folders; install all Windows updates and keep the firewall on; switch off AutoPlay and give customers a standard account that cannot install programs; and keep a clean backup of the café's own files under the 3-2-1 rule.

Computer Virus.q: What is a computer virus? Explain the types of malware and the symptoms of an infected computer.
Explain how an antivirus works and eight ways of protecting a computer from malware.

Computer Network.q: The device that sends data only to the port of the computer it is meant for is a
Computer Network.w: a switch reads MAC addresses; a hub copies to all ports.

Computer Network.q: The device that joins a school's LAN to the Internet using IP addresses is a
A MAC address is
A network inside one school building is a
In a star topology, if the central switch fails
Computer Network.w: every computer depends on the centre.

Computer Network.q: A 100 Mbps connection can download at most
Differentiate between a hub and a switch.
Computer Network.r: A hub copies every signal it receives to all its ports, so all computers share the speed and data can collide. A switch reads the MAC address and sends each frame only to the port of the destination computer, so it is faster and more private.

Computer Network.q: Differentiate between LAN and WAN with one example each.
Computer Network.r: A LAN (Local Area Network) covers a small area such as a room, building or school campus and is fast — for example a school computer lab. A WAN (Wide Area Network) covers a country or the whole world and joins many LANs — for example the Internet, or the network joining a bank's branches across Nepal.

Computer Network.q: Name two wired and two wireless transmission media.
Computer Network.r: Wired: twisted-pair (UTP) cable, coaxial cable, optical fibre (any two). Wireless: radio waves (Wi-Fi), Bluetooth, microwave, satellite, infrared (any two).

Computer Network.q: A school's Internet connection is 16 Mbps. What is the shortest time to download a 120 MB video?
What is a computer network? Explain any four network components.
Computer Network.r: A computer network is two or more computers and devices connected by wired or wireless media to share data, hardware, software and an Internet connection (1 mark). Any three components: server — a powerful computer that provides services such as files, printing or websites to others; client — a computer that uses those services; NIC — the network card that connects a device to the network and carries its MAC address; switch — the central device that sends data only to its destination; router — joins different networks, such as the school LAN and the Internet, using IP addresses; modem — converts digital signals for the telephone or cable line and back (3 marks).

Computer Network.q: Why is the Internet called a network of networks? Explain with ISPs, packets and TCP/IP.
Computer Network.r: (1) The Internet is not one network: it is millions of LANs and WANs of homes, schools, companies and countries joined together by routers. (2) ISPs (Internet Service Providers) such as Nepal Telecom and WorldLink connect users to the Internet, and ISPs exchange traffic with each other (in Nepal at npIX) and with other countries. (3) Data is broken into small packets, each carrying the sender's and receiver's IP addresses, which may travel by different routes and are joined again at the destination. (4) All these different networks can work together because they follow the same rules, TCP/IP: IP addresses and routes the packets, TCP checks that every packet arrives and puts them in order.

Computer Network.q: The network of a school's computer lab is a
Computer Network.w: a lab lies in one building, so it is a Local Area Network.

Computer Network.q: Which device sends data only to the port of the destination computer?
Computer Network.w: a switch reads the MAC address; a hub copies to every port.

Computer Network.q: The full form of NIC is
Computer Network.w: NIC is the Network Interface Card that joins a computer to the network.

Computer Network.q: Which medium carries data as pulses of light?
Computer Network.w: optical fibre carries light in a glass core.

Computer Network.q: Terminators are needed at both ends of the main cable in a
Computer Network.w: the terminators stop the signal bouncing back along the bus.

Computer Network.q: In a star topology the whole network stops when
o: the printer is out of paper
Computer Network.w: every computer depends on the central device.

Computer Network.q: A modem changes
o: digital signals into line signals and back
Computer Network.w: modulation and demodulation of signals for the line.

Computer Network.q: A phone connected to Bluetooth earbuds forms a
Computer Network.w: the devices of one person within about 10 m form a PAN.

Computer Network.q: Define a computer network. Write two advantages of a network in a school.
Computer Network.r: A computer network is a group of two or more computers and devices connected by wired or wireless media to exchange data and share hardware, software and other resources. In a school: one printer and one Internet line can be shared by all the lab computers, and a teacher can give an exercise to the whole class through a shared folder (any two advantages).

Computer Network.q: What is a NIC? What is a MAC address?
Computer Network.r: A NIC (Network Interface Card) is the circuit or card that connects a computer to the network medium, through an RJ-45 port or a Wi-Fi radio. A MAC address is the permanent 48-bit number given to each NIC, written as six pairs of hexadecimal digits such as 3C-52-82-9A-7F-10, which identifies it on the local network.

Computer Network.q: What are a server and a client? Give one example of each.
Computer Network.r: A server is a powerful computer that provides services such as files, web pages or email to other computers, e.g. the web server that holds a school's website. A client is a computer or phone that requests and uses those services, e.g. a student's phone opening that website.

Computer Network.q: Write two differences between wired and wireless media, with one example of each.
Computer Network.r: Wired media carry signals along a cable and keep devices in one place; wireless media carry signals through the air and let devices move. Wired media are usually faster, steadier and safer from eavesdropping; wireless media are quicker to set up but affected by walls and distance. Example of wired: UTP cable; of wireless: Wi-Fi (any two differences with the examples).

Computer Network.q: What is a modem? Why does a fibre connection need an ONT instead?
Computer Network.r: A modem (modulator–demodulator) converts the computer's digital signals into signals that a telephone or cable line can carry, and converts them back on arrival. A fibre line carries light, not electrical signals, so an ONT (Optical Network Terminal) is needed to convert light into electrical signals and back.

Computer Network.q: Give two reasons why the star topology is used in most computer labs.
Computer Network.r: A faulty cable or computer cuts off only that one computer, so the rest of the lab keeps working; and computers are easy to add, remove and check, because each has its own cable to the switch. (Also: a switch gives every computer full speed.)

Computer Network.q: A 600 MB video is downloaded on a 40 Mbps connection. Find the shortest download time.
Computer Network.r: 600 MB × 8 = 4,800 Mb. Time = 4,800 Mb ÷ 40 Mbps = 120 s = 2 minutes.

Computer Network.q: Why is the Internet called a "network of networks"?
Computer Network.r: The Internet is not one network but millions of separate networks — home and school LANs, the networks of ISPs and companies, national and international WANs — owned by different people and joined by routers. Because all of them follow the same TCP/IP rules, data can pass from any one of them to any other.

Computer Network.q: What is network topology? Explain bus, ring and star topologies with neat diagrams.
Computer Network.r: Network topology is the pattern in which the computers and devices of a network are connected (1 mark). Bus: all computers are attached to one backbone cable with a terminator at each end; it needs the least cable, but one break in the backbone stops the network (draw a line with four computers and two terminators). Ring: each computer is joined to the next and the last to the first; data travels one way round, passed on by each computer; one broken link can stop the whole ring (draw six computers in a loop with an arrow). Star: each computer has its own cable to a central switch or hub;

Computer Network.q: Explain any four network devices with their functions.
Computer Network.r: Any four: NIC — connects a computer to the network medium; carries a MAC address. Hub — joins the computers of a star LAN and copies all data to every port. Switch — joins the computers of a LAN and sends data only to the destination's port using its MAC address. Router — joins different networks, such as a LAN and the Internet, reads IP addresses and chooses the best path. Modem — converts digital signals into signals for a telephone or cable line and back; on fibre an ONT does this. Wi-Fi access point — lets wireless devices join a wired LAN.

Computer Network.q: What are transmission media? Explain twisted pair, coaxial and optical fibre cables.
Computer Network.r: Transmission media are the paths along which data travels between devices: wired (guided) or wireless (unguided) (1 mark). Twisted pair: four pairs of insulated copper wires twisted to reduce noise, inside a plastic jacket; cheap, up to 1 Gbps over 100 m, RJ-45 connector; used for LAN cables. Coaxial: a copper core with insulation, a braided metal shield and a jacket; the shield keeps out interference; used for cable TV. Optical fibre: thin glass strands carrying pulses of light in a core surrounded by cladding; the fastest medium, reaches many kilometres and is not affected by electrical noise or lightning, but costly; used for ISP backbones and FTTH.

Computer Network.q: Explain LAN, MAN and WAN with one example of each. Write one difference between LAN and MAN.
Computer Network.r: LAN: a network within a room, building or campus, up to about 1 km, owned by one organisation, very fast — e.g. a school computer lab. MAN: a network covering a city or valley that joins many LANs — e.g. a cable-TV network in Kathmandu Valley, or a bank's branches in one city. WAN: a network across a country or the world, using links of many organisations — e.g. the Internet, or a bank's network joining branches in all seven provinces. One difference: a LAN covers one building or campus and is owned by one organisation, while a MAN covers a whole city and joins the LANs of many places (or: a LAN is faster than a MAN).

Computer Network.q: What is a computer network? Explain eight advantages and seven disadvantages of networking.
Explain bus, ring and star topologies with their advantages and disadvantages.
Describe the network devices and the transmission media; differentiate LAN, MAN and WAN.

Number System.q: The base of the hexadecimal number system is
Convert $(1110101101)_2$ into octal and hexadecimal.
Number System.r: Octal: groups of three from the right: 001 110 101 101 → 1, 6, 5, 5, so $(1655)_8$. Hexadecimal: groups of four from the right: 0011 1010 1101 → 3, A, D, so $(3AD)_{16}$. (Both equal 941 in decimal.)

Number System.q: How many megabytes and kilobytes are there in 2 GB?
Convert $(3AF)_{16}$ into binary and octal, and check your answer through decimal.
Which digit is not used in the octal system?
In hexadecimal, the symbol D stands for
How many bits make one byte?
To convert a binary number into octal, its bits are grouped in
Number System.w: $8 = 2^3$, so each octal digit is 3 bits.

Number System.q: Which of these units is the largest?
Number System.w: the order is GB, TB, PB, EB.

Number System.q: What is a number system? Define base (radix) with one example.
Number System.r: A number system is a way of writing numbers with a fixed set of digits and rules. Its base (radix) is the number of different digits it uses: binary has base 2 (digits 0 and 1), and decimal has base 10 (digits 0 to 9).

Number System.q: Why do computers use the binary number system?
Number System.r: A computer is made of electronic switches that have only two states, off and on, which are easy to make and to tell apart; they are written as 0 and 1. Storage also uses two states (magnetised one way or the other, charge or no charge), so all data is stored and processed as binary digits.

Number System.q: Convert $(1011101)_2$ into octal and hexadecimal.
Convert 3 MB into KB and into bytes.
How many bits are there in 2 KB? Show the working.
Number System.r: 2 KB = 2 × 1024 = 2,048 bytes, and each byte is 8 bits, so 2,048 × 8 = 16,384 bits.

Number System.q: Convert $(420)_{10}$ into binary, octal and hexadecimal, and check one of your answers by converting it back.
Why is each octal digit worth exactly 3 bits and each hexadecimal digit exactly 4 bits? Convert $(\mathrm{A7F})_{16}$ into octal through binary.

p: Write the units of memory from the bit to the yottabyte in order, with the relation between each pair.
A 32 GB memory card stores songs of 4 MB each. How many songs can it hold?
Why does a "1 TB" hard disk show only about 931 GB on a computer?
Number System.r: (a) 1 nibble = 4 bits; 1 byte = 8 bits; 1 KB = 1024 bytes; 1 MB = 1024 KB; 1 GB = 1024 MB; 1 TB = 1024 GB; 1 PB = 1024 TB; 1 EB = 1024 PB; 1 ZB = 1024 EB; 1 YB = 1024 ZB. (b) 32 GB = 32 × 1024 = 32,768 MB; 32,768 ÷ 4 = 8,192 songs. (c) Disk makers count 1 TB as 1,000,000,000,000 bytes (powers of 1000), but the computer divides by 1024 three times to show GB: $10^{12} \div 1024^3 \approx 931$ GB. The disk is not smaller; the two figures use different units.

Number System.q: Compare the binary, octal, decimal and hexadecimal systems in a table (base, digits, largest digit, one use). Write $(100)_{10}$ in each of the other three systems.
Explain decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal number systems. Why does a computer use binary?
Convert numbers between decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal with full working.
Explain the units of computer memory and convert between binary, octal and hexadecimal directly.
Convert the binary number $11010_2$ to its decimal equivalent.

Computer Graphics.q: A school logo that must stay sharp on a badge and on a banner should be made as
With a colour depth of 8 bits, a pixel can show
The uncompressed size of an 800 × 600 picture with 24-bit colour is
The free vector-drawing program that saves SVG files is
Computer Graphics.w: Inkscape; GIMP and Paint are raster editors.

Computer Graphics.q: For a photograph on a website, where small file size matters most, the usual format is
Computer Graphics.w: JPEG compresses photos strongly (with some loss).

Computer Graphics.q: The format that keeps every detail and allows a transparent background is
Computer Graphics.w: PNG is lossless and supports transparency.

Computer Graphics.q: A small moving sticker with few colours is usually a
Computer Graphics.w: GIF supports simple animation in up to 256 colours.

Computer Graphics.q: How many bytes does an uncompressed 800 × 600 picture with 24-bit colour need? Give the answer in KB too.
Computer Graphics.r: Pixels = 800 × 600 = 480,000; 24 bits = 3 bytes per pixel, so size = 480,000 × 3 = 1,440,000 bytes; ÷ 1024 = 1,406.25 KB (about 1.37 MB).

Computer Graphics.q: Differentiate between JPEG and PNG.
Computer Graphics.r: JPEG uses lossy compression: it throws away fine detail to make photographs very small, and it has no transparency. PNG uses lossless compression, keeps every pixel exactly, supports transparent backgrounds, and suits logos, screenshots and diagrams.

Computer Graphics.q: Differentiate between GIMP and Inkscape.
Computer Graphics.r: GIMP (GNU Image Manipulation Program) is a free raster editor for photographs and paintings, working pixel by pixel with layers. Inkscape is a free vector editor for logos, posters and diagrams that stay sharp at any size; it saves SVG files.

Computer Graphics.q: Write the full forms of BMP, JPEG, PNG, GIF and SVG, with one feature of each.
Computer Graphics.r: BMP — Bitmap: uncompressed, so files are very large. JPEG — Joint Photographic Experts Group: lossy, small files for photographs. PNG — Portable Network Graphics: lossless, supports transparency. GIF — Graphics Interchange Format: only 256 colours, supports simple animation. SVG — Scalable Vector Graphics: vector format, sharp at any size, used on websites.

Computer Graphics.q: Write the steps to make a Dashain greeting card in Paint and save it as a PNG file.
Computer Graphics.r: (1) Open Paint and set the page size with Resize (or Image Properties). (2) Use the Fill tool to colour the background, and the shapes tool (rectangle, star) with Colour 1 and Colour 2 for a border and decorations. (3) Use the Text tool (A) to type "Happy Dashain" and a short wish, choosing font, size and colour; draw a kite or a jamara with the brush or pencil. (4) File → Save As → PNG picture, type a name such as dashain.png and click Save.

Computer Graphics.q: The smallest unit of a raster picture is a
Computer Graphics.w: a pixel (picture element) is the smallest unit of a digital picture.

Computer Graphics.q: Which of these is a vector graphics program?
Computer Graphics.w: Inkscape edits shapes; Paint, GIMP and Pixlr edit pixels.

Computer Graphics.q: The full form of PNG is
Which format can store a short animation?
Computer Graphics.w: GIF can hold several frames and play them in turn.

Computer Graphics.q: A photograph from a phone camera is usually saved as
A picture that stays sharp however much it is enlarged is a
Computer Graphics.w: vector shapes are redrawn at every size.

Computer Graphics.q: Define computer graphics. Write any two of its uses.
Computer Graphics.r: Computer graphics are pictures, drawings, charts and animations created, stored, edited and displayed with a computer. Uses (any two): advertising banners; animated films and games; CAD drawings of buildings; digital maps; X-ray and CT images in hospitals; diagrams in e-learning lessons.

Computer Graphics.q: What is a pixel? What does a screen resolution of 1366 × 768 mean?
Computer Graphics.r: A pixel (picture element) is the smallest unit of a digital picture, holding one colour. A resolution of 1366 × 768 means the screen has 1366 pixels across and 768 pixels down, 1,049,088 pixels in all.

Computer Graphics.q: Write any two differences between raster and vector graphics.
Computer Graphics.r: Raster graphics are made of pixels, while vector graphics are made of shapes described by numbers. A raster picture blurs or pixelates when enlarged, while a vector picture stays sharp at any size. (Also: raster suits photographs, vector suits logos and diagrams.)

Computer Graphics.q: Write the full forms of BMP, JPEG, GIF and SVG.
Computer Graphics.r: BMP — Bitmap; JPEG — Joint Photographic Experts Group; GIF — Graphics Interchange Format; SVG — Scalable Vector Graphics.

Computer Graphics.q: Name two free graphics programs and say whether each one is a raster or a vector program.
Computer Graphics.r: GIMP — a raster (photo-editing) program; Inkscape — a vector (drawing) program. (Paint, which comes free with Windows, is also raster.)

Computer Graphics.q: What are the uses of the Fill with colour tool and the Colour picker tool in Paint?
Computer Graphics.r: Fill with colour pours the chosen colour into a closed area, such as the inside of a circle. The Colour picker copies a colour from the picture and makes it the current colour, so the same shade can be used again.

Computer Graphics.q: Differentiate between lossy and lossless compression, with one format of each.
Computer Graphics.r: Lossless compression makes a file smaller while keeping every pixel exactly, e.g. PNG (or GIF). Lossy compression throws away small details to make the file much smaller, and the original cannot be got back, e.g. JPEG.

Computer Graphics.q: Find the size in KB of an uncompressed 800 × 600 picture in 24-bit colour (1 KB = 1024 bytes).
What is a layer in GIMP? Give one advantage of using layers.
Computer Graphics.r: A layer is like a transparent sheet laid over a picture; each part of the picture can be on its own layer. Advantage: one part, such as the text, can be moved, changed or hidden without disturbing the rest of the picture.

Computer Graphics.q: What is colour depth? How many colours can an 8-bit picture show?
Computer Graphics.r: Colour depth is the number of bits used to store the colour of one pixel. An 8-bit picture can show $2^8 = 256$ colours.

Computer Graphics.q: What are raster and vector graphics? Explain each with two examples and write any four differences between them.
Computer Graphics.r: Raster graphics are pictures made of a grid of pixels, each holding one colour; examples: a phone photograph, a scanned certificate. Vector graphics store pictures as shapes — points, lines, curves and filled areas — described by numbers; examples: a school logo, a map of Nepal's provinces. Differences (any four): (1) raster is made of pixels, vector of shapes; (2) raster pixelates when enlarged, vector stays sharp; (3) raster files of photos are large, vector files are usually small; (4) raster suits photographs, vector suits logos, icons and diagrams; (5) raster is edited in Paint or GIMP, vector in Inkscape or Illustrator;

Computer Graphics.q: Describe the image formats BMP, JPEG, PNG, GIF and SVG: give the type, the kind of compression and one use of each.
Computer Graphics.r: BMP (Bitmap): raster, uncompressed, very large files; used by simple Windows programs. JPEG (Joint Photographic Experts Group): raster, lossy compression, 16.7 million colours, no transparency; used for photographs. PNG (Portable Network Graphics): raster, lossless, supports transparency; used for logos, screenshots and diagrams. GIF (Graphics Interchange Format): raster, lossless but only 256 colours, supports animation; used for stickers and short animations. SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics): vector, stored as text instructions, sharp at any size; used for logos, icons and maps on websites.

Computer Graphics.q: Write the steps to draw a greeting card in Paint using shapes, colours and text, and to save it as a PNG file. Name the tools you use.
Computer Graphics.r: (1) Open Paint from the Start menu and set the canvas size with Image properties (Ctrl+E). (2) Fill the background with the Fill with colour tool. (3) Draw hills, a kite or a house with the Shapes tools (curve, polygon, oval, rectangle), choosing Size and Colour 1; hold Shift for a perfect circle or square. (4) Fill each closed shape with colour. (5) Add the greeting with the Text tool, choosing font, size and colour. (6) Correct mistakes with Ctrl+Z or the Eraser, using the Magnifier for detail. (7) Save: File → Save as → PNG picture → type the name → Save.

Computer Graphics.q: Compare Paint, GIMP, Inkscape and Canva in a table: type, cost, need for the Internet and best use.

Multimedia.q: Pictures drawn one by one and shown quickly so that they seem to move form
Multimedia.w: animation; video is recorded from real life.

Multimedia.q: A film watched from beginning to end without any choices is
Multimedia.w: linear: a fixed order.

Multimedia.q: An E-Paath lesson in which you click to answer and choose what to see next is
Multimedia.w: interactive: it responds to the user.

Multimedia.q: The free program for recording and editing sound is
Multimedia.w: Audacity is a free audio editor.

Multimedia.q: To play sound, a computer needs
Multimedia.w: the sound card makes the signal; speakers play it.

Multimedia.q: Telemedicine and medical images are uses of multimedia in
Multimedia.w: health care.

Multimedia.q: Differentiate between linear and interactive multimedia.
Multimedia.r: Linear multimedia plays from beginning to end in a fixed order, and the user only watches, like a film or a TV advertisement. Interactive multimedia lets the user control it — click, choose, answer — like a game, a website or the E-Paath lessons.

Multimedia.q: Differentiate between animation and video.
Multimedia.r: Video is recorded from real life with a camera. Animation is made of drawn or computer-made pictures shown quickly, usually 12 to 30 a second, so that they seem to move.

Multimedia.q: Name two input devices and two output devices used for multimedia.
Multimedia.r: Input: microphone, webcam, digital camera, scanner, graphics tablet (any two). Output: monitor, speakers, headphones, projector (any two).

Multimedia.q: Write two uses of multimedia in health.
Multimedia.r: Any two: medical images such as X-ray, CT and MRI scans; telemedicine — video consultations with distant doctors; training doctors and nurses with videos and 3D models; health awareness campaigns with videos and animations.

Multimedia.q: Explain the uses of multimedia in education, entertainment and business.
Multimedia.r: Education: interactive lessons (E-Paath), videos and animations, projectors in classrooms and online classes make learning interesting and easier to understand. Entertainment: films, music, video games, YouTube and virtual reality. Business: advertisements, product videos on shopping sites such as Daraz, presentations and tourism videos (one or two explained points for each; health or communication may replace one).

Multimedia.q: Write two advantages and two disadvantages of multimedia. How many bytes does one minute of uncompressed CD-quality stereo sound need (44,100 samples a second, 16 bits, 2 channels)?
Multimedia.r: Advantages: it holds attention and makes learning interesting; it explains hard ideas with pictures, sound and motion; it suits learners who learn by seeing, hearing or doing; it can reach a large audience. Disadvantages: making it takes time, skill and costly equipment; its large files need storage and fast Internet; too many effects can distract (any two of each, 2 marks). Size: 44,100 × 16 × 2 × 60 ÷ 8 = 10,584,000 bytes, about 10.1 MB (2 marks).

Multimedia.q: Which of these is not one of the five elements of multimedia?
Multimedia.w: a printer is hardware; the five elements are text, graphics, audio, video and animation.

Multimedia.q: Moving pictures recorded from real life with a camera are called
Multimedia.w: video is recorded with a camera; animation is drawn.

Multimedia.q: Which device is an output device?
Multimedia.w: a projector gives the picture out to the viewers.

Multimedia.q: VLC media player is used to
Multimedia.w: VLC plays almost every audio and video format.

Multimedia.q: A free program for recording and editing sound is
Multimedia.w: Audacity is a free, open-source audio editor.

Multimedia.q: Which file format is used for sound?
Multimedia.w: MP3 is a compressed sound format.

Multimedia.q: An E-Paath lesson in which the student drags and answers is an example of
Multimedia.w: the lesson responds to what the student does.

Multimedia.q: The part of a computer that changes sound between analogue and digital form is the
Multimedia.w: the sound card converts sound to numbers and back.

Multimedia.q: What is multimedia? Name its five elements.
Multimedia.r: Multimedia is the combined use of two or more forms of media to present information, usually with a computer. Its five elements are text, graphics, audio, video and animation.

Multimedia.q: Write two differences between video and animation.
Multimedia.r: A video is recorded from real life with a camera, while an animation is made of drawn or computer-generated pictures. Video shows real people and places (a cricket match); animation can show anything that can be drawn, including imaginary things (a cartoon, a moving diagram of the heart).

Multimedia.q: Differentiate between linear and interactive multimedia with one example each.
Multimedia.r: Linear multimedia plays from start to end in a fixed order and the viewer only watches, e.g. a TV advertisement. Interactive multimedia lets the user choose and responds to clicks and answers, e.g. an E-Paath lesson or a video game.

Multimedia.q: Name any two input devices and two output devices used in multimedia.
Multimedia.r: Input: microphone, webcam, digital camera, scanner, graphics tablet (any two). Output: monitor, speakers, headphones, projector (any two).

Multimedia.q: What is the use of
Multimedia.r: (a) A graphics card (GPU) draws pictures, 3D scenes and video frames on the screen quickly. (b) A sound card changes sound from the microphone into digital form and changes digital sound back into sound for the speakers.

Multimedia.q: Write any two uses of multimedia in education.
Multimedia.r: Interactive lessons such as E-Paath make learning interesting and give practice with feedback; teachers show videos, animations and simulations with a projector; students join online classes and watch tutorials (any two).

Multimedia.q: Write any two uses of multimedia in health.
Multimedia.r: Doctors study X-ray, ultrasound, CT and MRI images on screens; telemedicine lets a remote health post consult a specialist by video call; doctors and nurses are trained with videos and 3D animations; awareness videos teach people about vaccination and hygiene (any two).

Multimedia.q: Name one program for each job: playing a video, editing sound, editing video, making a 3D animation.
Multimedia.r: Playing a video: VLC media player. Editing sound: Audacity. Editing video: OpenShot (or Kdenlive or CapCut). 3D animation: Blender.

Multimedia.q: A 2-minute voice recording uses 22,050 samples per second, 16 bits per sample and 1 channel (mono). Find its uncompressed size in KB (1 KB = 1024 bytes).
Define multimedia. Explain its five elements with one example of each.
Multimedia.r: Multimedia is the combined use of two or more forms of media — text, graphics, audio, video and animation — to present information, usually with a computer (1 mark). Text: letters, numbers and symbols, e.g. the title and instructions of a lesson. Graphics: still pictures such as photos, diagrams and maps, e.g. a labelled diagram of a flower. Audio: sound — speech, music and effects, e.g. a teacher's recorded explanation. Video: moving pictures recorded with a camera, e.g. a recorded science experiment. Animation: drawn or computer-made pictures shown quickly so they seem to move, e.g. an animated water cycle.

Multimedia.q: What is a multimedia system? Describe the input, output and storage devices and the software it needs.
Multimedia.r: A multimedia system is a computer (or phone or tablet) with the hardware to capture, store and play sound, pictures and video, and the software to make, edit and play multimedia. Input devices: microphone (sound), webcam and digital camera (pictures and video), scanner (printed pictures), graphics tablet (drawing). Output devices: monitor, speakers and headphones, projector and printer. Inside: a fast CPU, enough RAM, a graphics card and a sound card. Storage: hard disk or SSD, memory cards, pen drives and cloud storage, because media files are large.

Multimedia.q: Explain the uses of multimedia in education, entertainment, business and health, with one example of each.
Multimedia.r: Education: interactive lessons such as E-Paath, videos and simulations shown on projectors, and online classes make learning interesting. Entertainment: films, music videos, cartoons and video games, watched on TV, YouTube and phones. Business: adverts, product photos and videos on Daraz, presentations, training videos and video conferences. Health: X-ray, CT and MRI images on screens, telemedicine between remote health posts and city hospitals, and training of doctors with 3D animations.

Multimedia.q: Write any four advantages and any four disadvantages of multimedia.
Multimedia.r: Advantages: (1) makes information interesting and holds attention; (2) explains difficult ideas with pictures, sound and movement; (3) suits learners who learn by seeing, hearing or doing, and gives practice with feedback; (4) one product can reach a very large audience. Disadvantages: (1) making it needs time, skill and costly equipment; (2) files are large and need much storage and fast Internet; (3) it needs electricity and devices, which not everyone has; (4) too many effects distract, and long screen time harms health.

How many such MP3 songs fit on a 16 GB memory card? (1 KB = 1024 bytes, 1 MB = 1024 KB, 1 GB = 1024 MB)

Program Design Tools.q: The flowchart symbol for a decision is the
Program Design Tools.w: a diamond has two labelled exits, yes and no.

Program Design Tools.q: The flowchart symbol for input and output is the

The property that an algorithm must end after a fixed number of steps is
The first step of program development is
Program Design Tools.w: first understand the input, process and output.

Program Design Tools.q: "Repeat these steps until the counter reaches 10" is an example of
Structured English with keywords such as IF … ENDIF is called
Write any two features of a good algorithm.
Program Design Tools.r: Any two: finiteness — it ends after a limited number of steps; definiteness — every step is clear and has only one meaning; input and output — it states what it receives and produces at least one result; effectiveness — every step can actually be carried out.

Program Design Tools.q: Write two differences between an algorithm and a flowchart.
Program Design Tools.r: An algorithm is written in words as numbered steps, while a flowchart is drawn with standard symbols joined by arrows. An algorithm is quicker to write and change; a flowchart makes branches and loops easier to see.

Program Design Tools.q: Write an algorithm to find the average of four numbers.
Program Design Tools.r: Step 1: Start. Step 2: Read A, B, C and D. Step 3: SUM = A + B + C + D. Step 4: AVG = SUM ÷ 4. Step 5: Display AVG. Step 6: Stop.

Program Design Tools.q: What is pseudocode? Write pseudocode to find the sum of two numbers.
Program Design Tools.r: Pseudocode is an algorithm written in short, structured English statements with keywords such as INPUT, PRINT, IF … ENDIF and WHILE … ENDWHILE; it looks like a program but cannot be run. Example: BEGIN / INPUT A, B / SET S = A + B / PRINT S / END.

Program Design Tools.q: Write an algorithm and draw a flowchart to find the sum of the even numbers from 2 to 50.
Program Design Tools.r: Algorithm. Step 1: Start. Step 2: Set S = 0 and I = 2. Step 3: Is I ≤ 50? If no, go to step 6. Step 4: S = S + I. Step 5: I = I + 2, and go to step 3. Step 6: Display S. Step 7: Stop. Flowchart. Start → rectangle "S = 0, I = 2" → diamond "Is I ≤ 50?" → Yes: rectangle "S = S + I" → rectangle "I = I + 2" → arrow back to just above the diamond; No: parallelogram "Display S" → Stop. The output is 650, which a QBASIC version of this algorithm also printed.

Program Design Tools.q: Explain the steps of program development.
Program Design Tools.r: (1) Problem analysis: understand the problem and list its input, process and output. (2) Program design: plan the steps with an algorithm, flowchart or pseudocode. (3) Coding: write the program in a language such as QBASIC. (4) Testing and debugging: run it with test data and remove errors. (5) Documentation: write comments and a user guide. (6) Implementation and maintenance: install it, then fix and update it when needed.

Program Design Tools.q: A finite set of step-by-step instructions for solving a problem is called
Program Design Tools.w: that is the definition of an algorithm.

Program Design Tools.q: Which flowchart symbol is used for a decision?
Program Design Tools.w: the diamond holds a yes/no question.

Program Design Tools.q: Which flowchart symbol is used for "Read N" or "Print SUM"?
Program Design Tools.w: input and output use the parallelogram.

Program Design Tools.q: The feature that an algorithm must end after a limited number of steps is
Program Design Tools.w: finiteness means the steps come to an end.

Program Design Tools.q: Which is the first step of program development?
Program Design Tools.w: the problem must be understood before it is designed or coded.

Program Design Tools.q: A small circle in a flowchart is a
Program Design Tools.w: a connector joins two parts of a flowchart on the same page.

Program Design Tools.q: Structured English statements such as IF … THEN … ENDIF that cannot be run on a computer are called
What is an algorithm? Write any two features of a good algorithm.
Program Design Tools.r: An algorithm is a finite set of clear, step-by-step instructions for solving a problem, from Start to Stop. Any two features: it has input and output; every step is definite (one meaning only); it is finite (it ends); every step is effective (can be carried out).

Program Design Tools.q: Draw the symbols for terminal, input/output, process and decision, and write the use of each.
Program Design Tools.r: Terminal — an oval, used for Start and Stop. Input/output — a parallelogram, used to read data or display results. Process — a rectangle, used for a calculation or assignment. Decision — a diamond, used for a yes/no question with two exits.

Program Design Tools.q: Write any two differences between an algorithm and a flowchart.
Program Design Tools.r: An algorithm is written in words as numbered steps, while a flowchart is drawn with standard symbols joined by arrows. An algorithm is quicker to write and change, while a flowchart is easier to follow, especially for branches and loops.

Program Design Tools.q: Write an algorithm to find the area of a rectangle.
Program Design Tools.r: Step 1: Start. Step 2: Read the length L and breadth B. Step 3: A = L × B. Step 4: Display A. Step 5: Stop.

Program Design Tools.q: What is selection? Give one example from daily life.
Program Design Tools.r: Selection is a control structure in which a condition is tested and one of two (or more) paths is followed depending on whether it is true or false. Example: if the traffic light is green, cross the road; otherwise wait.

Program Design Tools.q: What is a loop? What is an infinite loop?
Program Design Tools.r: A loop is a group of steps that is repeated while a condition is true (or a fixed number of times). An infinite loop is a loop whose condition never becomes false, usually because the update step is missing, so it repeats for ever.

Program Design Tools.q: Write an algorithm and draw a flowchart to find the area and circumference of a circle of radius R.
Program Design Tools.r: Algorithm. Step 1: Start. Step 2: Read R. Step 3: A = 3.14 × R × R. Step 4: C = 2 × 3.14 × R. Step 5: Display A and C. Step 6: Stop. Flowchart. Start (oval) → Read R (parallelogram) → A = 3.14 × R × R (rectangle) → C = 2 × 3.14 × R (rectangle) → Display A, C (parallelogram) → Stop (oval), joined top to bottom by arrows. Test: R = 7 gives A = 153.86 and C = 43.96.

Program Design Tools.q: Write an algorithm and draw a flowchart to check whether a person is eligible to vote in Nepal (age 18 years or more).
Program Design Tools.r: Algorithm. Step 1: Start. Step 2: Read AGE. Step 3: Is AGE ≥ 18? If yes, display "Eligible to vote"; otherwise display "Not eligible". Step 4: Stop. Flowchart. Start → Read AGE (parallelogram) → diamond "Is AGE ≥ 18?" → Yes exit to a parallelogram "Display Eligible to vote"; No exit to a parallelogram "Display Not eligible" → both paths join → Stop. Test: AGE = 20 gives Eligible; AGE = 16 gives Not eligible.

Program Design Tools.q: Write an algorithm and draw a flowchart to find the factorial of a number. Trace it for N = 4.
Program Design Tools.r: Algorithm. Step 1: Start. Step 2: Read N. Step 3: Set F = 1 and I = 1. Step 4: Is I ≤ N? If no, go to step 7. Step 5: F = F × I. Step 6: I = I + 1, and go to step 4. Step 7: Display F. Step 8: Stop. Flowchart. Start → Read N → rectangle "F = 1, I = 1" → diamond "Is I ≤ N?" → Yes: rectangle "F = F × I" → rectangle "I = I + 1" → arrow back up to just above the diamond; No: parallelogram "Display F" → Stop. Trace for N = 4: I = 1, F = 1; I = 2, F = 2; I = 3, F = 6; I = 4, F = 24; I = 5 fails the test, so the output is 24.

Program Design Tools.q: What is a flowchart? Write any four rules for drawing a flowchart and any two of its advantages.
Program Design Tools.r: A flowchart is a pictorial representation of an algorithm using standard symbols joined by flow lines (1 mark). Any four rules: one Start and one Stop; use standard symbols only; flow from top to bottom and left to right with an arrowhead on every line; a decision has two labelled exits (Yes/No); flow lines do not cross — use connectors; write short statements inside the symbols (2 marks). Any two advantages: the logic is easy to understand; mistakes are easy to find; it helps explain the plan to others; it documents the program (1 mark).

Program Design Tools.q: What is an algorithm? Explain its features, and the symbols and rules of a flowchart.
Write the algorithm, flowchart steps and pseudocode of programs that use sequence, selection and repetition.

Fundamentals of Computer Programming.q: The language written only in 0s and 1s is
Fundamentals of Computer Programming.w: the only language the CPU runs directly.

Fundamentals of Computer Programming.q: MOV and ADD are mnemonics of
Fundamentals of Computer Programming.w: mnemonics are short codes of assembly language.

A program adds two numbers when it should multiply them; it runs and gives wrong answers with no message. This is
Fundamentals of Computer Programming.w: the logic is wrong, so the answer is wrong.

Python was created by
Finding and correcting the errors in a program is called
Differentiate between machine language and assembly language.
Fundamentals of Computer Programming.r: Machine language is written in binary (0s and 1s), is understood directly by the processor and needs no translator. Assembly language uses short words called mnemonics, such as MOV and ADD, and needs an assembler to translate it into machine code. Both are low-level and machine-dependent.

Fundamentals of Computer Programming.q: Differentiate between a syntax error and a logical error, with an example of each.
Fundamentals of Computer Programming.r: A syntax error breaks the grammar rules of the language, so the program does not run, for example PRNT for PRINT. A logical error is a mistake in the method, so the program runs but the output is wrong, for example A = L + B for the area of a rectangle.

Fundamentals of Computer Programming.q: Name the QBASIC data types with their type symbols.
Write any three features of high-level languages, and name four high-level languages with the person who created each.
Fundamentals of Computer Programming.r: Features (any three): English-like words and mathematical signs; easy to write, read and correct; portable (machine-independent); must be translated by a compiler or interpreter; one statement does the work of many machine instructions (2 marks). Languages (2 marks): BASIC — John Kemeny and Thomas Kurtz (1964), whose QBASIC version came from Microsoft (1991); Python — Guido van Rossum (1991); C — Dennis Ritchie (1972); Java — James Gosling (1995).

Fundamentals of Computer Programming.q: Find the errors in this program, name their type, and write the correct program with its output for radius 7.
The translator that converts assembly language into machine language is
Fundamentals of Computer Programming.w: an assembler translates mnemonics into machine code.

Fundamentals of Computer Programming.q: Which translator converts the whole program at once and makes an object program?
Fundamentals of Computer Programming.w: a compiler translates everything at once.

Fundamentals of Computer Programming.q: QBASIC programs are run by
Fundamentals of Computer Programming.w: QBASIC is an interpreter, running one line at a time.

Fundamentals of Computer Programming.q: Which of these is a low-level language?
Fundamentals of Computer Programming.w: assembly language is close to the machine; the others are high-level.

Fundamentals of Computer Programming.q: Dividing a number by zero while a program is running causes
Fundamentals of Computer Programming.w: the error appears only while the program runs.

Fundamentals of Computer Programming.q: A program runs to the end but prints a wrong answer because of a wrong formula. This is
Fundamentals of Computer Programming.w: the program runs, but the method is wrong.

Fundamentals of Computer Programming.q: Python was created by
Write any two differences between a low-level and a high-level language.
Fundamentals of Computer Programming.r: A low-level language (machine or assembly) is close to the hardware and machine-dependent, while a high-level language uses English-like words and is portable. Low-level programs are hard to write and correct but run very fast; high-level programs are easy to write and correct but must be translated by a compiler or interpreter.

Fundamentals of Computer Programming.q: What is a language processor? Name its three types.
Fundamentals of Computer Programming.r: A language processor (translator) is a program that converts a program written in assembly or a high-level language into machine language. Its three types are the compiler, the interpreter and the assembler.

Fundamentals of Computer Programming.q: Write any two differences between a compiler and an interpreter.
Fundamentals of Computer Programming.r: A compiler translates the whole program at once, while an interpreter translates and runs one line at a time. A compiler makes an object program that runs without it, while an interpreter makes no object program and is needed every time. (Also: a compiler lists all errors after checking the whole program; an interpreter stops at the first error.)

Fundamentals of Computer Programming.q: What is assembly language? Why does it need an assembler?
Fundamentals of Computer Programming.r: Assembly language is a low-level language that uses short words called mnemonics (such as MOV, ADD, SUB) in place of binary instructions. The processor understands only machine language, so an assembler must translate the mnemonics into binary before the program can run.

Fundamentals of Computer Programming.q: Define syntax error and logical error with one example each.
Fundamentals of Computer Programming.r: A syntax error breaks the grammar rules of the language, for example PRIMT "Hello" instead of PRINT "Hello". A logical error is a mistake in the method, so the program runs but gives a wrong result, for example AVG = A + B / 2 instead of AVG = (A + B) / 2.

Fundamentals of Computer Programming.q: What is a run-time error? Give two examples.
Fundamentals of Computer Programming.r: A run-time error is an error that occurs while the program is running, when it is asked to do something impossible, and it stops the program with a message. Examples: dividing a number by zero; the square root of a negative number; storing a number too large for its variable (overflow).

Fundamentals of Computer Programming.q: What is debugging? Write any two ways of debugging a program.
Fundamentals of Computer Programming.r: Debugging is the process of finding and correcting the errors (bugs) in a program. Any two ways: reading the error messages; dry running the program with a trace table; printing the values of variables at different points; stepping through it line by line (F8 in QBASIC) or using breakpoints (F9).

Fundamentals of Computer Programming.q: Define constant and variable with one example of each.
Fundamentals of Computer Programming.r: A constant is a value that does not change while the program runs, for example 25 or "Nepal". A variable is a named memory location whose value can change while the program runs, for example AGE in AGE = 14.

Fundamentals of Computer Programming.q: Write any four rules for naming a variable in QBASIC.
Fundamentals of Computer Programming.r: Any four: it must begin with a letter; it may contain letters, digits and a full stop; it may be up to 40 characters long; it must not contain spaces or other symbols except a type symbol at the end; it must not be a keyword such as PRINT or END.

Fundamentals of Computer Programming.q: Name the five data types of QBASIC with their type symbols.
What is a programming language? Explain machine language, assembly language and high-level language, giving one advantage and one disadvantage of each.
Fundamentals of Computer Programming.r: A programming language is a set of words, symbols and rules used to write instructions for a computer (1 mark). Machine language: written in 0s and 1s; advantage — runs directly and fastest, needs no translation; disadvantage — very hard to write and correct, and machine-dependent. Assembly language: uses mnemonics such as MOV and ADD; advantage — easier than binary while still fast; disadvantage — machine-dependent and needs an assembler. High-level language: English-like statements, such as QBASIC and Python; advantage — easy to write, read and correct, and portable; disadvantage — must be translated by a compiler or interpreter and runs a little slower.

Fundamentals of Computer Programming.q: Explain compiler, interpreter and assembler. Which translator is used for QBASIC programs and which for C programs?
Fundamentals of Computer Programming.r: A compiler translates the whole high-level program at once into an object program (such as an.exe file), lists all errors after checking, and the object program then runs fast without the compiler. An interpreter translates and carries out one line at a time, stops at the first error, makes no object program and is needed every time the program runs. An assembler translates assembly-language mnemonics into machine code (3 marks). QBASIC programs are run by an interpreter; C programs are translated by a compiler such as GCC (1 mark).

Fundamentals of Computer Programming.q: What are testing and debugging? Explain the three types of programming error with one example each.
Fundamentals of Computer Programming.r: Testing is running a program with test data whose correct results are known and comparing the outputs; debugging is finding and correcting the errors (1 mark). Syntax error: breaking the rules of the language, found by the translator, e.g. PRIMT for PRINT. Run-time error: an impossible operation while the program runs, which stops it with a message, e.g. dividing by zero. Logical error: a wrong method; the program runs but gives wrong output and no message, e.g. AVG = A + B / 2 (3 marks).

Statistics.r: Mean. The sum is $35+42+48+55+60+62+65+68+70+72+74+75+78+80+82+85+88+90+92+95=1416$, so $\bar x=\frac{1416}{20}=70.8$. Median. With $n=20$ (even) it is the mean of the 10th and 11th values: $\frac{72+74}{2}=73$. Why they are close. The values rise steadily with no extreme value and no gap, so there is no outlier to pull the mean away from the middle of the list. When data are spread evenly like this, the mean and the median agree closely; when they differ a lot, look for an outlier.

With $n=10$ the median is the average of the 5th and 6th values: $\frac{15+15}{2}=15$. The mode is the most frequent value, 15 (it occurs three times). Statistics.r: (a) $\sum f=3+5+8+3+1=20$. $\sum fx=6+15+32+15+6=74$. Mean $=\dfrac{74}{20}=3.7$.(b) Mean $=\dfrac{12000+14000+15000+16000+143000}{5}=\dfrac{200000}{5}=\text{Rs }40{,}000$. The median is the middle value of the ordered data: Rs 15,000. The median is the better average here: the one very high income pulls the mean up to Rs 40,000, which describes none of the families, while Rs 15,000 is a typical family.

A shopkeeper marks his goods 40 % above the cost price and then allows a discount of 20 % on the marked price. Find his profit percent, and explain why the profit is not 20 %.
Profit and Loss.r: Take CP $=$ Rs 100. Then $\text{MP}=100\times1.40=\text{Rs }140$, and the discount is 20 % of the marked price: $0.20\times140=\text{Rs }28$, so $\text{SP}=140-28=\text{Rs }112$. Profit $=112-100=\text{Rs }12$, that is 12 % on the cost. Why not 20 %. The 40 % is added to the cost price while the 20 % discount comes off the marked price, which is the larger number: $0.40\times100=40$, but $0.20\times140=28$, so only 12 remains. Percentages added and subtracted in this way only cancel when they are measured on the same base.

Profit and Loss.r: (a) Discount $=15\%\times40000=\text{Rs }6000$, so SP before VAT $=40000-6000=\text{Rs }34{,}000$.(b) VAT $=13\%\times34000=\text{Rs }4{,}420$ (VAT goes on the discounted price).(c) Bill $=34000+4420=\text{Rs }38{,}420$.(d) Profit $=34000-30000=\text{Rs }4000$, and profit $\%=\dfrac{4000}{30000}\times100=13\tfrac13\%$ (profit is always found on the cost price, and the VAT is not part of the shopkeeper's profit).

Unitary Method.r: Going: $240\div60=4$ hours. Returning: $240\div40=6$ hours. Total time $=4+6=10$ hours for $240+240=480$ km, so average speed $=480\div10=48$ km/h. Unitary Method.q: A hostel has food for 60 students for 24 days. After 8 days, 20 students leave. For how many more days will the remaining food last the remaining students?
Unitary Method.r: Total food $=60\times24=1440$ student-days. In 8 days the 60 students eat $60\times8=480$ student-days, leaving $1440-480=960$. The remaining students number $60-20=40$, so the food lasts $960\div40=24$ more days (inverse variation: fewer students, more days). The whole stay is $8+24=32$ days.

Congruency and Similarity.q: A vertical pole 2 m high casts a shadow 3 m long at the same time as a tower casts a shadow 21 m long. Using similar triangles, find the height of the tower, and state which angles you used.

Congruency and Similarity.r: Given: $AB=CD$, $AB\parallel CD$. To prove: $\triangle ABC\cong\triangle CDA$. Proof: (i) $AB=CD$ (given). (ii) $\angle BAC=\angle DCA$ (alternate angles, since $AB\parallel CD$ and $AC$ is the transversal). (iii) $AC=CA$ (common side). So $\triangle ABC\cong\triangle CDA$ by SAS. Corresponding parts of congruent triangles are equal, so $BC=DA$. This shows that a quadrilateral with one pair of opposite sides equal and parallel has its other pair equal too — it is a parallelogram.

p: A pole 3 m high casts a shadow 2 m long. At the same time a tree casts a shadow 14 m long. Find the height of the tree.

Congruency and Similarity.r: (a) The sun's rays make the same angle, so the pole with its shadow and the tree with its shadow form similar right triangles: $\dfrac{\text{height of tree}}{3}=\dfrac{14}{2}$, so the height $=3\times7=21$ m.(b) All squares are similar: every angle is $90^\circ$ and the ratio of corresponding sides is the same for any two squares. Rhombuses are not all similar: their sides are equal, but the angles can differ (a rhombus with $60^\circ$ and $120^\circ$ angles is not similar to one with $80^\circ$ and $100^\circ$). Similar figures need equal angles and proportional sides together.

Coordinates.r: (a) $x<0$ and $y>0$: the second quadrant. Reflection in the $y$-axis: $(3,4)$. Reflection in the $x$-axis: $(-3,-4)$. Reflection in the origin: $(3,-4)$.(b) $d=\sqrt{(9-(-3))^2+(3-(-2))^2}=\sqrt{12^2+5^2}=\sqrt{144+25}=\sqrt{169}=13$ units.

Tessellation.r: One brick to the next is a translation (a glide reflection also occurs in a normal brick wall, because alternate courses are offset). A mirror pattern is a reflection.
