A room 4 m long and 3 m wide is to be paved with square tiles of side 25 cm. Find the number of tiles, the number to buy if 5% extra is added for breakage, and the cost at Rs 45 per tile. State the number of lines of symmetry and the order of rotational symmetry of a square tile and of a regular hexagonal tile.
Tessellation.r: Floor $=400\times300$ cm; along the length $400\div25=16$ tiles and along the width $300\div25=12$ tiles, so $16\times12=192$ tiles. Extra $5\%$ of 192 $=9.6$, so buy $192+9.6=201.6\approx202$ tiles. Cost $=202\times45=\text{Rs }9{,}090$. A square tile has 4 lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry of order 4. A regular hexagonal tile has 6 lines of symmetry and order 6.

Tessellation.q: Which of the following is the definition of a tessellation?
o: A pattern formed by repeating a single geometric shape without any gaps or overlaps.
A shape that can cover a surface completely with no gaps or overlaps when combined with other shapes.
A three-dimensional figure that can fill space completely without any gaps or overlaps.
A method to calculate the area covered by overlapping geometric shapes.
Tessellation.w: A tessellation specifically refers to the arrangement of shapes covering a plane without gaps or overlaps.

Tessellation.q: What is required for a set of polygons to form a tessellation?
o: The sum of the interior angles at the vertices where they meet must equal 360 degrees.
Each polygon must have an equal number of sides.
All polygons must be regular polygons.
There must be exactly three different types of polygons in the set.
Tessellation.w: For polygons to form a tessellation, their angles must fit together perfectly around a point without leaving gaps.

Tessellation.q: How many regular polygons can tessellate a plane independently?
Tessellation.w: Only three regular polygons—equilateral triangles, squares, and regular hexagons—can tessellate a plane independently.

Transformation.q: A triangle has vertices $A(1,1)$, $B(4,1)$ and $C(1,3)$. (i) Reflect it in the $y$-axis and give the image. (ii) Find the area of both triangles and compare them.
Transformation.r: (i) Reflection in the $y$-axis changes the sign of $x$: $A'(-1,1)$, $B'(-4,1)$, $C'(-1,3)$. (ii) The object has a horizontal side $AB=3$ and a vertical side $AC=2$, so $\text{area}=\frac12\times3\times2=3$ square units. The image has $A'B'=3$ and $A'C'=2$, so its area is also 3 square units. Conclusion. The areas are equal, which is what a reflection must give: it is a rigid motion, so every length and every area is unchanged, even though the figure faces the other way.

Transformation.q: If a figure undergoes a dilation centered at the origin with a scale factor of $-3$, which of the following statements is true about its image?

It is three times smaller than the original figure.
It is inverted and three times larger than the original figure.
It remains the same size as the original figure.
Transformation.w: A negative scale factor indicates an inversion, and the magnitude of the scale factor indicates how much larger the image is compared to the original.

Bearing and Scale Drawing.r: South-east is 135°; 25° west of north is $360-25=335°$.

Bearing and Scale Drawing.q: A walker goes 6 km north and then 8 km east. Find his distance and bearing from the start.
Bearing and Scale Drawing.r: The two legs are at right angles, so distance $=\sqrt{6^2+8^2}=10$ km. From a scale drawing (say 1 cm to 1 km), the protractor gives a bearing of about 053°.

Bearing and Scale Drawing.q: A ship sails 120 km on a bearing of 090° and then 160 km on a bearing of 180°. Using a scale of 1 cm to 20 km, draw the route and find the distance and bearing of the ship's final position from its starting point.

p: Write the three-figure bearings of north-east, south-west and north-west.
The bearing of $B$ from $A$ is $070^\circ$: find the bearing of $A$ from $B$.
The bearing of $A$ from $B$ is $130^\circ$: find the bearing of $B$ from $A$.
Bearing and Scale Drawing.r: (a) North-east $=045^\circ$, south-west $=225^\circ$, north-west $=315^\circ$ (bearings are measured clockwise from north, in three figures).(b) The back bearing is found by adding $180^\circ$ to a bearing below $180^\circ$: $070+180=250^\circ$.(c) The back bearing of $130^\circ$ is $130+180=310^\circ$. (For a bearing above $180^\circ$ subtract $180^\circ$.)

p: A tree 12 m tall is drawn to the scale 1 cm: 2 m. Find the height in the drawing and write the scale as a ratio.
A path measures 7.5 cm on this drawing: find its real length.
A plot 30 m by 18 m is drawn at the scale $1:500$: find the sides of the drawing.
Bearing and Scale Drawing.r: (a) $12\div2=6$ cm. As a ratio: $2\text{ m}=200$ cm, so 1 cm: 200 cm is $1:200$.(b) $7.5\times2=15$ m.(c) $30\text{ m}=3000$ cm, and $3000\div500=6$ cm; $18\text{ m}=1800$ cm, and $1800\div500=3.6$ cm. The drawing is a rectangle 6 cm by 3.6 cm.

Bearing and Scale Drawing.q: A hiker walks 3 km due east and then 4 km due north.
p: Find how far she is from the start.
Find the bearing of her finishing point from the start, to the nearest degree.
Find the bearing of the start from the finishing point. Describe the scale drawing you would use.
Bearing and Scale Drawing.r: (a) The two legs form a right angle, so the distance is $\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=\sqrt{25}=5$ km.(b) The finishing point is 3 km east and 4 km north of the start. The angle east of north is found from $\tan\theta=\frac34$, so $\theta\approx36.9^\circ\approx37^\circ$ and the bearing is $037^\circ$.(c) The back bearing is $037+180=217^\circ$. Scale drawing: use 1 cm: 1 km; draw a north line, mark 3 cm east then 4 cm north, join start to finish (5 cm), and measure the bearing with a protractor clockwise from north.

Bearing and Scale Drawing.q: What is the bearing of point B from point A if point B is directly east of point A?
Bearing and Scale Drawing.w: Directly east translates to a bearing of $090^\circ$.

Bearing and Scale Drawing.q: Which of the following bearings is equivalent to a true bearing of $225^\circ$?
Bearing and Scale Drawing.w: A true bearing of $225^\circ$ corresponds to the South-West direction.

Relation and Function.q: Find $x$ and $y$ if $\left(\frac{x}{2}+1,\ y-2\right)=(3,\ x)$.
Relation and Function.r: First components: $\frac{x}{2}+1=3$, so $x=4$. Second components: $y-2=x=4$, so $y=6$.

Relation and Function.q: If $P=\{a,b,c\}$ and $Q=\{0,1\}$, find $Q\times P$ and $n(P\times Q)$.
If $f(x)=x^2-4x+3$, find the pre-images of 0 and of 3.
Relation and Function.r: Pre-images of 0: $x^2-4x+3=0$, $(x-1)(x-3)=0$, so $x=1$ or 3. Pre-images of 3: $x^2-4x=0$, $x(x-4)=0$, so $x=0$ or 4.

Relation and Function.q: A function is defined by $f(x)=ax+b$. If $f(2)=7$ and $f(-1)=-2$, find $a$ and $b$, then find $f(5)$ and the pre-image of 19.

State, with reasons, which of these are functions: $R_1=\{(1,1),(2,4),(3,9)\}$; $R_2=\{(4,2),(4,-2),(9,3)\}$; $R_3=\{(x,y): y=3\}$ on $\{1,2,3\}$; the circle $x^2+y^2=4$. Use the vertical line test where it helps.
Relation and Function.r: $R_1$: a function, each first component appears once. $R_2$: not a function, 4 has two images, 2 and $-2$. $R_3=\{(1,3),(2,3),(3,3)\}$: a function (constant), each input has the one image 3. The circle: not a function, the vertical line $x=0$ meets it at $(0,2)$ and $(0,-2)$.

Relation and Function.q: If $A=\{a,b\}$ and $B=\{1,2,3\}$, find $A\times B$ and $n(A\times B)$.
If $A=\{2,4\}$ and $B=\{1,3\}$, find $B\times A$ and show that $A\times B\neq B\times A$.
Relation and Function.r: $B\times A=\{(1,2),(1,4),(3,2),(3,4)\}$ and $A\times B=\{(2,1),(2,3),(4,1),(4,3)\}$. The pair $(1,2)$ is in $B\times A$ but not in $A\times B$, so the sets are not equal.

Relation and Function.q: If $n(A\times B)=6$ and $n(B)=3$, find $n(A)$ and the number of relations from $A$ to $B$.
Relation and Function.r: $n(A)\times3=6$, so $n(A)=2$. A relation is a subset of $A\times B$, which has 6 members, so there are $2^6=64$ relations.

Relation and Function.q: If $A=\{1,2,3\}$, $B=\{2,3,4,5,6\}$ and $R=\{(x,y): y=2x\}$ from $A$ to $B$, list $R$ and find its domain and range.
Find the inverse of $R=\{(1,2),(2,4),(3,6)\}$ and state its domain and range.
If $f(x)=4x-3$, find the pre-image of 9.
Relation and Function.r: $4x-3=9$, so $4x=12$ and $x=3$. The pre-image of 9 is 3.

Relation and Function.q: State, with a reason, whether $\{(1,5),(2,6),(2,7),(3,8)\}$ is a function.
Relation and Function.r: It is not a function, because the first component 2 has two images, 6 and 7.

Relation and Function.q: A function $f: A\rightarrow B$ is defined by $f(x)=x+3$, where $A=\{-1,0,1,2\}$. Find its range.
If $(x+y,\ 3)=(7,\ x-y)$, find $x$ and $y$. Taking $A=\{x,y\}$ and $B=\{1,2\}$, find $A\times B$ and $B\times A$, and verify that $n(A\times B)=n(B\times A)$.
Relation and Function.r: Equating components: $x+y=7$ and $x-y=3$. Adding, $2x=10$, so $x=5$ and $y=2$. Then $A=\{2,5\}$ and $B=\{1,2\}$. $A\times B=\{(2,1),(2,2),(5,1),(5,2)\}$ and $B\times A=\{(1,2),(1,5),(2,2),(2,5)\}$. Each has 4 members, so $n(A\times B)=n(B\times A)=4=2\times2$, although the two sets are different.

Relation and Function.q: A function is defined by $f(x)=ax+b$. If $f(1)=1$ and $f(3)=7$, find $a$ and $b$. Then find $f(5)$ and the pre-image of 10.

For $f(x)=2x-1$ with domain $\{-1,0,1,2,3\}$: (i) make a table of values, (ii) write $f$ as a set of ordered pairs, (iii) find the range, (iv) plot the points and explain why they pass the vertical line test.
Relation and Function.r: (i) $x$: $-1, 0, 1, 2, 3$ give $f(x)$: $-3, -1, 1, 3, 5$. (ii) $f=\{(-1,-3),(0,-1),(1,1),(2,3),(3,5)\}$. (iii) Range $=\{-3,-1,1,3,5\}$. (iv) The five points lie on a straight line rising 2 units for every 1 unit to the right. Their $x$-coordinates are all different, so any vertical line passes through at most one of them: the graph passes the test, as a function must.

Relation and Function.q: Let $A=\{1,2,3\}$ and $B=\{2,4,6,8\}$ and let $R=\{(x,y): y=2x,\ x\in A,\ y\in B\}$. (i) List $R$. (ii) Write its domain, co-domain and range. (iii) Find $R^{-1}$. (iv) Is $R$ a function from $A$ to $B$? Which type?
Relation and Function.r: (i) $y=2x$ gives $1\to2$, $2\to4$, $3\to6$, so $R=\{(1,2),(2,4),(3,6)\}$. (ii) Domain $=\{1,2,3\}$; co-domain $=B=\{2,4,6,8\}$; range $=\{2,4,6\}$ (8 is in the co-domain but is not an image). (iii) Interchange each pair: $R^{-1}=\{(2,1),(4,2),(6,3)\}$. (iv) Every member of $A$ has exactly one image, so $R$ is a function from $A$ to $B$; different members have different images, so it is one-to-one (but not onto, since 8 has no pre-image).

Find the general term and the 15th term of $2, 6, 10, 14, \ldots$.
Sequence and Series.r: The difference is 4 and each term is 2 less than $4n$: $t_n=4n-2$, so $t_{15}=58$.

Sequence and Series.q: Is 101 a term of $5, 9, 13, \ldots$? If so, which term?
Sequence and Series.r: $t_n=4n+1$. Setting $4n+1=101$ gives $n=25$, a natural number, so 101 is the 25th term.

Sequence and Series.q: Find the general term of $0, 3, 8, 15, 24, \ldots$ by the method of differences, find the 10th term, and evaluate the sum of the first four terms written in sigma notation.
Sequence and Series.r: First differences $3, 5, 7, 9$; second differences 2, so compare with $n^2$: the terms are each 1 less, so $t_n=n^2-1$. Then $t_{10}=99$, and $\sum_{k=1}^{4}(k^2-1)=0+3+8+15=26$.

Sequence and Series.q: Using $\sum_{k=1}^{n}k=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$, find (i) $\sum_{k=1}^{30}k$ (ii) $\sum_{k=1}^{12}(2k+3)$ (iii) the sum of all the multiples of 4 from 4 to 100.

Sequence and Series.q: Find the 20th term of $2, 5, 8, 11, \ldots$.
Find the next two terms of $1, 3, 6, 10, 15, \ldots$ and state the rule.
Sequence and Series.r: The differences are $2, 3, 4, 5$, so the next differences are 6 and 7: the next terms are 21 and 28. These are the triangular numbers, $t_n=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$.

Sequence and Series.q: Is 75 a term of $4, 9, 14, 19, \ldots$? Give a reason.
Sequence and Series.r: $t_n=5n-1$. Setting $5n-1=75$ gives $n=\frac{76}{5}=15.2$, which is not a natural number. So 75 is not a term (the 15th term is 74 and the 16th is 79).

Sequence and Series.q: Expand and evaluate $\sum_{k=1}^{4}(3k-1)$.
Write $\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{16}$ in sigma notation and find its value.
Sequence and Series.r: The $k$th term is $\frac{1}{2^k}$, so the series is $\sum_{k=1}^{4}\frac{1}{2^k}$. Its value is $\frac{8+4+2+1}{16}=\frac{15}{16}$.

Sequence and Series.q: A row of $n$ squares made of matchsticks uses $4, 7, 10, \ldots$ sticks for $n=1, 2, 3, \ldots$. (i) Find the general term. (ii) How many sticks are needed for 30 squares? (iii) How many squares can be made with 151 sticks?
Sequence and Series.r: (i) The difference is 3; comparing with $3n$, each term is 1 more, so $t_n=3n+1$. (ii) $t_{30}=91$ sticks. (iii) $3n+1=151$ gives $3n=150$, so $n=50$ squares.

Sequence and Series.q: Find the general term of $2, 6, 12, 20, 30, \ldots$ by the method of differences, find its 15th term, and find $\sum_{k=1}^{5}t_k$.
Sequence and Series.r: First differences $4, 6, 8, 10$; second differences 2, so compare with $n^2$: the leftovers $2-1=1$, $6-4=2$, $12-9=3$, $20-16=4$, $30-25=5$ are $n$. So $t_n=n^2+n$. Then $t_{15}=225+15=240$, and $\sum_{k=1}^{5}t_k=2+6+12+20+30=70$.

Sequence and Series.q: The first row of a hall has 20 seats and each row has 3 more seats than the row in front. (i) Write the sequence and its general term. (ii) How many seats are in the 12th row? (iii) Which row has 62 seats? (iv) Write the number of seats in the first 5 rows in sigma notation and find it.

The general term of a sequence is $t_n=n^2+2n$. Write the first four terms and $t_{10}$. Which term is 143? Is 100 a term of the sequence?
Find the general term of each sequence and use it to write the 8th term: (i) $3,7,11,15,\dots$ (ii) $2,6,18,54,\dots$ (iii) $1,4,9,16,\dots$ (iv) $1,\frac12,\frac13,\frac14,\dots$
Sequence and Series.r: (i) The common difference is 4 and the first term 3, so $t_n=3+4(n-1)=4n-1$; $t_8=31$. (ii) Each term is 3 times the one before, so $t_n=2\times3^{n-1}$; $t_8=2\times3^7=4374$. (iii) The squares of the natural numbers: $t_n=n^2$; $t_8=64$. (iv) $t_n=\frac1n$; $t_8=\frac18$.

Limit.q: If $\lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)=2$ and $\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)=3$, then $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)$
Limit.w: the two sides disagree, so there is no single limit.

Limit.q: As the number of sides increases, the perimeter of a regular polygon inscribed in a circle of radius 7 cm approaches (take $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$)
Limit.w: the polygons tend to the circle: $2\pi r=2\times\frac{22}{7}\times7=44$ cm.

Limit.q: Write the next three terms of $\frac{1}{3}, \frac{2}{4}, \frac{3}{5}, \frac{4}{6}, \ldots$ and state the limit of the sequence.
Limit.r: The $n$th term is $\frac{n}{n+2}$, so the next terms are $\frac{5}{7}$, $\frac{6}{8}=\frac{3}{4}$, $\frac{7}{9}$. Since $\frac{n}{n+2}=1-\frac{2}{n+2}$ and $\frac{2}{n+2}\rightarrow0$, the limit is 1.

Limit.q: Evaluate $\lim_{x\to5}\frac{x^2-25}{x-5}$.
Limit.r: $\frac{(x-5)(x+5)}{x-5}=x+5\rightarrow10$.

Limit.q: Evaluate $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{4n-1}{n}$.
Limit.r: $\frac{4n-1}{n}=4-\frac{1}{n}\rightarrow4$.

Limit.q: Evaluate (i) $\lim_{x\to3}\frac{x^2-5x+6}{x-3}$ (ii) $\lim_{x\to-1}\frac{x^2-1}{x+1}$ (iii) $\lim_{x\to4}\frac{x^2-3x-4}{x-4}$.
Limit.r: (i) $\frac{(x-2)(x-3)}{x-3}=x-2\rightarrow1$. (ii) $\frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x+1}=x-1\rightarrow-2$. (iii) $\frac{(x-4)(x+1)}{x-4}=x+1\rightarrow5$.

Limit.q: A function is defined by $f(x)=2x+1$ for $x<2$ and $f(x)=7-x$ for $x\geq2$. (i) Find $f(2)$. (ii) Find what $f(x)$ approaches as $x\rightarrow2^-$ and as $x\rightarrow2^+$. (iii) Does $\lim_{x\to2}f(x)$ exist, and does it equal $f(2)$?
Limit.r: (i) $x=2$ uses the second rule: $f(2)=7-2=5$. (ii) From the left, $2x+1\rightarrow2(2)+1=5$; from the right, $7-x\rightarrow5$. (iii) Both sides approach 5, so the limit exists and equals 5, which is also $f(2)$: the graph has no break at $x=2$.

Limit.q: $\lim_{x\to2}(3x+4)$ equals
$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}$ equals
Limit.w: $\frac{1}{n}$ becomes as small as we like.

Limit.q: Write the next three terms of $\frac{1}{2}, \frac{3}{4}, \frac{7}{8}, \frac{15}{16}, \ldots$ and state the limit of the sequence.
Limit.r: The $n$th term is $\frac{2^n-1}{2^n}$, so the next terms are $\frac{31}{32}$, $\frac{63}{64}$, $\frac{127}{128}$. The gap to 1 is $\frac{1}{2^n}$, which tends to 0, so the limit is 1.

Limit.q: Find the limit of the sequence $t_n=\frac{2n+1}{n}$ by writing $t_n=2+\frac{1}{n}$.
Limit.r: $t_n=2+\frac{1}{n}$; as $n\rightarrow\infty$, $\frac{1}{n}\rightarrow0$, so $\lim_{n\to\infty}t_n=2$.

Limit.q: Evaluate $\lim_{x\to4}\frac{x^2-16}{x-4}$.
Limit.r: $\frac{(x-4)(x+4)}{x-4}=x+4$, so the limit is $8$.

Limit.q: Evaluate $\lim_{x\to1}\frac{x^2+2x-3}{x-1}$.
Limit.r: $\frac{(x+3)(x-1)}{x-1}=x+3$, so the limit is $4$.

Limit.q: For $f(x)=\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}$, explain the difference between $f(2)$ and $\lim_{x\to2}f(x)$.
Limit.r: $f(2)=\frac{0}{0}$ is not defined: the function has no value at 2. But for $x\neq2$, $f(x)=x+2$, so values of $x$ near 2 give $f(x)$ near 4: $\lim_{x\to2}f(x)=4$. The graph is the line $y=x+2$ with a hole at $(2,4)$.

Limit.q: From which term onwards are the terms of $\frac{n}{n+1}$ within 0.001 of 1?
Limit.r: The gap is $\frac{1}{n+1}$. We need $\frac{1}{n+1}<\frac{1}{1000}$, so $n+1>1000$ and $n>999$. From the 1000th term onwards.

Limit.q: Write in limit notation: "as $n$ increases without bound, $\frac{3}{n}$ gets closer and closer to 0".
Limit.r: $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{3}{n}=0$.

Limit.q: A regular hexagon is inscribed in a circle of radius 5 cm. Find its perimeter, and state what the perimeters of inscribed polygons of 12, 24, 48, … sides approach.
Limit.r: Each side equals the radius, so the perimeter is $6\times5=30$ cm. The perimeters approach the circumference $2\pi\times5=10\pi\approx31.42$ cm.

Limit.q: For $t_n=\frac{n}{n+1}$: (i) write the first six terms as decimals correct to 3 places; (ii) find the gap $1-t_n$ for $n=9$, 99 and 999; (iii) state the limit; (iv) explain whether any term equals the limit.
Limit.r: (i) $0.5, 0.667, 0.75, 0.8, 0.833, 0.857$. (ii) $1-t_n=\frac{1}{n+1}$, giving $0.1$, $0.01$ and $0.001$. (iii) The gap tends to 0, so $\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n}{n+1}=1$. (iv) No term equals 1, because the gap $\frac{1}{n+1}$ is positive for every $n$. The limit is approached but never reached.

Limit.q: A square of area 1 is shaded in steps: half of it, then half of what is left white, and so on. (i) Write the shaded areas after 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 steps. (ii) Write the white area after $n$ steps. (iii) State the limit of the shaded area. (iv) After how many steps is the white area first less than 0.01?
Limit.r: (i) $\frac{1}{2}, \frac{3}{4}, \frac{7}{8}, \frac{15}{16}, \frac{31}{32}$, that is $0.5, 0.75, 0.875, 0.9375, 0.96875$. (ii) White area $=\frac{1}{2^n}$. (iii) $\frac{1}{2^n}\rightarrow0$, so the shaded area $1-\frac{1}{2^n}\rightarrow1$. (iv) $\frac{1}{2^n}<\frac{1}{100}$ needs $2^n>100$; $2^6=64$ is too small and $2^7=128$ works, so after 7 steps.

Limit.q: Let $f(x)=\frac{x^2-5x+6}{x-2}$. (i) Show that $f(2)$ is not defined. (ii) Make a table of $f(x)$ for $x=1.9, 1.99, 1.999, 2.001, 2.01, 2.1$. (iii) Find $\lim_{x\to2}f(x)$ by factorising. (iv) Describe the graph of $f$.
Limit.r: (i) $f(2)=\frac{4-10+6}{0}=\frac{0}{0}$, which is not defined. (ii) $-1.1, -1.01, -1.001, -0.999, -0.99, -0.9$. (iii) $x^2-5x+6=(x-2)(x-3)$, so for $x\neq2$, $f(x)=x-3$ and $\lim_{x\to2}f(x)=2-3=-1$, which agrees with the table. (iv) The graph is the straight line $y=x-3$ with a hole at the point $(2,-1)$.

Limit.q: A car park charges Rs 20 for up to and including 2 hours and Rs 40 for more than 2 hours, up to 4 hours. Let $F(t)$ be the fee for $t$ hours. (i) Find $F(1.5)$, $F(2)$ and $F(2.5)$. (ii) What does $F(t)$ approach as $t\rightarrow2^-$ and as $t\rightarrow2^+$? (iii) Does $\lim_{t\to2}F(t)$ exist? Give a reason.
Limit.r: (i) $F(1.5)=20$, $F(2)=20$ (up to and including 2 hours), $F(2.5)=40$. (ii) As $t\rightarrow2^-$, $F(t)\rightarrow20$; as $t\rightarrow2^+$, $F(t)\rightarrow40$. (iii) No. The left-hand and right-hand values approach different numbers, so there is no single number that $F(t)$ approaches; the limit does not exist, even though $F(2)=20$ exists.

Limit.q: For the sequence $t_n=\dfrac{3n+2}{n}$ find $t_1$, $t_{10}$, $t_{100}$ and $t_{1000}$. What number do the terms approach? Write the result with the limit notation and explain why the terms never reach it.
Limit.r: $t_1=\frac51=5$; $t_{10}=\frac{32}{10}=3.2$; $t_{100}=\frac{302}{100}=3.02$; $t_{1000}=\frac{3002}{1000}=3.002$. The terms approach 3, so $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{3n+2}{n}=3$. Since $\frac{3n+2}{n}=3+\frac2n$ and $\frac2n$ is always positive, every term is a little larger than 3: it comes as close as we please but never equals 3.

Limit.q: Find (i) $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to2}\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}$ using a table of values for $x=1.9,\ 1.99,\ 2.01$, and then by factorising, (ii) $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to3}(2x+1)$, (iii) $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to1}\frac{x^2-1}{x-1}$.
Limit.r: (i) For $f(x)=\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}$: $f(1.9)=\frac{-0.39}{-0.1}=3.9$; $f(1.99)=3.99$; $f(2.01)=4.01$. The values approach 4 from both sides. By factorising, $\frac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x-2}=x+2\to4$ (we may cancel because $x\ne2$ when finding a limit). So the limit is 4, although $f(2)$ itself is not defined. (ii) $2(3)+1=7$. (iii) $\frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x-1}=x+1\to2$.

Limit.q: A regular polygon with $n$ sides is drawn inside a circle of radius 1 unit. Its area is $\frac n2\sin\frac{360^\circ}{n}$. Find the area for $n=3,6,12,24$, say what number the areas approach as $n$ grows, and find $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{x^2+3x}{x}$.
Limit.r: Area $=\frac n2\sin\frac{360^\circ}{n}$: for $n=3$, $1.5\times0.8660=1.299$; $n=6$, $3\times0.8660=2.598$; $n=12$, $6\times0.5=3.000$; $n=24$, $12\times0.2588=3.106$. The areas increase and approach $\pi\approx3.1416$, the area of the circle, so the limit of the polygon areas is $\pi$. Finally, $\frac{x^2+3x}{x}=x+3$ for $x\ne0$, so the limit as $x\to0$ is 3.

Limit.q: Which of the following best describes the concept of limit in mathematics?
o: It is the maximum value a function can attain.
It is the behavior of a function as its input approaches a certain value.
It is the sum of all values a function takes over an interval.
It is the difference between the highest and lowest value of a function.
Limit.w: The limit defines the value a function approaches as the input variable gets closer to a specified value.

Find (i) the total marks $F+S$ (ii) the change $S-F$, explaining any negative entry (iii) the average marks $\frac{1}{2}(F+S)$.

Matrix.q: Write the unit matrix of order 3 and the scalar matrix of order 2 whose diagonal elements are $-3$.

Two shops sell pens, copies and bags. In Baisakh their sales were $B=[(120,80,15),(95,60,20)]$ and in Jestha $J=[(140,70,18),(110,75,12)]$ (rows: shops; columns: pens, copies, bags). (i) Find the total sales of the two months. (ii) Find the change from Baisakh to Jestha and explain the negative entries. (iii) If the target for Asar is double the Jestha sales, find the target matrix.
Matrix.r: (i) $B+J=[(260,150,33),(205,135,32)]$. (ii) $J-B=[(20,-10,3),(15,15,-8)]$: the first shop sold 10 fewer copies and the second shop 8 fewer bags in Jestha; every other entry rose. (iii) $2J=[(280,140,36),(220,150,24)]$.

Matrix.q: If $A=[(2,0),(-1,3)]$ and $B=[(2,4),(3,-1)]$, verify that $3(A+B)=3A+3B$ and find the matrix $X$ such that $2X-A=B$.
Classify each of the matrices $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$, $T$, $U$, $V$, $W$ by every type that applies to it. Then find $T-5I$, where $I$ is the unit matrix of order 3, and comment on the result.
Matrix.r: $P$: square, upper triangular (its element below the diagonal is 0). $Q$: square. $R$: rectangular, $2\times3$. $S$: square, symmetric. $T$: square, diagonal, scalar, symmetric, upper and lower triangular. $U$: square, upper triangular. $V$: row, rectangular. $W$: column, rectangular. $T-5I=[(5,0,0),(0,5,0),(0,0,5)]-[(5,0,0),(0,5,0),(0,0,5)]=O$, the zero matrix; so $T=5I$: every scalar matrix is a scalar multiple of the unit matrix.

Matrix.q: If $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\5&2\end{pmatrix}$, find $A+B$, $A-B$ and $2A-3B$. State the order of each result.
Matrix.r: $A+B=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\8&6\end{pmatrix}$. $A-B=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\-2&2\end{pmatrix}$. For $2A-3B$: $2A=\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\6&8\end{pmatrix}$ and $3B=\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\15&6\end{pmatrix}$, so $2A-3B=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\-9&2\end{pmatrix}$. Every result is of order $2\times2$ (matrices are added and subtracted element by element, so they must have the same order).

Matrix.q: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$ verify that $A+B=B+A$, and show that $A+(-A)=O$ and $A+O=A$. Name the type of the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$ and of $\begin{pmatrix}5&0\\0&5\end{pmatrix}$.
Matrix.r: $A+B=\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\5&7\end{pmatrix}$ and $B+A=\begin{pmatrix}1&3\\5&7\end{pmatrix}$: equal, so addition is commutative. $-A=\begin{pmatrix}-1&-2\\-3&-4\end{pmatrix}$ and $A+(-A)=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}=O$ (the additive inverse). $A+O=A$ since adding zeros changes nothing (the zero matrix is the additive identity). The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$ is a symmetric matrix (it equals its transpose); $\begin{pmatrix}5&0\\0&5\end{pmatrix}$ is a scalar matrix (a diagonal matrix with equal diagonal elements).

Matrix.q: Which of the following represents the transpose of a matrix $A = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}$?
Matrix.w: Transposing a matrix swaps the row and column indices of the elements.

Coordinate Geometry.r: $m=\frac{-2-4}{3+1}=-\frac{6}{4}=-\frac{3}{2}$. The slope is negative, so the line falls to the right.

Coordinate Geometry.q: Write the equation of the line whose slope is $-2$ and whose $y$-intercept is 5.

Find the area of the triangle with vertices $(1,2)$, $(5,3)$ and $(3,7)$.
Write the equations of the lines through $(-2,4)$ parallel to the $x$-axis and to the $y$-axis.
Coordinate Geometry.r: Parallel to the $x$-axis: $y=4$. Parallel to the $y$-axis: $x=-2$.

Coordinate Geometry.q: Show that $A(2,1)$, $B(5,3)$ and $C(1,9)$ are the vertices of a right-angled triangle, and find its area in two ways.
Find the points of trisection of the segment joining $A(1,2)$ and $B(7,11)$, and the mid-point of $AB$.
Coordinate Geometry.r: $P$ (ratio $1:2$) $=\left(\frac{7+2}{3},\frac{11+4}{3}\right)=(3,5)$; $Q$ (ratio $2:1$) $=\left(\frac{14+1}{3},\frac{22+2}{3}\right)=(5,8)$. Mid-point $=\left(\frac{1+7}{2},\frac{2+11}{2}\right)=(4,\ 6.5)$, which lies between $P$ and $Q$, as it should.

Coordinate Geometry.q: Find the equation of the line through $(1,2)$ and $(3,8)$ in the form $y=mx+c$. State its slope and $y$-intercept, and check whether $(-1,-4)$ lies on it.
Coordinate Geometry.r: $m=\frac{8-2}{3-1}=3$; $2=3(1)+c$ gives $c=-1$. The line is $y=3x-1$, with slope 3 and $y$-intercept $-1$. At $x=-1$: $y=-3-1=-4$, so $(-1,-4)$ does lie on the line.

Coordinate Geometry.q: Show that $A(0,0)$, $B(4,1)$, $C(5,5)$ and $D(1,4)$ are the vertices of a rhombus but not of a square, and find its area.
Find the area of the quadrilateral with vertices $A(1,1)$, $B(6,2)$, $C(5,6)$ and $D(2,5)$ (i) by dividing it into two triangles along $AC$, (ii) by the arrow method.
Coordinate Geometry.r: (i) $\triangle ABC=\frac{1}{2}\left|1(2-6)+6(6-1)+5(1-2)\right|=\frac{21}{2}$ and $\triangle ACD=\frac{1}{2}\left|1(6-5)+5(5-1)+2(1-6)\right|=\frac{11}{2}$, total $16$ square units. (ii) Cross terms $(2-6)+(36-10)+(25-12)+(2-5)=-4+26+13-3=32$, area $=\frac{1}{2}\times32=16$ square units.

Trigonometry.r: (i) LHS $=\frac{(1-\sin\theta)+(1+\sin\theta)}{(1+\sin\theta)(1-\sin\theta)}=\frac{2}{1-\sin^2\theta}=\frac{2}{\cos^2\theta}=2\sec^2\theta=$ RHS. (ii) LHS $=\sec^2\theta-\tan^2\theta$ (difference of two squares) $=1=$ RHS, using $1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta$.

Vector.q: Find the unit vector in the direction of $\binom{5}{12}$.
If $\vec{a}=\binom{3}{4}$ and $\vec{b}=\binom{-2}{1}$, find $|\vec{a}|$, $|\vec{b}|$, $\vec{a}+\vec{b}$ and $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}|$, and show that $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}|<|\vec{a}|+|\vec{b}|$.
Vector.r: $|\vec{a}|=5$, $|\vec{b}|=\sqrt{5}\approx2.24$, $\vec{a}+\vec{b}=\binom{1}{5}$, $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}|=\sqrt{26}\approx5.10$. Since $5.10<5+2.24=7.24$, the inequality holds: two sides of a triangle are together longer than the third.

A trekker walks 6 km east and then 8 km north. (i) Write the two walks as column vectors and draw their sum by the triangle law. (ii) Find the distance walked and the magnitude of the displacement. (iii) Find the direction of the displacement.
Vector.r: (i) $\binom{6}{0}$ and $\binom{0}{8}$; drawn head to tail, the resultant runs from the start to the end: $\binom{6}{0}+\binom{0}{8}=\binom{6}{8}$. (ii) Distance walked $=6+8=14$ km; displacement $=\sqrt{36+64}=10$ km. (iii) $\tan\theta=\frac{8}{6}=\frac{4}{3}$, so $\theta\approx53.13^\circ$ north of east.

Vector.r: $\vec a+\vec b=\binom{2-1}{3+4}=\binom17$. $\vec a-\vec b=\binom{2+1}{3-4}=\binom{3}{-1}$. $3\vec a=\binom69$ and $2\vec b=\binom{-2}{8}$, so $3\vec a-2\vec b=\binom{6+2}{9-8}=\binom81$. $|\vec a+\vec b|=\sqrt{1^2+7^2}=\sqrt{50}=5\sqrt2\approx7.07$.

Transformation.q: Define isometric and non-isometric transformations, with one example of each.
Transformation.r: An isometric transformation keeps the distance between every two points, so the image is congruent to the object; example: rotation. A non-isometric transformation changes distances, so the image differs in size; example: enlargement with scale factor 2.

Transformation.r: $AB=\sqrt{9+16}=5$. The images are $A'(-1,3)$ and $B'(-4,7)$, and $A'B'=\sqrt{(-4+1)^2+(7-3)^2}=\sqrt{9+16}=5$. The length is unchanged.

Transformation.q: The triangle $ABC$ has vertices $A(2,1)$, $B(5,2)$ and $C(3,4)$. (i) Find its image after reflection in the $x$-axis. (ii) Find its image after reflection in the $y$-axis. (iii) Draw all three triangles on one graph. (iv) Show that $AB=A'B'$.
Transformation.r: (i) $A'(2,-1)$, $B'(5,-2)$, $C'(3,-4)$. (ii) $A''(-2,1)$, $B''(-5,2)$, $C''(-3,4)$. (iii) The object is in quadrant I, the first image in quadrant IV and the second in quadrant II, as in the reflection figure of section 9.2. (iv) $AB=\sqrt{3^2+1^2}=\sqrt{10}$ and $A'B'=\sqrt{3^2+(-1)^2}=\sqrt{10}$, so $AB=A'B'$.

The point $P(3,2)$ is reflected in the $y$-axis to $P_1$; $P_1$ is rotated through $+90^\circ$ about the origin to $P_2$; $P_2$ is translated by $\binom{1}{-4}$ to $P_3$. Find $P_1$, $P_2$, $P_3$ and the distance $PP_3$.

A triangle with vertices $(1,1)$, $(3,1)$, $(1,2)$ has the image $(2,2)$, $(6,2)$, $(2,4)$. (i) Compare the lengths of corresponding sides and the areas. (ii) Is the transformation isometric? (iii) Name it and write its rule.
Transformation.r: (i) Object: base $3-1=2$ and height $2-1=1$, area $\frac{1}{2}\times2\times1=1$. Image: base $6-2=4$ and height $4-2=2$, area $\frac{1}{2}\times4\times2=4$. Every length is doubled and the area is multiplied by 4. (ii) No: lengths change, so it is non-isometric; the image is similar but not congruent. (iii) An enlargement with centre $O$ and scale factor 2: $(x,y)\rightarrow(2x,2y)$.

Statistics.r: (i) Kathmandu: range $27-23=4$°C, coefficient $\frac{4}{50}=0.08$. Jumla: range $22-12=10$°C, coefficient $\frac{10}{34}\approx0.29$. Statistics.w: The mode is the value that appears most frequently in a data set.

Scientific Learning.q: A tentative, testable explanation of an observation is called a
Scientific Learning.w: a hypothesis can be tested; a theory is already well tested.

Scientific Learning.w: the independent variable is changed by the experimenter.

Scientific Learning.w: a quantity deliberately held constant is a controlled variable.

Scientific Learning.w: the conclusion judges the hypothesis against the data.

Scientific Learning.q: Which of the following is not a quality of a good scientist?
Scientific Learning.w: science accepts a claim only with evidence.

Scientific Learning.q: What is the process of experiencing an object, event or process carefully through the sense organs?
Scientific Learning.w: this is the definition of observation.

Scientific Learning.q: Which method suits a study of whether the farmers of a region use more chemical or organic fertiliser?
Scientific Learning.w: the data must be collected directly from many farmers.

Scientific Learning.q: Which of these would you stop your friend from doing in the laboratory?
o: using a test-tube holder while heating
Scientific Learning.w: chemicals may be poisonous or corrosive.

Scientific Learning.q: What should be done while performing a chemical reaction that produces fumes?
o: do it in a fume hood
Scientific Learning.w: a fume hood carries harmful fumes out of the room.

Scientific Learning.q: Which is the first step of a scientific study?
Scientific Learning.w: every study begins by noticing something.

Scientific Learning.q: In the algae research, the bottle with only pond water is the
Scientific Learning.w: nothing is added to it, so the others are compared with it.

Scientific Learning.q: Distinguish between
Scientific Learning.r: (a) Observation is studying an object or event carefully with the sense organs (or instruments) without changing it; it gives information and leads to a guess. A test is a fixed scientific procedure to check whether that guess (hypothesis) is true, e.g. dipping litmus in lemon juice. (b) Research is an in-depth study of a question, often with experiments, following steps from goal setting to conclusion; it may be done in a laboratory. A survey collects data directly from people or places through questionnaires, interviews, discussion or observation, and draws a conclusion from them.

Scientific Learning.q: Give reasons:
p: Precautions should be taken while doing experimental work.
A report is prepared after an experiment or survey.
Observation is the first step in scientific learning.
Scientific Learning.r: (a) Laboratory chemicals, glass and burners can cause injury, fire or poisoning, and careless work also gives wrong results. (b) A report records the objective, method, results and conclusion so that others can understand, check and repeat the work, and so that the findings can be used. (c) All scientific work starts from something noticed; observation gives the information from which questions and hypotheses are made.

Scientific Learning.q: What is observation? Why is it important in scientific work?
Scientific Learning.r: Observation is the process of experiencing an object, event or process very carefully using the sense organs. It is important because it gives the first information about a thing, helps us make hypotheses and records the results of tests and experiments.

Scientific Learning.q: What is done in scientific work when observation does not give enough information?
Scientific Learning.r: A hypothesis is made from the observation, and a test or experiment is carried out to check it. Instruments such as a hand lens or microscope may also be used to observe more closely.

Scientific Learning.q: What precautions should be taken while carrying out a scientific experiment?
Scientific Learning.r: Follow the given method; wear an apron, gloves and goggles; never taste or directly smell chemicals; use a test-tube holder and point the tube away from people; take care with burners and hot objects; do reactions that give fumes in a fume hood; keep hot apparatus off the bare table; wash hands afterwards.

Scientific Learning.q: List the things that should be done and should not be done in the laboratory.
Scientific Learning.r: Do: wear a lab coat, follow instructions, know the emergency exit, use holders and tongs, keep the bench clean, wash hands after work. Do not: eat or drink, taste or smell chemicals, play or tease, handle materials carelessly, put hot apparatus directly on the table.

Scientific Learning.q: What should we pay attention to while doing research?
Scientific Learning.r: Have a clear question and objective; follow the steps in order; collect data honestly; keep a control for comparison; repeat if it fails and improve the method; be patient; write a report and name the sources used.

Scientific Learning.q: In what conditions is a survey conducted? What are survey tools? Give examples.
Scientific Learning.r: A survey is done when the information is spread among many people, households or places (e.g. waste management in a community, use of fertiliser by farmers) and must be collected directly. Survey tools are the means of collecting data: questionnaire, interview, group discussion and observation.

Scientific Learning.q: A class must be held in the absence of the science teacher. Prepare a worksheet for a practical class on the study of plant and animal cells.
Scientific Learning.r: Title: Study of plant and animal cells. Objective: to observe and draw an onion-peel cell and a human cheek cell. Materials: onion, clean toothpick, slides, cover slips, iodine or methylene blue, water, forceps, needle, microscope. Steps: (i) Peel a thin layer from the inside of an onion scale, place it in a drop of water on a slide, add a drop of iodine, cover gently. (ii) Scrape the inside of your cheek gently with the flat end of a clean toothpick, spread it on another slide, add methylene blue and cover. (iii) Observe both under low power then high power. Questions for the worksheet: Draw and label each cell.

Scientific Learning.q: Describe the steps of the scientific method with an example. Why are observation and a fair test important?
Write eight rules of laboratory safety and explain the common apparatus and the measurement of length, mass and time.

Information and Communication Technology.q: Which of the following is an input device?
Information and Communication Technology.w: a scanner feeds data in; the other three put data out.

Information and Communication Technology.q: The memory whose contents are lost when the power goes off is
Information and Communication Technology.w: RAM is volatile; ROM and storage keep their contents.

Information and Communication Technology.q: Which one is a web browser?
Information and Communication Technology.w: Firefox is a browser; Google is a search engine.

Information and Communication Technology.q: A collection of related data stored so it can be searched is a
Information and Communication Technology.w: a database is organised for storage and retrieval.

Information and Communication Technology.q: Sharing another person's photograph online without permission is
Information and Communication Technology.w: consent is required; this is a privacy violation.

Information and Communication Technology.q: What is the main function of a set-top box (STB)?
Information and Communication Technology.w: an STB receives, decodes and displays the signal.

Information and Communication Technology.q: What is the fixed address of a website called?
Information and Communication Technology.w: URL, the Uniform Resource Locator.

Information and Communication Technology.q: Which cybercrime means threatening, defaming or humiliating someone through social media?
Information and Communication Technology.w: cyberbullying.

Information and Communication Technology.q: Which technology makes machines able to understand and act with human-like intelligence?
Information and Communication Technology.w: artificial intelligence.

Information and Communication Technology.q: Which of the following is an advantage of cloud computing?
Information and Communication Technology.w: data and programs can be reached from anywhere in the world.

Information and Communication Technology.q: Differentiate between
Information and Communication Technology.r: See the tables in 2.1.3 and 2.2. (a) A scanner is an input device that changes a hard copy into a soft copy; a printer is an output device that changes a soft copy into a hard copy. (b) A search engine is a program that finds pages on many websites by keyword (Google); a website is a collection of web pages with its own URL that holds information (www.moecdc.gov.np).

Information and Communication Technology.q: Differentiate between
p: computer code of conduct and cyber law
Information and Communication Technology.r: (a) VR creates an artificial 3-D world that a person experiences through a headset; AI makes a machine think, learn and decide like a human. (b) The code of conduct is a set of moral guidelines for using computers, without legal punishment; cyber law is the law of the state, and breaking it is punished by jail or fine. (c) A robot is a machine run by a program, without feelings, that does repetitive or dangerous work without tiring; a human is a living being who thinks and feels, and gets tired.

Information and Communication Technology.q: What kind of technology is an ATM? Write its important functions.
Information and Communication Technology.r: An ATM is an electromechanical (computer-based) banking technology. Functions: withdraw and deposit cash, check balance, give a mini statement, pay bills, transfer funds, change PIN.

Information and Communication Technology.q: List the main parts of a photocopy machine.
Information and Communication Technology.r: Glass plate (platen) and cover, light source and lens, light-sensitive drum with electrostatic charge, toner, fuser (heat and pressure), paper tray, control panel with Start button, output tray.

Information and Communication Technology.q: What is a printer? Mention its function.
Information and Communication Technology.r: A printer is an output device that produces a hard copy of a digital file. It prints text and pictures in black and white or colour; types are dot-matrix, ink-jet and laser.

Information and Communication Technology.q: What is a search engine? Explain the need for search engines with an example.
Information and Communication Technology.r: A search engine is a software system that finds information on the internet by keywords. It is needed because we often do not know the website address; e.g. typing "Curriculum Development Centre" in Google gives the link www.moecdc.gov.np, saving time.

Information and Communication Technology.q: Write the main features of an ISP.
Information and Communication Technology.r: High-speed internet; e-mail addresses; protection from phishing and malware; web hosting; charges according to the data package.

Information and Communication Technology.q: Mention the opportunities and benefits of social media.
Information and Communication Technology.r: A strong medium of expression and discussion; quick news and notices; brand development and advertising for businesses; customer feedback; learning (e.g. NCED Virtual on YouTube); keeping in touch with family abroad.

Information and Communication Technology.q: Write the full forms: ATM, WWW, URL, Wi-Fi, ISP, AI, VR.
Information and Communication Technology.r: Automated Teller Machine; World Wide Web; Uniform Resource Locator; Wireless Fidelity; Internet Service Provider; Artificial Intelligence; Virtual Reality.

Information and Communication Technology.q: Mention the dangers to internet security and the ways to avoid them.
Information and Communication Technology.r: Dangers: malware (viruses, worms, Trojan horses, spyware); phishing by false messages; identity theft; hacking; botnets. Ways to avoid: strong and different passwords; two-factor authentication; update software; use antivirus and a firewall; back up data; do not open unknown links or attachments; never share PIN or OTP.

Information and Communication Technology.q: What is artificial intelligence? What is its main objective? Write any four fields where AI is used.
Information and Communication Technology.r: AI is the making of programs or machines that can do tasks needing human intelligence — understanding language, recognising objects, deciding and solving problems. Its main objective is to make machines that think and learn like humans so that work becomes faster and more accurate. Fields: health care (diagnosis), agriculture (crop monitoring), finance (chatbots, trading), education (virtual tutors), travel, games, robotics.

Information and Communication Technology.q: What is robotics? Mention some important tasks done by robots.
Information and Communication Technology.r: Robotics is the branch of computer science and engineering dealing with the design, construction, operation and use of robots. Tasks: welding, painting and assembling in factories; helping in surgery; planting and harvesting; packing and sorting goods; exploring space and the deep sea; defusing bombs and rescue work.

Information and Communication Technology.q: What is virtual reality? Write the sectors in which it is used.
Information and Communication Technology.r: VR is a computer-made 3-D imitation of an environment that a user experiences through a headset and sensors as if it were real. Sectors: military training and PTSD therapy, education (virtual field trips), sports training and broadcasting, mental health (anxiety, phobia), medical surgery training, fashion, architecture.

Information and Communication Technology.q: What is cloud computing? Write two services and two advantages of cloud computing.
Information and Communication Technology.r: Cloud computing is using remote servers on the internet to store, manage and process data and programs instead of a local computer. Services: online file storage (e.g. Google Drive), e-mail, web hosting, running software online. Advantages: low cost (pay only for use); access from anywhere; reliable backup; strong security.

Information and Communication Technology.q: Describe the main tools of ICT. Explain the working of a search engine, website and ISP.
What is cybercrime? Explain eight rules of safe and ethical use of the internet, with the cyber law of Nepal.
Explain robotics, virtual reality, artificial intelligence and cloud computing with uses.
Which of the following devices is primarily used to convert digital data into analog signals?
Information and Communication Technology.w: A modem is used to convert digital signals into analog signals for transmission over analog networks.

Information and Communication Technology.q: In a computer network, what does OSI stand for?
Information and Communication Technology.w: OSI stands for Open Systems Interconnection, which is a reference model that standardizes the functions of a telecommunication or computing system.

Information and Communication Technology.q: Which protocol is used for transferring files between computers on a network?
Information and Communication Technology.w: FTP stands for File Transfer Protocol and is specifically designed for transferring files between computers on a network.

Information and Communication Technology.q: What type of IP address is used for multicast communication?
Information and Communication Technology.w: IP addresses in the Class D range (224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255) are reserved for multicasting.

Living Beings and Their Structure.w: Hooke saw empty cork cells in 1665.

Living Beings and Their Structure.q: Which structure is present in a plant cell but absent in an animal cell?
Living Beings and Their Structure.w: the rigid cellulose cell wall is a plant feature.

Living Beings and Their Structure.q: The powerhouse of the cell is the
Living Beings and Their Structure.w: respiration releasing energy occurs in mitochondria.

Living Beings and Their Structure.q: A group of similar cells performing the same function is a
Living Beings and Their Structure.w: similar cells with one function form a tissue.

Living Beings and Their Structure.q: Which one is a unicellular eukaryote?
Living Beings and Their Structure.w: Amoeba is a single-celled protist with a true nucleus.

A common feature of the nuclear membrane and the cell membrane is that they
Living Beings and Their Structure.w: both control the passage of substances.

Living Beings and Their Structure.q: Which function of the nucleus helps the growth of the body?
Differentiate:
Living Beings and Their Structure.r: (a) Cytoplasm is the semi-liquid between the cell membrane and nucleus, holding organelles; nucleoplasm is the liquid inside the nucleus, holding the nucleolus and chromatin. (b) Chloroplast is a green plastid with chlorophyll that makes food; chromoplast is a coloured (non-green) plastid that colours flowers and fruits for pollination and dispersal. (c) See the table in 3.1.3: wall is non-living, tough, freely permeable, only in plants/fungi/bacteria; membrane is living, thin, semi-permeable, in all cells. (d) Organelles are living parts with a special job (mitochondria, ribosome); inclusions are non-living substances in the cytoplasm (water droplets, salt crystals, stored food, wastes).

Living Beings and Their Structure.q: Give reasons:
p: The cell wall gives a fixed shape to plant cells.
The cell is the basic unit of life.
Cells, tissues and organs must be coordinated for life processes.
Living Beings and Their Structure.r: (a) They join amino acids to make proteins. (b) It is tough, rigid and non-living and surrounds the membrane like a box. (c) The cytoplasm holds the enzymes, raw materials and organelles where the chemical reactions occur. (d) Every organism is made of cells and every life process takes place in cells. (e) Each life process needs many cells working as tissues, tissues working as organs and organs working as a system; if one level fails, the process stops.

Living Beings and Their Structure.q: Where are mitochondria found in a cell? Write their functions.
Living Beings and Their Structure.r: In the cytoplasm of both plant and animal cells. Functions: oxidise glucose with oxygen to release energy stored as ATP (power house); contain DNA that passes on some hereditary characters.

Living Beings and Their Structure.q: Which organelle digests itself, and why?
Living Beings and Their Structure.r: The lysosome. It is full of digestive enzymes; when the enzyme level becomes very high, or the cell is old or damaged, the membrane breaks and the enzymes digest the cell itself — so it is called the suicidal bag.

Living Beings and Their Structure.q: Write the role of the Golgi body and the vacuole.
Living Beings and Their Structure.r: Golgi body: secretes mucus, saliva, sweat and tears; sorts and packs proteins; helps form the new membrane or cell plate in division. Vacuole: stores cell sap, balances water and salts, and collects wastes before they are removed.

Living Beings and Their Structure.q: Why is the nucleus called the brain of the cell? What happens if a cell has no nucleus?
Living Beings and Their Structure.r: It controls and coordinates all activities of the cell and carries the hereditary material. Without a nucleus the cell cannot divide or control its work, and soon dies (e.g. mature red blood cells live only about 120 days).

Living Beings and Their Structure.q: Differentiate between bacteria and virus.
Give reasons:
p: A virus is called an infectious particle, not an organism.
We should not eat stale, smelly food.
The five-kingdom system gives a proper place to almost all organisms.
Fruits do not spoil if dried well.
Living Beings and Their Structure.r: (a) It has no cell and no metabolism, and it shows life only inside a host cell. (b) Microbes have grown in it and made toxins, causing food poisoning. (c) It separates prokaryotes from eukaryotes, unicellular from multicellular, and gives fungi their own kingdom. (d) Microbes need water to grow; dried fruit has too little.

Living Beings and Their Structure.q: What is food poisoning? Write its causes and prevention.
Living Beings and Their Structure.r: Illness from eating food spoiled by microbes or their toxins. Causes: stale, uncovered or undercooked food; dirty hands or utensils; germs like Salmonella, Clostridium, norovirus. Prevention: eat fresh, well-cooked, covered food; wash hands; keep food cold; avoid smelly food.

Living Beings and Their Structure.q: How is amoeba useful to people?
Living Beings and Their Structure.r: Amoeba proteus eats bacteria, so it is used to control bacteria (e.g. in cleaning waste water).

Living Beings and Their Structure.q: Write the functions of the three kinds of plastids in a plant cell. What would happen to a plant with no chloroplasts?
Living Beings and Their Structure.r: Chloroplast: makes food by photosynthesis, gives green colour, helps make fatty acids and amino acids. Chromoplast: gives colour to flowers and fruits to attract insects and birds for pollination and seed dispersal. Leucoplast: stores starch, protein and fat. Without chloroplasts the plant could not make food, so it would not grow and would die; animals that depend on it would also suffer.

Living Beings and Their Structure.q: Write the merits and drawbacks of the two-kingdom system, and explain how the five-kingdom system corrected them.
Living Beings and Their Structure.r: Merits: first scientific system; simple; easy to tell plants from animals. Drawbacks: fungi put with plants; prokaryotic bacteria and eukaryotic algae put together; unicellular and multicellular not separated; lichens and Euglena had no place. Correction: Whittaker's five-kingdom system put prokaryotes in Monera, unicellular eukaryotes in Protista, fungi in their own kingdom Fungi, and kept only green multicellular plants in Plantae and multicellular consumers in Animalia.

Living Beings and Their Structure.q: What are the methods of food preservation? Describe one, and write the importance of food preservation. Why does fungus grow in a pickle jar, and how can it be stopped?
Living Beings and Their Structure.r: Dry, wet and cold preservation (table in 3.5). Wet preservation: the food is washed or boiled, dried, then kept in strong salt solution, lemon juice, vinegar or mustard oil in an airtight jar; e.g. lemon pickle. Importance: food lasts longer, nutrients are kept, seasonal food is available all year, loss to farmers is reduced and food poisoning is prevented. Fungus grows when moisture or air enters (wet vegetables, wet spoon, loose lid, too little oil or salt); prevent it by drying well, using enough oil and salt, an airtight lid and a dry spoon.

Living Beings and Their Structure.q: What is a microorganism? Give one example from each group, write four advantages of microorganisms, and name two diseases caused by each group.
Living Beings and Their Structure.r: Microorganisms are living beings too small to see without a microscope. Examples: virus — coronavirus; bacteria — Rhizobium; protozoa — Amoeba; fungi — yeast; algae — Chlamydomonas. Advantages: decomposition and soil fertility; nitrogen fixation; curd and cheese; antibiotics and vaccines; fermentation (bread, jaand). Diseases: virus — COVID-19, common cold; bacteria — typhoid, tuberculosis; protozoa — malaria, amoebic dysentery; fungi — ringworm, athlete's foot.

Living Beings and Their Structure.q: Draw and label plant and animal cells. Differentiate between them and write the functions of the organelles.
Explain the harmful and useful effects of microorganisms, the methods of food protection and the importance of vaccination.

Biodiversity and Environment.w: roughly 10 %; the rest is lost mainly as heat.

Biodiversity and Environment.w: Chitwan holds Nepal's largest rhinoceros population.

Biodiversity and Environment.q: Mikania (lahare banmara) spreading in Nepal's forests is an example of
Biodiversity and Environment.w: an introduced species spreading at the cost of native ones.

Biodiversity and Environment.q: Where was the 1992 Earth Summit on biodiversity held?
Faunal diversity is related to

o: planting it in the community forest
planting it in the forest where it was found
planting it in her kitchen garden
Biodiversity and Environment.w: the plant is moved out of its natural habitat.

Biodiversity and Environment.q: Which represents the significance of biodiversity?
o: fodder and firewood are obtained from forests
there is fear of wild animals

Biodiversity and Environment.q: What percentage of the world's plant species is found in Nepal?
Which aspect of sustainable development emphasises social justice?
Which point shows the importance of sustainable development for biodiversity?
Differentiate:
Biodiversity and Environment.r: (a) See the table in 4.2.1. (b) Genetic diversity is the variation among individuals of the same species due to genes (e.g. human skin colour, rice varieties); species diversity is the number and kinds of species in a place (e.g. deer, tiger, rhino and many birds in Chitwan).

Biodiversity and Environment.q: Give reasons:
p: There is variation among individuals of the same species.
Biodiversity and Environment.r: (a) Their genes differ slightly, and the environment also affects them. (b) Fire kills plants, seedlings, eggs and slow animals, destroys habitats and food, and leaves soil bare to erosion. (c) Its altitude changes from 59 m to 8848.86 m in a short distance, giving many climates (tropical to alpine), fertile soils and monsoon rain, so many habitats exist.

Biodiversity and Environment.q: What is biodiversity? Give examples. What is the role of species richness?
Biodiversity and Environment.r: Biodiversity is the variety of living beings in different habitats, including variety within species, between species and between ecosystems; e.g. rhinos and tigers in Chitwan, rhododendrons in the hills, yaks in the Himalaya. Species richness (many species) keeps food webs complex and the ecosystem stable and productive.

Biodiversity and Environment.q: Explain the present status of biodiversity in Nepal.
Biodiversity and Environment.r: Nepal has 0.1 % of the world's land but about 3.2 % of plant and 1.1 % of animal species, more than 118 ecosystems and 15 forest types; it ranks about 27th in the world. Endemic spiny babbler, rare rhino, tiger and wild yak, 32 rhododendron species and Marshi rice of Jumla show its richness.

Biodiversity and Environment.q: Differentiate:
p: social and environmental aspects of sustainable development.
Biodiversity and Environment.r: (a) See the table in 4.4. (b) The social aspect concerns people — ending poverty, equality, participation, culture, peace and justice; the environmental aspect concerns nature — conserving land, water, air, climate and biodiversity during development.

Biodiversity and Environment.q: Give reasons:
p: The environment must be considered in development work.
Sustainable development helps to establish social harmony.
Degradation of biodiversity affects sustainable development.
Biodiversity and Environment.r: (a) Development that destroys forests, rivers and slopes causes landslides and pollution, so the project itself does not last. (b) It shares resources and opportunities fairly, empowers women and marginalised groups and respects culture, so conflict decreases. (c) Food, water, medicine, tourism and soil fertility depend on biodiversity; when it is lost, the base for long-term development is lost.

Biodiversity and Environment.q: What is sustainable development? Give an example.
Biodiversity and Environment.r: Development that meets present needs without reducing the ability of future generations to meet theirs; e.g. building a road with drains, retaining walls and slope planting so that it lasts for many years.

Biodiversity and Environment.q: Write a food chain of four links and say what happens to it if the frog is removed.
Biodiversity and Environment.r: Grass → grasshopper → frog → snake. If frogs are removed, grasshoppers increase and damage the grass and crops, while snakes lose food and decline or move away.

Biodiversity and Environment.q: What are the methods of conserving biodiversity? Explain one, and write other measures of conservation.
Biodiversity and Environment.r: In-situ and ex-situ conservation. In-situ: organisms are protected in their natural habitat, e.g. national parks (Chitwan), wildlife reserve (Koshi Tappu), hunting reserve (Dhorpatan) and conservation areas (Annapurna); it is natural and cheap and protects all species, but poaching and fire are hard to control. Other measures: control poaching and illegal trade, create more protected areas, control overgrazing, fire and pollution, enforce strict laws, and educate people.

Biodiversity and Environment.q: Explain the causes of degradation of biodiversity in points.
Biodiversity and Environment.r: Any eight from the list in 4.2, each with a short reason (e.g. overgrazing destroys seedlings; invasive banmara displaces native plants).

Biodiversity and Environment.q: What are the principles of sustainable development? Describe any one.
Biodiversity and Environment.r: Ecosystem and biodiversity conservation; population control and human resource management; cultural conservation and public participation. Public participation: when people take part in a project and their culture is respected, they own and protect it — e.g. a village-built irrigation canal is maintained by the villagers and lasts long.

Biodiversity and Environment.q: What are the SDGs? Illustrate Nepal's efforts to achieve them.
Biodiversity and Environment.r: SDGs are 17 global goals with 169 targets and 232 indicators, adopted by 193 UN members in 2015 for 2016–2030. Nepal's efforts: Climate Change Council and cabinet meeting at Kalapatthar (2009); lowering Tsho Rolpa; community forests; periodic plans for poverty reduction, education and employment; National Environment Policy 2076 and Environment Protection Act 2076.

Biodiversity and Environment.q: Explain biodiversity, its levels and importance. Describe the threats to biodiversity and the ways of conserving it in Nepal.
Explain ecosystem, food chain and food web. Describe sustainable development and the Sustainable Development Goals.

Life Process.q: Where does fertilisation take place in flowering plants?
Life Process.w: inside the ovule, which lies in the ovary.

Life Process.q: Differentiate:
Life Process.r: (a) In fission the parent splits and disappears (amoeba); in budding a bud grows on the parent and separates, and the parent remains (yeast, hydra). (b) A bulbil is a small bud that falls and grows (agave, lily); a rhizome is a thick underground stem with buds lying flat under the soil (ginger). (c) Natural propagation happens by itself through roots, stems or leaves (potato, Bryophyllum); artificial propagation is done by people with tools (cutting, layering, grafting, tissue culture) to improve crops.

Life Process.q: Give reasons:
p: Asexual reproduction has no concept of male and female.
Growing potatoes from tubers is vegetative propagation.
Tissue culture is the most advanced method of vegetative propagation.
Life Process.r: (a) There is no formation or fusion of gametes; only one parent is involved. (b) The tuber is a stem (a vegetative part) and its eyes are buds that grow into new plants. (c) Grafted plants bear fruit early and have the high quality of the scion, so yield and income increase. (d) Thousands of disease-free, identical plantlets are produced from a tiny piece in a short time in any season.

Life Process.q: Name the method of asexual reproduction: yeast, paramecium, pineapple, banana, planaria, begonia, ginger, onion, sugarcane, Mucor, sweet potato, Spirogyra.
Life Process.r: Yeast — budding; paramecium — binary fission; pineapple — bulbils (and suckers); banana — sucker; planaria — regeneration; begonia — leaf; ginger — rhizome; onion — bulb; sugarcane — stem cutting (aerial stem); Mucor — sporulation (and fragmentation); sweet potato — root; Spirogyra — fragmentation.

Life Process.q: What are stock and scion? Write two advantages of grafting.
Life Process.r: The stock is the lower rooted part (a young seedling); the scion is the twig of a good-quality plant joined on it. Advantages: early fruiting; fruit of the desired quality; combines a hardy root with a productive shoot.

Life Process.q: Differentiate:
Life Process.r: (a) A gamete is a single reproductive cell (sperm or ovum); a zygote is the cell formed by fusion of two gametes. (b) The anther is the part of the stamen that makes pollen; a pollen grain is the tiny cell formed in it that carries the male gametes. (c) Autogamy: pollen to the stigma of the same flower; geitonogamy: pollen to another flower of the same plant.

Life Process.q: Give reasons:
p: Pollinating agents play a great role in pollination.
Both male and female are needed for sexual reproduction.
Internal fertilisation is safer than external fertilisation.
Life Process.r: (a) In cross-pollination pollen cannot move by itself; wind, water, insects and birds carry it. (b) The male gives the sperm and the female the ovum; only their fusion forms the zygote. (c) The gametes and embryo stay inside the female's body, protected from drying, cold and predators.

Life Process.q: What is gametogenesis? Where does it occur in plants and animals?
Life Process.r: Gametogenesis is the formation of gametes. In plants it occurs in the anther (pollen, male gametes) and ovule (egg); in animals in the testes (sperms) and ovaries (ova).

Life Process.q: Differentiate:
p: dispersal of mustard seeds and of kafal seeds.
Life Process.r: (a) Dispersal is carrying seeds away from the parent; germination is the growth of a seed into a seedling. (b) The plumule grows upward into the shoot; the radicle grows downward into the root. (c) Mustard seeds are thrown out when dry pods burst; kafal seeds are swallowed by birds and animals with the fruit and passed out elsewhere.

Life Process.q: Give reasons:
p: Seeds germinate if soaked in water.
Silk cotton seeds are dispersed far.
Eating sprouted seeds is more beneficial than dry seeds.
Life Process.r: (a) Water softens the coat, breaks dormancy and starts enzyme action. (b) They are light and covered with silky hairs, so the wind carries them. (c) Sprouting changes stored food into simpler forms and increases vitamins, so sprouts are easier to digest and more nutritious.

Life Process.q: Compare self-pollination and cross-pollination with their advantages and disadvantages.
Life Process.r: Self: pollen to the same flower or same plant; small dull flowers; no agent needed; seed setting is sure and parent characters are kept, but no new variety and vigour falls. Cross: pollen to another plant of the same species; bright, scented flowers with nectar; needs agents; gives new, stronger and better-adapted varieties, but depends on agents and may bring unwanted characters.

Life Process.q: What is double fertilisation? Describe the process.
Life Process.r: Two fusions in the ovule of a flowering plant. The pollen grain forms a pollen tube that grows through the style to the ovule; its nucleus forms two male gametes; one fuses with the egg to form the zygote (→ embryo) and the other fuses with the secondary nucleus to form the endosperm nucleus (→ endosperm). Then the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary the fruit.

Life Process.q: Write the methods of seed dispersal and explain any one with examples. Name the method for mango, chestnut, maple, gram, cobbler's pegs, sesame, pumpkin, coconut and pear.
Life Process.r: Wind, water, animals, gravity and bursting of pods (table in 5.4.2). Mango — gravity (and animals); chestnut — bursting/gravity; maple — wind; gram — bursting of pods; cobbler's pegs — animals (sticking); sesame — bursting of pods; pumpkin — animals/people; coconut — water; pear — animals.

Explain the structure of a seed, germination and the ways of seed dispersal. Write about nutrition and respiration in living things.

Force and Motion.q: Define reference point, relative velocity and retardation.
Force and Motion.r: A reference point is a fixed point, line or place with which the position of a body is compared. Relative velocity is the velocity of a body with respect to another body. Retardation is the rate of decrease of velocity (negative acceleration).

Force and Motion.q: Differentiate:
Force and Motion.r: (a) MA = load ÷ effort, affected by friction, always less than VR; VR = effort distance ÷ load distance, not affected by friction. (b) Input work = effort × effort distance (work put into the machine); output work = load × load distance (useful work done by it); output is less than input.

Force and Motion.q: Give reasons:
p: The efficiency of a lever is never 100 %.
A wheelbarrow is easier to push when the load is moved towards the wheel.
MA is always less than VR.
Force and Motion.r: (a) Some input work is always lost against friction, so output work is less than input work. (b) The load distance becomes shorter, so by $E\times E.D.=L\times L.D.$ less effort is needed. (c) Friction reduces MA but does not change VR.

Force and Motion.q: Which class of lever is a pair of scissors? What can a lever with MA more than 1 do? Write other advantages of a lever besides making work easy.
Force and Motion.r: First class (the pivot is between blade and handle). A lever with MA > 1 lifts a load larger than the effort (multiplies force). Other advantages: changes the direction of the force, increases speed or distance of movement (third class), and allows work at a convenient place (tongs keep hands away from fire).

Force and Motion.q: Give reasons:
p: The bottom of a dam is wider than its top.
A bucket fills faster on the ground floor than upstairs.
Force and Motion.r: (a) The small area of the studs gives large pressure, so they grip the ground. (b) A sharp edge has small area, so a small force gives large pressure to cut the soil. (c) Liquid pressure increases with depth, so the bottom must be strongest. (d) The depth of water below the tank (h) is greater at the ground floor, so pressure $hdg$ and the flow are greater.

Force and Motion.q: How can we show that a liquid exerts pressure? Write two applications of liquid pressure.
Force and Motion.r: Make holes at different heights in a bottle full of water; water comes out from all holes (pressure acts sideways) and spurts farthest from the lowest hole (pressure increases with depth). Applications: dams thick at the bottom; tanks kept high; divers' suits.

Force and Motion.q: What is atmospheric pressure? Write two uses of it.
Force and Motion.r: The pressure exerted by the weight of air on unit area of the earth's surface (760 mmHg at sea level). Uses: drinking with a straw, filling a syringe or fountain pen, pumping tyres.

Force and Motion.q: A bus covers 4.2 km in 7 minutes. Find its average velocity.
A car starts from rest and reaches 30 m/s in 12 s. Find its acceleration.
A car starts from rest with an acceleration of 5 m/s² for 6 s. Find its final velocity and average velocity.
Force and Motion.r: $v=u+at=0+5\times6=30$ m/s. Average velocity $=\frac{u+v}{2}=\frac{0+30}{2}=15$ m/s. (The answer printed in the textbook, 15 m/s and 7.5 m/s, would be correct only for an acceleration of 2.5 m/s²; with 5 m/s² the correct values are 30 m/s and 15 m/s.)

Force and Motion.q: Two motorcycles move at 50 km/h and 60 km/h. Find their relative velocity in the same and opposite directions.
Force and Motion.r: Same direction: $60-50=10$ km/h. Opposite directions: $60+50=110$ km/h.

Force and Motion.q: An effort of 75 N lifts a load of 300 N placed 25 cm from the fulcrum. Find the effort distance.
Force and Motion.r: $E\times E.D.=L\times L.D.$: $75\times E.D.=300\times25$, so $E.D.=\frac{7500}{75}=100$ cm $=1$ m.

Force and Motion.q: An effort of 300 N lifts a load of 900 N with a 2 m first-class lever; the load is 50 cm from the fulcrum and the effort is at the other end. Find MA, VR and efficiency.
Force and Motion.r: $L.D.=0.5$ m, $E.D.=2-0.5=1.5$ m. $MA=\frac{900}{300}=3$; $VR=\frac{1.5}{0.5}=3$; $\eta=\frac{3}{3}\times100\%=100\%$ (an ideal lever, friction neglected).

Energy in Daily Life.r: (a) A conductor lets heat pass easily (copper, iron); an insulator does not (wood, plastic, wool). (b) See the table in 7.3.4. (c) See the table in 7.3.2.

Energy in Daily Life.q: Give reasons:
p: Mud houses are cool in summer and warm in winter.
Tea cups are made of porcelain.
Light-coloured clothes are worn in summer.
Ventilators are made in the upper part of walls.
Transparent plastic covers an artificial greenhouse.
Energy in Daily Life.r: (a) Mud is a poor conductor, so heat does not easily pass in or out through the walls. (b) Porcelain is a poor conductor, so the tea stays hot and the cup is safe to hold. (c) Light colours absorb less heat radiation. (d) Warm used air is lighter and rises; it goes out through the upper ventilator while fresh air enters below (convection). (e) It lets the sun's short-wave radiation in but traps the long-wave heat given out by the soil and plants.

Energy in Daily Life.q: What is convection? How does wind blow? Write two applications of convection.
Energy in Daily Life.r: Transfer of heat in liquids and gases by the movement of heated particles. Wind: the sun heats the ground; the air above becomes warm and light and rises; cooler air from nearby flows in to take its place — this moving air is wind. Applications: boiling water, sea and land breezes, fans and air conditioners, refrigerators.

Energy in Daily Life.q: What is radiation? Write two applications. What is an electromagnetic wave? Give three examples.
Energy in Daily Life.r: Transfer of heat without a medium in the form of waves. Applications: sun heats the earth; warming near a fire; white clothes in summer; black solar cookers. An electromagnetic wave needs no medium and travels at $3\times10^8$ m/s in a vacuum: light, radio waves, X-rays (also infrared, gamma rays).

Energy in Daily Life.q: What is the greenhouse effect? Write its importance and two harmful effects.
Energy in Daily Life.r: The warming of the earth because greenhouse gases trap the heat radiated by it. Importance: keeps the average temperature about 15 °C instead of -18 °C so life can exist; greenhouses grow off-season vegetables. Harmful effects of its increase: global warming, melting glaciers and GLOF, sea-level rise, changed rainfall, lower crop yield.

Energy in Daily Life.q: Differentiate:
p: real and virtual image. Define principal axis, focus, centre of curvature and focal length.
Energy in Daily Life.r: See the tables in 7.5.1. Principal axis: the line through the pole and centre of curvature. Focus: the point on the axis where parallel rays meet (or seem to come from) after reflection. Centre of curvature: the centre of the sphere of which the mirror is part. Focal length: the distance from the pole to the focus.

Energy in Daily Life.q: Give reasons:
p: A concave mirror is used in a solar cooker.
A convex mirror is used as a rear-view mirror.
Convex and plane mirrors cannot form real images.
A concave mirror is used for shaving.
Energy in Daily Life.r: (a) It is a converging mirror; it collects the sun's rays at its focus and produces great heat. (b) It always gives an erect, diminished image and a wide field of view of the traffic behind. (c) Their reflected rays never actually meet; they only appear to meet behind the mirror. (d) When the face is within F, a concave mirror gives an erect, enlarged image.

Energy in Daily Life.q: Differentiate:
p: infrasound and ultrasound. Write three uses of ultrasound.
Energy in Daily Life.r: (a) Wavelength is the distance between two successive crests; amplitude is the maximum displacement of a particle from the mean position. (b) Infrasound is below 20 Hz (earthquakes, elephants); ultrasound is above 20 kHz (bats). Uses of ultrasound: USG of the womb, SONAR, killing bacteria, bloodless operations.

Energy in Daily Life.q: Why does the speed of sound stay the same when frequency changes? Why does sound become fainter as we move away from the source?
Energy in Daily Life.r: The speed depends only on the medium; since $v=f\lambda$ is fixed, a higher frequency gives a proportionally shorter wavelength. The energy spreads over a larger area and part is absorbed by the air, so intensity falls with distance.

Energy in Daily Life.q: The speed of sound in air is 332 m/s and its frequency is 10 Hz. Find the wavelength.
Energy in Daily Life.r: $\lambda=\frac{v}{f}=\frac{332}{10}=33.2$ m. (The textbook prints 33.3 m; the exact value is 33.2 m.)

Energy in Daily Life.q: A sound has a wavelength of 22 m and frequency 10 Hz. Find its speed.
Energy in Daily Life.r: $v=f\lambda=10\times22=220$ m/s. (The textbook's printed answer, 330 m/s, does not match the data; with 22 m and 10 Hz the speed is 220 m/s.)

Energy in Daily Life.q: If the speed of sound in air is 332 m/s, find the wavelengths of the shortest and longest sound waves that humans can hear.
Energy in Daily Life.r: Shortest wavelength at the highest audible frequency, 20 000 Hz: $\lambda=\frac{332}{20000}=0.0166$ m. Longest at 20 Hz: $\lambda=\frac{332}{20}=16.6$ m.

Energy in Daily Life.q: Draw ray diagrams for a concave mirror when the object is (i) beyond C (ii) at infinity (iii) between C and F, and write the nature of each image.
Energy in Daily Life.r: Use the three rules of 7.5.1. (i) Beyond C: image between F and C, real, inverted, diminished (figure in 7.5.1). (ii) At infinity: parallel rays meet at F — image at F, real, inverted, point-sized. (iii) Between C and F: image beyond C, real, inverted, magnified.

Energy in Daily Life.q: Write the causes, two effects and two ways to control sound pollution.
Energy in Daily Life.r: Causes: traffic and horns, factories, construction, loudspeakers and loud music. Effects: hearing loss and eardrum damage; high blood pressure, stress and sleeplessness; loss of concentration. Control: trees along roads, silencers and fewer horns, low-volume music and TV, industries away from settlements, awareness programmes.

State the laws of reflection. Explain the images formed by plane and spherical mirrors and by a convex lens, with uses.
