Classification of Elements and Periodici.q: Among the following, the lowest first ionisation energy belongs to
Classification of Elements and Periodici.w: Ionisation energy falls down group 1 as size grows; Cs (376 kJ mol⁻¹) is the lowest of these.

Classification of Elements and Periodici.q: Across a period from left to right, the atomic radius of main-group elements generally
Classification of Elements and Periodici.w: The nuclear charge rises while electrons enter the same shell, so Z_eff rises and pulls the shell in.

Classification of Elements and Periodici.q: Which of these elements is a metalloid?
Classification of Elements and Periodici.w: Silicon is a metalloid (semiconductor); Na is a metal, S and Cl are non-metals.

Classification of Elements and Periodici.q: Isoelectronic species have the same number of
Classification of Elements and Periodici.w: Isoelectronic means "equal electrons" (e.g. Na⁺, Ne and F⁻ have 10 each).

Classification of Elements and Periodici.q: The IUPAC temporary name of the element with atomic number 104 is
Classification of Elements and Periodici.w: 1-0-4 → un-nil-quad-ium: unnilquadium, symbol Unq (now rutherfordium). Ununquadium is element 114.

Classification of Elements and Periodici.q: The elements of group 16 are called
Classification of Elements and Periodici.w: Group 16 (O, S, Se, Te, Po) are the chalcogens ("ore-formers"); pnictogens are group 15, halogens group 17.

Classification of Elements and Periodici.q: The nearly equal atomic radii of zirconium and hafnium are due to
o: the screening effect of s electrons
Classification of Elements and Periodici.w: Poor screening by the 4f electrons shrinks the elements after the lanthanoids, so Hf (5d) ends up the size of Zr (4d).
Al₂O₃ dissolves in acids and in alkalis. Na₂O and MgO are basic; SO₃ is acidic.

Classification of Elements and Periodici.q: Explain the periodic trends in atomic radius, ionisation enthalpy, electron gain enthalpy and electronegativity with reasons and a Slater's-rule numerical.
Discuss the anomalous behaviour of the first element of a group, diagonal relationships and the change in the nature of oxides across the third period.

Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.q: According to the electronic theory of valency of Kossel and Lewis, atoms combine in order to
Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.w: The Kossel–Lewis theory: atoms transfer or share electrons to reach an octet (or duplet), the configuration of a noble gas.

Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.q: A coordinate (dative) bond is present in
Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.w: In NH₄⁺ the nitrogen lone pair is donated to H⁺. CH₄ and H₂O have ordinary covalent bonds; NaCl is ionic.

Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.q: The bond angle in a regular tetrahedral molecule such as CH₄ is
Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.w: 109.5° (109° 28′). 104.5° is water, 120° trigonal planar, 90° octahedral.

Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.q: The hybridisation of each carbon atom in ethyne (C₂H₂) is
Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.w: Each C forms two σ bonds (to C and H) and two π bonds: SN 2, sp, linear.

Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.q: A π bond is formed by the
o: axial overlap of s and p orbitals
Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.w: Sideways (lateral) overlap of parallel p orbitals; head-on overlap gives σ bonds.

Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.q: Which molecule has zero dipole moment?
Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.w: CO₂ is linear, so its two C=O moments cancel. Bent H₂O, pyramidal NH₃ and HCl are polar.

Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.q: Ice floats on water because
o: ice has stronger van der Waals forces
hydrogen bonding gives ice an open cage structure
Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.w: In ice each molecule is H-bonded tetrahedrally to four others, an open, low-density cage; water is densest at 4 °C, not 0 °C.

Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.q: The electron sea model explains the bonding in
Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.w: Metal kernels in a sea of mobile valence electrons (Drude–Lorentz model).

Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.q: The attraction between non-polar molecules such as I₂, or between noble-gas atoms, is due to
Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.w: Momentary dipoles inducing dipoles: London (dispersion) forces, the only attraction between non-polar particles.

Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.q: The shape of the SF₆ molecule is
Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.w: SN = ½(6 + 6) = 6, no lone pair: octahedral, all angles 90°.

Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.q: The hybridisation of phosphorus in PCl₅ is
Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.w: SN = ½(5 + 5) = 5: sp³d, trigonal bipyramidal.

Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.q: Which molecule does NOT obey the octet rule?
Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.w: Boron in BF₃ has only six electrons round it (incomplete octet).

Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.q: By Fajans' rules, the covalent character of an ionic compound increases when the cation is
Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.w: A small, highly charged cation polarises the anion strongly. Noble-gas cations polarise less than pseudo-noble-gas ones of the same size.

Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.q: XeF₄ is square planar because the xenon atom has
o: four bond pairs and no lone pair
four bond pairs and two lone pairs
four bond pairs and one lone pair
Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.w: SN = ½(8 + 4) = 6: octahedral arrangement with the two lone pairs opposite each other (trans), leaving the four F atoms in a square.

Chemical Bonding and Shapes of Molecules.q: Explain the VSEPR theory and the shapes of molecules, with hybridisation in BeCl₂, BF₃, CH₄, NH₃, H₂O, PCl₅ and SF₆.
Explain molecular orbital theory, the bond order of N₂, O₂ and the paramagnetism of O₂, and compare ionic, covalent and metallic bonds.

Redox Reactions.q: In terms of electrons, oxidation is
Redox Reactions.w: Oxidation is loss of electrons (OIL RIG); gain of electrons is reduction.

Redox Reactions.q: In the classical concept, which change is a reduction?
Redox Reactions.w: Removal of oxygen is reduction (CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O). The other three are classical oxidations.

Redox Reactions.q: An oxidising agent is a substance that
o: gains electrons and is itself reduced
Redox Reactions.w: An oxidant takes electrons from something else and is reduced in doing so.

Redox Reactions.q: The oxidation number of manganese in KMnO₄ is
A reaction in which the same element is both oxidised and reduced is called
In the reaction Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, the reducing agent is
Redox Reactions.w: Zn loses two electrons (0 → +2), so it is the reducing agent; Cu²⁺ is the oxidising agent.

Redox Reactions.q: The oxidation number of osmium in OsO₄, the highest found in any stable compound, is
Redox Reactions.w: x + 4(-2) = 0 → x = +8. Osmium in OsO₄ and ruthenium in RuO₄ reach +8, the highest oxidation number in stable compounds.

Redox Reactions.q: Oxygen has the oxidation number -½ in
Redox Reactions.w: In KO₂ the superoxide ion O₂⁻ carries -1 over two O atoms: -½ each. BaO₂ and H₂O₂ are peroxides (-1).

Redox Reactions.q: Which of these can act only as a reducing agent?
Redox Reactions.w: Sulphur at -2, its lowest state, can only lose electrons. SO₂ (+4) and S (0) can go up or down; H₂SO₄ (+6) can only go down.

Redox Reactions.q: Which of these can act only as an oxidising agent?
Redox Reactions.w: Mn in KMnO₄ is +7, its maximum, so it can only gain electrons. H₂O₂, SO₂ and HNO₂ are in intermediate states and can act both ways.

Redox Reactions.q: In the ion-electron method for an acidic solution, oxygen atoms are balanced by adding
Redox Reactions.w: Water supplies O; H⁺ then balances the hydrogen. OH⁻ is used only when converting to a basic medium.

Redox Reactions.q: The rusting of iron is an example of
Redox Reactions.w: Iron goes from 0 to +3 in hydrated Fe₂O₃ (rust) — it is oxidised; oxygen is reduced.

Redox Reactions.q: In the reaction 2FeCl₂ + Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃, iron(II) chloride is
o: oxidised, as an electronegative element is added
Redox Reactions.w: Adding an electronegative element (Cl) is oxidation in the classical sense; electronically Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻.

Redox Reactions.q: The oxidation number of iron in Fe₃O₄ is
Redox Reactions.w: 3x + 4(-2) = 0 → x = +8/3, an average: Fe₃O₄ is really FeO·Fe₂O₃, one Fe²⁺ and two Fe³⁺.

Redox Reactions.q: Explain oxidation number, and balance a redox equation by the ion-electron method (acidic and basic medium).
Discuss the types of redox reactions, including disproportionation, and solve a redox titration numerical using equivalents.

States of Matter.q: According to the kinetic theory, the average kinetic energy of gas molecules is directly proportional to
States of Matter.w: KE = (3/2)RT per mole: it depends on the absolute temperature only, not on P, V or the kind of gas.

States of Matter.q: The value of the gas constant R in L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ is
States of Matter.w: 0.0821 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. 8.314 is in J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and 1.987 in cal mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; 22.4 L is the molar volume.

States of Matter.q: Graham's law states that the rate of diffusion of a gas is
o: inversely proportional to its molar mass
proportional to the square root of its density
inversely proportional to the square root of its density
States of Matter.w: r ∝ 1/√ρ ∝ 1/√M. Option (b) misses the square root.

States of Matter.q: Real gases behave most nearly like an ideal gas at
States of Matter.w: At low pressure the molecular volume is negligible, and at high temperature the attractions hardly matter.

States of Matter.q: In the van der Waals equation the constant a corrects for
States of Matter.w: a corrects the pressure for intermolecular attraction; b corrects the volume for the size of the molecules.

States of Matter.q: A liquid boils at the temperature at which
o: its vapour pressure equals the external pressure
States of Matter.w: Boiling begins when bubbles of vapour can form inside the liquid, i.e. when its vapour pressure equals the pressure above it.

States of Matter.q: The SI unit of surface tension is
States of Matter.w: Force per unit length: N m⁻¹ (equivalently J m⁻²). N s m⁻² is the unit of viscosity.

States of Matter.q: When the temperature rises, the viscosity of a liquid
States of Matter.w: Warmer molecules overcome intermolecular attraction more easily, so the liquid flows more freely. (Gas viscosity does the opposite.)

States of Matter.q: A substance that absorbs moisture from the air and dissolves in it is called
States of Matter.w: Deliquescent solids, such as CaCl₂ and NaOH, dissolve in the water they absorb; hygroscopic ones only become damp.

States of Matter.q: Which of the following is an amorphous solid?
States of Matter.w: Glass has only short-range order and softens over a range of temperature. NaCl, quartz and diamond are crystalline.

States of Matter.q: The state of matter that flows like a liquid but keeps some orientational order of a crystal is
States of Matter.w: The liquid crystal (mesophase) lies between the crystalline solid and the isotropic liquid.

States of Matter.q: Crystals of washing soda lose water and crumble when exposed to air. This property is called
States of Matter.w: Efflorescence: Na₂CO₃·10H₂O gives up water of crystallisation to the air and turns powdery.

States of Matter.q: Dalton's law of partial pressures applies to
States of Matter.w: The partial pressures add only when the gases do not react with one another.

States of Matter.q: Diamond is an example of a
States of Matter.w: Every carbon is covalently bonded to four others in a giant 3-D network, hence extreme hardness and a very high melting point.

States of Matter.q: State the gas laws, derive the ideal gas equation and explain Graham's law, Dalton's law and deviations of real gases with numericals.
Describe the properties of liquids and the types of crystal lattice, and calculate packing efficiency and density of a unit cell.

Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium.q: At equilibrium, a reversible reaction has
o: both reactions proceeding at equal rates
Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium.w: Equilibrium is dynamic: both reactions continue at the same rate, so concentrations stay constant. Nothing has stopped and nothing is necessarily used up.

Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium.q: For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, the equilibrium constant $K_c$ is
Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium.w: Products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient: [NH₃]² on top, [N₂] and [H₂]³ below. Option (c) is the expression for the reverse reaction.

Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium.q: The unit of $K_c$ for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI is
Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium.w: $\Delta n = 2 - 2 = 0$, so the concentration units cancel and $K_c$ is dimensionless. Options (a) and (b) belong to reactions with $\Delta n = +1$ and $-1$.

Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium.q: If the reaction quotient $Q$ is greater than $K$, the reaction
Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium.w: $Q > K$ means there is too much product, so the reverse reaction runs until $Q$ falls to $K$. Option (a) is the case $Q < K$.

Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium.q: The equilibrium constant of a reaction changes when
Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium.w: $K$ depends only on temperature. Pressure, volume, concentration and catalyst change the position or the rate, never the value of $K$.

Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium.q: An increase in pressure shifts an equilibrium towards
o: the side with more gas molecules
the side with fewer gas molecules
Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium.w: Raising the pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules, because that side occupies less volume. If $\Delta n = 0$ there is no shift at all.

Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium.q: The catalyst used in the contact process is
Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium.w: Vanadium(V) oxide, V₂O₅, at about 720 K. Iron is the Haber catalyst and platinum–rhodium the Ostwald catalyst.

Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium.q: The catalyst used in the Ostwald process is
Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium.w: A platinum–rhodium gauze at about 800 K and 9 atm. It is expensive, so it is used as a fine gauze with a very short contact time.

Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium.q: The conjugate base of HCO₃⁻ is
Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium.w: Remove one H⁺ from HCO₃⁻ and CO₃²⁻ remains. H₂CO₃ is the conjugate acid, formed by adding H⁺.

Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium.q: According to Lewis, an acid is an
Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium.w: A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair, as BF₃ does from NH₃. This definition covers acids such as BF₃ and AlCl₃ that contain no hydrogen at all.
HSO₄⁻ can donate a proton (to give SO₄²⁻) or accept one (to give H₂SO₄). SO₄²⁻ and NH₄⁺ can only do one of the two.

Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium.q: At 25 °C, pH + pOH is equal to
Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium.w: Since $K_w = 10^{-14}$, $-\log[\text{H}^+] - \log[\text{OH}^-] = 14$, so pH + pOH = 14 at 25 °C. At other temperatures the sum is pKw, not 14.

Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium.q: For a conjugate acid–base pair at 25 °C, pKa + pKb is
Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium.w: $K_aK_b = K_w$ for a conjugate pair, so taking logs gives pKa + pKb = pKw = 14 at 25 °C.

Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium.q: For PbCl₂, the solubility product is
Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium.w: PbCl₂ gives one Pb²⁺ and two Cl⁻, so each concentration is raised to its coefficient: [Pb²⁺][Cl⁻]².

Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium.q: State the law of mass action and Le Chatelier's principle. Derive the relation between $K_p$ and $K_c$ and calculate the equilibrium concentrations.
Explain pH, buffer solutions, the solubility product and the common ion effect with numericals.

Volumetric Analysis.q: The equivalent weight of an acid is its molar mass divided by
Volumetric Analysis.w: An acid's n-factor is its basicity, the number of replaceable H⁺ per molecule. For a base it would be the acidity, the number of OH⁻.

Volumetric Analysis.q: The equivalent weight of H₂SO₄ (M = 98) is
Volumetric Analysis.w: Sulphuric acid is dibasic, so $E = 98/2 = 49$. Option (a) forgets the n-factor and (d) is the value for H₃PO₄.

Volumetric Analysis.q: The n-factor of K₂Cr₂O₇ in acidic medium is
Volumetric Analysis.w: Two chromium atoms go from +6 to +3, so 2 × 3 = 6 electrons are gained per formula unit. Option (a) counts only one chromium atom.

Volumetric Analysis.q: The equivalent weight of KMnO₄ in acidic medium (M = 158) is
Volumetric Analysis.w: Mn goes from +7 to +2, so $n = 5$ and $E = 158/5 = 31.6$. Option (b) is the value in neutral medium (n = 3).

Volumetric Analysis.q: The equivalent weight of anhydrous Na₂CO₃ (M = 106) is
Volumetric Analysis.w: The carbonate ion takes two protons, so $n = 2$ and $E = 106/2 = 53$. Option (a) uses n = 1, which is right only for NaHCO₃.

Volumetric Analysis.q: Molarity is the number of moles of solute per
Volumetric Analysis.w: Molarity is moles per litre of solution, not of solvent. The volume includes the solute.

Volumetric Analysis.q: Molality is expressed in
Volumetric Analysis.w: Molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent, so its unit is mol kg⁻¹ and it does not change with temperature.

Volumetric Analysis.q: One part per million is the same as
Volumetric Analysis.w: ppm is 1 mg per kg (or per litre of dilute aqueous solution). Option (c) is one part per billion.

Volumetric Analysis.q: Which substance is a primary standard?
Volumetric Analysis.w: Oxalic acid is pure, stable and non-hygroscopic. NaOH absorbs CO₂ and water, HCl is volatile and KMnO₄ decomposes.

Volumetric Analysis.q: The law of equivalence is written as
Volumetric Analysis.w: At the equivalence point the equivalents of the two reactants are equal: $N_1V_1 = N_2V_2$. Option (a) is true only for a 1: 1 reaction in molar terms.

Volumetric Analysis.q: The indicator used for a strong acid–weak base titration is
Volumetric Analysis.w: The salt of a weak base is acidic at equivalence (pH about 5), so the indicator must change in the acid region: methyl orange.

Volumetric Analysis.q: The indicator used for a weak acid–strong base titration is
Volumetric Analysis.w: The salt of a weak acid is basic at equivalence (pH about 8.7), so phenolphthalein, which changes at 8.3–10.0, is the right choice.

Volumetric Analysis.q: The number of equivalents of a solute is equal to
Volumetric Analysis.w: Equivalents $= N \times V$ in litres. Option (b) gives moles, not equivalents.

Volumetric Analysis.q: The equivalent weight of oxalic acid dihydrate (M = 126) is
Volumetric Analysis.w: Oxalate loses two electrons, so $n = 2$ and $E = 126/2 = 63$. Option (b) is the anhydrous value, 90/2.

Volumetric Analysis.q: Explain acid-base titration, the choice of indicator and the use of primary standards, with a numerical on purity.
Describe iodometric and complexometric (EDTA) titrations and determine copper and the hardness of water.

Chemical Kinetics.q: The rate of disappearance of a reactant is written with a negative sign because
o: the stoichiometric coefficient of a reactant is negative
the reactant concentration falls, so $d[R]/dt$ is negative
the rate constant of a reactant is negative
Chemical Kinetics.w: Concentration falls, so $d[R]/dt$ is negative; the minus sign makes the rate positive. Rate constants are always positive and coefficients are positive numbers.

Chemical Kinetics.q: The SI unit of the rate of a chemical reaction is
Chemical Kinetics.w: Concentration per unit time, mol L⁻¹ ÷ s. Option (c) is the unit of a first-order $k$; (d) of a second-order $k$.

Chemical Kinetics.q: The unit of $k$ for a zero-order reaction is
Chemical Kinetics.w: rate $= k$ for zero order, so $k$ carries the unit of rate itself.

Chemical Kinetics.q: The order of a reaction is
o: the number of molecules in the balanced equation
the sum of the concentration powers in the experimental rate law
the number of steps in the mechanism
Chemical Kinetics.w: Order is experimental. It equals the molecularity only for a single-step reaction.

Chemical Kinetics.q: The molecularity of a reaction
Chemical Kinetics.w: Molecularity counts whole species colliding in one step, so it cannot be 0 or a fraction. Zero and fractional orders exist because order is empirical.

Chemical Kinetics.q: The integrated rate equation of a zero-order reaction is
Chemical Kinetics.w: Integrating $-d[A]/dt = k$ gives $[A] = [A]_0 - kt$. Option (a) is the first-order law, (b) the second-order law.

Chemical Kinetics.q: According to collision theory, colliding molecules react only if they
o: have at least the threshold energy and a favourable orientation
Chemical Kinetics.w: Both conditions are needed: enough energy and the right geometry. Head-on collision alone is neither necessary nor sufficient.

Chemical Kinetics.q: The minimum energy that colliding molecules must possess in order to react is called the
Chemical Kinetics.w: The activation energy is the extra energy above the reactants' average energy needed to reach the threshold.

Chemical Kinetics.q: The short-lived, high-energy arrangement of atoms at the top of the energy barrier is the
Chemical Kinetics.w: The activated complex is a transient arrangement at the peak; an intermediate sits in a valley between two steps.

Chemical Kinetics.q: A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction by
o: providing an alternative path of lower activation energy
Chemical Kinetics.w: A catalyst offers a new path of lower $E_a$. It cannot alter $\Delta H$ or $K$.

Chemical Kinetics.q: The catalyst used in the Haber process is
Chemical Kinetics.w: Iron with molybdenum as promoter. V₂O₅ is the contact process, Pt the oxidation of SO₂ and catalytic converters, Ni the hydrogenation of oils.

Chemical Kinetics.q: The temperature coefficient of a reaction compares the rate constants at two temperatures differing by
Chemical Kinetics.w: The temperature coefficient is $k_{T+10}/k_T$, usually about 2 to 3.

Chemical Kinetics.q: A reaction whose rate does not depend on the concentration of the reactant is of
Chemical Kinetics.w: Rate $= k[A]^0 = k$, independent of concentration. This happens on a saturated catalyst surface.

Chemical Kinetics.q: The unit of the rate constant of a second-order reaction is
Chemical Kinetics.w: mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹ = $k$(mol L⁻¹)², so $k$ is in L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.

Chemical Kinetics.q: Define rate, order and molecularity. Derive the integrated rate law and half-life of a first-order reaction with a numerical.
Explain collision theory and the Arrhenius equation, the effect of a catalyst and calculate the activation energy.

Electrochemistry.q: In an electrolytic cell, oxidation takes place at the
Electrochemistry.w: Oxidation is loss of electrons and always happens at the anode. In an electrolytic cell the anode is the electrode connected to the positive terminal.

Electrochemistry.q: In a galvanic cell, the cathode is the electrode where
Electrochemistry.w: Reduction at the cathode in every cell. In a galvanic cell the cathode is positive and electrons arrive there from the external circuit.

Electrochemistry.q: The SI unit of quantity of electricity is the
Electrochemistry.w: The coulomb is the unit of charge; the ampere is charge per second.

Electrochemistry.q: The standard hydrogen electrode is assigned a potential of
Electrochemistry.w: Zero, by definition; it is the reference against which every other electrode is quoted.

Electrochemistry.q: In the standard hydrogen electrode, the H⁺ concentration and the H₂ pressure are
Electrochemistry.w: Unit activity of H⁺ (1 M in practice), H₂ at 1 atm, 298 K, on platinum black.

Electrochemistry.q: Standard electrode potentials are quoted as
Electrochemistry.w: IUPAC uses reduction potentials. An oxidation potential is the same number with the sign reversed.

Electrochemistry.q: The calomel electrode is used as a
Electrochemistry.w: It is a secondary reference: stable and portable, but its potential is about +0.24 V, not zero.

Electrochemistry.q: Metals placed above hydrogen in the electrochemical series
Electrochemistry.w: They have negative $E^\circ$ and are oxidised by H⁺. Copper and silver lie below hydrogen and do not.

Electrochemistry.q: The emf of the cell Zn | Zn²⁺ || Cu²⁺ | Cu is
Electrochemistry.w: $0.34 - (-0.76) = 1.10$ V. Option (b) is the zinc potential alone; (d) is the Zn–Ag cell.

Electrochemistry.q: A lead–acid accumulator is an example of a
Electrochemistry.w: It is rechargeable, so it is a secondary cell. Primary cells cannot be recharged.

Electrochemistry.q: The electrolyte in a lead–acid battery is
Electrochemistry.w: Dilute sulphuric acid; both electrodes become PbSO₄ on discharge and the acid is diluted.

Electrochemistry.q: The fuel used at the anode of a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell is
Electrochemistry.w: Hydrogen is oxidised at the anode and oxygen reduced at the cathode; the only product is water.

Electrochemistry.q: Rusting of iron is essentially
Electrochemistry.w: Anodic and cathodic sites on the surface form short-circuited galvanic cells, with iron as the anode.

Electrochemistry.q: In the rusting of iron, the iron acts as the
Electrochemistry.w: Iron dissolves as Fe²⁺ and releases electrons, so it is oxidised and is the anode.

Electrochemistry.q: Describe the Daniell cell, define standard electrode potential, and apply the Nernst equation with a numerical.
State Faraday's laws of electrolysis, explain conductance and Kohlrausch's law, and solve numericals.

Chemical Thermodynamics.q: A system that exchanges both matter and energy with its surroundings is
Chemical Thermodynamics.w: Open systems exchange both. A closed system exchanges only energy; an isolated system exchanges neither.
Temperature does not depend on how much substance is present. Mass, volume and internal energy all do.

Chemical Thermodynamics.q: The first law of thermodynamics is a statement of the conservation of
Chemical Thermodynamics.w: Energy is conserved; the first law is the law of conservation of energy written for a thermodynamic system.

Chemical Thermodynamics.q: A reaction with a negative $\Delta H$ is
Chemical Thermodynamics.w: A negative $\Delta H$ means heat leaves the system: exothermic.

Chemical Thermodynamics.q: The enthalpy of formation of an element in its standard state is
Chemical Thermodynamics.w: Zero, but only in the standard state. Diamond and ozone have non-zero values.
Enthalpy is a state function, so $\Delta H$ is path-independent; that is the first law applied to $H$.

o: $\Delta H$ forward is the negative of $\Delta H$ backward
Chemical Thermodynamics.w: Reversing a reaction reverses the sign of the heat change, because the initial and final states are swapped.
Entropy is energy per kelvin per mole; $\Delta S = q_{\text{rev}}/T$.

Chemical Thermodynamics.q: The enthalpy change when one mole of a substance is completely burnt in oxygen is the enthalpy of
Chemical Thermodynamics.w: Combustion, and it is always exothermic for a fuel.

Chemical Thermodynamics.q: The enthalpy of fusion of ice at 0 °C is about
Chemical Thermodynamics.w: 6.01 kJ mol⁻¹. 40.7 is the enthalpy of vaporisation; 2.26 is per gram, not per mole.

Chemical Thermodynamics.q: The standard enthalpy of combustion of methane is
Chemical Thermodynamics.w: -890.3 kJ mol⁻¹. -74.8 is the enthalpy of formation of methane, -393.5 that of CO₂.

Chemical Thermodynamics.q: At constant volume, the heat exchanged equals
Chemical Thermodynamics.w: No pressure–volume work is possible at constant volume, so all the heat appears as $\Delta U$.

Chemical Thermodynamics.q: The dissolution of ammonium nitrate in water is
o: equal to its enthalpy of fusion
Chemical Thermodynamics.w: The lattice energy outweighs the hydration energy, so the solution cools: the cold pack.

Chemical Thermodynamics.q: Which of these is an extensive property?
Chemical Thermodynamics.w: Mass scales with amount. Temperature, density and molar volume are intensive.

Chemical Thermodynamics.q: State the first law of thermodynamics, define enthalpy and apply Hess's law with a numerical.
Explain entropy, Gibbs free energy and spontaneity, and calculate the temperature at which a reaction becomes spontaneous.

Nuclear Chemistry.q: In a nuclear reaction, the quantities always conserved (summed on both sides) are
Nuclear Chemistry.w: nucleons (A) and charge (Z) balance; the measured mass shrinks by the binding-energy account (Physics §20.1).

Nuclear Chemistry.q: Emission of an α-particle decreases the atomic number by
Nuclear Chemistry.w: the helium nucleus carries off 2 protons (and A by 4).

Nuclear Chemistry.q: β⁻ emission from a nucleus increases its atomic number by one because a
Nuclear Chemistry.w: $n \rightarrow p + e^- + \bar\nu_e$: a new proton appears, the electron is the β⁻ particle.

Nuclear Chemistry.q: Which set lists only magic numbers (for nucleons)?
Nuclear Chemistry.w: the nuclear shell closures. (Noble-gas electron counts, option (d), are the chemical cousins, not magic numbers.)

Nuclear Chemistry.q: Radioactive dating of once-living matter uses the isotope
Carbon-14 is produced in the atmosphere by the action of cosmic-ray neutrons on
A smoke detector commonly uses the radioisotope
Nuclear Chemistry.w: americium-241 α-source ionizes the detector's air gap; smoke interrupts the ion current. (Kitchen physics of §12.2.)

Nuclear Chemistry.q: The isotope used to study phosphorus uptake (fertilizers) in plants is
Nuclear Chemistry.w: ${}^{32}P$ (β⁻, 14.3 days) is traced from fertilizer to leaf with counters/autoradiography.

Nuclear Chemistry.q: Which nuclide is doubly magic (magic Z and magic N)?
Nuclear Chemistry.w: Z = 82 and N = 126 are both magic — ${}^{208}Pb$ is the doubly-magic terminus of two decay series. (${}^4He$ and ${}^{16}O$ and ${}^{40}Ca$ are the smaller doubles.)
1934: aluminium bombarded with α gave radioactive ${}^{30}P$ (Nobel 1935).

Nuclear Chemistry.q: The tracer principle works because a radioisotope of an element has (chemically)

Verbal Reasoning.q: A man is facing north. He turns right, then right again, then left. Which direction is he facing now?
Verbal Reasoning.w: North → right → east → right → south → left → east. Facing south, a left turn points east.

Verbal Reasoning.q: Sunita walks 12 m east, then turns left and walks 5 m. How far is she from her starting point?
Verbal Reasoning.w: The legs are 12 m east and 5 m north: $\sqrt{12^2 + 5^2}$ = 13 m (the 5-12-13 triple). 17 m is the path length, not the distance.

Verbal Reasoning.q: Soon after sunrise, Hari stood facing his own shadow. Which direction was he facing?
Verbal Reasoning.w: In the morning the sun is in the east, so his shadow falls to the west; facing the shadow means facing west.

Verbal Reasoning.q: From her home, Asha walks 4 km north and then 3 km west. Where is she now with respect to her home?
Verbal Reasoning.w: 4 km north and 3 km west: $\sqrt{4^2 + 3^2}$ = 5 km, and north + west = north-west. 7 km adds the legs.

Verbal Reasoning.q: Pointing to a boy, Gita said, "His mother is the only daughter of my mother." How is Gita related to the boy?
Verbal Reasoning.w: The only daughter of Gita's mother is Gita herself, so Gita is the boy's mother.

Verbal Reasoning.q: Introducing a girl, Raju said, "She is the daughter of the only son of my father." How is the girl related to Raju?
Verbal Reasoning.w: The only son of Raju's father is Raju himself; the girl is the daughter of Raju.

Verbal Reasoning.q: A is B's brother. C is A's mother. D is C's father. How is D related to B?
Verbal Reasoning.w: C is the mother of A and B (they are brothers/sisters); D is C's father, so D is B's (maternal) grandfather.

Verbal Reasoning.q: If P × Q means "P is the father of Q" and P + Q means "P is the sister of Q", then A + B × C means
o: A is the mother of C
A is the aunt of C
A is the sister of C
A is the grandmother of C
Verbal Reasoning.w: A is the sister of B, and B is the father of C: A is C's father's sister — C's aunt.

Verbal Reasoning.q: If COLD is written as DPME in a code, how is WARM written in that code?
Verbal Reasoning.w: COLD → DPME moves every letter one place on (+1). W→X, A→B, R→S, M→N: XBSN.

Verbal Reasoning.q: If each letter is replaced by its opposite letter of the alphabet (A↔Z, B↔Y, C↔X, …), HEART is written as
Verbal Reasoning.w: Opposite letters add to 27: H(8)→S(19), E(5)→V(22), A→Z, R(18)→I(9), T(20)→G(7): SVZIG.

Verbal Reasoning.q: If A = 1, B = 2, …, Z = 26 and CAT = 24, then DOG =
Verbal Reasoning.w: CAT = 3 + 1 + 20 = 24, so the code is the sum of positions. DOG = 4 + 15 + 7 = 26.

Verbal Reasoning.q: If PAPER is written as REPAP in a code, how is NURSE written in that code?
Verbal Reasoning.w: The word is written backwards. NURSE reversed is ESRUN.

Verbal Reasoning.q: If "sky" is called "sea", "sea" is called "water", "water" is called "air", "air" is called "cloud" and "cloud" is called "rain", what do we drink when thirsty?
Verbal Reasoning.w: We drink water, and in this code water is called "air". Option (a) is the real name, not the code name.

Numerical Reasoning.w: The number × 1.2 = 360, so the number = 360/1.2 = 300. Taking 20 % off 360 (288) is the trap: the 20 % was of the original number.

Physical Quantities, Vectors and Kinemat.q: The dimensional formula of Planck's constant is
Physical Quantities, Vectors and Kinemat.w: $E = hf$, so $h = E/f = [ML^2T^{-2}]/[T^{-1}] = [ML^2T^{-1}]$, the same as angular momentum. (a) is energy and (d) is power.

Physical Quantities, Vectors and Kinemat.q: The number of significant figures in 0.003060 is
Physical Quantities, Vectors and Kinemat.w: leading zeros do not count; the digits 3, 0, 6 and the final 0 (after the decimal point) do: 4 significant figures.

Physical Quantities, Vectors and Kinemat.q: Which pair of quantities has the same dimensions?
Physical Quantities, Vectors and Kinemat.w: torque ($rF$) and work ($Fs$) are both [ML²T⁻²], though torque is a vector and work a scalar. Power has an extra T⁻¹; strain is dimensionless.

Physical Quantities, Vectors and Kinemat.q: A set of measurements is called precise when
o: its mean equals the true value
it is free of systematic error
it is made with a calibrated instrument
the repeated readings agree closely with one another
Physical Quantities, Vectors and Kinemat.w: precision is the closeness of repeated readings to each other; closeness to the true value is accuracy.

Physical Quantities, Vectors and Kinemat.q: In a vernier calliper, 10 vernier divisions coincide with 9 main-scale divisions of 1 mm each. Its least count is
Physical Quantities, Vectors and Kinemat.w: 1 VSD = 9/10 mm = 0.9 mm, so LC = 1 MSD - 1 VSD = 1 - 0.9 = 0.1 mm.

Physical Quantities, Vectors and Kinemat.q: Which of the following is NOT a vector quantity?
Physical Quantities, Vectors and Kinemat.w: current has a sense of flow but adds algebraically at a junction; it does not obey vector addition, so it is a scalar.

Physical Quantities, Vectors and Kinemat.q: The scalar product of two non-zero vectors is zero when the angle between them is
Physical Quantities, Vectors and Kinemat.w: $\vec A\cdot\vec B = AB\cos\theta = 0$ only for $\theta = 90^{\circ}$. At 180° it is $-AB$, not zero.

Physical Quantities, Vectors and Kinemat.q: At the highest point of its path, a body projected obliquely (no air resistance) has
o: a horizontal velocity and acceleration g downward
zero velocity and acceleration g downward
a horizontal velocity and zero acceleration
Physical Quantities, Vectors and Kinemat.w: only the vertical component vanishes at the top; $u\cos\theta$ remains, and gravity still gives g downward.

Physical Quantities, Vectors and Kinemat.q: For a fixed speed of projection and no air resistance, the horizontal range on level ground is greatest when the angle of projection is
Neglecting air resistance, the path of a body projected obliquely near the Earth's surface is a
Physical Quantities, Vectors and Kinemat.w: uniform horizontal velocity plus uniform vertical acceleration gives $y = x\tan\theta - gx^2/(2u^2\cos^2\theta)$, a parabola.

Physical Quantities, Vectors and Kinemat.q: The dimensional formula of the universal gravitational constant G is
Which of the following is a dimensionless quantity?
Physical Quantities, Vectors and Kinemat.w: strain is change in length / original length, a ratio of two lengths. Stress is [ML⁻¹T⁻²], surface tension [MT⁻²], angular velocity [T⁻¹].

Physical Quantities, Vectors and Kinemat.q: Dimensional analysis CANNOT be used to
o: find the value of a dimensionless constant in a formula
check the consistency of an equation
convert a quantity from one system of units to another
find how a quantity depends on others in a product-of-powers relation
Physical Quantities, Vectors and Kinemat.w: pure numbers such as $\frac{1}{2}$ or $2\pi$ have no dimensions, so they cannot be found; the other three are standard uses.

Physical Quantities, Vectors and Kinemat.q: Two vectors of equal magnitude P have a resultant that is also of magnitude P. The angle between them is
Physical Quantities, Vectors and Kinemat.w: for equal vectors $R = 2P\cos(\theta/2)$; $R = P$ needs $\cos(\theta/2) = \frac{1}{2}$, so $\theta/2 = 60^{\circ}$ and $\theta = 120^{\circ}$.

Physical Quantities, Vectors and Kinemat.q: Derive the time of flight, maximum height and range of a projectile and solve a numerical.
Explain dimensional analysis, its uses and limitations, and combine errors in a measurement.

Dynamics: Force, Momentum, Work, Energy.q: Newton's first law of motion gives the concept of
Dynamics: Force, Momentum, Work, Energy.w: the first law says a body keeps its state unless a net force acts: the property of resisting change is inertia (measured by mass).

Dynamics: Force, Momentum, Work, Energy.q: The SI unit of impulse is
Dynamics: Force, Momentum, Work, Energy.w: impulse = force × time, N s, the same as kg m s⁻¹ (the unit of momentum). N m is the unit of work or torque.

o: act on the same body and cancel each other
are unequal when the bodies accelerate
act on different bodies and never cancel each other
Dynamics: Force, Momentum, Work, Energy.w: the third-law pair acts on two different bodies, so the forces cannot cancel; they are equal at every instant, whatever the motion.

Dynamics: Force, Momentum, Work, Energy.q: A rigid body is in complete (translational and rotational) equilibrium when
o: the net force on it is zero
the net torque on it is zero
both the net force and the net torque on it are zero
Dynamics: Force, Momentum, Work, Energy.w: zero net force gives no linear acceleration; zero net torque gives no angular acceleration. A rigid body needs both.

Dynamics: Force, Momentum, Work, Energy.q: The area under a force–time graph gives

o: both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved
neither momentum nor kinetic energy is conserved
momentum is conserved and the bodies move together afterwards
kinetic energy is conserved but momentum is not
Dynamics: Force, Momentum, Work, Energy.w: momentum is conserved in every collision; in a perfectly inelastic one the bodies stick together and the loss of KE is the greatest.

Dynamics: Force, Momentum, Work, Energy.q: Two equal masses collide head-on elastically, one of them initially at rest. After the collision
o: the moving one rebounds with its own speed
Dynamics: Force, Momentum, Work, Energy.w: with $m_1 = m_2$ and $u_2 = 0$, the formulas give $v_1 = 0$ and $v_2 = u_1$: the velocities are exchanged (as in billiards).

Dynamics: Force, Momentum, Work, Energy.q: The coefficient of static friction $\mu_s$ and the angle of repose $\theta$ are related by
Dynamics: Force, Momentum, Work, Energy.w: at the angle of repose $mg\sin\theta = \mu_s mg\cos\theta$, so $\mu_s = \tan\theta$.

Dynamics: Force, Momentum, Work, Energy.q: For the same normal reaction, limiting friction between two surfaces is independent of
Dynamics: Force, Momentum, Work, Energy.w: the third law of friction: for the same normal reaction, the area of contact does not matter. Friction is proportional to $N$, so (d) is wrong.

Dynamics: Force, Momentum, Work, Energy.q: Compared with the coefficient of static friction, the coefficient of kinetic friction for the same pair of surfaces is
Dynamics: Force, Momentum, Work, Energy.w: $\mu_k < \mu_s$: it takes more force to start sliding than to keep sliding.

Dynamics: Force, Momentum, Work, Energy.q: Ball bearings are used in machines because
o: they increase the area of contact
rolling friction is much smaller than sliding friction
Dynamics: Force, Momentum, Work, Energy.w: bearings replace sliding with rolling, and rolling friction is far smaller; friction is reduced, not removed.

Dynamics: Force, Momentum, Work, Energy.q: The work–energy theorem states that the work done by the net force on a body equals the change in its
Dynamics: Force, Momentum, Work, Energy.w: $W_{net} = \Delta K$. Work by conservative forces alone equals $-\Delta U$, which is a different statement.

Dynamics: Force, Momentum, Work, Energy.q: A man stands on a weighing machine in a lift that falls freely. The machine reads
Dynamics: Force, Momentum, Work, Energy.w: in free fall both the man and the machine accelerate at $g$, so $R = m(g - g) = 0$: apparent weightlessness.

Dynamics: Force, Momentum, Work, Energy.q: Rocket propulsion is an application of
Dynamics: Force, Momentum, Work, Energy.w: the exhaust gases are pushed backward and the rocket gains equal forward momentum (equivalently, Newton's third law); kinetic energy is not conserved.

Dynamics: Force, Momentum, Work, Energy.q: State and prove the law of conservation of linear momentum. Discuss elastic and inelastic collisions with a numerical.
State the work-energy theorem, define power and solve a problem on a moving vehicle.

Rotational Dynamics.q: The moment of inertia of a thin uniform rod of mass M and length L about an axis perpendicular to it through its centre is
The moment of inertia of a thin uniform rod of mass M and length L about an axis perpendicular to it through one end is
Rotational Dynamics.w: $ML^2/12 + M(L/2)^2 = ML^2/3$, four times the value about the centre.

Rotational Dynamics.q: The radius of gyration of a thin uniform rod of length L about a perpendicular axis through its centre is
Rotational Dynamics.w: $k = \sqrt{I/M} = \sqrt{L^2/12} = L/(2\sqrt{3}) \approx 0.29L$. $L/\sqrt{3}$ is the value about an end.

Rotational Dynamics.q: The moment of inertia of a rigid body does NOT depend on
o: the position of the axis of rotation
Rotational Dynamics.w: $I$ depends on the mass, its distribution and the axis; for a rigid body it is the same at any angular velocity.

Rotational Dynamics.q: In rotational motion, the quantity that plays the part of mass is
Rotational Dynamics.w: $I$ resists angular acceleration ($\tau = I\alpha$) as mass resists linear acceleration ($F = ma$).

Rotational Dynamics.q: The dimensional formula of torque is
Rotational Dynamics.w: $\tau = rF$: $[L][MLT^{-2}] = [ML^2T^{-2}]$, the same as work, though torque is a vector.

Rotational Dynamics.q: The SI unit of angular momentum is
Rotational Dynamics.w: $L = I\omega$: kg m² s⁻¹ = (kg m² s⁻²) s = J s. J s⁻¹ is the watt.

Rotational Dynamics.q: The rotational kinetic energy of a body of moment of inertia I and angular velocity ω is
The angular momentum of a system is conserved when
o: the net external torque on it is zero
the net external force on it is zero
its moment of inertia is constant
Rotational Dynamics.w: $\tau_{ext} = dL/dt$, so zero external torque keeps $L$ constant. Zero net force conserves linear momentum.

Rotational Dynamics.q: The rate of change of angular momentum of a body equals
o: the net external torque on it
Rotational Dynamics.w: $\tau = dL/dt$ is the general form of Newton's second law for rotation.

Rotational Dynamics.q: An ice skater spinning on one toe pulls her arms close to her body. Her angular velocity
Rotational Dynamics.w: $I\omega$ stays constant (no external torque about the vertical axis); pulling the arms in lowers $I$, so $\omega$ rises.

Rotational Dynamics.q: A couple acting on a rigid body produces
Rotational Dynamics.w: the two forces of a couple add to zero (no translation) but their torque $Fd$ is not zero.

Rotational Dynamics.q: The radius of gyration of a body about a given axis depends on
o: the distribution of its mass about the axis
Rotational Dynamics.w: $k = \sqrt{I/M}$; the mass cancels, so $k$ depends only on how the mass is spread about the chosen axis.

Rotational Dynamics.q: The relation $L = I\omega$ in rotation corresponds, in linear motion, to
Rotational Dynamics.w: angular momentum $I\omega$ corresponds to linear momentum $mv$.

Rotational Dynamics.q: Define torque, moment of inertia and angular momentum. State the law of conservation of angular momentum with examples and solve a numerical.
State the parallel and perpendicular axis theorems and find the moment of inertia of a disc. Explain rolling motion with a numerical.

Fluid Statics and Dynamics.q: A hydraulic lift works on the principle of
Fluid Statics and Dynamics.w: the pressure applied at the small piston is transmitted undiminished to the large one, so $F_2 = F_1A_2/A_1$.

Fluid Statics and Dynamics.q: The dimensional formula of surface tension is
When the temperature of a liquid rises, its surface tension
Fluid Statics and Dynamics.w: surface tension falls (almost linearly) with temperature and vanishes at the critical temperature.

Fluid Statics and Dynamics.q: The excess pressure inside a soap bubble of radius r made from a solution of surface tension T is
Fluid Statics and Dynamics.w: a soap bubble has two surfaces, so the excess pressure is $2\times2T/r = 4T/r$. $2T/r$ is for a drop or an air bubble inside a liquid.

Fluid Statics and Dynamics.q: The angle of contact between mercury and clean glass is
Fluid Statics and Dynamics.w: about 140°: mercury does not wet glass, its meniscus is convex and it is depressed in a capillary.

Fluid Statics and Dynamics.q: For a given liquid, the height of capillary rise h and the radius r of the tube are related by
Fluid Statics and Dynamics.w: Jurin's law: $h = 2T\cos\theta/(r\rho g)$, so $hr$ is constant.

Fluid Statics and Dynamics.q: The SI unit of the coefficient of viscosity is
Fluid Statics and Dynamics.w: $\eta = F/(A\,dv/dx)$ has unit N s m⁻² = Pa s. The poise is the CGS unit (1 Pa s = 10 poise).

Fluid Statics and Dynamics.q: When a gas is heated, its viscosity
Fluid Statics and Dynamics.w: gas viscosity comes from molecules carrying momentum between layers; faster molecules at higher temperature carry more. Liquids behave oppositely.

Fluid Statics and Dynamics.q: The equation of continuity for fluid flow follows from the conservation of
Fluid Statics and Dynamics.w: what enters a tube per second must leave it: $\rho A_1v_1 = \rho A_2v_2$.

Fluid Statics and Dynamics.q: A venturimeter is used to measure
o: the surface tension of a liquid
the rate of flow of a liquid in a pipe
Fluid Statics and Dynamics.w: the pressure difference between its wide part and its throat gives the flow speed and hence the rate of flow.

Fluid Statics and Dynamics.q: The surface energy per unit area of a liquid surface is numerically equal to its
Fluid Statics and Dynamics.w: surface energy (J m⁻²) and surface tension (N m⁻¹) have the same dimensions and the same numerical value.

Fluid Statics and Dynamics.q: Small free drops of a liquid are spherical because of
Fluid Statics and Dynamics.w: surface tension makes the surface contract to the least area, and a sphere has the least area for its volume.

Fluid Statics and Dynamics.q: Water rises 6 cm in a capillary tube, but only 4 cm of the tube is above the water surface. The water
o: overflows from the top in a fountain
rises to 4 cm and its meniscus becomes flatter
rises to 4 cm and its meniscus becomes more curved
Fluid Statics and Dynamics.w: a capillary never overflows; the water stops at the top and the meniscus radius grows ($hR$ constant), so the meniscus becomes flatter.

Fluid Statics and Dynamics.q: A capillary tube stands in water inside a freely falling lift. The water in the tube
o: rises to the same height as on the ground
rises to half the usual height
rises to fill the whole length of the tube
Fluid Statics and Dynamics.w: in free fall the effective $g$ is zero, so nothing pulls the column down: $h = 2T\cos\theta/(r\rho g)$ grows without limit and the water fills the tube.

Fluid Statics and Dynamics.q: State and derive Bernoulli's theorem. Give its applications and solve a numerical.
Define viscosity and state Stokes' law. Derive the terminal velocity of a sphere falling in a liquid and solve a numerical.

Circular Motion and Simple Harmonic Moti.q: The SI unit of angular velocity is
Circular Motion and Simple Harmonic Moti.w: angle (radian) per second. rad s⁻² is angular acceleration.

Circular Motion and Simple Harmonic Moti.q: For a body in uniform circular motion, the quantity that stays constant is its
Circular Motion and Simple Harmonic Moti.w: the direction of motion changes all the time, so velocity, momentum and the acceleration vector change; only the speed (and KE) stay constant.

o: a pseudo force observed in a rotating frame
the reaction to the centripetal force
a real force that pulls bodies outward
Circular Motion and Simple Harmonic Moti.w: it is a fictitious force felt in a rotating (non-inertial) frame; the centripetal force has no outward "reaction" acting on the same body.

Circular Motion and Simple Harmonic Moti.q: The least speed that a stone on a string of length r must have at the lowest point to complete a vertical circle is
A road is banked at angle θ so that vehicles can turn at speed v on a curve of radius r without needing friction. Then
The greatest speed at which a car can take a level curve of radius r, if the coefficient of friction is μ, is
Circular Motion and Simple Harmonic Moti.w: friction supplies the centripetal force: $\mu mg = mv^2/r$, so $v = \sqrt{\mu rg}$.

Circular Motion and Simple Harmonic Moti.q: In SHM, the speed of the particle is greatest
o: halfway between the mean and an extreme

Circular Motion and Simple Harmonic Moti.q: In SHM, the acceleration of the particle is greatest
o: halfway between the mean and an extreme
Circular Motion and Simple Harmonic Moti.w: $|a| = \omega^2|x|$ is greatest, $A\omega^2$, at $x = \pm A$, where the particle is momentarily at rest.

Circular Motion and Simple Harmonic Moti.q: The period of a simple pendulum of length l is
Circular Motion and Simple Harmonic Moti.w: $T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}$ for small swings. (a) has $l$ and $g$ the wrong way round: $\sqrt{l/g}$ has the unit of time, $\sqrt{g/l}$ of frequency.

Circular Motion and Simple Harmonic Moti.q: The period of a seconds pendulum is
Circular Motion and Simple Harmonic Moti.w: a seconds pendulum takes 1 s for each swing, so its full period is 2 s.

Circular Motion and Simple Harmonic Moti.q: Resonance occurs when the frequency of the driving force
o: equals the natural frequency of the system
Circular Motion and Simple Harmonic Moti.w: at resonance the driver is in step with the natural oscillation and the amplitude is greatest.

Circular Motion and Simple Harmonic Moti.q: In a damped oscillation, with time
Circular Motion and Simple Harmonic Moti.w: resistive forces remove energy, so the amplitude dies away; the frequency changes very little.

Circular Motion and Simple Harmonic Moti.q: A car turns a corner on a level road. The centripetal force on it is provided by
o: the normal reaction of the road
the friction between the tyres and the road
Circular Motion and Simple Harmonic Moti.w: on a level road only static friction acts towards the centre; that is why cars skid on wet or icy bends.

Circular Motion and Simple Harmonic Moti.q: The speed of a body moving in a circle of fixed radius is doubled. The centripetal force needed becomes
Define simple harmonic motion, derive its equations and energy, and find the time period of a spring-mass system and a simple pendulum.
Explain centripetal force, the banking of roads and motion in a vertical circle with numericals.

Gravitation.q: The SI unit of gravitational potential is
Gravitation.w: potential is work per unit mass, J kg⁻¹. N kg⁻¹ is field strength, and N m² kg⁻² is G.

Gravitation.q: The value of the universal gravitational constant in SI units is
Gravitation.w: $G = 6.67\times10^{-11}$ N m² kg⁻². The value 9.8 is $g$ (a local acceleration), and option (b) carries the wrong units for $G$.

Gravitation.q: At a depth $d$ below the Earth's surface, the acceleration due to gravity is
Gravitation.w: only the sphere of radius $R-d$ pulls, giving $g(R-d)/R = g(1-d/R)$. Option (b) is the common error of applying the height formula downwards.

Gravitation.q: The escape velocity from the Earth's surface is about
Gravitation.w: $\sqrt{2gR} = \sqrt{2(9.8)(6.4\times10^6)} = 11.2$ km s⁻¹. 7.9 km s⁻¹ is the orbital speed.

Gravitation.q: The height of a geostationary satellite above the Earth's surface is about
Gravitation.w: the orbital radius is 42,200 km, so the height above the 6400 km radius is about 36,000 km.

Gravitation.q: The SI unit of gravitational field strength is
Gravitation.w: field strength is force per unit mass, N kg⁻¹, numerically equal to m s⁻².

Gravitation.q: Compared with its value at the poles, the value of g at the equator is
Gravitation.w: rotation supplies part of the centripetal acceleration at the equator, and the equatorial radius is larger; both reduce $g$ there.

Gravitation.q: Kepler's third law for satellites states that
Gravitation.w: $T^2 = (4\pi^2/GM)r^3$ for every satellite about the same central mass.

Gravitation.q: The escape velocity of a body from the Earth depends on
o: the mass and radius of the Earth
its mass and direction of projection
Gravitation.w: $v_e = \sqrt{2GM/R}$ contains only the planet's mass and radius; the body's mass cancels and the direction does not enter.

Gravitation.q: The value of g at a height equal to the Earth's radius is
Two satellites of different masses move in the same circular orbit. They have the same
o: kinetic energy and the same speed
Gravitation.w: $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$ has no mass in it, so the speeds are equal; $K = GMm/2r$ is proportional to the satellite's mass, so the kinetic energies differ.

Gravitation.q: Which statement about a satellite in a circular orbit is TRUE?
Gravitation.w: $E = -GMm/2r$ is negative for every bound orbit. $K$ is positive and $U$ is negative, so (a) and (c) are impossible.

Gravitation.q: As a satellite moves from a lower circular orbit to a higher one, its
o: speed and total energy both increase
speed increases and total energy decreases
speed and total energy both decrease
speed decreases and total energy increases
Gravitation.w: $v \propto 1/\sqrt{r}$ falls, while $E = -GMm/2r$ becomes less negative, that is, it rises.

Gravitation.q: The weightlessness felt by an astronaut in an orbiting spacecraft is because
o: there is no gravity beyond the atmosphere
the spacecraft moves at the escape speed
the spacecraft and the astronaut fall together with the same acceleration
Gravitation.w: g at 400 km is still 8.7 m s⁻²; the astronaut floats because both craft and astronaut are in free fall, so the normal reaction vanishes.

Gravitation.q: State Newton's law of gravitation. Derive the variation of $g$ with height and depth and solve a numerical.
Derive the orbital and escape velocities. Describe the geostationary satellite and Kepler's laws.

Elasticity.q: Hooke's law is obeyed up to the
Elasticity.w: the straight part of the stress–strain graph ends at the proportional limit; the elastic limit is slightly beyond it.

Elasticity.q: The dimensional formula of Young's modulus is
Elasticity.w: stress and strain have the same dimensions as pressure: $[ML^{-1}T^{-2}]$.

Elasticity.q: Compressibility is the reciprocal of
Elasticity.w: compressibility $=1/K$; a large bulk modulus means low compressibility.

Elasticity.q: Poisson's ratio is the ratio of
o: change in volume to original volume
Elasticity.w: lateral strain over longitudinal strain, with a minus sign in the definition to make it positive.

Elasticity.q: Poisson's ratio is
Elasticity.w: it is a ratio of two strains, so it is a pure number.

Elasticity.q: The SI unit of energy density is
Elasticity.w: energy per unit volume, J m⁻³, which equals Pa.

Elasticity.q: The slope of the linear part of a stress–strain graph gives
Elasticity.w: slope $=\frac{\text{stress}}{\text{strain}}=Y$ (or the relevant modulus).

Elasticity.q: The ratio of shear stress to shear strain is called
Elasticity.w: shear stress over shear strain is the modulus of rigidity, $G$.

Elasticity.q: For the same stress, a steel wire stretches less than a rubber band because steel has
Elasticity.w: the same stress gives strain $=\text{stress}/Y$; a larger $Y$ means a smaller strain. Steel is "more elastic" in this technical sense.

Elasticity.q: Young's modulus has the same dimensions as
Elasticity.w: $Y$ is stress per unit strain, and strain is dimensionless, so $Y$ has the dimensions of stress, the same as pressure.

Elasticity.q: In F = kx for a spring, k is called the
Elasticity.w: $k$ is the force constant or spring constant, in N m⁻¹.

Elasticity.q: Bulk modulus applies to
Elasticity.w: every state of matter resists a change of volume, so $K$ is defined for solids, liquids and gases.

Elasticity.q: A wire extends by 1 mm under a load of 50 N. Within the elastic limit, the extension under 150 N is
Elasticity.w: Hooke's law gives extension proportional to load: $3\times1 = 3$ mm.

Elasticity.q: Young's modulus of a wire depends on
Elasticity.w: $Y$ is a material constant (temperature aside). Length, diameter and load change the extension, not the modulus.

Elasticity.q: State Hooke's law and explain the stress-strain curve and the three elastic moduli.
Derive the energy stored in a stretched wire, define Poisson's ratio and solve a numerical.

Heat, Temperature and Heat Transfer.q: The SI unit of heat is
Heat, Temperature and Heat Transfer.w: heat is energy, so its unit is the joule. The watt is power and the kelvin is temperature.

Heat, Temperature and Heat Transfer.q: If body A is in thermal equilibrium with B, and B with C, then the zeroth law says
o: A and C are at different temperatures
A and C are in thermal equilibrium
heat flows from A to C
Heat, Temperature and Heat Transfer.w: the zeroth law makes thermal equilibrium transitive, so A and C must be at the same temperature.

Heat, Temperature and Heat Transfer.q: Absolute zero on the Celsius scale is
Heat, Temperature and Heat Transfer.w: absolute zero is 0 K, which is -273.15 °C.

Heat, Temperature and Heat Transfer.q: The ice point of water on the Kelvin scale is
The steam point of water on the Fahrenheit scale is
The range of a clinical thermometer is about
Heat, Temperature and Heat Transfer.w: a clinical thermometer covers only the narrow range of body temperature, 35–42 °C.
mercury solidifies at about -39 °C, which is why it cannot be used in very cold places; -115 °C is alcohol's freezing point.

Heat, Temperature and Heat Transfer.q: A liquid-in-glass thermometer works on the
Heat, Temperature and Heat Transfer.w: the liquid expands more than the glass, so the thread rises; the reading is the apparent expansion.

Heat, Temperature and Heat Transfer.q: A resistance thermometer uses the change of
Heat, Temperature and Heat Transfer.w: $R=R_0(1+\alpha\theta)$; the resistance is the thermometric property.

Heat, Temperature and Heat Transfer.q: A thermocouple thermometer works on the
Heat, Temperature and Heat Transfer.w: two junctions at different temperatures produce an emf by the Seebeck effect.

Heat, Temperature and Heat Transfer.q: A radiation pyrometer measures temperature using the
Heat, Temperature and Heat Transfer.w: the total radiated power depends on $T^4$, so measuring it gives the temperature without contact.

Heat, Temperature and Heat Transfer.q: The SI unit of thermal conductivity is
Heat, Temperature and Heat Transfer.w: from $H=kA\Delta\theta/L$, $k$ has units W m⁻¹ K⁻¹.

Heat, Temperature and Heat Transfer.q: Which of the following is the best conductor of heat?
Heat, Temperature and Heat Transfer.w: silver has the highest thermal conductivity of the four, about 406 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹.

Heat, Temperature and Heat Transfer.q: The absorptivity of a perfect black body is
Heat, Temperature and Heat Transfer.w: a black body absorbs all radiation of every wavelength.

Heat, Temperature and Heat Transfer.q: Explain conduction and thermal conductivity, and solve a problem on a composite rod. Compare conduction, convection and radiation.
State and explain Stefan's law, Wien's law and Newton's law of cooling with numericals.

Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.q: For an isotropic solid, the coefficient of cubical expansion γ is related to the coefficient of linear expansion α by
Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.w: length is one dimension, area two, volume three, so the coefficients go as 1: 2: 3. Option (b) is the area coefficient.

Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.q: The SI unit of the coefficient of linear expansion is
Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.w: α is a fractional change of length per kelvin, so the metre cancels and K⁻¹ is left.

Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.q: A circular hole is cut in a metal plate. When the plate is heated, the diameter of the hole
o: increases only if the hole is at the centre
Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.w: every linear dimension of the plate grows by the fraction αΔT, and the hole is one of them. A hole behaves like a disc of the same metal.

Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.q: A bimetallic strip of brass and iron is heated. Brass has the larger α. The strip bends with
Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.w: brass lengthens more, so it must form the longer (outer) arc. The strip curves towards the metal with the smaller α.

Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.q: Water has its maximum density at
Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.w: between 0 °C and 4 °C water contracts, and above 4 °C it expands; the turning point is the density maximum.

Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.q: The SI unit of specific heat capacity is
Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.w: heat per unit mass per kelvin: J/(kg K).

Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.q: The water equivalent of a calorimeter is
o: the mass of water with the same heat capacity as the calorimeter
the heat capacity of the calorimeter
the mass of water in the calorimeter
Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.w: the water equivalent is a mass of water whose heat capacity equals the calorimeter's. Option (c) is the heat capacity itself, in J K⁻¹.

Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.q: The specific latent heat of fusion of ice is
Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.w: 80 cal g⁻¹ × 4.2 = 336 J g⁻¹ = 3.36 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. The 10⁶ value in (a) is the latent heat of vaporization.

Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.q: The specific latent heat of vaporization of water at 100 °C is about
Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.w: 540 cal g⁻¹ × 4.2 ≈ 2.26 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹, about seven times the latent heat of fusion.

Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.q: The triple point of water is at
Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.w: 273.16 K at 611 Pa. Option (a) is the ordinary melting point at 1 atm.

Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.q: At the triple point of a substance
o: only the solid and liquid phases coexist
only the liquid and vapour phases coexist
all three phases coexist in equilibrium
the substance has no latent heat
Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.w: that is the definition: solid, liquid and vapour in equilibrium at one temperature and pressure.

Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.q: For the same rise in temperature, the cubical expansion is greatest in
Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.w: gases have γ ≈ 3.7 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹, some twenty times a liquid's and a few hundred times a solid's.

Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.q: Newton's law of cooling states that the rate of loss of heat by a body is proportional to
o: the fourth power of its absolute temperature
the square of the excess temperature
its excess temperature over the surroundings
Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.w: the driving difference is the body's temperature minus the surroundings'. Option (b) is Stefan's law, which Newton's law approximates for small excess.

Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.q: The heat capacity of a body is the heat needed to
Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.w: heat capacity is per kelvin for the whole body; per unit mass is the specific heat, option (a).

Thermal Expansion and Quantity of Heat.q: Define the coefficients of linear, area and volume expansion, show that $\alpha:\beta:\gamma = 1:2:3$, and explain the anomalous expansion of water.
State the principle of calorimetry, define specific and latent heats and solve a mixture problem with ice.

Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics.q: The value of the universal gas constant R is
Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics.w: R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Option (b) is Boltzmann's constant and (c) is Avogadro's number.

Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics.q: The pressure of an ideal gas of density ρ is
The number of degrees of freedom of a monatomic gas molecule is
Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics.w: a point atom can move in three independent directions only.

Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics.q: For a monatomic ideal gas, γ = Cp/Cv is
Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics.w: f = 3 gives γ = 1 + 2/3 = 1.67. Option (a) is the diatomic value.

Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics.q: For a diatomic ideal gas at room temperature, γ is about
Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics.w: f = 5 gives γ = 1 + 2/5 = 1.40, which is why air is treated as γ = 1.4.

Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics.q: Taking Q as heat supplied to the gas and W as work done by it, the first law is
Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics.w: heat in = rise in internal energy + work out.

Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics.q: For an ideal gas taken through an isothermal process
Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics.w: the temperature does not change, and for an ideal gas U depends only on T, so ΔU = 0.

Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics.q: In an isobaric process the work done by the gas is
Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics.w: at constant pressure the work is PΔV = nRΔT.

Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics.q: The work done by n moles of gas in a reversible isothermal expansion from V₁ to V₂ is
Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics.w: integrating P = nRT/V over the volume gives nRT ln(V₂/V₁).

Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics.q: The Kelvin–Planck statement of the second law says that no engine can
o: absorb heat from a hot body
reject heat to a cold body
convert all the heat absorbed into work
Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics.w: a cyclic engine must reject some heat to a sink; 100 % conversion is forbidden.

Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics.q: The efficiency of a Carnot engine working between T₁ and T₂ is
Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics.w: η = 1 - T₂/T₁ with absolute temperatures. Option (a) has the ratio upside down.

Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics.q: The coefficient of performance of a refrigerator is
Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics.w: COP is what you get (heat removed) divided by what you pay (work).

Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics.q: The entropy change in a reversible adiabatic process is
Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics.w: Q = 0, so ΔS = Q/T = 0. A reversible adiabatic process is isentropic.

Ideal Gas and Thermodynamics.q: The SI unit of molar heat capacity is
Derive the pressure exerted by an ideal gas on the basis of kinetic theory and find the rms speed and the mean kinetic energy per molecule.
State the first and second laws of thermodynamics, explain the thermodynamic processes and the Carnot engine, and solve a numerical.

Waves and Sound.q: In $y = A\sin(\omega t - kx)$, the quantity $\omega/k$ is the
Waves and Sound.w: $v = \omega/k$; multiplying $\omega$ by $t$ and $k$ by $x$ leaves a phase, and $\omega/k$ has the unit rad s⁻¹ ÷ rad m⁻¹ = m s⁻¹.

Waves and Sound.q: The SI unit of the intensity of a wave is
Waves and Sound.w: intensity is power per unit area, W m⁻². The watt alone is power; J m⁻² is energy per area, not per area per second.

Waves and Sound.q: Sound cannot travel through
Waves and Sound.w: sound is a mechanical wave and needs particles to compress; in vacuum there is nothing to vibrate, so no sound (light still passes).

Waves and Sound.q: A pipe closed at one end can produce
Waves and Sound.w: the closed end forces a node and the open end an antinode, which fits an odd number of quarter-wavelengths: $L = (2n-1)\lambda/4$. Even harmonics would need a node at both ends.

Waves and Sound.q: The loudness level in decibels is defined with the reference intensity
Waves and Sound.w: $I_0 = 10^{-12}$ W m⁻² is the threshold of hearing at 1 kHz, the zero of the dB scale.

Waves and Sound.q: The pitch of a musical note is determined by its
Waves and Sound.w: pitch is the ear's judgement of frequency. Intensity gives loudness and waveform gives quality.

Waves and Sound.q: Laplace corrected Newton's formula by treating the propagation of sound as
Waves and Sound.w: compressions follow too quickly for heat to flow, so $PV^{\gamma}$ is constant and $B = \gamma P$; that raises 280 m s⁻¹ to 331 m s⁻¹.

Waves and Sound.q: For a gas at absolute temperature $T$, the speed of sound is
Waves and Sound.w: $v = \sqrt{\gamma P/\rho}$ and $P = \rho RT/M$ give $v = \sqrt{\gamma RT/M}$. Option (a) omits $\gamma$, which is about 1.4 for air.

Waves and Sound.q: The distance between two consecutive nodes in a stationary wave is
Waves and Sound.w: the displacement repeats every half-wavelength, so nodes are $\lambda/2$ apart; node to antinode is $\lambda/4$.

Waves and Sound.q: Two points on a wave separated by $\lambda/4$ differ in phase by
Waves and Sound.w: a quarter of a wavelength is a quarter of $2\pi$, that is $\pi/2$.

Waves and Sound.q: In a stationary wave
o: the wave travels in one direction
there is no net transfer of energy
Waves and Sound.w: the two travelling waves carry equal energy in opposite directions; energy oscillates between kinetic and elastic forms but does not travel.

Waves and Sound.q: The end correction of a pipe of diameter $d$, open at one end, is about
Waves and Sound.w: the standard value is $e = 0.3d$ (equivalently $0.6r$) for each open end.

Waves and Sound.q: The unit of loudness level is the
Waves and Sound.w: the decibel. The watt is power, the hertz frequency and the pascal pressure.

Waves and Sound.q: A sound wave of frequency 170 Hz travels at 340 m s⁻¹. Its wavelength is
Derive the fundamental frequencies of vibrating air columns in open and closed pipes and of a stretched string.
Explain the Doppler effect and beats, and solve numericals on both.

Ray Optics: Reflection, Refraction and D.q: In the Cartesian sign convention, the focal length of a concave mirror is
Ray Optics: Reflection, Refraction and D.w: a concave mirror has its focus in front of it, on the side from which the light comes, which is the negative direction in the convention.

Ray Optics: Reflection, Refraction and D.q: A convex mirror always forms an image that is
Ray Optics: Reflection, Refraction and D.w: the reflected rays always diverge, so the image is virtual, erect and smaller than the object, lying between the pole and the focus.

Ray Optics: Reflection, Refraction and D.q: An object placed at the centre of curvature of a concave mirror forms its image at
Ray Optics: Reflection, Refraction and D.w: $u = -2f$ gives $v = -2f$: the image is at $C$, real, inverted and the same size.

Ray Optics: Reflection, Refraction and D.q: An object placed at the focus of a concave mirror forms its image at
Ray Optics: Reflection, Refraction and D.w: $u = -f$ gives $1/v = 0$, so $v = \infty$: the reflected rays are parallel.

Ray Optics: Reflection, Refraction and D.q: The critical angle $C$ for a medium of refractive index $\mu$ is given by
Ray Optics: Reflection, Refraction and D.w: at the critical angle the refracted ray grazes the surface, so $r = 90^{\circ}$ and $\mu\sin C = 1\cdot\sin 90^{\circ} = 1$.

Ray Optics: Reflection, Refraction and D.q: Total internal reflection occurs when light travels
o: from a denser to a rarer medium beyond the critical angle
from a rarer to a denser medium
Ray Optics: Reflection, Refraction and D.w: both conditions are needed: denser to rarer, and beyond $C$. At exactly $C$ the ray grazes the surface rather than being reflected.

Ray Optics: Reflection, Refraction and D.q: The apparent depth of a tank of real depth $d$, viewed from above, is
Ray Optics: Reflection, Refraction and D.w: the object appears raised to $d/\mu$. Option (a) would make the tank look deeper, which never happens.

Ray Optics: Reflection, Refraction and D.q: At the angle of minimum deviation, the ray inside the prism is
Ray Optics: Reflection, Refraction and D.w: the symmetrical path at minimum deviation passes parallel to the base of the prism.

Ray Optics: Reflection, Refraction and D.q: The power of a lens is
Ray Optics: Reflection, Refraction and D.w: power is the reciprocal of the focal length in metres, $P = 1/f$.

Ray Optics: Reflection, Refraction and D.q: The SI unit of the power of a lens is the
Ray Optics: Reflection, Refraction and D.w: one dioptre is one reciprocal metre, $\text{D} = \text{m}^{-1}$.

Ray Optics: Reflection, Refraction and D.q: Dispersion of light by a prism occurs because
o: the refractive index depends on wavelength
all colours travel at the same speed in vacuum
Ray Optics: Reflection, Refraction and D.w: $\mu$ varies with $\lambda$, so each colour leaves the prism at a slightly different angle. In vacuum all colours travel at the same speed.

Ray Optics: Reflection, Refraction and D.q: In the spectrum from a glass prism, the colour deviated most is
Ray Optics: Reflection, Refraction and D.w: violet has the shortest wavelength and the largest refractive index, so it is deviated most.

Ray Optics: Reflection, Refraction and D.q: Chromatic aberration is a defect of
Ray Optics: Reflection, Refraction and D.w: refraction depends on wavelength, so lenses disperse; mirrors reflect all wavelengths equally.
an achromatic doublet brings two colours to the same focus, removing chromatic aberration.

Ray Optics: Reflection, Refraction and D.q: Explain refraction, total internal reflection and the optical fibre. Derive the prism formula and solve a numerical.
Derive the lens formula and lens maker's formula, and explain dispersion with a numerical.

Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction a.q: The path difference required for constructive interference is
Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction a.w: constructive interference needs a whole number of wavelengths, $\Delta = n\lambda$; $(2n-1)\lambda/2$ is the destructive condition.

Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction a.q: A path difference of one wavelength corresponds to a phase difference of
Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction a.w: one wavelength is one full cycle, so $\phi = 2\pi\Delta/\lambda = 2\pi$.

Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction a.q: When the whole double-slit apparatus is immersed in water, the fringe width
Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction a.w: in water $\lambda$ falls to $\lambda/\mu$, and $\beta \propto \lambda$, so the fringes get closer together.

Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction a.q: In single-slit diffraction the first minimum occurs where
Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction a.w: pairing the slit into halves gives $\frac{a}{2}\sin\theta = \lambda/2$, hence $a\sin\theta = \lambda$. (a) is the double-slit path-difference condition misapplied.

Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction a.q: The width of the central maximum in single-slit diffraction, on a screen at distance D, is
Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction a.w: the first minimum is at $y = \lambda D/a$, and the central maximum extends symmetrically to both sides, so its full width is $2\lambda D/a$.

Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction a.q: The grating equation for the nth principal maximum is
Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction a.w: the path difference between neighbouring slits is $(a+b)\sin\theta$, set equal to $n\lambda$ for a maximum.

Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction a.q: Malus's law gives the intensity transmitted through an analyser as
Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction a.w: the transmitted amplitude is $a_0\cos\theta$, so the intensity is $I_0\cos^2\theta$.

Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction a.q: Brewster's law states that the polarizing angle satisfies
At the polarizing angle the reflected and refracted rays are
Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction a.w: the two rays are perpendicular at the polarizing angle; this is what allows the dipoles to radiate nothing into the reflected direction.

Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction a.q: Two independent sodium lamps cannot give a sustained interference pattern because
o: their phase difference changes at random
Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction a.w: each atom emits a train of about $10^{-8}$ s with random phase, so the phase difference is not constant.

Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction a.q: For fixed slit separation and screen distance, the fringe width is directly proportional to
Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction a.w: $\beta = \lambda D/d$, so $\beta \propto \lambda$. Frequency is inversely related to wavelength, so (c) is wrong.

Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction a.q: A Polaroid produces plane-polarized light from unpolarized light by
Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction a.w: a Polaroid absorbs the component along its aligned molecules and transmits the perpendicular one: selective absorption.

Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction a.q: In Newton's rings seen in reflected light, the centre of the pattern is
Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction a.w: at the centre the air film has zero thickness, which satisfies the dark condition, so the centre is dark.

Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction a.q: The angular fringe width in Young's double-slit experiment is
Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction a.w: the angle subtended at the slits by one fringe is $\beta/D = \lambda/d$.

Wave Optics: Interference, Diffraction a.q: Describe Young's double-slit experiment and derive the fringe width. State the conditions for sustained interference.
Explain single-slit diffraction, the diffraction grating, and polarisation with Brewster's and Malus' laws.

Current Electricity and Thermoelectricit.q: The drift velocity of free electrons in a metal carrying a steady current is of the order of
Current Electricity and Thermoelectricit.w: the drift speed is a fraction of a millimetre per second, about $10^{-4}$ m s⁻¹; $10^8$ m s⁻¹ is the speed of light and of the signal, not of the electrons.
the law is restricted to constant temperature; heating a filament makes its $I$–$V$ graph curve.

Current Electricity and Thermoelectricit.q: The resistivity of a conductor depends on
Current Electricity and Thermoelectricit.w: $\rho$ is a material property that varies with temperature; it is independent of length, area and shape.

Current Electricity and Thermoelectricit.q: Two resistors $R_1$ and $R_2$ joined in parallel have an equivalent resistance of
Current Electricity and Thermoelectricit.w: $1/R_p = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2$ gives $R_p = R_1R_2/(R_1+R_2)$, which is smaller than either.

Current Electricity and Thermoelectricit.q: Joule's law gives the heat produced in a resistor as
Current Electricity and Thermoelectricit.w: $H = I^2Rt$; the $V^2t/R$ form is equivalent but not offered here.

Current Electricity and Thermoelectricit.q: Kirchhoff's junction rule is a statement of the conservation of
