Current Electricity and Thermoelectricit.w: charge cannot pile up at a junction, so what enters must leave.

Current Electricity and Thermoelectricit.q: A galvanometer is converted into an ammeter by connecting
Current Electricity and Thermoelectricit.w: a shunt in parallel carries most of the current and protects the coil.

Current Electricity and Thermoelectricit.q: A galvanometer is converted into a voltmeter by connecting
Current Electricity and Thermoelectricit.w: a multiplier in series drops most of the voltage.
zero resistance means the ammeter does not alter the current it measures.
infinite resistance means it draws no current and so does not alter the pd.

Current Electricity and Thermoelectricit.q: The Seebeck effect is the production of an emf by
o: a current in a single metal
a temperature difference between junctions of dissimilar metals
Current Electricity and Thermoelectricit.w: the Seebeck emf needs two different metals and a temperature difference between the junctions.

o: absorption or release of heat at a junction carrying current
production of emf from a temperature difference
emission of electrons from a hot surface
Current Electricity and Thermoelectricit.w: the Peltier effect is heat absorbed or released at a junction when current passes; it reverses with the current.

Current Electricity and Thermoelectricit.q: At the neutral temperature of a thermocouple
Current Electricity and Thermoelectricit.w: at the neutral temperature $dE/d\theta = 0$, so the emf is at its peak.

Current Electricity and Thermoelectricit.q: The resistance of a metal wire rises with temperature because
Current Electricity and Thermoelectricit.w: heating increases the lattice vibration, collisions become more frequent, $\tau$ falls and $\rho = m/(ne^2\tau)$ rises.

Current Electricity and Thermoelectricit.q: Derive the relation between current and drift velocity, state Ohm's law and Kirchhoff's laws, and solve circuit numericals.
Describe the Seebeck, Peltier and Thomson effects and the thermoelectric curve of a thermocouple.

Magnetic Field and Magnetic Properties o.q: The magnetic force on a moving charge is zero when the angle between its velocity and the field is
Magnetic Field and Magnetic Properties o.w: $F=qvB\sin\theta$ vanishes when $\theta=0^{\circ}$ (or 180°), i.e. when the velocity is along the field.

Magnetic Field and Magnetic Properties o.q: A charged particle moves in a circle of radius r in a uniform field B. Its radius is
Magnetic Field and Magnetic Properties o.w: $qvB=mv^2/r$ gives $r=mv/qB$. Option (a) is the reciprocal and (c) is dimensionally wrong.

Magnetic Field and Magnetic Properties o.q: Two long parallel wires carry currents in the same direction. They
Magnetic Field and Magnetic Properties o.w: parallel currents attract. It is the opposite of the rule for like charges, which repel.

Magnetic Field and Magnetic Properties o.q: The torque on a coil in a magnetic field is maximum when the plane of the coil is
Magnetic Field and Magnetic Properties o.w: the torque is $NIAB\sin\theta$ with $\theta$ measured from the normal; the plane parallel to the field means the normal is perpendicular, so $\sin\theta=1$.

Magnetic Field and Magnetic Properties o.q: The deflection of a moving-coil galvanometer is proportional to the current because
o: the radial field keeps the torque proportional to the current
the coil has a large moment of inertia
the coil turns at constant speed
Magnetic Field and Magnetic Properties o.w: the radial field keeps $\sin\theta=1$, so $\tau=NIAB$ whatever the coil's angle, and the spring gives $\phi\propto I$.

Magnetic Field and Magnetic Properties o.q: The Hall voltage across a strip of thickness t carrying current I in field B is
Magnetic Field and Magnetic Properties o.w: balancing $qE_H=qv_dB$ and using $I=ne v_d t d$ gives $V_H=BI/net$; the width cancels.

Magnetic Field and Magnetic Properties o.q: The sign of the Hall voltage tells us
o: the sign of the charge carriers
Magnetic Field and Magnetic Properties o.w: electrons and holes are deflected to the same side but have opposite charge, so the polarity of $V_H$ reverses.

Magnetic Field and Magnetic Properties o.q: The susceptibility of a ferromagnetic material is
Magnetic Field and Magnetic Properties o.w: domain alignment gives $\chi$ of order $10^{2}$–$10^{5}$, positive.

Magnetic Field and Magnetic Properties o.q: Curie's law for a paramagnetic material states that its susceptibility is
Magnetic Field and Magnetic Properties o.w: thermal agitation opposes alignment, so $\chi=C/T$: cooling a paramagnet strengthens its response.

Magnetic Field and Magnetic Properties o.q: Above the Curie point, a ferromagnetic material becomes
Magnetic Field and Magnetic Properties o.w: above $T_C$ the domains break up and the material behaves as a paramagnet with $\chi=C/(T-T_C)$.

Magnetic Field and Magnetic Properties o.q: The area of a hysteresis loop represents
o: the energy lost per cycle per unit volume
Magnetic Field and Magnetic Properties o.w: the area is the work done per unit volume per cycle, dissipated as heat.

Magnetic Field and Magnetic Properties o.q: Soft iron is preferred for transformer cores because it has
o: a narrow loop and high permeability
Magnetic Field and Magnetic Properties o.w: a narrow loop means little hysteresis loss each cycle, and high permeability means a strong flux for a small current.

Magnetic Field and Magnetic Properties o.q: Steel is preferred for permanent magnets because it has
Magnetic Field and Magnetic Properties o.w: a large retentivity keeps the magnetism after magnetisation and a large coercivity resists demagnetisation.

Magnetic Field and Magnetic Properties o.q: The magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor is greatest when the conductor is
State the Biot-Savart law. Derive the magnetic field at the centre of a circular coil and inside a solenoid, and the force between two parallel wires.
Derive the motion of a charged particle in a magnetic field, and compare diamagnetic, paramagnetic and ferromagnetic materials.

Electromagnetic Induction and Alternatin.q: The SI unit of magnetic flux is
Electromagnetic Induction and Alternatin.w: the weber is 1 T m². Tesla is flux density, henry is inductance.

Electromagnetic Induction and Alternatin.q: Lenz's law is a consequence of the conservation of
Electromagnetic Induction and Alternatin.w: if the induced current aided the change, energy would be created; the opposition is energy conservation.

Electromagnetic Induction and Alternatin.q: In a transformer the ratio of secondary to primary voltage equals
Electromagnetic Induction and Alternatin.w: the emf per turn is the same in both coils, so $V_s/V_p=N_s/N_p$.
a steady DC gives a steady flux, $d\Phi/dt=0$, and no secondary emf.

Electromagnetic Induction and Alternatin.q: Eddy currents in a transformer core are reduced by
Electromagnetic Induction and Alternatin.w: thin insulated sheets break up the eddy-current loops.

Electromagnetic Induction and Alternatin.q: The SI unit of self-inductance is
The energy stored in an inductor of inductance L carrying current I is
The self-inductance of a solenoid of N turns, area A and length l is
Electromagnetic Induction and Alternatin.w: $L=\mu_0N^2A/l$; the $N^2$ comes from the flux per turn being proportional to $N$ as well.

Electromagnetic Induction and Alternatin.q: The rms value of an alternating current of peak value $i_0$ is
In a purely inductive circuit the current
Electromagnetic Induction and Alternatin.w: in an inductor the voltage leads the current by 90°, so the current lags.

Electromagnetic Induction and Alternatin.q: In a purely capacitive circuit the current
Electromagnetic Induction and Alternatin.w: in a capacitor the current leads the voltage by 90° (the mnemonic ICE).

Electromagnetic Induction and Alternatin.q: At resonance in a series LCR circuit
o: the impedance equals R and the current is maximum
Electromagnetic Induction and Alternatin.w: $X_L$ and $X_C$ cancel, leaving $Z=R$: the smallest impedance and the largest current.

Electromagnetic Induction and Alternatin.q: The resonant frequency of a series LCR circuit is
The average power in an AC circuit is
Electromagnetic Induction and Alternatin.w: only the component of current in phase with the voltage carries power.

Electromagnetic Induction and Alternatin.q: State Faraday's and Lenz's laws, derive the motional emf and explain self- and mutual inductance with the energy stored in an inductor.

Electrostatics and Capacitors.q: The force between two point charges in a medium of dielectric constant $K$, at the same separation, is
Electrostatics and Capacitors.w: the medium's polarisation weakens the force: $F = F_0/K$. $K$ for air is about 1, for water about 80.
$k = 9\times10^9$ N m² C⁻². Option (b) is $\varepsilon_0$ itself, not $1/4\pi\varepsilon_0$.

Electrostatics and Capacitors.q: The electric field at a point is the
o: force on any charge placed there
work done in bringing a unit charge there
force per unit positive charge there
Electrostatics and Capacitors.w: field is force per unit positive charge; a negative charge feels force opposite to $\vec E$.
potential is a scalar; only the field is a vector.

Electrostatics and Capacitors.q: The field due to an infinite plane sheet of charge density $\sigma$ is
Electrostatics and Capacitors.w: one sheet gives $\sigma/2\varepsilon_0$; the $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$ answer is for the field between two opposite plates.

Electrostatics and Capacitors.q: The field at distance $r$ from a long line charge of density $\lambda$ is proportional to
Electrostatics and Capacitors.w: $E = \lambda/(2\pi\varepsilon_0r)$; the $1/r^2$ law belongs to a point charge.

o: charge stored per unit potential difference

Electrostatics and Capacitors.q: The capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor is directly proportional to
Electrostatics and Capacitors.w: $C = \varepsilon_0A/d$: up with area, down with separation.

Electrostatics and Capacitors.q: Capacitors in series all carry the same
Electrostatics and Capacitors.w: the same charge passes through each capacitor in series; the voltages divide.

Electrostatics and Capacitors.q: Capacitors in parallel all have the same
Electrostatics and Capacitors.w: parallel branches share the same potential difference; the charges divide.

Electrostatics and Capacitors.q: The energy stored in a capacitor $C$ at potential difference $V$ is
Electrostatics and Capacitors.w: $U = \frac12CV^2$. Option (a) is the charge, not the energy.

Electrostatics and Capacitors.q: Charge is said to be quantised because it
o: occurs only in whole multiples of $e$
Electrostatics and Capacitors.w: charge comes in packets of $e$; no fraction of $e$ has ever been observed free.

Electrostatics and Capacitors.q: In charging by induction, the conductor acquires a charge
o: opposite in sign to the inducing charge
of the same sign as the inducing charge
Electrostatics and Capacitors.w: induction leaves the opposite charge; the inducing charge is never transferred.

Electrostatics and Capacitors.q: The leaves of a gold-leaf electroscope diverge because
o: they carry like charges and repel
Electrostatics and Capacitors.w: both leaves receive the same sign and repel; the divergence angle grows with charge.

Electrostatics and Capacitors.q: State Coulomb's law and Gauss's law. Find the electric field of a charged sphere and an infinite sheet and solve a numerical.
Derive the capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor, the effect of a dielectric, and the energy stored. Find the equivalent capacitance in series and parallel.

Electrons and Photons.q: Cathode rays are deflected towards the positive plate of an electric field, which shows that they are
Electrons and Photons.w: cathode rays bend towards the positive plate, so they carry negative charge. That is the observation Thomson built on.

Electrons and Photons.q: An electron moving parallel to a uniform electric field is
o: made to move in a circle
Electrons and Photons.w: the force $-e\vec E$ is along the field line for an electron, so the electron accelerates along the field (opposite to $\vec E$); there is no sideways force.

Electrons and Photons.q: An electron moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field follows a path that is a
Electrons and Photons.w: the magnetic force is always perpendicular to $\vec v$, so it acts as a centripetal force and the path is a circle. A helix needs a velocity component along $\vec B$.

Electrons and Photons.q: If the speed of an electron moving perpendicular to a magnetic field is doubled, the radius of its path becomes
Electrons and Photons.w: $r=mv/eB$, so $r\propto v$; twice the speed gives twice the radius, in the same time period.

Electrons and Photons.q: The time period of an electron moving in a uniform magnetic field is independent of its
Electrons and Photons.w: $T=2\pi m/eB$ contains no $v$: fast electrons circle in bigger circles but take the same time.

Electrons and Photons.q: The specific charge $e/m$ of cathode rays measured by Thomson is about
Electrons and Photons.w: $1.76\times10^{11}$ C kg⁻¹, about 1836 times the value for a hydrogen ion. (b) is the electron's mass, not its specific charge.

Electrons and Photons.q: Millikan's oil-drop experiment was designed to measure the
In Millikan's experiment the drop is held stationary so that
o: the viscous drag is zero and $qE=mg$
Electrons and Photons.w: at rest the drop has no viscous drag, so the only forces are $qE$ up and $mg$ down; they balance.

Electrons and Photons.q: The work function of a metal is
o: the maximum kinetic energy of a photoelectron
the energy of an incident photon
the energy needed to ionise a free atom
the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface
Electrons and Photons.w: the work function is a minimum escape energy from the surface, a few eV for metals.

Electrons and Photons.q: Photoelectric emission from a given metal takes place only when the incident light has
o: frequency at least equal to the threshold frequency
Electrons and Photons.w: a single photon must supply at least $\phi$, so $hf\ge\phi$; intensity cannot help.

Electrons and Photons.q: The stopping potential in a photoelectric experiment measures the
o: maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons
Electrons and Photons.w: $eV_0=K_{max}$, so the stopping potential is a direct measure of the fastest electrons' energy.

Electrons and Photons.q: For light of frequency above threshold, the saturation photocurrent depends on the
Electrons and Photons.w: current counts electrons, and the number of electrons follows the number of photons, i.e. the intensity.

Electrons and Photons.q: The threshold wavelength for a metal of work function $\phi$ is
When the intensity of light is increased at a fixed frequency above threshold, the quantity that does NOT change is the
o: maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons
Electrons and Photons.w: $K_{max}=hf-\phi$ depends only on frequency and metal; the other three all grow with intensity.

Electrons and Photons.q: Describe the photoelectric effect, state its laws and explain Einstein's equation. Solve a numerical.
Explain de Broglie's hypothesis, the Davisson-Germer experiment and the dual nature of matter.

Atomic Physics and X-rays.q: Bohr's quantisation condition for the allowed orbits of the hydrogen atom is
Atomic Physics and X-rays.w: the allowed angular momenta are $h/2\pi$, $2h/2\pi$, … so $mvr = nh/2\pi$. Option (a) misses the $2\pi$.

Atomic Physics and X-rays.q: The radius of the $n$th Bohr orbit of hydrogen is proportional to
Atomic Physics and X-rays.w: $r_n = 0.529n^2$ Å, so the radius grows as the square of the quantum number.

Atomic Physics and X-rays.q: The ionisation energy of a hydrogen atom in its ground state is
Atomic Physics and X-rays.w: removing the electron from $n=1$ to $n=\infty$ takes $0-(-13.6) = 13.6$ eV.

Atomic Physics and X-rays.q: The first excitation energy of hydrogen is
Atomic Physics and X-rays.w: the gap from $n=1$ to $n=2$ is $13.6(1-1/4) = 10.2$ eV. The 3.4 eV in (a) is the ionisation energy from $n=2$.

Atomic Physics and X-rays.q: The Lyman series of hydrogen lies in the
Atomic Physics and X-rays.w: every Lyman line ends on $n=1$, and the largest gaps give the shortest wavelengths, in the ultraviolet.

Atomic Physics and X-rays.q: The Balmer series of hydrogen ends on the level
Atomic Physics and X-rays.w: Balmer lines are jumps from higher levels down to $n=2$; that is why the visible hydrogen lines are Balmer lines.

Atomic Physics and X-rays.q: The series of hydrogen that ends on $n = 3$ is the
Atomic Physics and X-rays.w: Paschen lines end on $n=3$ and lie in the infrared.

Atomic Physics and X-rays.q: The series limit of the Balmer series is about
Atomic Physics and X-rays.w: the limit is the jump $\infty \to 2$: $1240/3.4 = 365$ nm. The 656 nm in (c) is Hα, the first line, not the limit.

Atomic Physics and X-rays.q: The value of the Rydberg constant is about
The de Broglie wavelength of a particle of mass $m$ and speed $v$ is
Atomic Physics and X-rays.w: $\lambda = h/p = h/mv$; (b) is the inverse, which would have units of m⁻¹ s.

Atomic Physics and X-rays.q: For an electron accelerated through a potential difference $V$, the de Broglie wavelength is proportional to
In a Coolidge X-ray tube, electrons are produced by
Atomic Physics and X-rays.w: the tungsten filament is heated and electrons boil off it (thermionic emission).

Atomic Physics and X-rays.q: The continuous X-ray spectrum is produced by
o: deceleration of electrons in the target
Atomic Physics and X-rays.w: bremsstrahlung: electrons lose any fraction of their energy on passing near a nucleus.
an inner-shell electron is knocked out, a higher electron falls in, and the fixed energy gap gives a sharp line.

Atomic Physics and X-rays.q: Describe Bohr's model of the hydrogen atom, derive the energy levels and explain the spectral series.
Explain the production of X-rays, the continuous and characteristic spectra, Moseley's law and Bragg's law.

Nuclear Physics and Radioactivity.q: The binding energy of a nucleus equals the
Nuclear Physics and Radioactivity.w: the vanished mass is the binding energy, $E = \Delta m c^2$.

Nuclear Physics and Radioactivity.q: The binding energy per nucleon is maximum for nuclei near
In beta-minus decay, the atomic number
o: is unchanged in value but A falls
Nuclear Physics and Radioactivity.w: a neutron becomes a proton: $Z + 1$, $A$ unchanged.

Nuclear Physics and Radioactivity.q: The mean life of a radioactive nucleus equals
In a nuclear reactor, the moderator serves to
Nuclear Physics and Radioactivity.w: slow (thermal) neutrons fission U-235 best; rods (b-option confusion) absorb.

Nuclear Physics and Radioactivity.q: The Sun's energy comes mainly from
Nuclear Physics and Radioactivity.w: the proton–proton chain fusing H into He at $1.5\times10^7$ K in the core.
high-energy photons emitted by de-exciting nuclei.
gray is absorbed dose; sievert is weighted dose (risk).

Nuclear Physics and Radioactivity.q: The continuous energy spectrum of beta particles is explained by the simultaneous emission of a
Nuclear Physics and Radioactivity.w: the antineutrino (in β⁻) takes a variable share (Pauli's prophecy, confirmed 1956).

Nuclear Physics and Radioactivity.q: Which particle starts the fission of U-235?
Nuclear Physics and Radioactivity.w: a thermal neutron tips U-235 into fission; the 2–3 emitted neutrons sustain the chain.

Nuclear Physics and Radioactivity.q: Isotopes of an element have the same number of
Nuclear Physics and Radioactivity.w: same Z, different N: same element, (nearly) same chemistry.

Nuclear Physics and Radioactivity.q: The half-life of a radioactive isotope can be changed by
o: none of these (it is a nuclear constant)
Nuclear Physics and Radioactivity.w: λ is fixed by the nucleus; ordinary physical/chemical means do not touch it.

Nuclear Physics and Radioactivity.q: Control rods in a reactor are made of materials such as boron or cadmium because they
Nuclear Physics and Radioactivity.w: boron-10 and cadmium greedily capture neutrons, throttling the chain.

Nuclear Physics and Radioactivity.q: Fusing two light nuclei or splitting a heavy one both release energy because both processes move the products
o: to higher BE per nucleon (towards iron)
Nuclear Physics and Radioactivity.w: products sit higher on the BE/$A$ curve; the gain in binding is paid out as energy.

Nuclear Physics and Radioactivity.q: State the law of radioactive decay and derive the relation between half-life, mean life and decay constant. Explain the types of radiation and solve numericals.
Define mass defect and binding energy, and explain nuclear fission and fusion with numericals.

Semiconductors and Logic Gates.q: In a metal at room temperature the conduction band is
o: separated by a gap of 3 eV
Semiconductors and Logic Gates.w: in a metal the highest band is only partly occupied (or two bands overlap), so electrons can move into empty states just above the filled ones. That is why metals conduct well.

Semiconductors and Logic Gates.q: The forbidden energy gap of a typical insulator is
Semiconductors and Logic Gates.w: insulators such as diamond have gaps of several electron volts (diamond about 5.5 eV), far more than thermal energy at room temperature.

Semiconductors and Logic Gates.q: The energy gaps of silicon and germanium are about
Semiconductors and Logic Gates.w: silicon 1.1 eV, germanium 0.7 eV. Germanium's smaller gap is why it conducts more at the same temperature.

Semiconductors and Logic Gates.q: In a p-type semiconductor the majority carriers are
Semiconductors and Logic Gates.w: the trivalent acceptor takes an electron and leaves a hole, so holes dominate in p-type material.

Semiconductors and Logic Gates.q: A pentavalent impurity atom in silicon is called
Semiconductors and Logic Gates.w: a pentavalent atom donates an electron to the conduction band, hence "donor".

Semiconductors and Logic Gates.q: The barrier potential of a silicon p–n junction is about
Semiconductors and Logic Gates.w: 0.7 V for silicon, 0.3 V for germanium. The barrier is set by the material, not by the applied voltage.

Semiconductors and Logic Gates.q: In forward bias the p-side of a diode is connected to the
Semiconductors and Logic Gates.w: forward bias means p to the positive terminal, which lowers the barrier and lets holes and electrons flow towards the junction.

Semiconductors and Logic Gates.q: When a p–n junction is reverse biased, the depletion region
Semiconductors and Logic Gates.w: the applied field adds to the built-in field and pulls majority carriers away, so the depletion layer widens.

Semiconductors and Logic Gates.q: The reverse saturation current of a diode is carried by
Semiconductors and Logic Gates.w: only minority carriers are available to be swept across in reverse bias, so the current is tiny.
one diode blocks one half of each cycle; two (centre tap) or four (bridge) are needed for full-wave.

Semiconductors and Logic Gates.q: A full-wave rectifier is fed with 60 Hz AC. Its output pulses are at
Semiconductors and Logic Gates.w: both halves are used, so there are two pulses per cycle: $2\times60=120$ Hz.

Semiconductors and Logic Gates.q: The Boolean expression for an AND gate is
Semiconductors and Logic Gates.w: AND is logical multiplication, $Y=A\cdot B$; $A+B$ is OR and $\overline{A\cdot B}$ is NAND.

Semiconductors and Logic Gates.q: The output of a NOR gate is 1 when
Semiconductors and Logic Gates.w: NOR is the negation of OR, and OR is 0 only when both inputs are 0, so NOR is 1 only for 00.

Semiconductors and Logic Gates.q: Which of the following is a universal gate?
Semiconductors and Logic Gates.w: NAND (like NOR) can build every other gate, so it is universal; AND, OR and XOR cannot.

Semiconductors and Logic Gates.q: Explain the formation of a p-n junction, its forward and reverse characteristics and its use as a rectifier.
Explain the action of a transistor as an amplifier and the logic gates, showing that NAND is a universal gate.

Particle Physics and Recent Trends.q: The number of quarks in the Standard Model is
Particle Physics and Recent Trends.w: six: up, down, charm, strange, top and bottom, in three generations of two.

Particle Physics and Recent Trends.q: The quark content of a proton is
Particle Physics and Recent Trends.w: two up quarks and one down: $+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{3}=+1$, the proton charge.

Particle Physics and Recent Trends.q: A positron is the antiparticle of
Particle Physics and Recent Trends.w: the positron has the electron's mass and the opposite charge; it is the first antiparticle found (1932).

o: do not feel the strong force
feel the strong force and are made of quarks
Particle Physics and Recent Trends.w: hadrons are the strongly interacting composite particles: baryons and mesons.
three quarks, as in the proton and neutron. A quark–antiquark pair is a meson.
a meson is a quark bound to an antiquark, which is why it has integer charge and baryon number zero.

Particle Physics and Recent Trends.q: The quark content of the $\pi^+$ meson is

Particle Physics and Recent Trends.w: about 70 km s⁻¹ for every megaparsec of distance; the unit must have distance in the denominator.

Particle Physics and Recent Trends.q: The accepted age of the universe is about
Particle Physics and Recent Trends.w: 13.8 billion years from the Planck measurements; 4.6 billion is the age of the Earth.

Particle Physics and Recent Trends.q: A neutron contains three charged quarks, yet it is neutral because
o: the quarks are neutral inside a nucleon
the strong force cancels the charge
Particle Physics and Recent Trends.w: $+\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{3}=0$. The quarks keep their charges; the total is zero, so the neutron is neutral.

Particle Physics and Recent Trends.q: When an electron and a positron annihilate at rest, the products are
Particle Physics and Recent Trends.w: energy $2m_ec^2=1.02$ MeV shared by two photons, emitted back to back so that momentum also balances.

Particle Physics and Recent Trends.q: A single free quark has never been observed because
o: quarks are confined by the strong force
quarks are too light to detect
Particle Physics and Recent Trends.w: the strong force between quarks does not weaken with distance in the usual way; pulling them apart makes new quark pairs instead of freeing one.

Particle Physics and Recent Trends.q: Beta decay, in which a neutron becomes a proton, is caused by the
Particle Physics and Recent Trends.w: the weak force changes quark flavour, turning a down quark into an up quark and emitting a $W^-$; the strong and electromagnetic forces cannot do this.

Particle Physics and Recent Trends.q: Gravity is negligible between two protons because
o: it is enormously weaker than the other forces
Particle Physics and Recent Trends.w: gravity is about $10^{-38}$ of the strong force; between two protons the electrical repulsion is some 36 powers of ten larger than their gravitational attraction.

Particle Physics and Recent Trends.q: Classify the fundamental particles and forces and describe the Standard Model.
Explain the Big Bang theory, the expansion of the universe, Hubble's law and dark matter with a numerical.

Evolutionary Biology.q: The phrase "hot dilute soup" for the primitive sea in which life began was used by
Evolutionary Biology.w: Haldane (1929) called the primitive ocean a "hot dilute soup" of organic molecules; Oparin's word was coacervate.

Evolutionary Biology.q: Which gas was absent from the primitive atmosphere according to the Oparin–Haldane theory?
Evolutionary Biology.w: the primitive atmosphere was reducing: CH₄, NH₃, H₂ and water vapour. Free O₂ came later, from photosynthesis.

Evolutionary Biology.q: Colloidal droplets of proteins and polysaccharides that Oparin regarded as forerunners of cells are called
Evolutionary Biology.w: coacervates are Oparin's; microspheres (option b) are Sidney Fox's proteinoid spheres.

Evolutionary Biology.q: In the Miller–Urey apparatus the electric spark between the electrodes stood for
Evolutionary Biology.w: the spark supplied the energy of lightning; the boiling water stood for the sea and the condenser for rain. (The gases were CH₄: NH₃: H₂ = 2: 2: 1 by pressure.)

Evolutionary Biology.q: The two amino acids found in greatest amount in Miller's original experiment were
Evolutionary Biology.w: glycine and alanine were the most abundant. No sulphur gas was used, so cysteine and methionine (a) could not form.

Evolutionary Biology.q: The swan-necked flask experiment that finally disproved spontaneous generation was performed by
Evolutionary Biology.w: Pasteur's swan-necked flask let air in but trapped dust and microbes in the bend; the broth stayed sterile.

Evolutionary Biology.q: The first living organisms on Earth were most probably
Evolutionary Biology.w: with no O₂ and a "soup" of organic food, the first cells were anaerobic heterotrophs; autotrophs came later.

Evolutionary Biology.q: Which pair consists of analogous organs?
o: flipper of whale and wing of bat
wing of butterfly and wing of sparrow
thorn of Bougainvillea and tendril of Cucurbita
forelimb of horse and arm of man
Evolutionary Biology.w: a butterfly wing is a fold of cuticle, a sparrow wing a feathered forelimb: same function, different origin. The others are homologous.

Evolutionary Biology.q: Which of the following is a vestigial organ in man?
Evolutionary Biology.w: the vermiform appendix is the vestige of a large herbivore caecum. Epiglottis, patella and uvula all work.

Evolutionary Biology.q: The connecting link between Annelida and Arthropoda is
Evolutionary Biology.w: Peripatus has nephridia and unjointed legs (annelid) with tracheae and a haemocoel (arthropod). Limulus is a living fossil, not this link.

Evolutionary Biology.q: Archaeopteryx is regarded as a connecting link between
Evolutionary Biology.w: feathers and wings of a bird with teeth, a long bony tail and clawed fingers of a reptile.

Evolutionary Biology.q: The first one-toed horse in the evolutionary series of the horse was
Evolutionary Biology.w: Pliohippus (Pliocene) was the first one-toed horse; Merychippus still had three toes.

Evolutionary Biology.q: "Ontogeny recapitulates phylogeny" was stated by
Evolutionary Biology.w: Haeckel's biogenetic law (1866). Von Baer said embryos resemble ancestral embryos, not adults.

Evolutionary Biology.q: The serum precipitin test used to show relationships between animals was introduced by
Evolutionary Biology.w: G. H. F. Nuttall (1904) showed anti-human serum reacts most strongly with ape sera.

Evolutionary Biology.q: Describe the Oparin–Haldane theory of the origin of life and the Miller–Urey experiment that supports it.
Describe the evidences of organic evolution (morphological, anatomical, palaeontological, embryological and biochemical).
Compare Lamarckism, Darwinism and Neo-Darwinism and explain how natural selection works.

Animal Diversity and Classification.q: Choanocytes (collar cells) are characteristic of the phylum
Animal Diversity and Classification.w: collar cells with a flagellum line the spongocoel of sponges and drive the water current. Ctenophores have colloblasts, not choanocytes.

Animal Diversity and Classification.q: Venus' flower basket is the common name of
Animal Diversity and Classification.w: Euplectella, a glass sponge with six-rayed siliceous spicules; Hyalonema is the glass-rope sponge.
Physalia is a polymorphic floating hydrozoan colony; Aurelia is the moon jelly, Adamsia a sea anemone.

Animal Diversity and Classification.q: Alternation of a polyp generation with a medusa generation (metagenesis) is seen in
Animal Diversity and Classification.w: Obelia alternates an asexual colonial polyp with a sexual medusa. Hydra and Metridium have no medusa; Pleurobrachia is a ctenophore.

Animal Diversity and Classification.q: The tapeworm whose scolex bears both hooks and suckers, and whose intermediate host is the pig, is
Animal Diversity and Classification.w: T. solium, the pork tapeworm, has an armed scolex; T. saginata (beef) has suckers only.
the filarial worm Wuchereria, carried by Culex, blocks lymph vessels.

Animal Diversity and Classification.q: A pseudocoelom is the body cavity of
Animal Diversity and Classification.w: the roundworm cavity is not lined by mesoderm on the gut side: a pseudocoel. Flatworms are acoelomate.

Animal Diversity and Classification.q: Parapodia are the locomotory organs of
Animal Diversity and Classification.w: Nereis, a polychaete, has paired lateral parapodia with many setae; earthworms have only setae, leeches suckers.

Animal Diversity and Classification.q: Kala-azar, endemic in the Terai of Nepal, is caused by
Animal Diversity and Classification.w: Leishmania donovani, a flagellate spread by the sandfly Phlebotomus. Trypanosoma causes sleeping sickness.

Animal Diversity and Classification.q: The only ciliate known to parasitise man is
Animal Diversity and Classification.w: Balantidium coli causes balantidial dysentery; Nyctotherus lives in the frog's rectum.

Animal Diversity and Classification.q: Book lungs are the respiratory organs of
Animal Diversity and Classification.w: scorpions and spiders breathe by book lungs; insects and millipedes by tracheae, prawns by gills.

Animal Diversity and Classification.q: Two pairs of legs on each trunk segment are found in
Animal Diversity and Classification.w: Julus, a millipede (Diplopoda), has two pairs per segment; Scolopendra, a centipede, has one.

Animal Diversity and Classification.q: A radula is found in most members of
Animal Diversity and Classification.w: the radula is the molluscan rasping tongue; bivalves lack it.
Pinctada; Ostrea is the edible oyster, Teredo the shipworm.

Animal Diversity and Classification.q: Describe the diagnostic features of the phyla Porifera, Cnidaria, Platyhelminthes and Aschelminthes, with examples.
Describe the features of the phyla Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca and Echinodermata, with examples.
Classify the phylum Chordata up to classes, giving the main features and examples of each.

Animal Tissues and Histology.q: The inner lining of blood vessels (endothelium) is made of
Animal Tissues and Histology.w: thin, flat cells allow exchange across capillary walls; cuboidal and columnar epithelia are too thick.

Animal Tissues and Histology.q: The urinary bladder is lined by
Animal Tissues and Histology.w: transitional epithelium stretches as the bladder fills; keratinised epithelium is confined to the skin.
the "respiratory epithelium": cells of different heights with cilia and goblet cells, all on one basement membrane.
the whole sebaceous cell breaks down to form sebum.

Animal Tissues and Histology.q: Mammary glands are an example of
Animal Tissues and Histology.w: the tip of the secreting cell pinches off with the milk fat; sebaceous glands are holocrine.

Animal Tissues and Histology.q: The most abundant cell of areolar connective tissue is the
Animal Tissues and Histology.w: fibroblasts secrete the fibres and matrix and outnumber every other cell type.

Animal Tissues and Histology.q: Heparin and histamine are secreted in connective tissue by
Animal Tissues and Histology.w: mast cells (like basophils) release heparin (anticoagulant) and histamine (inflammation).
tendons of dense white collagen fibres join muscle to bone; ligaments join bone to bone.

Animal Tissues and Histology.q: The pinna and the epiglottis are supported by
Animal Tissues and Histology.w: elastic fibres let the pinna and epiglottis bend and spring back.

Animal Tissues and Histology.q: The intervertebral discs are made of
Animal Tissues and Histology.w: collagen bundles make fibrocartilage the strongest cartilage, fit for the discs and pubic symphysis.
each Haversian system (osteon) of compact bone has a central canal with blood vessels; cartilage is avascular.
osteoblasts build bone; osteoclasts resorb it.

Animal Tissues and Histology.q: The protein of the bone matrix is
Animal Tissues and Histology.w: ossein (collagen) is the organic part of bone matrix; chondrin belongs to cartilage.

Animal Tissues and Histology.q: The most numerous white blood cells in human blood are
Animal Tissues and Histology.w: neutrophils are 60–65 % of WBCs; lymphocytes come second at 20–25 %.

Animal Tissues and Histology.q: Describe the structure, location and functions of the different types of epithelial and connective tissue.
Describe the muscular and nervous tissues of the human body, with a comparison of the three muscle types.

Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.q: The stage of Plasmodium that infects man is the
Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.w: sporozoites from the mosquito's salivary glands are injected with saliva. Gametocytes infect the mosquito, not man.

Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.q: The toxic pigment released when infected red blood cells burst is
Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.w: haemozoin, the residue of digested haemoglobin; haemocyanin is the copper pigment of molluscs.

Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.q: Benign tertian malaria is caused by
Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.w: P. vivax, 48-hour cycle, rarely fatal; P. falciparum causes the malignant form.

Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.q: Malarial fever recurring every 72 hours is caused by
Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.w: the 72-hour erythrocytic cycle of P. malariae gives quartan fever (every fourth day).

Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.q: Cerebral malaria and blackwater fever are complications of infection with
Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.w: sticky falciparum-infected RBCs block brain capillaries, and massive haemolysis darkens the urine.

Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.q: The oocysts of Plasmodium are formed on the
Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.w: the ookinete crosses the stomach wall and encysts on its outer surface; sporozoites later move to the salivary glands.

Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.q: The malarial parasite was first seen in human blood in 1880 by
Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.w: Laveran (1880); Ross (1897) found the oocysts in the mosquito.

Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.q: In the life cycle of Plasmodium the diploid stage is the
Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.w: the zygote (with the ookinete it becomes) is diploid; meiosis in the oocyst makes every later stage haploid.

Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.q: In Pheretima posthuma the clitellum occupies segments
Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.w: segments 14, 15 and 16 form the glandular clitellum, which has no setae.

Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.q: The female genital pore of Pheretima lies on segment
Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.w: a single mid-ventral female pore on segment 14, in front of the male pores.

Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.q: The male genital pores of Pheretima lie on segment
Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.w: one pair of male pores on segment 18, with genital papillae on 17 and 19.

Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.q: The spermathecal pores of Pheretima are
Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.w: four pairs, ventro-lateral, in the grooves between segments 5/6, 6/7, 7/8 and 8/9.

Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.q: The gizzard of the earthworm lies in segments
Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.w: the muscular grinding gizzard is in segments 8–9; the stomach follows in 9–14.

Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.q: The calciferous glands of the earthworm neutralise
Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.w: the CaCO₃ they secrete neutralises the humic acid of decaying leaves in the soil.

Plasmodium, Earthworm and Frog.q: Describe the life cycle of Plasmodium vivax and the types of malaria.
Describe the external features, body systems and economic importance of the earthworm (Pheretima).
Describe the external features and the digestive, respiratory, circulatory and excretory systems of the frog (Rana tigrina).

Digestive System.q: The pH of gastric juice is about
Digestive System.w: a fed stomach is at pH 1.5–2.5. 6.8 is saliva, 7.8–8.2 intestinal juice and 8.0–8.3 pancreatic juice.

Digestive System.q: The enzyme that converts trypsinogen into trypsin is
Digestive System.w: enterokinase (enteropeptidase) of the duodenal mucosa is the only activator of trypsinogen; trypsin then activates the other zymogens.

Digestive System.q: Bile is stored and concentrated in the
Digestive System.w: the gall bladder stores bile and concentrates it 5–10 times; the liver makes it.

Digestive System.q: Bile helps the digestion of fat by
Digestive System.w: bile salts lower surface tension and break fat into droplets, raising the area for lipase. Bile has no lipase, so (a) is wrong.

Digestive System.q: The largest gland of the human body is the
Digestive System.w: the liver, about 1.5 kg; the pancreas is a mixed gland but smaller.

Digestive System.q: Intrinsic factor, needed for the absorption of vitamin B₁₂, comes from
Digestive System.w: parietal cells. Without intrinsic factor, B₁₂ is not absorbed in the ileum and pernicious anaemia follows.

Digestive System.q: Digested fat is absorbed from the villus into the
Digestive System.w: fatty acids are rebuilt into triglycerides and packed as chylomicrons, which are too large for a capillary and enter the lacteal.

Digestive System.q: The duodenal hormone released by acid chyme is
Digestive System.w: secretin, from S cells, when duodenal pH falls below about 4.5; it drives bicarbonate secretion.

o: G cells of the pyloric antrum
Digestive System.w: G cells of the pyloric antrum. S cells make secretin, I cells cholecystokinin.

o: secretion of bicarbonate by the pancreas
secretion of HCl by the stomach
Digestive System.w: CCK contracts the gall bladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi; bicarbonate is secretin's job.

Digestive System.q: The milk-curdling enzyme of the infant's stomach is
Digestive System.w: rennin (chymosin) converts casein to calcium paracaseinate. Adults have little of it.

Digestive System.q: Most of the absorption of digested food occurs in the
Digestive System.w: the ileum, the longest part of the small intestine, with the greatest number of villi.

Digestive System.q: The optimum pH for pepsin is about
Digestive System.w: pepsin is a strongly acid protease, optimum pH 1.5–2; it is inactive at neutrality.

Digestive System.q: Bile pigments are formed from the breakdown of
Digestive System.w: haemoglobin is broken down to haem and globin; haem gives biliverdin and bilirubin.

Digestive System.q: Describe the human alimentary canal and the digestive glands with their functions.
Describe the digestion and absorption of carbohydrates, proteins and fats in the human body.

Respiratory System.q: The right lung of man has
Respiratory System.w: the right lung has upper, middle and lower lobes; the left has two, with a cardiac notch.
pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells; the cilia sweep the mucus upwards.
type II (septal) cells. Type I cells are the flat cells that form the exchange surface.

Respiratory System.q: The C-shaped rings of the trachea are made of
Respiratory System.w: hyaline cartilage, incomplete at the back so that the oesophagus can bulge into the trachea.

Respiratory System.q: The tidal volume of a resting adult is about
Respiratory System.w: 500 mL per quiet breath. 1100 mL is the expiratory reserve and 3000 mL the inspiratory reserve.

Respiratory System.q: The residual volume of the lungs is about
Respiratory System.w: about 1200 mL stays in the lungs and cannot be breathed out, so a spirometer cannot measure it.
VC = TV + IRV + ERV = 4600 mL. It never includes the residual volume.

Respiratory System.q: The diaphragm is supplied by the
Respiratory System.w: the phrenic nerve, from spinal roots C3–C5.
it contracts and flattens, increasing the vertical diameter of the thorax.

Respiratory System.q: Most of the oxygen in blood is carried
Respiratory System.w: about 97 % as oxyhaemoglobin; only 3 % is dissolved.

Respiratory System.q: Most of the carbon dioxide in blood is carried as
Respiratory System.w: about 70 % as bicarbonate, 23 % as carbamino compounds and 7 % dissolved.

Respiratory System.q: The respiratory centre is situated in the
Respiratory System.w: the medulla oblongata; the pons only modifies the rhythm.

Respiratory System.q: The chief stimulus to the respiratory centre is a rise in
Respiratory System.w: a small rise in CO₂ raises H⁺ and drives ventilation; a fall in O₂ matters only below about 60 mmHg.

Respiratory System.q: Carbonic anhydrase, which speeds up the formation of bicarbonate, is found in the
Respiratory System.w: inside the red cell, which is why the chloride shift is needed to balance the charge.

Respiratory System.q: Describe the human respiratory organs and the mechanism of breathing, with the lung volumes.
Explain how gases are exchanged and transported in the blood and how breathing is regulated.

Circulatory System.q: The pacemaker of the human heart is the
Circulatory System.w: the SA node, in the wall of the right atrium, depolarises fastest and so sets the rhythm.

Circulatory System.q: The left atrioventricular valve is also called the
Circulatory System.w: the bicuspid or mitral valve, on the left side; the tricuspid is on the right.

Circulatory System.q: The heart is enclosed in a sac called the
Circulatory System.w: the pericardium, with fibrous and serous layers and a film of fluid between them.

Circulatory System.q: At 75 beats per minute, one cardiac cycle lasts
Circulatory System.w: 0.8 s, made up of atrial systole 0.1 s, ventricular systole 0.3 s and diastole 0.5 s.

Circulatory System.q: The P wave of an ECG represents
Circulatory System.w: atrial depolarisation, which just precedes atrial systole.

Circulatory System.q: The QRS complex of an ECG represents
Circulatory System.w: ventricular depolarisation. Atrial repolarisation is hidden inside the same complex.

Circulatory System.q: The T wave of an ECG represents
Circulatory System.w: ventricular repolarisation; the ventricles recover before the next beat.

Circulatory System.q: The impulse is delayed on its way from the atria to the ventricles at the
Circulatory System.w: the AV node conducts at only 0.05 m s⁻¹, giving a delay of about 0.1 s.

Circulatory System.q: The normal blood pressure of a young adult is
Circulatory System.w: 120/80 mmHg. 140/90 is the threshold for hypertension.

Circulatory System.q: Blood pressure is measured with a
Circulatory System.w: the sphygmomanometer, with a cuff and a mercury or digital gauge.

Circulatory System.q: The universal donor for red cells is
Circulatory System.w: O negative red cells carry no A, B or D antigen, so no recipient has antibodies against them.

Circulatory System.q: The universal recipient of blood is
Circulatory System.w: AB positive plasma has no anti-A, anti-B or anti-D.

Circulatory System.q: Rh incompatibility between mother and fetus causes
Circulatory System.w: anti-D from a sensitised Rh-negative mother destroys fetal red cells.

Circulatory System.q: The most numerous formed element of blood is the
Circulatory System.w: about 5 million red cells per mm³, against 4000–11 000 white cells.

Circulatory System.q: Describe the structure of the human heart and explain the cardiac cycle and cardiac output.
Compare arteries, veins and capillaries; explain blood pressure and the common cardiovascular disorders.
Describe the composition and functions of blood and the ABO and Rh blood groups.

Excretory System.q: The structural and functional unit of the kidney is the
Excretory System.w: the nephron is the functional unit; the renal corpuscle (b) is only its first part, the glomerulus plus Bowman's capsule.
Bowman's capsule is the cup-shaped beginning of the tubule; the glomerulus is the capillary tuft inside it.

Excretory System.q: Which part of the nephron is freely permeable to water but not to solutes?
o: descending limb of the loop of Henle
ascending limb of the loop of Henle
Excretory System.w: the descending limb has aquaporins but no solute carriers, so only water leaves. The ascending limb (b) is the opposite.

Excretory System.q: The greatest part of the reabsorption of the filtrate takes place in the
Excretory System.w: the PCT recovers 65–70 % of the filtrate because of its brush border and dense mitochondria.

Excretory System.q: Glucose is reabsorbed from the filtrate by
Excretory System.w: glucose is moved by secondary active transport with Na⁺ (SGLT) in the PCT; it is never reabsorbed by diffusion alone.

Excretory System.q: Glucose first appears in the urine when its plasma concentration exceeds about
Excretory System.w: the renal threshold is about 180 mg/dL; above it the carriers are saturated and glucose spills into the urine.

Excretory System.q: Antidiuretic hormone is released from the
Excretory System.w: ADH is made in the hypothalamus but released from the posterior pituitary, which stores it.

Excretory System.q: ADH makes the collecting duct more permeable to
Excretory System.w: ADH inserts aquaporin-2 channels, so water is reabsorbed and the urine becomes concentrated.

Excretory System.q: A person who passes 15–20 litres of dilute urine a day most probably lacks
Excretory System.w: 15–20 L of dilute urine is the classic picture of diabetes insipidus, an ADH deficiency.
aldosterone comes from the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex; the medulla (a) makes adrenaline.
the juxtaglomerular cells of the afferent arteriole store and release renin.

Excretory System.q: Angiotensin I is converted to angiotensin II mainly in the
Excretory System.w: angiotensin-converting enzyme sits on the endothelium of the lung capillaries.

Excretory System.q: Atrial natriuretic peptide is secreted by
Excretory System.w: ANP is released by atrial muscle cells when they are stretched by a rise in blood volume.

Excretory System.q: The normal daily volume of urine in an adult is about
Excretory System.w: 1–2 L a day, about 1 % of the filtrate; 15 L (a) suggests diabetes insipidus.

Excretory System.q: Describe the human excretory organs and the structure of a nephron.
Explain the formation of urine and its regulation, and describe the common renal disorders.

Nervous System and Sense Organs.q: The structural and functional unit of the nervous system is the
Nervous System and Sense Organs.w: A neuron integrates and conducts the nervous signal; axon is only one part of it.

Nervous System and Sense Organs.q: The central nervous system consists of the
Nervous System and Sense Organs.w: The CNS is the brain and spinal cord; nerves and most ganglia belong to the PNS.

Nervous System and Sense Organs.q: The number of pairs of human spinal nerves is
Nervous System and Sense Organs.w: There are 31 spinal pairs: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 1 coccygeal.

Nervous System and Sense Organs.q: Cerebrospinal fluid is produced mainly by the
Nervous System and Sense Organs.w: Choroid plexuses in the ventricles secrete most cerebrospinal fluid.

Nervous System and Sense Organs.q: The principal respiratory and cardiovascular centres are located in the
Nervous System and Sense Organs.w: The medulla contains cardiac, vasomotor and respiratory centres.

Nervous System and Sense Organs.q: Balance, posture and fine coordination are controlled chiefly by the
Nervous System and Sense Organs.w: The cerebellum coordinates movement and maintains posture and balance.

Nervous System and Sense Organs.q: Hunger, thirst and body temperature are regulated mainly by the
Nervous System and Sense Organs.w: The hypothalamus is the principal homeostatic and autonomic integrating centre.

Nervous System and Sense Organs.q: The primary visual cortex is located in the
Nervous System and Sense Organs.w: Visual cortex lies mainly in the occipital lobe.
Corpus callosum fibres interconnect corresponding regions of the cerebral hemispheres.

Nervous System and Sense Organs.q: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons arise from the
Nervous System and Sense Organs.w: Sympathetic outflow leaves the thoracic and upper lumbar spinal cord.
Acetylcholine is the usual parasympathetic postganglionic transmitter.

Nervous System and Sense Organs.q: The normal resting potential of a neuron is about
Nervous System and Sense Organs.w: The inside of a resting neuron is about 70 mV negative to the outside.

Nervous System and Sense Organs.q: Rapid depolarisation of an axon is caused mainly by
Nervous System and Sense Organs.w: Opening voltage-gated sodium channels produces rapid Na⁺ entry and depolarisation.

Nervous System and Sense Organs.q: Myelin around a peripheral nerve fibre is produced by
Nervous System and Sense Organs.w: Schwann cells myelinate peripheral axons; oligodendrocytes do so in the CNS.

Nervous System and Sense Organs.q: Describe the central, peripheral and autonomic nervous systems of man.
Explain the generation and conduction of a nerve impulse and the working of a synapse.
Describe the structure and working of the human eye and ear.

Endocrine System.q: Endocrine glands release their secretions directly into the
Endocrine System.w: Endocrine glands are ductless and deliver hormones to blood.

Endocrine System.q: The gland traditionally called the master gland is the
Endocrine System.w: The pituitary controls several other endocrine glands, although the hypothalamus controls it.

Endocrine System.q: Growth hormone is secreted by the
Endocrine System.w: Somatotroph cells of the anterior pituitary secrete growth hormone.

Endocrine System.q: Milk production by mammary glands is stimulated mainly by
Endocrine System.w: Prolactin stimulates milk production; oxytocin causes milk ejection.

Endocrine System.q: The hormone that increases water reabsorption in collecting ducts is
Endocrine System.w: ADH inserts water channels and increases collecting-duct water reabsorption.

Endocrine System.q: Uterine contraction during labour and milk ejection are promoted by
Endocrine System.w: Oxytocin contracts uterine and mammary myoepithelial smooth muscle.

Endocrine System.q: Iodine is essential for synthesis of
Endocrine System.w: Thyroxine/T₄ contains four iodine atoms and requires dietary iodide.
Calcitonin from thyroid C cells lowers blood calcium.
The four parathyroid glands secrete PTH.

Endocrine System.q: Aldosterone is produced mainly by the
Endocrine System.w: Aldosterone is the mineralocorticoid of the zona glomerulosa.

Endocrine System.q: The principal glucocorticoid of humans is
Endocrine System.w: Cortisol is the main human glucocorticoid.
Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla secrete adrenaline and noradrenaline.

Endocrine System.q: Insulin is secreted by which islet cells?
Glucagon increases blood glucose mainly by acting on the
Endocrine System.w: Glucagon stimulates hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

Endocrine System.q: Describe the endocrine glands of man, their hormones and functions.
Describe the common disorders caused by hormone imbalance and the feedback control of hormones.

Reproductive System.q: The primary male reproductive organs are the
Reproductive System.w: Testes are the male gonads producing sperm and testosterone.

Reproductive System.q: Developing germ cells are nourished and supported by
Reproductive System.w: Sertoli cells are the nurse/support cells of the tubule.
Interstitial Leydig cells secrete testosterone under LH.

Reproductive System.q: Spermatozoa mature and are stored mainly in the
Reproductive System.w: The epididymis is the main site of sperm maturation and storage.

Reproductive System.q: Most fructose in human semen is supplied by the
Reproductive System.w: Seminal-vesicle fluid is rich in fructose.

Reproductive System.q: Enzymes that help a sperm penetrate oocyte coverings are stored in the
Reproductive System.w: The acrosome contains enzymes used in the acrosome reaction.

Reproductive System.q: Mitochondria supplying ATP for sperm movement are concentrated in the

Reproductive System.w: Ovaries produce oocytes and female sex steroids.

Reproductive System.q: Fertilisation in humans normally occurs in the
Reproductive System.w: The ampulla of the uterine tube is the normal fertilisation site.

Reproductive System.q: The blastocyst normally implants in the
Reproductive System.w: Implantation occurs in the secretory endometrium.

Reproductive System.q: The thick muscular layer of the uterus is the
Reproductive System.w: Myometrium is the smooth-muscle coat of the uterus.
Continuous spermatogenesis starts with pubertal gonadotropin activation.
Two meiotic divisions and spermiogenesis yield four sperm.

Reproductive System.q: Describe the male and female reproductive systems of man.
Describe spermatogenesis and oogenesis and compare them.
Describe the ovarian and menstrual cycles and their hormonal control.

p: Define tidal hypothesis. Explain the mountain building process focussing on the evolution of the Himalaya.
Paper 2081 Chaitra ENCE 102.r: Tidal hypothesis. The tidal (encounter) hypothesis for the origin of the planets was proposed by James Jeans (1919) and Harold Jeffreys (1929). It says that the Sun was once a lone star; a much larger passing star came very close, and its gravitational (tidal) pull drew a long, cigar-shaped filament of hot gas out of the Sun. The filament, thicker in the middle, broke up into blobs that condensed into the planets (the largest Jupiter and Saturn from the centre of the filament, the small Mercury and Pluto from its ends), and the intruder went away. The satellites formed from smaller tidal pulls of the planets.

Paper 2081 Baishakh CE 103.r: Quick lime (calcium oxide, CaO). It is the product obtained by burning (calcining) pure limestone at 900–1000 °C, $\text{CaCO}_3\rightarrow\text{CaO}+\text{CO}_2$. Properties: white, porous lumps; combines violently with water (slaking) with large heat and a volume increase of 2 to 2.5 times, $\text{CaO}+\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightarrow\text{Ca(OH)}_2+\text{heat}$; absorbs moisture and CO$_2$ from air and air-slakes into powder; caustic. Uses: for making hydrated lime and lime putty, in lime mortar and lime-sand bricks, whitewash, as a flux in steel making, soil stabilisation and water softening. It is not used directly in masonry, because it must be slaked first.

Paper 2081 Baishakh CE 103.r: Importance of steel. Steel (iron with up to about 1.5 % carbon) is the most important engineering metal because it has high strength in both tension and compression, is ductile and tough, can be rolled into sections of any shape (I-beams, angles, channels, bars, plates), can be welded, bolted and riveted, has a high strength-to-weight ratio (long spans, tall buildings), is produced in a factory with uniform quality, allows fast erection and is fully recyclable. It is used for reinforcement of concrete, structural frames, bridges, roofing, pipes, tanks and machinery. Its drawbacks are corrosion and loss of strength at high temperature (it must be painted and fire proofed).

p: Explain briefly the manufacturing of cement by WET PROCESS with its flow diagram. In what conditions it is considered a better process than the dry process?
Paper 2081 Kartik CE 103.r: Wet process of manufacture of cement. In the wet process the raw materials are made into a slurry with water. Steps: 1. Raw materials are limestone (calcareous: about 75 to 80 %) and clay (argillaceous: about 20 to 25 %). 2. Crushing and mixing with water. Limestone is crushed in crushers to small pieces; clay is washed in a wash mill with water to form a slurry. Both are ground in a ball or tube mill into a fine slurry containing 35 to 50 % water. 3. Blending in slurry tanks. The slurry is stored in tanks, the lime content is tested and corrected by adding clay or limestone, and the mix is kept homogeneous by compressed air or agitators. 4. Burning in the rotary kiln.

Proportion: select the cement: sand ratio for the work (1:3 to 1:4 for plastering and foundations, 1:4 to 1:6 for superstructure walls), measured by volume in boxes. 2. Materials: use fresh cement (not lumpy), clean, sharp, well graded sand free from silt, clay and organic matter, and clean potable water (no oil, acid, alkali or salt). 3. Mixing: mix dry sand and cement to a uniform colour, then add water and mix to the right workability. Water-cement ratio about 0.4 to 0.5 (just enough to be workable); avoid too much water. 4. Use within time: mortar must be used within 30 minutes of adding water (the initial setting time);

p: Explain in brief about the storage and handling of fat lime.
Paper 2081 Chaitra ENCE 103.r: Fat lime (high calcium lime) is made by burning almost pure limestone; the quicklime produced is slaked to give a smooth, white, rich paste. Storage and handling follow its behaviour with moisture, CO$_2$ and heat. Storage - Quicklime must be kept dry: it absorbs moisture and CO$_2$ and air-slakes into a useless powder. Store in lumps in a dry, closed, well-roofed shed with a raised plank or concrete floor and thick walls, away from rain and from combustible materials, and use it as soon as possible. Powdered quicklime and hydrated lime are stored in air-tight bags or drums, in a dry place.

p: Define wet weather and dry weather flow in sewer system.
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENCE 305.r: - Dry weather flow (DWF): the flow in a sewer in the absence of the rainfall (or the 7 days after the rain): the domestic sewage + industrial / commercial wastewater + the ground water infiltration. It is the base load used to design the treatment plant and to check the minimum velocity. - Wet weather flow (WWF): the flow during and just after the rain: the DWF plus the storm-water runoff (in a combined sewer) or the inflow and the extra infiltration through the manholes, the cracks and the illegal connections (in a separate sewer). It is many times larger than the DWF, and the combined sewers are designed for it (storm regulators pass the excess, above about 6 × DWF, to the stream).

Hence it is used because it - prevents the surcharge and the flooding of the downstream sewer and of the treatment plant, so the size and the cost of the downstream sewer and the plant are much reduced (they are designed for about 6 DWF, not the full storm flow);

p: What does the Big-Omega notation determine in an algorithm analysis? Explain divide and conquer approach of an algorithm.
Paper 2083 Baishakh ENCT 252.r: Big-Omega notation gives an asymptotic lower bound on the growth of a function (the running time of an algorithm). $f(n) = \Omega(g(n))$ means that there exist constants $c > 0$ and $n_0$ such that $$\begin{gathered}f(n) \ge c \cdot g(n) \\ \text{for all } n \ge n_0\end{gathered}$$ So the algorithm needs at least about $g(n)$ steps for large inputs; $\Omega$ is used to state the best-case time or to prove that a problem cannot be solved faster than a given rate. Example: $f(n) = 3n^{2} + 2n$ is $\Omega(n^{2})$ because $3n^{2} + 2n \ge 3n^{2}$ for all $n \ge 1$ ($c = 3$, $n_0 = 1$).

Paper 2082 Chaitra ENEE 306.r: (a) Factors in selecting the length of air gap of an induction motor The air gap is much smaller than in other machines, because the whole magnetising current comes from the stator supply. The gap length $l_g$ is a compromise between several factors: 1. Power factor. The magnetising MMF is mostly spent in the gap, so $I_m \propto B\,l_g\,k_g$. A small gap gives a small magnetising current and therefore a high power factor. This is the main reason the gap is made as short as possible. 2. Overload capacity. The leakage reactance (differential/zig-zag leakage) falls with a smaller gap, so the maximum torque (pull-out) and overload capacity increase. 3. Cooling.

A filter is a circuit (or system) that passes signals of some frequencies with little loss (the passband) and rejects or strongly attenuates signals of other frequencies (the stopband). Its behaviour is described by the transfer function $H(s)$ or the magnitude response $|H(j\omega)|$. p: What are the characteristics of Butterworth low pass approximation?
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENEX 301.r: Characteristics of the Butterworth low-pass approximation The magnitude-squared function of an $N$th order Butterworth low-pass filter is $$|H(j\omega)|^2 = \frac{1}{1 + \left(\dfrac{\omega}{\omega_c}\right)^{2N}}$$ 1. Maximally flat passband: the first $2N-1$ derivatives of $|H|$ at $\omega = 0$ are zero; the response is monotonic, with no ripple in either the passband or the stopband. 2. 3-dB point: at $\omega = \omega_c$ the gain is $1/\sqrt2$ ($-3.01$ dB) for every order $N$. 3. Roll-off: the attenuation in the stopband increases at $20N$ dB/decade ($6N$ dB/octave). A larger $N$ gives a steeper transition, and the response approaches the ideal brick wall. 4.

p: Define the virtual height of the ionosphere and derive the expression for relation between the skip distance ($D$) and critical frequency ($f_{crt}$) assuming Earth is not curve.
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENEX 303.r: Virtual height. When a radio wave is sent obliquely into the ionosphere, the electron density increases with height, the refractive index decreases, and the wave bends gradually and returns to Earth. The virtual height $h'$ is the height of an imaginary sharp reflecting surface from which the wave would be reflected, if it were to travel along the straight incident and reflected paths (the straight-line extensions) without bending. It is greater than the true (actual) height of the reflecting point, because the wave slows down (group velocity $<c$) in the ionized layer. It is measured with an ionosonde as $h' = c\,t/2$, where $t$ is the pulse round-trip time.

Lattice (reflection) coefficients by the step-down recursion. $K_m = \alpha_m(m)$ and $$\alpha_{m-1}(i) = \frac{\alpha_m(i) - K_m\,\alpha_m(m-i)}{1 - K_m^2}.$$ Order 3: $K_3 = \alpha_3(3) = \dfrac13$, $1 - K_3^2 = \dfrac89$.

p: Define Gibb's phenomenon. The desired frequency response of a HPF is given by $$H_d(e^{j\omega}) = \begin{cases} e^{-j3\omega}, & \omega_c \le |\omega| \le \pi \\ 0, & |\omega| < \omega_c \end{cases}$$ Design a linear phase FIR filter using hamming window for $M = 7$ and $\omega_c = 2$ rad/sample.
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENEX 304.r: Gibbs phenomenon. When an ideal (infinitely long) impulse response is truncated by a rectangular window to obtain a finite-length FIR filter, the frequency response shows ripples in the passband and stopband. Near the discontinuity (band edge) there is an overshoot of about $9\%$ of the jump (so about $0.09$ for a unit step in $H_d$). Increasing the length $M$ makes the ripples narrower and closer to the edge but does not reduce the peak overshoot. It is reduced only by using a smooth window (Hamming, Hanning, Blackman) in place of the rectangular one, at the cost of a wider transition band. Design.

p: What do you understand by optimum filter? Describe Remez exchange algorithm for FIR filter design using a flowchart.
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENEX 304.r: Optimum filter. A filter whose coefficients are chosen to minimise some error measure between the desired and the actual response. For FIR filters the optimum (equiripple) filter minimises the maximum weighted error over the passband and stopband (Chebyshev / minimax criterion). The error is spread evenly as ripples of equal height, so for the same order (length) it gives the smallest peak ripple, or for the same ripple the smallest order, compared with window methods. It is designed by the Parks-McClellan (Remez exchange) algorithm. Remez exchange algorithm. The amplitude response of a linear-phase FIR filter is a trigonometric polynomial $A(\omega) = \sum_{k=0}^{r}a_k\cos k\omega$.

Design a digital IIR low pass filter using bilinear transformation based on Butterworth approximation to meet the following specifications: passband magnitude characteristics that is constant to within 1 dB for frequencies below $\omega = 0.2\pi$ and stopband attenuation of at least 15 dB for frequencies between $\omega = 0.3\pi$ and $\pi$. Use bilinear transformation.
Find 8-point DFT using DIF-FFT of the sequence $x[n] = \{1, 2, 3, 2, 1\}$.
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENEX 304.r: $x[n] = \{1,2,3,2,1\}$ is padded with zeros to $N = 8$: $x = \{1,2,3,2,1,0,0,0\}$. $W_8 = e^{-j\pi/4}$, so $W_8^0 = 1$, $W_8^1 = \frac{1-j}{\sqrt2}$, $W_8^2 = -j$, $W_8^3 = \frac{-1-j}{\sqrt2}$. In decimation in frequency each butterfly takes $a = x[n]$, $b = x[n+N/2]$ and gives $a+b$ and $(a-b)W_N^{n}$. Stage 1 ($N/2 = 4$): $g[n] = x[n] + x[n+4]$ and $h[n] = (x[n] - x[n+4])W_8^n$.

For a saturated liquid–vapour mixture, the quality (dryness fraction) $x$ is the mass fraction of the vapour in the mixture: $$\begin{gathered}x = \frac{m_g}{m_f + m_g} = \frac{m_g}{m_t} \\ 0 \le x \le 1\end{gathered}$$ ($x = 0$ saturated liquid, $x = 1$ saturated vapour). The moisture content (wetness fraction) is the mass fraction of the liquid, $y = m_f/m_t$, so $$ \boxed{y = 1 - x} $$ Specific volume of the mixture. The total volume is $V = V_f + V_g$, that is $m_t v = m_f v_f + m_g v_g$.

p: Define rock stress and describe various in-situ measurement methods of rock stress.
Paper 2082 Bhadra ENCE 152.r: Rock stress. Rock stress is the force per unit area acting within the rock mass. The in-situ (virgin) stress is due to the weight of overburden, $\sigma_v = \gamma z$ (about $27$ kPa/m), the horizontal stress $\sigma_h = k\sigma_v$ (with $k$ commonly $0.3$ to $3$, higher near the surface in tectonically active regions such as the Himalaya), plus tectonic, residual and topographic stresses. Induced stresses arise around excavations. Knowledge of the magnitude and direction of the principal stresses is required for design of tunnels, caverns, underground powerhouses and slopes. p: Describe Hoek-Brown failure criterion. Discuss the importance of mechanical properties of rock in civil engineering.
Paper 2083 Baishakh ENCE 152.r: Hoek-Brown failure criterion. An empirical criterion for the strength of intact rock and rock masses under triaxial stress. In terms of the major and minor effective principal stresses at failure, $$\sigma_1' = \sigma_3' + \sigma_{ci}\left(m_b\frac{\sigma_3'}{\sigma_{ci}} + s\right)^a$$ where $\sigma_{ci}$ is the uniaxial compressive strength of the intact rock, and $m_b = m_i\exp\!\left(\dfrac{GSI - 100}{28 - 14D}\right)$, $s = \exp\!\left(\dfrac{GSI - 100}{9 - 3D}\right)$, $a = \tfrac12 + \tfrac16\left(e^{-GSI/15} - e^{-20/3}\right)$.

p: Write down the importance of discontinuities characters that affect rock mass classification. Discuss the tunnel excavation methods and support system in rock mass class IV based on Rock Mass Rating (RMR) classification.
Paper 2083 Baishakh ENCE 152.r: Importance of discontinuity characters in rock mass classification. Rock masses fail mainly along discontinuities (joints, bedding, faults, foliation), so their character controls strength, deformability and permeability: - Orientation (dip and dip direction): determines whether blocks can slide, topple or fall in a slope or tunnel (rated by the orientation adjustment). - Spacing and RQD: give the block size; closer spacing means a weaker, more deformable mass. - Persistence: continuous discontinuities make sliding surfaces. - Roughness and aperture: control the shear strength and the water flow. - Infilling and weathering: soft or clay infill and altered walls greatly reduce friction.

p: Define earthquake. How do you calculate earthquake magnitude (Richter Scale)?
Paper 2083 Baishakh ENCE 152.r: Earthquake. An earthquake is the sudden release of strain energy stored in the Earth's crust, usually by slip on a fault, which radiates as seismic waves (P, S, Love, Rayleigh) and shakes the ground. The point of rupture at depth is the focus (hypocentre) and the point on the surface vertically above it the epicentre. Richter (local) magnitude. Richter defined $$M_L = \log_{10}A - \log_{10}A_0(\delta)$$ where $A$ is the maximum trace amplitude (mm) on a Wood-Anderson seismograph and $A_0(\delta)$ the amplitude of a standard reference event ($M = 0$, amplitude $1\ \mu$m) at the same epicentral distance $\delta$.

p: Write short notes (Any Two): (a) Seismic Refraction Tomography (SRT); (b) Elastic Modulus; (c) Landslide Dam Outburst Flood (LDOF). <!-- SOLUTIONS -->
Paper 2083 Baishakh ENCE 152.r: All three are answered (any two are required). Seismic Refraction Tomography (SRT). A seismic source (hammer, weight drop, small explosive) generates P-waves that travel through the ground; the first arrival times at a line of geophones are recorded. Where velocity increases with depth, waves refract along the layer interface and return as head waves. Unlike classical refraction, tomography inverts all first-arrival times (using ray tracing and iteration) to produce a 2-D velocity section $V_p(x,z)$ with smooth lateral and vertical velocity variation.

o: To determine the depth to bedrock beneath a site.
To measure the compressive strength of rock samples.
To assess the permeability of soil layers.
To evaluate the shear strength of soil.
General.w: Seismic refraction surveys are primarily used to determine the depth to bedrock by analyzing the velocity of seismic waves through different materials.

General.w: Sandy gravel has larger pore spaces, allowing water to flow more easily compared to the other materials listed.

General.q: In geotechnical engineering, the unconfined compressive strength (UCS) test is commonly used for which type of material?
General.w: The UCS test is particularly useful for determining the strength of cohesive soils like clays that do not have significant internal friction.

General.q: What is the main purpose of performing a triaxial compression test on soil samples in geotechnical engineering?
o: To determine the Young's modulus of soil
To assess the shear strength parameters of soil
To evaluate the thermal conductivity of soil
To measure the bulk density of soil
General.w: The triaxial compression test is primarily conducted to obtain shear strength parameters such as cohesion and angle of internal friction for soil samples.

p: What is surveying and principle of surveying? Differentiate between plane and geodetic surveying.
Paper 2082 Bhadra ENCE 153.r: Surveying is the art and science of determining the relative positions of points on, above or beneath the surface of the earth by measuring distances, angles and directions, and of representing them in the form of a plan or map (or setting them out on the ground). Principles of surveying. 1. Working from the whole to the part: control stations are fixed first with the greatest accuracy, and the details are then located within this frame by less accurate methods, so that errors do not accumulate. 2. Fixing a new point from at least two known points by two independent measurements (lengths or angles), with a third as a check.

p: Discuss the importance of offsets; list the types. What is the principle of plane table surveying, and what are the advantages over the chain surveying?
Paper 2082 Bhadra ENCE 153.r: Importance of offsets. In a chain survey the chain lines form the skeleton, and the details (buildings, boundaries, roads, streams, trees) are located by measuring their lateral distances (offsets) from the chain lines. Offsets are therefore the only way by which the details are fixed and plotted, and their accuracy decides the accuracy of the plan. Types. (i) Perpendicular offsets, set out at $90^\circ$ with the cross staff, optical square or the 3-4-5 tape method; (ii) oblique offsets, measured at any angle by the tie-line method from two points of the chain line, when a perpendicular cannot be set. They are classified also as short (up to about 15 m) and long offsets.

p: What is local attraction? Draw sketch only for the graphical adjustment of closing error in compass traverse when closing error is exactly horizontal. In a link traverse ABCDEF the two points A (1000 mE, 2000 mN) and B(2000 mE,1000 mN). The angles to the right at stations are: 125°30' at B, 237°45' at C, 145°15' at D and 55°30' at E. FB of EF = 339°00'20". Check whether the observations for angles are correct or not. If not, compute the correct bearing of all lines.
Paper 2082 Bhadra ENCE 153.r: Local attraction. The deflection of a magnetic needle from the magnetic meridian caused by magnetic substances near it (steel structures, iron ore, electric cables, pipelines, keys, steel tapes, the chain and arrows). It makes the F.B. and B.B. of the line differ from exactly $180^\circ$, and is detected by $\text{F.B.}-\text{B.B.}\neq180^\circ$, and corrected by the included-angle method or by the bearing of a line that is free from attraction. Graphical adjustment of the closing error (Bowditch's rule, error exactly horizontal). The traverse is plotted ABCDE with the end falling at E', away from A by the closing error $EE'$.

Paper 2082 Bhadra ENCE 153.r: Level book (rise and fall / HI). Because the staff is 5 m long and the ground slopes continuously down, the readings increase until they approach the length of the staff, then the instrument has to be moved: after the 4th reading (2.52 to 1.25) and the 8th reading (4.685 to 0.625). So: set-up 1: BS 0.385, IS 1.030, IS 1.925, FS 2.52; set-up 2: BS 1.25, IS 2.87, IS 3.66, FS 4.685; set-up 3: BS 0.625, IS 2.005, IS 3.110, FS 4.485 (last point, RL 2208.000). The RLs are therefore worked backwards from the last station: $RL_{\text{before}}=RL_{\text{next}}+(\text{next reading}-\text{previous reading})$ within a set-up (the ground falls with increasing reading).

Paper 2082 Bhadra ENCE 153.r: Total station. An electro-optical instrument that combines an electronic theodolite (horizontal and vertical angles), an EDM (slope distance) and a microprocessor with memory in one unit, so that angles and distance are measured together and the horizontal distance, vertical difference, and the coordinates $(N,E,Z)$ of the target are computed and stored. Uses: topographic and detailed surveys; traversing and control; setting out of buildings, roads, bridges and tunnels; deformation monitoring; volume and area computation; as-built and cadastral surveys; resection and remote elevation measurement;

p: Define tacheometry. What is the principle of tacheometry? A staff was held vertically at a distance of 100 m and 300 m from the tacheometer and staff intercepts with the telescope horizontal were 0.995 m and 3.00 m respectively. The instrument was then set over a station P of RL 1950.50 m and height of instrument was 1.42 m. The stadia readings of a staff held vertically at a station Q were 1.00, 1.83, 2.67 m while the vertical angle was -10°00'. Find the distance PQ and RL of PQ.
Paper 2082 Bhadra ENCE 153.r: Tacheometry is a method of rapid surveying in which the horizontal distance and the difference of elevation of a point are determined from angular and staff observations of a theodolite fitted with stadia hairs (a tacheometer), without chaining or levelling. Principle. The stadia hairs make a fixed small angle; the staff intercept $s$ between the upper and lower hairs is proportional to the distance of the staff from the instrument: $D=ks+C$ ($k=f/i$, $C=f+d$). For an inclined sight at angle $\alpha$ with a vertical staff: $$\begin{gathered}D=ks\cos^2\alpha+C\cos\alpha \\ V=\tfrac12ks\sin2\alpha+C\sin\alpha\end{gathered}$$ Instrument constants.

Paper 2082 Bhadra ENCE 153.r: | | Triangulation | Trilateration | |---|---|---| | Principle | The network is made of triangles; one base line is measured accurately and all the angles are measured. The sides follow from the sine rule and the coordinates from the azimuth of one side | The same network, but all the sides are measured with EDM (or total station);
