Paper 2083 Baishakh ENCE 153.r: Primary classification of surveying. Surveying is classified first by the basis on which the earth's curvature is treated and then by the nature of the work: | Basis | Plane surveying | Geodetic surveying | |---|---|---| | Earth's surface | Taken as a plane; curvature ignored | Curvature of the earth (spheroid) is considered | | Area | Normally up to about 250 km² | Large areas, over about 250 km² | | Level surface | Level line taken as straight; plumb lines as parallel | Level line is a curve;

p: What are the methods of horizontal distance measurement in sloping ground? What type of significant figures are you used in the distance measurement? A car is travelling at a speed of 60 km per hour. A 4 cm long line represents the distance travelled in two hours; construct a scale upto 10 hours. The scale should be able to read the distance travelled in one minute. Show the distance 476 km and the distance in 4 hours and 4 minutes on map.
Paper 2083 Baishakh ENCE 153.r: Horizontal distances on sloping ground. 1. Direct (stepping) method. The tape is held horizontally and the distance is measured in steps, with a plumb bob used to transfer the point to the ground (suitable for steep slopes). 2. Slope measurement and reduction. The slope distance $L$ is measured along the ground together with the angle of slope $\theta$ (clinometer or theodolite), or the difference of level $h$ between the ends (by levelling). The horizontal distance is $L\cos\theta$, or $\sqrt{L^2-h^2}$, or by the hypotenuse allowance $L-\dfrac{h^2}{2L}$ for flat slopes. 3. Indirect methods: tacheometry (stadia), EDM or total-station horizontal distance, and triangulation or trilateration.

p: Explain the principles of chain survey and plane table survey with supporting sketches. Also mention the suitability of these survey.
Paper 2083 Baishakh ENCE 153.r: Principle of chain (linear) survey. It is a method in which the area is divided into a network of triangles (a well-conditioned triangle has no angle below $30^\circ$ and none above $120^\circ$) and only linear measurements are made, with a chain or tape. A triangle is rigid and is fixed by its three sides alone, so the plan can be drawn from the lengths only. Main (survey) lines run through the area and details are fixed from them by offsets, with check lines to control accuracy. Angles are never measured. Principle of plane table survey. The field work and plotting are done at the same time on a drawing board (table) levelled over the station.

p: If there is bearing of initial line and angle to the right are known; establish the relation to calculate bearing of other lines. The F.B & B.B. of the lines of a closed compass traverse are as follows: Calculate the correct bearings. | Line | F.B. | B.B. | |---|---|---| | AB | 33° 00' | 214° 30' | | BC | 124° 30' | 303° 15' | | CD | 180° 00' | 1° 00' | | DA | 289° 30' | 107° 45' |
Paper 2083 Baishakh ENCE 153.r: Relation for bearings (angles measured to the right). Let the bearing of the line $AB$ be $\theta_{AB}$ and let $\beta_B$ be the clockwise (right-hand) angle at $B$ between the back line $BA$ and the forward line $BC$. The back bearing of $AB$ is $\theta_{AB}\pm180^\circ$, and the bearing of $BC$ is the back bearing plus the angle to the right: $$\begin{gathered}\theta_{BC}=\theta_{AB}\pm180^\circ+\beta_B \\ (\text{if the sum exceeds }360^\circ\text{, subtract }360^\circ)\end{gathered}$$ Take $+180^\circ$ if $\theta_{AB}<180^\circ$ and $-180^\circ$ if $\theta_{AB}>180^\circ$.

p: Describe the loop levelling and level circuits. What is the basic fundamental consideration in this type of surveying?
Paper 2083 Baishakh ENCE 153.r: Loop levelling. A levelling that starts at a bench mark (BM), runs through a series of change points and returns to the same BM (or to the starting point) is a closed loop. The algebraic sum of rises and falls should be zero, so the closing error is the difference between the computed and the known RL of the starting BM; this is distributed in proportion to the number of set-ups (or distance). It is used to check the accuracy of levelling in a limited area and to establish a bench mark near a site. Level circuit.

p: List the features of total station. Why back station and occupied station are important in digital data recording in the total station?
Paper 2083 Baishakh ENCE 153.r: Features of a total station. A total station combines an electronic theodolite, an EDM (electronic distance meter) and a microprocessor with data storage in one instrument. - Measures horizontal angle, vertical angle and slope distance together; computes horizontal distance, vertical difference, and coordinates $(N,E,Z)$ on the spot. - Reflector-based (prism) and reflectorless (up to a few hundred metres) distance measurement; accuracy typically 2" to 5" and $\pm(2\text{ mm}+2\text{ ppm})$. - Built-in programs: resection (free station), remote elevation (RDM), missing line measurement, area and COGO, setting-out (stakeout) of points and alignment.

p: What is the principle of stadia method? The vertical angles to vanes fixed at 1 m and 3 m above the foot of the staff held vertically at a station P were - 1°45' and + 2° 30' respectively. Find the horizontal distance and the reduced level of P if the RL of the instrument axis is 1450.00 m.
Paper 2083 Baishakh ENCE 153.r: Principle of stadia. The stadia method is a tacheometric method of finding distances from the optical geometry of the telescope. The line of sight cuts a staff at two stadia hairs; the intercept $s$ of the staff between the upper and lower hairs is proportional to the horizontal distance from the instrument. With the hairs fixed at a small distance $i$ apart in a telescope of focal length $f$, similar triangles give $D=\dfrac{f}{i}s+(f+d)$, i.e. $D=ks+C$, where $k=f/i$ (usually 100) is the multiplying constant and $C$ the additive constant (zero for an anallatic telescope).

p: Describe the principle of the triangulation and trilateration method.
Paper 2083 Baishakh ENCE 153.r: Triangulation. The area (or the line to be controlled) is covered by a chain of connected triangles or quadrilaterals. In the principle of triangulation, the length of one side (the base line) is measured accurately, and all the angles of the triangles are measured with a precise theodolite. The lengths of all the other sides then follow by the sine rule: $$\frac{a}{\sin A}=\frac{b}{\sin B}=\frac{c}{\sin C}\ \Rightarrow\ b=a\frac{\sin B}{\sin A}$$ and the coordinates of the stations follow from the azimuth of one side (astronomical observation). The accuracy is checked by a check base measured at the far end: the computed length is compared with the measured length.

Paper 2081 Baishakh EE 103.r: For a balanced load, the two-wattmeter readings give $$\begin{gathered}P = W_1 + W_2 \\ Q = \sqrt3\,(W_1 - W_2) \\ \tan\varphi = \frac{\sqrt3\,(W_1 - W_2)}{W_1 + W_2}\end{gathered}$$ (the load is inductive, since $W_1 > W_2$ with both positive). (i) Per-phase average power. $$\begin{gathered}P_{total} = 2100 + 1550 = 3650\ \text{W} \\ P_{ph} = \frac{3650}{3} = \mathbf{1216.7\ W}\end{gathered}$$ (ii) Per-phase reactive power. $$\begin{gathered}Q_{total} = \sqrt3\,(2100 - 1550) = 952.6\ \text{var} \\ Q_{ph} = \frac{952.6}{3} = \mathbf{317.5\ var}\ \text{(lagging)}\end{gathered}$$ (iii) Power factor.

p: Describe the operating principle of a single-phase transformer. Derive the condition for which the efficiency of the transformer is maximum.
Paper 2081 Baishakh EE 103.r: Principle. A transformer works on mutual induction (Faraday's law). An alternating voltage $V_1$ applied to the primary drives an alternating magnetising current, which sets up an alternating flux $\Phi = \Phi_m\sin\omega t$ in the laminated iron core. The flux links the secondary winding as well. By Faraday's law it induces an emf in every turn, so $$\begin{gathered}E_1 = 4.44 f N_1 \Phi_m \\ E_2 = 4.44 f N_2 \Phi_m \\ \frac{E_2}{E_1} = \frac{N_2}{N_1} = \frac{V_2}{V_1} = \frac{I_1}{I_2} = K\end{gathered}$$ There is no electrical connection between the windings: energy is transferred by the common flux at constant frequency.

p: A 3-phase, 400 V, 80 kW, 50 Hz, 4-pole induction machine delivers rated output power at a slip of 0.05. Determine the:

Paper 2081 Baishakh EE 103.r: Given: $V_L = 400$ V, $P_{out} = 80$ kW, $f = 50$ Hz, $P = 4$ poles, $s = 0.05$. (a) Synchronous speed. $$N_s = \frac{120f}{P} = \frac{120 \times 50}{4} = \mathbf{1500\ rpm}\quad(\omega_s = 157.1\ \text{rad/s})$$ (b) Motor speed. $$N = N_s(1 - s) = 1500\,(1 - 0.05) = \mathbf{1425\ rpm}$$ (c) Frequency of the rotor current. $$f_r = sf = 0.05 \times 50 = \mathbf{2.5\ Hz}$$ (d) Rotor induced voltage at the operating speed. The stator phase voltage (star-connected stator) is $400/\sqrt3 = 230.9$ V.

p: Describe back emf in a dc motor. Explain the significance of back emf in a dc motor. Draw a constructional diagram of synchronous generator mentioning its components.
Paper 2081 Baishakh EE 103.r: Back emf. When the armature of a DC motor rotates, its conductors cut the main-pole flux, so an emf is induced in them according to the generator action. By Lenz's law this emf opposes the applied voltage (the cause producing the rotation), hence it is called the back (counter) emf: $$\begin{gathered}E_b = \frac{P\Phi Z N}{60A}\ \text{volt} \\ V = E_b + I_aR_a \ \Rightarrow\ I_a = \frac{V - E_b}{R_a}\end{gathered}$$ Significance of back emf. 1. It makes the motor self-regulating. If the load rises, the motor slows, $E_b$ falls, $I_a = (V - E_b)/R_a$ increases and so does the torque until it balances the load. If the load falls, the opposite happens. Speed settles automatically. 2.

p: Explain the generation of AC voltage. A coil having a resistance of $5\ \Omega$ and inductance of $30$ mH in series are connected across a $230$ V, $50$ Hz supply. Calculate current, power factor, and power consumed.
Paper 2081 Kartik EE 103.r: Generation of AC voltage. Faraday's law: an emf is induced in a conductor when it cuts magnetic flux. Take a rectangular coil of $N$ turns, area $A$, rotating at constant angular speed $\omega$ in a uniform magnetic field $B$. When its plane makes angle $\theta = \omega t$ with the neutral position, the flux linked is $\phi = BA\cos\omega t$, so $$\begin{gathered}e = -N\frac{d\phi}{dt} = NBA\omega\sin\omega t = E_m\sin\omega t \\ E_m = NBA\omega\end{gathered}$$ The emf is zero when the coil sides move parallel to the field (neutral position), maximum when they cut the field at right angles, and reverses each half revolution.

p: Derive the condition for maximum torque in an induction motor. Describe the torque slip characteristics of a three-phase induction motor.
Paper 2081 Kartik EE 103.r: Torque equation. In a three-phase induction motor, with $E_2$ the rotor emf per phase at standstill, $R_2$ and $X_2$ the rotor resistance and standstill leakage reactance per phase, and $s$ the slip, the rotor at slip $s$ has emf $sE_2$ and reactance $sX_2$: $$\begin{gathered}I_2 = \frac{sE_2}{\sqrt{R_2^2 + (sX_2)^2}} \\ \cos\varphi_2 = \frac{R_2}{\sqrt{R_2^2 + (sX_2)^2}}\end{gathered}$$ The torque is proportional to $\Phi I_2\cos\varphi_2$, and $\Phi \propto E_2$, so (from the rotor power input $P_2 = 3I_2^2R_2/s$ and $T = P_2/\omega_s$): $$T = \frac{3}{\omega_s}\cdot\frac{sE_2^2R_2}{R_2^2 + s^2X_2^2}$$ Condition for maximum torque.

p: Explain working principle of a synchronous generator. A 4 pole $230$ V dc shunt motor, lap wound has $980$ conductors. The flux per pole is $20$ mWb. Determine the torque developed by the armature in Nm when the current drawn by the motor is $26$ A. The armature resistance is $0.12\ \Omega$ and the field resistance is $130\ \Omega$.
Paper 2081 Kartik EE 103.r: Working principle of a synchronous generator (alternator). It works on Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction. The rotor carries a field winding fed with DC (through slip rings), so it forms alternate N and S poles. A prime mover (turbine) rotates the rotor at the constant synchronous speed $N_s$. The rotating field flux cuts the stationary three-phase armature conductors placed in the stator slots, and an emf is induced in each phase. The three phase windings are displaced by $120^\circ$ in space, so the three emfs are displaced by $120^\circ$ in time.

p: Define and explain reverse breakdown effect. Describe how Zener diode works as a voltage regulator.
Paper 2081 Kartik EE 103.r: Reverse breakdown. A p–n junction diode under reverse bias passes only a very small reverse saturation current (leakage). If the reverse voltage is increased beyond a critical value, the breakdown voltage $V_{BR}$, the reverse current suddenly rises sharply while the voltage across the diode stays almost constant. This is the reverse breakdown effect. It is not destructive in itself; damage occurs only if the power $V_{BR}I_R$ exceeds the rating, so the current must be limited by an external resistor. Two mechanisms are responsible: 1. Avalanche breakdown (usually $V_{BR} > 6$ V; lightly doped, wide depletion layer).

p: State KCL and KVL. Explain different types of voltage and current sources.
Paper 2081 Chaitra ENEE 103.r: Kirchhoff's current law (KCL). The algebraic sum of the currents meeting at a node (junction) is zero; equivalently, the total current entering a node equals the total current leaving it: $$\sum I = 0\quad(\text{charge is conserved at a node})$$ Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL). The algebraic sum of all the voltages (rises and drops) around any closed loop of a circuit is zero; the sum of the emfs equals the sum of the potential drops: $$\sum V = 0\quad(\text{energy is conserved around a loop})$$ Example. In a loop with a 12 V battery and resistors 2 Ω and 4 Ω in series: $12 - 2I - 4I = 0$, so $I = 2$ A. At a junction where 5 A and 3 A enter, $I_{out} = 8$ A. Types of sources.

Paper 2081 Chaitra ENEE 103.r: Why "bipolar"? In a bipolar junction transistor (BJT) the current is carried by both types of charge carriers, free electrons (majority in n-type) and holes (majority in p-type), and the device has two p-n junctions (emitter-base and collector-base). "Bipolar" refers to this two-carrier conduction, in contrast to the unipolar FET where only one type of carrier (majority) carries the current. It is a three-layer device (npn or pnp): the emitter (heavily doped, emits carriers), the base (very thin, lightly doped) and the collector (moderately doped, largest area, collects carriers). Operation of an npn transistor in active mode.

p: Why are protective devices important in residential installation? Explain in brief different types of protective devices used nowadays.

Either can start a fire; a protective device cuts the supply within milliseconds to seconds. - They protect people from electric shock when insulation fails or a live wire is touched (earth-leakage protection); even a current of 30 mA through the body can be fatal. - They protect appliances and wiring (TV, refrigerator, computers) from overload, overvoltage, lightning and switching surges, saving the cost of replacement. - They isolate only the faulty circuit, so the rest of the house stays supplied;

p: Explain the phenomena of resonance in parallel circuit and also derive the expression for resonance frequency and the impedance at resonance.
Paper 2077 Chaitra EE 460.r: Parallel resonance. A circuit with a coil and a capacitor in parallel is in resonance when the supply voltage and the line current are in phase: the net susceptance is zero, the power factor is unity and the circuit behaves as a pure resistance. At resonance the energy swings between the magnetic field of the coil and the electric field of the capacitor, so the supply only supplies the losses (the coil resistance). Practical circuit. The branch currents are $I_{coil} = \dfrac{V}{R + j\omega L}$ and $I_C = j\omega CV$.

Paper 2082 Chaitra ENCE 203.r: General equation of the parabolic vertical curve. The rate of change of grade is constant along an equal-tangent parabola: $$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\frac{g_2-g_1}{L}=r$$ where $g_1,g_2$ are the grades (decimal, rising positive) and $L$ is the horizontal length of the curve. p: How DGPS is better for mapping and surveying than normal GPS? What is the application of remote sensing in Civil engineering?
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENCE 203.r: DGPS against normal (standalone) GPS. In standalone GPS a single receiver computes its position from pseudo-ranges that contain common errors: satellite clock and orbit (ephemeris) errors, and ionospheric and tropospheric delay (and selective availability, when it was on). The accuracy is 5 to 10 m horizontally. In Differential GPS (DGPS) a reference (base) station is placed on a point of exactly known coordinates. It compares the range computed from every satellite with the true range and finds a correction for each satellite. These corrections are sent (by radio, mobile network or satellite) in real time, or applied in post-processing, to the rover, which applies them.

p: Describe the principle of GPS. Explain about the component of GPS. How you can apply the remote sensing in the field of civil Engineering?
Paper 2082 Kartik ENCE 203.r: Principle of GPS. The GPS fixes the position of the receiver by three-dimensional trilateration from satellites (the distances from known satellite positions). Each satellite continuously transmits its position (the ephemeris) and the time of transmission $t_s$ on the L1 (1575.42 MHz), L2 (1227.60 MHz) and L5 carriers. The receiver measures the time of arrival $t_r$, giving the pseudo-range $$\rho_i=c\,(t_r-t_s)=\sqrt{(x_i-x)^2+(y_i-y)^2+(z_i-z)^2}+c\,\delta t$$ where $(x_i,y_i,z_i)$ is the position of satellite $i$, $(x,y,z)$ the unknown position and $\delta t$ the clock error of the receiver (the receiver clock is a cheap quartz clock).

Elevations (front, rear and side), showing the heights, finish and the ground and roof levels. 4. Sections (at least two: one through the staircase), showing the floor-to-floor heights, plinth, sill, lintel and parapet heights. 5. p: What is common data environment? Write its advantages. <!-- SOLUTIONS -->

Advantages: one source of truth, so everybody works on the latest version; no duplicate or conflicting files; better collaboration and communication among the architect, structural, MEP engineers, contractor and client;

p: What is Computer Aided Design and Drafting? Explain its uses in civil engineering.
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENCE 204.r: Computer Aided Design and Drafting (CADD) is the use of computer hardware and software to create, modify, analyse, optimise, store and plot the design and the drawings of a project. Computer aided design is the creative and analytical part (modelling, checking, optimising a design) and computer aided drafting is the production of the accurate drawings (plans, sections, details) from it. AutoCAD, Civil 3D, Revit, SW-DTM and STAAD are common examples in civil engineering.

p: Write specific use of 2D drawings in civil engineering and list out common 2D, CADD software.
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENCE 204.r: Specific uses of 2D drawings in civil engineering: floor plans, elevations and sections of buildings; site, location and layout plans; foundation and structural reinforcement details; road plan and profile, cross-sections; canal, drainage and pipe-network layouts; survey and contour maps; working (construction) drawings, shop drawings and as-built drawings for submission to the municipality and for tendering. Common 2D CADD software: AutoCAD, AutoCAD LT, BricsCAD, DraftSight, ZWCAD, LibreCAD, Civil 3D (2D and DTM), MicroStation, SW-DTM (survey and road design software developed in Nepal).

p: Explain different types of coordinate system in AutoCAD.
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENCE 204.r: Coordinate systems in AutoCAD 1. World Coordinate System (WCS): the fixed default system with the origin (0,0,0) at the lower-left of the drawing, X to the right (east), Y upward (north) and Z out of the screen. Angles are measured counter-clockwise from the east (0°). 2. User Coordinate System (UCS): a movable and rotatable system defined by the user (UCS command: origin, 3 point, object, view, Z-axis, world). It is used for drawing on an inclined plane or in 3D and to make the point (0,0) convenient for the job.

p: Write in details how to create a block in AutoCAD. Explain its advantages.
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENCE 204.r: Creating a block in AutoCAD (steps) 1. Draw the object (door, window, tree, north arrow, column symbol) at full size, preferably on layer 0 so that it takes the properties of the layer on which it is inserted. 2. Type BLOCK (B). In the Block Definition dialog box: enter the Name (e.g. DOOR-900); click Pick point and select the base (insertion) point; click Select objects and pick the drawing, then Enter; choose Convert to block, Retain or Delete; set the block unit (mm or m) and the Annotative / Allow exploding options; give a description; click OK. 3. Place it with INSERT (I): select the block name, give the insertion point, scale (X, Y, Z) and rotation (or tick Specify on-screen). 4.

p: Define Building Information Modeling (BIM) and common data environment (CDE).
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENCE 204.r: Building Information Modelling (BIM) is a process of creating and managing an intelligent, 3D digital model of a facility, in which every element (wall, beam, door, pipe) carries information about its geometry, material, cost, schedule and maintenance. Plans, sections, elevations, schedules and quantities are all extracted from the same model, so they are always consistent. Revit, ArchiCAD, Tekla Structures, Civil 3D and Navisworks are BIM tools.

p: Write steps to create A3 layouts in AutoCAD with scale of 1:100.

Create a layer VPORT for viewports and TITLE for the border (set VPORT not to plot). 2. Click a Layout tab (or right-click → New layout, rename it A3-1:100). Delete the default viewport. Insert the A3 border and the title block (INSERT, at 0,0, units mm) on the layer TITLE. 4.

p: List the constituents of concrete and their function.
Explain concrete as three phase system.
Paper 2081 Chaitra ENCE 205.r: (a) Constituents of concrete and their functions. | Constituent | Function | |---|---| | Cement (OPC, PPC; 300 to 450 kg/m³) | the binder: reacts with water (the hydration) and forms the paste (the C-S-H gel) which coats and binds the aggregate, gives the strength and the setting | | Fine aggregate (the sand, about 35 % of the aggregate) | fills the voids between the coarse particles, gives the workability and cohesion, reduces the shrinkage, the segregation and the cost | | Coarse aggregate (the crushed stone or gravel, 10 to 40 mm) | the bulk (60 to 75 % of the volume), gives the strength, the volume stability, the economy and the wear resistance;

p: What are the methods for testing workability of concrete? Briefly explain the method of slump test.
Paper 2081 Chaitra ENCE 205.r: Methods for testing the workability (IS 1199): 1. Slump test: the measure of the consistency (the plain concrete, the 25 to 125 mm); 2. Compacting factor test: the degree of the compaction under the standard work (the low workability, 0.7 to 0.95); $CF=\dfrac{W_{partially\ compacted}}{W_{fully\ compacted}}$; 3. Vee-Bee consolometer test: the time in seconds (the Vebe) for the cone to be remoulded to a cylinder by the vibration (the very dry, the low workability mix); 4. Flow table test: the percent spread of the concrete on the table after 15 drops (the high workability and the flowing concrete: 100 to 150 %); 5.

p: Differentiate between nominal mix and design mix of concrete. Explain IS Code method for mix design of concrete.
Paper 2081 Chaitra ENCE 205.r: Nominal mix and design mix. | | Nominal mix | Design (engineered) mix | |---|---|---| | Basis | the fixed volumetric proportions (1:1.5:3 (M20), 1:2:4 (M15), 1:3:6 (M10)) given by the code | designed by the calculations and the trial for the required strength, the workability and the exposure | | Strength | the assumed (the minimum guaranteed);

p: Explain the effect of gel/space ratio in the strength of concrete. Describe the shrinkage and creep in concrete.
Explain ferro-cement concrete with their applications. <!-- SOLUTIONS -->
Paper 2081 Chaitra ENCE 205.r: Ferrocement. A thin reinforced-cement composite made of the rich cement-sand mortar (the cement: sand = 1: 1.5 to 1: 2.5, w/c 0.4 to 0.45) reinforced with the closely spaced layers of the continuous small-diameter wire mesh (the hexagonal chicken mesh, the welded or the woven square mesh with the 0.5 to 1.5 mm wires) and the skeletal steel (the 6 mm bars); the thickness is 10 to 50 mm; the volume fraction of the steel is 2 to 8 %, and the specific surface of the reinforcement is large (the 1 to 2 cm²/cm³).

p: Explain the basic requirements of coarse and fine aggregates in concretes.
Explain why the information on grading of aggregate is necessary.
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENCE 205.r: (a) Basic requirements of aggregates (IS 383). Coarse aggregate (retained on the 4.75 mm sieve): (1) strong, hard and durable rock (the crushing value $\le45$ % for the ordinary and $\le30$ % for the wearing surface, the impact value $\le45$ %, the abrasion value $\le50$ %); (2) clean: free from clay, silt, organic matter, coal, mica and the soluble salts (the chlorides and the sulphates); (3) good shape: cubical or angular and rough-textured (for the bond), the flakiness and the elongation index limited (about 30 to 40 %); (4) well graded between the nominal sizes (e.g. 20 mm, 40 mm);

p: Discuss segregation and bleeding effects during concreting.
Explain the importance of curing of concrete structures.
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENCE 205.r: (a) Segregation is the separation of the constituents of the fresh concrete (the coarse aggregate separates from the mortar) so that the mix is no longer uniform. Causes: the wrong grading, too wet or too dry mix, a drop from a height (more than 1 to 1.5 m), the long chute or the barrow transport, the over-vibration, the rough handling. Effects: the honeycombing, the weak and porous concrete, the poor bond with the steel, the non-uniform strength, the low durability and the loss of the surface. Prevented by the proper grading, the controlled water, the careful transport and the placing, the limited drop.

p: Write the procedure of DoE method for mix design of concrete.
Why trial mixes are important before concreting in structures? How they are different from nominal mix?
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENCE 205.r: (a) DoE (British Department of the Environment) method of mix design (the steps): 1. Target mean strength: $f_m=f_{ck}+k\,s$, with the margin $k s$ ($k=1.64$ for the 5 % defective, $s$ the standard deviation, e.g. 5 MPa for the M25, or from the previous test data). 2. Free water–cement ratio: from the chart (the relation of the strength and the w/c for the cement type, the aggregate and the age, e.g. 28-day), and check against the maximum w/c for the durability (the exposure, IS 456). 3. Free water content: from the table by the slump or Vebe, the maximum size and the type of aggregate (crushed or uncrushed), corrected for the mixed aggregates ($\tfrac23W_f+\tfrac13W_c$). 4.

p: Explain the effect of creep in concrete.
Explain the effect of size of aggregate on strength of concrete.
Explain the process of concrete maturity.
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENCE 205.r: (a) Effect of creep. Creep is the time-dependent increase of the strain under a sustained load (it continues for years: about 50 % in 2 months and 75 % in 1 year, and it is mostly recoverable by 25 to 30 %). Effects: (1) the increased deflections of the beams and the slabs (2 to 3 times the elastic deflection in the long term); (2) the loss of the pre-stress in the pre-stressed concrete (a major cause); (3) the redistribution of the stress from the concrete to the steel in the columns (the steel may yield), the reduction of the effective stiffness, the cracking and the increased the buckling;

p: Explain quality control and quality assurance in concrete constructions.
Explain the procedure of testing of concrete for compressive strength.
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENCE 205.r: (a) Quality control (QC) and quality assurance (QA). Quality control is the set of the operational techniques and the inspections and tests used to check that the materials and the workmanship meet the specification during the production and the placing (the sieve analysis, the slump test, the cubes, the batching accuracy, the temperature, the curing, the testing of the cement); it is corrective, done by the contractor or the site laboratory, based on the statistical acceptance (IS 456: the mean $\ge f_{ck}+0.825s$ and the individual $\ge f_{ck}-3$ MPa).

p: Discuss on emerging concrete technologies. <!-- SOLUTIONS -->
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENCE 205.r: Emerging concrete technologies. 1. Self-compacting concrete (SCC): the highly flowable concrete (the superplasticiser, the viscosity agent, the powder) which fills the formwork and the congested reinforcement without the vibration; the better finish, the fast, the less noise and the labour. 2. High-performance and the ultra-high-performance concrete (HPC/UHPC): the low w/c (0.2 to 0.3), the silica fume, the fibres; the compressive strength 60 to 200 MPa, the very low permeability and the long durability; the slender and the long-span members. 3.

p: Explain the gradation of coarse aggregates based on their shapes and their impact in the strength of concrete.
What is bulking of sand? Describe the method of determination of fineness modulus of coarse aggregates.
Paper 2082 Kartik ENCE 205.r: (a) Gradation and the shape of the coarse aggregate. Coarse aggregate is graded (the particle size distribution by the sieves 80, 40, 20, 10, 4.75 mm, IS 383) as the single-sized (the nearly uniform, e.g. 20 mm), graded (the all-in, the continuous: e.g. 40 to 4.75 mm) and gap-graded (the intermediate size missing). Shape classes (IS 2386, BS 812): rounded (the river gravel, the smooth, the low voids, the good workability, the poor bond), irregular, angular (crushed) (the rough, the good interlock and bond, the higher water demand), flaky (the thickness less than 0.6 of the mean size) and elongated (the length more than 1.8 of the mean size).

p: Explain the role of water cement ratio in the strength of concrete. Explain segregation and bleeding of concrete and their effects.
Paper 2082 Kartik ENCE 205.r: Role of the water-cement ratio. The strength of the concrete is governed mainly by the w/c ratio (Abrams' law): $$\begin{gathered}f_c=\frac{K_1}{K_2^{\,w/c}}\quad\text{(Abrams)} \\ \text{or in the gel/space form: }f_c=f_{c0}x^3\end{gathered}$$ For the fully compacted concrete, a lower w/c gives the higher strength (the less capillary porosity, the denser paste and the better bond); each 0.1 increase in w/c lowers the strength by about 10 to 15 MPa in the range 0.4 to 0.7. The water needed for the hydration is about 0.23 to 0.25 (the chemical combined 0.23 plus the gel water 0.15, total 0.38 for the full hydration without the capillary pores);

p: Explain DoE method for concrete mix design.
Paper 2082 Kartik ENCE 205.r: DoE method of the mix design (the British DoE "Design of Normal Concrete Mixes"; the steps): 1. Target mean strength: $f_m=f_{ck}+1.64\,s$ (5 % defectives), $s$ from the test records (or 5 to 6 MPa for the standard). 2. Free water/cement ratio from the figure of the strength against the w/c (the 28-day value for the cement type and the aggregate type, by the interpolation between the lines), and the maximum w/c from the durability (IS 456 table). 3. Free water content from the table of the slump or Vebe, the maximum aggregate size (10, 20, 40 mm) and the aggregate type; for the mixed (the crushed and the uncrushed): $W=\tfrac23W_f+\tfrac13W_c$. 4.

p: Explain load deformation behavior of hardened concrete. Describe shrinkage and creep in concrete with the help of sketches.
Paper 2082 Kartik ENCE 205.r: Load-deformation (stress-strain) behaviour of the hardened concrete. Concrete under the uniaxial compression gives the non-linear stress-strain curve: - up to about 30 to 40 % of the ultimate stress the curve is nearly linear and elastic (the micro-cracks at the aggregate-paste interface (the bond cracks) are stable): the modulus $E_c=5000\sqrt{f_{ck}}$ MPa (IS 456); - from 40 to 75 % the bond cracks grow and the curve bends (the stable crack propagation, the mortar cracking starts at about 50 %); - at 75 to 90 % the mortar cracks join up (the unstable crack growth, the volume starts to increase: the critical stress);

p: Describe non-destructive tests for concrete and its applications in concrete structures.
Paper 2082 Kartik ENCE 205.r: Non-destructive testing (NDT) assesses the strength, the quality and the condition of the concrete in the structure without damaging it (the existing structures, the doubtful concrete, the cubes that failed). 1. Rebound (Schmidt) hammer (IS 13311 Part 2): the spring-driven hammer's rebound number $R$ (the surface hardness) is read on the 12 points, and the strength is read from the calibration curve (the accuracy of $\pm25$ %); quick, cheap, to check the uniformity and the comparison, only the surface (the carbonated and the wet surface affects it). 2.

p: Describe emerging technologies in concrete. <!-- SOLUTIONS -->
Paper 2082 Kartik ENCE 205.r: Emerging technologies in concrete. 1. Self-compacting concrete (SCC) with the superplasticisers and the viscosity-modifying agents: flows into the formwork and the congested bars without vibration. 2. High-performance and ultra-high-performance concrete (HPC and UHPC): the low w/c, the silica fume and the fibres; 60 to 200 MPa, the very high durability. 3. Fibre-reinforced concrete (steel, glass, polypropylene, basalt) and the engineered cementitious composites (the bendable concrete, ECC): the toughness and the crack control. 4.

General.q: What is the term used to describe the time required for fresh concrete to lose its plasticity?
General.w: Setting time specifically refers to the period when fresh concrete loses its plasticity.

General.q: In the context of concrete technology, what does the term 'workability' refer to?
o: The ability of concrete to resist cracking under stress
The ability of concrete to flow and be placed without segregation
The speed at which concrete sets after mixing
The strength developed by concrete over time
General.w: Workability is defined as the ease with which fresh concrete can be mixed, placed, compacted, and finished without segregation or bleeding.

p: Justify the roles of water from the WASH perspectives.
Paper 2082 Bhadra ENCE 254.r: WASH = Water, Sanitation and Hygiene. Water is the common base of all three: - Water: safe drinking water prevents the water-borne diseases (diarrhoea, typhoid, cholera, hepatitis A) and gives the quantity for drinking, cooking and cleaning (a minimum of 45 lpcd in rural Nepal, 20 lpcd at the basic level); - Sanitation: water carries the wastes (the flush toilet, the sewer) and is needed for the cleaning and the operation of the sanitation facilities; safe water supply must be protected from the faecal contamination from the latrines; - Hygiene: hand-washing with soap, bathing, washing clothes, food hygiene and menstrual hygiene all need an adequate and accessible water;

p: Define the technical and legal considerations in selecting water sources with examples.
What are the base period, design period in water quantity estimation, and their purposes?
Paper 2082 Bhadra ENCE 254.r: - Base period: the period of the past records (the census data of the previous decades) used to project the trend of the population and the demand: usually the last 3 to 5 censuses (the basis of the forecast). Purpose: to determine the growth rate and the per-capita demand trend. - Design period: the number of future years for which the system is designed, i.e. the time from the commissioning to the time when the capacity is fully used: intake, dams and the treatment plant 15 to 30 years; the pipes, the reservoirs and the buildings 20 to 30 (50 for the dam); the pump and the mechanical parts 10 to 15 years; in Nepal, 15 to 20 years for the rural schemes, and 20 to 25 years for the urban.

p: Define advanced oxidation process and disinfection kinetics.
Paper 2082 Bhadra ENCE 254.r: Advanced oxidation process (AOP). A group of treatment processes that generate highly reactive, non-selective hydroxyl radicals ($\cdot$OH, E° = 2.8 V) in situ, which oxidise the organic and the micro-pollutants that resist the ordinary oxidation, e.g. $\text{O}_3/\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$, $\text{UV}/\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$, $\text{UV}/\text{O}_3$, the Fenton ($\text{Fe}^{2+}/\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$), the photocatalysis ($\text{TiO}_2$/UV). They destroy the pesticides, the pharmaceuticals, the dyes, the taste and the odour compounds, and the emerging pollutants, ideally to $\text{CO}_2$ and water. Disinfection kinetics. The rate at which the microorganisms are inactivated by a disinfectant.

p: What is meant by smart water distribution system? And list its main features.
Paper 2082 Bhadra ENCE 254.r: A smart water distribution system combines the conventional water network with sensors, smart (AMR/AMI) meters, remote-controlled valves and pumps, communication networks (IoT, SCADA) and data analytics (GIS, hydraulic models, AI) to monitor and to control the supply in real time. Main features: (1) real-time monitoring of the flow, pressure, level and the water quality (the chlorine, turbidity, pH); (2) smart metering with automatic reading and the billing and the consumption analytics; (3) leak and burst detection and the non-revenue water reduction, with the DMAs; (4) pressure management with the PRVs and the variable-speed pumps (the energy saving);

p: Define palatable and potable water with example.
Paper 2083 Baishakh ENCE 254.r: Palatable water is water that is pleasant to drink: it is clear, colourless, free from objectionable taste and odour and at a suitable temperature, but it is not necessarily safe. Example: clear, cool water from a well that tastes good but contains pathogenic bacteria (or a colourless water with dissolved arsenic) is palatable but not potable. Potable water is water that is safe to drink, free from pathogens, toxic chemicals and excessive minerals, and meeting the drinking-water standard (the Nepal Drinking Water Quality Standard 2062, WHO guidelines). Example: tap water after filtration and chlorination with residual chlorine 0.1 to 0.5 mg/L and zero E. coli per 100 mL.

p: What is the importance of understating yield in drinking water system?
Paper 2083 Baishakh ENCE 254.r: The yield is the quantity of water that a source can deliver safely in the driest period (the dependable yield, e.g. the minimum spring discharge measured in the dry season, the safe yield of a well, or the 7-day 10-year low flow of a stream). Its importance: - the source is selected and the scheme is sized on the yield: the design demand (with the future growth) must be less than the dependable yield; if the yield is overestimated, the supply fails in the dry season, the cost is wasted and conflicts arise;

p: Explain the significance of peak factor in water supply system.
Paper 2083 Baishakh ENCE 254.r: The peak factor is the ratio of the peak (maximum) demand to the average demand: maximum day factor ($1.2$ to $1.5$, or $1.5$ to $2$ in Nepal's rural schemes) and the peak hour factor ($2$ to $3$, higher for small villages, e.g. $3$ for $<$ 2000 persons). Significance: - the distribution pipes, the pumps and the service reservoir are designed for the peak hourly flow, the intake, the treatment plant and the transmission main for the maximum daily demand; so the factor sets the sizes (and the cost) of each component; - it ensures that the required residual pressure is maintained at peak time and in the periods of the highest use (the morning and evening);

p: Justify the environmental significance of emerging pollutants.
Paper 2083 Baishakh ENCE 254.r: Emerging pollutants (contaminants) are new or newly recognised substances found in water that are not yet covered by the standards: pharmaceuticals and the personal-care products, hormones and endocrine disruptors, pesticides, PFAS ("forever chemicals"), micro- and nano-plastics, antibiotic-resistant bacteria and genes, nanomaterials and industrial additives. Environmental significance. They occur in very small concentrations (ng/L to $\mu$g/L) but they are persistent and bio-accumulative, and the conventional treatment (coagulation, sand filtration, chlorination) does not remove them.

p: Define the membrane filtration and electrodialysis process in water treatment.
Paper 2083 Baishakh ENCE 254.r: Membrane filtration. A pressure- or vacuum-driven process in which water is forced through a semi-permeable membrane that retains the particles, the microorganisms or the dissolved substances according to the pore size: microfiltration (0.1 to 10 $\mu$m: bacteria and turbidity), ultrafiltration (0.01 to 0.1 $\mu$m: viruses and colloids), nanofiltration (about 1 nm: hardness, organics) and reverse osmosis (below 1 nm: dissolved salts, with the pressure higher than the osmotic pressure). The permeate is the treated water, the retentate the concentrate. Electrodialysis (ED).

p: State the primary functions of District Metered Areas (DMAs) in a smart water distribution system.

Paper 2081 Chaitra ENCT203.r: (a) Lexical analyzer and DFA. The lexical analyzer (scanner) turns the character stream of the source code into tokens. Each token class (identifier, number, keyword, operator,...) is described by a regular expression, and every regular expression is equivalent to a finite automaton. The scanner generator (Lex/Flex) converts all expressions into one NFA, then into a DFA, which is the scanning engine: the DFA reads characters from the start state, remembers the last accepting state it passed through (longest-match rule) and, when no move is possible, returns the token of that accepting state, backing up the input to the end of that lexeme.

p: Define equivalence and partial-equivalence relation. Using mathematical induction show that for every integer $n \ge 0$ the number $4^{(2n+1)} + 3^{(n+2)}$ is a multiple of 13.
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENCT203.r: Equivalence relation. A relation $R$ on a set $A$ is an equivalence relation if it is - reflexive: $(a,a)\in R$ for every $a \in A$, - symmetric: $(a,b)\in R \Rightarrow (b,a)\in R$, - transitive: $(a,b)\in R$ and $(b,c)\in R \Rightarrow (a,c)\in R$. It splits $A$ into disjoint equivalence classes (for example "has the same remainder mod 3" on the integers). Partial-equivalence relation (PER). $R$ is a partial equivalence relation if it is symmetric and transitive but need not be reflexive. A PER is an equivalence relation on the part of $A$ that it relates to something, namely its domain $\{a: (a,a)\in R\}$.

Paper 2082 Chaitra ENCT203.r: Turing machine with storage in the states. The finite control can remember a fixed, finite amount of information, if each state is a tuple $[q,\,x]$ where $q$ is the control state and $x$ is a stored symbol (or several symbols). The states are written $[q_0,a]$, $[q_0,b]$,... and the machine is an ordinary TM, only the state set is a product $Q\times\Gamma^k$. p: State halting problem. Explain the closure properties of recursively enumerable languages.
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENCT203.r: Halting problem. Given a Turing machine $M$ and an input $w$, decide whether $M$ halts (accepts or rejects, but does not loop forever) on $w$. $\textit{HALT}=\{\langle M,w\rangle: M\text{ halts on }w\}$ is undecidable (it is recursively enumerable but not recursive). Proof sketch. Suppose a decider $H(\langle M,w\rangle)$ exists. Build $D(\langle M\rangle)$: run $H(\langle M,\langle M\rangle\rangle)$; if $H$ says "halts" loop forever, otherwise halt. Run $D$ on its own code: $D$ halts on $\langle D\rangle$ iff $H$ says it does not halt, a contradiction. So $H$ cannot exist. Closure properties of recursively enumerable (RE) languages.

Paper 2082 Bhadra ENCT 251.r: Counter example. To disprove $\forall x\, P(x)$ it is enough to find one element $c$ in the domain for which $P(c)$ is false; $c$ is the counter example. Example: for $P(x)$: "$x^{2} > x$" over the reals, $x = 1$ (or $x = \tfrac12$) is a counter example, so $\forall x\,(x^{2} > x)$ is false. Witness. To prove $\exists x\, P(x)$ it is enough to exhibit one element $c$ with $P(c)$ true; $c$ is the witness (an existence proof). Example: for $P(x)$: "$x^{2} = 2$" over the reals, $x = \sqrt{2}$ is a witness, so $\exists x\, (x^{2} = 2)$ is true. The argument. Let $p$: you send me an e-mail message, $q$: I finish writing the program, $r$: I go to sleep early, $s$: I wake up feeling refreshed.

Paper 2082 Bhadra ENCT 251.r: Formal definition of a DFA. A deterministic finite automaton is a 5-tuple $M = (Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F)$ where - $Q$ is a finite, non-empty set of states, - $\Sigma$ is a finite input alphabet, - $\delta: Q \times \Sigma \to Q$ is the transition function (exactly one next state for every state and symbol), - $q_0 \in Q$ is the start state, - $F \subseteq Q$ is the set of accepting (final) states. A string $w$ is accepted if $\hat\delta(q_0, w) \in F$. Design. The language is $L = \{w \in \{a,b\}^{*}: w \text{ does not start with } aba\}$.

p: Derive the explicit formula for the Fibonacci series using recurrence relation.
Paper 2082 Bhadra ENCT 251.r: Recurrence. The Fibonacci numbers satisfy $$\begin{gathered}F_n = F_{n-1} + F_{n-2} \quad (n \ge 2) \\ F_0 = 0,\ F_1 = 1\end{gathered}$$ This is a linear homogeneous recurrence of order 2 with constant coefficients. Try $F_n = r^{n}$: $$r^{n} = r^{n-1} + r^{n-2}$$ Dividing by $r^{n-2}$ gives the characteristic equation $$r^{2} - r - 1 = 0$$ $$r = \frac{1 \pm \sqrt{5}}{2}$$ Let $\varphi = \dfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$ (golden ratio) and $\psi = \dfrac{1-\sqrt5}{2}$.

p: Define wheel graph. Draw 3-dimensional hypercube ($Q_3$). Show that the total number of edges in any complete graph is $\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}$.
State and prove Euler's Formula for planar graph.
Paper 2082 Bhadra ENCT 251.r: Euler's formula. For a connected planar graph with $v$ vertices, $e$ edges and $f$ faces (regions, including the outer unbounded face) drawn in the plane without crossings, $$v - e + f = 2$$ Proof (induction on the number of edges $e$). Basis. A connected graph with $e = 0$ is a single vertex: $v = 1$, $f = 1$, so $v - e + f = 1 - 0 + 1 = 2$. (A tree with $v$ vertices has $e = v - 1$, $f = 1$, and $v - (v-1) + 1 = 2$ also holds.) Inductive step. Assume the formula holds for all connected planar graphs with $e - 1$ edges, and let $G$ be a connected planar graph with $e \ge 1$ edges. Case 1: $G$ has no cycle. Then $G$ is a tree, $e = v - 1$ and $f = 1$, so $v - e + f = v - (v-1) + 1 = 2$.

Prove that $\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{3}$ is irrational using proof by contradiction.
Paper 2083 Baishakh ENCT 251.r: Claim: $\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3}$ is irrational. Proof by contradiction. Assume $\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3} = r$ with $r$ rational ($r > 0$). Then $\sqrt{3} = r - \sqrt{2}$. Squaring both sides: $$3 = r^{2} - 2r\sqrt{2} + 2 \;\Rightarrow\; 2r\sqrt{2} = r^{2} - 1 \;\Rightarrow\; \sqrt{2} = \frac{r^{2} - 1}{2r}$$ Since $r$ is rational and non-zero, the right-hand side is rational, so $\sqrt{2}$ would be rational. But $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational: if $\sqrt{2} = a/b$ in lowest terms, then $a^{2} = 2b^{2}$, so $a$ is even, $a = 2c$; then $b^{2} = 2c^{2}$ and $b$ is even too, contradicting lowest terms. This contradiction shows that the assumption is false.

Claim $P(n)$: $1^{2} + 2^{2} + \cdots + n^{2} = \dfrac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}$ for all integers $n \ge 1$. Basis step ($n = 1$). LHS $= 1^{2} = 1$; RHS $= \dfrac{1\cdot2\cdot3}{6} = 1$. So $P(1)$ is true. Inductive step. Assume $P(k)$ is true for some $k \ge 1$: $$1^{2} + 2^{2} + \cdots + k^{2} = \frac{k(k+1)(2k+1)}{6}$$ Add $(k+1)^{2}$ to both sides: $$\begin{aligned}1^{2} + \cdots + k^{2} + (k+1)^{2} &= \frac{k(k+1)(2k+1)}{6} + (k+1)^{2} \\ &= \frac{(k+1)\left[k(2k+1) + 6(k+1)\right]}{6} \\ &= \frac{(k+1)\left(2k^{2} + 7k + 6\right)}{6} \\ &= \frac{(k+1)(k+2)(2k+3)}{6}\end{aligned}$$ This is $P(k+1)$, since $\dfrac{(k+1)((k+1)+1)(2(k+1)+1)}{6} = \dfrac{(k+1)(k+2)(2k+3)}{6}$.

State Dirac's and Ore's theorem. Is $K_5$ and $K_{3,3}$ planar graph? Justify your answer.
Paper 2083 Baishakh ENCT 251.r: Dirac's theorem. If $G$ is a simple graph with $n \ge 3$ vertices and the degree of every vertex satisfies $\deg(v) \ge n/2$, then $G$ has a Hamiltonian circuit. Ore's theorem. If $G$ is a simple graph with $n \ge 3$ vertices and $\deg(u) + \deg(v) \ge n$ for every pair of non-adjacent vertices $u, v$, then $G$ has a Hamiltonian circuit. (Dirac's theorem is a special case of Ore's: if every degree is at least $n/2$, every pair has degree sum at least $n$.) Both are sufficient, not necessary, conditions. Is $K_5$ planar? No. $K_5$ has $v = 5$ and $e = 10$. For a simple connected planar graph with $v \ge 3$, $e \le 3v - 6 = 9$.

A network with only two resistor values: $R$ in series along the ladder and $2R$ in each shunt leg; the $2R$ leg of the bit $b_i$ is switched to $V_{ref}$ (bit = 1) or to ground (bit = 0); the last leg (the LSB end) is terminated with an extra $2R$. p: What do you understand by sample and Hold circuit? Explain the role of multiplexer in a data acquisition system with a neat sketch.
Paper 2081 Chaitra ENEE 201.r: Sample-and-hold circuit. A circuit which samples the analogue input at a command instant and holds the sampled value constant for the required time. A MOSFET switch, a hold capacitor $C_H$ and input and output buffer amplifiers form it: in the sample mode the switch is closed and $C_H$ charges, so the output follows the input; in the hold mode the switch is open, $C_H$ keeps the voltage and the output buffer holds it (the droop rate is $I_{leak}/C_H$). It is needed because an ADC needs a steady input during its conversion time, otherwise the error is more than 1 LSB for any changing signal; the aperture time and the acquisition time of the switch limit its speed.

The generator builds up its own voltage from the residual flux, through its field current $I_f = V/R_f$ taken from its own terminals. If a load is connected during the build-up: 1. The load (and armature) current produces an armature-resistance drop and armature reaction, which lower the terminal voltage, so the field current, and hence the flux, cannot rise: the voltage fails to build up (or settles at a very low value). 2. With a heavy load of low resistance across the terminals, the voltage at which the field and load share the generated emf collapses; the machine may also overheat because of the heavy current with a small emf.

Paper 2082 Kartik ENEE 202.r: Need of a starter. At the instant of starting the speed is zero, so the back emf $E_b = k\Phi\omega = 0$ and the armature current is limited only by $R_a$: $$I_{a,start} = \frac{V}{R_a}$$ Since $R_a$ is very small (for example 0.12 Ω at 200 V gives 1667 A, or about 180 times the full-load current), this would burn the armature and commutator, produce a very large torque and shock, and cause a heavy voltage dip on the supply. A starter inserts an external resistance in series with the armature at starting, limiting the current to 1.5 to 2 times the rated current, and cuts it out in steps as the motor speeds up and $E_b$ builds up. It also provides no-voltage and overload protection.

p: What do mean by armature reaction? How does armature reaction vary in a synchronous generator when supplying loads at different power factors?
Paper 2082 Bhadra ENEE 253.r: Armature reaction. The effect of the armature (stator) mmf on the main field flux is called armature reaction. A loaded alternator has a current-carrying armature winding that sets up a rotating mmf $F_a$ which rotates at synchronous speed, so it is stationary with respect to the field mmf $F_f$. The resultant air-gap flux is the phasor sum of the two, so its magnitude, distribution and position change with the load current and the power factor.

p: Two station generators A and B operate in parallel. Station capacity of A is 50 MW and that of B is 25 MW. Full load speed regulation of station A is 3% and B is 3.5%. Calculate the load sharing if the connected load is 50 MW, no load frequency is 50 Hz. Comment on the answer.

It separates the armature leakage-reactance drop from the armature-reaction mmf, and it takes the saturation of the magnetic circuit into account (the emf method does not, so it is pessimistic). Data needed from tests 1. Open-circuit characteristic (OCC): the generated emf against the field current $I_f$ at rated speed. 2. The excitation system of a synchronous machine is the equipment that supplies the d.c. field current to the rotor: a main exciter (a d.c. generator on the shaft, or a static/brushless a.c. exciter with rectifier), the field rheostat or automatic voltage regulator (AVR) controlling the field current, the slip rings and brushes (or rotating diodes), and the field-suppression and protection equipment. In a synchronous motor it also supplies the d.c. field for pull-in and runs the motor as an adjustable power-factor machine. Effect of changing excitation at constant load (constant $P$, constant $V$, constant $f$).

p: Write 3 advantages of abc to dq0 transformation. Prove that I$_{abc}$ = [T] i$_{dq0}$
Paper 2082 Bhadra ENEE 253.r: Three advantages of the abc to dq0 (Park) transformation 1. It converts the time-varying inductances of a salient-pole machine (which depend on $\theta$) into constants, so the machine equations become ordinary linear differential equations with constant coefficients. 2. Balanced sinusoidal a.c. quantities become d.c. quantities ($i_d$, $i_q$), so PI controllers can be used (vector / field-oriented control) and the steady state is an equilibrium point instead of an oscillation. 3. The three-phase system is reduced to decoupled axes: $d$ and $q$ (flux and torque producing parts) and the zero-sequence axis ($0$) for unbalance, which simplifies fault, stability and transient studies;

p: Describe operating principle and characteristics of shaded pole single phase motor with necessary diagrams.
Paper 2082 Bhadra ENEE 253.r: Shaded-pole single-phase motor. Construction: a salient-pole stator with a concentrated single-phase coil; a shading coil (one short-circuited copper ring or band) embraces about one third of each pole face. The rotor is a squirrel-cage rotor. Principle. The alternating main flux $\Phi_m$ is divided into $\Phi_u$ (unshaded part) and $\Phi_s$ (shaded part). The flux through the shaded part induces an emf $E_s$ in the shading ring, which is $90^\circ$ behind $\Phi_s$. The short-circuit current $I_s$ it drives lags $E_s$ by the ring's impedance angle and produces its own flux, so the net shaded-part flux $\Phi_s$ lags the unshaded flux $\Phi_u$ by a small angle $\gamma$ (about $30^\circ$).

p: What is hunting in synchronous machines? Explain in details and how they reduced.
Paper 2083 Baishakh ENEE 253.r: Hunting. When a synchronous machine is running synchronously, the rotor holds a fixed load angle $\delta$ with respect to the stator rotating field. A sudden change of load or of prime-mover torque makes the rotor swing about its new equilibrium position: it overshoots, the synchronising torque pulls it back, it overshoots the other way, and so on. This periodic oscillation of the rotor about the synchronous speed is called hunting (phase swinging). Mechanism (swing equation).

p: Illustrate the concept of d axis and q axis in synchronous machine. Why dq0 plane in synchronous machine is needed?

The axis of the rotor field pole is the direct axis (d-axis), where the air gap is smallest and the reluctance is least. The axis 90 electrical degrees from it, along the interpolar space, is the quadrature axis (q-axis), where the reluctance is largest. In the usual convention the q-axis leads the d-axis by 90° and the emf $E_f$ lies on the q-axis.

Paper 2081 Chaitra ENEX 101.r: Barkhausen criteria. An amplifier of gain $A$ with a positive-feedback network of feedback factor $\beta$ produces sustained oscillations at a frequency $f_0$ if at that frequency 1. the magnitude of the loop gain is unity, $\ |A\beta| = 1$, and 2. the total phase shift around the loop is $0^\circ$ or an integer multiple of $360^\circ$ (the feedback is positive). (If $|A\beta| < 1$ the oscillations die out; if $|A\beta| > 1$ they grow until the amplifier saturates, so for start-up $|A\beta|$ is made slightly greater than 1 and the amplitude is then limited by non-linearity.) Paper 2081 Baishakh EX 101.r: Trans-conductance ($g_m$). The ratio of the output current to the input voltage of a two-port device or amplifier (a voltage-controlled current source, VCCS). Its unit is the siemens (A/V): $$g_m = \frac{I_{out}}{V_{in}}$$ For a BJT $g_m = \dfrac{\Delta I_C}{\Delta V_{BE}} = \dfrac{I_C}{V_T}$ (about 40 mS per mA at room temperature); for a FET $g_m = \dfrac{\Delta I_D}{\Delta V_{GS}}$. Its unit is the ohm: $$r_m = \frac{V_{out}}{I_{in}}$$ An op-amp transimpedance amplifier (photodiode amplifier) has $V_o = -I_{in}R_f$, i.e. $r_m = -R_f$. Gain.

p: Why BJT is bipolar and FET is unipolar? Design β-independent type DC biased common collector amplifier. Given parameters are: V$_{CC}$ = 20 V, I$_C$ = 2 mA, and β = 100. Use firm biasing method.

Both electrons and holes take part in conduction across the two p-n junctions, hence bi-polar. p: Explain the role of bypass capacitor in amplifier circuits. Draw the small signal equivalent circuit of a common base amplifier circuit and find its input impedance, output impedance and voltage gain.
Paper 2083 Baishakh ENEX 151.r: Role of the bypass capacitor. A bypass capacitor (for example C$_E$ across R$_E$ in a CE stage) offers a very small reactance X$_C$ = 1/(2πfC) at the signal frequency, so it short-circuits the a.c. signal to ground around the resistor while it is an open circuit for d.c. Hence (i) the biasing resistor R$_E$ keeps the Q-point stable (d.c. negative feedback) and (ii) the signal sees no emitter degeneration, so the full gain is obtained (A$_v$ = -R$_C$/r$_e$ instead of -R$_C$/(r$_e$+R$_E$)). In the common-base amplifier the base capacitor C$_B$ is a bypass capacitor that holds the base at a.c. ground. It is chosen so that X$_C$ ≤ R/10 at the lowest signal frequency.

A thin n-type channel is physically built in between them (by diffusion or implantation). A very thin layer of SiO$_2$ (about 10 to 100 nm) covers the channel, and the metal gate is deposited on the oxide. Source and drain have metal contacts; the substrate is usually connected to the source. Because the gate is insulated by the oxide, the gate current is practically zero (input resistance about 10$^{10}$ to 10$^{15}$ Ω).

p: Describe the operation of mod-12 asynchronous counter using negative-edge triggered T flip-flops with neat logic circuit diagram and timing diagram.
Paper 2081 Chaitra ENEX 203.r: Mod-12 asynchronous (ripple) counter with negative-edge triggered T flip-flops. $2^4=16>12$, so four flip-flops $FF_0\ldots FF_3$ ($Q_0$ is the LSB) are used, all with $T=1$ (toggle mode). The external clock drives $FF_0$; the output $Q_0$ clocks $FF_1$, $Q_1$ clocks $FF_2$ and $Q_2$ clocks $FF_3$. A negative-edge triggered flip-flop toggles when its clock input goes from 1 to 0, i.e. when the previous stage output falls from 1 to 0, so the chain counts up in binary $0000\to0001\to\ldots\to1011$. Resetting at 12: the counter must skip the states 1100 to 1111.

A crystal oscillator followed by a frequency divider chain (decade dividers) produces an accurate time base, for example a 1 s or 0.1 s pulse; a gate-control flip-flop (the time-base pulse toggles it) generates the gate signal, which is the second input of the AND gate. A decade counter (BCD counters) counts the number of pulses that pass through the AND gate during the gate time;

p: What is an ASCII code? Design 3-bit binary to Gray code converter with truth table.
Paper 2082 Kartik ENEX 203.r: ASCII code. ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) is a 7-bit alphanumeric code (128 characters; an 8th bit may be used for parity or for the extended set). It represents the digits 0-9 ($30_{16}$-$39_{16}$), the upper-case letters ($41_{16}$-$5A_{16}$), the lower-case letters ($61_{16}$-$7A_{16}$), punctuation and control characters (CR $=0D_{16}$, LF $=0A_{16}$, ESC $=1B_{16}$). Example: 'A' $=100\,0001_2=65_{10}$, '0' $=011\,0000_2=48_{10}$. It lets computers, keyboards and printers exchange text. 3-bit binary to Gray converter. Gray code: $G_2=B_2$ and each other bit is the XOR of two adjacent binary bits.

Examples are registers, counters, sequence detectors. Types: synchronous (common clock) and asynchronous; Mealy and Moore machines. Positive-edge-triggered JK flip-flop. The parallel data inputs are $D_3D_2D_1D_0$, each connected to the D input of its own flip-flop, and the outputs are $Q_3Q_2Q_1Q_0$ (all four available at the same time). Paper 2082 Bhadra ENEX 253.r: Effective address (EA) is the actual memory address of the operand, computed from the address field of the instruction and the addressing mode: the mode field tells the control unit how to turn the instruction's address field into the operand. The common modes are given below, with a worked example: the instruction is stored at address 200 (its address field 500 is at 201), so after fetching PC = 202; register R1 = 400, index register XR = 100, with memory contents M[399] = 450, M[400] = 700, M[500] = 800, M[600] = 900, M[702] = 325, M[800] = 300.

p: Differentiate between hardwired control unit and microprogrammed control unit. Describe address sequencing with the help of block diagram.
Paper 2082 Bhadra ENEX 253.r: Function of the control unit. The control unit is the part of the processor that directs the operation of everything else. For each instruction it (1) fetches the instruction and decodes the opcode, (2) generates, in the correct order and at the correct clock pulse, the control signals (register load enables, ALU function select, memory read/write, bus gating, I/O strobes) that open the data paths for each micro-operation, (3) sequences the instruction cycle (fetch, decode, execute, interrupt), and (4) responds to external signals such as interrupts, reset and bus requests, using the flags of the status register for conditional operations.

p: Explain associative cache mapping technique with suitable example. Describe the Least Recently Used (LRU) replacement algorithm with case example of miss and hit.
Paper 2082 Bhadra ENEX 253.r: Associative (fully associative) cache mapping. A main-memory block can be placed in any line of the cache. The memory address is split only into a tag (the block number) and the word offset, $\text{Address} = \text{Tag} \,|\, \text{Word}$. To look up a word, the tag is compared simultaneously with the tags of all cache lines using an associative memory (content-addressable memory); a match is a hit and the word offset selects the word, otherwise it is a miss and a block is fetched, replacing a line chosen by a replacement algorithm when the cache is full. Advantage: most flexible, no conflict misses, best hit ratio.

p: Write down the flowchart of Booth's Multiplication algorithm. Multiply $7 \times -5 = -35$ using Booth's Multiplication algorithm.
Paper 2082 Bhadra ENEX 253.r: Flowchart of Booth's algorithm: Booth's algorithm multiplies two signed numbers in two's complement. It scans the multiplier bits in pairs $Q_0 Q_{-1}$ ($Q_{-1}$ is an extra bit appended on the right, initially 0): pair $10$ marks the start of a run of 1s (subtract the multiplicand, $A \leftarrow A - M$), pair $01$ marks the end of a run of 1s (add, $A \leftarrow A + M$), and $00$ or $11$ means no operation. After each step the register $A, Q, Q_{-1}$ is arithmetic-shifted right by one bit (the sign bit of $A$ is copied). After $n$ cycles the $2n$-bit product is in $A{:}Q$.

p: Explain about how multicore processors improve the hardware performance with respect to parallelism and power consumption. <!-- SOLUTIONS -->
Paper 2082 Bhadra ENEX 253.r: Multicore processors and hardware performance. The performance of a single core was raised for decades by higher clock frequency and deeper instruction-level parallelism, but both ran into the power wall (dynamic power $P = C V^{2} f$ with the supply voltage $V$ having to rise with $f$, so power grows roughly as $f^{3}$), the memory wall and the limited instruction-level parallelism in programs. A multicore processor puts several simpler cores on one chip instead. Parallelism. Each core executes its own thread, so the chip does several streams of instructions at the same time: thread-level parallelism (and data-level parallelism with SIMD units in each core).

Paper 2083 Baishakh ENEX 253.r: Set associative mapping. The cache is divided into $S$ sets of $k$ lines each ($k$-way set associative). A main-memory block can go into exactly one set (set = block number mod $S$) but into any of the $k$ lines of that set. It is a compromise between direct mapping (fast, but conflict misses) and fully associative mapping (flexible, but an expensive comparison of all tags).

Explain the different types of pipeline hazards with example.
How does DMA overcome the problems of programmed I/O and interrupt-driven I/O in computer organization.
Paper 2083 Baishakh ENEX 253.r: Programmed I/O. The CPU starts the transfer and then busy-waits (polls the device status) for every byte or word; data goes device, CPU register, memory, so the CPU is occupied for the whole transfer. Interrupt-driven I/O. The CPU starts the operation and continues with other work; the device interrupts when it is ready, and the CPU runs an interrupt service routine that moves one word. There is no busy waiting, but the CPU still moves every word and pays the overhead of saving and restoring the context at each interrupt (a big transfer needs thousands of interrupts). DMA (direct memory access).

p: State the divergence theorem. A uniform sheet of charge $\rho_s = 20\epsilon_0$ C/m$^2$ is located in the plane $x = 2$ in free space. Paper 2082 Bhadra ENEX 254.r: Divergence theorem. The total outward flux of a vector field through a closed surface equals the volume integral of its divergence over the enclosed volume: $$\oint_S\vec D\cdot d\vec S = \int_V(\nabla\cdot\vec D)\,dv$$ Sheet. $\rho_s = 20\epsilon_0$ gives a uniform field of magnitude $\dfrac{\rho_s}{2\epsilon_0} = 10$ V/m: $\vec E_s = +10\,\hat a_x$ for $x > 2$ and $-10\,\hat a_x$ for $x < 2$.
