Define bar pendulum. Prove that there are four points in a bar pendulum having the same time period. OR Prove that the average kinetic and average potential energies of a particle executing simple harmonic motion are equal.
Paper 2082 Shrawan SH 402.r: Bar pendulum. A bar pendulum is a compound (physical) pendulum made of a long uniform metal bar with holes drilled at equal intervals along its length. It can be suspended from any hole and made to oscillate in a vertical plane about a horizontal axis through that hole. Time period. Let the bar of mass $m$ be suspended at a point $O$ at distance $l$ from the centre of gravity $G$, and let $k$ be the radius of gyration about the parallel axis through $G$. For a small angular displacement $\theta$ the restoring torque is $mgl\theta$, and the moment of inertia about $O$ is $I = m(k^2 + l^2)$.

p: A circuit has $L = 12\ \text{mH}$, $C = 1.6\ \mu\text{F}$ and $R = 1.5\ \Omega$. (i) After what time $t$ will the amplitude of the charge oscillations drop to one half of its initial value? (ii) To how many periods of oscillation does this correspond?
Paper 2082 Shrawan SH 402.r: Charge in a damped LCR circuit: $q = q_0e^{-Rt/2L}\cos(\omega't + \phi)$, so the amplitude is $q_0e^{-Rt/2L}$. (i) Amplitude $= \tfrac12q_0$: $$e^{-Rt/2L} = \frac12\ \Rightarrow\ t = \frac{2L\ln2}{R} = \frac{2(12\times10^{-3})(0.6931)}{1.5} = 1.109\times10^{-2}\ \text{s}$$ $$\boxed{t\approx11.1\ \text{ms}}$$ (ii) Angular frequency of the damped oscillation: $$\omega' = \sqrt{\frac1{LC} - \frac{R^2}{4L^2}} = \sqrt{5.208\times10^{7} - 3.9\times10^{3}} = 7.217\times10^3\ \text{rad/s}$$ Period $T = \dfrac{2\pi}{\omega'} = 8.707\times10^{-4}$ s. Number of periods $$n = \frac tT = \frac{1.109\times10^{-2}}{8.707\times10^{-4}}\approx12.7$$ $$\boxed{\text{about 12.7 periods (roughly 13)}}$$

p: Give an account of bad acoustic properties of a hall and discuss the methods to improve these defects.
Paper 2082 Shrawan SH 402.r: Acoustics of a hall. A hall has good acoustics if every listener hears the sound clearly, with adequate loudness and without distortion. The common defects are: 1. Excessive reverberation. Sound persists after the source stops because of repeated reflections. If the reverberation time is too long, successive syllables overlap and speech becomes unintelligible. If it is too short the hall sounds dead. Sabine's formula gives $$T = \frac{0.161\,V}{\sum\alpha_iS_i}$$ where $V$ is the volume (m³), $S_i$ the area of surface $i$ and $\alpha_i$ its absorption coefficient. The optimum value is about $0.5$ s for small rooms and $1$–$1.5$ s for concert halls. 2. Echoes.

p: Explain the formation of Newton's rings in a reflected system of monochromatic light. Prove that in reflected light the diameters of the dark rings are proportional to the square root of natural numbers. OR Show that the intensity of the second-order maximum of Fraunhofer's single-slit diffraction is $\left(\dfrac2{5\pi}\right)^2$ times the intensity of the central maximum.
Paper 2082 Shrawan SH 402.r: Formation of Newton's rings. A plano-convex lens of large radius of curvature $R$ is placed with its convex surface on a flat glass plate, so a thin air film of varying thickness $t$ is formed, with $t = 0$ at the point of contact and $t$ increasing symmetrically outwards. Monochromatic light is allowed to fall nearly normally (through a $45^\circ$ glass plate) on the lens. Rays reflected from the lower surface of the lens and from the upper surface of the glass plate interfere. The locus of constant film thickness is a circle, so a system of alternating dark and bright concentric rings is seen, with a dark spot at the centre.

p: A plane transmission grating having 5000 lines/cm is used to obtain a spectrum of light from a sodium lamp in the second order. Calculate the angular separation between the two sodium lines whose wavelengths are $589\ \text{nm}$ and $589.6\ \text{nm}$.
Paper 2082 Shrawan SH 402.r: Grating element $d = \dfrac{1\ \text{cm}}{5000} = 2\times10^{-4}\ \text{cm} = 2\times10^{-6}\ \text{m}$. For order $n = 2$: $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$. $$\sin\theta_1 = \frac{2(589\times10^{-9})}{2\times10^{-6}} = 0.5890\ \Rightarrow\ \theta_1 = 36.086^\circ$$ $$\sin\theta_2 = \frac{2(589.6\times10^{-9})}{2\times10^{-6}} = 0.5896\ \Rightarrow\ \theta_2 = 36.129^\circ$$ $$\Delta\theta = \theta_2 - \theta_1 = 0.0425^\circ$$ Check with the dispersion formula: $$\Delta\theta\approx\frac{n\,\Delta\lambda}{d\cos\theta} = \frac{2(0.6\times10^{-9})}{(2\times10^{-6})(0.808)} = 7.4\times10^{-4}\ \text{rad} = 0.0425^\circ$$ $$\boxed{\Delta\theta\approx0.043^\circ\approx2.6'\ (\approx153'')}$$

p: Two lenses of focal lengths $8\ \text{cm}$ each are identical and co-axially separated by $4\ \text{cm}$. Determine the equivalent focal length of the combination. If the image is formed at infinity at a particular position of the object, find the object distance.
Paper 2082 Shrawan SH 402.r: Two thin lenses, $f_1 = f_2 = f = 8$ cm, separated by $d = 4$ cm. Equivalent focal length. $$\frac1F = \frac1{f_1} + \frac1{f_2} - \frac d{f_1f_2} = \frac18 + \frac18 - \frac4{64} = \frac{12}{64} = \frac3{16}$$ $$\boxed{F = \frac{16}3 = 5.33\ \text{cm}}$$ Object distance for an image at infinity. Final image at infinity means the rays leaving lens 2 are parallel, so the intermediate image $I_1$ formed by lens 1 must lie at the first focal point of lens 2, i.e. $8$ cm in front of lens 2. Lens 2 is $4$ cm beyond lens 1, so $I_1$ is $8 - 4 = 4$ cm in front of lens 1 (on the object side), a virtual image: $v_1 = -4$ cm.

p: Determine the electric field at a point on the axial line of a uniformly charged disc of radius $R$. OR Derive an expression for the electric potential on the axial line of an electric linear quadrupole. Also extend it for large distance.
The potential at any point due to a charge is given by $V = 2x^2y$. Determine the acceleration gained by an electron along the $x$-direction at the point $(-1,2)$.
Paper 2082 Shrawan SH 402.r: $V = 2x^2y$. The $x$-component of the electric field is $$E_x = -\frac{\partial V}{\partial x} = -4xy$$ At $(-1,\,2)$: $E_x = -4(-1)(2) = +8\ \text{V/m}$ (taking $V$ in volts and $x$, $y$ in metres), along $+x$. Paper 2082 Shrawan SH 402.r: Charging of a capacitor through a resistor. A capacitor $C$ is connected in series with a resistor $R$ and a battery of emf $V_0$ through a switch closed at $t = 0$, with the capacitor initially uncharged. At an instant $t$ let the charge on the capacitor be $q$ and the current $i = \dfrac{dq}{dt}$. By Kirchhoff's voltage law $$V_0 = iR + \frac qC = R\frac{dq}{dt} + \frac qC$$ $$\frac{dq}{dt} = \frac{CV_0 - q}{RC}\ \Rightarrow\ \int_0^q\frac{dq}{CV_0 - q} = \frac1{RC}\int_0^tdt$$ $$-\ln\frac{CV_0 - q}{CV_0} = \frac t{RC}$$ $$\boxed{q(t) = CV_0\left(1 - e^{-t/RC}\right) = q_0\left(1 - e^{-t/RC}\right)}$$ where $q_0 = CV_0$ is the final charge.

Paper 2082 Shrawan SH 402.r: Physical significance of the wave function $\psi$. - $\psi(\vec r,t)$ is the complex amplitude of the matter wave associated with a particle. It has no direct physical meaning by itself and is not measurable. - The quantity $|\psi|^2 = \psi\psi^*$ is the probability density: $|\psi|^2dV$ is the probability of finding the particle in the volume $dV$ at the point $\vec r$ at time $t$ (Born's interpretation). - Since the particle must be somewhere, $\psi$ is normalized: $\displaystyle\int|\psi|^2dV = 1$ over all space. - A physically acceptable $\psi$ must be single-valued, finite, continuous, with a continuous first derivative, and must vanish at infinity (so that it is square-integrable).

The ligand donates a lone pair into a vacant hybrid orbital of the metal ion; the geometry is fixed by the hybridisation, and the magnetism by the number of unpaired electrons, $\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM. (i) $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{4-}$. Oxidation state of Fe: $x-6=-4$, so $\text{Fe}^{2+}$, configuration $3d^6$. $\text{CN}^-$ is a strong-field ligand, so it forces the pairing of the $3d$ electrons (all six $d$ electrons occupy three $3d$ orbitals in pairs) and frees two $3d$ orbitals. These, along with one $4s$ and three $4p$ orbitals, undergo $d^2sp^3$ hybridisation. Six $\text{CN}^-$ donate pairs into these six hybrid orbitals (inner-orbital complex).

p: What are the important characteristics of explosives? Write the preparation and uses of TNT and Gun cotton.
Paper 2081 Bhadra SH 403.r: Characteristics of a good (important) explosive. 1. It must be stable to heat, shock, friction and storage, so that it can be handled and transported safely, and it must not deteriorate on storage. 2. It must be sensitive to a suitable detonator (primary explosive) and explode only when needed. 3. The decomposition must be highly exothermic, giving a large amount of heat (high temperature). 4. It must produce a large volume of gaseous products ($\text{CO}_2$, $\text{CO}$, $\text{N}_2$, steam) per unit mass, so that a high pressure builds up. 5. The reaction must be very fast (high velocity of detonation, $\sim$ $6$-$9$ km s$^{-1}$). 6.

p: Define lubricants and mention their functions. In which situation grease and solid lubricants are used? What are the requisites of a good paint?
Paper 2081 Bhadra SH 403.r: Lubricants. Substances that are applied between two moving or sliding surfaces to reduce friction and wear between them. They may be liquid (mineral oils, vegetable and animal oils, synthetic oils), semi-solid (greases) or solid (graphite, $\text{MoS}_2$). Functions of lubricants. 1. Reduce friction and wear and tear of moving parts, which increases machine life. 2. Reduce the loss of energy as heat, so the efficiency of the machine improves. 3. Act as a coolant, carrying away the heat produced. 4. Act as a seal (e.g. in piston rings, cylinders), prevent leakage and keep out dust and moisture. 5.

p: What is geometrical isomerism? Write the conditions required to show geometrical isomerism. Write all the possible stereoisomers of 2-bromo 3-chloro pentane.
Paper 2081 Bhadra SH 403.r: Geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism. A type of stereoisomerism in which compounds have the same structural formula but differ in the relative arrangement of atoms or groups in space about a double bond or a ring, because rotation about it is restricted. The isomer with the similar groups on the same side is cis (or Z), on opposite sides is trans (or E). Examples: cis- and trans-but-2-ene, maleic acid (cis) and fumaric acid (trans), cis- and trans-$[\text{Pt(NH}_3)_2\text{Cl}_2]$. Conditions for geometrical isomerism. 1. There must be restricted rotation about a bond: a C=C (or C=N, N=N) double bond, a ring, or a rigid metal complex. 2.

p: Describe the reaction mechanism of hydrolysis of methyl bromide with aqueous sodium hydroxide. Write the differences between S$_\text{N}$1 and S$_\text{N}$2 reactions mechanism.
Paper 2081 Bhadra SH 403.r: Hydrolysis of methyl bromide with aqueous NaOH: S$_\text{N}$2 mechanism. $\text{CH}_3\text{Br}$ is a primary (methyl) halide with practically no steric hindrance and cannot form a stable carbocation, so the substitution goes by a bimolecular, one-step (concerted) mechanism: $$\text{CH}_3\text{Br}+\text{OH}^-\to\text{CH}_3\text{OH}+\text{Br}^-$$ $$\text{rate} = k\,[\text{CH}_3\text{Br}][\text{OH}^-]\quad(\text{second order})$$ Mechanism. The nucleophile $\text{OH}^-$ attacks the electron-poor carbon from the side opposite to the leaving group Br (back-side attack, $180^\circ$).

p: What is an elimination reaction? Explain the mechanism of dehydrohalogenation of tertiary butyl bromide with caustic potash. <!-- SOLUTIONS -->
Paper 2081 Bhadra SH 403.r: Elimination reaction. A reaction in which two atoms or groups are removed from adjacent carbon atoms of a substrate (without being replaced) to form a multiple bond (a double bond). Dehydrohalogenation of an alkyl halide, loss of $\text{H}$ and $\text{X}$ using a base such as alcoholic KOH, is the commonest example: $$\text{R–CH}_2\text{–CH}_2\text{–X}+\text{KOH(alc.)}\to\text{R–CH}{=}\text{CH}_2+\text{KX}+\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Dehydrohalogenation of tert-butyl bromide with caustic potash (alcoholic KOH). The tertiary halide $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CBr}$ has nine equivalent $\beta$-hydrogens, and the strong base removes one of them.

By convention it is quoted as the reduction potential $E^\circ$; it measures the tendency of the species to be reduced. Galvanic vs electrolytic cell.

p: What is buffer capacity? Calculate the pH change in a buffer solution made by mixing $150\ \text{ml}$ of $0.5\ \text{M}$ acetic acid and $450\ \text{ml}$ of $0.1\ \text{M}$ sodium acetate in which $10\ \text{ml}$ of $0.2\ \text{M}$ HCl is added. ($K_a = 1.8\times10^{-5}$)

Calculation.

p: What are transition elements? Why are all the transition elements not considered as typical transition elements? Why are cupric salts blue in colour while cuprous salts are colourless?
What are low and high explosives? Write the preparation and uses of TNT and TNG.
Paper 2082 Baishakh SH 403.r: Low explosives. They burn (deflagrate) rapidly but not instantaneously (rate below about $1$–$2$ km/s) and produce a pushing action; no shock wave is formed. They are used as propellants, in fireworks and for blasting soft rocks. Examples: gunpowder (black powder), smokeless powder, safety fuse. High explosives. They detonate, with decomposition faster than the speed of sound ($3$–$9$ km/s) and a powerful shattering (brisance) effect, and are comparatively insensitive (need a detonator). Examples: TNT, TNG (nitroglycerine), RDX, PETN, dynamite, picric acid. TNT (2,4,6-trinitrotoluene).

What are the requisites of good paints?

Reduces friction and the wear and tear of surfaces (and the power loss) by forming a thin film that separates the rubbing surfaces. 2. p: What isomerism is shown by 3-hexene and why? Write all the possible enantiomers and diastereomers of 3-bromo-2-butanol.
Paper 2082 Baishakh SH 403.r: Isomerism in 3-hexene. $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}{=}\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ shows geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism, because rotation about the C=C double bond is restricted by the $\pi$ bond and each double-bond carbon carries two different groups (H and ethyl), so two spatial arrangements exist: cis-3-hexene (the two ethyl groups on the same side, $Z$) and trans-3-hexene (opposite sides, $E$). (It also shows position and chain isomerism with other hexenes.) Stereoisomers of 3-bromo-2-butanol, $\text{CH}_3\text{–C}^\text{H(OH)–C}^\text{HBr–CH}_3$.

In an S$_\text{N}$1 reaction the rate depends on only one species, the substrate (first order): $\text{rate} = k[\text{R–X}]$. It takes place in two steps through a carbocation intermediate and is typical for tertiary haloalkanes. Example: tert-butyl bromide with water or aqueous NaOH.

Paper 2082 Shrawan SH 403.r: Negative catalysis vs catalytic poisoning. | Negative catalysis | Catalytic poisoning | |---|---| | A substance (inhibitor or negative catalyst) decreases the rate of a reaction. | A substance (poison) destroys the activity of a positive catalyst. | | It acts on the reactants or the reaction path (for example by destroying a chain carrier). | It acts on the catalyst surface (strongly adsorbed, blocking the active sites). | | Example: glycerol or acetanilide retards decomposition of H$_2$O$_2$; tetraethyl lead retards knocking. | Example: As$_2$O$_3$ poisons Pt in the contact process; CO poisons Fe in the Haber process (H$_2$S poisons Fe).

p: What is a non-biodegradable polymer? Give the preparation and uses of polystyrene and epoxy resins.
What are transition elements? Explain the colour of transition elements on the basis of d to d transition.
Paper 2082 Shrawan SH 403.r: Transition elements. The elements that have partly filled $d$ orbitals in their ground state or in any of their common oxidation states are called transition elements (the $d$-block elements Sc to Cu in the 3d series, and so on). Zn, Cd, Hg (d$^{10}$) are not true transition elements. Colour and $d$–$d$ transition. In a free ion, the five $d$ orbitals are degenerate. In a complex, the ligands' field splits them into two sets, $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ (octahedral), separated by an energy $\Delta_o$ (crystal field splitting).

p: What are d-block elements? Why does the number of unpaired electrons make the compound paramagnetic? Calculate the magnetic moment if the metal ion contains five unpaired electrons.
Paper 2082 Shrawan SH 403.r: $d$-block elements. The elements of groups 3–12 in which the last electron enters the penultimate $(n-1)d$ subshell are called $d$-block elements (general configuration $(n-1)d^{1-10}ns^{1-2}$). They comprise the 3d, 4d, 5d and 6d series. Unpaired electrons and paramagnetism. An electron has a spin and therefore a magnetic moment. Two electrons in the same orbital have opposite spins, so their moments cancel, and an atom or ion with all electrons paired is repelled slightly by a magnetic field (diamagnetic).

p: Define primary explosives, low explosives and high explosives. Write the preparation and uses of nitrocellulose.
Paper 2082 Shrawan SH 403.r: Explosives. An explosive is a substance that, on suitable initiation by heat, shock or friction, undergoes very rapid exothermic decomposition producing a large volume of hot gases, a sudden pressure rise and a loud report. - Primary (initiating) explosives: extremely sensitive to heat, shock or friction; explode on slight stimulus and are used to set off other explosives (detonators, percussion caps). Examples: mercury fulminate $\text{Hg(ONC)}_2$, lead azide $\text{Pb(N}_3)_2$, lead styphnate. - Low explosives: burn (deflagrate) at a comparatively slow rate (below about $1$–$2$ km/s) with a pushing effect, producing gas without a detonation wave.

p: Explain why S$_\text{N}$1 reaction gives the products with both retention and inversion of configuration but S$_\text{N}$2 gives only inversion of configuration. Write the mechanism of the reaction between tertiary alkyl halide and aqueous sodium hydroxide.
Paper 2082 Shrawan SH 403.r: S$_\text{N}$1 versus S$_\text{N}$2 stereochemistry. S$_\text{N}$1 (unimolecular nucleophilic substitution) takes place in two steps. In the slow step the leaving group departs to give a planar $sp^2$ carbocation (achiral at that carbon). The nucleophile is free to attack this flat cation from either face with nearly equal probability: attack from the face from which the leaving group left gives retention, attack from the opposite face gives inversion, so a (nearly) racemic mixture results. (A slight excess of inversion occurs because the departing ion pair shields the front face.) S$_\text{N}$2 (bimolecular) is a single-step, concerted reaction.

p: What is meant by bimolecular elimination reaction? Describe the mechanism for the dehydrohalogenation of a $3^\circ$ alkyl halide. <!-- SOLUTIONS -->
Paper 2082 Shrawan SH 403.r: Bimolecular elimination (E2). An E2 reaction is a one-step (concerted) elimination in which a strong base removes a $\beta$-hydrogen at the same time as the leaving group departs from the $\alpha$-carbon, forming a C=C double bond. The rate depends on the concentrations of both the alkyl halide and the base (second order): $$\text{rate} = k[\text{R–X}][\text{B}^-]$$ Dehydrohalogenation of a tertiary alkyl halide.

p: Show that $x\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} + y\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} = \sin 2u$, where $u = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x^3 + y^3}{x - y}\right)$.
If $x = r\cos\theta,\ y = r\sin\theta$, then find $\dfrac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(r,\theta)}$.
Paper 2082 Bhadra ENSH 151.r: (a) $f = \tan u = \dfrac{x^3 + y^3}{x - y}$ is homogeneous of degree $3 - 1 = 2$. By Euler's theorem $xf_x + yf_y = 2f$, i.e. $\sec^2u\,(xu_x + yu_y) = 2\tan u$, so $$x\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + y\frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = 2\sin u\cos u = \sin2u$$ (b) $\dfrac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(r,\theta)} = \begin{vmatrix}\cos\theta & -r\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta & r\cos\theta\end{vmatrix} = r\cos^2\theta + r\sin^2\theta = \boxed{r}$.

p: Find the moment about the $x$-axis of the lamina bounded by $y = x$ and $y = x^2$ with density $\rho(x,y) = 1$.
Find the area of the region bounded by the curves $x = y^2$ and $x = 2y - y^2$.
Paper 2082 Bhadra ENSH 151.r: (a) The curves meet at $x = 0$ and $x = 1$, with $x^2\le y\le x$. The moment about the $x$-axis is $$M_x = \iint y\rho\,dA = \int_0^1\int_{x^2}^x y\,dy\,dx = \int_0^1\frac{x^2 - x^4}{2}\,dx = \frac12\left(\frac13 - \frac15\right) = \boxed{\frac1{15}}$$ (b) The curves meet where $y^2 = 2y - y^2$, i.e. $y = 0$ and $y = 1$, and for $0<y<1$ we have $y^2 < 2y - y^2$. Integrating with respect to $x$ first, $$A = \int_0^1\left[(2y - y^2) - y^2\right]dy = \left[y^2 - \frac{2y^3}{3}\right]_0^1 = \boxed{\frac13}\ \text{square units}$$

p: A particle moves along the curve $x = 3\cos t,\ y = 3\sin t,\ z = 6t$. Find the velocity and acceleration at time $t = \dfrac\pi3$.
If $\vec F = \operatorname{grad}(x^3 + y^3 + z^3 - 3xyz)$, then find $\operatorname{div}\vec F$.
Find the work done by the force $\vec F = x^2\vec i - xy\vec j$ along the path $C$ given by $x^2 + y^2 = 1,\ z = 0$.
Paper 2082 Bhadra ENSH 151.r: (a) $\vec r = (3\cos t, 3\sin t, 6t)$. $\vec v = (-3\sin t, 3\cos t, 6)$; at $t = \tfrac\pi3$: $\vec v = -\tfrac{3\sqrt3}{2}\vec i + \tfrac32\vec j + 6\vec k$, speed $\sqrt{9 + 36} = 3\sqrt5$. $\vec a = (-3\cos t, -3\sin t, 0)$; at $t = \tfrac\pi3$: $\vec a = -\tfrac32\vec i - \tfrac{3\sqrt3}{2}\vec j$, magnitude $3$. (b) $\vec F = \nabla\phi = (3x^2 - 3yz,\ 3y^2 - 3xz,\ 3z^2 - 3xy)$, so $$\operatorname{div}\vec F = 6x + 6y + 6z = \boxed{6(x + y + z)}$$ (c) $W = \oint_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r = \oint_Cx^2\,dx - xy\,dy$.

p: State the existence conditions of the Laplace transform. Obtain the Laplace transform of $t\sin3t$.
Find the inverse Laplace transform of $F(s) = \cot^{-1}(s+1)$.
Paper 2082 Bhadra ENSH 151.r: (a) Existence: $\mathcal L\{f\}$ exists if $f(t)$ is piecewise continuous on every finite interval $[0, b]$ and of exponential order, i.e. $|f(t)|\le Me^{at}$ for $t\ge T$ (these conditions are sufficient). Since $\mathcal L\{\sin3t\} = \dfrac{3}{s^2 + 9}$ and $\mathcal L\{tf(t)\} = -\dfrac{d}{ds}F(s)$, $$\mathcal L\{t\sin3t\} = -\frac{d}{ds}\left(\frac{3}{s^2 + 9}\right) = \boxed{\frac{6s}{(s^2 + 9)^2}}$$ (b) Let $F(s) = \cot^{-1}(s+1)$. Then $F'(s) = -\dfrac{1}{1 + (s+1)^2}$ and $\mathcal L^{-1}\{F'(s)\} = -e^{-t}\sin t$. Since $\mathcal L^{-1}\{F'(s)\} = -t f(t)$, $$t f(t) = e^{-t}\sin t \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{f(t) = \frac{e^{-t}\sin t}{t}}$$

p: Find the rank of the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2 & -1 & 3\\ 2 & 4 & 1 & -2\\ 3 & 6 & 3 & -7\end{pmatrix}$.
Reduce the quadratic form $Q(X) = 17x_1^2 - 30x_1x_2 + 17x_2^2$ into canonical form.
Express the function $f(x) = 4 + 2x + x^2$ in terms of Legendre's polynomials.
Find the extreme values of the function $x^2 + y^2 + z^2$ subject to the condition $x + y + z = 1$.
Paper 2082 Bhadra ENSH 151.r: Let $f = x^2 + y^2 + z^2$, $g = x + y + z - 1$. From $F = f - \lambda g$: $2x = \lambda,\ 2y = \lambda,\ 2z = \lambda$, so $x = y = z$. The constraint gives $3x = 1$, so $x = y = z = \dfrac13$ and $\lambda = \dfrac23$. $$f\left(\tfrac13, \tfrac13, \tfrac13\right) = 3\cdot\frac19 = \boxed{\frac13}$$ This is the minimum value (it is the squared distance from the origin to the plane $x + y + z = 1$, namely $(1/\sqrt3)^2$); the function has no maximum on the plane since $x^2 + y^2 + z^2\to\infty$.

p: Prove that the necessary and sufficient condition for a vector function $\vec a$ of a scalar variable $t$ to have constant direction is $\vec a\times\dfrac{d\vec a}{dt} = \vec0$.
State Green's theorem in the plane and, using it, find the area of the hypocycloid $\left(\dfrac xa\right)^{2/3} + \left(\dfrac yb\right)^{2/3} = 1$.
Paper 2082 Bhadra ENSH 151.r: Green's theorem. If $P(x,y), Q(x,y)$ have continuous first partial derivatives on a region $R$ bounded by a piecewise smooth simple closed curve $C$ traversed counter-clockwise, then $$\oint_C(P\,dx + Q\,dy) = \iint_R\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)dx\,dy$$ Taking $P = -y,\ Q = x$ gives $A = \dfrac12\oint_C(x\,dy - y\,dx)$. For the hypocycloid, $x = a\cos^3t,\ y = b\sin^3t$, $0\le t\le2\pi$: $dx = -3a\cos^2t\sin t\,dt$, $dy = 3b\sin^2t\cos t\,dt$, so $x\,dy - y\,dx = 3ab\sin^2t\cos^2t\,dt$.

p: Using the Laplace transform, solve the initial value problem $x'' - 3x' + 2x = e^{-t}$, $x(0) = 0$, $x'(0) = 1$.
Solve the differential equation $y'' + xy' + y = 0$ by using the power series method.
a: Prove that $J_{5/2}(x) = \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{\pi x}}\left\{\dfrac{3 - x^2}{x^2}\sin x - \dfrac3x\cos x\right\}$, where the symbols have their usual meanings. <!-- SOLUTIONS -->
Paper 2082 Bhadra ENSH 151.r: Let $y = \sum a_nx^n$. Then $y'' = \sum(n+2)(n+1)a_{n+2}x^n$, $xy' = \sum na_nx^n$. Coefficient of $x^n$: $(n+2)(n+1)a_{n+2} + (n+1)a_n = 0$, so $$a_{n+2} = -\frac{a_n}{n+2}$$ Even terms: $a_2 = -\dfrac{a_0}{2},\ a_4 = \dfrac{a_0}{2\cdot4},\ a_6 = -\dfrac{a_0}{2\cdot4\cdot6}$, i.e. $a_{2k} = \dfrac{(-1)^ka_0}{2^kk!}$, which sums to $a_0e^{-x^2/2}$. Odd terms: $a_3 = -\dfrac{a_1}{3},\ a_5 = \dfrac{a_1}{3\cdot5},\ a_7 = -\dfrac{a_1}{3\cdot5\cdot7}$. $$\boxed{y = a_0\left(1 - \frac{x^2}{2} + \frac{x^4}{8} - \cdots\right) + a_1\left(x - \frac{x^3}{3} + \frac{x^5}{15} - \frac{x^7}{105} + \cdots\right) = a_0e^{-x^2/2} + a_1\left(x - \frac{x^3}{3} + \frac{x^5}{15} - \cdots\right)}$$ OR.

p: If $u = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x^2 + y^2}{x + y}\right)$, then show that $x\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} + y\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} = \tan u$.
If $u = xyz,\ v = xy + yz + zx,\ w = x + y + z$, find the Jacobian $\dfrac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)}$.
Paper 2083 Baishakh ENSH 151.r: (a) $f = \sin u = \dfrac{x^2 + y^2}{x + y}$ is homogeneous of degree $n = 1$. Euler: $xf_x + yf_y = f$, i.e. $\cos u\left(xu_x + yu_y\right) = \sin u$: $$x\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} + y\frac{\partial u}{\partial y} = \frac{\sin u}{\cos u} = \tan u$$ (b) $\dfrac{\partial(u,v,w)}{\partial(x,y,z)} = \begin{vmatrix}yz & xz & xy\\ y+z & x+z & x+y\\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}$. Paper 2083 Baishakh ENSH 151.r: Let $f = x^2 + xy + y^2 + 3z^2$, $g = x + 2y + 4z - 60$. Setting the partial derivatives of $f - \lambda g$ to zero: $2x + y = \lambda,\ x + 2y = 2\lambda,\ 6z = 4\lambda$. From the first two, $3x = 0$, so $x = 0$, $y = \lambda$, $z = \tfrac{2\lambda}{3}$. The constraint: $2\lambda + \tfrac{8\lambda}{3} = 60 \Rightarrow \lambda = \tfrac{90}{7}$. The stationary point is $$\left(0,\ \frac{90}{7},\ \frac{60}{7}\right),\qquad u = \frac{90^2 + 3\cdot60^2}{49} = \boxed{\frac{2700}{7}\approx385.7}$$ Since $f$ is a positive-definite quadratic form on the constraint plane, this is the minimum (there is no maximum).

p: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\int_x^\infty\dfrac{e^{-y}}{y}\,dy\,dx$ by changing the order of integration.
Paper 2083 Baishakh ENSH 151.r: The region is $0\le x\le y<\infty$. Changing the order: $y$ from $0$ to $\infty$, $x$ from $0$ to $y$: $$I = \int_0^\infty\frac{e^{-y}}{y}\left[\int_0^ydx\right]dy = \int_0^\infty\frac{e^{-y}}{y}\cdot y\,dy = \int_0^\infty e^{-y}\,dy = \boxed{1}$$

For $P, Q$ with continuous first partial derivatives on a region $R$ bounded by a piecewise smooth simple closed curve $C$ (counter-clockwise), $$\oint_C(P\,dx + Q\,dy) = \iint_R\left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)dx\,dy$$ Choosing $P = -y$, $Q = x$: $A = \dfrac12\oint_C(x\,dy - y\,dx)$. For the astroid $x = a\cos^3t,\ y = a\sin^3t$: $x\,dy - y\,dx = 3a^2\sin^2t\cos^2t\,dt$, so $$A = \frac{3a^2}{2}\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2t\cos^2t\,dt = \frac{3a^2}{2}\cdot\frac\pi4 = \boxed{\frac{3\pi a^2}{8}}$$

p: Find the Laplace transform of $\dfrac{1 - e^t}{t}$.
Find the inverse Laplace transform of $\dfrac{s}{(s+2)^3}$.
Paper 2081 Ashwin SH 151.r: (a) $\mathcal L\{1 - e^t\} = \dfrac1s - \dfrac1{s-1}$. Using $\mathcal L\{f(t)/t\} = \int_s^\infty F(p)\,dp$, $$\mathcal L\left\{\frac{1-e^t}{t}\right\} = \int_s^\infty\left(\frac1p - \frac1{p-1}\right)dp = \Big[\ln\frac{p}{p-1}\Big]_s^\infty = -\ln\frac{s}{s-1} = \boxed{\ln\frac{s-1}{s}}\quad(s>1)$$ (b) Write $s = (s+2) - 2$: $\dfrac{s}{(s+2)^3} = \dfrac{1}{(s+2)^2} - \dfrac{2}{(s+2)^3}$. By the first shifting theorem, $\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\dfrac1{(s+2)^2}\right\} = te^{-2t}$ and $\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\dfrac{2}{(s+2)^3}\right\} = t^2e^{-2t}$: $$\boxed{\mathcal L^{-1}\left\{\frac{s}{(s+2)^3}\right\} = (t - t^2)e^{-2t}}$$

Paper 2081 Ashwin SH 151.r: Let $f = x^2 + xy + y^2 + 3z^2$ and $g = x + 2y + 4z - 60$. Form $F = f - \lambda g$ and set its partial derivatives to zero: $$2x + y = \lambda,\qquad x + 2y = 2\lambda,\qquad 6z = 4\lambda \;\Rightarrow\; z = \frac{2\lambda}{3}$$ From the first two, $2(2x + y) = x + 2y \Rightarrow 3x = 0$, so $x = 0$, $y = \lambda$. The constraint gives $0 + 2\lambda + \dfrac{8\lambda}{3} - 60 = 0 \Rightarrow \dfrac{14\lambda}{3} = 60 \Rightarrow \lambda = \dfrac{90}{7}$.

p: Prove that the necessary and sufficient condition for a vector function $\vec a$ of a scalar variable $t$ to have a constant direction is $\vec a\times\dfrac{d\vec a}{dt} = \vec 0$.
Paper 2081 Ashwin SH 151.r: Let $\vec a = a\,\hat e$, where $a = |\vec a|$ and $\hat e$ is the unit vector along $\vec a$. Then $\dfrac{d\vec a}{dt} = \dfrac{da}{dt}\hat e + a\dfrac{d\hat e}{dt}$ and $$\vec a\times\frac{d\vec a}{dt} = a\frac{da}{dt}(\hat e\times\hat e) + a^2\left(\hat e\times\frac{d\hat e}{dt}\right) = a^2\left(\hat e\times\frac{d\hat e}{dt}\right)$$ Necessity. If the direction is constant, $\hat e$ is constant, so $\dfrac{d\hat e}{dt} = \vec0$ and $\vec a\times\dfrac{d\vec a}{dt} = \vec 0$. Sufficiency. Suppose $\vec a\times\dfrac{d\vec a}{dt} = \vec0$ and $a\ne0$. Then $\hat e\times\dfrac{d\hat e}{dt} = \vec0$.

p: Find the area of the astroid $x^{2/3} + y^{2/3} = a^{2/3}$ using Green's theorem.
Paper 2081 Ashwin SH 151.r: By Green's theorem the area enclosed by a simple closed curve $C$ is $A = \dfrac12\oint_C(x\,dy - y\,dx)$. Parametrise the astroid as $x = a\cos^3t,\ y = a\sin^3t$, $0\le t\le2\pi$. Then $dx = -3a\cos^2t\sin t\,dt$ and $dy = 3a\sin^2t\cos t\,dt$, so $$x\,dy - y\,dx = 3a^2\left(\cos^4t\sin^2t + \sin^4t\cos^2t\right)dt = 3a^2\sin^2t\cos^2t\,dt$$ $$A = \frac{3a^2}{2}\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^2t\cos^2t\,dt = \frac{3a^2}{2}\cdot\frac14\int_0^{2\pi}\sin^22t\,dt = \frac{3a^2}{8}\cdot\pi$$ $$\boxed{A = \frac{3\pi a^2}{8}}$$

p: Using the Laplace transform technique, solve the initial value problem $y''(t) - y'(t) + 6y(t) = e^{-t}$, $y(0) = 0$, $y'(0) = 0$.
Paper 2081 Ashwin SH 151.r: Take Laplace transforms with $y(0) = y'(0) = 0$: $s^2Y - sY + 6Y = \dfrac{1}{s+1}$, so $$Y = \frac{1}{(s+1)(s^2 - s + 6)} = \frac{1/8}{s+1} - \frac{1}{8}\cdot\frac{s - 2}{s^2 - s + 6}$$ (partial fractions: $1 = A(s^2 - s + 6) + (Bs + C)(s+1)$ gives $A = \tfrac18$, $B = -\tfrac18$, $C = \tfrac14$.) Complete the square: $s^2 - s + 6 = \left(s - \tfrac12\right)^2 + \tfrac{23}{4}$, and $s - 2 = \left(s - \tfrac12\right) - \tfrac32$.

p: Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}3 & 2 & 2\\ 1 & 4 & 1\\ -2 & -4 & -1\end{pmatrix}$.
Solve $y'' - 4xy' + (4x^2 - 2)y = 0$ by the power series method. <!-- SOLUTIONS -->
Paper 2081 Ashwin SH 151.r: Let $y = \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nx^n$. Substituting into $y'' - 4xy' + (4x^2 - 2)y = 0$ and equating the coefficient of $x^n$: $$(n+2)(n+1)a_{n+2} - 4na_n + 4a_{n-2} - 2a_n = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; a_{n+2} = \frac{(4n+2)a_n - 4a_{n-2}}{(n+1)(n+2)}$$ (with $a_{-1} = a_{-2} = 0$). Computing: | $n$ | $a_{n+2}$ | |---|---| | $0$ | $a_2 = a_0$ | | $1$ | $a_3 = a_1$ | | $2$ | $a_4 = \dfrac{10a_2 - 4a_0}{12} = \dfrac{a_0}{2}$ | | $3$ | $a_5 = \dfrac{14a_3 - 4a_1}{20} = \dfrac{a_1}{2}$ | so $y = a_0\left(1 + x^2 + \dfrac{x^4}{2} + \cdots\right) + a_1\left(x + x^3 + \dfrac{x^5}{2} + \cdots\right)$.

p: State Euler's Theorem for Homogeneous function of two variables. If $u = \sec^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{x^3 + y^3}{x + y}\right)$ then show that $x\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} + y\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} = 2\cot u$
Paper 2078 Chaitra SH 451.r: Euler's theorem. If $f(x,y)$ is homogeneous of degree $n$ with continuous first partial derivatives, then $$\boxed{x\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} + y\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = nf}$$ Proof of the problem. Let $f = \sec u = \dfrac{x^3 + y^3}{x + y}$. Under $x\to tx,\ y\to ty$, $f\to\dfrac{t^3(x^3+y^3)}{t(x+y)} = t^2f$, so $f$ is homogeneous of degree $2$.

p: What are the criteria for a function $f(x,y)$ to have local maximum and minimum value? Using the criteria, evaluate the extreme value of $x^2 + y^2 + z^2$ subject to the condition $x + y + z = 1$.
Paper 2078 Chaitra SH 451.r: Criteria. Let $f(x,y)$ have continuous second partial derivatives. A stationary point $(a,b)$ satisfies $f_x = 0$ and $f_y = 0$. With $r = f_{xx}$, $s = f_{xy}$, $t = f_{yy}$ evaluated at $(a,b)$: - $rt - s^2>0$ and $r<0$: local maximum; - $rt - s^2>0$ and $r>0$: local minimum; - $rt - s^2<0$: saddle point (no extremum); - $rt - s^2 = 0$: the test fails (examine further). Extreme value. On $x + y + z = 1$, $z = 1 - x - y$, so $$f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2 + (1 - x - y)^2$$ $$\begin{gathered}f_x = 2x - 2(1 - x - y) = 4x + 2y - 2 = 0 \\ f_y = 4y + 2x - 2 = 0\end{gathered}$$ Subtracting: $x = y$; then $6x = 2$, $x = y = \dfrac13$, $z = \dfrac13$.

p: What advantage do we get by changing Cartesian integrals into polar form? Change the following integral into Polar and hence evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^a\int_0^{\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}}\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\,dy\,dx$
Paper 2078 Chaitra SH 451.r: Advantage of polar form. When the region of integration is a circle, sector or annulus, or the integrand contains $x^2 + y^2$, the polar limits become simple constants and the integrand simplifies (e.g. $\sqrt{x^2+y^2} = r$); integrals that are difficult or impossible in Cartesian form become elementary. Also $dx\,dy = r\,dr\,d\theta$. Change of variables. The region: $0\le x\le a$, $0\le y\le\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}$ is the quarter circle $x^2 + y^2\le a^2$ in the first quadrant. In polar coordinates $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$: $0\le r\le a$ and $0\le\theta\le\dfrac\pi2$.

p: Find by triple integration, the volume of the sphere $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = a^2$
Paper 2078 Chaitra SH 451.r: Sphere $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = a^2$. By symmetry $V = 8\times$ (volume in the first octant): $$V = 8\int_0^a\int_0^{\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}}\int_0^{\sqrt{a^2 - x^2 - y^2}}dz\,dy\,dx = 8\int_0^a\int_0^{\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}}\sqrt{a^2 - x^2 - y^2}\,dy\,dx$$ With $\rho^2 = a^2 - x^2$ the inner integral is a quarter-disc area integral: $\displaystyle\int_0^{\rho}\sqrt{\rho^2 - y^2}\,dy = \dfrac{\pi\rho^2}4$. So $$V = 8\int_0^a\frac\pi4(a^2 - x^2)\,dx = 2\pi\left[a^2x - \frac{x^3}3\right]_0^a = 2\pi\cdot\frac{2a^3}{3}$$ $$\boxed{V = \frac43\pi a^3}$$ (Spherical-polar check: $V = \displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\int_0^ar^2\sin\theta\,dr\,d\theta\,d\phi = 2\pi\cdot2\cdot\frac{a^3}3$.)

Find the radius and interval of convergence of the power series: $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(-1)^n(x+1)^n}{2^n}$. <!-- SOLUTIONS -->
Paper 2078 Chaitra SH 451.r: $$\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(-1)^n(x+1)^n}{2^n} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty\left(-\frac{x+1}{2}\right)^n$$ This is a geometric series with ratio $\rho = -\dfrac{x+1}2$; it converges iff $|\rho|<1$: $$\left|\frac{x+1}{2}\right|<1\ \Rightarrow\ |x + 1|<2\ \Rightarrow\ -3<x<1$$ Radius by the ratio test: $\left|\dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| = \dfrac12\Rightarrow R = 2$ (centre $x = -1$). Endpoints. $x = 1$: the series is $\sum(-1)^n\cdot1 = -1 + 1 - 1 + \cdots$, whose terms do not tend to $0$ (diverges). $x = -3$: the series is $\sum(1)^n = 1 + 1 + \cdots$ (diverges). $$\boxed{R = 2,\qquad\text{interval of convergence }-3<x<1}$$ (Its sum inside the interval is $\dfrac{\rho}{1 - \rho} = -\dfrac{x+1}{x+3}$.)

p: State Euler's Theorem for a homogeneous function in two variables. If $u = \cos^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{x+y}{\sqrt x + \sqrt y}\right)$ prove that: $x\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} + y\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} = -\dfrac12\cot u$.
Paper 2079 Chaitra SH 451.r: Euler's theorem. If $f(x,y)$ is a homogeneous function of degree $n$ (i.e. $f(tx,ty) = t^nf(x,y)$) with continuous first partial derivatives, then $$\boxed{x\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} + y\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = n\,f}$$ Proof of the problem. Let $f = \cos u = \dfrac{x+y}{\sqrt x+\sqrt y}$. Replace $x\to tx$, $y\to ty$: $f(tx,ty) = \dfrac{t(x+y)}{\sqrt t(\sqrt x+\sqrt y)} = t^{1/2}f(x,y)$, so $f$ is homogeneous of degree $n = \tfrac12$.

p: Find the extreme value of $x^2 + xy + y^2 + 3z^2$ connected by the relation $x + 2y + 4z = 60$.
Paper 2079 Chaitra SH 451.r: Minimize / extremize $f = x^2 + xy + y^2 + 3z^2$ subject to $g = x + 2y + 4z - 60 = 0$. Lagrange's method: $F = f + \lambda'g$, or equivalently $\nabla f = \lambda\nabla g$: $$\begin{gathered}2x + y = \lambda \\ x + 2y = 2\lambda \\ 6z = 4\lambda\end{gathered}$$ From the first two: subtract $2\times$(first) from second: $x + 2y - 4x - 2y = 2\lambda - 2\lambda\Rightarrow-3x = 0$, so $x = 0$. Then $y = \lambda$ and $z = \dfrac{2\lambda}3$. The constraint: $$0 + 2\lambda + \frac{8\lambda}{3} = 60\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{14\lambda}3 = 60\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda = \frac{90}7$$ $$\begin{gathered}x = 0 \\ y = \frac{90}7 \\ z = \frac{60}7\end{gathered}$$ Nature.

p: Evaluate: $\displaystyle\iint_Ry\,dy\,dx$ where $R$ is the region bounded by parabola $y^2 = 4x$ and $x^2 = 4y$.
Find the volume of ellipsoid $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} + \dfrac{z^2}{c^2} = 1$ using triple integration.
Show that the lines $\dfrac{x-5}{4} = \dfrac{y-7}{4} = \dfrac{z+3}{-5}$; $\dfrac{x-8}{7} = \dfrac{y-4}{1} = \dfrac{z-5}{3}$ are coplanar. Find the plane in which they lie.

Define the term 'Great Circle'. Find the equation of the sphere having the circle $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + 10y - 4z - 8 = 0,\ x + y + z = 3$ as a Great Circle.
Paper 2079 Chaitra SH 451.r: Great circle. The section of a sphere by a plane passing through its centre is called a great circle: it has the same centre and radius as the sphere (the largest possible circle on it). Any sphere through the given circle is $S + \lambda P = 0$: $$x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + 10y - 4z - 8 + \lambda(x + y + z - 3) = 0$$ Its centre is $\left(-\dfrac\lambda2,\ -\dfrac{10+\lambda}2,\ \dfrac{4-\lambda}2\right)$.

p: Find the equation of the cone with vertex at $(1, 2, 3)$ and guiding curve $y^2 = 16x,\ z = 1$.
Find a power series solution for $y'' - 4y = 0$.
Paper 2079 Chaitra SH 451.r: Assume $y = \displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nx^n$. Then $y'' = \displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty(n+2)(n+1)a_{n+2}x^n$. Substitute in $y'' - 4y = 0$ and equate the coefficient of $x^n$ to zero: $$(n+2)(n+1)a_{n+2} - 4a_n = 0\ \Rightarrow\ \boxed{a_{n+2} = \frac{4\,a_n}{(n+1)(n+2)}}$$ Even terms: $a_2 = \dfrac{4a_0}{2} = 2a_0$, $a_4 = \dfrac{4a_2}{12} = \dfrac{2a_0}{3}$, $a_6 = \dfrac{4a_4}{30} = \dfrac{4a_0}{45}$. Odd terms: $a_3 = \dfrac{4a_1}{6} = \dfrac{2a_1}{3}$, $a_5 = \dfrac{4a_3}{20} = \dfrac{2a_1}{15}$. $$\boxed{y = a_0\left(1 + 2x^2 + \frac23x^4 + \frac4{45}x^6 + \cdots\right) + a_1\left(x + \frac23x^3 + \frac2{15}x^5 + \cdots\right)}$$ with $a_0, a_1$ arbitrary.

p: Express $f(x) = 5x^3 + x$ in terms of Legendre's Polynomials.

Define vector triple product. Prove that $\hat i\times(\vec a\times\hat i) + \hat j\times(\vec a\times\hat j) + \hat k\times(\vec a\times\hat k) = 2\vec a$ where $\hat i, \hat j, \hat k$ are mutually unit vectors along the co-ordinates axes.
Paper 2079 Chaitra SH 451.r: Vector triple product. For three vectors, $\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c) = (\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec b - (\vec a\cdot\vec b)\vec c$. It is a vector in the plane of $\vec b$ and $\vec c$, perpendicular to $\vec a$, and generally $\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c)\ne(\vec a\times\vec b)\times\vec c$. Proof. Using the formula, $\hat i\times(\vec a\times\hat i) = (\hat i\cdot\hat i)\vec a - (\hat i\cdot\vec a)\hat i = \vec a - a_1\hat i$, where $\vec a = a_1\hat i + a_2\hat j + a_3\hat k$. Similarly the other two terms are $\vec a - a_2\hat j$ and $\vec a - a_3\hat k$.

p: Find the directional derivative of $\phi = x^2yz + 4xz^2$ at $(1, -2, -1)$ in the direction of $2\hat i - \hat j - 2\hat k$.
Paper 2079 Chaitra SH 451.r:
$\phi = x^2yz + 4xz^2$: $$
abla\phi = (2xyz + 4z^2)\hat i + x^2z\,\hat j + (x^2y + 8xz)\hat k$$ At $(1,-2,-1)$: $$ egin{gathered}\phi_x = 2(1)(-2)(-1) + 4(1) = 4 + 4 = 8 \ \phi_y = (1)(-1) = -1 \ \phi_z = (1)(-2) + 8(1)(-1) = -10\end{gathered}$$ $$
abla\phi = 8\hat i - \hat j - 10\hat k$$ Unit vector along $2\hat i - \hat j - 2\hat k$: $\hat u = \dfrac{2\hat i - \hat j - 2\hat k}{\sqrt{4 + 1 + 4}} = \dfrac13(2,-1,-2)$. $$D_{\hat u}\phi = 
abla\phi\cdot\hat u =  rac{16 + 1 + 20}{3}$$ $$ oxed{D_{\hat u}\phi =  rac{37}{3}\approx12.33}$$

p: Find the interval and radius of convergence of the power series: $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{2^n(x-3)^n}{(n+4)}$. <!-- SOLUTIONS -->
Paper 2079 Chaitra SH 451.r: Series $\sum\dfrac{2^n(x-3)^n}{n+4}$: $a_n = \dfrac{2^n}{n+4}$, centre $x = 3$. $$\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| = \frac{2^{n+1}}{n+5}\cdot\frac{n+4}{2^n} = 2\cdot\frac{n+4}{n+5}\to2\ \Rightarrow\ R = \frac1{2}$$ The series converges absolutely for $|x - 3|<\dfrac12$, i.e. $\dfrac52<x<\dfrac72$. Endpoints. - $x = \dfrac72$: $(x - 3) = \dfrac12$, the series is $\sum\dfrac1{n+4}$, which diverges (harmonic series, $p = 1$). - $x = \dfrac52$: $(x-3) = -\dfrac12$, the series is $\sum\dfrac{(-1)^n}{n+4}$, an alternating series whose terms decrease to $0$: it converges (Leibnitz test). $$\boxed{R = \frac12,\qquad\text{interval of convergence }\frac52\le x<\frac72}$$

p: State Euler's theorem for a homogeneous function of two variables of degree $n$. If $u = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt x - \sqrt y}{\sqrt x + \sqrt y}\right)$, show that $x\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} + y\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} = 0$.
Paper 2080 Ashwin SH 451.r: Euler's theorem. If $f(x,y)$ is a homogeneous function of degree $n$ with continuous first-order partial derivatives, then $$x\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} + y\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = nf$$ Proof sketch. Put $f(tx,ty) = t^nf(x,y)$ and differentiate with respect to $t$ at $t = 1$: the left side gives $xf_x + yf_y$ by the chain rule and the right side gives $nf$. Application. Let $z = \sin u = \dfrac{\sqrt x-\sqrt y}{\sqrt x+\sqrt y}$. Replacing $x,y$ by $tx,ty$ gives $\dfrac{\sqrt t(\sqrt x-\sqrt y)}{\sqrt t(\sqrt x+\sqrt y)} = z$, so $z$ is homogeneous of degree $0$. By Euler's theorem $$xz_x + yz_y = 0\cdot z = 0$$ Since $z = \sin u$, $z_x = \cos u\,u_x$ and $z_y = \cos u\,u_y$.

p: Find the extreme value of $x^2 + y^2 + z^2$ subject to the conditions $x + z = 1$, $2y + z = 2$.
Paper 2080 Ashwin SH 451.r: Method 1: elimination. From the conditions, $x = 1 - z$ and $y = \dfrac{2-z}{2}$, so with $z = t$ $$f(t) = (1-t)^2 + \frac{(2-t)^2}{4} + t^2$$ $$f'(t) = -2(1-t) - \frac{2-t}{2} + 2t = \frac92t - 3 = 0\ \Rightarrow\ t = \frac23$$ $f''(t) = \dfrac92 > 0$, so this is a minimum. Then $z = \dfrac23$, $x = \dfrac13$, $y = \dfrac23$ and $$f = \frac19 + \frac49 + \frac49 = 1$$ Method 2: Lagrange multipliers. $F = x^2+y^2+z^2 + \lambda(x+z-1) + \mu(2y+z-2)$. Then $$2x + \lambda = 0,\quad 2y + 2\mu = 0,\quad 2z + \lambda + \mu = 0$$ so $x = -\lambda/2$, $y = -\mu$, $z = -(\lambda+\mu)/2$. The constraints $x+z=1$ and $2y+z=2$ give $2\lambda + \mu = -2$ and $\lambda + 5\mu = -4$.

p: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^a\int_0^{\sqrt{a^2-x^2}} y^2\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\,dy\,dx$ by changing it into polar form.
Using a multiple integral, find the volume bounded by the cylinder $x^2 + y^2 = 4$ between the planes $y + z = 8$ and $z = 1$.
Paper 2080 Ashwin SH 451.r: The solid stands on the disc $D: x^2+y^2\le4$; its bottom is the plane $z=1$ and its top is the plane $z = 8 - y$. The height at $(x,y)$ is $(8-y) - 1 = 7 - y$ (positive on $D$ since $|y|\le2$). $$V = \iint_D(7-y)\,dA = 7\iint_DdA - \iint_Dy\,dA$$ $\iint_D dA = \pi(2)^2 = 4\pi$, and $\iint_Dy\,dA = 0$ because $D$ is symmetric about the $x$-axis ($y$ is odd). In polar form the same result: $\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^2(7-r\sin\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta = 7\cdot2\pi\cdot2 - 0 = 28\pi$. $$\boxed{V = 28\pi\ \text{cubic units}\approx 87.96}$$

p: Find the image of the point $(2,-1,3)$ in the plane $3x - 2y - z = 9$.
Paper 2080 Ashwin SH 451.r: Let $P = (2,-1,3)$ and the plane be $3x - 2y - z - 9 = 0$ with normal $\vec n = (3,-2,-1)$. The foot of the perpendicular and the image lie on the line $\dfrac{x-2}{3} = \dfrac{y+1}{-2} = \dfrac{z-3}{-1} = k$, i.e. $Q = (2+3k,\ -1-2k,\ 3-k)$. Substituting $Q$ into the plane for the foot: $$3(2+3k) - 2(-1-2k) - (3-k) - 9 = 14k - 4 = 0\ \Rightarrow\ k = \frac27$$ The foot is $\left(\dfrac{20}7,-\dfrac{11}7,\dfrac{19}7\right)$.

p: Define coplanar lines and skew lines. Show that the lines $\dfrac x1 = \dfrac{y-2}{2} = \dfrac{z+3}{3}$ and $\dfrac{x-2}{2} = \dfrac{y-6}{3} = \dfrac{z-3}{4}$ are coplanar and also find their point of intersection and the equation of the common plane.
Obtain the equation of the sphere through the circle $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 9$, $x - 2y + 2z = 5$, as the great circle. Also determine its centre and radius.
Paper 2080 Ashwin SH 451.r: Every sphere through the circle $x^2+y^2+z^2 = 9$, $x-2y+2z = 5$ has the form $$x^2+y^2+z^2 - 9 + \lambda(x - 2y + 2z - 5) = 0$$ Its centre is $\left(-\dfrac\lambda2,\ \lambda,\ -\lambda\right)$. For the given circle to be a great circle, the centre must lie in the plane $x-2y+2z = 5$: $$-\frac\lambda2 - 2\lambda - 2\lambda = 5\ \Rightarrow\ -\frac{9\lambda}2 = 5\ \Rightarrow\ \lambda = -\frac{10}9$$ The sphere is $$x^2+y^2+z^2 - 9 - \frac{10}9(x - 2y + 2z - 5) = 0$$ $$\boxed{9(x^2+y^2+z^2) - 10x + 20y - 20z - 31 = 0}$$ Centre: $\left(-\dfrac\lambda2,\lambda,-\lambda\right)$ with $\lambda = -\dfrac{10}9$ gives $\left(\dfrac59,\ -\dfrac{10}9,\ \dfrac{10}9\right)$.

p: Obtain the equation of the right circular cylinder of radius $4$ and axis the line $x = 2y = -z$.
Paper 2080 Ashwin SH 451.r: The axis $x = 2y = -z$ can be written $\dfrac x2 = \dfrac y1 = \dfrac z{-2}$ (dividing by 2), through the origin with direction $\vec d = (2,1,-2)$, $|\vec d| = 3$. A point $P(x,y,z)$ lies on the cylinder when its distance from the axis is $4$: $|\vec r\times\vec d|^2 = 16|\vec d|^2$. $$\vec r\times\vec d = \begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\x&y&z\\2&1&-2\end{vmatrix} = (-2y - z,\ 2z + 2x,\ x - 2y)$$ $$(2y+z)^2 + 4(x+z)^2 + (x-2y)^2 = 16\cdot9 = 144$$ Expanding, $$4y^2 + 4yz + z^2 + 4x^2 + 8xz + 4z^2 + x^2 - 4xy + 4y^2 = 144$$ $$\boxed{5x^2 + 8y^2 + 5z^2 - 4xy + 4yz + 8zx = 144}$$ Check by the other form $x^2+y^2+z^2 - \dfrac{(2x+y-2z)^2}{9} = 16$, which expands to the same equation.

p: Define a power series. Apply it to solve the differential equation $y'' + xy' + y = 0$.
Paper 2080 Ashwin SH 451.r: Power series. An infinite series $\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n(x-x_0)^n = a_0 + a_1(x-x_0) + a_2(x-x_0)^2 + \cdots$ is called a power series in $(x - x_0)$; it converges for $|x-x_0|<R$, where $R$ is its radius of convergence. Solution of $y'' + xy' + y = 0$. Let $y = \displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nx^n$, so $y' = \sum na_nx^{n-1}$, $y'' = \sum n(n-1)a_nx^{n-2}$. Then $$\sum_{n=0}^\infty(n+2)(n+1)a_{n+2}x^n + \sum_{n=0}^\infty na_nx^n + \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nx^n = 0$$ Equating the coefficient of $x^n$ to zero: $$(n+2)(n+1)a_{n+2} + (n+1)a_n = 0\ \Rightarrow\ a_{n+2} = -\frac{a_n}{n+2}$$ $a_0$ and $a_1$ are arbitrary.

p: Express the function $f(x) = x^3 + 5x^2 + 4x + 1$ in terms of Legendre's polynomials.
Prove that Bessel's function $J_{5/2}(x) = \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{\pi x}}\left\{\dfrac{3-x^2}{x^2}\sin x - \dfrac3x\cos x\right\}$, where the symbols have their usual meanings.
Paper 2080 Ashwin SH 451.r: Bessel's function of order $n$: $J_n(x) = \displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^\infty\frac{(-1)^r}{r!\,\Gamma(n+r+1)}\left(\frac x2\right)^{n+2r}$. Using $\Gamma\!\left(r+\tfrac32\right) = \dfrac{(2r+1)!\sqrt\pi}{2^{2r+1}\,r!}$ and $\Gamma\!\left(r+\tfrac12\right) = \dfrac{(2r)!\sqrt\pi}{4^r\,r!}$ in the series, $$\begin{gathered}J_{1/2}(x) = \sqrt{\frac2{\pi x}}\sum_{r}\frac{(-1)^rx^{2r+1}}{(2r+1)!} = \sqrt{\frac2{\pi x}}\sin x \\ J_{-1/2}(x) = \sqrt{\frac2{\pi x}}\sum_{r}\frac{(-1)^rx^{2r}}{(2r)!} = \sqrt{\frac2{\pi x}}\cos x\end{gathered}$$ The recurrence relation is $J_{n+1}(x) = \dfrac{2n}xJ_n(x) - J_{n-1}(x)$.

p: Define scalar triple product and vector triple product for vectors. Prove that $[\vec a+\vec b,\ \vec b+\vec c,\ \vec c+\vec a] = 2[\vec a,\ \vec b,\ \vec c]$.
Paper 2080 Ashwin SH 451.r: Scalar triple product. For vectors $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$, $[\vec a\ \vec b\ \vec c] = \vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c)$, a scalar equal to the (signed) volume of the parallelepiped on them. It equals $\begin{vmatrix}a_1&a_2&a_3\\b_1&b_2&b_3\\c_1&c_2&c_3\end{vmatrix}$ and is unchanged by cyclic permutation. Vector triple product. $\vec a\times(\vec b\times\vec c) = (\vec a\cdot\vec c)\vec b - (\vec a\cdot\vec b)\vec c$, a vector lying in the plane of $\vec b$ and $\vec c$. Proof.

p: Prove that the necessary and sufficient condition for a vector function $\vec a$ in the variable $t$ to have constant direction is $\vec a\times\dfrac{d\vec a}{dt} = \vec 0$.
Paper 2080 Ashwin SH 451.r: Necessity. If $\vec a$ has constant direction, $\vec a = s(t)\,\hat e$ with $\hat e$ a constant unit vector. Then $\dfrac{d\vec a}{dt} = s'\hat e$ and $$\vec a\times\frac{d\vec a}{dt} = ss'(\hat e\times\hat e) = \vec 0$$ Sufficiency. Let $\vec a = a\hat u$ where $a = |\vec a|$ and $\hat u$ is the unit vector along $\vec a$. Then $\dfrac{d\vec a}{dt} = a'\hat u + a\dfrac{d\hat u}{dt}$ and $$\vec a\times\frac{d\vec a}{dt} = aa'(\hat u\times\hat u) + a^2\left(\hat u\times\frac{d\hat u}{dt}\right) = a^2\left(\hat u\times\frac{d\hat u}{dt}\right)$$ If this is $\vec 0$ (and $a\ne0$) then $\hat u\times\dfrac{d\hat u}{dt} = \vec 0$.

p: Find the interval and radius of convergence of the power series $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(-1)^n(2x+1)^n}{3^n}$. <!-- SOLUTIONS -->
Paper 2080 Ashwin SH 451.r: $\displaystyle\sum\frac{(-1)^n(2x+1)^n}{3^n} = \sum\left(-\frac{2x+1}3\right)^n$ is a geometric series with ratio $r = -\dfrac{2x+1}3$ (or by the ratio test $\left|\dfrac{u_{n+1}}{u_n}\right| = \dfrac{|2x+1|}3$). It converges when $\left|\dfrac{2x+1}3\right|<1$, i.e. $|2x+1|<3$, $-3<2x+1<3$, so $-2<x<1$. In the form $|x - (-\tfrac12)|<\tfrac32$ the radius of convergence is $R = \dfrac32$, centred at $x = -\tfrac12$. Endpoints. - $x = 1$: $2x+1 = 3$ and the terms are $(-1)^n$, which do not tend to $0$: divergent. - $x = -2$: $2x+1 = -3$ and the terms are $(-1)^n(-1)^n = 1$, which do not tend to $0$: divergent. $$\boxed{R = \frac32,\qquad\text{interval of convergence }(-2,\ 1)}$$

p: State Euler's theorem on homogeneous functions of two variables and use it to show $x\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial x} + y\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial y} = \sin2u$, where $u = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{x^3+y^3}{x-y}$.
Find the maximum value of $f(x,y,z) = xyz$ subject to the condition $x + y + z = 9$.
Find the distance of the point $(1,-2,3)$ from the plane $x - y + z = 5$ measured parallel to the line $\dfrac x2 = \dfrac y3 = \dfrac z{-6}$.
Show that the lines $\dfrac{x-1}{2} = \dfrac{y-2}{3} = \dfrac{z-3}{4}$ and $\dfrac{x-2}{3} = \dfrac{y-3}{4} = \dfrac{z-4}{5}$ are coplanar. Find the equation of the plane in which they lie.
Find the centre and radius of the circle $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + x + y + z = 4$, $x + y + z = 0$.
Paper 2080 Chaitra SH 451.r: The sphere $x^2+y^2+z^2 + x + y + z - 4 = 0$ has centre $C\left(-\tfrac12,-\tfrac12,-\tfrac12\right)$ and radius $R = \sqrt{\tfrac34 + 4} = \dfrac{\sqrt{19}}{2}$. The distance of $C$ from the plane $x+y+z = 0$ is $$p = \frac{|-\tfrac32|}{\sqrt3} = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}$$ The centre of the circle is the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to the plane: $C + t(1,1,1)$ with sum zero, $-\tfrac32 + 3t = 0$, $t = \tfrac12$, i.e. $(0,0,0)$. The radius is $$r = \sqrt{R^2 - p^2} = \sqrt{\frac{19}{4} - \frac34} = 2$$ $$\boxed{\text{centre }(0,0,0),\quad\text{radius }2}$$ (Directly: on the plane, $x + y + z = 0$ so the sphere reduces to $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 4$.)

p: Find the equation of the cylinder whose generators are parallel to the line $\dfrac x1 = \dfrac y{-2} = \dfrac z3$ and whose guiding curve is $x^2 + 2y^2 = 1$, $z = 3$.
Paper 2080 Chaitra SH 451.r: The guiding curve is $x^2 + 2y^2 = 1$, $z = 3$. Let $P(x,y,z)$ be on the cylinder; the generator through it has direction $(1,-2,3)$ and meets the plane $z = 3$ at $$Q = (x - t,\ y + 2t,\ z - 3t)\quad\text{with}\quad z - 3t = 3\;\Rightarrow\;t = \frac{z-3}{3}$$ $$\begin{gathered}x_1 = x - \frac{z-3}{3} = \frac{3x - z + 3}{3} \\ y_1 = y + \frac{2(z-3)}{3} = \frac{3y + 2z - 6}{3}\end{gathered}$$ Since $Q$ lies on $x^2 + 2y^2 = 1$: $$\left(\frac{3x - z + 3}{3}\right)^2 + 2\left(\frac{3y + 2z - 6}{3}\right)^2 = 1$$ $$\boxed{(3x - z + 3)^2 + 2(3y + 2z - 6)^2 = 9}$$

p: Prove that the vectors $\vec b\times\vec c$, $\vec c\times\vec a$, $\vec a\times\vec b$ are coplanar if the vectors $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ are coplanar.
Paper 2080 Chaitra SH 451.r: Let $\vec a,\vec b,\vec c$ be coplanar, so $[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c] = \vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c) = 0$. Three vectors are coplanar iff their scalar triple product is zero, so we compute $$\big[\vec b\times\vec c,\ \vec c\times\vec a,\ \vec a\times\vec b\big] = (\vec b\times\vec c)\cdot\big[(\vec c\times\vec a)\times(\vec a\times\vec b)\big]$$ Using $\vec X\times(\vec a\times\vec b) = \vec a(\vec X\cdot\vec b) - \vec b(\vec X\cdot\vec a)$ with $\vec X = \vec c\times\vec a$: $\vec X\cdot\vec a = 0$ and $\vec X\cdot\vec b = [\vec c\,\vec a\,\vec b] = [\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]$, so $(\vec c\times\vec a)\times(\vec a\times\vec b) = [\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c]\,\vec a$.

p: Prove that the necessary and sufficient condition for the vector function of a scalar variable $t$ to have a constant direction is $\vec a\times\dfrac{d\vec a}{dt} = \vec 0$.
Paper 2080 Chaitra SH 451.r: Necessary. If $\vec a$ has constant direction, $\vec a = \varphi(t)\hat e$ with $\hat e$ a constant unit vector. Then $\dfrac{d\vec a}{dt} = \varphi'\hat e$ and $\vec a\times\dfrac{d\vec a}{dt} = \varphi\varphi'(\hat e\times\hat e) = \vec0$. Sufficient. Let $\vec a = a\hat e$ with $a = |\vec a|$ and $\hat e$ the unit vector along $\vec a$. Then $$\vec a\times\frac{d\vec a}{dt} = a\hat e\times\left(a'\hat e + a\frac{d\hat e}{dt}\right) = a^2\,\hat e\times\frac{d\hat e}{dt}$$ From $\hat e\cdot\hat e = 1$, $\hat e\cdot\dfrac{d\hat e}{dt} = 0$, so $\dfrac{d\hat e}{dt}\perp\hat e$ and $\left|\hat e\times\dfrac{d\hat e}{dt}\right| = \left|\dfrac{d\hat e}{dt}\right|$.

p: If $f = x^3 + y^3 + z^3 - 3xyz$, find $\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{grad}f)$ and $\operatorname{curl}(\operatorname{grad}f)$.
Paper 2080 Chaitra SH 451.r: $$\operatorname{grad}f = \nabla f = \big(3x^2 - 3yz,\ 3y^2 - 3zx,\ 3z^2 - 3xy\big)$$ $$\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{grad}f) = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(3x^2 - 3yz) + \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(3y^2 - 3zx) + \frac{\partial}{\partial z}(3z^2 - 3xy) = 6x + 6y + 6z$$ $$\boxed{\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{grad}f) = \nabla^2f = 6(x+y+z)}$$ $$\operatorname{curl}(\operatorname{grad}f) = \begin{vmatrix}\vec i&\vec j&\vec k\\ \partial_x&\partial_y&\partial_z\\ 3x^2-3yz&3y^2-3zx&3z^2-3xy\end{vmatrix} = (-3x+3x)\vec i + (-3y+3y)\vec j + (-3z+3z)\vec k$$ $$\boxed{\operatorname{curl}(\operatorname{grad}f) = \vec 0}$$ (as it must be for any scalar function with continuous second derivatives).

p: Find the solution of the differential equation $y'' + 16y = 0$ using the power series method.
Express the function $f(x) = x^3 - 5x^2 + 6x + 1$ in terms of Legendre's polynomials.
Show that $J_{5/2}(x) = \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{\pi x}}\left\{\dfrac{3-x^2}{x^2}\sin x - \dfrac3x\cos x\right\}$, where the symbols have their usual meanings.
Find the radius and interval of convergence of the series $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty\dfrac{(x-1)^n}{\sqrt n}$. <!-- SOLUTIONS -->
Paper 2080 Chaitra SH 451.r: Ratio test: $\left|\dfrac{u_{n+1}}{u_n}\right| = |x-1|\sqrt{\dfrac n{n+1}}\to|x-1|$. The series converges absolutely for $|x-1|<1$, so the radius of convergence is $R = 1$, i.e. $0<x<2$. Endpoints. - $x = 2$: $\displaystyle\sum\frac1{\sqrt n} = \sum\frac{1}{n^{1/2}}$, a $p$-series with $p = \tfrac12\le1$: divergent. - $x = 0$: $\displaystyle\sum\frac{(-1)^n}{\sqrt n}$ is alternating with $\dfrac1{\sqrt n}\downarrow0$: convergent (conditionally), by Leibnitz's test. $$\boxed{R = 1,\qquad\text{interval of convergence }[0,\,2)}$$

p: State Euler's theorem for homogeneous functions and use it to show that $x\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} + y\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \sin 2z$ for $\tan z = \dfrac{x^3+y^3}{x+y}$.
Find the minimum value of the function $x^2 + y^2 + z^2$ under the condition $x + y + z = 3a$.
Evaluate $\displaystyle\iint_R xy\,dx\,dy$, where $R$ is the region over the area of the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$ in the first octant (quadrant).
Paper 2081 Chaitra SH 451.r: The region is the quarter of the ellipse in the first quadrant: $0\le x\le a$, $0\le y\le\dfrac ba\sqrt{a^2-x^2}$. $$\iint_Rxy\,dx\,dy = \int_0^ax\left[\frac{y^2}2\right]_0^{\frac ba\sqrt{a^2-x^2}}dx = \int_0^a\frac{x}{2}\cdot\frac{b^2}{a^2}(a^2-x^2)\,dx = \frac{b^2}{2a^2}\left[\frac{a^2x^2}{2} - \frac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^a = \frac{b^2}{2a^2}\cdot\frac{a^4}{4}$$ $$\boxed{\iint_Rxy\,dx\,dy = \frac{a^2b^2}{8}}$$

p: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^a\int_y^a\dfrac{x}{x^2+y^2}\,dx\,dy$ by changing the order of integration.

Show that the lines $\dfrac{x-5}{4} = \dfrac{y-7}{4} = \dfrac{z+3}{-5}$ and $\dfrac{x-8}{7} = \dfrac{y-4}{1} = \dfrac{z-5}{3}$ are coplanar. Find their point of intersection and the equation of the plane in which they lie.
Find the shortest distance between the lines $x + a = 2y = -12z$ and $x = y + 2a = 6z - 6a$.
Find the equation of the sphere having the circle $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + 7y - 2z + 2 = 0$, $2x + 3y + 4z - 8 = 0$ as a great circle.
Find the equation of the right circular cylinder whose guiding curve is the circle $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - x - y - z = 0$, $x + y + z - 1 = 0$.
Paper 2081 Chaitra SH 451.r: The axis of a right circular cylinder through a given circle is perpendicular to its plane; the plane $x+y+z = 1$ has normal $(1,1,1)$, so the generators are parallel to $(1,1,1)$. Let $P(x,y,z)$ lie on the cylinder, and let the generator through $P$ meet the plane at $Q = (x-t, y-t, z-t)$. Since $Q$ is in the plane, $x+y+z-3t = 1$, i.e. $t = \dfrac{s-1}{3}$ with $s = x+y+z$. $Q$ must also lie on the sphere $x^2+y^2+z^2-x-y-z = 0$: $$\sum(x-t)^2 - \sum(x-t) = \sum x^2 - 2ts + 3t^2 - s + 3t = 0$$ With $3t = s-1$: $-2ts + 3t^2 = \dfrac{(s-1)(-2s + s - 1)}{3} = -\dfrac{s^2-1}{3}$ and $-s + 3t = -1$.

p: Solve the differential equation $y'' - y = 0$ by the power series method.
Express $f(x) = 5x^3 + 3x$ in terms of Legendre's polynomials.
a: Solve in series Legendre's equation $(1-x^2)y'' - 2xy' + n(n+1)y = 0$.

p: Prove Bessel's function $J_{3/2}(x) = \sqrt{\dfrac{2}{\pi x}}\left(\dfrac{\sin x}{x} - \cos x\right)$.
Find the set of reciprocal system to the set of vectors $2\vec i + 3\vec j - \vec k$, $-\vec i + 2\vec j - 3\vec k$, $3\vec i - 4\vec j + 2\vec k$.
Paper 2081 Chaitra SH 451.r: Let $\mathbf a = (2,3,-1)$, $\mathbf b = (-1,2,-3)$, $\mathbf c = (3,-4,2)$. The reciprocal system is $\mathbf a' = \dfrac{\mathbf b\times\mathbf c}{[\mathbf a\,\mathbf b\,\mathbf c]}$, $\mathbf b' = \dfrac{\mathbf c\times\mathbf a}{[\mathbf a\,\mathbf b\,\mathbf c]}$, $\mathbf c' = \dfrac{\mathbf a\times\mathbf b}{[\mathbf a\,\mathbf b\,\mathbf c]}$.

p: Prove that the necessary and sufficient condition for the vector function $\vec a(t)$ of the scalar variable $t$ to have constant direction is $\vec a\times\dfrac{d\vec a}{dt} = \vec 0$.
Paper 2081 Chaitra SH 451.r: Necessary. If $\vec a(t)$ has constant direction, write $\vec a = \varphi(t)\,\hat e$ with $\hat e$ a constant unit vector. Then $\dfrac{d\vec a}{dt} = \varphi'\hat e$ and $\vec a\times\dfrac{d\vec a}{dt} = \varphi\varphi'(\hat e\times\hat e) = \vec 0$. Sufficient. Let $\vec a = a\,\hat e$ where $a = |\vec a|$ and $\hat e$ is the unit vector in the direction of $\vec a$.

p: Find the directional derivative of $\varphi(x,y,z) = xy^2 + yz^3$ at the point $(2,-1,1)$ in the direction of the vector $\vec i + 2\vec j + 2\vec k$.
Paper 2081 Chaitra SH 451.r:

abla\varphi = \left(\dfrac{\partial\varphi}{\partial x},\dfrac{\partial\varphi}{\partial y},\dfrac{\partial\varphi}{\partial z}ight) = (y^2,\ 2xy + z^3,\ 3yz^2)$. At $(2,-1,1)$: $$

p: Find the half range Fourier sine series of the function $f(x) = x$ in the interval $(0, 2)$.
Find the Fourier cosine integral of $f(x) = e^{-ax}$ for $x>0$, $a>0$.
For a complex variable, show that $f(z) = \sin z$ is analytic.
Find the image of the circle $|z - i| = 1$ under the mapping $w = \dfrac1z$.
Show that $\displaystyle\int_C\frac{1}{z-a}\,dz = 2\pi i$ where $C$ is a unit circle $|z - a| = 1$.
Paper 2081 Chaitra ENSH 201.r: (a) Write $\sin z = \sin(x + iy) = \sin x\cosh y + i\cos x\sinh y$, so $u = \sin x\cosh y$, $v = \cos x\sinh y$. The partial derivatives are $$\begin{gathered}u_x = \cos x\cosh y = v_y \\ u_y = \sin x\sinh y = -v_x\end{gathered}$$ The Cauchy–Riemann equations hold for all $(x, y)$ and the partials are continuous, so $\sin z$ is analytic everywhere (an entire function). (b) The circle is $x^2 + (y-1)^2 = 1$, i.e. $x^2 + y^2 = 2y$. It passes through $z = 0$, so its image under $w = 1/z$ is a straight line. With $w = u + iv = \dfrac{x - iy}{x^2 + y^2}$, we have $v = -\dfrac{y}{x^2 + y^2} = -\dfrac{y}{2y} = -\dfrac12$.

p: Expand the function $f(z) = \dfrac1z$ about $z = i$ in Taylor's series.
Find the residue of $f(z) = \dfrac{3z-4}{(z-2)(z-3)}$ at each of the singularities.
Paper 2081 Chaitra ENSH 201.r: (a) Put $z = i + (z - i)$ and expand for $|z - i|<1$: $$\frac1z = \frac1{i + (z-i)} = \frac1i\cdot\frac{1}{1 + \dfrac{z-i}{i}} = -i\sum_{n=0}^\infty\left(-\frac{z-i}{i}\right)^n = -i\sum_{n=0}^\infty i^n(z-i)^n$$ (using $(-1/i)^n = i^n$). Hence $$\boxed{\frac1z = -i + (z - i) + i(z-i)^2 - (z-i)^3 - i(z-i)^4 + \cdots,\qquad |z - i|<1}$$ (b) $f(z) = \dfrac{3z-4}{(z-2)(z-3)}$ has simple poles at $z = 2$ and $z = 3$. $$\text{Res}_{z=2} = \frac{3(2) - 4}{2 - 3} = \boxed{-2},\qquad\text{Res}_{z=3} = \frac{3(3) - 4}{3 - 2} = \boxed{5}$$

p: Solve the partial differential equation $\dfrac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2} = 12x^2(t+1)$ subject to $u(0,t) = \cos2t$ and $u_x(0,t) = \sin t$.
Find the solution of the equation $3u_x + 2u_y = 0$, by the method of the separation of the variables.
If $Z[x(k)] = X(z)$, show that $x(1) = \displaystyle\lim_{z\to\infty}z[X(z) - x(0)]$, where the symbols have their usual meaning.
If $Z[x(k)] = X(z)$ and $y(k) = \displaystyle\sum_{m=0}^kx(m)$, then show that $Y(z) = \dfrac{z}{z-1}X(z)$.
Find the Fourier series for $f(x) = x^2$ in the interval $-\pi<x<\pi$ and deduce the relation $\dfrac{\pi^2}{12} = \dfrac1{1^2} - \dfrac1{2^2} + \dfrac1{3^2} - \dfrac1{4^2} + \cdots$
Paper 2081 Chaitra ENSH 201.r: $f(x) = x^2$ is even on $(-\pi, \pi)$, so $b_n = 0$. $$\begin{gathered}a_0 = \frac2\pi\int_0^\pi x^2dx = \frac{2\pi^2}3 \\ a_n = \frac2\pi\int_0^\pi x^2\cos nx\,dx = \frac2\pi\left[\frac{x^2\sin nx}n + \frac{2x\cos nx}{n^2} - \frac{2\sin nx}{n^3}\right]_0^\pi = \frac{4(-1)^n}{n^2}\end{gathered}$$ $$\boxed{x^2 = \frac{\pi^2}3 + 4\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(-1)^n}{n^2}\cos nx = \frac{\pi^2}{3} - 4\cos x + \cos2x - \frac49\cos3x + \cdots}$$ Deduction.

p: Find the Fourier integral of $f(x) = \begin{cases}e^{-x}; & x>0\\ 0; & x<0\end{cases}$ and hence show that $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\frac{\cos\omega x + \omega\sin\omega x}{1 + \omega^2}\,d\omega = \begin{cases}\pi e^{-x} &;x>0\\ \dfrac\pi2 &;x = 0\\ 0 &;x<0\end{cases}$
Find the Fourier transform of $f(x) = e^{-ax}$ and use the result to show $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\frac{dx}{(a^2 + x^2)(b^2 + x^2)} = \frac{\pi}{2ab(a+b)}$.
Prove that $u = y^3 - 3x^2y$ is harmonic function. Find its harmonic conjugate and hence construct corresponding analytic function $w = f(z)$.
Paper 2081 Chaitra ENSH 201.r: $u = y^3 - 3x^2y$. Then $u_x = -6xy$, $u_{xx} = -6y$, $u_y = 3y^2 - 3x^2$, $u_{yy} = 6y$, so $u_{xx} + u_{yy} = 0$ and $u$ is harmonic. Harmonic conjugate $v$. By the Cauchy–Riemann equations $v_y = u_x = -6xy$, so $v = -3xy^2 + h(x)$. Also $v_x = -u_y = 3x^2 - 3y^2$, i.e. $-3y^2 + h'(x) = 3x^2 - 3y^2$, so $h' = 3x^2$, $h = x^3$. $$\boxed{v = x^3 - 3xy^2 + c}$$ Analytic function. $$w = f(z) = u + iv = (y^3 - 3x^2y) + i(x^3 - 3xy^2)$$ Since $z^3 = (x^3 - 3xy^2) + i(3x^2y - y^3)$, we have $iz^3 = -(3x^2y - y^3) + i(x^3 - 3xy^2) = u + iv$. Hence $$\boxed{f(z) = iz^3 + c}$$

p: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{d\theta}{5 + 4\sin\theta}$, using method of contour integration in the complex plane.
a: Evaluate $\displaystyle\oint_C\frac{\sin z}{z^2}\,dz$, where $C$ is any closed path not passing through 0.
Paper 2081 Chaitra ENSH 201.r: Put $z = e^{i\theta}$: $d\theta = \dfrac{dz}{iz}$, $\sin\theta = \dfrac{z - z^{-1}}{2i}$, and $\theta: 0\to2\pi$ becomes the unit circle $|z| = 1$. $$I = \oint_{|z|=1}\frac{1}{5 + \dfrac{4}{2i}\left(z - \dfrac1z\right)}\frac{dz}{iz} = \oint\frac{dz}{5iz + 2z^2 - 2} = \oint\frac{dz}{2z^2 + 5iz - 2}$$ The denominator factorises as $2(z + \tfrac i2)(z + 2i)$, with poles $z = -\tfrac i2$ (inside $|z| = 1$) and $z = -2i$ (outside).

p: Derive one dimensional wave equation representing the vibration of the particles of a string.
a: Derive Navier-Stokes equation of fluid flow.
Paper 2081 Chaitra ENSH 201.r: Derivation of the one-dimensional wave equation. Consider a tightly stretched elastic string of linear density $\rho$ and constant tension $T$, lying along the $x$-axis and displaced slightly so that the transverse displacement is $u(x,t)$. Take an element $PQ$ of length $\delta x$. The tensions at $P$ and $Q$ act along the tangents, at small angles $\alpha$ and $\beta$ to the $x$-axis. - Horizontal: there is no horizontal motion, so $T\cos\beta - T\cos\alpha = 0$ (for small angles, $\cos\approx1$), hence $T$ is constant along the string. - Vertical: the net force is $T\sin\beta - T\sin\alpha$, which equals mass times acceleration, $\rho\,\delta x\,\dfrac{\partial^2u}{\partial t^2}$.

p: Solve one dimensional heat equation $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial t} = \dfrac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2}$, subject to $u(0,t) = u(\ell,t) = 0$ and $u(x,0) = u_0\sin\dfrac{\pi x}{\ell}$.
Paper 2081 Chaitra ENSH 201.r: Let $u = X(x)T(t)$. Then $XT' = X''T$, so $\dfrac{X''}X = \dfrac{T'}T = -\lambda^2$ (a negative constant, for a solution that decays with time). Hence $X'' + \lambda^2X = 0$, $X = A\cos\lambda x + B\sin\lambda x$, and $T = Ce^{-\lambda^2t}$. Boundary conditions. $u(0,t) = 0\Rightarrow A = 0$. $u(\ell,t) = 0\Rightarrow B\sin\lambda\ell = 0\Rightarrow\lambda = \dfrac{n\pi}\ell$. The general solution is $$u(x,t) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n\sin\frac{n\pi x}\ell\,e^{-n^2\pi^2t/\ell^2}$$ Initial condition. $u(x,0) = \sum b_n\sin\dfrac{n\pi x}\ell = u_0\sin\dfrac{\pi x}\ell$. Comparing coefficients: $b_1 = u_0$ and $b_n = 0$ for $n\ge2$. $$\boxed{u(x,t) = u_0\,e^{-\pi^2t/\ell^2}\sin\frac{\pi x}\ell}$$

p: In the series $f(x) = \dfrac{a_0}2 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty(a_n\cos nx + b_n\sin nx)$, find the coefficient $b_n$ for the function $f(x) = e^{-x}$ where $x\in(0, 2\pi)$.
Find the Fourier integral representation of $f(x) = \begin{cases}1 & \text{for } |x|<1\\ 0 & \text{for } |x|>1\end{cases}$
Solve the integral equation $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty f(x)\cos\alpha x\,dx = e^{-\alpha}$, $\alpha>0$.
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENSH 201.r: (a) For $f(x) = e^{-x}$ on $(0, 2\pi)$ (period $2\pi$), $b_n = \dfrac1\pi\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}e^{-x}\sin nx\,dx$. Using $\displaystyle\int e^{-x}\sin nx\,dx = -\frac{e^{-x}(\sin nx + n\cos nx)}{1 + n^2}$: $$b_n = \frac1\pi\left[-\frac{e^{-x}(\sin nx + n\cos nx)}{1 + n^2}\right]_0^{2\pi} = \frac1\pi\cdot\frac{n\left(1 - e^{-2\pi}\right)}{1 + n^2}$$ $$\boxed{b_n = \frac{n\left(1 - e^{-2\pi}\right)}{\pi(1 + n^2)}}$$ (Similarly $a_n = \dfrac{1 - e^{-2\pi}}{\pi(1 + n^2)}$.) (b) $f$ is even, so $f(x) = \dfrac2\pi\displaystyle\int_0^\infty A(\omega)\cos\omega x\,d\omega$ with $A(\omega) = \displaystyle\int_0^1\cos\omega t\,dt = \dfrac{\sin\omega}\omega$.

p: Define harmonic function. Show that the function $u(x,y) = e^x\cos y$ is harmonic.
Find the bilinear transformation which maps the points $z = 0, -1, i$ into $w = i, 0, \infty$.
Find the residue of $f(z) = \dfrac{2z+1}{(z-3)(z+5)}$ at each of the singularities.
Find the Taylor series expansion of $f(z) = \dfrac1{z-3}$ centered at the point $z = 4i$.
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENSH 201.r: (a) Simple poles at $z = 3$ and $z = -5$. $$\text{Res}_{z=3} = \frac{2(3) + 1}{3 + 5} = \boxed{\frac78},\qquad\text{Res}_{z=-5} = \frac{2(-5) + 1}{-5 - 3} = \boxed{\frac98}$$ (b) Write $z - 3 = (z - 4i) + (4i - 3)$: $$\frac1{z-3} = \frac1{(4i - 3)}\cdot\frac1{1 + \dfrac{z - 4i}{4i - 3}} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{(-1)^n(z - 4i)^n}{(4i - 3)^{n+1}}$$ $$\boxed{\frac1{z-3} = \frac1{4i-3} - \frac{z - 4i}{(4i-3)^2} + \frac{(z-4i)^2}{(4i-3)^3} - \cdots}$$ valid for $|z - 4i|<|4i - 3| = 5$ (the distance to the singularity $z = 3$).

p: Solve the partial differential equation $\dfrac{\partial^2z}{\partial x\partial y} = \sin x\sin y$ given that $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} = -2\sin y$ when $x = 0$; $z = 0$ when $y = \dfrac\pi2$.
Write down the classification rules for general second order partial differential equation and hence use it to classify the equation $u_{xx} + x^2u_{yy} = 0$.
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENSH 201.r: (a) $\dfrac{\partial^2z}{\partial x\partial y} = \sin x\sin y$. Integrate with respect to $x$: $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} = -\cos x\sin y + f(y)$. At $x = 0$: $-\sin y + f(y) = -2\sin y\Rightarrow f(y) = -\sin y$. So $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} = -(1 + \cos x)\sin y$. Integrate with respect to $y$: $z = (1 + \cos x)\cos y + g(x)$. At $y = \dfrac\pi2$: $z = 0 + g(x) = 0\Rightarrow g = 0$. $$\boxed{z = (1 + \cos x)\cos y}$$ (b) Classification rules. For $Au_{xx} + Bu_{xy} + Cu_{yy} + Du_x + Eu_y + Fu = G$ the discriminant $B^2 - 4AC$ decides: - $B^2 - 4AC>0$: hyperbolic (e.g. wave equation); - $B^2 - 4AC = 0$: parabolic (e.g. heat equation); - $B^2 - 4AC<0$: elliptic (e.g.

p: Find $x(0)$ and $x(1)$ of Z-transform of $x(t) = 1 - e^{-t}$.
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENSH 201.r: (a) Sampling with $T = 1$: $x(k) = 1 - e^{-k}$, so $X(z) = \dfrac z{z-1} - \dfrac z{z - e^{-1}}$. $$x(0) = \lim_{z\to\infty}X(z) = 1 - 1 = \boxed{0}$$ $$x(1) = \lim_{z\to\infty}z\left[X(z) - x(0)\right] = \lim_{z\to\infty}z^2\left[\frac{1}{z-1} - \frac{1}{z - e^{-1}}\right] = \lim_{z\to\infty}\frac{z^2\left(1 - e^{-1}\right)}{(z-1)(z - e^{-1})} = \boxed{1 - e^{-1}\approx0.632}$$ These agree with $x(k) = 1 - e^{-k}$ at $k = 0, 1$. (b) $\dfrac{X(z)}z = \dfrac1{(z-1)(z-2)} = \dfrac1{z-2} - \dfrac1{z-1}$, so $X(z) = \dfrac z{z-2} - \dfrac z{z-1}$. For the causal sequence ($|z|>2$): $$\boxed{x(k) = 2^k - 1,\qquad k = 0, 1, 2,\ldots}$$

p: If $f(x) = x + x^2$ for $-\pi\le x\le\pi$, then find the Fourier series of $f(x)$.
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENSH 201.r: $f(x) = x + x^2$ on $[-\pi, \pi]$. The part $x$ is odd and $x^2$ is even. $$\begin{gathered}a_0 = \frac2\pi\int_0^\pi x^2dx = \frac{2\pi^2}3 \\ a_n = \frac2\pi\int_0^\pi x^2\cos nx\,dx = \frac{4(-1)^n}{n^2}\end{gathered}$$ $$b_n = \frac2\pi\int_0^\pi x\sin nx\,dx = \frac2\pi\left[-\frac{x\cos nx}n + \frac{\sin nx}{n^2}\right]_0^\pi = \frac{2(-1)^{n+1}}n$$ $$\boxed{x + x^2 = \frac{\pi^2}3 + 4\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(-1)^n}{n^2}\cos nx + 2\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}n\sin nx}$$ (Writing out: $\dfrac{\pi^2}3 - 4\cos x + \cos2x - \cdots + 2\sin x - \sin2x + \tfrac23\sin3x - \cdots$.)

p: Find Fourier cosine integral of $f(x) = e^{-kx}$, $k>0$, $x>0$ and use it to evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\frac{\cos\omega x}{k^2 + \omega^2}d\omega$.
Find Fourier sine transform of $f(x) = e^{-x}$ and hence use the result in Parseval's identity to show $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\frac{x^2\,dx}{(x^2+1)^2} = \frac\pi4$.
Express the function $\dfrac1{z^2 - 3z + 2}$ in Laurent series form in the region $1<|z|<2$.
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENSH 201.r: Partial fractions: $\dfrac1{z^2 - 3z + 2} = \dfrac1{(z-1)(z-2)} = \dfrac1{z-2} - \dfrac1{z-1}$. In the annulus $1<|z|<2$: - $|z|<2$: $\dfrac1{z-2} = -\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac1{1 - z/2} = -\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{z^n}{2^{n+1}}$; - $|z|>1$: $-\dfrac1{z-1} = -\dfrac1z\cdot\dfrac1{1 - 1/z} = -\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty z^{-(n+1)}$. $$\boxed{\frac1{z^2 - 3z + 2} = -\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{z^n}{2^{n+1}} - \sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac1{z^n} = \cdots - \frac1{z^2} - \frac1z - \frac12 - \frac z4 - \frac{z^2}8 - \cdots}$$

p: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{\cos2\theta}{5 + 4\sin\theta}d\theta$ using method of contour integration in the complex plane.
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENSH 201.r: Put $z = e^{i\theta}$: $\cos2\theta = \dfrac{z^2 + z^{-2}}2$, $\sin\theta = \dfrac{z - z^{-1}}{2i}$, $d\theta = \dfrac{dz}{iz}$. Then $iz(5 + 4\sin\theta) = 5iz + 2z^2 - 2 = 2(z + \tfrac i2)(z + 2i)$. $$I = \oint_{|z|=1}\frac{(z^4 + 1)}{2z^2}\cdot\frac{dz}{2(z + \tfrac i2)(z + 2i)} = \oint\frac{z^4 + 1}{4z^2(z + \tfrac i2)(z + 2i)}dz$$ Poles inside $|z| = 1$: $z = 0$ (double) and $z = -\tfrac i2$ ($z = -2i$ is outside).

p: Using Z-transform technique, solve the difference equation $x(k+2) - 4x(k+1) + 4x(k) = 0$ under $x(0) = 0$, $x(1) = 1$.
Solve one dimensional heat equation $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial t} = c^2\dfrac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2}$ completely.
a: Solve the wave equation $u_{tt} = c^2u_{xx}$ under boundary conditions $u(0,t) = 0$, $u(\pi,t) = 0$ and initial conditions $\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial t} = 0$ at $t = 0$ and $u(x,0) = x$ for $0<x<\pi$.
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENSH 201.r: Let $u = X(x)T(t)$ in $u_t = c^2u_{xx}$: $\dfrac{X''}X = \dfrac{T'}{c^2T} = k$. Three cases: 1. $k = 0$: $X = Ax + B$, $T = C$, so $u = (Ax + B)C$ (steady state, linear profile). 2. $k = p^2>0$: $X = Ae^{px} + Be^{-px}$, $T = Ce^{c^2p^2t}$, so $u = (Ae^{px} + Be^{-px})Ce^{c^2p^2t}$. This grows without bound with time and is not physical. 3. $k = -p^2<0$: $X = A\cos px + B\sin px$, $T = Ce^{-c^2p^2t}$, so $$\boxed{u(x,t) = \left(A\cos px + B\sin px\right)e^{-c^2p^2t}}$$ which is the physically acceptable (decaying) solution. If the ends are kept at $0$, i.e.

p: Derive Navier-Stoke's equation of motion for fluid flow. <!-- SOLUTIONS -->
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENSH 201.r: Derivation of the Navier–Stokes equation. Take a small fixed fluid element $dx\,dy\,dz$ of a fluid of density $\rho$ and velocity $\vec V = (u, v, w)$. Newton's second law for the element gives $\rho\dfrac{D\vec V}{Dt}\,dx\,dy\,dz = $ (body force) + (surface forces). - Acceleration (material derivative): $\dfrac{D\vec V}{Dt} = \dfrac{\partial\vec V}{\partial t} + (\vec V\cdot\nabla)\vec V$. - Body force (gravity): $\rho\vec g\,dx\,dy\,dz$. - Surface forces come from the stress tensor $\sigma_{ij} = -p\,\delta_{ij} + \tau_{ij}$.

p: Find half range sine series for the function $f(x) = \pi - x$ in $0<x<\pi$.
Find Fourier integral representation of $f(x) = e^{-|x|}$.
Show that the function $u(x,y) = 2x + x^3 - 3xy^2$ is harmonic.
What will be the image of circle $|z - i| = 1$ under the mapping $w = f(z) = \dfrac1z$ in complex plane?
Expand $f(z) = e^{-z}$ in a Taylor's series about $z = 0$.
Find the residue of $f(z) = \dfrac{3z-4}{(z-1)(z-2)}$ at each of its singularities.
Paper 2082 Kartik ENSH 201.r: (a) Simple poles at $z = 1$ and $z = 2$: $$\text{Res}_{z=1} = \frac{3(1) - 4}{1 - 2} = \boxed{1},\qquad\text{Res}_{z=2} = \frac{3(2) - 4}{2 - 1} = \boxed{2}$$ (b) Both poles $z = 1$ and $z = 2$ lie inside $|z| = 3$. $$\text{Res}_{z=1} = \frac{e^1}{1 - 2} = -e,\qquad\text{Res}_{z=2} = \frac{e^2}{2 - 1} = e^2$$ $$\oint_C = 2\pi i\left(-e + e^2\right) = \boxed{2\pi i\,e(e - 1)}$$

p: Classify the PDE: $x^2\dfrac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2} + 3\dfrac{\partial^2u}{\partial x\partial y} + x\dfrac{\partial^2u}{\partial y^2} + 17\dfrac{\partial u}{\partial t} = 100u$.
Solve the PDE: $y^2u_x - x^2u_y = 0$ by the method of separation of the variables.
Paper 2082 Kartik ENSH 201.r: (a) Compare with $Au_{xx} + Bu_{xy} + Cu_{yy} + \cdots = 0$: $A = x^2$, $B = 3$, $C = x$. The discriminant is $$B^2 - 4AC = 9 - 4x^2\cdot x = 9 - 4x^3$$ - Hyperbolic where $9 - 4x^3>0$, i.e. $x^3<\tfrac94$ ($x<1.31$); - Parabolic on $x^3 = \tfrac94$; - Elliptic where $x^3>\tfrac94$ ($x>1.31$). So the type depends on the region. (The terms $17u_t$ and $100u$ are lower-order and do not affect the classification.) (b) Let $u = X(x)Y(y)$: $y^2X'Y = x^2XY'$, so $\dfrac{X'}{x^2X} = \dfrac{Y'}{y^2Y} = k$. Then $X' = kx^2X\Rightarrow X = Ae^{kx^3/3}$ and $Y' = ky^2Y\Rightarrow Y = Be^{ky^3/3}$. $$\boxed{u(x,y) = C\exp\left[\frac k3\left(x^3 + y^3\right)\right]}$$

p: Find $x(\infty)$ using the final value theorem of $z$-transform when $x(t) = 1 - e^{-at}$.
Apply $Z$-transform to find the sum of infinite series: $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^\infty e^{ak}$ for $a>0$.
Paper 2082 Kartik ENSH 201.r: (a) For the sampled signal $x(k) = 1 - e^{-ak}$, $X(z) = \dfrac z{z-1} - \dfrac z{z - e^{-a}}$. The final value theorem: $x(\infty) = \displaystyle\lim_{z\to1}(z-1)X(z)$ (valid since the poles of $(z-1)X(z)$ lie inside the unit circle for $a>0$). $$(z-1)X(z) = z - \frac{(z-1)z}{z - e^{-a}}\ \to\ 1 - 0 = 1$$ $$\boxed{x(\infty) = 1}$$ This agrees with $\lim_{t\to\infty}(1 - e^{-at}) = 1$. (b) The Z-transform of $x(k) = 1$ ($k\ge0$) is $X(z) = \displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^\infty z^{-k} = \frac z{z-1}$ for $|z|>1$. The series $\sum e^{ak}$ is obtained by putting $z^{-1} = e^{a}$, i.e. $z = e^{-a}$, giving $\dfrac{z}{z-1}\Big|_{z = e^{-a}} = \dfrac{1}{1 - e^{a}}$.

p: An electrostatic field in a plane is given by the potential function $\phi(x,y) = 3x^2y - y^3$. Find the corresponding stream function and complex potential $f(z)$.

Cauchy–Riemann: $\psi_y = \phi_x = 6xy$ and $\psi_x = -\phi_y = -3x^2 + 3y^2$. $$\psi = 3xy^2 + h(x)\ \Rightarrow\ \psi_x = 3y^2 + h'(x) = -3x^2 + 3y^2\ \Rightarrow\ h' = -3x^2,\ h = -x^3$$ $$\boxed{\psi = 3xy^2 - x^3}$$ $$f(z) = (3x^2y - y^3) + i(3xy^2 - x^3)$$ Since $z^3 = (x^3 - 3xy^2) + i(3x^2y - y^3)$ and $-iz^3 = (3x^2y - y^3) - i(x^3 - 3xy^2)$, $$\boxed{f(z) = -iz^3 + c}$$ Or. A bilinear transformation $w = \dfrac{az + b}{cz + d}$.

p: Derive the recurrence relation for solving one dimensional heat equation using Bender-Schmidt method and use it to solve the following problem for five time steps taking $\Delta x = h = 1$. $$\begin{gathered}u_t = 0.25\,u_{xx} \\ u(0, t) = u(5, t) = 0 \\ u(x, 0) = x(5 - x)\end{gathered}$$ <!-- SOLUTIONS -->
Paper 2082 Kartik ENSH 202.r: Derivation. The heat equation $u_t = c^2u_{xx}$ is discretised with a forward difference in time (step $k$) and a central difference in space (step $h$): $$\frac{u_{i,j+1} - u_{i,j}}{k} = c^2\frac{u_{i+1,j} - 2u_{i,j} + u_{i-1,j}}{h^2}$$ With $\lambda = \dfrac{c^2k}{h^2}$: $$u_{i,j+1} = \lambda u_{i-1,j} + (1 - 2\lambda)u_{i,j} + \lambda u_{i+1,j}$$ This (explicit Schmidt) scheme is stable for $\lambda \le \tfrac12$. The Bender-Schmidt choice $\lambda = \tfrac12$ removes the middle term: $$\boxed{u_{i,j+1} = \tfrac12\left[u_{i-1,j} + u_{i+1,j}\right]}$$ Problem. $c^2 = 0.25$, $h = 1$, so $\lambda = \tfrac12$ requires $k = \dfrac{\lambda h^2}{c^2} = \dfrac{0.5}{0.25} = 2$.

The explicit scheme for $u_t = \alpha^2u_{xx}$ is $$\begin{gathered}u_i^{j+1} = \lambda u_{i-1}^j + (1 - 2\lambda)u_i^j + \lambda u_{i+1}^j \\ \lambda = \frac{\alpha^2 k}{h^2}\end{gathered}$$ which is stable for $\lambda \le \tfrac12$. Write $A = LU$ with $L$ unit lower-triangular, then solve $Ly = b$ (forward) and $Ux = y$ (backward). $$A = \begin{pmatrix} 4 & -5 & 7 \\ 9 & 4 & 1 \\ 7 & 10 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad b = \begin{pmatrix} 27 \\ 30 \\ 48 \end{pmatrix}$$ First row of $U$ = first row of $A$: $u_{11} = 4,\ u_{12} = -5,\ u_{13} = 7$.
