Paper 2082 Bhadra ENSH 253.r: Bayes' theorem. If $A_1, \dots, A_n$ are mutually exclusive and exhaustive events with $P(A_i) > 0$ and $B$ is any event with $P(B) > 0$, then $$P(A_i|B) = \frac{P(A_i)\,P(B|A_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}P(A_j)\,P(B|A_j)}$$ It updates the prior probability $P(A_i)$ to the posterior $P(A_i|B)$ once $B$ is known. The denominator is the total probability $P(B)$. Let $D$ = "touch screen is defective": $P(A) = 0.30$, $P(B) = 0.40$, $P(C) = 0.30$, $P(D|A) = 0.08$, $P(D|B) = 0.06$, $P(D|C) = 0.12$.

Paper 2083 Baishakh ENSH 253.r: Normal and standard normal distribution. A normal variable $X\sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ has density $f(x) = \dfrac1{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/2\sigma^2}$, a bell curve symmetric about $\mu$ with spread $\sigma$. Every normal distribution is converted to the standard normal $Z\sim N(0, 1)$ by the transformation $$\begin{gathered}Z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma} \\ \phi(z) = \frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2}.\end{gathered}$$ So one table of $\Phi(z) = P(Z \le z)$ serves all normal distributions: $P(X \le x) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\right)$. The standard normal is the special case $\mu = 0$, $\sigma = 1$. Problem.

The essential steps: Step 1. Check the assumptions. (i) The samples are independent random samples; (ii) each population is (approximately) normal; (iii) the populations have equal variances (homogeneity, e.g. Levene or Bartlett test, or the rule $s_{max}/s_{min} < 2$). Step 2. State the hypotheses. $$\begin{gathered}H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 = \cdots = \mu_k \\ H_1: \text{at least one mean differs}\end{gathered}$$ and choose the significance level $\alpha$ (usually $0.05$). p: An assembly plant receives its voltage regulators from three different suppliers: 60% from supplier $B_1$, 30% from supplier $B_2$, and 10% from supplier $B_3$. It is known that 95% of the voltage regulators from $B_1$, 80% from $B_2$, and 65% from $B_3$ perform according to specifications. Find the probability that:
A randomly selected voltage regulator received by the plant performs according to specifications.
A voltage regulator that performs according to specifications came from supplier $B_3$.
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENSH 304.r: Let $S$ = "regulator performs according to specification". $P(B_1)=0.60,\; P(B_2)=0.30,\; P(B_3)=0.10$ and $P(S|B_1)=0.95,\; P(S|B_2)=0.80,\; P(S|B_3)=0.65$. (a) Total probability. $$\begin{aligned}P(S) &= \sum_{i=1}^{3}P(B_i)P(S|B_i)\\ &= 0.60(0.95) + 0.30(0.80) + 0.10(0.65)\\ &= 0.570 + 0.240 + 0.065\end{aligned}$$ $$\boxed{P(S) = 0.875}$$ (b) Bayes' theorem. $$P(B_3|S) = \frac{P(B_3)\,P(S|B_3)}{P(S)} = \frac{0.065}{0.875}$$ $$\boxed{P(B_3|S) = 0.0743}$$ About $7.4\%$ of the good regulators come from supplier $B_3$, close to its $10\%$ share of supply but a little less, because $B_3$ has the worst performance.

p: An important factor in solid missile fuel is the particle size distribution. Significant problems occur if the particle sizes are too large. From production data in the past, it has been determined that the particle size (in micrometers) distribution is characterized by $$f(x) = \begin{cases} 3x^{-4}, & x > 1 \\ 0, & \text{elsewhere.} \end{cases}$$
Verify that this is a valid density function.
What is the probability that a random particle from the manufactured fuel exceeds 4 micrometers?
Paper 2082 Chaitra ENSH 304.r: (a) Validity. A function is a pdf if $f(x)\ge0$ for all $x$ and $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx = 1$. For $x>1$, $3x^{-4}>0$, and $f=0$ elsewhere, so $f(x)\ge0$ everywhere. Now $$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx = \int_1^{\infty}3x^{-4}\,dx = 3\left[\frac{x^{-3}}{-3}\right]_1^{\infty} = \left[-x^{-3}\right]_1^{\infty} = 0 - (-1) = 1.$$ Both conditions hold, so $f(x)$ is a valid density function. (b) $$P(X>4) = \int_4^{\infty}3x^{-4}\,dx = \left[-x^{-3}\right]_4^{\infty} = 4^{-3} = \frac{1}{64}$$ $$\boxed{P(X>4) = 0.015625 \approx 1.56\%}$$

General.q: Given a binomial distribution with parameters $n=10$ and $p=0.6$, what is the probability of obtaining exactly $7$ successes?
General.w: Using the formula $P(X=k) =  inom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k}$, we calculate $P(X=7) =  inom{10}{7} (0.6)^7 (0.4)^3 = 0.215$.

General.q: In a Poisson process with an average rate of occurrence $\lambda=5$ events per hour, what is the probability of observing exactly $3$ events in one hour?
General.w: The probability of exactly $3$ events in a Poisson process with $\lambda=5$ is given by $P(X=3)= rac{e^{-5}5^3}{3!}=0.140$.

Paper 2081 Ashwin EX 154.r: (a) Virtual ground. In an inverting amplifier (non-inverting input grounded) the open-loop gain A is very large, so the output is finite only if the differential input v$_d$ = v$_o$/A ≈ 0. Hence the inverting terminal is at the same potential as the grounded non-inverting terminal, v$_-$ ≈ v$_+$ = 0 V, although no wire connects it to ground. This is the virtual ground (a virtual short). No current flows into the input terminal (infinite input resistance), so the input current flows entirely through R$_f$: i = v$_i$/R$_1$ = -v$_o$/R$_f$ and the inverting gain is v$_o$/v$_i$ = -R$_f$/R$_1$. The input resistance seen by the source is R$_1$.

Paper 2082 Baishakh EX 154.r: Why a large-signal model is needed. The diode current follows the Shockley equation i$_D$ = I$_S$(e$^{v_D/nV_T}$ - 1), which is non-linear. When the signal is large compared with the thermal voltage (V$_T$ ≈ 26 mV), the diode cannot be linearised about one Q-point, so the exponential curve is replaced by straight-line (piece-wise linear) approximations called large-signal models. Each model is a combination of an ideal diode (a switch that is closed for forward bias and open for reverse bias) with a battery and a resistor.

Paper 2082 Baishakh EX 154.r: Operation of the LED. An LED is a p-n junction made of a direct-band-gap compound semiconductor (GaAs, GaAsP, GaP, AlGaInP, GaN). When it is forward biased, the barrier falls and electrons from the n-side and holes from the p-side are injected across the junction. Near the junction the injected electrons recombine with holes, and in a direct-gap material each recombination releases the energy as a photon: $$\begin{gathered}E=h\nu\approx E_g \\ \lambda\ (\mu\text{m})=\frac{1.24}{E_g\ (\text{eV})}\end{gathered}$$ So the colour is set by the band gap: GaAs (1.4 eV) is infrared, GaAsP red (about 1.8 V forward drop), GaP green, GaN blue (about 3.2 V).

p: Explain the construction and operation of an n-channel depletion type MOSFET with necessary diagrams.
Paper 2082 Baishakh EX 154.r: Construction. The n-channel depletion-type MOSFET (D-MOSFET) is built on a lightly doped p-type substrate. Two heavily doped n⁺ regions form the source and the drain, and a thin n-type channel is diffused between them during manufacture, so a conducting channel already exists at V$_{GS}$ = 0. A very thin insulating layer of SiO$_2$ covers the channel and carries the metal gate, so the gate current is of the order of 10$^{-12}$ A (input resistance 10$^{10}$ to 10$^{15}$ Ω). The substrate is usually joined to the source.

p: Write any four properties of ideal Op-Amp. Design a circuit diagram for summing amplifier to generate output voltage V$_o$ = 2V$_1$ - 4V$_2$ + 5V$_3$, where V$_1$, V$_2$, V$_3$ are input signals.
Paper 2082 Baishakh EX 154.r: Properties of an ideal op-amp (any four): (1) infinite open-loop voltage gain A$_{OL}$ = ∞; (2) infinite input impedance (zero input currents); (3) zero output impedance; (4) infinite bandwidth (flat gain from d.c. to any frequency); (5) infinite CMRR and PSRR; (6) zero input offset voltage and zero output when the inputs are equal (v$_1$ = v$_2$ gives v$_o$ = 0); (7) infinite slew rate and no noise or drift. Because A$_{OL}$ = ∞ with finite output, v$_+$ = v$_-$ (virtual short) and i$_+$ = i$_-$ = 0. Design. A single inverting summer gives only negative coefficients: v$_o$ = -R$_f$(V$_1$/R$_1$ + V$_2$/R$_2$ + V$_3$/R$_3$).

Paper 2082 Code 0041 'C'.r: The Sunrise at Poon Hill Three years ago, in the winter holidays, I joined my cousins for a trek to Poon Hill in Myagdi. I was a city boy who thought a walk was something to be done on flat roads, so I started the trip with doubts and a heavy bag. The first day began easily, but the stone steps to Ulleri seemed never to end. My legs burned, my breath came in gasps, and I wanted to turn back. A porter, hardly older than I, passed me with a load twice the size of mine and smiled. "Slowly, slowly," he said. I felt ashamed of my complaining and walked on, one step at a time. On the second morning we woke at four and climbed in the dark with torches.
